Endlessly replayable rogue-lite with turn-based battles interspersed through a choose-your-own-adventure game, which follows a group of explorers as they discover treasures and people around the world. Engaging mechanics, great visuals, and some entertaining interactions and storylines make this game definitely worth a look!

I found Renowned Explorers to be a fantastic strategy game with a good mix of tactical RPG battles (in the style of Disgaea, Final Fantasy Tactics, etc.), RPG-style leveling and character-building elements, and visual novel style storytelling where choices as well as skill checks matter. The game has quite a bit of resource management (in the style of FTL) and risk management, adding a definite "management" element to the tactics. (Sidenote: Those who complain about the RNG are missing the point that you've got to accept the fact that luck matters and focus on making wise management choices to minimize the risk of failure.)
The game is a perfect length of maybe 10 hours per playthrough with a huge amount of replayability and an emphasis on collections and achievements to keep things interesting. There are quite a few characters, each with their own skills, forcing you to play each game a little differently than the last. Then, if you get bored with the base game, the Emperor's Challenge expansion adds even more replayability by giving each game a unique set of objectives different from those of the base game.

I quite liked this game. I have the core version without any expansions ( for now :-p) but it gave me lots of hours of fun and I still feel I have plenty of things to explore and many adventures to have in the future.

Simple fun from the 90s. I'm a trivia buff, so this was right up my ally. Not to mention, the stupid humor (I use stupid in a positive way here) is quite refreshing and enjoyable.

The game is fun, and definitely follows the YDKJ pattern, but the movie trivia does become only more dated and obscure with time, as even what were newer movies when the game was made are now decades old. Even if you're really into movies, you will still be lucky to get more than a handful of correct answers in a full game, despite the impression caused by the screenshots. This is especially true if you don't watch and rewatch classic films and the popular movies from the 70s, 80s, and 90s on a regular basis. It's still very good, and I definitely look forward to playing the multiplayer and hopefully letting others narrow down the answers a bit for me sometimes, but it seems fair to warn everyone that this is not the type of trivia game where one can reasonably expect to be really "good" at it. If you cannot have fun while being utterly clueless and guessing the wrong answers to silly questions, you will despise the game very quickly.

Oh my god, this game is fantastic! This is the first Hitman game I've played completely and the only other one I've played was a few hours of Hitman: Absolution and I found that game to be quite boring so my expectations wasn't that high going into this game but by god, this is one of the best games I've ever played! Everything in this game is just great, great gameplay, fantastic level design, fantastic story, fantastic soundtrack to set the mood and pretty good graphics for a 2006 game to accompany it all.
I'm gonna be honest, the tutorial level starts quite dull and is a pretty poor level to show of this fantastic game with but even that has some highlights like the guy you have to assassinate, you actually feel for this guy, yes you feel for someone in a ♥♥♥♥ing tutorial level. But as soon as the tutorial is over then this game goes from good to absolutely unbelievable.
For me, what makes this game such a masterpiece is the story and the level design, and these two things are tightly woven together to accompany eachother with cutscenes inbetween each mission that tells a story told from this games villain to a journalist looking for the next big story to report on where the villain talks about all the hits Agent 47 does in this game and the journey the villain and his organisation goes on to try and catch this mythical killer clone. The story is also told from the perspective of Agent 47 and his contracter from the ICA organisation and how they are losing operatives from left to right and how they are being slowly hunted down by someone and the very last level, by god it was absolutely fantastic. Such a great way to end a fantastic game.
Did I say that the level design was great? Because it really is, each level in this game lets you approach your target in many different ways so the replayability is up there among the greatest games out there. My favorite missions are the Mardi Gras mission and the last mission before the credits level (Not gonna spoil the setting of that great mission). Before each mission you are able to equip and upgrade different equipment for you to take with you on your mission so if you want to try and take out your target from a distance with a sniper rifle you can do that, if you want to sneak near the target with a uniform you stole from a guard you subdued and take him/her out with your fiber wire or some poison then you can do that as well. Or if you just want to have fun you can spend a ♥♥♥♥ ton of money upgrading your M4 and just gun every single person down. The options are almost infinite but keep in mind that the more professional you are when it comes to taking out your target the more money you will get.
The game has a map function built into the game but I highly recommend that you don't use it, it's so fun trying to identify your target through a picture you have in your briefing log and sneaking around the level trying to find where they might be and being able to see where your target is on the map is really really boring in my opinion. The only mission where I'd say it's okay to use the map is on the Hotel mission because that level is huge and there is a total of four different floors where your targets might be so there you can use it because otherwise it would be so frustrating trying to find your target by breaking in to every single hotel room on the level.
tl;dr
Positive:
+Fantastic level design
+Fantastic story
+Fantastic moody soundtrack
+Amazing replayability thank to all the different ways you can take out your targets
+Great gameplay
+Good graphics for a game from 2006
Negative:
-The AI can be a bit unpredictable and quirky, for some reason I can be spotted directly above the target several floors up

I'm really torn over whether to give this game a positive or negative review. Hitman: Blood Money is an amazing game... one of the best games ever made in my opinion, but it has one massive flaw which I will touch on later. Note that I will give this game a positive review but please, read until the end as depending on your hardware configuration the game may prove itself to be unplayable for you.
Let's get it out of the way that the graphics aren't bad - they have a nice style to them - but they aren't the greatest. Lots of noticeable aliasing and the in-game AA drops your framerate immensely. Force AA in your graphics card's control panel... you will get much better results. I could run 32x anti-aliasing with minimal hit through the Nvidia Control Panel, but my frames would halve from 60 to 30 using the in-game maximum of 8x anti-aliasing. If you don't use in-game AA and have a relatively modern computer of any power whether it be a budget laptop or a multi-thousand-dollar gaming PC, you should be able to run this game pretty well due to its' age (not my problem if your PC can't, though - just have to put that out there).
The sound is terrific... the sound effects, the positions of sounds, the clarity of everything that's going on, is great. I had it turned up using headphones, and I heard a dog barking in the distance (on the level "A New Life" if anybody's wondering)... I had to mute it and look outside as I legitimately thought it was a real dog barking outside my house.
As for the gameplay (which is what really matters), it's a very innovative game with sandbox elements like no other. The story I could care less about; what's awesome is the gameplay. It's not sandbox in the sense that it's open world like in Grand Theft Auto, but in the sense that you get a huge, detailed level with lots of things to do and a million ways to go through with it. If you don't follow a guide, you will have to look long and hard to find someone who played whatever mission by taking the exact same route as you did. Between knocking out guards, using weapons, using the environment around you, spiking drinks, etc., each mission is extremely replayable.  Maybe you're the slip in, lure the target, cap him, and slip out kind of guy. Maybe you prefer to put a little bit of something in that fellow over there's drink so he'll go into the back room to puke his guts out or whatever so you can nab him. Maybe you'd prefer to toss a bomb in the pool and hit the detonator as you're nearing the extraction point to go out with a bang. Maybe you need to go over to the neighbor's house across the street, collect some tranquilizer darts, then go up into the child's treehouse to get his air rifle, use the tranquilizer darts to make the nasty puppy go night-night so you can slip past him, knock out a guard, and take his clothes and go into the building to kill your target pretending you're one of theirs.
If you're not interested yet, this game is not for you.
Also... if you're an Nvidia owner, this game is not for you unless you like rolling back drivers. Apparently an issue with the newer drivers makes this game crash sometimes on the newspaper screen at the end. Some missions do it, some don't. I shaved my time from 30+ minutes killing and knocking out loads of people down to 3 minutes two clean kills on "A New Life" because it kept crashing at the newspaper screen. I had to switch to my Intel HD 4000 integrated graphics to play that one so it wouldn't crash - and I refuse to roll back drivers as my newer games won't work. Unless you have a dedicated older-games rig or don't mind rolling back drivers, steer clear from this game if you're an Nvidia owner. I can't count how many times I went through that one mission for it to crash at the end, at literally the last screen before you are allowed to hit "Save". If you're an Nvidia owner using more recent drivers and don't mind taking a gamble, it comes pretty cheap and there are Steam refunds after all. If you have an Optimus laptop like I do, just switch it to your HD 4000 - half the framerate but it doesn't crash after you spend all that time trying to finish the mission.

I recommend this game. It is beautiful; however, I don't think I can play it again.
The models in KotOR are blunt and textures grafted onto this low-polygon frame might look too detailed; instead, the environments recognise their simple shapes and embrace a diorama aesthetic, which product contains a comfortable experience. Players enjoy two cohered game materials: combat, which is turn based, and exploration, which is extended by the combat rather than interrupted, as in most role-playing games. Characters retain their personality in battle. Although control over everybody is proxied sometimes to scripts you can decide with whom to fight, so you feel possession in respect of each party member. I am displeased, however, that my character, whom I speak as, has absolutely zero personallity relative to Carth or Mission. What the main character says accesses the plot and the feelings of the other characters, whom I would rather be. Perhaps the game would be more interesting if you could initiate conversation as any charater, the protagonist being each of the Knights.
The game has two tutorials, neither of which you can skip. One on the Endar Spire and then a secondary one, or an extension at the beginning of the Taris questline. The game falls in between a time when games were deliberately secretive about how to play, and the age of 20-hour tutorials. It is fairly in favour of giving any player the chance to understand basically what is going on, while return players can read the feedback dialog to understand in detail the d20 system. It tries to show players a number of ways in which you may access your goals or defeat enemies; tragically, many of these experiences are repeated throughout the game with no variation, such as overloading power conduits or building a robot. For one, such interractions do not take advantage of the tactile environment: rather than amassing unique robot parts through the level the player collects generic "parts", currency best spent by engineer characters. Likewise, computer hacking is done by contributing computer spikes in an amount inversely proportionate to the character's skill. Here, the game is asking us to loot every crate or body to find the items and then be sure to bring along a party member who has good computer skills. I do not see how this is fun in any way except for the raw reward of encouraging sound effects.
As a human player you are not often given an opportunity to think or anticipate a novel result. Sometimes you are given a mathematical puzzle to solve, and if you can it is gratifying, but the knowledge used to overcome these obstacles comes from outside the game entirely. As you effect a solution the procedure is simulated on monitors that you engage with: press 1 to overload the coduit; press 2 to release gas. These seem like convenient functions on a standard security panel. Your options are each prescribed to you, and once decided one tends to erase the other options. Free choice is restricted to future matters and you cannot remedy the past through intuition, even where that appears to be possible according to the rules of the game. Much of the game is experienced in another immersion of blue light: the level up screen, the feats page, the map, the inventory screen. These places are distractions from the gorgeous environments with which i could directly engage were I not transported to a datapad view. I can't just get in a swoopbike or manually pilot the Ebon Hawk, cut down a Dantooine baobab or manipulate a door lock. Almost every opportunity for a more interesting game is elided in favour of a cutscene or a list of options.
The "game" of KotOR is, I think, achieving conciliation between the player and his or her allies and the galaxy at large. You do this by selecting dialogue from four or five options. I can think of no better system to effect to a player's will and promote it as the enclosed limit of acceptable text-based RPGs (the character moving freely in 3D). I think this was not emphasized enough, actually, or not sufficiently associated with the combat. There are times when Carth becomes disturbed that you behave like Opie Hughes, or counsels caution, but in fact the game progresses more or less the same way so long as you don't kill Juhani. You can't save Taris or simply join Malak. Even though you can go to other planets your movement is usually quite linear from the hangar to the star map. Other times, progress comes randomly and without any meaningful sleuthing, like on Taris where finding the Sith trainee is a matter of talking to all the canteen patrons with a non-generic name. Generally, the UI gets in the way. Obeying the quest log is duller than being mindful of the environment, watching the exit to the Sith barracks for soldiers to rob, for example. Collecting and equipping items is tedious compared to just picking up a vibroblade while, dare I say, being bound to armour until returning to the ship to change.
The foregoing notwithstanding, I had a great time playing KotOR when I was 12 and still like most of it now, but the way the pieces are put together makes it very hard for me to enjoy it as a returning player.

A game that gets way more hate than it deserves, Battleborn is definitely a Gearbox game with innovation, humor, and lots of hidden easter eggs and lore. Gearbox had the misfortune of being bullied by a bigger company's fandom and had their product completely overshadowed. (Not very different from the days of WoW being 'the only MMO worth playing, or whatever.) But they are still very much dedicated to their fans and support them in every way they can.
Things to do:
Run through maps with friends in the campaign mode while trying to save the last star.

If you are looking for a terrible example of licensed shovelware, here it, Kick♥♥♥♥♥2, the stinky king of the trash hill.
Released over a year after the second movie bombed in theaters, Freedom Factory decided to grace the gaming scene with this piece of interactive entertainment, but forgoing anything that has to do with actual fun and entertainment.
Here is the♥♥♥♥♥♥list:
-Absolutely horrendous voice over on all the main characters, especially Kick♥♥♥♥♥himself who sounds like an annoying Spanish kid trying his hardest to fit in The Hamptons. I imagine the conversation that occurred at Freedom Factory went like this: Producer: "Great job on the Spanish voice over, you brought out the vigilante in you. So, can you do the English, Italian and German too?" VO: "Uh, well, you know.. Product: "Excellent, I'll schedule you for a couple more hours. Jorgeeeee! We're good on localization! Cancel the American's contract."
-Terrible script and sound bites. The writer tried their hardest to inject every possible unrelated pop-culture reference in every goddamn scene.
-Uninspired level design that is on par with The Elder Scrolls: Daggerfall when it comes to visual quality and consistency. Everything is so sickeningly bland and heavily reused in the four areas the game kicks you through, that you will appreciate the few and badly illustrated comic scenes in between. I've fallen through the game's geometry 3 times at least, losing time and patience, while trying to tip-toe through the scenery.
-Slow and clunky camera controls plus the occasional forced camera angle for street fighter-style segments. The camera doesn't move with your character when elevated either.
-Terrible controls that cannot be changed on PC. That's right, you are stuck with whatever default Alt/E/Space controls they developers deemed "optimal" for your experience. They didn't even bother to provide you with a menu for that.
-Fight combos are IMPOSSIBLE to pull with keyboard controls, you absolutely need a gamepad for that. I truly believe that the developers didn't test the game with that setup.
-Music plays the same 3 oddly-misplaced tracks over and over, while the voice overs just punched more salt into my bleeding ears.
-Movement and pace throughout the entire game is absolutely slow and pointless: you run like a turtle, your fights are agonizing and running through the world presents no excitement or purpose, aside from finding some random Wi-Fi spots and graffiti to cover.
On the upside, the graphic style and main character's design were OK and fitting for the comic book style, it's a pity they did not fill the world with anything exciting or worthy of the comic book.
The entire game feels so badly and quickly manufactured that you'll feel like burning every dollar you spent on this crap. A fitting metaphor presented itself every time Kick♥♥♥♥♥used the stairs saying "Why the hell am I doing this, heh!" Indeed, Kick♥♥♥♥♥ why the ♥♥♥♥ am I?

Greetings Everyone!  Next stop, Supreme Commander 2 the sequel to…well the original but more importantly a spiritual sequel to Total Annihilation; all three of which are mass battle RTS where the overall strategy is more important than micromanaging your units.  Instead of managing a few units and ensuring they are using their spells and abilities at the right moment while jump kiting the enemy models into turrets you are given hundreds of units with an overall goal.  This style may not be as click intensive but it is fun and impressive to watch huge battles.
All the bots:  As a mass battle RTS I’d consider this the best of its class.  There are a lot of decent mass battle RTS out there but this game does all the popular mechanics and quality of life design choices that I feel is needed.  It may not be the flashiest (I’d say that belongs to Ashes) but the mechanics are solid, the units behave correctly and (for the most part) the game has easy way to accomplish your strategy without making it a matter of how fast you are or intense your micro is.
What’s in a story:  So, unless you are a hardcore fan of the fiction you really aren’t going to know or really even care why you are doing what you are doing.  This really isn’t a problem but does create a more boring style of missions for the campaign, very often your missions devolve into killing your opponents ACU (their commander) which ends up not being that difficult as the AI doesn’t really try to protect itself very well.  There are some secondary objectives as well; these tend to be things that would make accomplishing the end goal easier but are not required and only give you rewards in the way of research points.
Commander Under Attack:  The game is fun, overall well designed and will scratch that mass battle itch if you have one.  Nothing more satisfying then just watching a battle that has been raging on in the center of the map for 20 minutes as you sneak a small group of units to the side to destroy a critical manufacturing building to gain the advantage.  If I had to level complaints…the campaign can be a bit annoying on higher difficulties where you can mission fail for having your own ACU destroyed at a moment of forgetfulness or seeing an ally ACU being dumb and getting themselves killed (Maddox…really?).
Overall, I recommend this game to any RTS fan, especially if you are one to enjoy mass battles.  It doesn’t have the scene of the more popular games and doesn’t have that level of mastery of more competitive RTS but I enjoy it and chances are if you want to order a hundred units to go headlong into death while you churn out another hundred for wave two then you will too!  Enjoy!

Youll get a better experience with watching someone else play the game. Youll get the references and humor from everyones favorite nerd in the same manner without the dull game. Let me explain WHY it's dull.
The people who made it clearly didnt spend very much time creating fun mechanics. I love difficult games. Got every achievement in dark souls, beaten super meat boy, and I even beat I wanna be the guy. But all those games have VARIETY. I go into a new stage or area and get killed by something different.
In the AVGN game, you die in 2 ways, falling to your death, or deathblocks. 90% of your deaths are to SPECIFICALLY those 2 things alone. You wont die to any cool enemies or a platforming puzzle, youll die to deathblocks and pits that ARE THE GAME. You could remove everything else and the game would be just as difficult. It is NOT imaginative when your deathblock "puzzle" is jump, jump, dont jump, jump, over and over again. Any mechanic in the game only serves the fact that you need to avoid deathblocks while avoiding them in a stage at some point. Fire and deathblocks? Check. Slippery floor and deathblocks? Check. Gravity and deathblocks? Check. Poorly lit rooms and deathblocks? Check. Spikes and deathblocks? Check. Rockets and deathblocks? Check. 2 silver surfer sections filled with deathblocks? Check. Enemies and deathblocks? Check. Unkillable THING that moves in a circular pattern around deathblocks? Check. Deathblocks and deathblocks? Check. You literally cant go 5 seconds of running in any stage without avoiding deathblocks. ITS BORING.
It's 8 stages of random mechanics and deathblocks, followed by all of them in a single 9th stage that has twice as many deathblocks.
Sure the bosses were a little neat, (except Fred ♥♥♥♥s, he was just more annoying than anything considering you will NOT beat him the first time you get to him) but youd get to see them by watching someone else play the game. And when you finally do win, you dont feel on top of the world, you feel cheated. It was less skill and more about memorization and I could play Simon Says if I just wanted that.

As a longtime fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd show, I was looking forward to this game when I had heard that it was in development. When I finally got my copy, I realized very quickly that my money was well spent.
This game was definitely made with fans of the show in mind, but, it can be enjoyed by anyone who has a love for old school 2D platformers. Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is a challenging, 2D platformer where you take control of the Nerd himself (or one of the characters that show up on the show, even people like Mike Matei, that you can unlock.)
If you have played a platformer on the NES before, you can imagine what you can expect from this. The difference being that it has the AVGN humor, and tropes from the show. For instance, AVGN's main weapon is a NES Zapper. His life are bottles of Rolling Rock. Levels are based on games he has reviewed in the past, even things he has only talked about- Such as the most ridiculous trap room a game developer could ever make... and they made it in this game.
The game is a blast to play, and as I said, it is challenging! Although, I do think that there are a few too many checkpoints in the game, and this makes the challenge a little lower-the final levels of the game are madness!
So, if you are a fan of AVGN, you will love this. If you are a fan of challenging 2D platformers from the NES era, you will love this.
Forewarning, this game is DEFINITELY for the mature gamer. Lots of Swearing and potty humor, so if that isn't your thing, you may want to pass this up as there is quite a lot of it. But, otherwise, this game is a fun throwback to my childhood gaming days, with AVGN's brand of humor, and LOTS of references to the show, even very obscure references, these guys really fit a little bit of everything into this little gem.

Okay so I am a big Telecomm fan and I have done my fair share of research about the technology developments which centered around the Cold War Era really.  It was all about how can we spread information quickly and securely which is why I was a little giddy when I cught the secret achievement.
. Seeing a title that combines this Cold War tech idea with a futuristic model really made me feel like this was some sort of modern-technology-apocalypse and all that was left were those spool machines we leave running, computing, and executing on analog bands because no one else is using them now. Yet, I couldn't get enough from the environment to really put my hands on a theory and I liked it.
Not every art piece like this will really have a definitive plot, story, or lore, and I can respect that.  This one left enough open to really create my own dialogue and lore about this robot.  Maybe what we were doing was performing a pre-written line of executable commands based on an internal clock that was set in a one-midnight-to-midnight scenario or maybe it was a chunk of self-aware technology that previously vaporized the humans and their civilizations but this piece did not harbor that anger is now confused as to why there are no more squishy people walking around.  The latter is sort of a Space Oddyssey meet iRobot meet Chappy thing...
Whatever the case, the art, the puzzles, and sound work were all very well done and even if this was a resume piece that these guys/gals can walk in to some media executives offices and say "Hey man, look what we can do." then it's still going to get my praise.  You got me to play it, think about it, and write about it all in one sitting.

I keep coming back to this game after having played it for 50+ hours, so it obviously has something going for it.
The game starts by picking a captain and two assistants from a pool of explorers with different pros and cons; they then go on 6 expeditions from a pool of areas of varying difficulty and rewards.
The goal of each expedition is to get from the start to the end of an area while picking up as many rewards and treasures along the way. Once in a while the party gets an encounter, which plays out as a turn based battle on a randomized map.
Different characters have different abilities belonging to one of the attitudes aggressive, friendly, and devious with a particular damage type. Characters may be more or less vulnerable to particular damage types, and depending on which category of skills your party predominantly use to solve an encounter different rewards may be given.
On the maps a lot of tiles are skill challenges where the skills of the characters determine chanse of success. There are many kinds of skills - enough that you're probably not going to be good at everything.
Every playthrough plays slightly differently thanks to how the maps are randomized; while the highlights of a map are always present somewhere it is never obvious what the best way to traverse the map from the start to the end node
is, and as the party only has a limited amount of rations (one is consumed every turn on the map, and if you run out a random character gets a random cumulative penalty for the rest of the expedition, some challenges may give some rations as a reward) luck is a big factor in how well an expedition turns out.
In between expeditions the party goes to a world map where gold can be spent on buying equipment giving better stats or bonus skill levels, fame can be used to recruit followers giving the party some kind of bonus, or research points can be used to write papers giving the party bonus stats, and it is the only way to obtain additional rations.
The game features a lot of funny writing, and some events may vary slightly depending on who is in your party.  Different party compositions do better in different areas, and different areas of the same difficulty have different kinds of rewards and enemy attitudes.
It does not require a lot of energy to play, and is a great way to relax when you are tired.
I do have some complaints too; Due to how combat is set up a lot of enemies can one shot the weaker characters, even while wearing armor. AI will attack characters randomly, so glass canons quite often get killed, and there doesn't seem to be much to do to prevent it from happening. This typically becomes a problem after you have already completed 2-3 expeditions, but can still bite you earlier than that if you're unlucky. It just feels cheap to have someone randomly walk up to one of my characters and just keep knocking them down. Each time a character is knocked down a unique resource that is hard to replenished is reduced by one, and when you run out it's game over. Characters can be revived by another character, but many boss battles are lost because the boss randomly decides to keep whacking the weakest character, and there is simply nothing to do about this if the character is to contribute at all.
The themed maps leave little choise for a party - an aggressive focused party is for example not going to have a good time fighting a ghost they are unable to hit, so for every party there is  a fairly obvious path that is optimal, and deviating from it typically quickly puts an end to the expedition due to one shotting enemies.
These are fairly minor complaints about an otherwise very nice game, but they begin to grate after a while, and I hope the developers will some day patch the combat to be a bit less unfair.

KOTOR is a strange anathema for BioWare where there are so many great ideas from previous games as well as new ones exemplified in its future buried under a lot of horribly implemented features. It somehow does enough to intrigue me to finish it, but not enough to revisit the different paths.
I’m left with a strange thought that from all the series between BioWare and Obsidian it was Obsidian’s take that felt more like a BioWare game than the one created by the developers themselves.
As someone who had played most of KOTOR 2 and finally finished KOTOR 1, it amazes me how much quality as well player choice is sorely lacking from the first. However, it’s not something I think should be attributed with incompetence as this game is from the weird limbo time of games being an old and modern RPG.
The most obvious source of its shoddy quality is the core gameplay itself. It feels more like an unbalanced, simplified Dragon Age: Origins’ gameplay with three party members with the feats, skills and item management from the Neverwinter Nights/Baldur’s Gate games. The drawbacks of stat and perk choices that relied more on managing numbers is overshadowed by the 3D gameplay with a clunky interface and AI behavior that rewards spamming stun abilities rather than any positioning or target-decision tactics. The reward of combat is more often attributed to exploiting tactics, gear or dumb luck than any real sense of victory.
Even if you solely care for the experience of BioWare, your choice of companions are some of the weakest in any game, including Andromeda, and unlike in Baldur’s Gate their token attributes offer nothing compelling to explore as you play. For starters, many companions come off as token characters like the Twelik, the Pilot, the Wookie, the Mandalorian, and the not-R2D2 bot. If they’re not dull alien characters, then you are given three Jedis who range from arrogant Padawans with little or no personality to a cranky smartmouth with some character. The few characters with actual personality such as the assassin droid are so few it cannot hold your interest, and KOTOR2 takes so many of these trope characters and fleshes them out that I can’t help but find these characters forgettable.
It’s these and many other things that BioWare gets right that cements how poor of a game KOTOR is; however, what bothers me the most as a RPG is how much it punishes you from developing your own character as well as they handled your choices.
As ridiculous as it sounds, what if I want to play a Star Wars game that does not involve becoming a Jedi?
As a beloved fan of Dark Forces 1 and 2, I like being a lovable scoundrel with a blaster as fast as my quips, and the bonus of Force abilities is something I am not against in a Star Wars RPG. However, and this is the root of my problem, KOTOR1 is so focused on you being a Jedi that it affects the gameplay, the storyline, and worst of all, the options you are given.
In the beginning hours, the options you are given focus more on developing your combat and non-combat skills as a non-Jedi character. This is the peak of the RPG experience that it was my favorite part of the game. It’s when you are forced to undergo the transformation into a Jedi, which is so shallow compared to the arduous task in KOTOR2, that the game restricts the options are you given in small, tangible ways.
Overtime, the restrictions become more apparent as you play. Weapons that are not lightsabers become poorly balanced in fights, sometimes even immune to certain enemies, and their stats are so convoluted in comparison to lightsabers that they become forgotten. Items like grenades, mines, etc. cannot always be reliable for scripted encounters. Armor suffers the same issue of weapons as well as a restriction on Force abilities. Worst of all, the extent of paths as well as dialogue options once you’re free to explore the galaxy boil down to two, a Jedi answer or a Sith answer.
This last aspect is worse than the Renegade/Paragon system of Mass Effect as it sets a restriction on your role-playing. There are discussions or options in quests that open up the role-play for nuances, but for the majority of quests it boils down into naively good choices or maliciously evil options that the game heavily relies on to a fault. Even more saddening is how little the good-evil alignment affects your party members except for two scripted moments of the game that doesn’t take into account how you developed a character but which fork in the road you choose.
In spite of all these glaring issues with KOTOR1, there are reasons why I finished it and ultimately enjoyed my experience, and it’s because of moments when genuine intrigue happens in the lore, especially the nuances of the Sith and Jedi; the quest-design; and the storyline.
When it comes to BioWare games, the lore has always felt sidelined for a simpler plot in spite of how much more interesting the lore is and how it can add to the game. In KOTOR 1, however, the plot manages to connect the lore in an effective manner. Most planets you explore like Dantooine,  Manaan and Korriban all have different lore-building storylines as well as perspectives into the Jedi vs Sith dichotomy that has been solidified in the films and only explored in the expanded universe of Star Wars. KOTOR takes what has been accepted as the good-guy vs. bad-guy scenario and expands upon the lore to flesh out the justifications and philosophies of each side. The plot will even change, somewhat, based on the order you visit these planets in small but rewarding means as well as how you view the dilemma ex. if you visited the Sith Academy first or visited it last. Even the other planets that do not touch upon this core dilemma like Kashyyyk and Tatooine takes time to explore the beliefs and conflicts beyond the balance of the Force.
The development of the lore is also benefited by excellent quest design. While not all of them are rewarding or difficult, compared to modern games that throw hundreds of kill quests, quests in KOTOR feel more considerate of expressing yourself with options as well as adding some complicated quests. Some may influence the game only slightly, others may affect the game more drastically such as gaining one or two companions. The best quests by far are the ones that test your observation and reasoning skills as you navigate crime-scenes and cross-examine witnesses and claims to come to the answers. As a result of the vast quality of excellent quests that vary in how difficult and rewarding they are, the experience of playing KOTOR nowadays rivals the Radiant Quests of Bethesda as well as the frivolous quests in Dragon Age: Inquisition.
Probably what is more widely considered as the best quality by most is the story of KOTOR, and for the most part, I agree. The story relies solely on one developed twist that affects the player’s expression before and after the reveal exactly like Baldur’s Gate. The best I can say about the story that doesn’t ruin it is the twist contextualizes the player’s role and avatar in a literal and a metaphorical manner to the game. Having played BG before KOTOR, the effect isn’t as strong as it was meant to be but the thoughts that it left me afterwards was effective to make me think over moments throughout the plot. However, most people probably have played KOTOR than BG, so the nostalgia is warranted.
For all these moments of brilliance and overall intrigue into the Star Wars universe, I feel they happen more in the sequel than in the original, but whenever these flashes occur they truly do elevate KOTOR into one of the best Star Wars experiences to date.

Let my words attempt to describe the degree to which this game is bad:
This game has, at its core, the soul of an outstanding multiplayer experience, carefully forged by demonic powers into the form of a boring waste of your time. You will see SO MUCH about this game that is promising, only to feel very let down in the end.
If I'm being generous and carefree in my grading:
Graphics: 10
Gameplay: 6
Character design: 7 - I should mention also that items aren't as satisfying as I wish they were.
Single player levels: 5 - bonus points for interesting levels, extra point loss for those interesting levels being unbelievably boring about half the time.
Multiplayer matchmaking 1 - Makes every other matchmaking system suddenly seem awesome to me. You have about a 50% chance of going up against a HIGHLY skilled/experienced/leveled team, with absolute know-nothing noobs on yours. I'm not talking know-nothings like you find in other matchmaking games, where you sometimes have people screw up badly or who think they know everything and get themselves killed foolishly. I'm talking about people who, like you, won't understand what the heck is going on, or how on earth the other team is so far ahead of you. Nobody on your team will understand their strats; and if you play long enough to figure out the strats, you'll be even more frustrated, because nobody else will understand them. In dota, lol, counterstrike, at least you know exactly why you suck. In this, you will be against the best frequently (or people who feel like the best relative to you), and have no idea why they're better than you.  The 1 point I gave it is for actually creating matches in a reasonable timeframe, despite the small and decreasing player base.

It's a rail shooter -- think Time Crisis but with a lot less time spent in cover. If you're a prodigy at clicking on heads, nearly all your reloads will be when you move from wave to wave, not ducking behind flimsy shelter. The end result is Blue Estate moves faster and more hectic than the Time Crisis games. Where they were about survival, Blue Estate is about piling on headshots as quickly as possible.
Story mode spins a yarn as sleazy as it is funny, of a burnout mob scion and the trail of bodies that follows him from the top to the bottom and back up. Add in different mechanics per level and per boss fight to mix it up. Story mode felt deeper and more rewarding than Arcade mode, but also more challenging. Arcade mode throws the wacky mechanics and story interludes out for a nonstop shooting spree whose continuity won't make a lick of sense. Oddly enough, Normal felt like a struggle on story mode but S-rank scores come really easily on Arcade on CrazyTrain difficulty.
Blue Estate is a blast but its story mode is pretty short and the extreme downward shift in difficulty from story to arcade means Arcade mode doesn't offer as much replay as it ought to. Pick it up on a sale and you won't regret it.

It honestly hurts me to say this, but I cannot recommend this game in its current state. Cossacks was my first RTS as a kid while everyone else was playing Age of Empires 2. I had hundreds of hours in the original + Art of War + Back to War.
Cossacks 3 is simply a graphics upgrade of Cossacks 1. Animations and graphics are new. AI, UI, gameplay, units, buildings, stats, technologies, upgrades are all the same. That's not a bad thing, the original Cossacks was amazing! But after 15 years, it sucks seeing the AI creating the same old formations and sending the same old periodic attack waves in single-player random maps. It was cool when I was ten, but now it's just sad.
What breaks this are the bugs and technical issues. I have a 3840x2160 display (ASUS PB287Q) and can only run certain resolutions - eg 2560x1440, 1920x1080. Other resolutions don't work - buttons don't highlight, can't click anything. Updating monitor and GPU drivers didn't do anything. I get bad framerate on an overclocked i7-2600k + GTX 980 Ti and have seen others complain of poor performance on even better setups. Mouse scrolling is a nightmare, you have to get it just right or it stutters and lags - seems like this maybe ties into the resolution issue. I have to use WASD keyboard scrolling (makes me feel like I'm playing an RTS on a console) and remap hotkeys, neither of which I like doing. I couldn't access multiplayer at all on launch day. Of less importance are the residual balance issues from a decade and a half ago - most nations have 500 max pop after building two Town Halls and two 17c Barracks, whereas Russia has 200 max pop? DC merc dragoon spam still ridiculously OP?
I can't tell my friends to buy this right now. If the technical issues are fixed (especially resolution and FPS), I can definitely recommend this.

So first of all, I must say that the name of the game is misleading, this isn't really Cossacks 3, but more like Cossacks 1 HD. That said, it is a lot more HD than the other HD remakes of classic games out there, which are just high resolution patches for the old game. This is a complete remake in a new engine, and definitely worth the price if you want the classic Cossacks 1 experience in a shiny new package. If you search through some things the devs have said in the past, they were actually quite clear about this, but I still think they should have named it something other than Cossacks 3.
This release did get off to a bit of a shaky start, with a major lack of communication about anything from the devs, hardly any information on their website, no pre-release hype, some brief messages explaining the release would be delayed because they were still squashing bugs, but it's here now, and it seems like they are committed to fixing various issues and improving the game.
I'll start with the things I'm not so keen on:
* the graphics are quite pretty, but very static feeling, it somehow feels like the game is in 2D, even though it isn't. The terrain is very flat, and the trees and buildings are completely static other than a few waving flags.
* there is some old school clunkiness that I don't expect of a remake in an entirely new engine. This makes me wonder if they only remade the graphical side, but the rest is still just 15 year old code from Cossacks 1. Units seem to just give up if you queue up a few too many buildings (which you will with the number of houses you need late game), and pathfinding is sometimes a bit odd. Aligning ferries to the shoreline can be fiddly too. I'm fairly sure at least some of these issues come the original Cossacks game.
* the AI feels pretty bad. I have only tried against the easiest AI for now, by "bad" I'm not commenting on the difficulty, which obviously should be fairly low, but rather the fact that it acts in an unconvincing manner. It looks to me like it ignores fog of war, and just knows where my stuff is, and it will just send troops near the coast to get bombarded by my ships. AI was one of the things the devs claim to have reworked, so maybe they will continue to improve it, but currently I can't recommend it if you compare it to the AI in StarCraft 2 or Planetary Annihilation, which feels a lot like a real player.
OK, so these issues aside, I still have to give this a positive review, because it's Cossacks, and Cossacks is a great game. For those of you not familiar with the concept, it is somewhat like Age of Empires, in that you gather resources and construct buildings, and it also features an upgrade to the 18th century, much like ages in AoE. Where it is very different is in the scale of the game, you can have up to 10 000 units in the same game (shared between all players, I believe), so that's a whopping 5k units each in a 1v1. Units are organised in formations, which not only offers interesting tactical play, but also makes it much easier to control so many units, compared to say Total Annihilation with the 5k unit patch, which is a mess to control because the game was designed to have 200 units. You have infantry, cavalry and artillery, as well as quite powerful ships. You can also capture enemy artillery, peasants and buildings if they have no soldiers defending, so you should probably guard any outposts with some troops. There are also walls and towers, although these can be quite expensive.
All in all a very enjoyable RTS, and I don't know of another one that scratches the same itch. Would recommend in spite of a few issues. Also worth mentioning that the game is open to modding, so we'll hopefully see some cool mods pop up in the near future.

Cossacks 3 is a very fun and challenging game. Its mechanics have lots of depth to them. For example, you must have a officer and a drummer commanding your troops in order to put them in a certain formation, Cannons can be captured if left unattended by your men, musketmen will only fight with melee if you have upgraded them with bayonets from your blacksmith, and your infantry can run out of ammunition if you don't have a steady supply of coal and metal.
The campaigns are diverse and challenging to play. Each one can take quite a while to complete, even if you are a veteran of the Cossack franchise. The tutorials explain everything very well so you wont have much trouble learning the games basics.
There are a few bugs in the game currently, but nothing that can't be fixed with an update or two.
I would recommend this game to anyone that loves AoE, Civilization, or Rise of Nations.

I've played 102 hours, so this game must be doing something right.
It's a turn based group RPG adventure game. Think turn based combat, and dice rolling for risks and rewards during the adventure.
I wish the game had more content - more places to explore etc. It feels like it quickly gets quite repeative.
Addicting "one more turn" quality just like 4x games, but without the big time commitments. Games are quick and also easily saved and resumed since there's not a ton to plan and manage.
I was positively surprised by the depth of this tactical roguelite. It's rewarding and more difficult to master than it seems.

RE: International Society is a turn-based game that let's you discover, research, befriend or fight different places and people all around the globe. While the playthroughs are made to be quick and your campaigns only last for 5 explorations (or less if you're playing Adventure Mode), there is a high replayability. There are always new secrets, treasures and encounters to discover.
You can decide how you want to build your team, approach other characters and win encounters. To me that's one of the most enjoyable things in the came; the variety of everything. There are so many ways you can collect Renown and climb your way to the top.
The Tutorial is a bit long and the "Combat" System uses Moods and Emotion skills, which seem a bit complicated at first, but you get into it right away and it's understandable once you use them a couple times.
All in all a very enjoyable and fun game, for casual and more strategic gamers.

The cutsy cartoonish graphics are amusing, and the game doesn't take itself seriously enough to raise any of the ugly quetsions this sort of genre might normally garner (colonialism ho!)
But what I really love about this game is the surprisingly large number of ways you can break the game by taking advantage of the various powers, story cards, the six zillion upgrades, and the fairly in-depth combat system.
I partiuclarly enjoy that verbal combat is not only just as effectve but actually complements physical attacks. The various challenges, the large variety of characters with unique abilities, the various paths you can go on the islands lead to a very interesting style of game play that had me playing this game far more times than I expected to.

Well, I'll open with what I didn't like. While amusing and actually fairly innovative, the "combat" encounters were, for the most part, heavily skewed towards Deception, Diplomacy, or a combination of those two. If in amongst your many types of party you decided that you wanted to go full colonialism and try an aggressive playthrough, you'll quickly realise it's untenable. Also, the roguelike nature can be a little restrictive; while you can go on and do the other expeditions after your campaign finishes, you'll find that does somewhat reduce replayability instead.
These however are not big enough issues to warrant not recommending the game, especially when it's on sale. It's surprisingly enjoyable, there's a lot of stuff you can do, and it's an amusing, endearing, memorable game. It doesn't take itself too seriously, it's got some appreciable humour, and most importantly it's rather fun. I can't speak for the paid DLCs, but the fact that the game gets both free and paid new content is a definite vote in its favour; a lot of indie games receive disappointing care following release, even abandonment (yes, I'm looking at you Battle Brothers devs), so seeing a small game like this getting some support is heartening.

Considering I was doing my best to avoid the Overwatch hype train and wanted to see Battleborn get the exposure I thought it was going to deserve, upon actually playing the full release of the game I could not help but feel dissapointed . It truly feels like there could have been a game worth playing here but so many little things ended up dragging it down and left me with a very 'meh' final opinion once I finished the story.
If you enjoyed the Borderlands series but disliked the open world aspect, then you would probably get along well with battleborn for a few hours. However, every mission sees you backtracking repeatedly just to fight waves of the exact same enemies you thought in the mission before and that just made a lot of the campaign feel recycled, repetative and dull with a lackluster ending that cuts a pretty cool villains story way too short. Each boss had the Borderlands issue where they didn't do anything exciting. They mostly soaked bullets for five minutes. And do people still think escort missions are fun?
The characters you play as however are all charming, though some do feel much less appreciated than others. Especially when they constantly repeat the same joke or seem to feel unkillable with their gear sets and chosen abilities. Since nobody is really playing the multiplayer, any new player would be matched with people that have clocked 100+ hours already usually ending in a one sided stomp. Which is also a darn shame since the multiplayer 'moba style' game mode was such a cool idea. But nobody cared. Overwatch would be out soon.
Though I'm unsure if that really mattered. Even if Overwatch came out a few months later, Battleborn would have run out of steam fast. The selling point of a campaign fell far from the finish line for me whilst the multiplayer was fun but suffered from character balancing and matchmaking issues.
In conclusion, I sadly regret preordering this game even though I wanted to praise it so much.

I definitely recommend this game!
As is to be expected from Gearbox, this game is a masterpiece. This is one of those game where everything is just right (Game play wise). That said, I only play this game for the multiplayer part, where, i think, the game excels. The story mode is ok, i guess, and, while many people enjoy it, I see it as a means to get achievements and the like.
As for the multi: have u ever played a competitive game and thought, "I wish I had to try and practice different approaches because, after a while this fells like it always the same tactics"? Its clear, for me, that the developers had the same thought and went and made a game worthy of it.
The game features different characters (around 30) and it is amazing (well actually that's what Gearbox does better)  how they managed to make each one unique. Literally, there's no 2 character alike. Each has its own abilities, it's own learning curve, it's own tactic and set of skills and it's own unique personality. Classic shooter, sword fighter, brawler, sniper, assassin, healer, buffer, tank, etc.
One of the most important aspects of the game is how each character interact and complement each other. With so many characters and only 5 to chose on each fight, the combinations are endless.
Pros:
+Unique characters with their own personality.
+Tactics and team based fight make the game a pleasure to learn and play with each battle bringing something new to chew on.
+Beautiful graphics and sound effects give the game an amazing fell while playing (read next).
+The visuals and sound really give feedback of what is happening in the field (though this might take some time to get used to)
Cons:
-(The elephant in the room) Low Players base make waiting ques a little bit of a pain (Though if u play on the right server on the right time, when u probably will, these r somewhat normal).
-Hard steep learning curve makes it really hard for newcomers to actually give it a try beyond the first few fights. (I have to be honest about this one, I still have my moments too after 500 hours).
Conclusion: This game is a jewel IF u like a challenge. And i'm not talking about the challenge of playing against harder opponents or a punishing A.I. I'm talking about the challenge of having to actually understand what works and what doesn't and adapt ur strategy as u learn more advanced ones and how to positively interact with your team.
If u r like me don't think it twice and get this game.

Blue Estate is a solid exemplar of the near-dead Rail Shooter genre. While it features all it needs to, it doesn't make an effort to add anything too innovative to the genre.
One of the game's first victims is political correctness. The game's writing is sexist, racist and full of outdated stereotypes. If you have an issue with this, consider yourself warned. If not, you are in for a great ride. Although the humour can be a bit hit-and-miss at times. The game also rarely gives you more time between jokes than you need to shoot the enemies, which can feel a bit irritating and shoe-horned in. The lines are delivered by fitting voice actors who all do a great job at bringing the characters to life. Anyway, the general quality is pretty impressive for the price tag.
The game sports two modes in three difficulties. The Story mode is rather short with up to three hours maximum and can be played either solo or in local Co-Op with shared life bar. Finishing one of the seven missions will unlock the Arcade variant of the level, in which you race against the clock, prolonging the countdown with kills while raking up highscores. After around 5 hours you should have seen everything there is. Which leaves you either going after the various achievements or competing on the leaderboards if you want more.
If you are looking for some quick mindless fun, don't look any further. Especially if the game is on discount. But if you are looking for some meaty experience with a deep epic story, you won't find it here.

Blue Estate is an on-rails shooter in the same vein as the House to the Dead series. It offers your regular shooting mechanics alongside cover and QTE (either a cursor direction or mouse movement) to pick up ammo or interact with the levels.
Given the price of the game you'd think presentation would suffer but it doesn't. There is a full cast of character audio narrating throughout the game which really adds to what could be quite a shallow and hollow experience. The game, much like House of the Dead, does everything it can to not take itself seriously. It's good, dumb fun with guns. Graphically everything is modeled and texutred way above the price point, levels are full of detail and stylised with a few flourishes here and there.
Gameplay, with the addition of the few other mechanics mentioned above, is as you'd expect. You move through the levels on a set path, enemies coming at you or popping up from behind scenery. At times you can rack up bonuses by meeting certain 'mini-game' criteria such as getting headshots only for a group of targets. If you don't like on-rails shooters this won't convince you otherwise. If you're indifferent or a fan I'd say give this a purchase.
Downsides? There's always some I guess. I'd have to criticise the deafening startup logos. Yeah, petty, but DAMN! why so loud? If you're easily offended I'd suggest Church or a local support group instead, consider this a trigger warning. Legitimately I'd say the reload (R.Mouse) and weapon switch (dbl click R.Mouse) can be a bit clunky, especially as some weapons require you to hold the right mouse button down to reload. Sometimes the levels are also a bit too cluttered resulting in it being hard to see what you're shooting at. It's also of course an on-rail shooter, that means limited replayability unless you enjoy chasing scores and stats.
In summation. Get this, it's polished, funny, stupid, entertaining and well put together. Well worth it at full price, an instant purchase if discounted.

So, I finally took the time to give my opinion about this game in more than just a like.
Guacamelee definetely was one of the best games I was able to experience in the last two years, it´s artstyle is just one of the things that keep me thinking exactly that. The artstyle gives room for a lot of different and wonderful colours and creative charcters and definetely fits the crazy topic very well. It also allows the game to have a fast and smooth gameplay and keeps you interested all the way.
As it has been said previously, the gameplay certainly does its job more than just good and allows a quick fighting and (for the most part) good platforming. The special moves that you learn through the game are all useable in both aspects and are shown especially awesome within the fighting of the game as they provide different combos and awesome ways of torturing your enemy. In the platforming most of the moves are placed very good, though there could have been better ways to include some of them even better.
The soundtrack of the game beautifully underlines every single place you´re in, wether it would be the human world or the world of the dead. It makes use of many mexican styles and can even be quite complex at times, giving every instrument a wonderful job to get you even deeper into the game.
The last part to discuss would be the story, and as there is of course not much of it due to the game´s genre being an action platformer, it is certainly supported by a lot of good humor and sympathetic characters and forms a nice setting for the game as a whole. In addition there are a lot of little references to other games that you are able to find in the game which do cary a great humor too.
To sum it all up, I really liked this game a lot, it always kept me excited and had something that I was interested in. It has a very good and smooth gameplay which never gets too slow or boring, given by the feedback you get.
So, long opinion, short message: Buy the game!!!

First review! (was gonna do Deus Ex but they took it off)
Recently finished, not 100%
Story, boy saves girl, doesnt really matter in this type of game
Art style, like it or you don't, there are screen shots available. I like it personally, works with the whole (Mexican/mariachi/wrestler) theme which we don't see alot of. Easter eggs and other game references through out the some of the levels.
Music, terrific again works with the theme
Gameplay, 2D platformer/beat'em up
Platforming is hard, for me, becuase I suck, not the game's fault, the controls are fine (I used a xbox controller), timing is the key here, sometimes it's frustrating but there are plenty of checkpoints and if you die falling off a platform you'll just respawn at the previous platform you were standing on before you jumped off; unless you fell on another platform that is way down at the bottom of the level, and because there is no fall damage, you won't die and just gonna have to make your way back up.
Fighting mechanic, basic puches and 4 special moves combined together along with jumps and rolls/dodges to create about 20 or so combos; there's fun side quest that serves as a tutorial for you to try out these combos, but other than that, it's not really necessary to memorize them since after the damage upgrades, which can be acquired pretty early in the game by spending orbs that you get from killing enemies (the higher the combo the more orb you get after the battle) and the abusing of the throw mechanic (which knocks down/back other enemies but does stop the combo), most enemies will be dead way before you finish the combo. Boss fights are not that hard either, learn their attack pattern dodge, lay down a combo, repeat.
Finding and getting to the treasure is the best part of the game for me, even though at that point of the game you don't really need the orbs/health/stamina upgrades that the treasure chests contain; but it's alot of fun because they requires you to use a combination of moves you've learned through out the game to pull it off. Which brings me to a problem I have with the game - the map. One way to find the hidden paths is by indentifying the blurred-pixelated spots on the map that aren't explored , but some of the areas on the map are also blurred-and pixelated looking, places like the edge of cliff, both ends of a stage, down at a bottomless pit, in the middle of the sky... So alot of time are spent on jumping off cliffs or the edges and looking for walls to grab onto just to use one of the game mechanics (SPOILER) to ___ across the stage just to clear up the map to make sure you didn't miss anything. And that still won't clear up the whole map!
Replayability, low, unless you want to try out a harder difficulty, since the game doesn't allow you to go back to collect all the treasues you missed or finish the challenges after entering the final stage
Final score 9/10 half a poitn for map; half a point for challenge room difficulty (yeah there's a challenge room) and replayability

Hitman: Blood Money
Stealth Action
IO Interactive
Square Enix
is the 4th game in the Hitman franchise released in 2006, developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix.
Some has been killing the agents of ICA, and it's your job as Agent 47 to go around the globe trying to find who is behind this conspiracy. And yes, this is as clichéd as it sounds. But you don't come here for the story itself, but for its settings, which are fantastic: you go to Las Vegas, a wedding on the , the White House, an Opera House, a boat on the Mississipi, a Mardi Gras parade in New Orleans... All the 13 levels have fantastic locations that are very memorable, even though the story is incredibly forgettable.
Surprisingly, the game still looks gorgeous after 10 years. And sure, while a couple of textures aren't in HD, the character animations and the post-processing effects show how much care was put into creating this game. I also love how every single level looks and feels different.
Your goal is very simple: kill the designated targets as stealthly as possible and leave the area unnoticed. You are free to choose which playstyle to use: equip an assault rifle and go on a loud killing-spree, find a vantage point and snipe from afar, go upclose and personal to garrote them, or, even better, make it look like an accident.
The best example of this is the
mission: you are at the theatre during the rehersal of Puccini's classic opera "Tosca", and one of the two targets is playing the lead role, who gets executed with a pistol. In order to make it all look like an accident, you can switch the prop gun with a real WWI handgun. You can guess what happens next.
This is just one of many things that makes Blood Money a fantastic game to just play around with and to experiment to get different outcomes. There are also other details, like being able to carry only one heavy weapon (shotgun, assault and sniper rifle) that can't be stored in your suit since it's too big. There are also upgrades to buy before each level to reduce recoil, improve damage or get silencers.
And, in case you didn't know,
. I didn't know this when I first played the game, but it sure helps if you get into some tough gunfights.
The AI makes the game very challenging: they hear gunshots, they recognise you based on the outfit you are wearing, they follow blood trails and they change how they react based on who dies. And, in case you get seen, you can try to shoot your way out of it, even though going full-on stealth is the best way to play this. Also, there is a save system that can be used in each level to correct some mistakes and to try without fear certain playstyles.
The sound effects are top notch, as well as the voice acting, and the soundtrack by Jesper Kyd is beautiful, from the Main Theme to Apocalypse, as well as Ave Maria by Schubert.
Multiple ways to kill your enemies, easter eggs and secrets will keep you coming back to this game for years to come.
Overall, this is easily one of the best stealth games of all time thanks to the variety of levels, weapons and excellent AI. A must play for every gamer and stealth fan.

I can't recommend enough that more people play this game.

Retention is a "choose your own adventure" type of game in which revolves a story where a man doesn't really look back into his memories. Then one day, he falls out of his bicycle and various moments fly through his head. Will he get his memories back?
As I said earlier, Retention doesn't really last long when you play, but provides you a nice experience. It is known for it's unique gaming genre, "Game-Photo Album" where the game attempts to create an experience with the use of only photos and it does a great job on that.
There's 8 endings to this game (4 good and 4 bad) according to the store page, but so far, I've only found 4 of them (3 good and 1 bad, but I may need to play through it more to find the other endings). This game contains one original unique soundtrack and can also be emotionally powerful for some people that go through this game at least once. Oh and let's not forget about the trading cards to go along with it.
In conclusion, this game's simple, strange, but yet, unique at the same time.
If you don't mind paying a dollar for a good experience and/or trading cards, then I'd say you should.

So, originally, my review for this game was going to be negative based on the intro of it, in the underground segment. It is VERY lack luster as the sequel to the original F.E.A.R.. Firefights are boring, the AI sucks, gunplay feels boring, and movement is floaty. Also, you can't lean in this game, which takes a lot more points off of it than it should.
BUT
Then I got out into the streets, and played the bit where you pilot a mech, and the fantastic music track from the first game plays. It was pretty radical. Afterwards, I found myself enjoying the game more and more.
So, to start off with, a big reason why I wasn't going to recommend this game is because of the writing, and the quote there at the top sums up why I would bring up the writing as a downside. In the first game, the writing was very solid. The only goofy things was some dialogue from characters... that was said like twice throughout F.E.A.R. and its two expansions, which, all combined, is upwards of a 20 hour experiance. Here, it's immediatly boring. The story presented is unoriginal, and the characters are terribly written. "Snake Fist" is my new most hated video game "assistant" character in anything. It doesn't help that his voice actor is awful, though, none of the voice acting is very good, so I guess it figures.
The horror element is also lack luster, though the bits where Alma is showing up and walking around is interesting. There are also some elements that are very DOOMish, which is kinda cool really, even though it feels like its from a completly different game.
Speaking of which, nothing in this game really feels like the sequel to F.E.A.R..
What this feels like, and I'm not saying this is how it went down, but I'm assuming that the same people did not head this game and the first. I'm pretty sure both are Monolith, but people working on it are very different. This game feels like they had been working on a really bland shooter, and needed something more to be going for it, so they slapped on the F.E.A.R. branding, developed some horror bits, and shipped.
So, again, the gameplay is boring, the artstyle is nothing interesting/special, and the writing/story is tacky.
These were the thoughts I had upon playing to first part of the game, which takes place in underground corridors.
Upon emerging into the streets, the game immediatly felt better.
To start things off, the city looked destroyed, which was a gripe I had with the first game. After a nuclear blast sweeps the town, in F.E.A.R. 1, you go out into the city streets, and it looks like nothing has changed... other than a few things (like the somewhat iconic crashed plane). In this game, the city looks devestated. Speaking of that plane, when you emerge into the city, you see one fly very close overhead, and hear it crash land, which is a very nice touch.
Anyways, the more open environments and different weapons other than an♥♥♥♥♥machine gun do add a lot to the eb and flow of shooting dudes.
Getting to the topic of the dudes you shoot in this game, I'd like to complain about them for a brief moment.
The AI in the first game are one of the things that set that game apart from others. It was very good. It would respond to the player based upon where they were, what they were doing, and would call out tactics to try and overcome you. They would also get panicked as you killed their squad mates, which I found really interesting. They also wouldn't just blandly stand still for you to kill easily. They would move around, much like they would in real life.
In F.E.A.R. 2, they just ♥♥♥♥ing stand around.
On top of that, they don't respond to the player. They boringly shoot at you, pile up with each other to be slaughtered, and sometimes hurl a casual grenade your way. And the dialogue they have is just the same script, which, without the same actions, feels like the script printed out for the voice actors (I believe there was a whole 2 of them) who did the voices for enemies was a copy paste job.
That being said, shooting their stupid asses and having them explode into blood or discombobulate is pretty satisfying.
That being said, some of the weapons are better than others, but talking about that would probably be boring so I'm not going to. I will say though that there is a literal rip off of a BFG in this game, and it is just the worst.
My two biggest complaints are some that I had for the first game as well, and might for the third, but, A) Reasoning for Alma wanting to kill the main character is loose (especially since this game ends with her♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the character you play as and becoming pregnant, and if that was her intention all along, I can't even fathom why she'd be trying to kill you all throughout the game), and in the first game it makes even less sense, considering you're her first born son, and B) the F.E.A.R. team, specifally trained to deal with paranormal threats seem pretty suprised when dealing with Alma, almost like they never thought they'd see a spooky ghost or something. To sum this up, there are holes in the writing. Not huge I suppose, but irritating ones.
There are some good visual effects, and it is a polished, and a *good* game, it's just a really lackluster sequel. It has some good implementations of horror elements, the story is a little boring, but where it goes is pretty interesting. And, unfortunately, the characters in this game are not very good. "Snake Fist", or TERRY, stands out the most, but mostly as a meme, similar to the fat guy in the first game.
A quick note about the DLC, Reborn... It's not very good. In fact, I would call it bad. It's super short, poorly written, and not very fun to play. Where it goes is important to know story wise, I guess, but it's really uninteresting. Content wise, we're looking at like, an hour of gameplay... It's just one of those things that I think I would forget I ever played in a couple years.
Final take -
I don't think I personally like this game, but I can still acknowledge it as good.
While I would call the first F.E.A.R. fantastic, a solid 9 on 10 I think, this game is simply good, being about a 6, maybe even a 7.

Buy it, just buy it. If you're apprehensive because of the whole rail-shooter aspect, don't be. It's very well implemented and the gesture gameplay definitely shakes it up. Blue Estate is one of those rare gems that will likely sit in your library til one night you're too bored to play "Insert period appropriate hot new triple a game that everyones been hyping" anymore and install it on a whim. It's memorable like Shadow Warrior in it's ridiculousness but without having to worry about getting bored, ever.
It's a ride, the entire game is a rollercoaster ride. It doesn't stop being funny, doesn't stop to ask you for microtransactions, and not once will you regret buying it. This is a real video game. It's short, yes, but so was portal and they're both that way because the devs didn't needlessly pad it out so people would still be playing when they released dlc and all that hootennanny.
The characters are definitely what made it for me, but the controls are tight, and the gameplay isn't repetitive (a rail shooter, surprising, I know). You'll pick up the controls easy and be jetting along at the same speed of the game in no time. I got worried a little ways in when they swapped Tony with Clarence for a couple missions, thought it was MGS2 all over again but not so.
Anyways, play this when you want to experience a slice of really great cake-pie stuff that was cooked in just the right way to be fun, and nothing less. It will leave you wanting more, yes, but that's just more credit to how good it is. Dear LORD somebody tell me they've got another episode in the works.

I typically avoid games like this, but Renowned Explorers seduced me with it's fantastic art style.
And I am glad it did.
Despite the frustrating RNG-powered resource management system that FTL-like games often sport, the pros of this game make up for it's cons. Characters, despite not uttering any words (maybe have some voice acting in next game? I'd love to see what they come up with /hint), have very distict personality and traits, and make every playthrough different.
The combat system in this game is a "social strategy" (©megakoresh, patent pending, all rights to use the term reserved, etc. etc.). Its a term I use for games where you can win fights without physically hurting enemies. In this case, in addition to straight up physical attack, you can also try to charm enemies, seduce them, or drive them to depression. Your actions affect overall mood of the encounter, which in turn affects how the enemy will respond, as well as significantly swings all friendly and enemy stats in one direction or the other. It's a fantastic system, that lets developers deliver character and story exposition through gameplay without even needing any dialogue. Ingenious!
On top of that the game sports a great sense of humour, incredible lovely art style (my favourite in all 2D games I played so far), and a great pace. The devs have also added a lot of extra free content since release and there are some DLCs available, that I'm actually gonna go buy (didn't know they came out already). Absolutely recommend it without hesistation. A great, cute, uplifting and clever game, equally fit for long sessions and 20 minute long dips.
