Renowned Explorers is a kind of mash up of turn based combat encounters, skill based choose your own adventure events and resource management. It makes for quite a good mix.
You pick 3 explorers from a selection of about 20 with each explorer having different strengths and skills. The goal in each playthrough is to complete 5 expeditions while trying to get as high a score as you can. The expeditions throw up different encounters and events which can net you resources or treasures but you run the risk of losing supplies or resolve.
The combat encounters also have an interesting twist. Each character has three types of attacks aggressive, devious and friendly which work like rock,paper and scissors. To add to this each battle has a mood that changes based on the types of attacks used. Different moods will either hinder or buff your party. It adds another layer of depth to the combat.
So overall Renowned Explorers is an interesting game which is surprisingly deep adnd challenging. Worth picking up if you enjoyed games like The Banner Saga.

Renowned Explorers has many good features going for it; the cartoon graphics are fun, well thought out and lend it a sense of the old Saturday morning cartoons you watched as a kid (I am going to assume the average player is not a kid because the content of the game would be a little dry for someone under 12).
It also has a sense of humor, is stylish and actually tries to place a little bit of historical content to its settings.  But in the end, it isn't enough.  Remember that part about dry?  This game is more than dry, ultimately it is boring.
After putting about six hours into it and trying several team members, I have lost interest.  The settings change, but other than that, the expeditions don't.  Choose a path, follow it, read some text and hope you brought the right expert for the RNG/Price is Right wheel spin.  Succeed, get a treasure where it is not clear how its buffs really help you.  Fail, maybe take a ding to one of your stats.  Either way, more often than not you will next enter the fight mode.
The fight mode will be familiar to anyone who has ever played Heroes of Might and Magic.  Walk your guy across a hexagon grid, choose your attack.  Despite there being three main schools of attacks, the type you prefer really doesn't matter.  If you do something violent, deceptive or friendly, there is no real long term effect on your character or game.  Just pick the one that does the most damage in the current situation.
And that is the rub.  The designers have put a lot of time building up the three types of attacks, with all the requisite buffs.  They also added something of a "mood" system, meaning your enemies will react differently to each school, both at the start of the battle and while it wages on.  For instance, you can start off with friendly "attacks", but after a little while of complimenting the enemies and otherwise buttering them up, you will get a 25% boost to deceptive attacks.  This mean is it in your interest to now start insulting your enemies instead.  Kill one of them?  Don't worry, go back to complimenting the rest and they soon forget you ran their buddy through.  So long as you ignore heavy specialization, you will be able to pick whichever takes the most off the enemy health bar at the moment and ride out the fights.
They should have sacrificed the complex buff system.  Honestly, unless your are really into minutiae or min/maxing, there is no reason or incentive to learn it.  Instead, they should have made the three attack schools much more unique and meaningful.  The type of attack your character uses should have real ramifications both inside and outside each micro battle.
TLDR; Pros: graphics work for the game setting, dry humor.  Cons: Quickly repetitive and boring.  Needless detail in attack schools and buffs fails to really affect your game, so no real reason to learn it.  Not worth riding the DLC train, probably just more of the same.

This game get some unfair lambasting when inevitably compared with Blizzard's similar Overwatch - but for anyone that has played both, you get a very clear sense that this is NOT trying to be Overwatch at all.  It has a clear identity - borrowing heavily from Borderlands in humour and art direction; and a unique character line-up that has more invested in it than one might expect from initial review.
Is it for everyone?  That is a hard "no";  it is very much a large arena for similar and repetitive PVE & PVP standard fare - but if that is your jam then Battleborn will not disappoint you badly.  It is character driven, which means unlike a CoD or most MOBA style games, you are limited and advantaged by your selection and proficiency at that very set style.  The missions can run long, and sometimes appear sparsely populated; but this is made up for with constant audio messages and dialogue informing you of the evolving narrative. The real asset is the potential that this game has-little to sell on if the core is not appealing at this stage to prospective gamers, but the updates from original release alone indicate a developer that is interested in nurturing their creation.  The inclusion of limited but essential support purchases for missions put co-operative teamwork under scrutiny in a dynamic manner-help your own advance, keep your fund or contribute to team success.  This kind of feature either galvanises or tears potential power teams apart or building fledgling alliances up.
Battleborn is a solid example of the genre, but, as mentioned above, hurt by the mainstream release of the highly anticipated Overwatch.  From about two million players in the Beta stage, it is unfortunately now difficult to find player matches online quickly.  However, this does have a silver lining.  Low player base is a negative, but the community that does exist around the game is built on a strong ethos of building a very social and accessible group.  If you can bring your friends to the game or develop with the current pool, this is a game that rewards investment over the long term.
I know many people hate this game for several reasons, despite that I still had fun.

Let's start with the bad...the community is small, which makes queue times for pvp matches unfortunately long.
Now for the good...the community is small, which gives you a rare opportunity to get to know a large percentage of the player base, which is why Battleborn's community feels uniquely tight-knit. I have also found the playerbase to be exceptionally welcoming and friendly. Probably because there is an understanding that you need friends to queue up for games if you don't want to wait a long time, which I consider to be another fortunate consequence of a small playerbase.
Game modes:
Despite the frequent comparisons to Overwatch and Paladins (which I do agree are similar to one another), Battleborn shares little in commmon with the two, which becomes immediately apparent when you become familiar with the game modes. Battleborn is equal parts PvP and PvE.
On the PvP side, you will find game modes that resemble MOBAs in that you are usually trying to push minion waves through one or more lanes until you've gained enough ground to ultimately destroy the enemy's sentries. This will feel familiar to anyone who has played Leage of Legends, DOTA 2 and/or Smite. There is also a capture mode, which is pretty straight forward.
On the PvE side, you will have access to the PvP modes listed above (vs. bots) which offers a very casual, light-hearted experience of the PvP modes. Additionally, there is an entire campaign that can be completed solo (on normal difficulty) or cooperatively (on advanced difficulty). Loot improves with difficulty. The campaign consists of various story missions, which feel like dungeon runs. Each mission offers unique loot, which provides incentive for replaying them later. (I'll mention the significance of loot later). After you've had your fill of story mode missions, you also have the option of completing Operations (DLC/Season Pass), which are essentially hard mode missions that scale in difficulty and reward the more times you run them. Again, each Operation offers the chance at loot unique to that mission, which is incentive to play them multiple times.
Loot:
The loot in this game presents an interesting overlap between the PvE and PvP content. In both the PvE and PvP modes, you are able to create gear loadouts, which is essentially a buid utilizing three items of your choice. Unlike the typical MOBA experience (where builds are involved), rather than simply choosing items from a predefined item set, you only have access to items that you have personally looted during your adventures in PvE or loot packs, which are awarded periodically as you progress through the game, whether in PvE or PvP. Furthermore, similar to the Diablo loot system, each individual item's stats are randomly generated within a certain range. For example, you may have two "Super Huge Fists of Smashing" which has attack damage and cooldown reduction as stats (which might be between +3% and +6%), but one's attack damage and cooldown reduction are +5%, whereas the second copy of the same item, might have +3.5% to the same stats. Once again, this provides incentive to play the game, or run PvE missions in order to get specific items for a build you're working on, that will hopefully have max stats.
Unlockables (characters/skins/taunts)
All but a few characters are available immediately upon firing up the game. I believe there are five characters that are unlocked through DLC/Season Pass content. Most skins and taunts are awarded for completing various tasks in game with specific characters. A few skins/taunts are purchasable via the currency purchasable by real life money. This in game currency is also awarded through the completion of daily quests/achievements, but in small incriments.
Conclusion:
As a fan of Borderlands, I have been following the development of Battleborn, which released in May of 2016. I was skeptical of the game at launch, and it took me until March of 2017 to bite, and I'm glad I finally did. Despite, and in some ways, because of the small playerbase at the moment, the game is in a good place. Lots of fun to play, and lots of good people to meet along the way. I highly recommend picking up Battleborn, especially if you can get the Digital Deluxe for $10 or $20.
If you happen to take the plunge, feel free to add me in game!

The original F.E.A.R. would be a tough act to follow for any game, not just a sequel. Between the intense, engaging gun battles and the kitschy but ultimately effective scares, it was a unique delight built from familiar parts. It would only make sense to carry over the incredible enemy AI and oppressive atmosphere and god-killing shotgun to build an even bigger, bolder game. And perhaps that was what they intended, but it’s clear right from the start that something was lost in translation. F.E.A.R. 2 never quite manages to rise above the basics of the genre the way its predecessor did, but that’s still enough to make a competent shooter.
Let’s start with a spoiler alert for the original F.E.A.R., because it’s going to be impossible to talk about the weird♥♥♥♥♥♥that happens in this one without it. You play Michael Becket, Delta Force operator, on a mission to extract background villain Genevieve Aristide from certain death at the hands of an angry Armacham. This happens just a few minutes before the end of F.E.A.R. 1, meaning you get a front-row seat to the ghost nuke from the end of the previous game. The rest of your adventure is through the bombed-out hellhole Alma has turned the city into, murdering your way through Armacham troops, Replica forces, and wilder things in the hopes of somehow stopping scary ghost lady.
One thing I will give F.E.A.R. 2 credit for is running with the bug♥♥♥♥ ending of the first, Alma stinger and all. The spirit bomb not only hollowed out the city but turned the living to ash, leaving ghostly projections and even some reanimated corpses to battle. It’s a far cry from the mostly grounded foes of F.E.A.R. 1, leaving you in doubt of what you may encounter around the next corner. Several levels feature wall-crawling zombie test subjects that creep me out something fierce, while in other places you fight charging specters or scampering corpses that possess others like grim puppet masters. These encounters give the game some much needed tension, though at the cost of making it feel a bit cheesier.
I say much-needed because the scares of the first game are largely absent here. Well, maybe not absent but not nearly as competent. Don’t expect any stand-out spooks like Alma in the vents or at the top of that one ladder. F.E.A.R. 2 happily ignores loads of prime opportunities to scare in favor of obnoxious new visual effects painted over your screen. Terror time is telegraphed with red flashes around your vision, followed by some flickering lights or Alma appearing for a second or something else subdued. The tension is further eroded by the presence of your team in a number of areas, fighting alongside you and quipping about dead chicks and sticking it to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
It still tries though, and the same can be said about the combat. F.E.A.R. 2 is still built around a foundation of slo-mo combat, but some subtle changes have wiped away some of that immortal badass feel from the first game. You seem to move slower and engage enemies at greater ranges, eliminating a lot of fun melee opportunities. The weapons are balanced differently, with the standard assault rifle and submachine gun proving to be reliable but boring workhorses throughout the game. Meanwhile, the two shotguns take more hits to kill enemies and the exotic weapons are dialed down in power and impact. Supposedly the masterful AI of the first game was brought over as well, but if that’s true then I’d have to guess that level design holds them back from actually showing what they can do because they feel no different from typical CoD fodder.
Hopefully I’m not giving too negative a vision of the game, but viewing it through the bloody lens of the first game makes it hard not to miss the omissions. This remains a quality FPS, just one that veers more towards something like Call of Duty or Medal of Honor than the grim and gritty horror shooter that came before. Kicking in slo-mo to pound bullets into heads and then returning to normal time as the bodies hit the floor is still a crowd-pleaser, and there are a few additions like turret battles and two giant mech rampages to help break things up. They certainly don’t help the atmosphere much but I can’t deny the fun in mulching waves of soldiers with a rack of chainguns.
The graphics also skew more towards modern shooters than the sharp contrasts in the first game, featuring plenty of brown-brick walls and rubble and gratings. It’s the icing on a purely perfunctory cake, one that does everything it needs to without owing too much to its predecessor. I’m sure you must be sick of hearing about the first F.E.A.R. by now but that’s because there’s never been a proper follow-up or competitor, just this functional successor with decent combat and a wild story. F.E.A.R. 2 is plenty fun as a shooter, it just lacks the magic which made the first F.E.A.R. a classic.

F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin
+ I enjoyed the levels which showcased the city exterior, urban street warfare was cool. Seeing the widespread destruction was a welcome change from being inside so much. Commanding the elite power armoured mech was super fun too.
~ The graphics are very mediocre. The stylistic choices by the developers seem strange - the artistic representation of the game world is dull.
~ The shooting is a mix of fun and meh. It feels odd at times and some guns are very arcadey, but the gore is great. I can personally attest to the fact that there are rubber bullets, 7-8 headshots with an assault rifle won't drop an enemy (on hard difficulty). Laser weapons or the .50 cal sniper are brutally powerful, although ammo is scarce.
- For some reason the developers designed an annoying visor HUD which informs the player about health, current medkits and other information. It sounds great, but it is ugly and obstructive, blocking my view.
-  For the most part the hard difficulty is actually well-balanced, however there are some incredibly stupid fights which will require you to reload the game repeatedly when you die. They are a fantastic source of frustration and a supreme waste of time, especially the final engagement in the game. I finished 99% of it on hard, but turned it down to easy at the end because I just couldn't be bothered grinding it for no reason.
- This game really lacks a good soundtrack like the original. F.E.A.R's in-game music was epic and really set the tone for each mission, but F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin drops the ball, even using recycled music from its predecessor instead of innovating.
Overall Score 6/10

This is a great light gun game, and i say "light gun" because it's essential for enjoying this game to the full. I love light gun games, games such as time crisis, house of the dead and virtua cop were among some of my favorite games period and i feel that this genre has been left out in the cold for far too long.
This game plays very much like virtua cop, were it focuses on accuracy and precision rather than a duck and cover mechanic like in time crisis. Head shots are key to getting combos quickly and timing your reload is paramount to survival. Often you'll be met with on screen notifications showing you where to swipe the screen, these come individually, in quick succession or continuous like spinning a valve to open a gate. You can only carry two weapons which is a shame, though you won't need a lot of weapons anyway. The style of the game reminds me of house of the dead overkill, which had a grind house feel to it. So for the most part the game doesn't take itself seriously and perhaps you shouldn't either.
If you like light gun games, do yourself a favor, get this game and a aimtrak light gun
you won't regret it, and please don't use a mouse and keyboard or xbox controller you'll only be experiencing a fraction of the fun if you do so.

Guacamelee! is very much not shy about being a Metroidvania, but it still is a great standalone game with its own unique mechanics that are gradually introduced and it comes naturally using them to solve puzzles. The combat is great, and I enjoyed every fight, even if the final boss was a big and somewhat frustrating ramp up in difficulty I managed to defeat him in one sitting. It is also just a well written lighthearted game, as I feel it should be, aside from a couple moments. The visuals are bright and colorful, and the music is good too.
But where this game really shines, is when you have unlocked many of the powers and have to use them all in combination to get through some of the later platforming sections. They're used in truly brilliant ways here. Although sometimes I felt it could have gone further, it was just a lot of fun getting through the last few areas. It helps that falling does not kill or even hurt you. Of course colliding with a thorny vine or some spikes or an enemy's attack still will, so it's not as if there's no risk.
Overall, this game surprised me with how well made it was. Now I was expecting a decent game, but this was great. I played it whenever I could.

Anytime recently when I felt like playing Minecraft I've felt like building cities, castles, and towns. You can use creative mode for that but without anyone to inhabit your houses and buildings, it feels... Pointless. You can play survival to extend the amount of time to build your cities and towns, but the same result occurs over-time and you don't feel any reason to keep building and creating. You find that you want to explore, loot, spelunk in Minecraft more than build. And that is where this game is different.
Colony Survival is focused on building a town or city for colonists that can then inhabit and serve under you. They might farm, mine, guard, own shops, etc.  Your growth is limited by the amount of food you are able to produce which therefore requires a great deal of time and energy to achieve. You are also limited during the night as zombie like creatures invade and try and kill your colonists, while they sleep. Very simple dynamics that becomes fairly challenging pretty quickly.
Currently I would not say the price is worth it to everyone. There are no animals, the colonists can be buggy, there is no weather system, and few blocks and materials to build with. For more than a decade, James Rolfe, AKA the Angry Video Game Nerd, has been reviewing some of the worst games ever made.  Now, he is not playing the games, but is in the games.  While playing a bad game is one thing, being inside one is another story.
With the game being based on the Nerd’s show, the game uses material from the various episodes.  This is what will make the game most appealing to fans of the show.  Throughout the game, references to the show make its presence felt.   From stages like Boo! Haunted House coming from his comments to characters like Stuttering Craig as the Ghost of Christmas Past, everything about the game feels like an interactive version of the show.  Even things like the
deathtrap make its way into the game.  To go even further, some people from the show like Guitar Guy are playable characters adding extra variety and strategy.  If you are a fan of the Nerd, part of the fun will come into to finding and determining where all the references are from.
One thing that is surprising about the game is the quality of the music.  Even though this is supposed to be like an 8-bit game, the music is at a level above that.  The way that the music is designed could easily fit into any electronic setting.  For those that found themselves enjoying the music from the
series, the music will be a perfect fit.
Since this is modeled after 8-bit games, the game also has their challenge.  Excluding the tutorial, every level in the game is hard.  Even with the easy setting’s generous checkpoints and lives, trying to clear a single area can be unforgiving at times.  A prime example of this is in the Haunted House level.  In that stage, the player needs to walk through a long corridor.  While in there, a series of death blocks with make navigating difficult.  That would make it hard enough as is.  However, these blocks are only visible when within a few steps away.  On top of that, make of the floor blocks will collapse when standing on them.  This makes it that either the player has to have fast reflexes or memorized the layout.  With such steep challenge, only those with high skill or tolerance will be able to finish.
Nerd fans will definitely enjoy the game the most, but platforming fans in general will enjoy it.  Its high difficulty is a problem, so casual players might find it too much to handle.  Just remember that he was originally the Angry Nintendo Nerd, and this game personifies the expression “Nintendo Hard.”

I recommend this game I guess, but, there's something I want to say in this review. If you aren't someone who likes to build... This game isn't for you. Even playing with other peoples super awesome creations will only be fun for about 10 seconds, until you realize that wow, this map is really small for me to be flying a super fast plane, and wow, there's not a lot to destroy with this giant death machine I have. Sure, the levels are fun but there aren't many of them, and again, it won't take long. Also, it feels like it's taking forever for the devs to make these levels. I mean, they aren't exactly complicated or hard to complete at all. One of them literally is just, here's a crank, figure out how to turn it.
Now with that being said, if you like to build.. HOLY JESUS! There is a lot you can do in this game. Someone built a ♥♥♥♥ing bumble bee transformer, AND IT WORKS! One person built an actual Millennium Falcon! Not only does it look SPOT ON, but it WORKS SO PERFECTLY! Thanks to the skins people can do whatever they want to the games assets, like change the color, texture, and even the model itself. From what I can tell you can also add mods to the game that add in new effects too, like a sweet new engine particle.
Right, so these great complicated machines are super cool and all, but here's the problem. Because the game is in EA, it doesn't exactly run... well. That Millennium Falcon I mentioned before lags the heck out of my computer. However though, I think this is a minor problem. Thanks to the clever inclusion of the ability to slow down the game to reduce the pressure on the computer, it will help those with weaker machines. It sucks the game will be slow, but it'd be worse if it was 3FPS slideshow mode. It's not like it's an FPS where you need the precision or anything. You really just want to be able to play with some cool stuff and mess around, and the game lets you do that.
Overall, I'd recommend this game to those who like to build things, and whom are willing to really dive into this game really far and understand the inner workings of it. I WOULDN'T recommend this to those who are just looking to control some machines and mess around. I know I literally just said the game lets you do that, but still, you'll find yourself bored pretty quick once you realize there isn't anything to do with that tank you just downloaded.

After sinking 75 hours into this game I feel it deserves a review.
I had seen this game on my 'recommended' list for a while but was put off by the cartoonish and casual look. When I finally got it during a steam sale a few weeks ago I wasn't expecting much but felt I would get a dozen or so hours out of it before it became stale. My first few runs were indeed fairly standard casual fare. By the third run I had beaten the game (a lucky run) and felt I had seen everythiing this game had to offer. I was convinced that it would be shelved along many of the other games that once beaten I would never return to again.
That's when I saw the weekly community challenge. I was intrigued, especially when I saw the huge scores some people managed to submit. I was miles away from those score and couldn't immediately understand how people did this. So I went back and started to analyse the game mechanics in more detail. And that's when I realized that below the casual look was a very deep and complex game with many interlocking components. To get one of those high scores you had to understand those relationships and plan ahead. Both character development and resource management were important and balancing short-term vs long-term advantages was key. And most of all I started to realize that while luck and randomness do play a role, good preparation could mitigate this to a degree where it never became frustrating. My next few runs were all focussed on maximizing my chances of succeeding in challenges, starting to get a feeling for what perks would be best suited for which expeditions and events and which resources were best to invest in for each playstyle.
What strikes me the most is that despite the fact that the same challenges and events come up after a while it never really feels repetitive. At each point there are real and meaningful decisions to be taken. I cannot quite put my finger on it but there is something here that means that each run feels very different. And going back to the community challenges, those are a great way to keep the game fresh, forcing you to approach the game slightly differently.
The combat too is quite well thought out, mixing both standard turn-based tactics with a attitude management system that again looks simple on the surface but is actually quite deep once you understand the mechanics. A seemingly overwhelming encounter can be beaten by shifting the mood to constantly keep an advantage over the opponents.
I don't have the expansions yet, I hear they add a lot to the game, allowing even more options and advanced strategies, but even after 75 hrs I still have enough fun with the base game that I don't feel I need them yet.

This game just exudes charm with its whimsical, freewheeling adventures and approach to character.  Despite the relative short length of any one campaign, no two adventures are exactly the same and I found myself coming back for more just to see if I could pass a skill check that I failed before, and what would happen if I did?
Simply moving across the various maps and encountering the little stories+skillchecks is fun enough for me in itself, but it is also a tactical RPG and in that the game excels more than I was expecting. The novel approach to tactical gameplay in Renowned Explorers is incredibly interesting--instead of focusing on, say, weapon types, encounters revolve around setting and reacting to the mood of the battlefield.  In addition to the challenge of making sure you use the right kind of action to set the mood to give your party a potentially life-saving speech buff, you're also trying to make sure that the overall mood of the battle resolves in a way to net you particular rewards.  It's a lot more complex than I gave it credit for at first, and quite addicting.
This is a gem of a game that's fun and entertaining at any skill level.

Renowned Explorers is a good game, where good is defined as "a series of interesting choices." It's like an infinite fractal of interesting choices. You choose characters who have disparate abilities and define a theme for your party. You choose which resources to pursue. You choose how to make those resources more valuable. You choose where to get those resources from. You choose how to fight. You choose when to take risks and make choices that can make risks into sure bets.
This is a game about choice and the rush of seeing results from your choices. Choose this game.

Cossacks 3 is a 3D/HD/remastered version of 'Cossacks: Back To War', which is an absolute must-have for a nostalgic RTS gamer such as myself. It is an awesome game, and I already had the pleasure to play some skirmishes that instantly brought back delicious memories of my late childhood's lan games.
I cannot deny, however, that I was a bit disapointed by the lack of additions/improvements - other than graphics - to the original game concept. I was expecting at least some new units, researches and/or buildings, but I guess I'll have to wait for upcoming updates and already announced DLCs to satisfy that thirst.
For an "early-bird", the quality and stability are very acceptable, save for the multiplayer, which's UI is ludacris, in addition of lacking any kind of functionalities such as password-protected or friends-only servers. Furthermore: no LAN support, really? This one flaw always pisses me off, whatever the game!!!
The worst point though, if you ask me: Portugual! Yup, I don't know why, but Portugual isn't playable no more... Like, why in the nine goddam hells would you not include the one nation I prefered playing in 'Cossacks: Back to War'? Where is the cannon-mounted port that still haunts my memories?
Though I really prefered the one from the original game, the OST is of good quality, but dramatically lacks of "punch" according to me - or was it inspiration?
That said, I'd sincerily recommend it to nostalgic RTS gamers - for it is a playable and graphically endurable version of the first of the kind - but I'd warmly encourage younglings and/or non-initiated to skip it, at least for now.
A special note to devs: even though it is awesome you are trying to answer most of negative reviews with copy/paste replies, PLEASE, make sure to hire one guy who has at least a high-school level of english. I know mine is not flawless, far from it, but the display of your skills just made my eyes bleed and my brain melt.

F.E.A.R. 2 is a very solid shooter that is a worthy continuation of its predecessor.
The good:
- Very decent visuals even for today's standards - some nice textures, nice particle effects and many destructible elements.
- Great atmosphere - same old FEAR 1 jump scares and some tasty gore.
- Many memorable moments, that push the story forward and keep it interesting.
- Varied environment.
- Attention to detail - looks like the developer really sprinkled some love into this game. Example: In the opening chapter if you take your time running arround exploring and destroying the envoronment (e.g. a car parked in front of the building) before joining the rest of the squad, your team mates will make some comments like: "You took your time", "He was busy vandalising the place", when otherwise they wouldn't say anything. I think it's a nice touch.
- Great soundtrack - "Snake Fist" during the final battle is epic :)
The bad:
- AI pretends to be as sophisticated as in FEAR 1, but it clearly isn't. Enemy soldiers frequently sit in one place camping or just charge into your position. They may do some fancy backflips or turn over a piece of furniture to use as cover, but it looks very scripted and fake (and has a questionable effect). It is a bit of a shame as in FEAR 1 you had to watch your flanks and keep moving. In FEAR 2 however squad members don't seem to cooperate. They also don't seem to react to your flashlight (they did in FEAR 1).
The neutral:
- Guns for me felt a bit less impactful than in FEAR 1 - might be my own preference though.
- Guns in general are pretty standard, with a couple of exceptions.
- Slomo makes your enemies light up like christmas trees - I understand that it's a stylistic choice and it is designed to help the player, but slomo is so overpowered, that I don't think there is any need for that.
- New cover system sounds good on paper, but in reality is pretty useless. I haven't even used it once.
- Mech - I am not a fan of mech in FPS games, but in FEAR 2 it is digestible.
Overall I would give FEAR 2 a solid 8/10.

Rollercoaster Tycoon is an important game for me. It is that game what I install everytime something bad happened, when I'm ill or when I want to destress. Install RCT 1, 2 or 3 and you have a smile on your face in a minute I can guarantee you.
The game has it's own character. The colors, the happy peeps, balloons and the cartoony artstyle without being a casual game at all is proven a strong a concept and I think after many years this game is still a lot's of gamers favorite.
It was RCT that I saw on friends PC's screens, even on them who never play any other video game.
RCT World fails in every aspect to reproduce the freedom and creativity and addictive feeling of the older RCT games.
Even when the game did not suffered from technical bugs, 3D glitches, broken sound/music, bad optimization and way too less content it was a bad game. It's missing spirit, comedy, freedom and everything what makes the RCT series great.
The peeps are boring to look at. They don't have any style themself. It seems the dev team could not choose between realistic and cartoony and choose to design a mix of photorealistic characters with cartoony movement models. Everything moves too fast even on slow setting on a slow engine. I did met the sys req. for the game (the minimum) but whatever graphic setting I use after I place my first rollercoaster the game can't deliver anymore.
Object placement and path placement is ridiculous. The terrain tools very user unfriendly. You can't place path where you want, even if it seems to fit perfectly the engine don't allow you to place anything on random places. Tools you have like a grid and a snap grid makes this even more worse.
You can only place objects directly to the ground. You cannot place anything on top of something else. You can't even place banks, lights, carbage bins anymore on paths when the path is higher then the ground level. You can not build anything anymore in the game itself. (It's advertised that you can build anything in any other 3D tool and import it).
There is almost non to zero customization. You can't choose the main building, the entrance building, thematic entrances, place of entrances etc etc. It's all setup for you so the only thing you can do is build a prefab item. No creative building anymore.
You can't assign staff, can't train staff, can't change the colors of them. It's all setup. Same for food stalls, ticket stalls, peeps etc etc.
The management tools are not complete. The menu to read info about your parc is very hard to read. It's just a plain spreadsheet directly imported from the engine to the game. No nice menu's, no humor, no cartoony style and just a plain and simple click and place building game with a tycoon parc theme around it.
Last but not least the amount of content you get at the moment is 1/30 part of the original RCT games. You have 6 rollercoasters to choose from, 4 different terrain types (instead of 18 in RCT 3), a few thrill and a few junior and family rides. All rides are fixed and you cannot change anything yourself. But even if you could the amount of content provided by the game itself is so minimum. You can choose between some rocks and some trees and a handfull of decoration pieces.
Theme parc building should be something that makes you happy and should be happened smooth and relax. This game is slow, frustrating, ugly and simply misses anything that could make a game like this fun.
Very laggy. Cluncky controls. Nothing like RCT2 (The Classic)  A real shame the direction they went.  Wish I could get a refund.

text:
The game is roughly 35-40 minutes long. Most of that time is spent confused. The description of the game is that you are a lonely robot trying to find purpose, and that its an atmospheric game. These are all lies.
You randomly set up anntennas, randomly search for radio signles and then you randomly become a robot and just walk around. The puzzles give no hint of what to do. There is one puzzle where you have to change the sound of 2 monotone blocks. Yet it gives no indication why they need to be changed or what too. No where in the game do you hear these sounds ever again so it is not a case where you needed to listen to find the answer, or look around for clues. It becomea a guessing game.
The next puzzle is a combination, which again is a guessing game, with no hints if your hitting the code in the right order. There are potentially thousands of combinations it could be with no help as to what it is.
The game is just bland. You walk around and do unimaganitive puzzles. There is no story. you don't contimplate your exsistance you are on no known quest. The ending is just setting up more anntennas. You achieve nothing, discover nothing except feeling like a fool for wasting 40 minutes of your life.
Its free though and you can get all the acheivments in one sitting so whatever. If your Mrs is taking her time to get prepared for a night out this will tide you over til shes done.

I respect the authors and the work that went into this game, but it feels to me like this is the kind of game you show to a friend for feedback before continuing to a bigger project. Or what in the days used to be a mix tape of your band for publicity on your work. I don't like consuming publicity and it seems to me like the authors wanted solely to get their work out there with this game. I understand them, but that doesn't make it fun and consequently a propper entertainment product for Steam to present.
Regarding the "game" in itself it features a total of 4 puzzles and they can hardly be called that. As any short game, they favor the slow avatar movement speed to make it seem longer. It doesn't. And everyone creating a short game should not force us to go through their game at a reduced speed. It just makes me bored. Pressing a key for a long time just to get from A to B in order to progress is not my idea of fun.
Futhermore, the universe felt bland to me and the antenna animations were so chopped that I actually thought I had a drop in frame rate, but I stayed at 50fps constantly. Which also leads to the question as to why it didn't reach at least my screen's refresh rate of 60...
In the end, this is another game from Steam's catalgue of silly offers and there is no way I can recommend it to anyone. Only download and play this if you feel like doing the devs a favour. Kinda like when you go see your neighbours' children's play. You know it won't be excellent, but you want to be nice at the expense of some of your time, which could have been used to do anything else much more productive.

Cons

If you are one who enjoys supreme commander and supreme commander forged alliance, and want to get this game, prepare for a very different experience.
The main difference is the research system. Unlike SC and SCFA you don't have tier units and factories. You now have the research system, which you use to unlock the ability to build better units and structures. You build research stations to increase the rate you get points in it, so you can start unlocking units faster. While I still enjoy it, I don't find it to be as fun.
Another change is how resources are handled. Instead of still being able to build if you don't have the mass or energy to handle, with it draining from your storage supply, you gain it and spend it all at once to build a structure, and there is no storage. This makes base building, especially for stating out, relatively slow, because you need to wait for the mass and energy to come in before you can build. While its only an intial problem, because if you are like me, you will get more mass and energy than you know what to do with, aside from building experimentals.
And the experimentals aren't nearly as fun. First off, they are built from a factory instead of having to build them from an engineer or your ACU. This makes them feel less satisfying to build, especially considering most of the units that transfer over from SC and SCFA are hugely downgraded (the fatboy II isn't nearly as amazing as the fatboy). And there are some balance issues with how much things cost and some unit/structure power. Some units either cost what seems to be too much or too little, and some of them are broken. The new soulripper is the best air unit in the entire game period, as no other air unit matches its dps, and a group of them charging the enemy acu will destroy it insanely quickly. Finally, the Aeon/illuminate Loyalty gun, (or way laser as I call it), is the most overpowered thing in the game. It has a large range and  quickly captures ground units and structures that are in its radius, and while it can't capture air units, the fact that it can capture experimentals before they can even get to it to attack, its completely unfair.
Overall, I do enjoy Supreme commander 2, but the best out of the three is Supreme commander forged alliance. While I do say add this to your library (and get the dlc, adds some fun stuff) if you are a SC fan like me, just go in knowing its very different from the previous two games.

The best review I can give this game is to say that it is one of the most incredibly-executed platformers I have played in a very long time. Unfortunately, that review is also tinged by the fact that it is a very short game.
Guacamelee is a metroid-vania-style game, where you have a free and open world to explore, and your level of exploration is determined only by the upgrades you have gained for your character. However, the world itself feels rather small. There are several "dungeon" areas to explore, but the main hub world in which they all exist is not much of an experience. You'll be constantly running through the same areas, and while there may be one or two new things to do after each dungeon, it often does not feel satisfying to dive down a pit just to destroy a particular-colored block that hides a room with a single heart/skull piece (which upgrade your health/stamina).
The game does have a Challenge mode, which you can play to unlock additional costumes, but it just didn't feel strong enough or consume enough time for me, and I was left feeling as if I wanted more from the game.
HOWEVER, that being said, the rest of the game is fantastic. The actual level design of the dungeons themselves is stellar, slowly integrating every ability and upgrade your character acquires until you're dealing with incredibly complex (but entirely doable) challenges where you are constantly hopping between dimensions, running up walls, and jumping between said walls (which each exist in a separate dimension, forcing you to switch mid-jump) while avoiding deadly spikes and enemies the entire way. It may sound overwhelming, but the exceptional pace of the game perfectly prepares you for the challenges you will face.
Enemies range between push-over easy to complex and difficult, and the game not only understands how to place enemies to get the best bang for the proverbial buck, but it also recognizes how to use them in interesting and innovative ways. There are moments where you cannot fight enemies, and they simply become another aspect of a platforming challenge.
When you are fighting, however, it really shines. What begins as a simple three-hit combo game quickly transforms into a complex beat-em-up featuring a plethora of techniques that can each, themselves, be used in a variety of ways. Bosses, in particular, will put your reflexes and knowledge of the game's controls to the test as they unleash hell upon you in fascinating and intricate ways. That said, the level of difficulty is balanced by a system that does not punish you too severely for failing a challenge. There are no "lives" in Guacamelee, and you are instead replaced either at a save point, or at the beginning of the challenge that bested you.
Speaking of controls, these controls are TIGHT. I highly suggest you use a controller, as this is the type of game that just feels RIGHT with a controller in-hand. Each individual movement of the character feels incredibly well established and tested, ranging from simple run-speed and jump arcs to the range and directionality of throws and special attacks. Not once did I experience a buggy jump or a wavering character due to shaky movement. Your hit box is perfectly established, and when you fail, you never feel as if it's the game's fault.
Overall, Guacamelee is a fantastic game. It's short, to be sure, and I wish there were a few more levels and a bit more of the world to explore. That said, it was definitely a labor of love, and I completely adored playing it.

Both Metroidvania and Dia de los Muertos are equally rad concepts in my book, so Guacamelee seemed like the game for me when it went on sale. I burned through main quest in the course of an evening (to those disappointed by its ho-hum ending, there is an alternate available to the thorough explorers out there). The game's elegantly simple combat is certainly a lot of fun, its world-switching mechanic is fluid and intuitive, and its brevity means Guacamelee doesn't wear out its welcome.
If the title falls short anywhere noticable, it's in its attempts at humor. The merciless string of internet memes reskinned to fit the sugar-skull aesthetic just didn't do it for me. At the same time, Guacamelee takes its references a little too far in places; a cute homage to Super Mario Bros. involving an axe, a bridge, a giant lizard, and some lava is one thing, but completely pinching the statues from Metroid kind of kills the joke.
These ultimately amount to minor gripes, as the core gameplay and very pretty art-style make this Metroidvania-in-miniature well worth the $6 and change I paid for it.

Renowned Explorers is an Exploration game with a Choose Your Own Adventure style story and Tactical Combat. I like it very much and it "feels" almost like FTL (exploration) mashed up with Civ V (Tactical Combat, Multiple Paths to Victory) to me, but is unique enough to stand as its own thing.
The game is played by choosing a location to explore, traveling from node to node while managing your supplies and trying to get the most rewards out of a location before heading to the final confrontation. Sometimes a thing just happens and you get a reward, sometimes you have a challenge which you must pick a charecter and roll on the adventure wheel for success with a higher chance of success based on that charecters skills and the choices youve made, sometimes you must face combat which can be resolved in one of three ways: Aggressive, Friendly or Devious. Ultimatly you are looking for treasure and rewards which also help to make you stronger for future expiditions. After 5 sussecsful expiditions the game completes and if you managed to get enough Renown you win the game. If your resolve ever runs out or all your charecters fall in battle you lose the game.
It can sound very complicated but you can freely play on lower difficulties without having to master all the systems. Also the higher risks you take in the game the greater the rewards you get, but it is entirely possible to win by playing it safe. Renowned Explorers is very fun for me and I would reccomend everyone to try it out if it sounds appealing to you.

Fantastic game with an unexpected amount of depth. A solid title, currently an 8/10 that would become a 9/10 with some more updates.
Despite seeming like a simple board-game, combat is surprisingly strategic and requires significant planning and thought rather than some boring hack and slash. You have to take into account the mood and combat tactics you and your enemy are using, gear for your party, specific weaknesses the enemy might have, status effects that you apply, taking advantage of AOE effects and much more.
The characters that you can select have quite a few overlapping skills (a few more new skills assigned to different characterws would be appreciated), but it's not too bad. The biggest saving grace here is the incredible stylized art which makes every scientist, soldier, scout, or speaker feel unique in their own way. You've got the big, burley (but well-meaning) Russian bear, a stuffy, German school-teacher, the beautiful Latin seductress (Hola!), the insane eletricity-obsessed scientist, and much more.
The number of "expeditions" could be a bit higher. Considering that the game is rogue-like and you'll be replaying quite a bit, the game suffers from a feeling of redundancy too soon that could be remedied with additional maps. Currently there are 3 maps for every challenge rating (total of 13 I believe, there are only 2 five-star and four-star challenge expeditions), but after your first 6 or so runs it may get a bit stale.
There is a bit of a learning curve, but that's to be expecting in a rogue-like game. Your first three or four adventures will end in disaster, but you simply accept your mistakes and improve upon them the next time!
Overall, great game for it's price, especially on sale. The two main gripes one may have is if you are not keen on luck-based games (which a substantial portion of this game is based on) and the medicore number of expeditions. (note, they are slowly making more, but some are hidden behind paid DLC) Still, the positives far outweight the negatives.

A cross between tactics games and FTL-style exploration, RE:IS is a fun and humorous game about exploring exotic locations and preparing for the next journey. The fun, easy-to-grasp game mechanics have a surprising amount of depth to them, both in encounters and in the exploration map. The game's great sense of style compliments the slightly humorous and cartoony gameplay and narrative, with characters straight out of Tintin and adventures out of Ducktales. Do you happen to meet some friendly highlanders on your way to a lost Scottish artefact and talk some sense into them with seduction? Insult and berate wolves into leaving you alone while you excavate forgotten ruins? Or just fight like a gentleman (or a thug) to clear your way to treasure?

Retention is as much of a game as those old picture slideshow disks from the early era of the CD-ROM. The “game” is practically nothing but a showcase of roughly 300 pictures compiled to 100 sets.
Each set randomly modifies the photos to contain one unaltered, one black & white, and one with distorted colours. What you choose from each set affects the outcome of the framing story, which is a short, but powerful allegory: a man falls with his bicycle and suffers temporary amnesia.
So… that’s it, really. Retention is nothing but a big photo album allegory about memories and how we value them. Not a game but an artistic expression that costs only one dollar to experience.

Blue estate is a on rails shooter based on a comic series. It's remnicent of hardboiled fiction but is incredibly sardonic and comedic in tone. The game controls really well and the on rails setpeices are fantastic, then juxtoposed against things like your hair falling down, blocking your vision. In short it has a good story, great homour, tight controls (well on mouse and keyboard. there is leaf control support, but i hear it is not particularly intuitive), brilliant gameplay, doesnt feel repetitive as there are 2 characters you switch between, and different weapons for each level. Very solid concept and fundamentals, but it is (July 2017) EARLY Early Access in terms of content. I think the devs are on the right track but I will add suggestions/limitations anyway:
- The number of blocks/jobs is very limited. Jobs/management are the fun part of this game, so there definitely needs to be more.
- Colonists have no personality and there is no way to manage them efficiently. For example, you can't assign people to jobs, they assign themselves. There should be a UI for this. It would be a nice touch if colonists had variable looks and names, maybe even skills or preferences that would make them better at some jobs rather than others and level up over time.
- I would like to see in the future more high-tier "culture" type jobs; musician, artist, priest, etc. Maybe that sort of thing could affect colonist "happiness" and therefore productivity.
- There should be clothing/armor.
- More types of food, perhaps variety of food available could affect colonist happiness. Drinks (alcohol)? I would really like to build a tavern but it would be kind of pointless currently.
- Farm and war animals? It would be cool to ride around horses. Also, guards should be able to be given patrol routes.
Overall, I'd give it about 3-6 more months of development before buying. It is not worth the price with the current content, but by all indications, it is getting there.

I have nearly 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews - Game 9
Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures
Purchase Date: 8/25/2014
The first splash screen I see is "Rated F for ♥♥♥♥balls".  I did not realize at the time what valuable information I was being given.
The first thing I realize is, this game is clearly intended to be played with a controller.  The main menu flashes "PRESS START".  After some quick trial and error, I figured out that the Enter key means start.  After a couple of quick screens to explain the story (such as it is), the game starts with a tutorial level.
The main character provides some expletive filled commentary as you run, jump, and shoot your way through the level.  It didn't take me long to die due to a mistimed jump, which caused me to fall through the floor.  That means instant death in this game.  You also have a number of beers, which you can think of like hearts in a Zelda game.  Every time you hit something bad, you'll lose a beer.  If you lose all of your beers then you die, and get sent back to the last checkpoint.
It became very clear that the game intends for me to die.  A lot.  Every time I die, the main character gives an expletive filled comment about how much the game sucks.  After dying the 20th or so time at the same checkpoint, you start to get his point.
The graphics and sound are fine, and do a good job of evoking the retro feel the game goes for.  It does look and sound like a game you would have played on the old NES.  Which I think is also the point of the insane difficulty as well.  I should mention, the game does give you a choice of difficulty, so there is an "Easy" mode.  But it doesn't really make a difference.  Easy mode just means you get unlimited continues and more beer.  But more beer doesn't keep you from missing a jump and dying.  A lot.
Once I made it through the tutorial level, I was presented with a list of levels to choose from.  I appreciated the fact that I could make the choice myself, and the game wasn't completely linear.  Each level has a different theme.  For example one level is based on Castlevania, and contains a lot of the same traps and fiends you'd expect to see in a Castlevania game.  Another level is based on D&D and has an appropriately fantasy theme.
I do have to give props to the workmanship put into the game.  I think it took a lot of work to make a game this hard.  The level design is very good in that regard.
I only ended up playing about 40 minutes of this game.  After sampling a few levels, I realized I didn't need to play any longer to understand what I was in for.
Ultimately I can't recommend this game.  But I want to be clear that the reason I'm not recommending the game isn't because of it's difficulty, but rather I think it has a limited appeal.
You should buy this game if you are:
*15 years old
*A fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd
*Are looking for a video game to take you back to the days of throwing your controller at the TV when you were trying to get past that level in Battletoads.
If you are not any of these things, then this game was not intended for you.
If you are a small child go right ahead and buy this game. But if you are an adult male like myself and you buy this game for yourself........let's just say you won't enjoy it.

I have spent many hours with sweat dripping onto my keyboard and my teeth grit in visible pain as I saw the infamous death screen pop up, reminding me just how bad I was at this game.
AVGN Adventures is the perfect homage to the "bad games" of the 80's. It takes everything that could possibly be frustrating about them: cheap deaths, unnavoidable projectiles, leaps of faith, and above all else: levels that can utlimately be beaten in a matter of minutes (But in the real world, can take you about an hour at least after dying about 100 times), and mashes it into 10 obnoxious levels. Even when it is making fun of the "bad games" it does it in good taste. It rewards you for your unreasonable dedication to beating the levels and has more quality to it than actual abominations from the 80's.
The plot is kinda obscene, but with the Angry Video Game Nerd involved, what isn't? The nerd gets grabbed (by his junk specifically) by his game and is yanked into "VideoLand" where he must fight his way out and defeat the game's creator at the very end. Wild, huh? Regardless, tight controls, kickin' music, hilarious and well animated sprites, colorful backgrounds, and the little things like the unique phrases that appear upon each death at the bottom of your screen and the pause menu loop (those of you that have played this know what I'm talking about), and the misspelling of "Congratulations" as you beat each stage takes this game from being another steaming turd to a diamond. . . shaped like a turd.
This is a satire of videogames done right. It is a painful experience, but is one of those painful experiences where you go through it on purpose just so you can show off your scars to all your friends afterwards. Because not many people out there can say "I have beaten AVGN Adventures!" Only 5.1% of game owners actually have the achievement of beating the game on normal mode.
This game? I would say a solid 9/10. It is not perfect to me, but it is soo good. I also give it a 9/10 simply because I am kinda biased with the AVGN and this cushion is designed to offset my bias :p. If this baby is on sale, you should definitely give it a play, but I can't guarantee that you will get very far. . . Nonetheless, enjoy!

I liked Limbo, I really did. It didn't need much of a story, or any real fancy gameplay dynamic. Just some nice art style involving silhouettes and simple black/white backgrounds. It can be described as having a minimalistic art style. Antenna does the same, though with far less content.
Personally, I looked a little deeper into what this game is about. The description for the game: "A machine ponders its loneliness. It scans the radio spectrum for an answer to its question."
I think a little imagination is needed to fully encapsulate what this game is about and what it attempts to achieve. The robotic creature scuttling along seems to act as a sort of caretaker for the structure which the game revolves around. You control the creature to raise radio antennae and activate generators, to power up/turn on parts of the structure and to strengthen the radio waves needed to access the underground area and progress.
The games' greatest flaw is definitely the lack of content. Plenty more is need. However the content that is there is good. The puzzles were fun and I'm sure a story could have been made to accompany extended gameplay to give this game more than half an hours worth of gameplay. But for what its worth, I enjoyed it. For a free, short game, you can't go wrong and I just don't see why people write negative reviews when this game didn't relieve them of a single cent/rupee/rand/ruble/peso etcetera, and didn't take much of their time. As for unique, I dunno man. If you're after a unique game these days, you're in for a struggle. But I suppose there will always be whiners and whingers.

How did I ignore this game for so long?  It is one of the best "rock, paper, scissors" strategy games I've ever played.  It is certainly one of the most fun strategy games I've ever played.
The goal of the game is simplicty itself.  Explore different locales to gain renown and become the most renowned explorer.  You gain renown from treasures you find.  You also gain renown from choices you make on a research tree as well as from helpers and associates you hire.  The associates mostly just amplify the choices you make in the research tree.  I'm not explaining this very well, but it is super fun.
The game has a ton of replayability.  There are so many combinations of explorers and each group you pick plays differently.  You get to buy items for your explorers, and the small inventory space makes for some tough decisions on how to equip them.  Items can boost attack, defense, amplify certain skills and even add additional skills to an explorer. It's a cool system and adds a lot to the game.
Even when you can beat the game every time every time with your favorite crew, it will take a lot of play until you can beat every time with a random crew.
Three thumbs up, good value and a ton of fun.  Check it out the next time it goes on sale.

It's pretty fun.  Anytime you get mass amount of muskets firing at each other is always a good time. The army sizes can be pretty intense, but it takes forever to build up to anything huge if you start from scratch. It took me 2 hours to get to a point where i could start pumping out units like crazy.
PROS
ARMY CAP?- There is none as far as i could tell. Granted, I only went to 900s, but that took me two hours to get to. It's awesome.
CAPTURE MECHANIC- So. You can capture buildings and units. And you don't even need a monk to convert it or prevent conversion. Just run over to it.
RESEARCH- This game has tons of research in it. Mainly in the Academy and for each unit to improve.
CONS
ARMY MANAGEMENT- is kind of poor Your officers and drummers (key to putting your units in squad) like to stand in the front, die a lot so it's always a pain to reform that squad. Then, trying to form up an army  out of multiple squads is more of a hassle. A lot of the time I had units overlapping each other.
Not to mention the workers. By the end of a match I had it felt like a chore to see which mines I had open and getting the peasants over there. I couldn't click on idle peasants and automatically assign them to fill up the empty mines, which would've been nice when you have 250ish workers.
UNITS- Cannons are unbalanced. You can't form up huge squads due to 1 cannon=20 guys in one hit. Or just get a bunch of melee cavalry and just charge in and kill them all since they'll never hit moving targets.
VARIETY- And there's no real difference between factions so far that I've seen out of the 3 factions I've seen. The buildings look different from each other, and units are called by different names (Peasants/serfs),  I haven't seen unique units, unique bonuses, or unique buildings. Some buildings felt lacking while others felt more complete.
INFORMATION- Next topic is scoreboard. So you get a little tab on bottom right saying you're score based on buildings, units, etc. But there's no real end summary or graph like there's one in Age of Empires or SC2.
SUMMARY-
Overall it's a fun game, even though it feels incomplete at parts. If you like age of empires 2, you'll like this. I'd get just the regular version if I were you. Although, this review was based off of around 2-3 hours of gameplay,  so I haven't nitpicked it. Thanks for reading! (:

This game is so undeniably "meh" that I'm not sure whether to recommend it or not. It has its moments, but if you're like me, the entire time you will be reminiscing about how absolutely amazing the first game was. Gone are the incredibly tense firefights where slo-mo changes the game. Instead, there is COD like gunplay that poses next to no challenge whatsoever, and a story which has moments where I was laughing rather than being spooked. And, the weapon selection is poor- gone are several awesome guns from the first game like the AUG, grenade launcher, and akimbo pistols, and in their place are forgettable guns like the automatic shotgun and a new variant of the beam cannon which is useful for about 5 seconds (the sniper is the one new gun that's actually really good).
So, for now, I am not going to recommend the game, although there were parts which were enjoyable. If you're interested in the series and are looking for a decent FPS to take 8-9 hours of your life away, then go for it. I'd honestly say that you're better off playing the first game through again though.

This game is Borderlands gameplay and humor meets MOBA.  Lots of quirky and fun characters with unique abilities that set them apart from each other.  This game is NOT Overwatch, as the community was quick to point out.  However, the stigma has stuck with it.  I had my fun with 86 hours into the game.  I met some great people and had quite a few furious and rewarding matches.
That's all in the past.  Now, this game is a ghost town.  It's sad to see that so many people have abandoned it when there's so much to it.  Single player and co-op missions gives you a storyline and a goal to play through.  And when you're done with that then hop into the PVP modes, with the more prominent being moba-inspired.  I really enjoyed this game.
However, I did NOT enjoy Gearbox dropping the price $30 just 2 months after launch.  I bought 3 copies for my buddies at launch so we could all get on and get our game on.  That's fine, I got my money's worth from it.  And then the matchmaking nightmare began.  Pugging in this game is a nightmare, with matches taking forever to find, and once you're in them they become extremly 1-sided.  Then there's the cheesing as well.  Last I played this game, a sniper could stay back in their base and literally snipe your first turret with 0 counterplay.  3 patches in and this still wasn't addressed.  I don't know about now but that there was the reason I avoided playing the most popular and enjoyable map.
All in all, this was a very fun experience a launch, but it's become a ghost-town for matchmaking.  If you are looking for a decent co-op experience and enjoyed Borderlands then pick this up.  You'll like the roster of characters and humerous co-op missions (that do grow a bit stale after your 20th run-through).  Every once in a while I do get the urge to hop on my knife-throwing mushroom ninja(Miko4lyfe) but then the negative memories of all the unaddressed issues this game had come flooding back and I move on to something else.  Purchase at your own risk, but in the end it was still a good game.

Good game, not as good as I remember
Graphics: When this game debuted, the visuals were great, and they still hold up to the test of time.  The game runs well at 1080p/60 FPS.  Visuals are good enough to still be immersive, which is important in a horror game.
Sound: Audio was good for its time, but most modern audio is good, so it is nothing remarkable now.  Soundtrack is not as haunting as the first FEAR, though.
Atmosphere: Well done.  If they intention was to sow despair as you and your team attempt to stop a "demigod" from wreaking havoc on the world, they did well.  Destruction is everywhere, and creepyness exists in almost every level, to a certain extent.  Not as scary as the first FEAR though.
Story: Competent at the very least.  It all makes sense and is somewhat intriguing, but not much different than your typical "super secret agency doing super secret stuff" exposition.  Ironically, I got many Outlast or "Murkoff Corp" vibes from this game.  I would not be surprised if those games drew influence from the FEAR storyline.
Gameplay: Solid.  More FPS than the first FEAR, with some less horror sequences.  Not enough to say this isn't a FEAR game, but a noticeable departure from the first.  Gunplay is alright, but the grenades are a nuisance.  I assume to immitate real life, but when you throw a grenade it doesn't always go where you aim--You will throw it either to the left or the right, a little up or a little down.  Annoying in a firefight as you sometimes throw it right into a wall to much frustration.  I played on veteran, and the difficulty is a little unfair sometimes.  Shotguns will usually one-shot you, even with full armor.  An NPC will randomly get off a few shots on you as you are filling his mouth with lead, which doesn't make much sense.  I've been sniped and grenaded through walls.  Certain enemy animations include invincibility frames, some animations don't.  Very frustrating to not know exactly when you can or can't attack an enemy.  There is absolutely no stealth factor, enemies will see your toe and within milliseconds be putting fire into you.  Sometimes you don't ADS when you press the right-mouse-button (this is an old game and I believe the default ADS is shift, so that may be the reason for this unusal bug).  I've fallen through a level before.
If you are a general FPS fan, you will probably find this game enjoyable.
If you are a FEAR fan, you will find this game enjoyable but not as creepy as the first.  It does certainly have its moments, but not as frequent as FEAR.
If you are a horror fan, you probably won't enjoy this game unless you also like FPS.
The game is on the shorter side, but that's not always a bad thing, as there is very little downtime.  You're either in a horror sequence, or a firefight sequence 90% of the time.
FPS = 8.8/10
Horror = 7.5/10
Final score = 8.2/10

Antenna is a short puzzle game from indie developer LWNA. Given its short life span of 15-20 minutes, there is little to say about the game, as there is very little content present. You initially set up an antenna, find the correct frequency, and then you end up controlling a semi-arachnid type robot. You wander a desolate landscape, setting up more antennas and generators, and sometimes solve small sound puzzles.
The art style is of the modern, "stylish" silhouette variety, much akin to Nihilumbra and Limbo. The foggy, gloomy, blue background instills the alone and depressed direction of the game. While not solving puzzles, the sound is very quiet and ambient, save for the hums and buzzes of generators and frequencies in the background when you pass by power stations. The puzzles themselves aren't overly complicated, but they aren't exactly fun either. The title in and of itself isn't exactly fun, it's just mediocre and existing.
Sure, Antenna is free and that's great for those of us without deep pockets. Quite honestly, not many people would've paid for the game anyway; if they had, they'd probably have requested a refund when finding out it only lasts 20 minutes. I will hand it to LWNA for not gouging gamers for a title so short, unlike the dollar games that have been popping up left, right, and center. While Antenna isn't a bad game, it's not very fun either, nor is it unique. If you're an achievement hunter, there's no harm in wasting time on this one for the easy achievements; if you're a passerby, give something else a whirl.

It's an amazing game, especially considering it's sale price now at $2.99. It draws inspiration from Castlevania, Metroid, Megaman, Mario Bros., and other indie games like VVVVVV and Super Meat Boy. You can see all of these game references and more not only in the great art that's everywhere, but in the way it plays out. The simple game expands to be amazingly complex, and Hard Mode and leaderboards add extra challenge value--although the story is good enough to play through again just to see it all unfold like the first time. That said, for a great classic experience such as this, please use a gamepad/controller.
It's not just a brawler, but a platformer and puzzler. Although references in the game are generally a homage to Nintendo and the internet, the game has enough content to feel like a 2D Batman: Arkham series game. The only downside is just the same: there's little in the way of getting a feel for your character, since what little dialogue choice you have doesn't seem to make a significant difference. That said, it's a game that does what it intends to do. A wired Xbox360 controller is ideal for button layout and plug-and-play drivers to instantly get playing with no setbacks. Simply plug it in, calibrate, and go.
In a technical standpoint, the game is made in Adobe Flash. That said, there's a particular art and function that indie veterans will feel familiar with, but brawler games are rare for this kind of base. That said, one particular minor problem the game has is slowdown stuttering, with the same flavor as the kind you saw way back on old NES systems. Perhaps all of our insane 300+ hit flawless combos cause too much stress as a game session carries on. Regardless, the fix is simple and easy: just restart the game. You need to completely exit to your desktop, stopping at the main menu won't fix it.
The game has additional small features such as leaderboards and the ability to make skins for this game and post them on the Steam Community Workshop. The leaderboards are essentially a global speedrun board for various kinds of completions. The Community Skins workshop so far seems to only be for player characters, and workshop crafters use Flash to make their stuff. I recommend you only keep a handful of these mods installed at a time for game stability. You can easily manage these through your subscribed files panel.
Overall, I give this game a solid endorsement. It has a classic feel that's polished enough to compare to many great games, and there's so much variety here it feels like many games all at once. Currently with the Summer Sale going on, it's well worth the $2.99 (75% off) you're paying for it. The full price seems proper for the quality, so you're getting an amazing deal. Please do get a game controller though, chances are you're going to need it.
