I needed my Mass Effect fix and this was the closest game I could find. My goal was to rush through this game so I could play KotOR 2, but I was pleasantly surprised with what it had to offer. I ended up taking my time and enjoying the journey.
PROS:
+ BEAUTIFUL music. It's top notch. It's easily the best aspect for me.
+ I loved the story. It's what kept me playing. If the story wasn't on point, I wouldn't have finished the game and likely would have uninstalled.
+ Like most BioWare games, the characters are wonderful. I enjoyed getting to know their lore in between missions. It's a bit like Mass Effect where you talk to a character and then have to complete a mission before you can unlock further dialogue.
+ Voice acting was top notch. There are some exceptions, but nothing that ruined my experience.
+ The game has mod support. I recommend checking out Snigaroo's modding guide on Reddit. Just Google "kotor modding guide reddit" and it should be the first link.
+ The UI is clean and well organized. It takes up minimal screen space and is intuitive.
+ The side quests were decent. I actually wanted to do them outside of wanting XP and karma.
+ I love games with karma system.
+ No inventory limit.
CONS:
- No 1080p support. You have to mod the game in order to get it to work. A YouTuber by the name of "Xuul" has a very good video on how to accomplish this.
- I disliked the combat system. I haven't played a game like this before, but the way it works is that you pick which attacks you're going to do and these attacks get queued up for your characters to execute. It's not exactly real time combat. It felt clunky, targeting was a pain, and it didn't feel like I had the level of control that I wanted over what my characters were doing. A positive aspect of the combat is that you can pause the screen while you assign attacks and targets for each of your squad members. The system is very similar to Mass Effect.
- You can't tell the squad to cancel combat and get them to exit like you can in Mass Effect. You can press F to cancel combat, but you have to take control of your team one by one in order to completely exit combat. This was highly annoying in early game when I needed to retreat to regroup, but I had to do it one by one which often resulted in an ally dying and me not being able to exit the area because you have to have all your squad.
- Speaking of which: "[You must gather your party before venturing forward]" is a highly annoying message that I kept getting every time I would try to leave an area. Basically, your squad must be within a certain minimum vicinity from you before you can leave. If not, you get that message. This happened to me quite often since the squad AI is slow and often takes forever.
- Quest management sucks in this game. This seems to be a recurring problem in quite a few BioWare titles. Luckily, there are mods that fix some of the problems such as removing quests you won't be able to complete and having the quest list free of clutter.
- There's no adequate fast travel. You can travel back to your ship and sometimes to previous locations, but there isn't a way to fast travel throughout a given map. This makes navigating maps cumbersome since you have to backtrack quite a bit to turn in quests. This artificially inflates  the play time of the game, but not in a good way.
- The game does a horrible job at telling you when you've levelled up.
- I dislike silent protagonists. It doesn't make the game feel immersive to me. It's actually the contrary.
- Disappointing loot with no real / substantial difference in stats. For example, you'll end up getting a truck load of lightsabers with no real stat differences. Armors/outfits and their upgrades are an after-thought.
Conclusion: It feels like I had more bad things to say about the game than good. To be honest, I quite enjoyed the game despite some of the faults. Not enough to replay it multiple times like I did with ME1, but it's still a great game. The gameplay was mediocre, but the story made it worth enduring. I recommend playing this.

From the legacy of Chris Sawyer and the entire series of Roller Coaster Tycoon comes the latest sequel: World. Unfortunately, this is nothing but a name now. RCTW fails on so many levels. I purchased the game in the EA and it never reached functionality.
It's clear to see where the faults come from. Atari had three separate developers for the project and after Area 52 and Pipeworks dropped out, Nvizzio Creations took over the reins. Built on the Unity engine with unproven developers and seemingly unknowing, the game has glitches and the path system never functioned the way anyone who plays it wants it to.
Four months after release and over a year since the initial Early Access release, the game is still not optimised. This game is still unplayable. You cannot place anything where you want to. In order to have staff in this game, you must construct giant bulky ugly buildings for each of the type of workers.
One bright spot that RCTW has is its superior roller coaster building system. Instead of using the old piece-by-piece system from earlier iteration, RCTW boasts a new spline system. They still have the old system as an option. This is one spot that Planet Coaster loses in battle. Planet Coaster has a good piece-by-piece system but still has an old system.
Peeps look terrible, and still to this day have animation glitches where they warp or levitate. Peeps in RCT3 (developed by the people who developed Planet Coaster) had substance. Peeps before were well-created. These peeps aren't characters. They don't interact with the game like they did in the first three games.
Atari made a ton of money on this game, so it's a success for them. But, for us fans expecting the best game of the series, it's a huge failure. This game is a letdown for so many. Atari can tell Nvizzio to add so much content, but in the end this game will never live up to the hype behind it two years ago.

It has been some time since the release of RCTW Early Access and I feel the game has reached a level where a review is warranted. There have been many negative reviews, and I can see the frustrations that led many to leave such, but a lot of those seem to have dismissed the game after a few moments of play. Not giving the game a chance to show off its potential.
And in Early Access, potential is what we want to consider, The foundation that RCTW has laid is such that it may very well grow into that potentail we can glimpse. Should UGC become full, and each day we see more pieces added, should Piece by Piece building with the UGC be solved, and each update we see that happening. Then the foundation could lead to overwhelming success.
At present, for those who are creative, the park builders, I would say the game has enough that you can find many hours of contentment playing it. For those who are problem solvers and want to play scenarios, we are not quite there yet with needing AI to balance better, with the scenarios to be tweaked better.
But for the $50 price, it is closer each to day to be the successor to RCT3. At present the trajectory that it is on, may never get us to being equal or better than RCT3. But perhaps one rung below it. Though should more coaster types, more rides, more more more be released, then it might even surpass RCT3 for at present the graphics are better. Should the gameplay expand, UGC be optimized and the others items that we can see the potential to better happen, then yes, we shall have a GAME!

Each mission being worth 3-5 playthroughs, as, you have several unique ways of killing each target. You'll really feel the urge to replay and see how many different ways you can kill someone. This game has a good story, good soundtrack, tight controls for the pc version, fun combat, each level is a fun large sandbox dying to be explored, and you'll be dying to see how many different paths you can take through the levels, and how many different ways you can kill your target. The general question is simply: Do I recommend other people to play it? Short answer: No.
Long answer: Depends! Last time I played an on-the-rail shooter was in an arcade many years ago, and I've played many of them before. Do I think they're generally fun? Yes. Do I think this game is that fun? Not really.
The humor of this game didn't really strike me much, except for a few scenes here and there. So I guess one of my biggest problems with the game is simply that it didn't "click" with me, and not much else I can do on that end. However, I'm sure there are many people that would find it to be hilarious.
But besides that, I also just didn't like much of the Story mode of the game. Some of my dislikes go along with the humor, but they also affected the gameplay - for instance, Tony's hair always falling down in front of the camera as a cheap gag got really annoying really quickly. It isn't necessarily difficult to move it away, but that doesn't mean it can't get bothersome.
In terms of positives, the game does have some nice graphics and sound, and the voice acting isn't bad. Many people compare PDH and PD2 together saying one is better than the other. They're both great games, however, they both exel in their own fields. In this review, I'll cover what PDH does better than PD2.  Firstly, we have the fluidity of the animations. Hot damn, those animations feel good. Just the feeling of reloading an AMCAR so quickly and effectivly gives me a great feeling of satisfaction. When chaining these animations together, it feels fluid, not jerky. On the contrast, the PD2 animations can feel jerky when put together making it not as satisfying to move around, reload, shoot. Secondly, we have the desync. This is a HUGE problem with PD2, however, I have found no instances where it is nearly as bad in PDH. People move where they are, not where they've been. Everything feels like it's not run clietside, but rather on a server where everyone has the same ping and latency. Lastly, we have the difficulty. PDH is MUCH harder than PD2, and it shows. The average success rate for heists is about 25%. Playing on normal doesn't just make the cops mindless drones like in PD2. This may be due in part to the low health and armor of the characters, but it shows. The game is rewarding and punishing. Now, for the downfalls. PDH doesn't have as many hesits as PD2, not as many weapons, not as many gagets. It doesn't even have skills. However, it instead has a RPG like level system which makes you work to level up all your skills. It is rewarding and difficult to get where you want. In the end, PDH is a much better feeling game to play, however, it does not have the new shiny look of PD2 with all its new heists and weapons. This game is for those who want a challenge from the normal rinse repeat of PD2. Not for the faint of heart (you've been warned!).

I downloaded the game earlier and played through two runs, hoping to get a contribution in for the community challenge #71 going on this week.
What I didn't expect was to spend over three hours having way more fun and being way more engrossed than I thought I would.
This game is a beauty for anyone who enjoys turn-based strategy board games, or even turn-based strategy in general. Oregon Trail is something I kept thinking of while playing. There's definitely inspiration from board games in RE, though, and along with the characters and the witty writing, as well as the unique battle mechanics, there's a huge amount of charm to find in this game.
That's not to say this game is forgiving. Not in the slightest. There's a lot to grasp starting out (thankfully the tutorials are straightforward and not too drawn-out), and I'm sure some meta tactics are out there to maximize your resources in various ways. There's a lot to explore (see what I did there?) in terms of the game's depth through its mechanics, and you can always improve your score, so replayability isn't that big of an issue. And for anyone who may somehow find themselves exhausting that replayability, there's DLC packs to continue the enjoyment at very reasonable prices.
Renowned Explorers: International Society is well worth your money, but more importantly, it is certainly worth your time. If you like this kind of game, don't hestitate to pick it up.

I needed my Mass Effect fix and this was the closest game I could find. My goal was to rush through this game so I could play KotOR 2, but I was pleasantly surprised with what it had to offer. I ended up taking my time and enjoying the journey.
PROS:
+ BEAUTIFUL music. It's top notch. It's easily the best aspect for me.
+ I loved the story. It's what kept me playing. If the story wasn't on point, I wouldn't have finished the game and likely would have uninstalled.
+ Like most BioWare games, the characters are wonderful. I enjoyed getting to know their lore in between missions. It's a bit like Mass Effect where you talk to a character and then have to complete a mission before you can unlock further dialogue.
+ Voice acting was top notch. There are some exceptions, but nothing that ruined my experience.
+ The game has mod support. I recommend checking out Snigaroo's modding guide on Reddit. Just Google "kotor modding guide reddit" and it should be the first link.
+ The UI is clean and well organized. It takes up minimal screen space and is intuitive.
+ The side quests were decent. I actually wanted to do them outside of wanting XP and karma.
+ I love games with karma system.
+ No inventory limit.
CONS:
- No 1080p support. You have to mod the game in order to get it to work. A YouTuber by the name of "Xuul" has a very good video on how to accomplish this.
- I disliked the combat system. I haven't played a game like this before, but the way it works is that you pick which attacks you're going to do and these attacks get queued up for your characters to execute. It's not exactly real time combat. It felt clunky, targeting was a pain, and it didn't feel like I had the level of control that I wanted over what my characters were doing. A positive aspect of the combat is that you can pause the screen while you assign attacks and targets for each of your squad members. The system is very similar to Mass Effect.
- You can't tell the squad to cancel combat and get them to exit like you can in Mass Effect. You can press F to cancel combat, but you have to take control of your team one by one in order to completely exit combat. This was highly annoying in early game when I needed to retreat to regroup, but I had to do it one by one which often resulted in an ally dying and me not being able to exit the area because you have to have all your squad.
- Speaking of which: "[You must gather your party before venturing forward]" is a highly annoying message that I kept getting every time I would try to leave an area. Basically, your squad must be within a certain minimum vicinity from you before you can leave. If not, you get that message. This happened to me quite often since the squad AI is slow and often takes forever.
- Quest management sucks in this game. This seems to be a recurring problem in quite a few BioWare titles. Luckily, there are mods that fix some of the problems such as removing quests you won't be able to complete and having the quest list free of clutter.
- There's no adequate fast travel. You can travel back to your ship and sometimes to previous locations, but there isn't a way to fast travel throughout a given map. This makes navigating maps cumbersome since you have to backtrack quite a bit to turn in quests. This artificially inflates  the play time of the game, but not in a good way.
- The game does a horrible job at telling you when you've levelled up.
- I dislike silent protagonists. It doesn't make the game feel immersive to me. It's actually the contrary.
- Disappointing loot with no real / substantial difference in stats. For example, you'll end up getting a truck load of lightsabers with no real stat differences. Armors/outfits and their upgrades are an after-thought.
Conclusion: It feels like I had more bad things to say about the game than good. To be honest, I quite enjoyed the game despite some of the faults. Not enough to replay it multiple times like I did with ME1, but it's still a great game. The gameplay was mediocre, but the story made it worth enduring. I recommend playing this.

Both Rollercoaster Tycoon World (RCTW) and Planet Coaster (PC) are halfway through their alpha stages (or beta, the difference in meaning has become insignificant over the last years) and both games show great promises and annoying bugs at the same time, which is completely normal for any game under development of course. PC has just seen the release of its second alpha (the second out of three) and RCTW has had major and minor updates over the last two months, since it has entered early access on Steam. Let's start with pointing out what PC delivers and lacks at this point in time.
PC is a game which features a more or less cartoonic graphic style and is mainly focused on building custom scenery and constructions by using various structural elements and decorative items. This way no two parks will look the same and the possibilities are numerous (not endless, as that's technically impossible), especially with the latest update in which it has been made a lot easier to fine tune the movement of objects on multiple axes. The amount of different structural elements to obtain such a desired beautiful park is quite decent, although it remains to be seen how many will still be added in the future before its final release in autumn 2016, as the amount of newly added objects was amazing during the first alpha, but rather disappointing in the second. Another main focus within the game is the animations of the park guests. These are far from optimal at this point, but it's obvious to see that the creators tend to accomplish guests who accurately reflect their mood, appear to be responsive to their environment (including the rides of course) and behave as natural as possible. This feature still needs development, but it's too soon to tell whether they succeeded or failed, as the park management (which includes this feature as far as I'm concerned) will be released in the third alpha stage next summer, so I will leave this part of the consideration for now. Moving on to the flat rides it seems the developers were bereft of any resourcefulness, as most rides are mere copies of previous rollercoaster tycoon games (RCT 1, 2 and 3) and in the second alpha they even added a second Ferris' Wheel, whereas one would have been more than enough (and don't forget that another flat ride - the Whirley Rig - is also a Ferris' wheel to tell the truth). Is it really that hard to come up with rides that are actually different from predecessors and at least somewhat different from other rides? Let me give you another example: the newly added Insanity ride is just a copy from previous rollercoaster tycoon games and it's also remarkably similar to the Hammer Swing. Why don't they add rides which they've actually come up themselves instead of merely copying others and/or existing rides (just compare the Brain Surge from Nickelodeon Universe to the Psychola ride in the game). To be fair, the same mistake was made with the development of RCTW, as they added two slides (whereas one would have been more than sufficient) and they failed to provide rides which are different and interesting enough from my perspective, just as the developers of PC did. The number of flatrides is still quite low within both games, but I'm sure this will improve on both fronts. Finally, let's move on to my biggest disappointment of PC: the coaster builder. It contains some nice features, such as being able to change colours of the tracks and the supports (although the colours of the carts can't be changed for some unknown reason) and there's a good amount and variety of coaster types, but the building itself is downright frustrating and tedious, as you constantly have to move the cursor from the screen to the interface at the bottom of the screen and back again to build track sections. The building process is also rigid and doesn't feel natural due to a lack of flexibility and a poorly designed interface. This feature has barely been improved upon since the release of Rollercoaster Tycoon 3 in 2004, which is clearly an impairment in this game. The second alpha delivered us the finished coaster builder according to the developers, so apparently they deem it to be completed.
Let's now move on to RCTW. This game features a style similar to parks like Six Flags or Hersheypark (as opposed to PC which is more in the direction of Disneyland or Disney World) and is mainly focused on the coaster builder, although various flatrides and scenery items have been included of course. The coaster builder is not perfect (which will be improved in upcoming updates), but building coasters has quite a natural and flexible feel to it, does possess a good interface to make use of all the different functions the spline based building tool has to offer and provides the option to change colours as well. This feature has clearly been improved upon since its last installment of 2004, whereas PC failed to do this. On the other hand, the flexibility and possibilities PC offers for scenery items and custom constructions are not included in RCTW, as the latter does provide a freeform placement system, but is not aimed at allowing players to make their own buildings within the game at this point in time. This feature will be added to the game later on, probably once the game is pulled out of Early Access, which will happen given the amount of regular updates since its release (although many claimed it never would). Moreover, the animation of the peeps (park guests) is fairly poor in RCTW in comparison to PC. They behave and move unnaturally and need quite a few improvements, but the developers are still working on this. My aforementioned criticism on the flatrides also applies to RCTW. Several other missing features are more striking in both games, however, as both games don't include water, dark or transport rides (although both the developing teams promised to add these to the final product of games) and both games don't contain any kind of weather system or simulation (this feature has been promised for RCTW, but not for PC at the moment).
So, which game would I recommend to you ? Both, as long as the promises that have been made regarding both games are met. Which game should you buy? That's up to you (I bought both games). To me it all comes down to preferences. Do you prefer a theme park builder which mainly focuses on beautiful scenery items and custom buildings just like Disney World, then go for Planet Coaster. If the building of amazing coasters and parks such as Six Flags is more to your liking, then go for Rollercoaster Tycoon World. I truly believe that both games are on the same level at this point in time, as both contain both good and bad features and both offer promises and bugs, which is utterly normal for games under development (as I already said). Let's hope that we will have two good theme park building games coming out at the end of this year.

I highly recommend getting this game some time in the future. Even now, in Early Access, there is a surprising amount of content and the concept has a lot of potential. Two things that really caught my attention were the graphics and controls. It looks and plays better than a lot of "finished" games.
I've seen a lot of people compare it to Minecraft, but really the similarities are only skin deep. They both have cube-based worlds and some focus on surviving. Aside from that, the gameplay and pacing are radically different. Colony Survival is about managing your units (colonists, who can have various jobs) and building a practical and efficient base (that can still look very nice). Your character is not an invincible warrior, he is a fragile king, and the danger of falling or getting attacked by monsters is very real and frightening.
The creators have done an excellent job of making shaders appropriate for a cube-based world. All the little details are there: your "eyes" adjusting to different light levels, the blinding effect of looking at something light from a dark area, the rays of sun coming in through gaps, the focusing of your "eyes" on the surface in front of you (blurring things at different distances). It looks better than any other cube-based game I have seen.
The blocks are proper 3D models. They're not just 6 flat planes--they have bumpmaps that work very well to create a feeling of texture through lighting. It's clear that the creators have put genuine effort into making this a quality game.
However, there are some minor issues that still need to be worked out. Blocks diagonally adjacent to one another have ugly edges when viewed up close due to the way the edges of the blocks are defined, among other small problems.
It is sometimes hard to tell what item you have selected because the outline around the currently selected slot is faint. This might be fixed by adding tooltips or making the outline easier to see.
The water needs a lot of work. The opaque, bumpmapped water blocks just don't look good from up close.
The movement is acceleration-based and feels very nice right away. It doesn't take any getting used to and it's fairly easy to get close to a ledge without falling off, as the game does not have Minecraft-style crouching.
The inventory can be finnicky. It sometimes takes a few tries to get something or put it down in another slot. I'm not sure if this is due to the hitboxes on the slots being off or if it's failing to register clicks somehow.
The best single-phrase description I can give is "First Person Real Time Strategy." There is very little emphasis on your own character. You do not need to make tools for yourself--those are for colonists. Inventory space is not an issue. Your main responsibility in terms of manual labor is building the colony (this might change once colonists can build from blueprints). You need to design an effective defense. Right now it is easy to "cheese" the system by making a maze, but this may be fixed in the future. Most of your responbility lies in managing your colonists. You need to have enough food coming in to sustain them all, and you need to position your archers correctly.
The pacing of the game in the early stages is very nice. The amount of monsters spawned is based on the number of colonists, so you are safe to build your base and get it ready before recruiting any colonists (and thus letting monsters spawn). However, unless you go out of your way to make something that looks nice, it's easy to have the game "done" and your colony defended very quickly. Just build a 2 high wall and put a bunch of archers around a single entrace with a maze in front. There needs to be some reason to expand the colony and have high, strong walls around it. Perhaps new monsters that can climb walls or jump. Perhaps more complex processes for grinding wheat and baking bread that require more space. As it stands, a single, small building will work forever, and that leaves you with little desire to continue into the late game.
As a lot of other people have pointed out, multiplayer is very much unfinished. There is no way to share resources, have colonists work together, or prevent griefing. However, the creators have said that they will actively work on this. I see huge potential for multiplayer in this game. I would like to see more resources, some of them rare, to give incentives to trade with other players (perhaps automatically with "trader" colonsists?).
Going on with the idea of trade, I think having more biomes with biome-exclusive resources would be a huge step forward. It would give players a reason to explore in singleplayer and trade in multiplayer. There should also be resources that take a lot of effort and time to process, allowing specialization and, again, giving a reason to expand the colony and give the process its own building or other area.

After playing a while of this, I can only describe it as a Minecraft mod idea that was too hard to implement into Minecraft itself, so they made their own game for it. And that's perfectly fine. I like Minecraft and this is a unique twist on the concept. I dunno if that's actually what happened, but I wouldn't be surprised.
I don't normally review games until I've completed them, nor do I like to review early access games as they're an incomplete experience. This one, however, makes me want to review it to support it and encourage others to try it too. At time of writing I have all but one achievement, but that just requires me to stockpile some more food.
Let's get the first big hurdle out of the way. This looks like Minecraft. A lot like Minecraft. It uses metre-cubed blocks for everything and features a procedurally-generated world with grass, dirt, stone, woods and lakes. It also has biomes like snow and rainforest, but I've yet to find them. Every night zombies attack and try to kill your colonists and destroy your banner. And that's where this game deviates from Minecraft.
While you're all alone in the former aside from a few brain-dead animals and some big-nosed villagers, Colony Survival is all about the collective. The main drive is ensuring food and safety for your burgeoning colony comprised of...admittedly brain-dead workers. If you play right, you'll never need to collect a single grain of wheat or fire a single arrow in defence.
To keep everything running smoothly, you hire colonists to perform these jobs and others for you...or for the colony, I guess. You place a quiver and an archer will stand at that post forevermore, firing on any zombies that come within range. You allocate a field and a farmer will plant and harvest wheat. Millers turn the wheat into flour, bakers make bread from that and so on. This is a bit like Minecraft meets Factorio, which is weird as Factorio is always described as Minecraft Tekkit but bigger... This game is massively more simplistic than Factorio, however.
I said that I'd completed almost all the achievements, and that's in about 8 hours of playtime. At the moment, there is not a lot here. But again, that's perfectly fine; what is here is fun, addictive and has a lot of room to expand and improve. I couldn't stop playing this last night and now I have a beautiful little colony with golden fields, cherry trees and 67 eager young idiots who take very circuitous paths to stuff.
As this game is very early in development (v0.2.3 at time of writing), I don't begrudge the issues I'm about to recount, but I feel they should be recounted nonetheless. The pathfinding is painfully bad; I had colonists walking three quarters of the way round my perimeter to get in instead of taking the path a third of the length. I have guys who bagsy the beds meant for (and much closer to) the miners because, as the crow flies, they're technically closer. Doesn't matter that there's a giant ditch between them meaning they need to walk a bloody long way to get there.
The game is also very easy. I had two archers early on and have NEVER had a problem with zombies. More zombies attack based on the number of colonists, but I kept on top of it with so much ease that they might as well not be there. You can also set it so zombies attack during the day and in double numbers, but these are on world creation and I don't think they can be toggled later.
The shader can also be a bit obnoxious, but that's getting into some very subjective and petty griping. 8 hours of play and that's about all the bad stuff I have to say, because there isn't that much in this game yet.
Overall, this game shows great promise. I've seen many games that could be called 'Minecraft rip-offs' and while this is a solid contender for the title, it's one of the few that I really want to see grow, expand and earn the right to quash the comparison.
~~ Ideas For The Devs ~~
Just in case the developers are reading this, I had some suggestions for the future. I dunno how many of these are already planned, but take what you will.
1. Pathfinding. While it might be tempting to keep adding more features, I think this should be a priority. A couple of my other suggestions would require better pathfinding.
2. Carriers. I read that you want to do something with the crates to make them more realistic. How about they act like item dumps and other colonists could carry items to a central storage. Think of the carriers from Settlers, for example.
3. Central Storage. Some kind of vault room could be cool. I really like the creative-style collective inventory for the player, but the colonists should have somewhere to ferry items to/from.
4. Auto-Builders. I read that you already plan on adding colonists who can build to a plan. If that's true, nevermind.
5. Happiness. Instead of just adding more zombies or something like that to increase difficulty, some kind of happiness or approval system would be cool. Luxury items, decoration and extra food could all contribute to happiness while cramped housing, shared quarters and working outside (for non-farming jobs) could reduce it. Happy colonists could work faster but unhappy ones could revolt.
6. Pathfinding. See number 1. Sorry. Just really important.
7. Hitboxes. Not being able to place a block because you're standing in the 1m cubed hitbox of the torch, for example, should be fixed. Also being able to place and remove fields without removing the wheat. But that's kinda minor.
8. Area Clearing Tools. These could be a player-only thing. Some kind of axe to chop down a whole tree or clear a 3x3 dirt or stone area would be good. Something to make the manual labour bit a bit less time-consuming.
9. Bed Allocation. After my annoyances with the miner's village being overrun by shopkeepers, I think being able to set beds or areas for certain jobs would be very good; miners bunk together, farmers in their huts, etc.
That's all I got at the moment. I shall update this with more as I think of stuff.

If you have FEAR 1 and are interested in this at all, don't go higher than 90% on
a big steam sale. This is a really sad follow up to the horror FPS masterpiece
that was FEAR 1. The FEAR 1 Expansions, Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate had
their problems, but compared to this, they shine brightly. While FEAR 2 does have
some great horror moments, it's not worth trudging through this entire game to get
to them. IF You really need to, buy it, and then just watch a longplay of this on
Youtube. You'll safe yourself a headache.
Everything about this game feels rushed. It seems like they hired level
designers just for this game, cause the game's Singleplayer maps are beautiful
and detailed. But I got the impression that the mappers didn't really fully
utilize the AI. From my understanding, it's the same AI system, but not properly
used in FEAR 2. In FEAR 1, Enemies would spread out and hunker down, wait for
you, use supressing fire to keep you down, and order their own units in real
time, based on the situation. In FEAR 2, it seems like the AI has a short
attention span. Unable to stay in cover for very long, and throws grenades more
often than I care to count. It doesn't feel as co-hesive as it did in FEAR 1.
FEAR 2 would've been a spectacular expansion to FEAR 1. That's what it feels
like, a well crafted expansion, but its not a true sequel. It's more of a
side-step than anything else. The only thing particularly new that is sequel
worthy, is what it does at the very end. Not gonna spoil it, but I'm just gonna
say it would've been amazing if it was the end of an expansion, leading into
a new game (preferably not the embarrassment that was FEAR 3). I have a hunch
that WB was over Monolith's shoulders saying, hey, lets make the scares bigger
and more hollywood-y, same goes for the action. Heyyy about the action, Let's
have a pilotable mech in the game, cause everyone loves mechs!!
If I'm being really honest, I did like piloting the mech. It was fun, more fun
than the casual shooting on foot. Monolith should've just made a mech game
instead of FEAR 2. There's not enough mech games on the market, but landfill
amounts of generic shooters, ohhh boy we got enough of those.
The difficulty in this game is up and down. It seems as though they wanted to
make combat nonsensically harder for the player, and easier for the AI (almost
as if the AI is playing on their own easy mode the entire run through). Some
more refinement in the gun mechanics, would've made this a true gem. As I
mentioned, the AI isn't all that great, and their armor are stupid bullet sponges.
That's not to say I had trouble with my supplies in ammo, but headshots don't
mean much in this game, unless it's from a sniper rifle or laser rifle. They kinda
do seem to have extra damage, but not by much. I was getting by shooting
them in the leg or arm honestly. I'm not gonna even mention the fact that they
removed the ability to lean, even though the enemies still can, and do quite
often, while blind firing behind cover.
Oh, and don't bother playing this on hard difficulty, I just gave in and switched
to normal. If nothing else than to combat the AI's seemingly perfect aim to your
head (which seems to be more vulnerable than theirs). And to combat the shotguns,
cause they SUCK! They're basically useless, requiring two or three shots on most
enemies, sometimes four or five, even in close quarters. The Auto-Shotgun you get
later on doesn't help matter all that much, turning it into a shotgun rifle, just
save your self the pain and use the Assault Rifle or the SMG. Hammerhead nailgun
is useless, as it requires a stupid amount of bullets to take enemies down. I
never found much use in the flamethrower, since enemies can put the flames out.
The Laser gun is super neat, but it doesn't have much ammo in the game. The Pulse
rifles rip through almost anything, but only seem to have no more than 10 or 20
ammo in the entire run of the game, and there's only a total of two times where
you'd actually need to use it anyway.
The sound is great, the music was okay (most of it was just remixes from FEAR 1), the
graphics are top notch, the scares are well done, the voice acting is kind of up and
down in places, but mostly good. All that effort is kind of wasted when you have
terrible game mechanics, which is pretty sad. If it didn't have the FEAR title in it, it
would've fell off the radar as a generic shooter, represenative of its era in shooters.
On it's own, it's not a bad game. There are some neat moments here and there. But
not worth a full play through.
I'm not gonna even touch FEAR 3, unless it's 90% or higher. Maybe 95%, or 97%. My
review of that will likely be a short nope with a thumbs down.

I may not have many hours into this like the first game, but here we go.
F.E.A.R. 2 is a pretty decent game. Sure, its not the perfect sequel us F.E.A.R. fans expected, but its still fun. Its just that it lost some of the original games charm along the way. How did this happen? Well, heres the kicker: This is supposed to be the console version of F.E.A.R. 2, which had a pc version that would have differed greatly from the console version. Why else do we have such a dudebro storyline and no quicksaving or manual saving?
Anyways, I got a little sidetracked. F.E.A.R. 2 puts you in the role of Micheal Becket, a member of Dark Signal, a sub-squad of F.E.A.R. The mission? Nab Genevieve Aristide, a high ranking member of Armacham. The only problem is that Armacham does not like this, so they send in a WHOLE FRIGGIN BLACK OPS ARMY TO KILL DARK SIGNAL. However, things go awry as the replicas come back in bigger numbers as well, and they have some uprgrades to complement their massive numbers now. Now Micheal must make his way through the city of Fairport, avoiding the war going on between the two armies.
Okay, enough story stuff, since the rest is spoiler heavy. Now, what about the gameplay itself? Well, its like F.E.A.R. 1's, but somewhat dumbed down. We still have slow mo, melee attacks and intense violence and destruction, but something new and...UNFITTING mixes in as well. We have true ADS, a cover system, and a sprinting bar. Along with this, the A.I, legendaryingly known for its many ways to kick your♥♥♥♥♥ has seen a massive reduction in its intelligence, now making them more stupid bots than anything. Weapons seem to be less powerful, and their sounds are just pitiful.
Now you probably think I hate this game. I don't really. Because under the odd additions and weird guns, comes a plot that, once past the dudebro stuff, becomes ♥♥♥♥ing dark and mature as hell, and a combat system that actually picks itself up later on. Your guns become more powerful and actually sound like guns, the enemy variety goes through the roof later on and the locations add a very foreboding and dark feeling to the game. Along with this, and these two save the game entirely, are the school levels and mech suit riding segments. YES, YOU READ ME RIGHT, A ♥♥♥♥ING RIDEABLE MECH SUIT. Tired of dieing to the A.I too easily? HERES A GIANT SELF HEALING PIECE OF DESTRUCTION THAT WILL MAKE YOU ♥♥♥♥ YOUR PANTS WHENEVER YOU MOVE. The aftermentioned school levels are also brilliant, with a killer atmosphere and terrifying spooky moments that WILL make you feel as if as though something will kill you if you don't finish the level.
Overall, this game is worth it, but don't expect the amazing sequel we all craved for back then.

Short Version: Noises and parallax background. Couple of "puzzles". Play it, don't play it... matters little.
Long version: The game's appearance is intriguing, but since it's so short, there is little exploration of potentially interesting environments. The sound design is also interesting -- a nice ambience. Gamplay wise, it comes down to pressing buttons when promted to, like a QTE without time limits. The two only segments that are remotely resemblant to puzzles are accompanied with no hints or instructions of any sort, so you are pretty much left to brute force the solution. Once you've used brute force on the two puzzles (or cheated), the game is over, and leaves you hanging, with no apparent resolution to whatever our little robot wanted.
Also, once the game terminated itself, I could still hear the game sounds playing, the little ambient music...
Verdict: There is some value to playing this, if you want to explore the visual aspect, or the sound design aspect, but otherwise... I'd just play it, and when you stay stuck for more than two minutes, just find the solution online.
Overall for me, this game would be rated 8/10 'Good'.

Since I'm a HUGE fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd, I decided to purchase this game recently. And after a few days, I'm definitely not disappointed.
The game is very reminiscent of many old NES sidescrollers, mainly Mega Man, as it uses the "choose your level" kind of gameplay like Mega Man does. And there's also.. running while shooting a zapper like in Mega Man.. yey. It makes it rather fun to play, while being rather nostalgic at the same time, which is also added on by the 8-bit style of this game. I also like the bit of challenge within the game, as some of the levels do make you think what you need to do, and being careful in general, giving a bit of strategy.
Another thing I like is how it has references to the actual show, with the powerups like the "Glitch Gremlin" and "Super Mecha Death Christ 2000," as well as having some of the characters such as Mike Matei, and even the levels do reference some of the games he's played. Not to mention, some of the things he says within the game and the cutscenes add some decent humor as well.
So, overall, It's a fun game that is definitely a good purchase if your a fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd, or even if you're not a big fan, but you like to play old NES games like Mega Man. Either way, it's still a good purchase.

-The game is based in the future.

-Multiplayer Mode
-Hella long Campaign that lets you play from all three factions.
-Build heavy units that let you rain hell on the enemy! (King Kriptor lmao)
-Smart and responsive AI.
CONS-
-Not many people play this game anymore so it's hard to find a match online.
-Campaign gets boring fast as you continue into the missions.
-Although the game lets you build research stations that lets you grow your research faster, it still takes a long time.

I purchased this game because I'd picked up "The Curious Expedition". I enjoyed TCE, in spite of some harsh flaws, and noted that many reviews mentioned "Renowned Explorers" as being a similar and superior version of the idea. It went on sale, and I took the plunge.
It's a bit prettier if you don't like seeing aliased edges. Looks like vector art to me, coupled with some cut-out style ragdoll animations. I can see how some might find that objectively superior to little blots of pixels that wiggle a little and pop up and down once to indicate a combat action. It wasn't an issue for me.
RE also has a more tactical combat. TCE's combat system is pretty bad: it's simple, heavily random, and leans toward brutal outcomes. I still like it more, because RE's combat isn't even combat. It's a combat system that pretends you're all really just having a row. The outcomes aren't brutal, they're mostly carebear. You win by emotionally overwhelming your opponents. Yes, most of your attacks are either meant to make your opponents feel so bad they run away in tears, or feel so grateful to you for pumping up their ego that they wouldn't dream of interfering.
And you have to deal with their mood. Yes, your strategy changes depending on whether the bad guys are friendly or cranky. Except, it doesn't. Mostly it's just a matter of which type of attack you use most. Sometimes it's the red button. Sometimes it's the blue. Sometimes it's the green. It all depends on which one will break their spirit the most, as determined by what kind of spirit they brought you to break.
There's another couple layers of rock-paper-scissor tacked on, so that there are different buffs/debuffs for different... (*sigh) moods. Yes, the vibe in the air, the interaction of the opponent's emotional state and the emotional state your opponents percieve you have, has a 25-30% influence on some action or another.
There's a small novelty value to the window dressing at first--but only as long as you think of it as quirky window dressing. If you actually think of it as a game where most battles are won by alternately praising and verbally abusing or intimidating your opponents, then suddenly it's somewhere between catty and psychopathy. Do you really want to roleplay as someone who gets what they want through bullying and emotional manipulation? Is that even someone you want to pretend to be? If so, good news! They finally made a game for the pathologically passive aggressive, and this is it!
If, on the other hand, you prefer to pretend to better than you are, or much much worse, this isn't going to cut it. The paladins are going to puke their armor, and villains are likely to be dissappointed at how little damage they get to do, and how shallow the manipulations are. It's not like you're weaving together a detailed conspiracy and watching your puppets dance as you tug their emotions with subtlety from the background. It's more two groups of children shouting on the playground and alternating between "poopy head" and "Hey bae!" with the occasional "I'm gonna bang your mom" for good measure.
Think I'm exaggerating? I don't blame you. But keep in mind most of these emotional attacks also inflict (yes, inflict) emotional states ranging from enthusiastic to enraged to terrified, and most of them also have buffs or debuffs.
Did I mention your party members heal each other by saying nice things to one another? And the battle resolution is never about death or injury, they just run off the field weeping in joy, fear, anger or confusion about all the mixed signals. Basically it's a little too close to how I see people resolve conflicts in real life. Not the sort of realism I was looking for.
Even worse is their boss encounter system. Most encounters are mop up type missions where you keep going untill everyone else has run off in some flavor of tears. Boss encounters continue until the Boss is weeping, sometimes into the shoulder of a consoling henchman. Excuse me, hench-person. They all summon more henchpeople during the fight. That's what makes it a boss encounter. That's the main difficulty lever.
Granted, it does make the combat tougher. It doesn't keep it interesting.
Renowned Explorers does stand above The Curious Expedition in variety of storylines. I saw lots of repetition in the first hour or two of TCE. In three hours of RE, I was still seeing new storylines and events.
However, I think RE might have ruined this niche genre. No, not rogue-likes--this is not a roguelike. That would be like saying tag is like cribbage. This genre is "popularity contest", the realization of which is what has killed my interest.
It's not as obvious in TCE, where your primary means of gaining popularity is returning from adventures abroad with a shipload of treasure and lots of exciting stories to tell. But in RE, where about a third of your resources go to hiring an entourage provide buffs to your income--and you purchase them with 'status'... it's a little too blunt for me.
In TCE, you spent your money on real equipment: rope, climbing gear, torches, food, etc. In Renowned Explorers, you buy accessories to improve your stats. Things like "good boots", "memento", "decent book"--yeah... the paint is really peeling off now. This is a game for your inner middle school mean girl.
I do acknowledge they've corrected my internal misspelling of renowned. I guess that's worth something.

We can take for granted that an early access game will be rough round the edges, and we must be prepared for plenty of quirks and bugs.
However one has to wonder just how far into the development this game is, when core functionality is so fundamentally broken.
Take as an example, when you begin a campaign, besides a extreme stutter, which I will get into shortly, after picking one of just three areas to start in, you will often find yourself with only one build option; rides.
Granted, the intention is of course that different creation options will unlock for you as you progress in the game, however on numerous occasions, besides the rides category, the other options would unlock much later than necessary (that is assuming they ever unlock). Like in the previous Rollercoaster Tycoon games, you need to place rides and shops far enough from the paths to provide space for a substantial length of an entrance queue. After placing a number of rides, you may notice that you have no means of drawing a path to them. What this leads to is hundreds of visitors entering the park after paying the £5 entrance fee, merely to walk back and forth on the small stretch of preset pathway at the entrace, getting increasingly tired and frustrated, and feeling understandably ripped off. To make things worse, if you have opened those rides in the vain hope that these visitors will get off the beaten path and make the trek across the grass to ride the helter skelter (heads up: they won't), soon enough the rides will inevitably break down simply from normal test usage. Nevermind, you can get mechanics on the job because it looks like the Buildings category finally opened up! Oh wait, you can't build a pathway. Right, that's really brought things to a halt.
The interface adds insult to injury when notifications pop up, giving you a series of requests like "hey, it's kinda dark, can you please add some lamps?" or "hey your customers can't get to this ride, can you build a pathway to it?", and "hey, your ride has broken down, can you get your mechanics on it?" - And my response to them all is "I WOULD IF YOU LET ME!".
In spite of this locked interface bug occurring a couple of times for me, I was lucky enough to start a campaign where the interface
function normally, and all the features unlocked for me within a reasonable time, more or less consistently. Besides the slightly cumbersome building/ride rotation mechanic (an 8 way snapping rotation would be preferable), and the fact that the auto rotation assignment (based upon the path you are placing the building next to) works less than half the time, the game actually feels surprisingly functional in spite of those finnicky issues. As for the coaster creation, it is fantastic! I had a blast designing an intricate coaster with ease. However it can be a little tedious to keep testing the ride every time you make a change to ensure that it works. It would be preferable if there were a feature that allowed you to simply test the last segment that you added, rather than the whole ride from the begining.
Indeed, it does not seem to be far-fetched to assume a finished product could be comparable to Cities: Skylines in terms of quality and design. There will undoubtedly need to be a lot more in the way of content, as there is not even close to the amount of building and ride option or design variation compared with the previous Rollercoaster Tycoon games- but of course a lack of content is to be expected in early access.
Perhaps one thing which really leaves a gaping hole, is the lack of in-depth creation. For example, the paths are laid with a line-drawing tool rather than a grid system which prevents creating little patio areas or plazas by hand, forcing you to use the preset ones. I am not sufficiently convinced that this will be changed in future patches or indeed upon the final game's release, because the Tycoon game industry seems to be moving towards this more "accessible" route, at the cost of player's creativity. I noticed this with Thrillville and Zoo Tycoon and other games of this style, but I would love Rollercoaster Tycoon World to prove me wrong and break away from this trend.
I mentioned before that the game was stuttering. Although my PC's hardware is decidedly outdated for this 'generation', the parts exceeded the minimum and recommended specs for the game. For perspective, I can run Cities Skylines on Very High settings with smooth and responsive performance, even when my city spans across 5 regions and is filled with tens of thousands of people. I can also run Grand Theft Auto V at very high settings at around 50FPS. So, I cannot say I was not disappointed that the performance for Rollercoaster Tycoon World is abysmal. The game is not bad looking (though I'd argue not nearly as attractive or impressive as Cities Skylines), it is perhaps the best looking theme park tycoon game, and to be honest, it is a more up-close and personal style of tycoon game, with far more attention to detail than others in the same vein, with a naturally more dynamic environment. When you zoom into your park, you can get a lot closer than many tycoon games usually allow, and you can witness how the branches of palm trees sway in the wind,  a person behind the desk at a ride's entrace with the ride's buttons and controls, and see the little gate swing open for the customers, see kids running with excitement holding the balloons or other souvenirs they bought, etc. I expect that the finished product will look beautiful with just a hint of polish here and there, and perhaps a bit more detail in buildings and shops (most of the shops are identicle besides the large mascot/statue on the top). I would, for example, to see t shirts actually displayed in the window of the t shirt shops, and fridges with drinks actually displayed in the drink stalls, and burgers being made in the burger stalls. I recall the game The Movies by Lionhead allowed you to zoom into a burger stall and see a man actually cooking the individual burgers.... that was over a decade ago, so I am sure that in the $CURRENT_YEAR, it shouldn't be too much to request that the team behind RCTW are able to put at least a similar amount of effort into detail that Lionhead was able to achieve 11 years ago. But sadly, even if they did, that would only make the performance issues worse.
It is already extremely uncomfortable for people who even meet the recommended system requirements, and even more-so when you choose to speed-up time. Freezes, unresponsive UI and generally horrendous stutter are present even on lower graphics settings.
In conclusion, there is a lot that needs to be fixed and improved. I would certainly recommend fanatics of the franchise to get the early access game if they have ridiculously strong hardware, as when the game GUI is not misbehaving, the game shows a lot of promise and it is certainly quite enjoyable. I apologise if most of the review is criticizing rather than praising, but I felt that the negative did outweigh the positive for the most part. So, unless you fall into the category of "fanatic with future-proofed hardware", avoid the game for now but keep your eye on it, as I expect great things to come.

if you are having problems with this game on windows 10, use the windows compatibility troubleshooter.   at first, this game wasn't working for me on windows 10.  I tried all the fixes I could find, and tried changing settings around, and doing all the nonsense required to make incompatible games work.  I gave up on the game and quit trying to fix it, and uninstalled it.  and then a couple weeks ago, I installed it again, twiddling with fixes and settings, running the config thing in compatibility mode, changing the compatibility to XP to run the windows compatibility troubleshooter, which didn't fix anything, but then I changed something else, set the compatibility mode to win 98, tweaked some settings, and used the config thing again that comes with the program.  and then I used the windows compatibility troubleshooter again, and it fixed whatever problems there were along with fixing some of the settings.  windows compatibility thing itself went in and changed some of the settings inside the game itself.  now the game works.  and I have no idea if anything I did resulted in the game working, or if a recently updated windows compatibility troubleshooter was what fixed everything.  the game works for me now, and its great.  windows 10 steam games locations default is C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common.  this game is the swkotor folder, and in there, right click on swkotor.exe / properties / compatibility / "run compatibility troubleshooter".  that properties window there will also show you what it changes things to if you go back there after you run the troubleshooter and close/reopen the properties window.

Battleborn died pretty quickly considering that 2 million people played the Beta. The first month averaged around 4,000 people and that number drastically dropped the following month while these days it averages at around few hundred people. This could be seen as dead on arrival.
I actually bought the game because I liked the Beta. I haven’t played since launch but I had my fun with it. For me it was only fun playing with friends or a group with comms because it is crucial to know where enemies are when to push, rotate, etc. Playing alone with clueless teammates and no teamwork was very frustrating. The games would end very dominantly whether it was us or the enemy team, close games with back and forth were rare.
The heroes are unique in design and abilities, they provide for different playstyles and tactics. There are also some hero combinations that are deadly and unbeatable. There were issues that some heroes were unbalanced in the beginning but that might have been somewhat fixed by now. There is also a single player co-op campaign which I didn’t care for that much but some people liked playing this game against AI.
I think the biggest issue for this game was its release time that battled Overwatch. A ton of people were unjustly comparing it to Overwatch because of similar artstyle and playstyle, while in reality they are completely different genres. The full price also didn’t help. If this game came out later in the year with a $40 price point from the start, it may have done better.
So since this game is pretty much dead I would recommend it only in a specific circumstance. If you want to get it with a group of friends and play together or have a group to play with. Singleplayer co-op is fun and there are still a few hundred people playing multiplayer so you should be able to find matches here and there. If you are by yourself however, don’t bother.

If you want a good on-rails shooter game on Steam, look no further - Blue Estate is the one to get.
Blue Estate is incredibly fun and does exactly what a game of the genre is supposed to do - provide the gamer with action-packed levels where it's all about quickly taking aim and gunning down enemies before they gun you down. And even while the game stays true to the simple premise of on-rails shooter games, it still provides variety within each level, as the player has moments where they can take cover to protect themselves and on other times the only protection they have is being a quick shot. The swipe motions, albeit not being anything too game-changing, does add an extra layer to the gameplay, but even more so are the special in-game moments like Shoot-a-mole or Showdown, where the player has to do something in specific like take enemies down in a specific order or pay attention to quickly shoot an enemy as he comes out of hiding.
The story is completely packed with humor in a way that it doesn't feel cheap - it's not mindless jokes thrown around randomlessly, it's actual humor included within the game's story, both when it comes to character dialogue and certain funny moments during each level.
Couch coop is, gladly, included - two players can play together with a keyboard, mouse and/or controller... And even a light gun, for those who do own one.
The only thing I don't like about the game is how they set the weapon change command to double clicking the right mouse button and it can't be changed, which can be a problem sometimes as a single right click is the command for reloading. Would be a lot better if I could just reload with R and change weapons with a single right click instead. Still, it's just a matter of getting used to it.

Loving the game so far. I played it all day with my little brother yesterday. Thanks for the hard work.  Some things I would like to see include: More monster variation to challenge different defense setups.  I put it on double monsters and night/day monsters) before I got a sense of challenge, so more guys like flyers, ranged mobs, or the spiders from minecraft would be cool, aoe ranged bombers, fire, and maybe a few random bosses appearing once the colony hits x size. More options for food would also be great. Apple trees that give food and wood when harvested for example, mercenaries you can buy at shop that shoot faster, live longer, etc. I can also see player built siege weapons or traps being really fun. flinging a fireball into a crowd of zombies that just pushed through a door (another thing I'd really like to see) would be immensely satisfying. I mentioned traps. I dont need anything too extravagent, a spike trap that needs reset, and bundle of logs coming down with a switch, a floodgate to swamp your ditch around the base with fire or water for x seconds, these would be cool.
Anyway, I know my review mostly consists of suggestions so let's give some recommendations. The gameplay is smooth and I didn't run into any obvious bugs. I wish hosting a multiplayer server didn't require me going out of the game and navigating to the .exe in steamapp/common. Watching your loyal guards shoot down hordes of zombies feels great, but I feel bad for them since they don't seem to need sleep like their buddies, so a rotating shift would be cool. Building is fun and easy and should remind people of minecraft, minus some of the more complicated additions. As I mentioned above there are a lack of food options to choose from and the shop doesn't feel as great as I thought it would be considering how much effort you need to get it going, so I wish I had more cool things that I could buy there to kill zombies.
Thanks for the game and I'm looking forward to additional updates!

In short: reasonable idea, was not executed well, somewhat in the "so-bad-its-good" category.

This game is a great followup to one of the best RTS games ever made (absolutely no bias). To people who like Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance, this game is recognizable to the previous game, but takes a number of liberties, which distinguish it from the original, but not nesesarily for the better. These changes include the removal of the Teir system in favor of a research tree (similar in a way to Civilization), the nerfing of Expirimental Units, and the removal of the resource-stream in favor of a more traditional stockpile system. These changes may rub the wrong way with diehard fans of the original (understandably), but they all work together to make a cohesive game, with nothing really feeling left out.
. If anything is really better because of these changes, it is the accessability of the game.
, and ends up forming a cohesive, understandable, and much more simple whole.

Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is at base a typical "very hard" platformer, not nearly hard enough to qualify as Platform Hell (I was able to beat three levels without trouble, and got most of the way through a fourth). It has standard indie-pixel graphics (which is to say, visually appealing, but much more pixelized than actual 8-bit games were). The controls are pretty solid, there are multiple characters you can rescue and then switch between mid-level, and a decent number of powerups and items.
The connection to the AVGN consists primarily of references; while there's not actually that much original humor in the game, there are plenty of times you'll be able to say "oh, yeah, I remember the episode where the Nerd made that joke." The game does contain the Nerd's trademark profanity (throughout the game's dialogue and randomly generated phrases upon death). It doesn't, however, contain much for the Nerd to really complain about; you'll die constantly, but still end up making steady forward progress.
Most of the game's difficulty comes from a single source: death blocks. Touch a death block and it's instant death, like the spikes in Mega Man. These things are EVERYWHERE -- lining the bottom of pits, lining the ceiling of hallways, in vertical rows you have to springboard over, in horizontal rows you have to ride conveyances over. Some of them just flat-out block the way, and fade in and out of existence; you have to dash from safe spot to safe spot while they're gone. Timing this @#$@ is absolutely vital.
So I can recommend this game as a standard hard platformer that'll take most good players 1-2 weeks to finish. If you aren't confident in your platforming skills this is NOT the place to try and hone them. You don't have to be familiar with the Nerd's oeuvre to understand it, but it'll seem pretty random and surreal if you aren't.
Warning: One level in particular, the one based on the Nerd's "Atari Porn" review episode, is absolutely nauseating. Seriously, at certain points I honestly felt like I was going to throw up. Play that level on an empty stomach or you may react to it the way the Nerd reacted to E.T. II in the movie.

This game got so many things right. I haven't found another RPG that keeps my attention through the full game. The story is fantastic. Some mechanics, such as the follower influence system, don't get fully fleshed out until the sequel, but the character developing process really drives the game. You get the feeling by the end of the game that your character is extremely and satisfyingly powerful, but the game never lets up in terms of difficulty.

I'm just amazed with how well this game has aged. All the characters are fleshed out and layered, the decisions and choices you make in the main story truly make you feel the magnitude of your actions, and each planet is so detailed and has its own unique environment. Also, the side quests are phenomenal and I think people are doing themselve a disservice if they're just playing the main story. The side quests really help with the character development and they showcase the unique characteristics of each world (that Trial side quest in Manaan and Swoop races were my favorite). I also can't get over the amount of hours it must have taken to record all the voices and have only a third of that dialogue come out the first time you play it.
Aside from graphics (which was never a priority for me), the only thing that show the game's age was the clunky items menu. Other aspects of the game that annoyed me included your characters maxing out at Level 20, the ineptitude of the friendly-AI when you don't control them, and the amount of backtracking that you'd have to do. But those nuisances don't deter from the game's overall experience.

KOTOR has perhaps the best written storyline of any video game that I've come across. I first played this title on the original xbox when I was just a kid. A BioWare classic if there ever was one. Plus, it has one of the best plot twists in all of gaming. The game is a bit old and the graphics sho it, but evrything else is there and it feels great. Every character has flaws and weaknesses, even your stalwart Jedi masters. There is no cosmic imperative, pushing you towards being a good guy; you can still 'save' the galaxy from the bad guys, and be as evil as you want. BioWare lets you choose how your reputation and personality grow, and they do it better than every other RPG making company out there. KOTOR has everything you want in an RPG, plus Star Wars. If you like Star Wars, you'll like this, if you like BioWare games or RPGs in general, you'll like this. This game lets you be a Jedi, a gunslinger, a Sith, or anything in between, and it does it in style. Some of the game mechanics will seem outdated, and some of them are, but it still doesn't leave you wanting more from how the game handle's. There's a lot of fun to be had in this game, and many different ways to go about it.
(Also, the fact that Fallout 4 exists but Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic 3 doesn't, is like, half of what I hate about the gaming imndustry's current climate.)

Since it's release on March 30th, RCT World has been getting eleven updates. Each update added some content, fixed some bugs, improved the game piece by piece. Workshop integration sort of works without issues now, and a blueprint/piece by piece mode, just as in planet coaster (but without the annoying♥♥♥♥♥denuvo) has been added. While Planet Coaster still has a bit more to offer than RCTW, RCTW doesn't use Denuvo, so that's already a bigger plus than any content PC has to offer. And since frontier develops it, I doubt there will be any more support after the final release of the game. Maybe in DLCs. Keep an eye out for RCTW, because it's slowly becoming more and more of a real RCT title.
RCTW is developing more and more, some progress has certainly been made in the past few weeks. Almost 2 months have passed since the originial release of RCTW and the game has been improved a lot from its original state. The devs make use of the bugtracker and have fixed most of the more severe and some small bugs the users have been complaining about whilist still adding new features and improving the overall game experience, which is reflected in the community and the content the users have created. It will still take a while for RCTW to become a solid game, but it gets closer with every update. As of now I will still put a "No" recommendation on it, as it is not completely worth its money yet.
RCTW got rushed into early access before it was supposed to, as retailers sold the game before it's release. Thus the current state of the game is rather terrible. It has a bunch of bugs, some more severe than others, workshop integration isn't fully functioning and the performance is rather bad.
RCTW adds a lot of new features to the RCT series though. More customization, more user generated content, more park management. The coaster editor now features a node based building system, similar to the one seen in NoLimits, which allows the user to create coasters with more freedom than ever. Of course the "Piece by piece" system still exists. Curved paths and grid-less scenario placing allow the player to put more detail into their parks and staff now requires buildings to "rest" in.
However, the worst thing about RCTW as of now is it's community. People expected the game to be complete and a fully functional successor of the RCT franchise. Of course they got disappointed when the earlier-than-early access version turned out to be.. not so great.
Unless you absolutely want it, I'd recommend you to wait and watch the game develop.

This is probably one of the more tragic releases in gaming... This game, is actually more of a middle child. From a risky release date, and being placed in between MOBAS and the Hero Shooter genre's (Overwatch), Battleborn has been put in the wrong place in peoples minds. Battleborn is a 5 player pve, pvp experiance, it's got some fantastic and quick humor by most of the characters in the campaign, and even in the multplayer too. Along with interesting humor, this game has unique mechanics, allowing you to play your character differently from everyone else. You can augment your character through the helix system, allowing 2-sometimes 3 different options to augment your primary abilties and then your ultimate. There's an item system in place, allowing further customisation. Most items are simliar, but can offer vastly different effects to aid your hero, either in pvp or pve. Being able to go into your character and play the way that suits you, and can augment the abilties further through the helix and items is like no other. It's amazing. Characters are fun and fluid, gameplay is fast paced and sometimes hilarious, and overall it would just be a pleasant experiance. If you desire something fun and fast paced with unique characters, please please play this game. It would greatly benefit actually trying the game and spreading how much fun it is, versus telling everyone it's an Overwatch ripoff.

One of my favorite F.E.A.R. games, F.E.A.R. 2 Project Origin is, to me, the perfect sequel.  The game begins thirty minutes before the Origin Facility explodes in F.E.A.R. while your team of Delta Force, not F.E.A.R., are on a routine hostage protection mission.  So the game begins with you and your teammates all in an APC as Delta Force as you go to Genevieve Aristeads private penthouse to take her into protective custody.  However, you aren't the first ones to make it there, as an ATC Black OPS team is there, killing civilians as they too try to capture Aristead.  After the facility explosion, you go to a hospital, which is actually a Replica training facility.  In the hospital, you can hear, and see ATC killing the staff there.  A couple of the doctors you see have a green target recital when you aim at them, but you can't kill the guy who kills them first sadly.  As you proceed through the game, you arrive at an Elementary School after you battle through a destroyed urban street.  I'll be the first to say, that after I played F.E.A.R. Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate, Fairport is a lot more destroyed than in those two games.  Anyway, at the Elementary, (which was praised for being very atmospheric.) you are going to be battling Replicas and ATC Forces as you look for the nurses office.  In the school, the developers added in this cool little cartoon with music and an announcer and animation on a TV screen in the school that looks like a Dr. Seuss cartoon.  It's not in a cutscene either.  OK, I think I made my point about what F.E.A.R. 2 is like so I'll explain on why it's my favorite.  I love this game because, well, it's just a really good game and I started playing it on my PS3 at a hard time in my life and this game really connected with me.
Before I go, I'll talk a little about the multiplayer.  While I'm pretty sure Online is down, you can still play over a LAN network, which is OK.  There are a variety of game modes, such as a traditional Team Death Match and Free For All, but there is also an interesting Capture the Flag mode.  In this games CTF, (Blitz) one team has two flags that the other team is trying to capture.  After one round, the teams switch sides so attackers are now defenders.  A nice little twist I think.  Many of the game modes are from or similar too Call of Dutys modes, such as a Search and Destroy mode.  In this games version of Search and Destroy (Failsafe), as far as I know, only one team attacks and one team defends.  The attacker team can also drop the bomb, which is handy if you don't want it or an ally wants it.  There is also no respawns.  They have a domination mode like in Call of Duty, but in this mode, both teams have A and C (1 and 3) already captured for their side.  The last unique mode I'll talk about, aside from Slow_Mo Death Match, is called Armor Front.  This is like the game mode War from Call of Duty 3 and World at War.  In Armor Front, both teams have to capture five control points.  However, control point 1 and 5 has a big machine gun in a protective position for your team to use once that area has been captured and is on your side (you can't take your enemies gun).  Control point 2 and 4 has a large EPA or Elite Power Armor for one of your team mates to drive around as the rest of you protect it and attempt to destroy your enemies EPA.  The turret is useful to help try to destroy it, but it is set up so it can only defend its control point.  Also, for multiplayer, you get all the DLC maps free, something the PS3 doesn't do.  Armor Front maps are also unique for that game mode only.
If you have ever played Call of Duty, the controls on controller are similar.  When you look at ally soldiers, a similar thing from Call of Duty shows up, you see their name and their rank logo, and you can't fire on any friendly characters.  I would recommend this game to anyone who likes horror or if you have a few friends, multiplayer.  I would also recommend all of the F.E.A.R. games, even Reborn, this games DLC campaign.  In fact, while the game improved on almost everything (gameplay, scares, atmosphere, ai, weapons) the game is downgraded on the lighting.  There is no dynamic lighting which means only rearely will you see shadows, but this could just be my PC.
