I think the thing I found most interesting about this game is how split the community is on it - roughly half thinks it's a solid improvement on the first while the other rough half thinks it took a step down and just wasn't very good. I happen to fit into the latter category. Allow me to explain.
This is my second F.E.A.R. experience (3 came first with my brother and then I played 1 after this), and I have to say, I enjoyed the first one more than this. The biggest reason to me is that it just doesn't look appealing. The first was crisp and clean in it's settings, effects, and carnage. This one just looked kinda like a blur most of the time - not necessarily that the textures were muddy, just that it all looked fuzzy. I also wasn't very impressed with the enemy AI - it felt like they didn't work together as well as in the first, but it may have just been me. The weapons and gunplay were about as solid as in the first (except for the shotgun. It went from shotfun in the first to "I'll pass, thanks") and you got to pilot a mech several times (best sections in the game, honestly lol).
Much like with the first (I reviewed it first lol), I came hoping for a solid horror FPS experience... But it's just not scary by today's standards. Granted, Alma got me pretty good once or twice, but those were jumpscares. Still no tension or dread - just lots of gore (which I have no problem with, don't get me wrong) and Alma skulking around/attacking yo♥♥♥♥♥
The story was still fair and further deepened the notion that Alma is a ridiculously tragic antagonist. Unfortunately, I still can't recommend it unless you're suuuper invested in Alma's story and enjoy following the follow ups of milestone games.

You are the leader of a plucky team of wayward adventurers, exploring the world in the name of... profit, science, or simply fame, the choice is yours. Diplomacy and trickery can be your weapons, or you can achieve victory through your honest and cheerful demeanor, but as a last resort shooting everything that moves is always an option.
A wide variety of tintin-esque action-serial adventures await you on the far flung reaches of the globe, but the clock is ticking and you have to balance resource constraints against your limited time, and weigh risky but profitable ventures against safer alternatives. Success means the cherished Adventurer of the Year trophy, failure, and you are but a side-note in the annals of history.
The production values are very high, the cast of characters rich and diverse, the missions plentiful and entertaining, and the combat system well rounded. Frankly, there's not much about this game I don't like.
What makes this game great:
* relatively short playthroughs, with huge replay value
* progression doesn't depend on how many mobs you kill
* just the right amount of randomization to keep things fresh
* nails the victorian-steampunk-explorer vibe
* chill soundtrack
What's holding it back:
* another dlc pack with more expeditions would be awesome
* lacks internationalization (but if you can read this you likely don't care)

Summary: Excellent game, with interesting gameplay mechanics, great graphics and sound, that is marred only by its failure to deliver enough content, or a truly random system of adventure generation to extend game play indefinitely.  8/10
Renowned Explorers is a phenomenal game that I'd highly recommend to anyone, though there are some issues with it.
The game has a very fun gameplay style which emphasizes personal preference and choice for playing the game.  There's no right way to play it, and any play style is rewarding and fun.  There's quite a bit of depth to the encounter system where you have to carefully manage the mood of your party, your enemies, as well as the general mood of the encounter.
The character system is well done, using a simple ability 'tree' to decide how to customize your characters as they gain experience, as well as a very pen and paper feeling perk system to highlight the skills of your characters.  Unfortunately, for me at least, the character system can feel a little shallow, with few choices and levels, each character has a very limited spread of paths they can take.  Some people would likely argue that the simplicity makes it more appealing, but I've always prefered more depth and complexity to games.
The campaign is fun, and relatively short (a few hours to beat it).  Much of the premise of the game revolves around the idea of the game being highly replayable, and while superficially it appears to be, after a number of plays, I find that the game begins to grow stale.  In terms of content, there are only 11 expeditions in the base game, 3 of which are mutually exclusive (you play the one that is most suited to your team's playstyle as the first expedition, the others can never be chosen), leaving you with only 8 choices for the rest of the game.  Within each expedition, there's quite a bit of variety, and no single expedition ever takes the same path, but they always reach the same destination.  Once you've played an expedition once, you always know how it will end and this takes away a lot of the fun of exploring.  After a few campaign playthroughs, its likely that you've played every expedition multiple times and have seen most, if not all, of the optional events within.
The campaign also offers a marathon mode, which allows you to continue exploring with your team, until you've completed every expedition, however the level cap is usually reached after 5, leading to no additional character progression, beyond events within expeditions.
Overall the game is excellent, and very worth the price.  Unfortunately it is lacking in content, which takes away from its 'endless adventures' premise.  The devs have released one expansion pack as of this review, with 2 new expeditions, and other is due in a few weeks with a 3rd new expedition, but I do not believe that a few new expeditions are going to be enough to improve the long term gameplay enough.  I would like to see them add additional variation to each expedition, allowing the random generator to also randomly generate the goal of the expedition, and add in a number of new goals and treasures to that end.  It would go a long way to improve the general randomness and unpredictability of the game, and greatly extend the game's lifespan, in my opinion.

This is probably one of the more tragic releases in gaming... This game, is actually more of a middle child. Battleborn is a 5 player pve, pvp experiance, it's got some fantastic and quick humor by most of the characters in the campaign, and even in the multplayer too. Along with interesting humor, this game has unique mechanics, allowing you to play your character differently from everyone else. You can augment your character through the helix system, allowing 2-sometimes 3 different options to augment your primary abilties and then your ultimate. There's an item system in place, allowing further customisation. Most items are simliar, but can offer vastly different effects to aid your hero, either in pvp or pve. Being able to go into your character and play the way that suits you, and can augment the abilties further through the helix and items is like no other. It's amazing. Characters are fun and fluid, gameplay is fast paced and sometimes hilarious, and overall it would just be a pleasant experiance. If you desire something fun and fast paced with unique characters, please please play this game. It would greatly benefit actually trying the game and spreading how much fun it is, versus telling everyone it's an Overwatch ripoff.

I figured I would give Retention a chance, just to see if the negative reviews are justified. In my opinion, the game doesn't warrant such bad reviews at all. It was an overall pleasant experience for me, somewhat like a more artistically experimental form of the visual novel. Call it a "Visual Photoalbum". All you know, is that your character has been injured with the last moments of their life rushing through their head--in the form of still photography. You get to choose specifically which photos to look more closely at, which in turn reveal a little more about the protagonist's past and state of mind.
Let me just say, the over 200+ photos that are included in the game are gorgeous to look at, and very thought-provoking. Commentary on the photographs themselves are very cryptic and limited, allowing you the freedom to ruminate on the meaning for yourself. It makes the game feel very personal. Will you choose to remember love? Friendships? Color? Beauty? Or will it all be forgotten in a haze. The music adds an interesting touch to the game as well.
There is replay value, if you want to be able to view all the individual pictures (it's worth it in my opinion). There are also multiple "endings" (the game automatically "ends" after 10 minutes), but this game isn't so much about getting to end but rather everything that leads up to that. Death and the afterlife have been explored in video games before, but I have never played a game which focuses solely on the remaining few minutes of life itself. It really makes you wonder, what will you recall in your own last moments? Do your memories really make you who you are?

This was clearly watered down to appeal to the modern military FPS audience. Some great things still remain like the melee combat (though still completely useless and impractical), the story revolving around the tortured character Alma (accompanied by a shocking ending), and a good cast of characters with good voice acting.
Replacing the data files and phone messages with text logs really broke the flow and immersion.
On its own its a decent shooter, but coming from Fear 1 i was very underwhelmed.

Very impressed with this so far. It's by the same studio that made Reus, and there are some familiar elements, unsure to what extent it takes the "you need to have the wiki open to play this" style that Reus had but I can say it's not zero. As far as this niche of fire emblemy rougelites goes, this looks like it might be the best of them.
Edit: After playing a lot more, I'm happy to recommend this as an excellent rougelike. Once you know the game pretty well the mechanics come together in a very coherent package, and many of the elements that make this genre work for me are present:
-Really encourages greed. The map is basically the same as FTL, except rather than just being stuck when you run out of fuel, you can keep moving but acquire a temporary debuff each move. Since there's always a boss at the end of each area, acquire too many of these debuffs and the boss will mulch you... but so many shinies! There are similar opportunities to be greedy in all the other scopes of gameplay.
-Adaptively set your own difficulty. Relating to the above, the basic goal of the game is actually pretty simple (get 2.5k points in 5 runs). Then the game gives you a subtle "but what if you got 10k points???" and thus you get to balance maximizing your score while not getting completely stomped because greed.
-Diverse playstyles. I've got a main team, and quite a few ideas I want to try. There's a big aspect of building team compositions, and most of them are viable depending on how greedy you are.
-RNG that creates variety but doesn't usually screw you. In terms of procedural generation, it makes the maps unique but all the things you'd want to prepare for are guaranteed and obvious in advance. The dice rolls can mostly be bypassed, and don't kill you outright so much as make combat harder (and you're gonna do that to yourself anyway).
-Informed decisions. Play for 5 minutes and you'll see what I mean.
-Nuanced combat. Sure early on you can just oneshot everything, but once you start getting greedy you'll have to find depth in the combat, and there's a lot of it. It's fire emblem except you can control enemy aggro, and have several emotion systems to leverage to win a 3v10.
So yeah, if you're into this sort of roguelike, pick this up. It's not meant to be played determined to get the highest possible score every time, but if you like making a vague plan and then seeing what you can accomplish in each run, RE:IS is the best of these I've seen.

After 6 hours of playing I'm ready to review Colony Survival.
Let's start with the pros-
-While textures are blocky, they are not perfect cubes and have a nice 3d effect
-Visually really good- god rays, depth of field, etc
-Easy to pick up and start playing
-Active developer (too many indie games don't have this!)
Now let's go with the cons-
-After building a base and making sure your colony will not starve, there is not much to do (as of 7/6/17)
-Only 1 enemy type (zombies)
-Not very many building materials
-No animals
-a $20 price tag for about 10 or so hours of gameplay before you "beat" the game
-after getting everything set up there is basically nothing for the player to do except add more colonists, but at a point that gets pointless and boring.
Some things that would be nice in future updates-
-animals (part of the dev's roadmap)
-a "happiness" system (have to keep your colonists happy)
-more building materials
-enemy variance (stronger enemies and enemies that look different)
-more crafting in general
-different gendered colonists (as of 7/6/17 only male colonists)
-a reason to explore (i.e. certain materials found in only certain parts of the world) (also part of the dev's roadmap)
-armor for colonists (also if the happiness system gets implemented it would be cool if the colonists started in rags and you had to make clothes for them.) {otherwise they would be unhappy}
-different weapons for colonists (i.e. swords)
-traps for enemies (i.e. spike pits)
-draw bridges
-other colonies that you could run a caravan to and trade with
All of that being said, I highly recommend this game, and I look foward to future updates.

Updating my review to reflect its current status.
Originally i had a negative review going, since i bought the game on release day and it was a buggy, glitchy, broken and unblanaced mess. Missing basic features (such as having units being visible behind structures), problems taken over from the older games and simply being unfinished and untested.
The team worked long on fixing the issues and i have to take notice of that and be fair with updating my review to reflect that.
Many issues have been fixed, the game got many additions that i think are good.
However, although i rate it positive here, take it as a more neutral rating.
The company behind the game is unable to put DLC out in a good way that is beneficial to the customer. I am ok with having new factions in a DLC with the atatched campaigns.
What i am not ok with are DLC features that are mechanics, options or quality of life improvements.
Which sadly is the case.
Next to that, there are still many things missing that were already named in an earlier review and often enough by people on the forums.
Such as more players, larger maps, a working map editor, shared faction control (many players controlling the same faction) and other things.
All of them were already availabe in earlier iterations of the series.
In the end, this game feels like a lighter version of the classic Cossacks, with graphical "improvements". "Improvements" because this only applies to stuff like resolutionsupport, modern texture quality and lighting.
What is worse are things like reload animations, drummer animations and sounds etc.
All of that is very dumbed down in presentation, which was better in the older games.
So when you are ok to have a modern version of the first Cossacks but with less options and features and dumbed down presentationquality, go for it.
Thats not nessecarily a problem. Thats because the game receives frequent updates and additions and therefor this lack of options and other problems are (or can be) temporary.
But keep in mind, that at this time and date, there are still things missing, the DLC policy of this company isnt very customer friendly, but its a better looking and modernized version that receives more attention and develops.

(Disclaimer, my first review. I feel passionately about how this game could be / could have been vs how it is, so I felt moved to actually leave a review for once. The review has been updated, the old one is after the TL;DR)
Wow. What can I say? I put up a review on the 21st of September explaining how the game had so much potential, but was yet to be realised (as you can see below), mainly due to all the bugs. At the time of writing, the 23rd of September, there have been (to my knowledge) 5 different patches, some with notes, some without, but 5 nonetheless. I haven't seen a company be this responsive to feedback in such a long time, and it really is amazing to see. I bought the game again and went back into it, just decided to play the campaigns, when it occured to me that the typos had gone, the glitches were not anywhere near as apparent. Still there in places, for example the first mission of the Dawn of the French Fleet campaign bugged, because at one point I had to repel an invasion, I did, and it didn't continue, maybe something for the devs to pick up on, not sure if I was dumb and misinterpreted or if that's a genuine bug or not.
Secondly, multiplayer has been established and it is surprisingly popular. The chat system works and is very used, mostly by people talking in cyrillic (I think that's what it is, someone in chat told me thats what it was anyway :P) so I don't understand them, but english is fairly common as well. I was so hyped about this game, having practically grown up facing off against my dad as England while I played as Algeria, spamming the crap out of my jannissaries and rushing him down before he could establish his base, but some times I would be too slow and he would crush the attack with his defenses, and lead a cavalry charge of mercenary cossacks directly into the heart of my base, wiping out all my peasants and leaving me helpless.
This game, Cossacks 3, is not a sequel. It should not be labelled as a sequel, and it definitely shouldn't have taken this long to release for what it is. It is a HD, 3D, re-textured version of Back To War, which is fantastic, apart from the fact it lacks a significant number of features that we love about Back To War. For a start, upon the time of writing, the multiplayer functionality of the game is non-existant, the servers haven't been set up. But, as a game released mere hours ago, this can be forgiven and overlooked, mainly as it will be rectified soon, I expect.
A big issue for me is the typos / grammar errors. It's picky and pedantic, but when your senior advisor for military informs you that your peasants are now prodiving you with food, the double-take kinda kills the immersion for me, that I am a commander and I lead my armies to victory. Again, picky and pedantic, and hopefully rectified soon.
As for actual game play, it is a mechanical twin of Cossacks: Back To War. Same infinite resource gathering, same method of spending, same kind of firing mechanics (using coal and iron), except for cannons now also require gold to fire, which I believe is new. Anyway, there are still formations that require drummers and officers etc., still cavalry that you can use to flank, or cavalry that you use to charge, so on and so forth. The campaigns are new, which is refreshing, the storylines are different and unique to one another. My only issue is that they are -exceedingly-, maybe even excessively difficult, even at "Normal" difficulty (which, by the way, is the easiest of the 4, ranging from "normal" to "impossible"... they aren't kidding). Maybe it's just my playstyle, maybe the campaigns are designed to be challenging from level 1, see if other people comment on the campaign and see if they share my thoughts.
I also feel like the games take a -lot- longer to get going than the old ones did, so if that appeals to you then by all means, just again, personal preference.
If you were to ask me "Do you think that Cossacks lived up to your expectations?" The answer would be an easy, immediate "No.". If, however, you were to ask me "Do you think the new Cossacks is a good remake of the old one?" Absolutely, it is almost identical, with very good graphics, with good running even on my average PC, comment / pm / whatever it is if you want my specs.
If you were to ask me "Should I buy it?" I would say no, not yet. Leave it a while to see how much attention it gets from the devs, watch the space for any updates, bug fixes etc. I bought the deluxe edition as soon as it was available and I've requested a refund. Not because the game is bad, not at all, but I would rather watch the game to see if it gets much attention.
TL;DR -> The game is exactly like the old one, should not be called a sequel. Runs very well with good graphics, but still very buggy as if a development version. Don't buy yet, wait, and watch for updates and see how much attention it gets.

Interesting experience! I was interested to see what was changed compared to the first game, and although it's still the same style, it felt different. One thing I'll say off the bat is that the animations weren't all that impressive as they tend to bug out when performing an action straight after sprinting for example, or a complete lack of a motion for sprinting, the gun is just stationary in a tilted position. So although the animations weren't great, I didn't really mind it as I'm not one for animations or graphics really, just nescessary to include in my review to let others know. The removal of the tilt feature was unescessary hoenstly, but the addition of the ability to knock over objects for defense was quite cool, and I saw enemies do that mroe often and found out that it wasn't a scripted sequence in the first game. There weren't that many guns in this game, and there were standard guns and guns brought back from the first game, but they were pretty cool and creative, and I'm glad they introduced a sniper rifle, love just poppin' heads with it, very satisfying, as there's allot more gore in this game compared to the first one, although it doesn't make much sense that their body gets completely blown apart with a shotgun at close range, but it's entertaining. Again, not really much fear in this game either, only got one mini jump, that's it. And this is mostly due to the fact that the atmosphere, combined witht he lack of scary sound when these events occur, overall makes it predictable and not scary. As for the plot, I actually really enjoyed it, as well as the plot twist at the end, was worth playing the whole way through. You also get to find out more about Alma in this game, and there's alllot of intel to read about as you gather it up throughout missions. There's more tactical enviornments in this game as well, and I'll admit this game is definately allot easier than the first game as the armor completely negates the damage taken from enemies, which makes you unkillable in allot of circumstances if you play smart. Only had to use a medkit a few times throughout the game. The game however, does indedd get allot more challenging as the missions progress which is awesome. I wish there was more oppertunity to use the special/heavy weapons, as I saved ammo in 2 of the special weapons all the way to the end of the game, which wasn't really worth it, as there wasn't a boss fight for the ending. The enviornemts are now less linear, with more exploration to be made to find intel and such, which is nice, but it's still drawn out not offering much replay value. I felt as if the enemies were allot less tougher in this game as they died more quickly at the beggining, but as I said, it gets more challenging as you progress. Overall, same with the first game, I enjoyed it! Wheather you'll like it or not is for you to decide.

I'm re-reviewing this because I feel like I didn't gush enough about it before. I'll let my playtime speak for itself. I'll also preface this with one very important thing:
It's like a way more colourful and slightly less 2d darkest dungeon and it will probably feel very familiar.
So what kind of game is Renowned Explorer? It describes itself as a rogue-like, but that's not strictly true. It's not a classic rogue-like, and arguably it doesnt really
like one. The game is split into three distinct modes, the expeditions themselves, combat during them and preparing for your next expedition. Combat is self-explanatory, pitting your team of explorers against many fantastic enemies. From angry Scotsmen in the highlands, to Voodoo Pirates in the Carribean, to.. well, some of the more incredible fights are actually best left to discover for yourself. Let's say you may be uncovering the truth about a few famous myths and legends!
There's three (and a half) currencies you earn throughout the game, each giving you some sort of boon when you spend them in between expeditions. Gold buys you items, either plain old armor and weapons or little trinkets which benefit your explorers in some way. Status buys you friends, either generic helpers who can make it so you earn even more money/status or ones that can do stuff a bit more unique. Research acts much like skill trees in any other game, in simple terms. You unlock a tree and then spend exponentially increasing amounts of research to improve it. The game does a really good job of explaining it so don't worry if that doesn't make sense.
Expeditions feel a lot like a choose your own adventure campaign, I'd honestly liken it to dealing with encounters in DnD. The map is split up into nodes and each one will (usually) have something on it. Sometimes your team stumbles upon a bunch of gold coins. Sometimes you come up against angry scorpions. Sometimes your team has a bit more of a choice.
As an example (and I'll spoilertag the end bit because it's really one of the best moments in the game when you find it - and actually its in one of the DLCs anyway which as an aside YOU REALLY SHOULD BUY): At one point in the game you find yourself face to face with someone blocking your path down a mountain. He insists that you must beat him in some ancient game. You can face off against him fairly, and having someone who knows tactics will do well. You could cheat, but, is cheating on an ancient boardgame really ever a good idea? OR:
. I'm spoilertagging that because it's a hidden choice, and the game is full of them. There are often points where it seems like you'll never be able to get past this normally and you're resigned to your fate, until you go there with a certain explorer...
Difficulty wise? It's hard, but it's not frustrating.. most of the time. It can be a bit annoying when you wipe to an encounter you really should have prepped better for, but since a full game takes about 1 to 2 hours, its no big loss. If you love achievements, there are a ton in this game. You only need to beat the game on the hardest mode with every single explorer for a captain!
And lets take that to talk about the characters. God, every single one of them is so fun and unique and full of charm. Each has their own upsides and downsides and, with the More to Explore dlc, their own campfire story which gives them a little bit more characterization than you'd normally get. It's hard not to feel your heart melt when you see your other two party members cheer on Emilia, the shy botanist from Poland, as she finds a super rare flower that she's been looking for forever.
Seriously, not only are the characters each unique and charming, they're also diverse. Honestly, how many games can you name featuring a main character from Ghana? Kwame is a diplomat hailing from an Ashanti tribe and he fits in perfectly with the rest of the cast. Bia is a freedom fighter from Greece. Kiwi came to the society from Samoa, making her own damn boat to sail to Australia and then on to London! The Emperor's Challenge DLC adds Phaillin, a deceptively charming speaker from Thailand and Suh Min-Jeong, the very young Korean scientist. I think you get the idea. Abbey Games should be commended for creating such a diverse and interesting cast! (well, there's no explicitly gay character yet.. although the charming Maria gets a campfire story that causes another crew member of any gender to fall in love with her- although she'll reject a female crew member saying she's 'out of that phase' now, which isnt great but its something at least)
In closing, I really really recommend this game. If any single bit of it looks interesting to you, you should buy it. Right now, it's 60% off which is an absolute steal in my eyes. Please buy this game.

A game about 19th-century globetrotting exploration ("rogue-like" in the sense that it has procedural content and optional permadeath, but it's not particularly hard to survive to the end). There's three main facets to this game:
First, there's a series of text-based events describing the people, places, and artifacts you encounter on your expeditions. You can make choices about how to respond, with the skills and personality traits of your crew unlocking extra options or providing bonuses.
Second, there's grid-based tactical combat. They've got a medium-weight combat system where each character has 3 basic moves and learns more specialized techniques as they level up. You can defeat opponents by beating them up, or by breaking their spirit with taunts and insults, or by winning them over with compliments and friendly banter. The moves you choose to use change your party's overall attitude, which can provide combat bonuses or penalties, influence enemy tactics, and change your rewards for the encounter.
Third, there's a resource management system. As you journey, you collect gold, fame, and research that can be used to upgrade your equipment, recruit an encourage, and research new abilities. Many of the things you can buy feed back into resource generation for future expeditions, so it's got a growth-optimization angle that reminds me a little of Civilization and similar games (though the actual mechanics are thoroughly different).
The skill system is notable: characters have skill ratings in general categories like Archaeologist, Diplomat, or Athlete, but your rating is simply a count of how many individual skills you have within that category (for instance, the Diplomat category has things like Languages, Customs, and Politics), which are sometimes individually important and also influence how you can rank up (there's no benefit to getting Diplomat: Languages from 2 different sources, but there is a benefit to getting both Diplomat: Languages and Diplomat: Customs).

If you're a fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd webseries, you'll like this game a lot. It does a great job of emulating the Nerd's typical brand of crude, geeky humour. The game is all about what the show is about: raging at old-school, hardcore gameplay that is often frustratingly hard.
It plays just like a classic Nintendo platformer, with levels poking fun at famous - as well as infamous - games of the 80's and 90's. What is great is that it throws these old-school frustrations at you without it being badly designed. It's done in such a way that it is hard not because it's poorly designed, like many of the Nerd's most despised games, but because it requires skill and some effort. It's not unfair if you start at the easiest settings.
The Nerd humour is recognizable in every element of the game: there's a randomly generated line of cursewords if you die, Mecha Jesus powerups, a laser-shooting shark in Hell, snowboarding on Santa's corpse, sh*t pickles and gratitious amounts of potty humour. Each level is distinct and full of geeky references to the show.
In the style of Capcom classics like Mega Man or DuckTales, you can start at any level you want, with an additional final level opening up once you beat all of them. Each one is based on different Nerd episodes and video games. At one point you are fighting Doom-inspired poop demons and a big-toothed Satan in Hell, the next moment you play through a colourful level reminiscent of Super Mario World and in another instance you find yourself shooting ghosts and zombies in a Castlevania-based world. There's even a level based on the 'Atari Porn Games' episode which really must be seen to be believed.
Hidden inside the game are three additional playable characters from the
universe as well as cameos of
stars. Fans of the Nerd will know what I am talking about. Power-ups include Super Mecha Death Christ and the Glitch Gremlin, two funny allies that attack all enemies on screen. There's also somewhat useless grenades, poking fun at that one useless power-up that every video game in the 80s and 90s seemed to have.
It's that parody element that makes this game so great. It's not just an old-school 'NES-hard' game, it's also a parody of every game ever made in that genre, both the classics and the ones that are the subjects of the Nerd's crudely graphic tirades. If you like that type of humour and are a fan of the show, this game is for you. If you are unfamiliar with the AVGN and the show's inside jokes, the game falls a bit short, however. Look past the Nerd twist given to classic gaming tropes and the levels turn out to be fairly similar in gameplay elements and are only different enough in the visual department.
If you like old-school, NES-hard platformers, you will feel right at home. You will die. A lot! At the easiest setting, you have unlimited lives, plenty of checkpoints and more health. The credits will roll in a few hours. Try normal, hard or one of the unlockable even harder (!) modes and you will face a much more meaty challenge that will leave even the most veteran gamer screaming in frustration.
There are plenty of similar old-school platform games available on Steam. Wether or not you want to buy this particular one ultimately boils down to the question of wether or not you are a fan of the Nerd. If you are, it's worth your ten bucks. If you aren't, it's just one of many games to choose from for fans of this genre. You won't get much of the inside jokes that make up much of what sets this game apart from others. Thankfully, the overlap between genre fans and the AVGN fandom is probably big enough to make this a game I can recommend.

I bought this game for 49 cents during the Steam Winter Sale. I haven't finished yet but I have played 6 hours of it. I'm a first person dungeon crawler enthusiast, and I was excited to see this game so cheap in a genre that is so starved of games.
Some background information, first. This game is produced in Smile Game Builder, and it uses mostly stock assets and music from what I've seen of Smile Game Builder, so it feels kind of like a tech demo for the software (I do not think the developer is affiliated with the producers of that software, however).
Town of Night is like most Wizardry-like games in that there is a homebase town that has an inn, church, shops, etc, and dungeons you can go into. Unlike most Wizardry-like games, however, you can actually explore this town in a top-down 16-bit RPG style (press Y while you're in town to switch to and from first-person mode! Not only does it show off the engine, but it's necessary to find some of the doors.) The dungeons are spread around the town and when you enter them you are locked in first-person view. The switch from top-down to first person view is reminiscent of the first Phantasy Star.
At the beginning of the game, you are thrust right into action, no cutscenes or anything like that. You start with one party member, but can quickly recruit three others by asking about town. I got a Blood Priestess, a Mage, and a Healer. There's also a Warrior. There may be other party members, but that's all I know of. Be careful when recruiting your party, as once characters are in, they're in. There's no switching party members as of this review. The character designs are cute, but once again, stock assets.
In the dungeons, there isn't a mini-map, however, unlike most games of this type, you will hardly miss it, nor feel the need to construct a map of your own. There is enough field of view and distinguishing landmarks, and the dungeons are short and linear enough that you can find your way without a map. Progression is mostly by keys and bosses, defeat the bosses, get the keys, dungeons are locked until you can get the keys. The focus is on combat, there haven't been any puzzles or other quests in the six hours I've played so far.
Battles are initiated by random encounters, which occur at a slightly annoying rate, however, the godsend is that you seem to have 100% chance to run away from (non-mandatory) battles. There also do not seem to be back attacks or pre-emptive attacks. The battles seem to be of padded sumo nature, After the beginning of the game, enemies hardly threaten you, and it takes a while for you kill enemies, especially bosses. There are some enemies where some of your attacks are strangely incredibly effective, and the characters feel unbalanced. The main character sucks (although he's gotten a bit better since he got the axe of 20% auto-KO on hit, although the axe seems to proc a lot more than 20% of the time), the Blood Priestess isn't good unless her Blood Suck deals hundreds of damage against the enemy you're fighting, the Mage seems to get poor value for her MP, and the Healer is very effective (you'll rely on her in these drawn-out battles).
I know I sound pretty negative about the game, but I do not believe it is bad, and I'm also grading on a curve for it being a 49 cent game (it's regular price is $1.99, still pretty cheap. You also get 3 trading card drops, so you get some of it back), and I've loved the time I put into it so far. The developer also seems to be committed to adding new content to the game, and I hope I can also point out other things that could be worked on.
Sometimes it isn't clear as to what to do next, although I haven't been stuck for too long each time. The developer also commits the mortal sin of placing items that seem to be important, but are merely decorative (such as the blue orbs in some of the dungeons, and the jail cells/cages). The game lacks polish, the title screen is kind of a mess, and some of the graphics don't seem to be optimized. In town, some of the shadows flicker, especially the ones under benches. One of the rooms in the haunted house slows the game down immensely, even in the transition to the battles it is slow, making the game pretty unbearable. Speaking of the haunted house, I am not sure if it is intended or not, but you can switch between the camera angles despite it being a dungeon. The script also needs some proofreading, with spelling and capitalization issues at times (such as the "sabre", which is lower case, when other items' names are capitalized.).
There isn't much of a story, although some of the better games in this genre have only had an excuse plot. Still, it would have been nice to know more about these characters, or have some in-party banter. Who is Corr? Why is Charlotte so eager for blood and torturing her enemies? and so on.
In conclusion, it's a pretty good first effort from a solo developer, and a fun way to kill some time for a low price. I can't wait to see what the developer does next with the lessons they learned from this.

Colony Survival is a (you guessed it) colony survival game with solid mechanics and an intriguing amount of potential.
Even in its incomplete state, the early game and mid game are a total blast. Since enemy numbers coincide with colonist count, the initial task of finding the right spot for your colony (defensible, scenic, and with easy access to resources) is actually a pleasant experience. Trying to build and populate your colony while keeping it safe can be beautifully tricky. It's surprisingly intense when you're digging a mine 50 meters underground, looking for iron to replenish your sentries' dwindling supply of arrows, and you start seeing your colonist numbers drop because zombies have overwhelmed your guards and are now flooding into the bunkhouses and killing your colonists in their sleep. There's a real sense of satisfaction to building a thriving town, alive with motion and industry, and finding a way to keep the zombie horde at bay that isn't "cheap" (i.e. digging a trench around your colony and making it traversible only by a zig-zagging bridge under a catwalk manned by a couple archers).
It's got its imperfections, of course. It runs into the same problem a lot of in-development sandbox games do: as soon as you've reached the outer boundaries of the finished content, there's that abrupt, disappointing plateau where the game isn't
exactly, but there's no motivation to keep playing. Although the block textures have beautiful sculpted depth you rarely see in cubic Minecraft-like games, the character and enemy designs (identical except in color) are particularly unappealing. Finally, the challenge feels rudimentary. The enemies are completely predictable, homogenous, and completely foiled by a two-block-high hedgerow. I'm going on faith that this is just an artifact of its early access status, and that more interesting enemies and a more sophisticated challenge will be forthcoming.
I'm eager to see where this game will go. Although it's never a good idea to speculate about early access games, it's hard to not imagine what Colony Survival
become. Varied enemies that can climb/fly over fortifications, break through walls, build stairs/bridges, or fire projectiles. Colonists that are born, cycle through unproductive childhood (perhaps apprenticed to other colonists to increase their skill at their future "career"), work for a few weeks as adults, then die. The need for water, requiring you to build near a lake or create a reservoir/aqueduct nearyour town (along with better water behavior). Travelers. Random events. Underground dangers. The need to set up multiple colonies and connect them by roads (for example, prairie colony A has arable land and can grow food, but only forest colony B is able to supply ample wood, and only mountainside colony C has access to a decent amount of ore). It's at times like theses that I really wish there was a mixed review option.
Where the part of me that thought "It's cheap, give it a chance, despite the awful reviews it had/has" is kicking me for not listening, the other is glad that I did at least give it a go. I believe everything deserves a look see, it's how you find amazing things afterall.
Moving right along, story wise you play as a man who has an accident and has his memory stolen from him, he runs in search of finding out who he is, about his past, the people he knows and his present. Now, at this point it gets a little confusing for me, as it's never explained anywhere if he is stuck under his bike looking through a photo album to regain his memory or if they are just pictures the player chooses to flash before his eyes.
Whilst it does somewhat try to give an opportunity to tell a man by his memories in the form of a photo album that the players personality can cause change to, it really fails to get any kind of story or meaning into it due to lack of depth or explainations, bar one liners on each picture.
Now, don't get me wrong, I do appreciate the idea of giving the player a kind of power to affect what the man will remember by them choosing a picture out of three in a set of 80 that may simply attract them, or one that they connect to. If they're a photographer, maybe one will stand out due to how the photo is put together or something along those lines. I also personally enjoyed some of the art and music in this photo album simulator, but anything more than that, it falls down miserably.

You could argue whether retention is artistic and is designed to make the player really think about what it is they are doing, or just a load of pretentious bull. For me, what it boils down to is the fact that there really isn't any gameplay to this so called game. All you're doing is clicking on photographs. Games like journey have proven that a game can be both deep, and enjoyable to play. At the end of the day, I can't say whether retention accomplishes what it sets out to do, but I can say that as a game, it is not worth playing.

If you like a well thought-out story with violent u-turns and great atmosphere (I suggest you to be playing at night with least distractions possible), then this is the title for you.
Combatwise - very graphical, which really adds to the atmosphere of the apocalypse. This is one of the few games that actually make you feel like a superhero, since the AI, although not as challenging as in the first game (less flanking, more like CoD AI), creates the feeling that you are a worthy opponent (which is logically explainable since you are the most promising candidate in Project Harbringer). Radio dialogues between your enemies make you feel like you are in an action movie. Imagine eliminating a group of enemies and one of the few survivors requesting a reinforsement, saying "he wasted the whole squad!". Details like that make this game the unique experience.
Better graphics (than in F.E.A.R 1) really help to make the apocalyptic mood more impactful. Lighting is more appropriate as well, which helps to swing mood of a level from hardcore firefight to paranoid loneliness.
Characters are very well though out, Colonel Vanek goes in the book of my favorites as one of the most likeable villans, although I would not call him a "bad guy" since he was pursuing the same goal as you but with less information on what exactly was going on. It would have been a brilliant idea to make a choice to team up with him, although a stubborn army man like him would have been impossible to reason with.  That kind of conflict makes the campaign feel like a race, since you need to be always faster than your enemies to keep the slim chance of rescuing the world, and the fact that you know what will happen if you lose that race makes you really feel like you are the part of the Delta Force.
That mix of storyline, characters, gore, apocalyptic setting and clear vision of your purpuse makes the game exciting to play from the beginning to the end (although the ending does not stand to the standard of the first 3/4, but be the judge youself - may be you will love it!).
Dead Space 2 can be easily compared to this title, as it presents the same perfect mix of horror and action.
I highly recomend to play this game. And although I did not get scared (since I play horror games a lot), I loved the atmosphere of violence, gore and apocalypse as it really immerses you in the world of Alma (literally!). If you are new to this genra - go get it now, I guarantee you won't be dissapointed.
Edit: After revisiting F.E.A.R 1 and all of its DLCs, its gotta be undertlined that the horror factor in this game is not as strong and as mentioned above, I did not get scared for once, whereas in the older games it happens to me a lot more often. In addition, the AI is a lot worse (or even absent), it is not even close to being a challenge. That's my biggest dissapointment, leaving alone the lack of "scarybility". If you are ready to give up the fancy graphics and fast paced combat - better go for the older games from F.E.A.R franchise, although as I have mentioned already - you won't be dissapointed, the atmosphere in F.E.A.R 2 is far superior.

While at first glance, "Secret of the Magic Crystals" appears to be a simplistic, repetitive game designed to entertain young children with little more than pictures of virtual ponies, it is, in fact, a brilliant critique of the socio-economic climates of the European Union.
At the beginning of the game, the player is informed that "[a] special meteor hit the atmosphere of the Earth a long time ago.", resulting in the main character's grandfather collecting 'magic crystals' from it. During this introduction, it is revealed that "[the] crystals give special abilities to horses..." This satirical critique of the oft-espoused claims of religious Fascist groups across Europe; that God has chosen some to benefit from the work of others through divine intervention, sets the tone for a thoughtful, hilarious and revelatory piece about the state of affairs in the European Union today. If you are studying the effects of the debt crisis on the people of Europe, this game is a must-play.

A game for little girls, you say? I think not. Completing this game requires testicular fortitude the likes of which few people can muster. If you are one of the elite who can manage this accomplishment, you will emerge a changed man: not happier, but wiser, and stronger for what you have endured. You will be able to say with pride that you have stood at the gates of hell and stared into its very mouth, and, rather than turn back and flee in cowardice, you strode in boldly and plumbed its blackest depths, heedless of the risks to your sanity and even your very soul. Be wary and guard against the torment and suffering this game may inflict, and mock not those who have mastered the hellish realms of these magic crystals and the writhing, horrific equine denizens that reside therein.

Watch empty barnes as you send your horse on what you can only assume to be white-knuckle thrill rides that would probably keep you on the edge of your seat! Wait patiently as arbitrary in-game seasons pass while you manage confusing statistics and spend money on flowers.

Literature and languages are not advanced enough to provide the vocabulary needed to describe this creation. It's a genre-defining masterpiece, and all other games crumble against the majesty that is Secret of the Magic Crystals.

This game is a delight! It manages to tickle my imagination in the way that a good children's book can while capturing the pleasure of a well designed board game.
The gameplay and mechanics are simple enough that a novice can complete the game easily within their first half-dozen attempts. But the high-end challenges nested within the game are enough to occupy any hardcore table top strategy gamer. The pacing at which these challenges unfold and reveal themselves to the player masterfully handled. And the Steam acheivements are well designed in that they help guide a gamer towards these challenges over time.
Even more enjoyable than the gameplay is Renowned Explorers sense of narrative. Character specific and skill specific narratives have been woven throughout the game. These are so much fun to discover and follow through to completion.
My only beef with the game related to the default settings. My first few playthroughs had the long combat animations turned on. I found these dragged out battles, making the game insufferably slow. Thankfully, the developers have made it so you can toggle these off. Once switched off, I find a full game, if successful, lasts about 1.5-2 hours. Considering the number of short indie titles & sometimes overly long civ-like strategy games in my library, I find that Renowned Explorers occupies a unique category and sweet spot in terms of the time commitment required versus the depth of play available.
I absolutely recommend this title and its expansion, More to Explore, to anyone.
One final note for families, this game is very wide in age appropriateness, offering good stuff for players aged 8 and plenty of fun stuff for any adults who enjoy good old fashioned adventure serials.

Short but sweet, Antenna is something that knows what it wants to do, does it and then leaves it at that. Part of the charm is that it doesn't really give much direct explanation as to what the player is to do, exactly. The game starts with a symbol over a black screen. It does not say if it's a loading image or if the game has begun and it's up to the player to interact by pressing buttons until something happens.
This continues in a less severe sense as it will offer what buttons may be used in the second phase of the game and then letting the player figure out how to proceed. The simplistic situations allow the player to understand the idea of how to go forward, but that is all. You may be given a radio style interface and two buttons that make signals, but it's up to you to figure out what the clue is to help you determine which frequency to settle on and what signal to use.
Once you do that, you move onto a Limbo style walk with minor puzzles that require you to listen. One puzzle requires matching a repetative tone, the other requiring an ear for scaling notes. Both relatively easy to figure out and complete, all with the unspoken goal of sending signals for an unknown reason, unless you read the game description.
Over all, it captures an empty scene except for this one robot marching around trying to make a connection. Whether it is for companionship or a preprogrammed duty, it is clear that it is set on this task as many antenna are marked into the ground and broadcasting signals.
Ignoring that it's a free game, I would say it's worth looking into.

The first 15 minutes were extremely confusing (especially seeing the ending)...but then I figured some things out about the gameplay...
There are 16 different endings, and 1 ending in which you have all 4 positive outcomes.  Trying to reach this ending requires either complete luck on what you pick (if you have no clue what criteria you're looking for and simply pick to the desirable qualities), or more likely, figuring out what each dimension requires.
This is a *very short* sociological game/puzzle that most people have no clue is actually a puzzle.  Puzzleception, lol.  Part of the amusement is how few people realize that there is indeed a game aspect to this, albeit short.
Since it does its job SO WELL of being mysterious, yet actually having intrinsic goals, I'm rating it 7/10.  However:
- It is very short (each game is max 10m30s, and usually less unless you're overthinking).  I figured out a 'best possible' ending permutation within about 33 minutes.
- You can't maximize or resize the window...this makes it painful to set up for a stream.
- There should be sound/music level options in the settings (it defaults to REALLY loud).
- Moving between slides should not be slowed down by the text animation...this makes it painful to scroll through the timeline in a normal way.  You have very limited time...I don't want to be stalled by the text animating one letter at a time.
- Perhaps better hints at the actual goal of the game would be a plus, but then again, I enjoyed being confused and then having the 'Aha!' Moment of figuring out what I needed to do.
- Replay value on this beyond finding the best possible and worst possible endings is near 0.
Well, that was pointless.  Other reviewers have already gone into detail about why it's pointless, which is just as well, because I'm too apathetic to bother.

Blue Estate is an on-rails shooter, the kind that is quite uncommon today. This Steam version is a re-release of the XBone version. The story is rather corny and the story missions are rather bland, but the game shines in arcade mode. It's actually more fun than House of the Dead.
The story mode is sometimes fun even if rarely funny, but as I mentioned the missions are too long and drag on and on. Fortunately there is the arcade mode. I was so bored after running through the story mode, which took me around 3hrs, that I almost missed the arcade mode completely. That would be a mistake as the arcade mode is great fun. Fast paced, crazy headshot nutshot extravaganza. Fun!
VISUALS
Everything seems pretty enough. It looks amazing compared to the last HotD, but then HotD was so horribly horrible that anything would look better. Fact is Blue Estate is quite nice to look at and smooth at all times. The levels are not that complex but still good looking.
AUDIO
Nice music all along, nothing spectacular but fitting the game pretty well. Sounds are allright, weapons sound cartoony, but meaty enough. Voice acting is spot on. All in all everything is aok in the audio department.
GAMEPLAY
The game controls surprisingly good albeit it has some sort of auto-aim which was a bit weird at first but quite handy later. The story mode is a bit fun-ish, but the diminishing returns quickly kick in and after a few minutes every minute is less enjoyable than the previous one. In the arcade mode you revisit some of the locales from the story mode and pop heads for high scores.
If you like on-rails shooters play this one. It's not an amazing game by any stretch of the imagination, but it is a guilty pleasure worthy of some monies.
Blue Estate - Random Game Footage:
Rather crude, but the humour is usually light hearted enough. The cover can feel a bit fiddly, but guns are good and overall I'm enjoying this on rails shooter.

Secret of the Magic Crystals is a brutal, bleak action combat RPG that pits your lone character against a universe full of violent demons. They range from former human soldiers to agile, double scimitar-wielding skeletons, pouncing flame-horses, octopus-headed ponies, embryonic plague-carrying monstrosities, even Death-Horse himself. The game's five worlds - all massive - are split into four different crystals, each guarded by a horribly large and hardcore boss horse.
Everything in the entire world is designed to kill you, quickly and often without warning. The only safe place is the Ranch, a haven for tormented souls. It acts as a hub from which you can access the five crystals, or buy and upgrade your character's tools and abilities to give them a slightly better chance of grooming hors. It is one of the most difficult modern videogames in existence, refusing to make even the slightest concession to your happiness or mental well-being.

I played this game in alpha during July '17. I had just finished Stardew Valley and was looking for something that would give me a similar experience for a few hours, and I'd say that Colony Survival did that (for around 4 hours).
The basic premise of this game is "idle game meets minecraft." It's in alpha, so there were relatively few features and mechanics.
Pros
- Open world and Minecraft-style building system allow for nice flexibility
- Provides a fun "optimization" experience ("hm, where is the bottleneck in my resource production? Ah, I need more grain, so I need more seeds, so I need more money, but I need more gold to make money," etc.)
- Simple combat (zombies attack your base at night) makes the difficulty more serious and compelling.
- This game is the only one I've ever played that _didn't_ implement bloom to be as annoying as possible; the day-night cycle made it most intense during early morning (when there'd be humidity and bright sun), and then it gets less intense as the day goes on.
Cons
- The UI is a little janky (forgiveable since it's two devs and in alpha). You have to drag items from your storage to your inventory to do any crafting, and the add/remove block system with mouse-clicks is a little unintuitive.
- The AI is also a little janky and frustrating at times - as far as I can tell, the zombies move non-stochastically (probably using some version of A* search), so they wind up hugging the walls of your base and attacking predictably. I was able to counter the zombie threat entirely by surrounding my base with a 2x1x1 moat and 1x1x10 bridge and then just stacking archers in front of it.
- Retasking your colonists from one job to another is _really_ frustrating. You either have to destroy the thing they're working on, or just add another job site and hire a new colonist.
Suggestions to the devs (obviously not all of these are doable, but any individual one would probably have kept me playing for at lease another hour or two):
- Make it possible to direct colonists or re-task them once assigned to a job.
- Make more weapons with different types of damage (melee weapons, different range weapons, etc), and make them upgradable.
- Make different kinds of enemies, especially ones with ranged attacks.
- Allow for buildings (other than the banner) to be destructible - this would force more strategic gameplay and base design.
- Maybe implement some feature where your colonists can level up themselves with regard to how efficient they are at tasks?
- Allow for multiple (with a maximum) colonists to work on certain job sites (i.e. I'm pretty sure my 10x10 farming sites can support more than one worker).
- This is my inner Stardew Valley nerd talking, but I'd definitely love it if there were livestock, a fishing system, and different regions to explore. :P
Overall, I would say it was an enjoyable experience. Don't go in (right now) expecting a AAA experience; it's a fun indie game that's worth a good few hours.
As this game is in Early Access, so far the dev's have shown great care for the game and I hope it turns out well through the coming months.

Guacamelee is a 2-D platforming action game set in a Mexican themed world, with a smaller emphasis on story than pure action (although there's still enough there to make you care). It follows the adventures of Juan, an everyday farmer who is resurrected after being killed by the evil Carlos Calacka, as he punches, jumps, and kicks his way to freeing the daughter of El Presidente.
The fighting in this game is superb - there is a great mix of normal attacks and more powerful special attacks that are unlocked throughout the game, and moment to moment action feels great. Trying to chain up a huge combo by pummelling enemies into the air, picking them up and throwing them into other enemies so they all land in a huge heap is fast, fluid, and feels amazing. There is a large variety in the enemies you face - starting off with standard brute enemies, and eventually leading up to giants with hammers, spikey armadillos with deadly, fast attacks, four armed sword wielding skeletons, and flying lightning priests. The game slowly introduces these enemies to match your rising skill level, and starts mix and matching them cleverly which leads to some genuinely difficult fights. That being said, on Normal mode (Hard mode is unlocked only after beating the game, and is much harder – enemies have more health, and you have less) the game is not very difficult, due to a forgiving checkpoint system and it will only take about 10 hours to finish the story. However, there are many collectibles hidden around the maps that can keep you occupied as you try for 100% - again, this will only take an additional 4 hours or so. There are also additional challenges (the El Infierno levels) that test your fighting, platforming, and thinking skills – these are easily the most difficult part of the game, and getting a gold medal in all challenges is a worthy achievement.
The art style in Guacamelee is one of the most striking things about the game – the graphics are crisp and look beautiful, all presented in a lovely and vibrant, if clichéd, Mexican style. The soundtrack is much the same – beautiful, and easy to listen to for hours on end. These two combine to form a convincing and engaging that makes the game fun to play for hours on end.
Summary:
- Beautiful aesthetics, both graphically and musically
- Fast, fluid and fun combat
- Great boss battles that test your fighting skills
- Responsive and challenging platforming.
A great mix of platforming and action, combined with a beautiful world make this a must buy, whether you like platforming and/or fighting games. This game is worth full price, and definitely grab it if it is on a sale.

If there was ever a game that I wished was a person, it'd be Guacamelee.
Not only is this side-scrolling, metroidvania piece of animated Mexican Folk Art a joy to play - but it's gorgeous as well. It's rare to find a titles with a sense of identity as strong as Guacamelee. Everything from the authentic wrestling to the campy characters is tightly packaged and shoved underneath the same umbrella. It all adds up for a colourful gem of a game which can quickly eat up hours of your time. The fact that much of the humour is Goat Based is a serious bonus.
Although not especially difficult, Guacamelee does have some excellent hidden gems. The search for Mask Fragments is fun, rewarding, and challenging. Although no where near Super Meat Boy, or I wanna Be The Guy difficulties there's still challenge to be had. The bit at the tallest point in the game was especially brutal. Satan's Tower of Doom is also a lot of fun if you're looking to immerse yourself in Guacamelee's combat system, or its traversal mechanisms.
My biggest complaint is that there's no actual Guacamole in the game. Not even as a health pick-up.

As far as real time strategy games go, you really cannot do much better than supreme commander 2.
Yes, square enix is basically gone.  Yes, the story line is more or less just there to say "this game has a story."  And yes, this game is old.
But it more than makes up for it with the massive armies you can command (1000 unit count, but realistically the max is 700 individual units since you need a little space for structures... like mass extractors and powerplants).  It has just the right amount of variety of units for each faction.
Truely exotic buildings, like a structure that can instantly teleport a massive army of small units or say 50 expeariemntals (one expeariemntal is worth 50-100 normal units... just imagine what that would do to a base... or a commander's unit) in to the very center of the enemies main base, or a artically cannon that shoots smaller units instead of projectiles, or a giant magnet/meatgrinder that sucks and destroys 100s of smaller units before it has to cooldown.

And ways to cheat resource limits, like energy to mass converters - which consume massive amounts of energy and need to be manually activated each time you use them - can provide you enough mass (resource) to make the next batch of elite units.
Giant robots.  Nukes.  Floating baby belle cheese rolls of death.  Artillary arrays.  Armadas.  Armies.  More nukes.   Walking battleships.  Sky-fleets.  Giant flying brains.

Russian pseudo psych quiz with images. Recommended if you like that sort of thing.
Do you know these psych quizzes you can find online or in magazines? You answer a bunch of questions with a), b) or c), and in the end the answer key tells you what kind of person you are, or what popular series character, etc. Retention is much like that, except you get no questions, instead your life is flashing before eyes, and the answers are images: 80 choices of 3 images each, and in the end your "life" is judged to be retained or forgotten, full of friendship or solitude, colorful or monochrome, and your memory of it is clear or corrupted.
The problems with Retention are numerous:
The game runs on a timer. In the settings on the intro screen, you can turn that off (and also change the language). I believe the timer is intended to make you pick images intuitively, from your gut feelings, and not think about your choices too much.
You can also change the language to the original Russian, or switch to Italian or Turkish translations.
Tip: Among the game files, there are instructions for making an OST CD.

I consider myself something of a hipster gamer. Okay, not something of. A complete and total hipster gamer. I love indie games and I love games that push the borders of what can be considered a game and I love weird narrative spins and just... everything about the sort of games that make your average gamer go "UGGGHHH NOT A GAME 0/10 BOOOOO" is the sorta thing I cherish. I mean, my top games of the past year or two include Mountain, Gone Home, and Hate Plus.
But even I can't stand Retention, the latest game to bring down the wrath of NOT A GAME gamers. First off, it's totally a game. The inputs are weird and disconnected because really you're looking through pictures and choosing them and its supposed to string together a story. It's no less of a game than any choice game; the system of inputs is just unique.
The problem is that the player is given absolutely no sense of coherent connections between the images. It's implied that they're a timeline of events, but there's no thread that holds them together except the occasional repeated model or vague theme. In terms of "narrative," nothing matches up.
So, if there's no narrative, maybe the game is better read as modern poetry. Maybe the game needs to be read as discordant elements brought together in a way where the meaning needs to be pieced together. Okay, cool idea. I still think it could be better executed because, again, there are few repeated motifs throughout the piece and poems work almost entirely based off invoking a series of signs and signifiers that links the reader back to previous works and images in a canon of both literature and language. The game struggles to do this. And that's okay, in certain ways, but it makes it incredibly hard to analyze and piece things together.
Retention is an interesting experiment, that's for certain. I think it deserves to exist and should exist and needs to exist. It's possibly an important step in disturbing and deconstructing our ideas of what makes games art by pushing a concept of game poetry forwards in a new way. Sadly, I just don't think this poem is any good.

This is a great fun game with possibly the best and most innovative turn-based combat I have ever played. Ever had the feeling you are just pressing the same attacks in the same order? Well not in Renowned Explorers. The unique combination of categories of attacks (attack, deceitful, friendly) + the overall mood of the combat which alters the effetiveness of attacks + the mood of the individual targets makes for an ever changing experience. The strategic placement on the map of zones that buff your characters plus obstacles adds another layer. Seriously there is nothing else like it.
The game is presented in a fun cartoon style that keeps it light and fresh with skill challenges being clearly labelled and then resolved via a spinning wheel of randomisation.
I highly recommend Renowned Explorers: International Society and the DLC More to Explore. Well worth your time. Fun but with depth, it is a cracking combination.

I seduced a nun, got spat on by a llama, fought Charles Darwin riding a dinosaur, and made grown men cry. 1000/10
But if you need more of a reason to buy this game, here's the breakdown: you play as a group of explorers, traveling the world, earning status and money while doing research, collecting treasures, and all around making a nuisance of yourself. It's a turn-based strategy game with a really interesting mechanic: moods and attitudes. Each side of the battle (you vs. them) each have one of three attitudes (friendly, devious and aggressive), and the combination of your attitude and the enemy's creates an overall mood (ex. hostile = both parties aggressive or persuasive = you friendly and them devious). Each mood has bonuses or penalties, and there's a rock-paper-scissors system so you know which way to shift your attitude to get the bonuses and avoid the penalties. (Friendly beats devious, devious beats aggressive, aggressive beats friendly.) You win battles with your built-in powers. There is some overlap between characters on the powers, but not a lot. There are area attacks, line attacks, and single-target attacks, and by default every character has one attack from each attitude, plus some bonus ones that fit their own personal strengths and personalities. (Yes, seduce is an attack you can actually use, and no, it's not gender specific). It's good for all kinds of different playstyles.
But that's just the battles!
The other main part of the game is exploring. You have 5 expeditions to a campaign (you can do more after that, but most of the achievements are turned off for anything past 5). Each expedition puts you on an island with tons of people to interact with, and depending on which three characters you have in your party, the outcomes can change. Ex. If you don't have a character with a high enough level in archaeology you won't find a really cool thingamajig, or there is one boss I didn't even realize I hadn't actually faced because I couldn't get past the skill checks to fight him. The options are basically things like "This person needs food. Help this person out (Lose 1 supplies. Reward: Gain status)" or "Help them out, but for a price (Lose 1 supplies. Reward: Gain 1 Collect)" or "Don't help them and move on." You can also do things like punch people in the face and start a fight, decide which people to send on supply runs, whether to skip a fight at the cost of supplies, etc. Your choices often require a spin of a chance wheel, with your various applicable skills increasing your percentage chance. Certain islands/areas that you travel to will have research, money, or status collectibles, each of which will help your party gain renown and come out on top in the eyes of the Renowned Explorer: International Society and beat your rival. There are also treasures you collect, which have special one-time or permanent bonuses (if you get the DLC you get to choose the bonuses from a list), which add to your renown.
There are also a ton of difficulty levels: easy, normal, classic, and impossible. Easy might make the battles easier, but I've still died plenty of times, and after 100 hours of play (including the DLC), I still haven't found all the treasures. In addition to the difficulty, there are two ways to play: Discovery mode (where you can restart a battle if you kill your party or run out of "resolve," which you can also collect), and Adventure mode, which makes it more like a Roguelike with no restarts. There are also TONS of achievements for both modes, and there are 20 achievement for winning the game with each of 20 characters in any mode and then 20 more for doing it with each of them in adventure mode, so there's going to be a lot of replays if you want to go to 100%.
Overall:
Pros:
+Great art.
+Adaptive music. Much of the music repeats, but it's adaptive, and will become more aggressive when the mood changes or more laid back when the mood drops back to more friendly terms.
+ TONS of depth. Playing with just one different character in your party can open up new avenues for the same interaction. Finishing a battle with a different attitude can give you different treasures, or open up new avenues of exploration like hints to hidden treasure.
+ Skill upgrades. Each character comes with a few built-in skills, which you can upgrade. Your character can be super amazing at one skill, or multi-talented in a bunch.
+ Items to purchase! Items give attack bonuses, defense, or additional skills. You have to upgrade shops with money to get better items, but items come with really good bonuses or tons of extra skills.
+ Entourages. You can spend status points to gain helpers and specialists who give you bonuses in research, collect, and status.
+ Research trees! Spend research points to collect renown faster, get bonuses for ending battles with a certain attitude, get extra skills, etc.
+ Unique characters! 4 classes, 5 different characters in each class, all with different weapons, behaviors, skills, homelands, an designs. No photocopied characters here. There's even more background to them in the DLC. Personality traits even affect your choices in interactions. Ex. A greedy character in your party will, in one case, go back for more treasure and decrease your chance to escape through a closing tomb door in time.
+ Your choices matter! You can only go on 5 expeditions. The first one is chosen at random, then you have your choice of 2-3 new expeditions, then after that one you have 2-3 additional choices, etc. So although there are a limited number of choices, you can decide whether to play it safe and explore only easy islands, or go for the big rewards and go for the hardest ones. Some of the expeditions are suited to different types of parties or attitudes (aggressive, devious or aggressive), or they may be tempting because they are high in money, or research, or status. Once you're on an island, you have a limited amount of supplies, so you can't search everywhere for treasure without getting serious penalties for the boss battle. Luckily, each spot is labeled with all the possible types of events that could happen there, so you have a hint of what may come, and can plan your route accordingly.
+ DLC is great. There should be another one coming out eventually, but the current one has two new expeditions (with tons of treasures and new mechanics, plus Charles Darwin riding a raptor). There are also collectible campfire stories to get more bonuses, skills, and backstory for your crew. These campfire stories do make it easier to beat the game without dying quite so much.
+ Great sound design. Characters don't talk, but they do make Sims-esque, barely intelligble noises during battle that are great.
+ TONS of achievements.
+ Interesting fight mechanics (see earlier)
Neutral:
~ Great variety of difficulty settings, but even easy is not free of death or total party death.
~ Some people might get bored by the lack of a long campaign. Just 5 expeditions and the game is *basically* over and you have to restart, and there aren't a ton of different exhibitions. I've played 117 hours thus far, so it doesn't bother me.
~ A lot of reading. It's nice that you can cycle through it really fast, and it has great flavor to it, and sometimes hints as to what choice to make for which outcome, but I skip it most of the time and just look at the choices. It often means missing vital information.
Cons:
- You can't move after you attack? What the hell?

Rail shooters. Yeah, so typically I wouldn't touch them with a ten-foot pole because the premise seems rather boring. I enjoyed the first Umbrella Chronicles game on the Wii, and I enjoyed CarnEvil in the arcades, but otherwise, I just dismissed the genre...until I watched a "let's play" of Jim Sterling playing through the first level of Blue Estate. Oh my word, this game's pedigree and production values are what all rail shooters should strive for. If you already like the genre, you should buy this when it's a price you're comfy with, because it's grand.
What's so great about it? Well, you play as two different characters throughout the game, and there are other characters involved as well, either present with your character in the level, or over a radio. Not only that, but you have a *very* geeky private eye narrating and adding commentary, as well as sarcastic and witty remarks from the "Federal Bureau of Procrastincation," if memory serves.  There's plenty of dialog, tons of action, some of which is quite stylized, a unique gun on every level which you can use as long as you have ammo, or else you default back to your infinite ammo normal guns (but if you're careful with your shots, you'll rarely run out and can use the ammo guns almost the whole time!).
Last but not least...the humor. This game is hilarious. Obviously, everyone has a different sense of humor, but I laughed aloud on multiple occasions and found myself smirking or grinning through much of the game. The comedy and gunplay go hand in hand as a real treat, and I'm so glad I finally played this game. I'm sure I'll end up circling back and playing through it again sometime in the future, because I had a great time with it, and it's just so charming with all of its comedy, action, and brevity. I dare say this may be the finest rail shooter I've ever played.
