The game features several campaigns with missions that include massive battles and tedious objectives. Random skirmishes against the AI and online multiplayer are also available. Groups of units need to have an officer and a drummer in order to be placed into formations, leaving smaller groups to be disorganized. This becomes more chaotic when units sometimes engage nearby enemies and sometimes do not. The game also does not indicate the income rate of each resource, which makes assigning peasants to collect the most needed item more difficult. Cossacks 3 is a game of resource collection: get the most stuff to build the most units. The game is extremely dawdling: collecting resources, constructing buildings, and recruiting units is all accomplished at a snail’s pace, even on the “fast” setting. In addition, resource requirements for additional military buildings (such as a third barracks) can be extremely high, which does not allow better players to outproduce their competition in terms of units, leading to stalemates during offensive maneuvers. Cossacks 3 plays identically to the previous games in the series, a massive sense of scale with some graphical upgrades. However, a slow pace, limited interface, and game balance issues hold Cossacks 3 back.

Hilarious, ridiculous, and crazy fun. Guacamelee is what you get when you implement Super Smash Bros-esque controls in a Metroidvania game. I played through the whole game co-op with a friend in one sitting, and it was fantastic. The main quest is short, but there are a lot of sidequests and collectibles scattered here and there to keep you entertained.
Praises:
+ Comedic gold. The characters and dialogue are pretty ridiculous, and there are a plethora of references to internet memes/jokes.
+ Simplistic art style, vibrant colors, and smooth animations. What's especially nice is the strong visual contrast between the world of the living and the world of the dead.
+ Challenging puzzles, both in solving and executing.
+ A pretty steady learning curve. By the end of the game, you have a lot of different moves and abilities at your disposal, but they are presented to you one by one throughout the course of the whole game so you aren't overwhelmed.
+ Two-player co-op is drop-in/drop-out style; great for old-fashioned "come over and play this game with me" fun.
Criticisms:
- A controller is basically a requirement to play. Trying to play with keyboard feels awkward, and you have less precise control of your throws (limited to the 8 directions of WASD as opposed to the full 360-degree control of a thumbstick)
- Many of the level designs are far too difficult for both players to coordinate. Most of the time, it was much quicker and easier for one player to turn themselves into a bubble so the other could navigate the level.
- I personally don't see this as a huge issue, but an online co-op option would be nice.
All in all, Guacamelee is a fantastic beat-em-up game that will keep you laughing behind your luchador mask.

Don't get fooled by this game's age or the fact that it is in the StarWars franchise - on the inside, it is an absolutely amazing old-school BioWare RPG with all the right elements that make a true ROLE-PLAYING game (not just a shooter with stats or a movie with fake choices). Some gameplay mechanics are even far ahead of modern RPGs.
You will be taken on a journey of choices as you watch your character and those around him/her grow and evolve according to your actions. It's true. The Force. The Jedi... All of it... Without spoiling anything, let me just say that this game's story contains one of the greatest plot twists ever. The writing in general really is great - even if you're not a huge fan of StarWars, you will definitely enjoy this game. In fact, some of the quests, dialogues and lore in this game actually made me appreciate the StarWars universe a lot more.
The NPCs and their interactions are as deep as in, say, Mass Effect. Some quests require a fair bit of thinking and will not always hold your hand. This really is the "old" BioWare feel.
Graphics are pretty oldschool but still very much bearable. The sound design is great and some of the voice acting is superior to most modern titles. So, with a small grain of nostalgia, this game can still feel great, even though it's quite old now.
TECHNICAL NOTE: On top of this version, make sure to find and install "KotOR 1 Restoration 1.2" - a community-made patch that fixes a lot of issues and restores some missing content. Also, you might want to look for a Widescreen mod (although I was fine playing it at less than full HD).

The interaction between characters are fun, you will have at least one favorite character here. There is a great plot twist in the game that not many can really see. I only played one route, but it was really exciting all along.
Gameplay: Will be a little frustrating for first timer, especially those not familiar with the D&D playstyle. You have to plan in advance what you want because haphazard levelling will make the game soooo hard starting mid-game. First time playing, I rarely hit anything and my damage is miniscule. Don't be afraid to abuse the Pause system.
Music & Sound: Classic Star Wars, what more can you ask?
Graphic: Still okay even by 2017 standard, even though some scenes will look a bit off or funny. At least there's not many horrendous bug in the characters' models. The sceneries can be a sight to behold.
There are some bugs here and there, like your character can bump into an invisible wall or the game can crash randomly. Just save often, you'll be fine.
Must if you like Star Wars and Western RPG.

Retention is... well to be honest I'm not exactly sure what it is. I could only find one definition of the word "Game" which even comes close to defining it: "A complete episode or period of play, ending in a final result".
Steam's store page lists it as a casual indie adventure. Casual and indie maybe, but adventure implies some kind of story at least, and... well, you'll see.
The game starts windowed at about 1280 by 800, and has no fullscreen option. In fact the only options it has are the language and whether you want it to force the ending after ten and a half minutes. Whether this is strictly necessary I'll let you decide yourselves after reading about a little of what could only very graciously be called "gameplay".
When you start a new game, you're given this: A picture of a leg and a bike. There's some backstory about how you've fallen off and need to go back through your memories to put things together again, but it's utterly irrelevant. You move through the memories either with the keyboard or clicking on the timeline at the top, and at each stage you're given one of three pictures to select. There's nothing else to do at this point. In fact, there's nothing else to do, period. Scroll through the pictures and pick one.
Very quickly, I got bored and started thinking up responses to the captions, each of which look like they're just a tag you'd put on facebook to remind yourself about it. And they're very pretentious comments at that.
Once you've selected your choice on all the pictures (or hit the ten and a half minute time limit if you managed to sit through it for that long), you get to the ending. Four more pictures which are selected based on your choices. Each of them is a binary black or white result, and just feels like you've just done one of those annoying Playbuzz quizzes to find out which Disney princess you are or some such rubbish, but doesn't even go into as much detail as them! "Your pictures were mostly black and white." Really? I hadn't noticed that, and you know why that is? It's because I actually don't care!
Or maybe this game has a deep understanding of my psyche and inner demons. I don't know.
The whole experience, because I refuse to further call this abomination a game, is a painful mess. Every time you click on a picture, you get the same tired old sound effect, which becomes irritating after only a couple of pictures. Although the music isn't bad, it has nothing to do with the rest of the content, instead just picked because... well, to be honest I have no idea why it was selected. It was probably the first music the developer came across and just bunged in to give the experience some sort of backing other than repetetive clicking noises.
Either way, on to the numbers.
Total time played: one hour.
Time for one playthrough: 630 beats of the heart. Yes, it actually says that. In real terms though, about 5 minutes.
Bugs found: 0. There's not really enough of anything to contain any bugs.
Sanity lost whilst reviewing: about 25%.
To sum up, Retention is a photocopy of an instagram of a snack that some random guy you've never met ordered in a cafe next to you. It's bland, boring, one-dimensional, and after seeing it once you have no desire to look at it again, if you ever did in the first place. In fact the only reason to have more than about ten minutes playtime logged on Retention is to get the Steam Trading cards and sell them for a few pennies. You never know, you might get a foil card and make back the wasted money you spent on getting the game in the first place.

I would suggest that you save that 67p for an actual game.  I bought Retention thinking that it probably isnt an amazing game, but often small, cheap games are enjoyable, and it looks like it would have a nice story behind it.  I was so wrong.  If there is a plot, I could not see it at all!
This "game", if you can even call it that, involves selecting one of out three pictures, over and over and over again, in order to get a short summary of that picture, which I kind of already understood from just looking at the photograph.  I got to the end of the game after about 15 minutes of tedious clicking, and was given a vague ending of some sort that didn't seem to mean anything at all!
Just don't buy this game.  it's really not worth your time or money.

I finished my first playthrough in about six minutes. With that experience, the only thing I can say with absolute certainty about this title is that I did not enjoy it.
The presentation is good and the game itself works fine, but it all seems a bit vague, to put it lightly. It's essentially a slideshow in which you decide on an injured man's memories. You are presented with a set of three photographs, from which you have to select one. This occurs numerous times, and makes up the entirety of the gameplay.
There are apparently a number of endings to unlock, but I honestly cannot find any motivation whatsoever to bring myself to work towards them. I understand that the story is to be partially constructed by the player. but I feel that more explicit explanations would have really helped to flesh out the narrative. Doing so may go against the game's vision, but not everyone (myself included) is able and/or willing to piece together a coherent narrative through a series of still images and some sparse accompanying text.
There is no denying that Retention is an original piece of work. As far as my experiences go, there is nothing else like it. However, that alone does not warrant a recommendation. This is a shame, as the method of delivery has so much promise.

"Strange pictures conceal the ideas of the artist."
It's a caption left under one of Retention's still frames, like a subtle acknowledgement that its developer knew the experience they were creating was likely going to have trouble communicating to its audience the ideas and emotions hidden underneath its disorganized film real. Shifting through photo after photo, bits of someone's life creeping through, literal and philosophical captions writing attempting to give way to a larger narrative of your own creation, it was hard to find meaning in the inscrutable frames I was haphazardly cycling through.
I don't wish to say that there's nothing here, as the haziest of structures makes me want to believe that at the very least its creator understands what it is, but whatever their intention the experience before me never revealed itself as anything but ten minutes spent scrutinizing seemingly unconnected images and then waiting to be informed as to whether or not the life I had just scanned through was one worth living. I'll have to get back to you on that one I'm afraid, though I haven't a lot of hope an answer is something I'll ever find.

The game takes the sensibilities of euro-style boardgaming and melds them with high-stakes tactics, and the resulting combination is too bumpy for me.

Explore the world and bring its treasures back to England! This is a game of joyous imperialism, a roguelike without the usual BS or difficulty cliff. The game has a tutorial and explains its mechanics! The mechanics are simple (sets of rock-paper-scissors) that have interesting interactions. Build your team, develop them with synergy, discover lands that change each game, and bring home treasures and stories.
Note that each game is fairly short. An expedition takes 30-60 minutes, five expeditions are your whole game, and you start over. There is no extended campaign or advancement across games. Each game stands on its own.

Graphics: 6/10. The graphics are fairly solid in this game, it's nothing too special. But for this game, it feels like the right balance between TOO good and TOO bad.

Notice people drifting and pull them over for fatigue, drugs or alcohal. You could even notice if they are on a phone, no seatbelt, speeding, or even just a car violation (such as a flat tire). The game takes into consideration the common laws from around the world. But here's the catch, the writings on the all of the documents they give you, all in German. I don't really read the license and all of that fun stuff, I just assume they are valid. Although the game is in German, it really doesn't get in the way of your entertainment. Oh, did I also mention police chases? Yes, a person could refuse to pull over and that brings you to solve the issue, pull them over the hard way, Despite all of these great things about the game, there is a single flaw. It gets boring after a little bit. You're used to pulling these kinds of people over and there's no story line to the game. You just raise your ranks and have as much fun as you can.
Addiction: 3/10, As soon as you play it you're all, "Oh this is pretty good." Then maybe after an hour you begin to say, alright this game is not as good as I thought it was, despite it's unattractive price of 20$.
Sounds: 8/10, Sounds run smoothly no problems with them. Common police/car sounds.
Music: 5/10, Really unattractive intro music right as you enter the game. No music during the gameplay.
Lag: 4/10, The lag to this game is insane if you have the default graphics on, I could barely move my dude when I played this. It's an easy fix although, just switch the graphics quality down and most importantly your view distance, then you'd be in good shape.

I was hoping for a new, fun Cossacks game. In reality, though, my expectations were lower, and I figured I'd end up with a slightly modernized remake of the old titles, with a few added improvements for modern machines.
Instead, I got a weak Unity rebuild that looks more like a high school project than a professional product.
Unit animations are limited, while pathfinding and collision mechanics are dysfuntional, with ships on land and formations that leave two or three soldiers marching in the wrong direction.
Graphics are terribly static, aside from the rather wooden units. The maps are smaller than expected, with units moving slowly and having tiny range to compensate. Everything feels like sprites instead of 3d models, and not particularly good ones at that.
Sound quality is especially bad. Music loops and overlaps itself. Drummers and officers are silent, instead of classic drumbeats and shouted orders. Muskets and cannons sound like firecrackers.
Localization is poor. Some unit names are still obvious placeholders, the campaign description read like Google translate, and either there is no documentation or I haven't been able to find it, either through Steam or in the game's folders. So unless you already know the difference between Prussian and Austrian units, you're not going to find out now.
Playtesting seems almost entirely absent. Ships on land. Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V allow you to literally copy-paste entire armies in the campaign and random maps. Unit highlighting is inconsistent, and anything behind a building is invisible.
I bought this expecting a less-than-stellar rehash of an old game, and was still disappointed.

Back in 2003, in the middle of the prequel time, where all hope was lost for the Star Wars franchise Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic was released. It was a light in the darkness. And to this day this game is the Magnum Opus of Star Wars, not only for the games, but Star Wars in general. A lot of people like my self love this game even after 14 years.
STORY:
The storyline of this game is iconic. It's not only iconic for Star Wars fans, but it has one of the most famous twist in gaming history. It is my favourite Star Wars story to this day with the Darth Vader story on second place. So what makes this story so great? This is a dark, grim story about redemption, friends, love, betrayal and learning about who you really are. This story is not only just a dark story where all is depressing, but there are some fun moments with your crew (I will talk about them in a bit). By including a morality system it makes the story even better.
CHARACTERS:
If you want to have a great story you need great and compelling characters. First of all i will not talk to much about the charcter and their storylines in the game because of spoilers. You can form their stories and how they all end in the game due to the morality system. The protagonist is either female or male which can customize a bit. But that doesn't have that big change to the story except some romance options. Whats so compelling about him/her is the story you learn throughout the game. And HK-47 is one of the best NPCs ever just sayin.
COMBAT:
Well this is probably the weakest part of the game for me (excluding the graphics). Well the combat is not exactly bad, but is not my type of combat. I'm not really type of the strategic turn-based combat. Some people like the combat and that is totally okay, but I'm not really into that type of combat. I prefer clean action like The Force Unleashed.
GRAPHICS:
I'm not really going to talk about the graphics because the game is 14 years old. You are not going to play this game for the graphics. But the graphics is not THAT bad actually. It's actually pretty decent, but it's not The Witcher 3 good obviously.
OVERALL:
Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic had a tremendous impact on my life. Everything from the story to the characters  and to the nostalgia. This game is a must buy for everyone. Not only for Star Wars fans, but for every gamer out there. BUY THIS GAME!
SCORE: 10/10
MESSAGE TO DISNEY:
Please make a Old Republic movie or TV-series.

PROS: The game's 2D feel definitely comes out like a classic game.  The controls are tight, and the music is just wonderful, fitting for each zone.
CONS: The game feels very cheap, and it fails to improve on some of the things people wanted to forget from classic games.  Knock back is a major problem, as everything will shove you back.  Enemy placement isn't a problem, but the over reliance on instant death blocks makes some parts an absolute joke until trial and error kicks in.  And although the harder difficulties are there for the challenge, YOLO mode is made to be quite the horror thanks to the problems.
ACHIEVEMENTS: The difficulty will cause a long and extended frustration.
FINAL: The game is well put together, however, the over reliance of annoying and cheap tricks used in the NES brings about it's failure to push the game to a standard of higher quality.  Instead of becoming a game to poke fun and improve the formula, it falls squarely into place.  A solid title, but one that could have been a great deal better.

The animation quality of the cutscenes is, however, somehow worse than in Sup Com 1 or FA. The missions, so far, are extremely bland. I've completed 5 of the 6 UEF missions and I'm barely 2 hours in the game. In Sup Com 1 it took me that long to even beat the first 1 or 2 missions, since the battlefield would constantly be expanding after achieving your objectives (which could screw you over big time). This time around, the first mission takes 10 minutes...I♥♥♥♥♥♥you knot. Mission 5 was 25 minutes and I chilled. All the epic from epic battles has been siphoned straight out of this campaign. I'm sure this is not such an issue in MP, but I don't know how big those maps are.
- The economy: They've ♥♥♥♥ing "revamped" the economy system...or rather they've dumbed it down...what made TA and Sup Com 1 so unique WAS their economy system. You had income and spending. If you spent more than you earned, you would slowly lose accumulated resources, until you hit rock bottom and your economy would tank. Things would still be completed, just slower. That was good. Wanna build a ♥♥♥♥ing mega artillery with 10 builders? Be prepared to have unlimited resources or face the consequences. On the other hand, you had a clear build path, and once your economy got going, say hello to mass production...you know, how it should be...in a damn war. In Sup Com 2 you instead gather resources automatically, but you can only spend those you actually HAVE. Like in Starcraft for example. Hey, this building or unit costs 1000 mass and 2000 energy, better wait till you've accumulated that before anyone starts building...♥♥♥♥ this.
- Builders and plants: In Sup Com 1 you could assign several builders for 1 building, thus speeding up construction time if you had a good economy. Now only 1 builder may build at a time. At least you can still have them support the unit plants...for no additional cost by the way. Mass producing units also doesn't seem viable anymore since, at least in the early campaign missions, it's impossible to produce enough to actually create a massive army of 400 or so units...
- Buildings: The number of buildings has been substantially reduced. Right now I have access to a mass extractor, an energy collector a research facility, land, air and naval base, a radar station, a sonar station, a shield generator and 2 defensive structures for land and air...yay. That is the amount of buildings Sup Com 1 had as Tier ONE. The tier system is gone by the way. Just build 1 construction plant and it can build everything.
- Units: Same as buildings. There are only about 5 land units, 3 air units, 3 naval units and experimentals, which are for the most part rather "meh". Building an experimental in Sup Com 1 was a serious commitment and its loss was a devastating blow. On the other hand, these ♥♥♥♥ers could almost eradicate entire armies or bases on their own if the enemy did not have a valid counter. Remember the spider bots? Oh man...the megaliths the Cybrans have now are just a sorry excuse. The UED Fatboy II is a lot weaker than the original Fatboy, has no shields, no hit points and can't produce anyunits. What happened? Did they just forget how to build the good stuff after 25 years of peace? The UEF King on the other hand is a fun experimental...way too strong. Where is the balance here? I think it's good to diversify the factions more, but you shouldn't do so at the expense of complexity. Where are my patrolling air scouts? Where are my almost impossible to hit interceptors? Where are my T3 missile turrets? Where are my nuclear power plants? Where are my BRICKS!? Where are my almost indestructible warships? And my heavy gunships? Why do my air units hover in the air when they're not engaging enemies? And why are they swarming in a 1 by 1 area around each other when they are fighting? And why are they only flying at 10 meters above ground? Why don't they have to resupply anymore? That was cool!
Interface: It's cleaner, but also more generic and sorely lacking tool tips. What does a Poseidon battleship do? No idea. What's the range? Does it have AA? Does it have torpedoes? Apparently yes, but the game doesn't tell you. There are less options here and I don't like it all that much.
Research: Instead of building up your base, you now continously earn research points with which to unlock new buildings and units, improve your existing units (with personal shields or more damage for example), reduce build times or improve your ACU. A shallow system you have to deal with in every mission and match from the very beginning again. You building the biggest experimental units now just takes about 15 minutes maybe.
Combat: This is actually the best part about the game. Units move effortlessly and don't get in the way of each other. No excessive "rat's tails" as far as I can tell. Animations and ordinance looks good. It's fun to watch...BUT!
Graphics: What the ♥♥♥♥ were they smoking? They've replaced the somewhat gritty graphics from Sup Com 1, which were a nod to Total Annihilation, with some sort of cartoony mess. The UEF forces are bright blue and yellow with VERY little detail on them (apart from weapons fire, which looks great). They look like LEGOs for ♥♥♥♥s sake. The Cybrans are this yellow smudge of vomit, instead of the imposing black and red with the circuits on the ground, the GAAT gun laser towers, etc. It's a disgrace really. Supreme Commander Dostya would not approve...and neither do I.
Oh Sup Com 2, what you could have been...if you want to experience this 90s era gameplay, play Sup Com: FA (it's a lot better than the base game and most mechanics actually work). And then play Total Annihilation and rejoice!
DOSTYA OUT!!!

Battleborn suffers from it's early high price tag and inevitable comparison to Overwatch. While I would say the visuals and "feel" of heros and abilities feels better in Overwatch, Battle born has a lot going for it:
mission storyline campaign thing. It's actually pretty fun and the levels are varied - my favorite being the big boss battles.
is actually pretty fun - if you can find a match... The game doesn't play like Overwatch at all. I don't even think Battleborn and Overwatch share a game mode to be honest. The most popular game mode is clearly the moba style multiplayer, where you have to take down their base sentries before they take down yours. You have little creeps that push automatically against theirs, and can hire bigger creep types by either hunting "jungle camps" called Thralls or buying bigger creeps with Shards - the currency you get during individual games.
Shards generate in hard form all over the maps, and destroying them gives you, and anybody around you, shards to use on upgrading the base, turrets, or "purchase" the items you equiped before the match. Stronger items cost more, and you won't have the perks from until later in the game. You also level up during the game based on performance, and get upgrades to your abilities and access to your ultimate ability (which is really not *that* much stronger.
Overall, the multiplayer mode is fun, but it's hard to find a match. If you can pick this up on sale for $15, and are looking for a game to play co-op, I would recommend it.

Renowned Explorers: International Society is a game that is stands out from the pack and is not like any other game you've played. One playthrough of the game only takes about 5 hours, but this isn't a game where you just play it once. You need to play through it multiple times to get the most out of it. The good thing is that there is tons of replaybility to the game.
First off, you have 16 characters to choose from in order to make a team of 3. Each one of those characters has unique starting stats, and different skill sets divided into four different classes. On *top* of that, each character has a special ability that gets put into place when they are the captain of the team, but in order to unlock 12 of the characters to use as captains, you need to play through one full game using those characters. So you have plenty of incentive to try different teams to see who works well together and unlock the additonal characters as captains.
In addition to that, since there are multiple locations you can visit in a single playthrough, but can only visit five in total, you can taking a totally different route each time. Even if you take the same route, the nodes on the maps can be different each time, or you might end up being able to tackle different challenges with different team members, or being able to take a different approach to certain situations can change things up significantly. In each of the five playthroughs I've had, I've experienced very little repetition.
Oh, and one more thing. You have multiple difficulty settings, ranging from Easy, up to Impossible. There's also two modes available; Discovery, which allows for saving/loading anytime, and Adventure, which is an Ironman-style, every decision counts type of mode that turns this into a roguelike. Since you can use any of the four difficulties on either of the two modes, you effectively have EIGHT different difficulty settings.
Of course, there has to be enjoyable gameplay to make you want to play through it again and again, and this game offers that in spades. You have a world map, where you can spend 'Insight' that you earn to acquire resources like status, gold, and research, all of which you can then spend in various shops to improve your crew members.
From there, you go to one of the expeditions, travel through various nodes exploring what you can based on your supplies, which deplete as you travel. Each node can offer different challenges and encounters that will reward you with resources and treasure as you progress towards the final boss of the map.
Now, your ultimate goal in all of this is acquire more then 2500 renown and become the worlds most renowned explorer, and you earn this renown through treasures, and from the various resources depending on how you play the game. It is actually fairly deep and complex so I'll leave it to you to figure out yourself, but once you get it figured out, it's very rewarding.
The most enjoyable part of the game, at least for me personally, is the encounter system. It's based around emotions; you can be aggressive, which is your standard just 'beat the crap out of everyone' type of thing; but then have devious abilities, which consist of taunting and mocking your opponent to make them angry, sad and scared; or you can even use friendly moves to make them worship you in amazement, or convince them that your cause is the best one. The battles can change drastically depending on which mood you use, and what your opponent decides to use. Also, resolving specific encounters in different ways offers different rewards, and depending on who is in your team of three, you might be better suited to one type of mood or another. There's a bit of a rock/paper/scissors deal with the emotions, but sometimes it's not as simple as using the right emotion at the right time. Again, I'll leave the intricate parts of this system for you to figure out.
If you hadn't figured it out yet, I 100% recommend this game to everyone who's a fan of turn based games, as this offers something completely different from the normal stuff you find. The replay value alone is worth the money, along with excellent developers, a welcome community, and weekly challenges available from the forums that you can try your hand at for bragging rights.
Bottom line: go buy the game and get to exploring!

This is a cool little game that combines rouge-like elements with tactical RPG battles.  The UI isn't as polished at it could be, but the gameplay more than makes up for it.  It's one of those games that you can play for an hour, and then walk away from if need be.  It's pretty difficult, but certainly rewarding.
Also in regards to the battle system, I think it's really cool that fighting isn't the only way to solve conflict.  You can get through battles by being 'nice' or 'devious' in addition to just smashing the opponent.  These three techniques are kind of a rock-paper-scissors kind of thing, so be wary of which one you're using for each encounter.
I'm only ~12 hours in at the time of this review, but I'm confident that I'll be playing plenty more.  Excellent game!

RE:IS is excellent at what it tries to do, but might not be right for everyone.
RE:IS is highly polished, runs flawlessly on Win10 and is a refreshing take on D&D style games where you send a group of explorers into dungeons/wilderness in search of treasure. With cartoonish charm, they have reduced death and violence and substituted  manipulation, charm and seduction instead. A welcome change to killing everybody all day all night! Violence is one of 3 options. Instead of Hit Points, the battle is won when Resolve (the will to go on) is reduced to 0.
With four classes to choose from, you create a team of 3 exlorers and send them on 5 expeditions, returning to town in between. In town, you improve your gear and skills and level up your toons. After 5 expeditions, the game is over. There are a few maps to choose from but not a huge number, but you can replay them with a different team, skills and gear later. There is some randomness to how the maps are generated and play, but each map is a story, and the bullet points of the story are the same each time. Each time you play the Hungarian Fort map, you are seeking The Alchemist, for example.
As an older gamer, I find some of the graphics and sound effects a bit childish but simultaneously charming. And the ability to use speech instead of violence is totally overdue in this kind of game - VERY refreshing. This game will not be a life-replacement game for most people, but it is fun, solid and without any bugs that I could find. None. Very easy to get 50 hours of fun. I will probably get 200 out of it utlimately. Some people complain about the RNG, but I did not find that to be a problem. Yes, if you chose a boss fight, you might get swatted hard, but if you prepared properly and chose wisely beforehand, you will probably be OK.

When I started to play, I fell in love with this game right from the start. Here is why:
1) gameplay mechanics. Simple to understand, yet different from any other games I have played. You can approach every fight the way you want - be friendly about it, scare them off or fight them directly. Mix in emotions and moods, and you have a hell of a fight.
2) art style. It is cartoonish, but in a good way.
3) great replay value, even if some playthroughs take away from you only 2 - 4 hours (you may want to increase difficulity or switch modes where the game takes longer time to complete and there are no chance of saving as well).
4) While some games give u the feeling of Deja Vu (the feeling - you have been there and done that), this game is a complete opposite - it gave me this unique experience.
Overall an A+ game. I would recommend this product to everyone who likes the thrill of excitement exploring and discovering new worlds.

Amazing game! Buy it!
It takes the "dungeon delver" genre to a truly unique place. If you like rogue-like games, or adventure games, or just want to try something new, buy it!
It does rely on reading comprehension, and the many new mechanics perhaps takes a while to master, but it has a good tutorial. Think while you play, and don't be afraid of losing, and you will be fine.
Now, it does have some flaws. Most notably, it lacks a real end game. The goal of the game is to get 2500 Renown in 5 expeditions, but if you play the game sort of half-decent, even on harder difficulties, you will get way more than that ( have ended with more than 4000 when playing Iron man mode). Sometimes you get to that amount on 4 expeditions, and if so, the last expedition loses much of its thrills. I was expecting something to happen after the fifth expedition and the end of the game, but no. If you have enough Renown, you win.
So, the real challenge of the game is not to gather 2500 Renown at all. The challenge is to survive till the end!
The game is still in development, and another expansion is in the works, so perhaps a new end game will be added. Even if not, the game is still loads of fun.
Buy it!

Turn-Based Strategy is one of my favorite game genres, dating back to the original Age of Mythology and Age of Wonders.  (I like a bit more of a fantastical edge to my strategy games).  I'm also a fan of old school RPG's like Icewind Dale and Baldur's Gate that require you to work with the strength and weaknesses of a team to be successful.  That being said, Renowned Explorers has elements of these games, but also somehow presents a concept I've never really seen before.  And they do it well.
The game is high in replayability, mental strategy, and unique gameplay.  It offers a range of difficulty settings, but even the lowest offering presents enough of a challenge to make it not seem like just a point-and-click.  I particularly enjoy the multitude of offerings to enhance your team at the end of each campaign, with the ability to spend the spoils of your exploration not just on items, but also on helpful followers, researched enhancements and paid jobs.
The only thing I've disliked so far is how they keep the goal of becoming the top explorer in a short amount of campaigns as part of the gameplay even after the tutorial, making continuation after that achievement seem a little less important, even though there are plenty of campaigns available at that time.  They also cap the growth of the group members to five  new skills, which is generally reached right at or soon after becoming "Top Explorer".  I haven't played the Adventure Mode, nor have I looked at what the DLC has to offer, so maybe some of this is remedied there.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a new, enjoyable twist on turn-based strategy.

RE:IS has more going for it than just the gameplay, though - the artwork in particular is incredible, and can honestly I am in love with the gorgeous art style and humurous atmosphere, as well as the color scheme and everything you can see on screen; it's all beautiful. As previously said I find it difficult to fault any part of the game, although as a warning to those not aware:
Renowned Explorers is set up to engage you in multiple playthroughs, and so each completion of a new game (with the DLC) adds more content during your 5 expeditions per game, and by the fourth or fifth playthrough you will have a much better understanding of the game and its mechanics. If this puts you off, for example if you prefer a larger campaign in your games, then maybe this is simply not the game for you. However if this excites you then go ahead and buy Renowned Explorers: International Society ASAP; it might just be up your alley.

This is one of those rare instances where I wish I had done as the negative reviews had suggested and not bought the game.
Sadly I thought that, because Retention was so cheap, it would be worth the risk of buying it.  That did not turn out to be true.  Now normally I enjoy games that go out of their way to be different and try something new.  While it is safe to say Retention is something different that does not make it good in any way.  A big problem with Retention is that it promises a story that never happens.  The game description says you're given the 'opportunity to tell a man by his memories', but I found that this just amounts to you picking one picture out of a group of three and then being given a small one sentence summary of the picture (as if you already couldn't tell just by looking at most of them).  The ending you recieve  after picking one picture out of all 85 groups of 3 doesn't help clarify the story in any way.  I've played through it multiple times now and I still can't decipher how or why I unlocked certain endings (and you can unlock multiple ones at once) and not others.
Confusion is honestly another reason why Retention is not a good game.  Again this is a game which in the description promises a 'user-friendly interface'.  I did not find that to be the case.  Right from the start the only helpful information given to you is how to move between slides and that you have to pick one picture out of a group of three.  The problem is that the game starts you at the very moment when the man presumably got into his biking accident.  You must then go back through all 85 of his memories (the pictures you'll get tired of looking at because they never change).  There are many problems with this.  First is the fact that it's very hard to tell what picture group you're on. It took me way too long to figure out that the only thing indicating what group you're on is a thin strip of white that appears below the square of film you're on.  Second is that if you somehow miss a picture group you're kind of screwed.  The only thing that separates picture groups you've selected a picture from, from ones you haven't is a tiny (very easy to miss) + sign.  Those two things coupled with being forced to flip through all the pictures you've already selected and seen to see if you've done enough to achieve an ending and in the end being denied one because you missed one group (out of 85) is downright frustrating.
In the end the only good thing I can say about Retention is that it has some pretty pictures and okay music.  There is also the fact it has cards, but even those can't make up for the fact that Retention is bad game.

87 cents wasted. I would give it away just to remove it from my collection if I knew how. I keep looking for the next "Dear Esther"  but am about to give up the search.  Retention just a bunch of pictures with stuff written to make them seem profound. This is the type of _retention_ that one goes to a doctor for when their bowels are impacted. Also no full screen.

Think metroidvania in 1080p, a flat, colorful, and borderless art style, tighter controls, and a contageous sense of humor. This game really shines in its gameplay. The game is a brawler at heart, and its tight controls lend itself to a easy-to-learn, hard-to-master combo system that is satisfying to traverse through as you purchase more moves. The story is not novel-worthy; it involves a few unconnected subplots that eventually lead up to facing the grand boss. The characters, however, are memorable and all have their own unique, though twisted and somewhat ADD, quirks.
The bosses are challenging and satisfying. There are moments when the game locks you in an enclosed space and force a battle between you and waves of enemies. Not only do these battles reward you with a pinata and a sense of satisfaction after, they also force you to learn the combos before you proceed (some enemies can only be broken with a certain type of move). There are rooms that are dedicated to puzzle-platform rewards. They're almost always completely optional but yield a nice reward (like a heart piece) and a sense of achievement after.

The 'balls' powerup is terrible (as it is supposed to be), the glitch gremlin can freeze things in or out of your way (really depends on timing), and Mecha-Death Christ is usually out of the way (dangerously), and provides a screen nuke for enemies that I can gun down without assistance.  The Super Scope is a nice boost of power, but goes away after just one hit from any hazard... you won't hold onto it for long.

Now, for those who are more interested in the gameplay than in the scatological humor, I think the platforming is pretty solid. It
ludicrously difficult, but it's not as cheap as you may expect from a game with a premise like this. Sure, there are some parts where you can't help but get hit (one of the witches in the last section of Beat'em and Eat'em springs to mind), but for the most part it's all about timing and pattern recognition. Some people might complain about the instant death blocks, but I didn't mind them.
The graphics are pure 16-bit goodness, but the real highlight here is no doubt the music. The theme songs for Thy Farts Be Consumed and Laughing Joking Numbnuts are just amazing.
My biggest complaint are perhaps the controls. The characters could use a bit more traction, and there are times when they don't turn around when you tell them to (this is mostly noticeable in boss battles). That being said, this doesn't completely ruin your experience like in other games.
So in short: yes, I would recommend this game to those looking for a challenge, though it's best enjoyed if you're familiar with the series.

Unit animations are limited, while pathfinding and collision mechanics are dysfuntional, with ships on land and formations that leave two or three soldiers marching in the wrong direction.
Graphics are terribly static, aside from the rather wooden units. The maps are smaller than expected, with units moving slowly and having tiny range to compensate. Everything feels like sprites instead of 3d models, and not particularly good ones at that.
Sound quality is especially bad. Music loops and overlaps itself. Drummers and officers are silent, instead of classic drumbeats and shouted orders. Muskets and cannons sound like firecrackers.
Localization is poor. Some unit names are still obvious placeholders, the campaign description read like Google translate, and either there is no documentation or I haven't been able to find it, either through Steam or in the game's folders. So unless you already know the difference between Prussian and Austrian units, you're not going to find out now.
Playtesting seems almost entirely absent. Ships on land. Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V allow you to literally copy-paste entire armies in the campaign and random maps. Unit highlighting is inconsistent, and anything behind a building is invisible.
I bought this expecting a less-than-stellar rehash of an old game, and was still disappointed.

For a price of 12.99 as of 1/24/17 this is a fantastic experience for any rts goer. Wether if you like turtling or rushing or zerging, this game offers a decent mix of options spanning across the three different factions. The only issue you may find in comparison to it's previous game is the smaller map sizes, slightly less variety of units, a rehaul of the resource storage and building system and the lack of mod support.

A good strategy game for beginner-intermidiate players. The futuristic campaign is not bad for a RTS, and offers a good challenge on harder difficulties. The three factions do not vary much in strategy in the early game though their mid to late tier units offer unique game changing opportunities from the brutal to the subtle. Thanks to a simple but effective interface, the game is also easy to play.
Skirmish/Multiplayer is a profound improvement to its Xbox 360 counterpart, having good pre-game options and a variety of maps and 4v4 compatibility (though the game's speed will definitely suffer with 5+ players). AI difficulty is reasonably balanced with customizable strategies for them to use. Internet connectivity in PvP multiplayer is typically not a problem either.
Unlike its predecessor, Supreme Commander 2 is less complicated and therefore game sessions are typically quicker though long, protracted battles are still possible with the huge 500 unit cap and available rush timers. More experienced players may become bored by the lack of diversity in strategies that limits replayability, as many battles (especially against AI) hinge on simply building a ton of one super unit or another. The DLC adds some interesting units and buildings though.
Overall a good value for a RTS fan or newbie looking to try somethings new, but not the most robust experience out there.

Renowned Explorers: International Society is not your typical party-based RPG/Adventure game. I'm not even a good example to review this product, since this this is not my game genre, but when I bought it I decided to take a shot in the dark and, oh boy, was I glad I did... This game can suck an entire day out of your life simply because you are having too much fun with it and not even realizing. The sense of progression (the RPG part) is extremely satisfying: Every time you get a new perk or a new item for your charecter, you end up rediscovering the entire game. The sense of a strong party is also really good, since after three or four "encounters" (battles), you get a hold of your entire deck and understand the roles which your charecters will assume once in battle to achieve maximum efficiency. Of course the game's focous is the adventure you see yourself in and the infinite deck of possibilities is what really makes it fun. Choosing who is going to do what in a certain event decides everything you'll get from an exploration. To top it off, I'd just like to add how the devs perfectly integrated a dynamic combat system, with nine different variables that affect the gameplay, all of which depend on a charecters emotional strength, mood and defense power. You can learn more about this in the store page or just buyin' the game already, cause that is going to be my final point: Even if nothing in this review called your attention, many other things in-game will, being why I strongly suggest that you should buy Renowned Explorers: International Society.

I hadn't heard of this game though any ad, or any commercial, i heard it though a family member who had been tracking the game for half a year or something before it came out, seriously, marketing team blew the donkey on this one.

First impression after 20 minutes in single-player and 40 minutes in co-op:
Blue Estate is a rail shooter aka shooting gallery. It's like you're in an action movie and get to shoot everyone, but what to do apart from that is being decided for you (you can actually do some more things when prompted, but you get no say in what to do). The writing and some gimmicks are humorous; basically, if you like the trailer, you're going to like the game. The low difficulty setting seems ok even for casual players.
This game has local co-op, which means if you have a friend over, they can pick up an Xbox controller and start shooting as well: the goons will spread their shots between you, you get separate health bars, but apart from that it's pretty much single-player with two guns, with the added difficulty of one player having to aim with the thumb-stick instead of a mouse. (Dual mice won't work - I checked.) Maybe it works better if one player or both have a light gun or the leap motion?
If you want this as a co-op game, I'd advise against it because the co-op is really light-weight, and the guy on the Xbox controller has drawn the short straw; but if you ever want (or need) to play a first-person shooter with only one hand, or you like the style, want to turn your brain off and just  go "blam blam blam" then this game will be fun.

Excessive, vulgar and especially pleased with his own nature, Blue Estate is a shooter on rails certainly more memorable for its attitude hopelessly stupid, between noir and screwball, not for its gameplay itself. As a shooter is in fact genuinely pretty ordinary and not particularly memorable (missing something in terms of rhythm, with levels guiltily long boss fight not exactly inspired), but the overall experience manages to entertain and amuse by virtue of its ingredients speziati.Se you are sensitive to certain types of content and will go for an evening of enjoying a dip in the brain strictly off, let us a little thought , but don't tell to your wife.

+ Rail shooter
+ Humour
- Takes a long time to initially start up each time, without obvious reasons
- Displayed messages and cutscenes (that otherwise add to the atmosphere and humour), can be annoying/blocking actual gameplay.
Playing with the mouse is very efficient.
I also tried playing with the Razer Hydra. The MotionCreator has no profile for Blue Estate yet, and the default / what I tried was not good yet. The view tilted (after you hit the border, the controler was not centered any more), and shooting the AK-47 seemed to be inconsistent; sometimes triggering single shot and sometimes automatic.

This is what rail shooters should be. So many past titles have made such a mess of this category that a lot of people stayed away from the genre. So Im glad that Blue Estate did it right, brought life back to rail-shooters, and reset the standards.
Every games' biggest challenge is replayability. And rail shooters are especially hard to corner that arena. But Blue Estate challenges you jsut enough to want to go back and replay levels just to get higher scores. I just finished a level and I was trying to get my accuracy as high as possible. I swore I was up to at least 60% accuracy. Nope. Turns out I was only at 44%. Dammit. Now I have to go back and replay the level. And I also have to get all the little bonuses that I missed (watched them slide out of view before shooting them and thinking "Crap!")
just get this game. The price is right and you will not be disappointed. Seriously. You get bonuses for shooting guys in the nuts. So far, as a rail shooter, it is absolutely perfect. The writing is good too. Sometimes games go over the top with their ridiculousness. This one doesnt. It takes it right to it's appropriate boundaries of stupid and stays there threatening to jump over the line.

After playing Rambo The Video Game, I was left hungry for an on-rail shooter that was actually good and fortunately Blue Estate has filled that void.
Now I first played the demo of Blue Estate on the PS4 in 2014 and found it virtually unplayable. The developers had opted  to utilise the Dual Shock 4's built in motion to control your aiming. But it felt awkward and it was no surprise every second comment on the Playstation Blog urged the developer to implement Playstation Move, which at the time of this review hasn't been patched int the PS4 version.
Despite the control issues, I was in love with the game's B-grade tone and no thrills game play, so when a PC version was announced with mouse controls, I jumped on the couch, threw my arms in the air and said yeeehaaa!!!
The PC port gives you a choice of 32bit or 64bit version plus V-sync, adjustable resolution and three graphical settings (low, medium, hard). This is to be expected from a port of a console game. Control options include a mouse, 360 controller and supported light guns, which sadly I don't own the latter for my PC. Mouse is the way to go, especially since you can do almost every input and quick time event with just the mouse, no need to use the keyboard, although the option is still there.
With the controls and graphic options out of the way, let's talk about the actual game. As I mentioned before Blue Estate has a B-grade feel with the story starting with an Italian mobster trying to get his prized stripper back. Blue Estate stirred up quite a bit of controversy with it's racial undertones, sexism and cheesy jokes. See what these critics failed to do, was switch off their brain and learn to laugh at the fake Italian accents, sex jokes and general craziness. Every AAA game and film tends to look the same, but B-grade stuff is so dodgy, it has a charm of it's own and same can be said about Blue Estate. Movie buffs will also enjoy some of the nods to various films and directors.
Blue Estate is an on-rail shooter, meaning the character moves automatically and your only job is to shoot everything that moves. I love Blue Estate, because it doesn't try to over-complicate the formula with RPG mechanics, stealth or innocent hostages like Rambo or Heavy Fire. If it moves, you shoot it and that's basically it. The way it should be.
The production values of Blue Estate are quite impressive for a $13 game: catchy music, strong voice overs and is powered by the Unreal Engine with surprisingly good textures.
It's no surprise the story mode can be finished in 3 hours, after all it's a $13 game. The game also local co-op (sadly no online), multiple difficulties levels and an arcade mode to fill your boots up, if you're hungry for more.
Overall Blue Estate delivers a basic, but enjoyable on-rail shooter that at least has decent production values and some evidence of care, which can't be said about Heavy Fire or Rambo. Obviously the racial undertones and sexism will offend many people, but if you switch your brain off, I guarantee you will have a good time with this one, mate.

Whom of you born in the 90's remembers the arcades? Or Arcade-cabinets for that matter. I do and I found myself looking back at those times long passed as I was playing Blue Estate the game. Giving me nostalgic memories, Is one of the surefire ways of getting my approval. HOWEVER, it is also one of the most effective ways of getting burned at the stake if they soil those memories.
Luckily for HE SAW, they managed to avoid the latter.
Blue Estate is a great blast from the past, giving back the good name of rail-shooters and arcade shoot'em'ups. I won't go over the story, since what there is, is minimal at best. Let's just summarize it into: A pulpy, over the top, humorous, d-movie, with a lot of shooting thrown in. The game is based on a comic, however I haven't had the pleasure of reading it.
But, I can say. That if the comics are as fun as the game, they will be added to my collections post-haste.
But what about the game? Well, I think it's already obvious that I love this game. And everything I say must be adhered with a good measure of bias.
The game is short for what it is, but can it be blamed for it? I shall paraphrase "I would rather pay for a short and well constructed piece, than something made to take hundreds of hours." And that works with this game. Although it took me  under 4 hours to finish the game on normal difficulty, including the arcade modes. I can say that I enjoyed it greatly.
The game ran well on my PC, right now I'm downloading it onto my laptop. So i will update the post afterwards to tell you how it ran.
EDIT: Laptop.
After setting quality to low, it ran fine. Once again, it is the integrated Graphics-chip that is the hurdle. (Intel HD Graphics)
The games visual quality is pretty good, however I did notice some strange blurriness with some areas. Otherwise the game ran perfectly fine, there were no noticeable framedrops anywhere (PC). (Unreal Engine at work..)
The games voice-acting is wonderfully cheesy, giving the characters some great personality. The music is somewhat mediocre at some points, however it manages to settle well with the areas. Giving them a bit more life than you would normally see in a rail-shooter.. NO! I SHALL NOT SAY THE NAME OF "THAT" GAME. NO! ARGH!!
Anyway, where was I?
ah yes..
Overall, I cannot recommend Blue Estate enough. The price 13€ might be a bit steep for some people, especially considering the games length. However I personally feel that the gameplay in itself is a good reason to get the game. The story is a bit so-and-so, but it gives a few good laughs and snorts, with its somewhat silly references now and again.
For those who want some funny and enjoyable arcade fun, Blue Estate is the game for you.

As a die hard fan of the RollerCoaster Tycoon series I was extremely excited to try out the latest installment in the series. I avoided the reviews and Lets Plays on youtube purposely so that I could judge the game by its merits alone.
That being said, there is unfortunately a lot wrong with the game.
The path system is a disaster and half the time it refuses to let me place paths in places that are unobstructed.
The peeps are completely lifeless while they are on rides and you can watch them cycle through various terrifying facial expressions while remaining dead silent the entire time. (Its honestly only a bad soundtrack away from being a horror movie.)
Perhaps this is just a glitch on my end, but half the time buildings and rides don't actually show you whether or not they are closed which led me to accidentally forget to open half the stuff in my park. (Oops!)
I also noticed that the days seemed... Shorter? Like, almost ridiculously short. I feel like they could be slightly longer. In order to see my park at night I have to lock the time set to night time or else you'd miss it if you looked away for two seconds.
There are so many little things that could be fine tuned, that would make this such a great game. I want to like this game so bad because a huge chunk of my childhood was spent playing both RCT2 and RCT3. RCTW is just not holding up compared to even RCT3.
I'm hoping the developers really are serious about improving the game because it has so much potential. Until then, I cannot recommend it.

In the barest of descriptions, this game is a piece of interactive fan-art. It distills 8+ years of content from it’s legacy, The Angry Video Game Nerd (produced by James Rolfe, who is a pretty awesome guy) into a Nintendo-length and Nintendo-hard adventure. For those who have watched the web-series, it’s a short walk down memory lane, a challenge to find all the references and easter eggs, and a way to experience the trials The Nerd has experienced over the lifespan of the series. It was lovingly produced to be an intentional experience, and for fans, it’s delightful.
It’s important to point out that this game is not for everyone. Like most fan-art, you can appreciate the aesthetics if you approach it unaware of the original work, but a lot of the heart, depth and meaning will be lost. Yes, the “retro” graphics are charming and the game handles well, and you may even see inspirations in the level design from games like Castlevania if that’s your generation. However, with no other perspective, you will soon be frustrated by the games seemingly poor level design. The game constantly cheats and frustrates you, killing you time and time again at no real fault of your own. Things appear skewed against you in some very unfair and unfun ways, never relenting.
For fans of the series, however, this is expected. This game emulates the experiences of The Nerd throughout the video series, constantly subjecting himself to terrible games from the genesis of home gaming under the premise of warning others against their trespasses. This game takes a sampling of those horrors and concentrates them into one experience, each level its own little snapshot of gaming hell. The joy of playing this game is largely derived from nostalgia, remembering the Olde Games and the despicable things that they did to you, that they made you do to beat them. We remember afternoons and evenings spent dedicated to conquering just one more level, despite the awful controls, the contrived traps and the straight-up horrendous level design. It’s all we had, and we didn't know better. This was just the way games were. We hated them, but we kept coming back, learning to love them like digital Stockholme-suffering prisoners.
Conceptually, the game helps us remember simpler times, and for that I do recommend it, but with a caveat: If you aren't from the Nintendo generation, or you haven’t seen the Angry Video Game Nerd web series, then I highly suggest you experience those things first.

Wonderful game, a joy to play.
Hand pick your team of 3 from 20 colorful fighters, scientists, diplomats, and scouts with a wide variety of backgrounds and abilities.  Explore mysterious maps and overcome both text-based skill check challenges and turn-based combat.  Use charm, guile, sheer brute force, or any combination to win over, scare off, or pulverize your enemies as you search for treasure, gather resources and, most importantly, work to uncover the mysteries of the lost world.  But be ready for anything - relying too much on a single strategy will leave you wide open against its "rock, paper, scissors" vulnerability.
Did you play FTL?  Of course you did.
has a very similar structure, in which each expedition is like a "sector".  There are numerous points of interest and limited supplies, forcing you to carefully manage where your explorations take you.
A new addition to the formula is the downtime between expeditions.  Return to London, write research papers, shop for better equipment, gain an entourage, share your findings with prestigious universities.  Fine tune your team to optimize for your particular goals.  (Example: my first team was led by a scientist, and geared towards collecting research, gathering followers and unlocking buffs to magnify the rewards from scientific challenges.)
RPG elements are not fantastically deep, but satisfy quite well enough in context.  Like FTL, this is a game made to buzz through half a dozen adventures, build up to a final tough confrontation, roll credits and start again with a new team and/or on a higher difficulty.
Just about worth it full price, a no-brainer on sale.  Play it!

Renowned Explorers: International Society is a humorous choose your own adventure style strategy game with rogue-like and RPG elements such as inventory management, turn based combat, dialogue choices, and unique character upgrades/skill trees. The game is set in a vibrant and quirky version of the late 19th century where both magic and quasi-steampunk technology abound, making for an incredibly colorful and interesting world full of weird and wonderful people and places to discover. It is well written, thoroughly enjoyable to play, and suitable for all ages.
The goal of the game is to achieve the title of "Most Renowned Explorer" by assembling a team of intrepid adventurers for the purpose of collecting treasures from various exotic locations around the globe. Each location has its own set of mysteries and treasures to uncover, and every character has his or her own individual backstory and unique personality that can affect their synergy with other characters, your interactions with the environment, and thus your overall chances of success. The team you choose and the decisions you make along the way will determine whether or not you rise to unprecendented heights of fame and glory, or fade into total obscurity... or worse.
The game also features an innovative turn-based combat system that incorporates emotion and mood into the tactical gameplay, allowing for battles to be resolved peacefully as well as by the usual violent means. The result is a 'rock, paper, scissors' style element to fighting that adds quite a lot more depth to combat than the standard RPG fare of merely switching between physical attacks and magic attacks. Choosing to resolve certain conflicts with a particular method can even unlock new dialogue and treasure-hunting opportunities, which makes having to choose between a well rounded team and a highly specialized one all the more compelling.
In conclusion, I highly recommend this title to anyone looking for a truly one of a kind, lighthearted, and endlessly replayable adventure/resource management/strategy game in the spirit of FTL: Faster Than Light or Reus. An instant classic, in my opinion, and one made even better with the addition of the DLC.
10/10

If I could sum this game up in just one word it would be 'LAZY'.
Now you may say it's impossible to review a game after just one hour, but I did play this when it first came out in order to do a youtube review however, after playing it back then I decided it simply wasn't worth my time.
I saw from the 3 updates the devs posted on steam that they had 'made improvements', so I figured, as a police enthusiast, I would check them out. Sadly, nothing felt improved and the word LAZY kept popping into my head at every hair raising turn.
So where to start?
Firstly, I'll get the good out of the way because that shouldn't take more than a few sentences.
As a cop enthusiast, I have to say the game has some elements that are neat and if the devs hadn't been so LAZY, those elements might have led to some interesting events. The ability to stop vehicles, check lights tires, trunk contents etc are all things I'd enjoy doing in a well developed police simulator, but sadly after the first couple of times, they became repetitive and annoying, mainly due to the character interactions which I'll cover in a bit.  I did like that you could follow a vehicle, trigger an observation and things like no seat belt worn would flag up.
Ok, now the now on to the bad.
Firstly, the optimization is terrible.  My rig which happily plays the latest big budget titles on high settings, managed barely a slide show when I ramped the graphics up to high on this one which is crazy given how pathetic and dated the graphics are. Ultra high is an option, but I could only laugh at the thought.
I'll mention the 20 mins I spent on google trying to figure out why I couldn't move my character only to discover you have to disconnect ANY other controller that's attached to your PC.
We move on to the game play itself.  The first thing you encounter is the facepalm, and I mean FACEPALM driving mechanics. They are truly terrible.  After treacherously weaving my way on to the autobahn, I suddenly released why the devs focused much of the driving on a repetitive straight stretch of road., though even on this straight road, trying to keep your vehicle in lane isn't without its challenges. For a simulator, I wanted to lead by example, demonstrating good careful driving which sadly I never achieved, quite often using the center barriers like bumper lanes at the local kids bowling plex.
Which leads me on the my next issue. The simulation. Of which by the way there is none. In fact, the word 'simulator' should be forcibly removed from the title. Let's start with the basics, and I really to mean 'basics'.
There are absolutely zero character animations in this game bar walking and running and even those look terrible.  The simplest and basic animations like getting in and out of your vehicle don't exist. Press F and you teleport from your driving seat to the exterior of your car, and the same in reverse when you get back in.   There are so many simple animations that could have made things a little more immersive such as holding up a radio to your face when speaking dispatch, administering a breathaliser / drug test, taking the drivers papers, checking tires, but nope, that was too far of a stretch for these guys. LAZY!
Then there's the actual interactions with the drivers.  The questions you ask and the answers you get are the same word for word rehashed sentences every single time. After only my first 5 or 6 traffic stops, I could literally predict what was going to be said.  There is obviously only one or two responses for each question in the database, so why the devs didn't bother to actually voice them is a complete mystery. Oh wait. LAZY!  If the driver is standing outside his car, which he will be if you're responding to a car accident, he just stands there with his hands pointing out by his sides, penguin fashion. Apparently having them turn to face you when you speak to them was too much of a stretch for the devs. instead they just stare across the autobahn as though you don't exist. LAZY!
Now lets not forget interaction with dispatch. Again it's the same rehashed replies, but what annoys me even more is that they are instant. Ask to check ID on someone, they reply the second you click your question. They could hace had you wait a few seconds, perhaps giving the response 'stand by whilst I check for you officer', but no. LAZY!
If you arrest someone, there's no cuffs, no animation, no escort to police vehicle,  they just instaport straight into the back seat, and the entire scene including their vehicle and cones you placed just vanishes into thin air.   Even traffic stops were you issue a simple ticket, sees the car just  'poof' and vanish. I mean seriously? Is it too complicated to script it so it drives off, back on to that long cornerless straight road? LAZY!
At the start of your shift, you get a female partner who also just appears in your car. She sits there the entire time and NEVER gets out to assist no matter how serious the incident.  LAZY!.  There's no interaction with her, no conversation, nothing. LAZY!
Every single one of the so called 'dynamically created' incidents that were given by dispatch on my first patrol took place at a petrol station, the suspect vehicle parked in the same parking spot each time.  To frustrate me more, each time the station was on the other side of the autobahn forcing me to drive past it for a few minutes until I reached an off ramp, only to go back the other way for another few minutes till I arrived at the damn thing. I did this so many freaking times it didn't take me long to realise every single off ramp / overpass / on ramp is exactly the same cut and paste job. Same rocks same Y shaped tree, same stretch of road. LAZY!
There's no script that simulates other road users knowing you even exist. Pull out on to the road or switch lanes in front of one and he'll just carry on ignoring your existence until he smacks in to you. LAZY!
After inspecting the contents of a vehicles trunk / boot just a handful of times, you come across the same grouped items over and over again. You'll be amazed just how many Germans carry a teddy bear back there. LAZY!
The driving controls are dangerous! I'm not talking about the steering here, I'm talking about things like switching your emergency lights on, siren, high beam etc. All done through a point and click menu / sub menu system which you're supposed to do whilst driving your highly volatile death trap on wheels. LAZY.
And finally ( could go on by the way). There's the German text you encounter. The game is in english (albeit a German cop sim) but you have to deal with ID's papers and tickets in German and unless you speak the laungage, you'll have no idea what they mean. LAZY!
So there we have it. Unless you're a complete and utter law enforcement fanatic, you should avoid this lazy train wreck of a game, in fact, avoid it even if you are!
I have precisely 55 mins of game play left for my youtube review before I turn this excuse for a simulator in for a refund.

This is not a game for those who are easily offended.  The game describes itself as “black-humored”, aka 'dark comedy', therefore, it will make light of subject matters usually considered taboo and controversial.
Blue Estate 'The Game' is a first-person rail shooter developed and published by 'HESAW' which serves as the prologue to a comic book series of the same title.  The game features a rail-based shooting mechanic with a story that revolves around black humor, mindless violence, and goofy comic dialogues.
The game places you in the shoes of Tony Luciano, the son of a big time Italian-American mafia Don. The game also lets you play as Clarence, a former Navy Seal turned hitman for the Luciano family that cleans up after Tony's messes.
+ Good graphics with a nice comic book art-style
+ Free comic download that supplements the story
+ Great humor and witty dialogue however...(See CON #3)
+ Voice acting is really good with excellent delivery
+ Very good sound effects
+ Pop culture references and Easter-eggs add to the humor
+ Arcade mode and challenges extends game-time...because (See CON #1)
+ Co-op gameplay
+ Supports multiple input devices (Kb&M, Gamepads, and Leap Motion, possibly even Light Gun, though I've never tried it)
- The story is very short...however (See PRO #7)
(Patched)
- The dark humor may not appeal to everyone
-/+ The gameplay mechanics of rail shooters didn't really change since the good-ol'-days, however, this game does try to spice things up with some mini-challenges here and there.
for a rail shooter and is a perfect party game if you have a Steam Machine or Living Room PC.  Though some people believe that the genre is from a by-gone age, I think that it just needs a proper subject matter and premise to breathe it new life.
Blue Estate ‘The Game’ is a great example on how to make the rail shooter genre relevant in our modern gaming age.  Featuring black (dark) humor with interesting characters and a 'more-or-less' over the top plot, it makes for a good 'B Movie-esque' experience that is both fun and enjoyable.
Priced at a fairly reasonable $12.99 price tag (or your regional equivalent), the game is well worth your attention if you are looking for a casual, arcade, and comical first-person action game.  It doesn't take itself seriously and it brings back the fun and excitement of classical arcade games such as Time Crisis and House of the Dead.  I highly recommend this at FULL PRICE and is a no-brainer during a SALE.

This is the first Hitman game i've ever played, and i liked it more than i thought i would. It's essentially a puzzle game set inside real-world sandboxes - you walk around in plain sight trying to figure out how to best distract or impersonate the guards to get to your target and then get back out again. It is very refreshing to play a game that has a true-to-life amount of civilians walking around in it instead of being stuck in abandoned city blocks or enemy bases. Of course, if you start attacking those civilians indiscriminately, you will be dead in no seconds flat. Really cool concept.
The unfortunate thing is that the game is designed around trial and error. You have to die over and over to figure out what places you are allowed to go, and to figure out the movements of your targets. You also get limited saves, so eventually it just gets frustrating. It's a testament to the game that even after i started using walkthroughs to figure out where to go without having to repeat sections over and over it was pretty fun. If you are into pure stealth spy games (there are no dialog options/conversation challenges), it's certainly worth the pittance it goes for these days.
