Played: Feb 2014
Pros:
+ Very comfortable controls that allow you to move intuitively (with controller)
+ Interesting visual style
Cons:
- Feels very short
- Some enemies get very stale by the end
- Story starts promising and ends nonsensical
This game bills itself as a “metroidvania” type platformer, and let’s face it: it pretty much is. Some areas are inaccessible until the correct special movement is unlocked, but ultimately there aren’t that many special moves, so many areas are open to you right from the start. You play as a luchador, so there won’t be any weapons to find, either; the few additional moves you can get in the game are all grapples (a move you can complete when smallish enemies have taken enough damage). The low number of moves contributes to the short feel of the game (probably about 8 hours for the first play-though), but man are they satisfying! Throwing a damaged enemy through a whole crowd of others and sending them flying like bowling pins should bring a grin to anybody who picks up this game.
On the other hand, there are only a few enemy types, and late-game difficulty increase consists largely of forcing you to take on more of them and introducing some unblockable types (read: fire-based attacks). As you get good, you’ll find that you can destroy many enemie types in 1-2 seconds, which is good, because otherwise you’d get really bored fighting the same 8-10 monsters.
The story starts out feeling epic, but pretty quickly you find you’re actually just rescuing Princess Peach from Bowser again. The boss minions of the main enemy have very crudely sketched reasons for working with him, nor is it ever clear just why your girlfriend was abducted in the first place. Furthermore, the devil is introduced as a character, then plays essentially zero role. Why introduce a pointless character you might ask? Maybe because the developers just wanted to… in any case this is not a game you should play because it “features elements of hispanic culture”-you won’t pick up any traditional lore at all.
Overall, the game is pretty darn good, and very memorable in some parts. You may find that you’ll get replay out of it if you go in for additional modes unlocked at the end of a run, but I’d try to get it for less than $10 if possible.

Great remake of the Original game. Personally, I find it a very succesful release.
There are some very minor problems that I feel are worth mentioning, but please note that I'm nitpicking, and overall the game is fantastic from what I've experienced in my first couple hours. Whilst there are a large amount of minor problems, it's important to remember that they are really, quite minor. They will be patched in the near future, and do not make the game 'unplayable' as some claim.
It may not have had the smoothest launch of all time, but then again what game does, these days. I am confident they will quickly and efficiently resolve the issues at hand.
Pro's:
- Overall gameplay:
The gameplay feels smooth. Optimization seems solid. So far no problems.
- Regiments:
There is nothing quite like being able to form individual regiments with their own officers and drummers. Very cool.
- Stunning visuals:
The game looks smooth, modernised whilst staying in touch with it's original style.
- Rifle sounds:
The sound of regiment after regiment firing sounds fanstastic.
- Nostalgic feel:
They succesfully managed to stay in touch with the feel and style of the original.
Cons:
- Minor bugs:
Currently, there are some minor problems and glitches. For example, at times the ships sort of 'hover' over the water rather than actually rowing, and the oars sort of warp back and forth. Looks a bit odd but you really have to zoom in to notice.
- Audio:
Like I said, the overall sound effects are great. I can't help but feel a little dissapointed when it comes to marching & cavalry however. Infantry drummers visually beat their drums, but it creates no actual drum audio, which would have been cool. Also, the sound of thousands of men marching or horses prancing about should have a fitting audio, and be noticeable. Currently it sounds like a handful of guys walk around or 3 horsemen are riding, rather than a full army. Would be nice to see this changed.
-Canons:
I can't help but be frustatred by the canons. Would it really have been so hard to implement two or three guys standing near them, acting as cononeers? I don't even demand they actually do anything, but it would have been nice to at least have them standing there. Currently the canons move on their own (magic?) and act as individuals , without actually being manned. To me this is really off putting. Would be nice to see this altered.

Renowned Explorers (RE) is my kind of game:  quirky, unique, slow-paced, easy to snack on, and just variable enough to motivate repeated plays.  Which is not to say it's without some flaws.
RE defies categorization.  You'll see it described as a "rogue-like" but I think that's a misnomer.  It certainly doesn't feel like one to me.  There's greater characterization and better narrative, and you have a distinct goal (win-condition) beyond just surviving for as long as possible.  Rather, it reminds me of big, theme-heavy adventure-RPG boardgames like Arkham/Eldritch Horror, Runebound, Fortune & Glory, etc.  Collect a party of heroes with different skill-sets, send them to unique locales where they will face challenges (i.e., skill checks) and gain experience & loot.  Then, level them up, buy better equipment, and set out for a tougher but more rewarding expedition.  GIven that I love boardgames, it's perhaps not surprising that I quite like RE.
For brevity's sake, here's my quick list of pros and cons...
Pros:
1.  The length of a single "campaign" feels just right to me.  In order to win, you need to complete 5 expeditions - with the additional goal of accruing enough Renown to rank higher than all your competitors.  In actual playtime, this can take you around 1-3 hours (depending on how leisurely you are about shopping).  That's perfect for a relaxing Saturday morning with a cup of coffee.
2.  There's a nice ebb and flow to RE.  You go on an expedition, which will involve ~7-15 "encounters" - some of which are battles and some of which are skill-checks.  You'll win most of your skill checks, but there's enough chance for failure that it's still tense when the RNG kicks in.  Combat is interesting and maybe a little muddled (more on that below), but you'll have only a few battles per expedition and, again, that feels just right.  Once the expedition is over, you fly back to London to spend research points, buy better equipment for your crew, and gather an entourage (which boost your ability to collect resources).  The back and forth between exploring and leveling feels great.
3.  There's a fantastic selection of characters to choose from, and it's here where a lot of the replayability in RE comes from.  There are different classes that comes with different starting skills (scientists, scouts, etc.).  There are glass cannons and tanks and everything in between.  You'll want to try another run-through with an entirely different cast.  And these crews will largely determine how you approach combat:  with friendly diplomacy, devious emotional manipulation, or outright violence.  Once you learn the systems of the game, you can start seeing synergies and possible strategies (e.g., choose 3 characters with the ability to terrify and unlock the research tree that enhances the power of terror).
4.  The difficulty seems tuned just right.  It's tough to win a campaign, but not so tough that you're discouraged and wondering if the designers are sadists.  It took me 3 play-throughs to win my first campaign on the "classic" (hard) difficulty.  It felt good winning and I thought that I had made a lot of solid decisions that helped me get that far.  After 15 hours of play, you'll be able to win most of the time unless you take big risks to try and max your renown.
Cons:
1. There's maybe not enough variability in the expeditions themselves.  I'm already a little tired of seeing the same locations and fighting the same bosses.  This game will really benefit from DLC and mini-content updates.
2.  There's definitely not enough variability in the equipment.  I was disappointed to discover that shops always carry the same stuff, and it never varies between games.  That seems like a missed opportunity to make every run-through feel different.  As it is, I'm already finding myself gravitating towards the same items/build-order on each playthrough.
3.  The combat is opaque at first - and once you discover how it works, I'm not sure if the added complexity is worth the price of admission.  It all depends on whether you're looking for another position-based tactical game (X-COM, etc.) or whether you're willing to try something new.  There's less emphasis on positioning and % hit-rate, and much more emphasis on trying to maximize damage output via manipulation of the innovative emotion system.  On your first couple playthroughs, you'll be largely confused about the variety of effects and modifiers - but if you persist, the tactical layers reveal themselves in a very satisfying fashion.
Overall, I strongly recommend the game.  A great mix of adventure-RPG-tactical gameplay.  One of my favorite gaming experiences of the year so far.

This is a unique game in many ways, and also very enjoyable. It's not the kind of game where fast clicking or amazing eye hand coordination is much help at all, and for me, that's fantastic. It's a strategy game with some story and a lot of humor, and I find I get very attached to the characters in my party very fast.
(such as screaming 'No Vlad, you can't have Ivan!!!')
The game is set up so you can select a party of three explorers of varying strengths, and you can choose throughout the game how they'll develop.
One of my favorite aspects is that you can choose to be very different explorers from game to game in how you 'battle' those who you encounter. You can be friendly, devious, or outright aggressive, meaning that talking is not a free action anymore and can in fact defeat an opponent, whether through messing with their head or convincing them that you're awesome and they should help you.
I highly recommend this game for its unique approach, its humor, and its art. Also, it's not 'America-centric' in its choices for your explorers, as they come from every continent and many different backgrounds, from a tiny Austrian magician to an Argentine diplomat's daughter to a wild Australian (and of course a loveable Russian giant).
Personally, my favorite explorers are Bia, Daisy, and Anna, but I haven't even gotten to playing all of them yet, so who knows if it'll stay that way.

Still, overall, a fun game, but if you're like me and bad at these sorts of games despite loving them, you will find yourself dying and starting campaigns over fairly consistently which can be a bit tedious due to the repetition.

By now, you’ve probably noticed that
is not a game that is renowned for its subtext or avant-garde design philosophy: it’s a standard, console shooter. There’s not a whole lot else to say really, but I’ll try and keep preaching as much as possible.
You play as Mr. Generic, yet another ♥♥♥♥ing prodigal test subject that just can’t seem to catch a break. Cursed with stunted legs and an eternity of walking slow as♥♥♥♥♥♥ you're tasked with doing something or rather, with Monolith clearly caring enough to fill you in during the occasional loading screen for the super, special task of
Simply put, you’re going through some rough times as a psychic nudist stalks you, and things don't improve once the tentacles start showing up and Prince “Snake Fist” Charming gets involved. (Just another day at the office, I guess.)
Visually,
looks quite good for its age and there's a nice burst of colour when compared to the grey palette of its predecessors. Combat isn't particularly enjoyable, but I honestly don't care enough to bother hating it. Enemies chatter over coms and demonstrate some decent AI, but you can literally just walk forward for the entire game, firing aimlessly and hit the slow-motion when needed. That's it.
As for how "scary" it is, I can't say. Just like playing the original games, I've coincidentally ended up playing them while tired and bored, so I sat there stone-faced and yawning the entire time. If blood and guts is your thing, you might enjoy the atmosphere b— what’s that? Damn. The power went out. Here comes the spooky sound design and light show.
Still, the gore and dismemberment is great and the satisfying crunch and splatter really helps immerse the player in the joys of corporate espionage and crimes against humanity. Mmhmm.
All jokes aside, I'd like to dedicate this review to the GameSpy client and the potential replay value that could've been had outside of the incredibly forgettable campaign. The ending is quite the surprise though, leaving you reeling at how short the game was. "Wait, is that it?" I hear you ask. Why, yes, my inquisitive friend! Yes, it was.
Dialogue is pretty hilarious and the writing isn't much better, featuring such gems as "Have you ever seen a hippopotamus fight?" and "You must be hurting for some hurting." Characters are clichéd, through and through, with Lt. "Zoey-not-Zoey" Stokes as the titillation/badass material.
also wins the award for the funniest boss fight in history, allowing you to gaze at a snivelling moustache during an infinitely looping series of QTEs.
I did enjoy hearing one of the NPCs from
though, but the influences don’t stop there either with a bit of throwback to the
series. (Let’s not forget the “prototype energy weapon” as well.)
doesn't do anything particularly wrong, but it doesn't do a whole lot right either; an exceedingly average experience even with the flashy engine and technical tricks. Thumbs down.

This is not a bad game, but it has serious limitations which are a) infuriating and b) extraordinary considering this is about the fifth version of the game.
My kids love the sandbox version, which allows them an unlimited budget to put together the teme park of their dreams and ride on the attractions they've created.  Frankly, $30 is quite a lot to pay for a kid's game.
The campaign game, whereby grown-ups attempt to achieve goals, seems buggy.  The first time I played it, it gave me the option to build a handful of rides, but no paths.  Even as the game was telling me that I needed to build paths so park visitors could reach the rides that I'd built, it was giving me no option to build a path.
The second time I played it, it gave me a paths option after a few minutes, and then a buildings option.  Then, after I'd built a few buildings, it took the buildings option away, and refused to restore it, even after I'd expanded the park substantially.  The game was telling me that my visitors were hungry, but denied me any opportunity to build restaurants.  The game told me rides were breaking down, but denied me any opportunity to build mechanic stations to provide the machenics to fix the rides.  Eventually, my park simply ground to a halt.
At no time did the campaign game provide me an opportunity to build a flower bed.  I see lots of screenshots above of luscious parks, with lamps, and decorations, and attractions, but my experience is that you can only create such scenes in the sandbox version in which everything is unlocked.  Althogh I played the campaign games to the point that I had fairly extensive parks, never could I have constructed the screenshots in the publicity.
Paths are the single, most-infuriating thing in the game.  In real life, you can build a path anywhere.  In Switzerland, they buld entire freeways across the Alps and through some of the world's largest mountains.  So why is constructing a dirt path across your theme park a great world of "You can't do that"?  You need to make very certain in advance of where your paths are going to go, and you can't add to many extensions to them without extensive demolitionand reconstruction.  Visitors on the path constitute obstructions, so if you're hoping to rebuild a major pathway, you have little option but to close the park and wait for the traffic to clear.  This will take a very long time and represent a potentially catastrophic loss of income, but it's the only way you can reconstruct a path!  Other problems with path construction are too numerous to detail here.  Suffice to say that probably noting in this game will raise your blood pressure  more than path construction.
All this said, the sandbox version is a lot of fun, in a SimCity kind of way.  If all you want to do is construct the theme park of your dreams, and then ride on all your attractions, it's great.  But I find it extraordinary that the developers have allowed the program's very obvious weaknesses to go ahead -- or even that the program's weaknesses weren't taken with in previous versions.  By the fourth version, you really shouldn't have to be enduring the frustration of non-functioning software! Actually, you shouldn't have to endure it in the first version.
It has the potential to be a really brilliant game.  Were it not for the bugs, it would be.  But it seems to have been released on a premise of, "It'll do."  The assumption seems to be that, if the graphics are brilliant (and they are superlative!), the public will forgive you if they don't actually work.  Well, I'm not a programmer.  I don't play a game for the joy of exclaiming, "Egad!  What good-quality graphics!"  When I pay $30 for a game, I expect it to have been thoroughly tested and to work perfectly.  And this game is anything but that.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This game took me literally by surprise! It has been quite a while since I played this type of game (rail shooter) and actually enjoyed it immensely.
You will play Tony Luciano (son of a jovial mobster) and Clarence, an ex-Navy Seal, in a 7- chapter story pack of black humour.
You will have the pleasure of calmly visiting the twin Dragon club to rescue your sensual dancer; you will be entertained in a prestigious golf club avoiding very small projectiles (bullets); and you will even be a health inspector in a chicken factory.
Make every shot count to maximise your combo. But be quick though, as you have a small amount of time between each kill. Go over the time limit and you will have to start your combo all over again. It is a bummer when you reach 150 hits in a row and miss the next one because of a stupid bottle. That’s right; make sure you kill these annoying bottle-throwers or you will get a bottle right in your schnoz!!
The game runs smoothly and has really nice and polished graphics. I personally like the artwork in each introduction. Oh, and the soundtrack is brilliant too! Absolutely Marvellous and plenty of fun!

People really hate on this game because it diverts from orignal by a lot, it makes a lot of stuff a bit easier and simpler. If you like a game that requires less build up and more action, like pretty much all modern rts then this is for you. If you like a slow start and more strategic elements that eventually lead to huge battles then maybe you should played the orignal or better yet the standalone expansion FA. This game is all about proper micro in the begining and massing units very early, its very easy to do this and you don't need to worry about a lot of stuff in the older games.
I for one think it was a good idea to make it easier to play, a lot of the mechanics in the older game were very dated to have continue. Veterancy is easier, it was made into experience which is gain through kills, even though its the same thing its easier to achieve then even FA. FA and supcom was a game all about economy, since a player with a better economy was going to outpace a player with a bad one. Time is the major factor in most RTS games since the start of the genre, and the time in SUPCOM was very precious even mores so since the maps were soo big, you had tier lists of units and resource management was very harsh. If you broke your limits you were penalized very badly for it, thus newer players were put off by this. The games went from several hours to under an hour for most games, which is good.
They eliminated the oversized maps, the maps are still big but units move faster and have more ways to get around, they elimnated the pointless tier list on units, so your units are relevant as long as you upgrade them consisently and they made resource management easier by paying stuff in lumps sums instead of letting you bleed your mass at a constant rate, thus crippling you if your overspent.
They made over 25 experiements and many of them are very unique and different, some olds ones come back in either the orignal game or the DLC, the DLC is worth getting btw. You can release them halfbaked which lets them come online faster but with a risk of being disabled every ten seconds or so, it allows you to defend yourself if you really need them online or if the factory is about to be destroyed.
The game engine is a vast improvement and the AI is way more difficult to fight in this game, in the old game you could bunker down with turrets and the AI would endless attack in the same way every time. Turtling is harder in this game, as shields don't level up like they used too and defense is always the same level of turrets, unless upgrading in the tech tree. The AI usually picks what it wants to focus on whether land, sea or air and it loves to used nukes whenever it can get them.
What i don't like about this game is i think the Cybran are OP, if they get a naval factory is pretty hard to comeback with both Illuminate or UEF. They get the navy legs upgrade so their ships can walk on land or the jump jets so they can fly over mountains and obstacles. They're like mini experimentals but way easier to mass and they have turrets, radar, aa, missles and the works. Its feel very unbalanced. I also don't like that the illuminate don't get a navy, their units just hover on water. I get that its very powerful for them but i feel they should be given a proper navy. I also feel like some experiemntal units are pretty useless, the king kriptor looks and acts like a colossus, its armed with dozen of weapons and firepower, its straight out of power rangers but it feels weak as hell compared to the DLC cybran monkey king which rekts all land experiementals on UEF and illimuniate. I understand its iconic but the cybran were already OP with the navy units but now they get this thing and it even stronger than its supcom stats, its outrageous.
I would buy this game even at its full price, i got a ton out of it and i find it better than the orignal and FA, i played those to death as well. This game is just way faster and easier to get into, most RTS feel the same way as this game did. The old supcom was an oddity for rts back in the day, it was still good though.

The game has potential to be something great... buuut with how it's looking so far, and from what i hear about the plans for it in the future, i can't possibly see myself enjoying this game very much. Why? i'll explain...
First off, the small little rides you can set up here and there (ferris wheels, gravitron, merry go round, etc) are all nice and work flawlessly... But the moment I try building a  coaster, it just starts eating up SO MUCH MEMORY.
Yes, this game uses up so much memory and processing, it's insane. It's definitely NOT optimized what so ever. I'm on a high end computer that can run just about every single game i have on here on max settings with flawless performance... but for some reason, this particular game, whenever I try building a coaster, or even spawn a premade one, it freezes up, crashes, and gives me a warning/error saying that too much memory is being used. Then java stops working, aaaand it dies all together. I learned this the hard way when I was spending a lot of time setting up paths, small rides, concessions, etc... and when i finally said "Alright, i think it's time to build a coaster!" Not even half way done with it, and it froze up and crashed and gave me that error.
At first I though it was just an instance, so i booted it up again and gave it another go. Same thing. Any time I tried making a coaster,  it just died. So there goes all that time on an unsaved game. Oh yeah, that's another thing. The game doesn't have an autosave feature and I feel that if it's going to crash like this often, it probably should have one.
To sum it all up...
It looks cool and all, but holy hell, it just sucks up so much memory, your computer can't handle it and ends up halting it's processing on it all together automatically. So if you don't have a good computer, a REALLY GOOD COMPUTER, with LOTS of memory, then this game isn't for you.
It's a shame... I was so excited about this game too. I love the RCT games and have been waiting for this one for years, only to see that it's in no way, shape, or form, ready to be played at all. And judging by what's being discussed by the devs, it's not going to be enjoyable in the years to come. =/

Well i spent over a week deliberating this one, in light of the mixed reviews. I ended up watching video reviews online to help me make up my mind.
I'm glad I bought this game. I prefer sims over any other genre, and I always thought a highway police sim would be cool.
Personally, I really can't understand why there's so many negative reviews. I guess a lot of them were written prior to the updates/patches, which appear to have corrected most of the bugs and glitches. It's really not a bad game at all if you're into simulators. And i think this is where most people make the mistake of reviewing it like a regular game instead of a sim.
It can become very tedious and involved, and you can easily lose track of time and your surroundings while playing it. But for me, that is essentially what simulators are all about. They do, after all, have to replicate their real life counterparts. So be prepared to spend looooong periods of time driving, inspecting vehicles and talking to drivers.
That's not ALL there is to do in this game though. You can stop ANY vehicle whenever and wherever you want on the autobahn. You can issue speeding tickets, warnings, fines for offences and defects, and of course arrest the serious law breakers for being under the influence of drink or drugs, or for trying to evade you when you go to pull them over. There's a variety of offences to be found, such as erratic driving, using a mobile phone while driving, not wearing a seat belt, and driving an overladen vehicle.
You can choose from either a marked or unmarked patrol car each time you leave the police station, and attend accidents, investigate reports of suspicious vehicles, and even pursue and recover stolen vehicles. In the boot/trunk of the car you'll find traffic cones, axle scales, and road warning lamps for securing accident scenes. You'll even be working a mix of day and night shifts.
Sooo, let's wrap this up.
Pros:
- Half decent graphics
- Variety of events and incidents to keep you entertained
- Extensive procedures for each task
- Ability to decide what action to take when dealing with drivers
- 40km of Autobahn to patrol
- Promotions awarded as XP increases
Cons:
- Blue light is distracting during in-car view
- Documentation in the game is displayed in German (licenses, waybills etc)
- Vehicle controls aren't great when using keyboard, so a wheel is recommended
- An understanding of German traffic law is almost essential with a few of the tasks, as the manual does not explain it
These are just a few thoughts off the top of my head following a few hours of gameplay.
In summary, I love this game. It does what any decent simulator SHOULD do. It puts you in someone else's shoes and gives you an insight into a different world. I can see myself playing this for a long time to come, and I personally believe the replay value will be quite high.
I only hope the developers might introduce some more scenarios and vehicles over time.
If you've been pondering this one. Get it. You won't regret it!

I am a huge strategy buff, and let me tell you, I have had a hard time finding a game that aces the RTS feel like SC2. I have nearly 500 hours in the game and have been playing it for what feels like forever. Especially when you combine the origonal in-game content with the DLC (I think its like $5 or something, theres no reason not to get it), you have such a fantastic range of buildings and units, affording you so much in the way of letting you pick your strategy.
The maps are fun and interesting, if maybe a little static, and a few really push you into a specific, predictable strategy, but every RTS game ive ever played has those.
The factions are very nice as well, each having the ability to suit multiple different play-styles, but they do certainly favor certain play styles. For instance, UEF favors highly armored, slow moving but hard hitting units, whereas the Cybran favors a huge mass of highly mobile assault bots, but can also bring some impressive gargantuans into play. The Illuminate favor a heavy tech tree, improving their units with research, as well as having some intense buildings and upgrades that can make them a force to be recconed with late game.
The game was pretty intense for its time, but I feel that hardware has definatly caught up to the software SC2 is running. I have a GTX 1060 with 3 internal GB, with 16 external sticks to back it up, and I can run everything on max even late game.
Now, my primary complaint with SC2 is that it has what I feel doesnt offer the HUGE, MASSIVE armies, capping players at 500 units, to include buildings as well as units. Most typically, I feel that it really doesnt bother me most times unless its very late game, or I am playing Cybran. If the game had a feature that allowed me to modify the unit count, this game would be 10/10.
TL;DR: SC2 is a fantastic RTS, killing alot of modern RTS games IMO. The mechanics are super solid and the game works really well. Awesome game.

The closest comparison I can draw from this game is to "Planetary Annihilation", which is also on Steam. It's a good comparison to make on account of the fact that P.A.'s developers have background experience on this game.
Both play very, very well, and very similar to one another. The big difference here, however, is that although the maps are smaller than Planetary Annihilation's planet(s), the combat and pace of the game is much more intense in my opinion. 10 minutes in and high volumes of artillery are upon you. What I find interesting is that this game has a different focus altogether when it comes to combat. Planetary Annihilation, to me, is sort of emphasizing base building and solidifying your claim on the planet you're on. RTS favorite StarCraft II has unit combos and rock-paper-scissors gameplay. This game's focus seems to be on technological warfare, if that makes sense. Like Planetary Annihilation and StarCraft II, this game still focuses on building bases, generating resources and building armies to use against your enemy. However it favors an interesting twist on the research/technology tree in that research points are generated by way of in-game buildings, and the research points are spent across five different tech trees. More of these buildings give more research points, which mean more upgrades, new units and new buildings.
Graphically and in terms of its engine this game is GREAT, especially in contrast to the two other strategy games I've used in comparison. Looks nice and runs very well on most systems. It doesn't by any means have super high-tech cutting edge graphixxx or whatever, but its graphics and in-game models most certainly meet the standard of the game's release year, 2010.
Ultimately this game remains obscure and unknown to most, which is a shame since it's the perfect game for people playing on somewhat older computers, and for people looking for very, very fast-paced combat.

So after having completed this game on Normal difficulty, I thought it only fair to leave some feedback on it.  Make no mistake: This is one of the hardest games ever.
At its core,
(
for short) is a platform and action game; comparing it to
is a fair reference.  You carry a simple blaster fasioned after the old Zapper light gun peripheral for the original NES.  You can occasionally pick up a rocket launcher in the design of the old Super NES peripheral, the SuperScope.  The platforming is tougher-than-nails, and very few of the stages are what I might call easy, even after multiple attempts.
The overall atmosphere and level design are very well done.  It's easy to see the retro influence in the stages.  For example, the sky stage features monsters fashioned after the Air Tikkis in
; another features a labyrinthine castle-like section clearly inspired by
.  The enemies in these stages are suitably varied, as well, and much of the game's music is also well done.  From an aesthetic point of view, the designers did a great job.
So now we need to discuss the afore-mentioned difficulty.  I find the challenge in this game to be completely uneven and outright sadistic at times.  The game is clearly meant to be retried over and over and over again; why else would you start out with 30 lives?  You're only ever given three units of health (indicated by beer bottles, of all things...); there is no way to earn more.  You lose a full unit with each hit and can only ever recover one at a time by finding beer bottles within a particular stage.  One-Ups are also extremely scarce.
The old standby of getting hit to become invincible for a couple of seconds works somewhat in this game, as well, though certain hazards ignore your invincibility frames and can still kill you on contact, similar to how spikes ignore invincibility in the original
.  Often, enemies will hit you and knock you into such a hazard; when hit in this game, you do recoil, whether on the ground or in the air, making it very easy to fall into a pit, as well.  Additionally, if you have picked up the rocket launcher, a single hit from an enemy takes it away; you don't even get to carry it until you lose a life.  Given that it's almost always positioned in a particularly nasty section of a stage, this makes it almost worthless as you are almost guaranteed to lose it as soon as you get it.
The introductory stage is deceptively easy; in fact, I completed it in one life on the very first try.  Once I reached the main part of the game, it took me many tries before I even found a stage I could complete.  You luckily can tackle stages in any order you choose, and you only have to restart a level entirely if you lose all lives within it.  For the most part, the checkpoints are plentiful enough that you rarely have to repeat lengthy sections, and you always restart at a checkpoint when you die, provided you have lives remaining.
One of the problems I found with the game, however, is with collision detection.  Even this is somewhat uneven; sometimes, you can get right up on a hazard, such as the skull blocks, but other times, having even a single pixel touching a hazard is death.  I found this to be particularly true with the Rainbow Beams in the final level; many times, I couldn't even TELL I had a pixel within range of one, then suddenly found myself exploding in bloody death.  Play control also seemed tepid sometimes.  I would try to turn in one direction only to have the game not respond at all.  My inconsistent experiences with these aspects of the game only added to the overall frustration.
But the primary reason that I can't recommend this game is simply the final boss.  It is almost without question the most unfair boss battle I have ever played in a game (I'll revisit this opinion once I finally complete
I'm sure...).  Even after I learned his patterns and put myself in the best position possible for the first couple of phases, his brutally strong defense, the trap-filled lair, and the near-impossible climax to the battle forced me to waste literally
of lives before I could finally win.  I ultimately felt that after all the time I had put into learning the individual stages and even being able to get to his lair within a reasonable number of lives, the effort was wasted as the final boss just decimated me again and again and again.  I feel like a small amount of luck was involved in the run that was ultimately successful.  I'm relieved that I never have to fight him again.
Another big issue I had was with random crashes.  I experienced more than a few during my playthrough, and all sent me back to the Windows Desktop.  This happened several times when I reached the boss of a level, or after I had managed to finally get through a particularly difficult section with many lives left in reserve, forcing me to do everything over again.  It even happened in the final stage after a particularly good run through the first few sections.  I would say I experienced roughly 10 such crashes.  Given that most games I play rarely, if ever, crash, this ended up being another obstacle to completing it.
If it weren't for the random crashes, and if it weren't for the almost impossible final boss, I could give this game at least a cautious recommendation.  But when the final challenge of the game makes everything you've done up to then feel pointless, that's when it goes from just a hard-core challenge to something more masochistic in nature.  After awhile, it just stopped being fun to try and overcome it.  As it is, I can only recommend this to the hardest-core gamers of this genre.  Just be prepared to want to break your controller in half.

Oh, Kotor. What do you say about this masterpiece?
If you are a younger gamer you are probably sick of hearing people say that today's RPG's are always missing something and that they where better before, playing Kotor is an excellent way of finding out why they say that. There's just so much love and care put into the story that you can really feel this was made back when making a great game mattered more than earning as much money as possible, the golden age before Bioware got in bed before EA and were imho the best RPG making company on the planet.
If it wasn't obvious I could wank this game for days, so what's not so great about it? Well, this is a game you want to play for the story. The overall plotline, the character interactions, all the little world details, not to mention the voice acting it all holds up very well and is what made this game so great. What holds up less well is the combat and the graphics, but don't get me wrong they were both great for their time, but by todays standards? This port really would have benefitted from widescreen support as 4:3 ratio on my screen makes everything look so small it's hard to see and as for the combat.. It's kind of boring. Building your character is still relatively fun though as it uses the classic DnD system with skills/feats and stat points.
After about an hour of playing I was used to the graphics and I don't think the graphics itself will hold anyone back from enjoying the game fully, unless you're a real graphics snob. The only real concern is the aspect ratio.
Flip flopping back to the topic of combat, I do not think it will hold back your enjoyment either as it's generally quite short and simple, it's never a chore it's just not very exciting either.. It's just there.
TLDR; If you want a good story with some great character interaction (and romances!), or just want to see where Mass Effect came from this is a must play classic. Don't take my word for it, just buy it! It's ridiculously cheap right now at 2.49€, and if you missed the sale while reading this don't worry, it's on sale often. Even if it's not it's definitely worth it's full price too.

An absolutely solid game that ended up having a one sided community and floundered with little marketing.
This game is very entertaining to play, interesting campaign (A bit heavy handed with its Borderlandsesque style) but from start to finish it was a solid co-op experience.
The multiplayer was equally exciting, there was a few exploits (Marquis killing secondary turret through a wall) But it was all very entertaining and solid. Characters felt balanced other than melee characters snowballing a bit.
But then the player numbers started to drop, and the good players got to good, and the new players were crushed.
The multiplayer setup did nothing to filter players into games at their skill levels. Eventually 5 man groups absolutely crushed, unless you were in your own pre-made, you had little chance of winning. I would say 30+ hours of my games have been so one sided it sucked any fun out of the game. With no competitive edge or ranking system people left in droves for games like Overwatch.
It's a shame I cannot recommend this game, because it held so much promise. If you don't mind jumping into a small community, grab the game, the campaign almost justifies owning it. With it's lower price point especially.

I tried this because Overwatch is getting stale and the development team sucks, so I wanted to see what the "dark side" looks like and I am not that familiar with MOBAs, so it's nothing new. Also, lets be real for a minute, Overwatch has a  huge number of players, but but the meta rarely changes, many classes are unviable, and the development team is anything but agile to even address minor things or even acknowledge problems, plus they have an in-house gaming engine which probably excaberates things.
PROS:
* I like what the game looks like, it looks cartoony and stupid in pictures but playing it, it's diferent. you gotta experience it
* I had one incredible Incursion game as Kleese and was like "YES, this could be my next main game IF THERE WERE MORE PEOPLE ONLINE".
* The character cast seems quite varied and I've already found several characters I really like playing, like Ambra and Kleese
* A lot of characters have pretty cool styles, like Orendi. The graphics for skills are also visually interesting.
* With the Helix Treeand the gear you can get, there is more strategy than using basic skills over and over, only problem is that the gear can kidn of unbalance things if you think about it.
CONS:
* This game is on life support for real, less than 1 year and it's already figthing signs of death. Needs a lot more players!
* Chaos Rumble mode (right now) is trash, you will get stomped or have no idea what is going on, plus there is Beatrix OVERLOAD. 0% fun.
* You get to vote on what modes to play and honestly I hate it. It's endless Incursion, which gets boring. Everybody only does Incursion it seems like.
* PvE seems simplistic and just way too easy (haven't tried advanced mode yet)
* Versus Draft mode is just poorly designed with it's long, drawn out character pick/ban screen... 4 minutes just staring at the character selection screen and there's no tutorial for it or anything so I accidentally banned somebody's Orendi.
* A lot of the character selection screens need to be redesigned, why are we selecting charcters with the R key or sometimes with the left click, but can't rechoose unless we click backspace? It's like they took something so basic and just made it complicated for no reason. PLUS THE WAIT TIME IS RIDICULOUS... sorry, but there is no need. Copy Overwatch or GTFO, it's not that complicated.
* The tutorial room is poor and includes a 60 second timer to go in and no way to change characters, really really bad. Even Overwatch's training room is better and that one is considered less than basic.
* The interface was recently revamped but still needs work IMO.
Overwatch and this game really are total opposites. Overwatch has the player base, instant gratification with hero kills being more common and feeling more satisfying, and a higher level of general game polish that Battleborn needs, where Battleborn simply has more things (abilities, the helix tree, PvP modes that feature bots, story mode). In an ideal world, while they are both different kinds of games, Battleborn could give Overwatch some competition because it's also fun in a different way. If the playerbase was only there... I'll recommend it just because I want to see it grow.

Mmmmmmeh.
The good: It runs at 1080p on my computer without any hitches, snags, or bugs. The stylized art is fairly attractive, with characters and locations both well-realized. Some of the jokes are worth a chuckle.
If you like on-rails lightgun-style games, this uses the style and adds a few wrinkles in in-level minigames, quicktime-style events, and switchable weapons.
The bad: You might note that as of this review, I've played "Blue Estate" for 2.9 hours. That is about how long it took to complete it on "normal" difficulty, going through eight stages.
You can make a good game that only takes 2.9 hours to complete. But despite the aforementioned attempts at humor, the running narrative, the weapon changes, etc., this amounts to 2.9 hours of fairly same-y game play in "story" mode, leading abruptly into a conclusion that rather obviously doesn't "conclude" anything plot-wise; neither character has accomplished anything towards their alleged goals by the end, and one is explicitly stated to be heading straight for new troubles.
Having completed the game, there's very little reason to stick around. Do you want to memorize enemy patterns so maybe you can get a four-star rating on each level? Play it at a harder difficulty so you can die slightly more often? Listen to the whiny-voiced narrator (whose annoying-ness the game attempts to mine for humor, with frequent interruptions "apologizing" for or "muting" him, as though the game wasn't responsible for the very quality it mocks) go through his schtick a second time?
I don't hate this game, but there are better offerings out there, even in this genre. "Typing of the Dead: Overkill" offers both a typing and a rail-shooter with a longer play time, better script, and more interesting boss fights. Call me if they offer a sequel that actually concludes... and then patch things to tie the two together.

NotGTAV is pretty much Snake if made by a team with no talent but decent humor. If you are not familiar with Snake well the point of it is to collect pieces to grow larger and avoid crashing into your own body. In this game your body is made of hobos, animals and other odd things. In levels you either walk around, push a shopping cart around or drive a car but the controls are exactly the same so it doesn't really matter. Thrown about the levels are obstacles to avoid and objects to collect or run over. And that's pretty much all you will be doing throughout the game though with different environments and jokes. The humor is the best part of this game though it is very hit or miss.
Controls are barely passable but the animations and the sense of speed make telling when to turn difficult. You may get used to the rhythm but  overtime you start moving faster causing you to lose your flow and hope that you have gotten used enough to the awful moving animation to survive. Levels also become harder to navigate as the game goes on but it does it in a very cheap fashion. All the while the most terrible music and sound effects I ever had the displeasure of hearing played. Most of the sound effects are made via mouth and the voice acting is just as bad. It was probably meant to be humorous but it is extremely irritating in my opinion.
In a few sections you can choose whether to go sneaky or brutal but going sneaky is a massive pain due to how the level is designed to be so small and touching a person kills you. Going brutal is more tolerable but it adds a bunch of people to run over and you must get every single one of them. That sounds a lot more fun on paper than it actually is due to the level design meant to annoy you and subpar controls. Even the options menu is annoying to read with how the font is written. Naming this game “NotGTAV” while not really having anything in common with GTA or even reference it all that much is a scumbag way to promote your terrible game. It wouldn't be a big deal if they made a fun game but this is quite possibly the worst game I have played on Steam and feels like a cash grab.
Yes, I am aware they stated 100% of the profits will be given to charity and if that's the case simply cut out the middle man and donate if you are inclined. This is an awful game and promoting this type of cash grab with a purchase is not something I would recommend to anybody. This is a sentence from their Steam page “By buying this game you can help us pay something back.”. And to that I say, well either start a fundraiser of some type or make a decent game instead of trying to pity people into buying rubbish. I know this may seem harsh to a lot of people but this is a really bad game that I probably wouldn't even recommend if it was free.
The trailers are probably the most entertaining part of this product and even then most of the footage is from Grand Theft Auto V. When low brow humor and terrible animations are your only talents you would be better off making a Youtube channel instead of utterly failing at making a Snake clone. Moving on from that, this is really a title with a very certain type of audience. That would be the people that are curious about this title and are willing to risk it for the small price or those that want to prove how edgy they are. If you are looking for a fun game or a decent clone of Snake you won't find anything to enjoy here. If you are looking for dark humor then you might find it here but would still have to play through the game to reach the jokes. Overall I can't recommend this to anybody.

If you're looking for an inventive turn based team strategy/adventure game with rogue-like elements, (or you might be after reading all of that), you can't go wrong with this one.  It's got deep wells of style, humor, and strategy, and it's set in a wonderfully re-imagined 19th century. That is to say, it's a 19th century nearly without heavy restrictions on women or colonized peoples and with 100% more cybernetic limbs and tesla weapons.  To be clear, this game is about colonizers and thieves of cultural artifacts, but it lets everyone in on the joke.  The art and animation are worthy of the experience, and the characters prove to have surprising depth.  The strongest suit here are the MANY options for building your party and playing them, with a ton of unique characters and an 'emotion' based combat that you've just never seen before.  It can be played for hours or for a few minutes.  You'll find a treasure trove of things to enjoy if you're still reading.  Without offering too many spoilers, in this game you can:
-Take a team of archaeologists to Egypt, ransacking treasures like the glory days of colonial nostalgia
-Help a sailor grow a beard
-Insult sheep to advance the game
-Have your German professor get everyone drunk
-Punch out a nun and have one of your characters feel awful about it for the rest of the game.
Bonus points from this anthropologist for having anthropology be the encounter-based research field, even though even 19th century anthropologists rarely engaged other cultures with their fists.  The devious approach, however....
Easily recommended.

Overall, it's quite a nice game. The art style is cartoonish and playful, and the mechanics are smooth and easy to use. The idea of three different approaches (Friendly, Devious, or Aggressive) to your expedition is unique, and it's fun seeing how your choice of emotion affects your opponents. The variety of characters is enjoyable as well, as they all have different personalities and looks.
But as nice as this all sounds, I can't recommend this game. My initial impression was "oh man! With this many characters and options to customize the difficulty, I'll be playing this game forever!". Unfortunately, I was wrong. After one incredibly short playthrough (took me about three or four hours), I was satisfied. Two days later I started a new game with new characters and a new Agressive approach. To my great disappointment, I found myself terribly bored within the first Encounter (what the battles are called in-game). All the dialogue and text between encounters was almost exactly the same, not to mention the story and plot stayed as dull as ever. I played on, but could not get myself to be nearly as intruiged as I had been during my first playthrough.
I'd rate Renowned Explorers a lowly 4/10, giving it credit for unique gameplay style that the developers did not expand nearly enough on and the aesthetic art style. The game definitely isn't worth it full price, and hardly worth it on a sale. Sure, put it on your wishlist and get it on sale if you curious, but keep in mind that it will most likely only offer you a few hours of time-killing at most.

Overall this game isn't for babies. This game isn't even for kids. This game is for adult gamers that like a challenge. If you're going to discount an entire game based on who someone said about one thing, then you're missing out on some important experiences in life. After playing Silent Assassin and Contracts, I was excited to play this game since it was even more highly rated. However, there were a number of very sloppy usability problems that made me give up for being frustrating and wasting too much time.
First, you can't permanently save your game mid-level. You have to complete an entire level before it records your progress. I have absolutely no idea why this is an intended requirement. All it does is waste your time as you try to complete a level all at once, instead of being able to make some progress then taking a break.
This "feature" particularily sucks because sometimes upon completing a level the game will crash, losing all progress. And then you have to start the level all over again.
Second, when you lose all your health, everything slows down into this death cam type mode. The problem is that this takes 10 - 15 seconds, and you cannot open up the menu to restart the level. You have to just wait there in frustration. And you can't escape to the menu for some other things like during reloading. It just shows the sloppy job they did there.
Third, when you do actually load a game, it is annoying because there are too many menus to go through. You have to open the menu, go down and down to load, then go down to choose the game to load (it doesn't automatically default focus to the last saved game like the previous Hitman games). Then are you sure you want to load? You have to go over to yes because it defaults to 'no'. Then after you load the game, it says "Game loaded successfully" and you have to press enter to select 'ok'. Why on earth do you need something that says "Game loaded successfully"? The whole loading of a game is very poorly done. In the previous Hitman titles it was like four keystrokes and bam, you are playing again. This is like 12, and you have to take your hand off the mouse to press enter right when it's loaded. Sometimes the screen is completely black after loading a game, and you have to reload it once or more.
The saving procedure is also sloppily done, because it saves then it seems like the menu turns off then back on instantaneously, then you have to hit ok. It just feels glitchy. You also have only 3 save slots while missions allow you to save up to 7 times. Do computers not have enough hard disk space?
Those are the main issues I had.
The AI and controls felt like a step back from the previous Hitman games I played.
For the AI, everyone seems to turn their head and just stare at you, even when walking in a crowd. It feels a little unpredictable when they will just start opening fire on you. Sometimes it isn't clear what triggered it.
The controls were a step back in my opinion. Using G, space, and E for different actions is confusing. Having to hold down right mouse instead of just click to get to inventory sometimes leads to mis-selects. You can't use caps-lock to run anymore, shift is the only option. You have to hold down control to sneak, instead of just pressing space. Holding down control is very akward. Pressing A, D, and W causes your body to face left, right, or turn around, instead of you body facing the same direction and you side stepping or walking backwards. Picking a lock now automatically opens a door, whereas it didn't in previous games. You can't look through key holes anymore either.
The story and writing also took a turn for the worse as well. You go from doing things like stopping nuclear weapons and taking out organized crime bosses to the first mission here which is literally shooting small time street thugs at an abandon carnival. Then when you get into the main game, it is an annoying series of flashbacks predicated on a r etarded caricature of a jounralist who is asking stupid questions. I feel like I'm playing just because of some ignorant idiot asking questions who shouldn't be involved with any important people at all. And he's talking to this over-the-top FBI guy in a wheelchair with a big scar on his face who is also a caricature of himself. After doing the first three or four missions, I really didn't even want to know how the story progressed. If it was watching this on TV I would have turned it off.
I guess the thing about the story that got to me is that Hitman is supposed to be an adult game, in other words, not for kids. So why do we have two comicbook characters telling us the story?

A little short compared to the content the first F.E.A.R game provides (completed F.E.A.R 2 in a little over 8 hours), but with the Reborn DLC things look OK.
Compared to the first game this one looks A LOT better, combat is flashy and feels really responsive. Most of the original weapons are present, but most of them are nerfed - the shotgun is noticeably weaker, which is fine considering that in my 3 difficulty runs in the first game I would use only the shotgun and the Penetrator occasionally. In F.E.A.R 2 the combat is also a lot more open spaced and the level design is a move forward in general, as the different office buildings from the first game do get quite tiring. The story is gripping enough and the horror elements do have their disturbing highlights, especially toward the end.
I do also want to make it clear that the game is pretty flawed in some regards. First, it's the supernatural enemies - the different ghosts and fast moving zombies, which appear about halfway through the game. The supernatural enemies, like in the first game, are just tedious to fight. They feel cheap, as the sound effects that give them out are really subtle and it's really easy for them to flank you and hit you a couple of times for free before you can fill their heads with bullets. In the short intervals when I had to fight them I was incredibly bored and was just hoping that some more gunfights with Replica soldiers would come soon.
Secondly, it's the AI. Compared to the first game it's actually a lot worse. Replica soldiers will rarely use grenades to get you out of cover. They will instead empty their clips in the wall or table you're behind and proceed to die to you while reloading. On the other hand, it's near impossible to sneak up on them anymore. A lot of times I would actually switch off my flashlight and try to sneak behind their squad for an elaborate flank only for them to immediately know I'm in the viscinity, saying nothing on the radio and just opening fire at me. Pretty disappointing, because the first game is still a cornerstone in believable AI, a decade later.
Overall I do recommend the game, it's a fun, kinda arcade-y shooter that looks great even 8 years later and counting. A bit on the short side, and with a few flaws, but coupled with the first F.E.A.R installment it's a quintessential game to play for fans of the action game genre.

About a year ago I played Her Story. I had heard amazing things about it. Best FMV game of the last 10 years, best mystery game of the year, one of the best stories in video game history. I played it and got the ending in about 25 minutes. Needless to say, I was slightly disappointed. But I felt like I had to be missing something, that there had to be good reason why it was so beloved. So the day before 2018, I booted it up again and took my time with it. I wanted to experience all of Her Story, and I did.
There was a lot more that I unpacked the second time around. I still stand by the plot twist being pretty predictable and would be a turn off for anyone that gets it early and goes "is that it?". But seeing all of it, there's legitimacy of another potential plot twist that I didn't fully realize in my original disappointment. I got much more entangled in the plot. I saw more emotion, more touching moments, more human flaws. I went from thinking Her Story as being a gimmick that just didn't convince me... to a genuinely great mystery game that was ominous, chilling and memorable. One of the most unique narrative/detective games you can play anywhere - and it goes for as cheap as $2. Give it a chance, and be patient. Don't rush and don't be stubborn. That's my only advice.

A really intriguing idea of a story being revealed in fragments is ruined by the developers refusal to allow the player to store the 250 odd clips in a user-friendly virtual sticker or reference book for easy access. Instead you can only view these thumbnails five at a time while they're simply stored along a massive horizontal line. Want to rearrange those clips into anything useful like chronological order (a core mechanics of the game) then you switch the thumbnails with another picture - one at a time - using the painstakingly tedious drag and drop method. Fun? No, not really.
There was so much to like here: the way the plot gradually revealed itself; the way she dressed in a different outfit for each interview; the clicking of the mechanical keyboard when typing into the retro monitor; even her acting was quite good. But that organisation system was an out and out deal-breaker for me turning a really interesting idea into a big disappointment. In short, the game was appealing enough to make me want to watch the full interviews on YouTube but not to actually want to take part in the journey to get there.

I enjoyed the experience and the brain bender of "wtf exactly is going on here." I came to a satisfying enough conclusion in a little under 4 hours of play. Given I got this on sale or free at some point; I have nothing negative to say beyond that the ending is a complete cliffhanger, which wasn't at all what I was expecting; but sure enough on reflection it added to the game in a way. I felt fairly certain I came to a sound theory and satisfying conclusion but was alarmed to find out that it didn't really mean that I "won" or "lost." That is a hard concept for most gamers to grasp after putting time and effort into something but I think it's kind of cool and I am enjoying reading theories that other people came up with (although some of them I feel are way off the mark compared to my own; so I guess in a small way I still get to feel like I accomplished something through "investigation"). Thanks for the unexpected hours of entertainment and intriguing suspense.
Note: Some people find this story to be too unrealistic to grasp; but I like wild fiction. It isn't any more of a stretch of a plot than something like a Chuck Palahnuik novel or a Lemony Snicket story would explore. Don't really expect a stranger than fiction or real life inspired story here. This is more like an interactive indy film and it is told out of order; kind of similar to the disjointed scenes in the movie "Momento" or any other nonlinear story.

Examples:
Pendles, newly added and is a snake like assassin and he focus on stealth and apearing when least expected. One of his passives is "Corner Sneak" which makes him almost completely invisible when he breaks line of sight with the enemy, ofcourse he becomes visible when he uses an ability or attacks.
Galilea, she is almost completely melee and is a defender of her team. She has a shield that she can use to block damage, as per usual with shields. BUT here is one of the twists you can give the shield, when you block damage you charge her "Dark Energy" thing (makes her deal dps in an area around her plus more). She can also throw it and stun people, as her only ranged attack on lvl 1.
Benedict, he is a bird with a rocket launcer. Not a new thing anymore with an airborn rocketeer, but it is a good idea after all. But they have nailed it with Benedict's playstyle. He is all about gliding in the air and firing rockets at the little kill-able ants, although the gliding actually feels more like flying to me. And he is the only almost fully airborn battleborn "with rockets and♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Now you might be thinking "HA, that is precisly like Pharah from Overwatch!". WRONG, her "flying" is more like managing a stat, rather than actual flying. With Benedict you just press and hold RMB and ther you go, you can then also use E to get some more altitude. Each character is unique and feels different to play as, even after you have played for 200h+ like me at the time writing this. Ofcourse there are the basics. Back in the 90s I was really into Virtua Cop &Time Crisis and gradually as the arcades died the genre disappeared. With a brief resurgence featuring House of the Dead overkill & Dead Space in the last gen there has not really been a stalwart of the genre in a long time. Enter Blue Estate the Game and let me start by saying that Blue Estate is my favourite rail shooter of all time.
The best way to describe Blue Estate the Game is Duke Nukem meets Time Crisis with Mafia stuff rather than Aliens. You probably already know if this is going to be your kind of game so firstly lets start by saying It does not revolutionise the genre, this isn’t some mind bending genre re-imagining but what it is the most enjoyable example of the genre I have ever played.
The game is broken into a number of different sections and sees you playing 2 characters. One of the key things about the game that really makes it stand out from other games in the genre is the gunplay. The guns in this game all feel distinctively different.
The story is openly ridiculous and is one of the main issues I have head people moaning about on the internet but to be honest as long as you take it for what it is and that’s absolute silliness its an enjoyable story to follow. You start the tale as Tony who is heading over to a Yakuza style strip bar after your head stripper at your skin joint was kidnapped. This then spills out into trying to recover Blue Estate the Head of the Mafia’s prize racehorse. Other sections of the game see you play as Clarence an ex-navy seal turned hit-man trying to clean up the mess started by Tony.
The game is enjoyable, fast and doesn't outstay its welcome. Controlling the game with the mouse works excellently and makes it play more like an FPS and the guns feel great.
There are also some enjoyable scenes where the game gives you bonus points for doing things such as killing enemies in a specific order and quickly stopping a Chihuahua from humping your leg… don’t ask. These work well and up the game's enjoyment. There are also hidden objects in each scene that you gain extra points for shooting which add to the replay story.
At £9.99 or your regional equivalent I feel this is excellent value for what you get. Sure this isn’t the longest story but when you consider how much say buying a Blu-ray or a trip to the cinema costs suddenly the price seems a lot more reasonable.
Blue Estate is by far the best rail shooter I have ever played and while it will not necessarily convert the masses for fans of the genre or someone looking for something which is fast, fun and different to your usual titles I cannot recommend it enough.

SUMMARY: A fun, clever, challenging, and character-filled "exploration and Tactical RPG roguelike" set in a fictional 19th century.  Manage a party of explorers, choose different ways to deal with enemies and challenges, unlock mysteries, and try to become the most renown explorer ever. There's a lot to do and find - and you can play an entire game in an hour or less . . . then do it again.  A must-buy for fans of good adventure/SRPG games.
Renowned Explorers: International Society takes place in a fictional 19th century where Exploring is the big thing, and most countries get along to sponsor investigations of the mysterious phenomena of the world - and find all sorts of amazing treasures.  You're running one of these adventuring groups seeking fame, fortune, and of course to show up that complete jerk Rivaleux with the great hair that keeps ruining EVERYTHING by finding it.
Plus, you get to do this your way.  The game is all about choice:
* Select a party of 3 adventurers from 4 differnt types (Scientists, Scouts, Fighters, and Speakers).  Each adventurer is a unique personality with special abilities, skills, looks, and even backstories you can unlock.
* Send them forth on adventures where you travel strange lands seeking fortune, fame, information, encounters, treasures, and occasionally lost sheep and llamas.
* Face assorted challenges that will test your skills and planning (or at least risk management), and weigh your options wisely.
* Exchange campfire stories to boost your abilities or find out more about your crew - and watch them develop
* Have them enter into conflict with assorted inhabitants and enemies, and decide how to handle the issues - friendliness, deception, or aggression.  Abilities and your options change as you use them and as the "mood" of battle shifts.  You could find yourself sending an enemy home in a body bag, off crying, or have them decide you're a great person and leave you alone.
* Improve your characters as they gain experience, with new skills abilities.
* Return home with treasures you find or select.
* Upgrade your research, hire helpers and specialists, buy equipment, and even deliver lectures to raise resources.  As you explore more, Exporer groups will help you out, further increasing options.
* Head towards the inevitable conflict with famous explorer and walking smug grin Rivaleux to show him up as best explorer!
* As you play keep unlocking more possible lead characters, extra stories to tell around the campfire, and more.
* Try and find every treasure and campfire story.  Oh and beat Rivaleux!
* Participate in various weekly challenges.
Renown explorers packs in adventure, mystery, choice, resource management, three kinds of conflicts, and plenty of humor - and a campaign takes at most an hour to play!  Since each game often unlocks more options after you play, you can try it again with a new mix of characters, new leaders, new stories, and randomized settings.
Along with the great game play is excellent graphic design, with a colorful cartoony world, a good soundtrack, and snappy writing.  The game is even self-aware of how bizarre it's world is, with characters commenting on and embodying old tropes of pulps and victorian adventure with gleeful self-awareness.
On top of all of this there's a great tutorial and clear controls, so it's easy to pick up for people who aren't always into the tactical RPG genre.
So who should by this game?
* First and foremost, if "easy to play/hard to master roguelike cartoony Tactical RPG with base management" pushes your buttons you should buy this.
*If you like a good character-optimizing and exploration-focused adventure game, you'll enjoy this.  Getting things "just right" is a challenge.
* If you're looking for a fun rouglike RPG - though this is more map-point exploring than corridor-crawling with tactical battle over simple click-and-fight.
It's hard NOT to reccomend this game to people, it's that much fun, that easy to pick up, that challenging.  Except to Rivaleux, he's a jerk.

This isn't the case with Renowned Explorers, so I'm going to tell you why it seems to be a perfect game for me and why you will love it, at least if our gaming preferences are similar.
It's easy to learn. You can get started right away, the tutorial blends in nicely with the campaign and is not too long. Also, if you don't play for a few weeks you won't have forgotten how to play or where you were in your campaign. The combat system is very creative and cute, easy enough to learn but you can play it the hard way if you want to. Replayability is high because of the many different ways you can build your team and the different approaches you can take. Since the expeditions are slightly randomized you can visit them again and again, with different teams and different approaches. It comes as a cute clicking game, but has actual depth and demands you have a plan and some tactics.
The graphics are absolutely cute, I love all the explorers, the other characters and the little animations of their attacks. It's varied and funny. This one time I insulted a nun and she got really sad. This game fulfiils my childhood dream of becoming a celebrated explorer and my adulthood dream of insulting random people.
The first DLC did not only bring new expeditions, but new mechanics as well, it's definitely worth the price. I hope the developers will continue to enrich this great game.

After playing F.E.A.R. and its non-canon expansion packs, I was stoked to play sequel to the amazing original. After having played it... I had a lot of fun with the sequel, but I felt that several things were inferior to the first game. Nonetheless, this is a solid game and I would still recommend playing it. I'm gonna talk about the pros first, cons next and lastly sum up my review.
First positive and for me the most notable: the visuals. This game is beautiful. Even for its time in 2009 its graphics still hold up pretty well, especially in comparison to the now very dated look of the first game. Additionally, most locations in the game have a much prettier and vibrant color palette varying from light blues, to orange, to red. Definitely a much more colorful game in comparison to F.E.A.R..
Secondly the action of this game was greatly improved. The first game had a tendency to be laggy during intense firefights or boss fights, and the overall combat was a little choppy. The sequel definitely made the firefights much smoother to improve the combat. I have but one complaint about the changes made to combat in F.E.A.R. 2 but I will cover that in a sec. They added a hit indicator when you are firing so it's easier to tell if you score a hit on an enemy, weapons now have the option of an alternate firing mode, you are able to interact with your environment to flip certain forms of cover to aid you in your fight, and the added variety of weapons and special grenades that you can cook to delay the explosion really improve the gameplay. My major complaint about F.E.A.R. 2 is the removal of the lean mechanic in the first game. It makes using corners less effective and instead wants to emphasize the usage of flipping cover instead.
These are the two major positives for the game, now for the two negatives.
My main issue is the blend of horror and action. I feel this game fell to a similar fate of Dead Space 3, as action is more focused than actual horror. While still definitely scary and creepy as hell at certain moments, action definitely takes a greater hold in this title.
Last is the story/ending. While fairly straight-forward and competent the story doesn't necessarily raise many questions during the gameplay, and it overall doesn't make a whole lot of sense while you start to learn more about what is going on, most notably in the character motivations on both sides. But I'm not gonna lie the ending of this game actually made me laugh. No spoilers, but the ending while somewhat intriguing and raising some questions such as my own reaction "Did that just really happen?", is just executed poorly and it felt silly what actually happened to end the game. While the answers are brought up again in the following game F.E.A.R. 3, it doesn't necessarily  have the effectiveness of the cliffhanger ending of the first game.
Overally this game is a very fun, kick♥♥♥♥♥shooter with some spooky♥♥♥♥♥moments, but the story and horror elements I feel definitely faltered in comparison to the original.
I'll give it a 7.5/10.

Guacamelee! is just too much fun. The combat is fluid and fun with tight controls. Platforming is kept fresh throughout the game with steady introductions of new techniques. Its story is well written with a good sense of humor and enjoyable Mexican setting. Quite simply, it's everything I'd want in a Metroidvania style game.

Combos, special moves (one of which is hilariously named Dashing Derpderp), double jumps, dodges, throws and grapples kept me engaged with the combat the entire way through. New moves are unlocked at such a pace that I never felt overwhelmed with too many options, nor bored with too few. Many of the new abilities also double as platforming tools. So just as you gain a wider range of battle skills, the platforming sections also evolve to require their use. There is a lot of great level design featured in Guacamelee! complete with plenty of enticing hidden treasures.

Even as a backseat element, the story shines with likeable characters and heavy doses of comedy. In particular, I enjoyed seeing some of the villains fleshed out enough to know a little of their backstory and how they came to follow Calaca (the primary antagonist). Guacamelee!'s soundtrack does a fair job of matching the setting and action but never hooked me enough to look into buying it. There is a nice atmospheric shift in the music as you swap between the world of the living and the dead. I think a person with very little familiarity with Mexican culture and the Spanish language will have no problems having a blast with this game. That being said, this is one case where I'm glad I took 2 years of Spanish in High School as I think it helped me understand or see the humor in a few situations.

I only have a few complaints with the game. The first is its native controller support, or lack thereof. From what I can tell only Xbox controllers will work automatically. I use a PS2 controller hooked up with a USB adaptor. This is the first game I've ever played where I had to use the external program x360ce (found online) to emulate an Xbox360 controller. Most games either work automatically or I can simply go to the in-game control options and set it up that way. Neither of those worked with Guacamelee! which is really unfortunate for a game that was designed for a controller.

Secondly, while I hesitate to call this a complaint, the platforming can be really hard at times. Whether that bothers you or not is entirely subjective. By and large I found the challenge to be gratifying except for just a couple of frustrating sections.

And finally, in a lot of ways calling a game too short can be both a critique and a compliment. For me Guacamelee! clocked in at 12 hours to achieve 100% completion on a normal difficulty playthrough. For an inexpensive indie game that's actually pretty good but as this review's title said: I still want more!
