Her Story uses the medium in a unique and interesting way to tell a story. Instead of telling you the story outright, it tells you small snippets of what is going on, and leaves you to put everything together in your head.
As a result the story is very ambiguous, and everybody will have a slightly different experience. It's a good story, with a lot of suspense and is just the right amount of creepy.
The acting is fantastic; despite only having one actor it never felt like it needed another. In fact I would even say that including another actor would have diluted the story by giving you too much information.
The lack of interactivity gets tiresome after a while, as the game isn't giving you much to do besides thinking about what is going on.
It takes a couple of hours to play, with no replayability, but it's a good couple of hours.

This is an interactive story told via video clips. Gameplay involves coming up with search terms and watching any new video clips you come across. If that doesn't sound like your thing, then don't get this.
All right, now that that's out of the way: I enjoyed this enough to finish it in what amounted to one long playthrough, with a break for dinner. I had been avoiding it because I was worried a full motion video game would be too repetitive for me, but it turned out to be more engrossing than I expected.
You play as someone who's been given access to police interview clips from 1994. The game starts you off with one search term, "murder," and as you watch the associated clips you gradually learn more keywords to try. Each video clip tells you a little more about the woman being interviewed, the murder that occurred, and the events that led up to that point. Although certain keywords may bring up lots of results, you can only ever see the first five results (although a code later allows you to see up to fifteen). Your efforts aren't timed, and you don't have a deadline. You have as much time as you need to browse the files, although a chat bubble does come up partway through the game, asking you if you've finished.
I enjoyed thinking up new keywords to try, and the design was fairly nice. A little eye icon made it easy to tell whether I'd come across any videos I hadn't seen before, I could save any files of particular interest in a little list below the main searching area (although I couldn't figure out how to remove videos from this area), and I could add whatever tags I liked to each video. I actually tagged each video with the date it was shot, but this turned out to be pretty useless. I only really had one tag that turned out to be pretty useful, my
tag, and that was mostly because I misunderstood what was going on in the first video I tagged that way. The tag made it much easier to find the video again and rewatch it once I knew more about what had happened. In general, I found keyword searching to be more useful to me than tag searching, although I'm fairly certain I wasn't using tags very well.
Pros:
+ Engrossing mystery.
+ The completionist in me enjoyed seeing if I could find every single video clip (I did!).
+ Nice acting.
+ Easy to tell which video clips you've seen before, so you don't end up rewatching stuff unless you want to.
Cons:
- Basic searching is pretty easy, but there were some things that I didn't figure out until later. A quick look through the guides tells me there were other aspects about searching that I
managed to figure out.
- I would have loved an epilogue or something similar. The ending throws a big revelation at you, but there's no additional info to go with it. Plus, I'm confused about what happened to

Like the previous title Reus from this studio, Renowned Explorers (REIS?) suffers from similar flaws in the shape of a steep learning curve which requires you to memorize a lot of some obscure game elements and mechanics. Also like Reus, it is a pleasantly unique and colorful game which art style is adapted to any age while gameplay definitely has some suitable to a mature audience depth to it. Note that I only played the game with the DLC "more to explore" and is fully part of this review.
So in RE you manage a team of 3 explorers from a pool of 20 and from 4 different classes each with it unique abilities, bonuses and (minimalistic) skill trees. You start with choosing a captain which gives you a specific bonus and 2 crew member and you jump in directly into the adventure with the supplies you have. Your main goal is to reach a point of the map where your final encounter for this expedition is while trying to gather as much tokens, treasures and bonuses as you can. At the end of each expedition, your tokens will be automatically converted into the 3 ressources of the game which are used to buy gear, hire helpers and specialists and perform research (all of which provides you various bonuses). You will also get "renown" from many of your actions and from the token conversion, which is actually a reflection of your score.
Between expeditions you can use all those ressources, plus one that is called "insight" which allows you to perform jobs to receive extra tokens, to improve your characters and team but also improve the token rewards for the next mission. Unfortunately a run in the game is pretty short as you will do 5 expeditions for the ladder ranking and you can then finish all the expeditions on the map if you like and this "reward at the end" system pretty much is not backed up by an actual proper game ending, as when you do your last expedition, unless you care about the score, you will simply not care about gathering anything and will just go to the end encounter as safely as possible.
Another thing I have noticed in my own (succesful) playthrough is that you may end up with too much of a ressource and no use anymore for it. Typically, with an economic and fame oriented team I ended up with several thousands of gold and reputation in reserve and nothing to spend it on in the last few expeditions so it was just accumulating. There as well, there could be improvements.
There is a nice system of unlock which is motivational as you need to complete some expeditions with some characters to be able to use them as captain and also unlock "campfire stories" (cards) which can give significant bonuses to your party. So there is plenty to do and some replay value in the game, although once you got a bit of experience you will easily recognize (and predict) all the events and encounters that you may find on each specific expedition, although randomly placed on the map, those are rigid and linear scripts. A bit more diversity/procedural generation would not hurt there as well as maybe more customisable starting options (i.e. expanded ladder for more expeditions).
"Combat" phases can be difficult especially when you want to keep a specific "mood" for the fight, as even with high defenses you are almost always outnumbered by the opponent forces and it comes down to placing and getting rid in anyways of enough opponent as fast as possible. The friendly, devious and aggressive stances are an interesting system as it encourages you to use certain abilities instead of others and in certain proportions even when the opponent are highly resistant (or even immune) to the attacks of those stances. Quite challenging are Boss fights and elite encounters which keep spawning minor mobs and are about balancing between eliminating reinforcements and taking on the high damage and life (spirit) boss to end the fight.
Several events trigger the RNG god and the odds are determined by the skill composition of your team members and it is up to you to decide (although sometimes you just have the choice between bad, worse and very worse) to have an audience or not with the divinity of randomness. Some of those events may even cause you to lose "resolve" (your life pool, which means game over when it reaches 0).
Despite the replay value (due to unlocks, as the content itself is pretty easy to discover in just a few runs), you can already feel the game is definitely meant to be further expanded (the world map has much more empty space to fill) by some other DLC(s). I hope that some of the game mechanics of the base game will be improved and some of the "issues" I highlighted (i.e. ressources becoming useless in the end game, lack of procedurally generated nodes, bad end game mechanics, etc.) will be acknowledged by the devs and fixed.
Though I may sound pretty critical of the product I still highly recommend it. If you are an optimizer or completionist, there is definitely material here to keep you busy for hundreds of hours. If you are just willing to go through the game once, well it is a very enjoyable experience and considering you may have to restart a few times it will also keep you busy for a bit of time.

Blue Estate. Boy oh boy oh boy, where do I even start with this one. Initial thoughts were that it was an interesting shooter with decent graphics and all and then the trailer showed that it had some humor, but that's about as good as the trailer gets. The real fun starts as soon as you actually start the first level.
Blue Estates is suppose to be based off of some novel and the plot revolves around a few mobster families fighting over various things such as a race horse (can't say name or else minor spoiler), a sexy busty Japanese dancer (super sexy), and other things. The game genre is known as a rail shooter, which you rarely hear about four a few reason. One, is that they are linear. People these days seem to gate linear things because of their freedoms as this, their freedoms as that. If you're too anal about that, then move along. If not, then listen up. The point of rail shooters is at the very least, to force you into situations where you have to adapt, and you get to see exactly what the creator wanted you to see. Anyway, enough ramble, time to review.
As stated earlier, its a rail shooter, so in each level you start off with a pistol that has infinite ammo. That's just standard protocall. Through out the level, you occasionally come across another weapon that can be used but with limited ammo. These are usually shotguns, ARs, rifles, and stuff like that. You move from place to place, and have to defend yourself against a lot of enemies as they charge after you, or pop up out of no where and shoot at you. Due to the nature of the game, and that having true unassisted aim would make the game really difficult for some gamers, they have a very generous aim system in which you have to aim close to the head with a general crosshair, and then allow the small crosshair to adjust slightly enough to get hopefully a headshot. This might make the game seem easy, but when enemies bob around, it can be hard to even get a lock on them so just good ol' aimming is required.
While in the levels, there are times where you have to do minor interactive things that are not exactly QTEs, but they involve moving the mouse in directions, or keyboard bindings. An example is that when the main Italian guy is running around, he sometimes has his long hair get in the way. A simple swipe, and poof, its moved. Opening a door, just swipe left and right and tah dah. Ammo and health packs are plentiful, maybe too plentiful, but they can be ignored if you please.
The trailer and screenshots show it all. Not super ultra HD 4k texture stuff, but enough to be fun and cartoony enough to enjoy.
The music, while simple is very effective at setting the mood and changes as you progress. The voice actors for the game, are amazing. Each of the characters have an unique enough voice to easily know who is who, and you don't even need to know a thing about them to figure out what type of person they are. Also, the humor, oh god the humor in this game is flat-out, hilarious. If you don't find a moment in the game to laugh about, then seriously, something's wrong with you.  No, Im serious, how could someone not find one part of the game funny? The humor is raunchy at times, but very clever and witty. There are a few moments that might rub people the wrong way, but the humor is done in good taste and pokes fun at all sorts of people.
Rail shooters have been an old-school game genre that have not gotten a lot of love, nor respect that they rightfully deserve. This game proves that the genre is not dead, and that you can enjoy a linear game with tons of humor. While I have yet to try the game on the hardest setting, I feel like the game is a bit too easy BUT you can make it harder by not picking up health packs, maybe not hiding while reloading, and stuff like that. This is definitely a good game that Im afraid will get bashed because the console version of it, didn't have the best of reviews, but still, this is PC version, not console. The price is one hell of a bargain for this, and if you enjoy rail shooters, humor, and a silly but fun story, then get this.

In its simplest form Her Story is you watching videos of a woman being interrogated by off-screen detectives. You watch 5 videos at a time, tag each one, and then load the next 5. The story unfolds over the course of 1 – 60 second videos, of which there are over 200!
Her Story is less of a game, and more of a chore. Tagging videos and “saving” them to the bottom of the screen, allows you to quickly go back and inspect the footage again. Unfortunately that's the entire game. There is little to mix things up, save for some desktop notes to read – none of which offer any help in spicing up the game.
Things start slow, very slow. I went through a few dozen videos before anything interesting started happening. Sometimes the sole character, Hanna overacts and sounds a little pretentious, which allowed me to enjoy some unintentional laughter. When you first start the game, you're given 5 videos, scattered over the course of a few days' worth of interrogations. (Un)fortuantely the developers give you the very last video clip upon starting the game. Her Story could have ended with a “wadda ending!” but instead, the falling action allows the game to fade out quickly.
At the low price of $2, Her Story allowed me to enjoy what I paid for. The story is great, and you really need to experience it for yourself to appreciate it. But that can be a downfall for some players. The “experience” is where most of the enjoyment is, because there is no “game play”. If you want something cheap, mildly entertaining with a good story- look no further. But be prepared to sift through 200+ video clips *ugh*.

After watching a ChilledChaos video on YouTube playing this game (and loving watching it), I decided to pick this game up along with other games as my "steam sale" bundle.
After playing over 10 hours of this game, I found it very addicting to play. It was like playing Minecraft for the first time, but having a twist of having to shelter, feed, and protect colonists. It starts nearly identical to Minecraft, but eventually starts to go off on its own road. There were a lot of things I was impressed with, such as the different jobs a colonist could have that benefits not only me but the rest of the population. It also has the same creativity as Minecraft, where you can build your colony however suits you.
There are some things that could be improved or did not go well with me. First off, the game gets kind of stagnent the more you play on your world. Hopefully since this game is in Early Access, the creators can add more items, jobs, etc. to the game to "spice" it up and make your world more long-lasting. Another thing that was kind of annoying was the lag spikes with having numerous wheat farms and the wheat all growing at the same time every day. Of course, I can't really complain when I have so many farms, but it's a bit of an annoyance. There are some other minor annoyances, such as the colonist pathfinding not being so direct, not being able to choose which job a colonist does, only one kind of enemy, etc.
If you like games like this and want to invest money in to an Early Access game, this would be the safest bet. There is so much room for improvement and additions in this game and could easily be worth $20 in no-time. I can't wait to see what direction this game heads towards!
Note: This is a singleplayer only review.

Old timey classic game, which never got the attention it should have gotten way back then.
It doesn't feel old, though, if you ignore the available screen resolution settings and some strange, and unchangeable, hotkey assignments.
Due to its age, the requirements of the game are low, and it should run on basically any modern computer (don't know about "modern Windows", though. It works perfectly in Wine on Linux, that's the way I play it.
It is best characterized as Tower Defense and Basebuilding RTS Mixup. The Basebuilding may be obvious to you from the screenshots, but it is also necessary to "terraform the land" to "Zero level" before you can even build anything. The Tower Defense part comes from the weaker AI, which almost always marches towards your nearest building or unit, and which makes this RTS more casual than other games of this genre. The missing AI power is "compensated" by the number and health of opponents. The unit system is also not standard, it consists of a very small number of squads, which you can move around the map, which means you can only cover a few strategic points with your mobile protection; static protection like turrets can not move and need infrastructure. A squad consists of three different types of base units and can morph into different unit types depending on which base units are in the squad, and a squad can only morph into one of those at a given time (no mixed squads, if you want to have different units at a point, you need to send two squads. Also, the number of units overall is very limited (artificially), which makes the squads small.
I recommend this game to everyone who wants to play a "different" type of RTS game, to anyone who wants to see a special part of the history of RTS gaming, and to anyone else, too. Especially, if you look at the price.

My favorite RTS of all time. Had it on disk for years before buying it again on Steam. Perimeter provides excellent story, an interesting and unique world, and fun mechanics all wrapped up into a game with far more flexibility than the average RTS. You can really choose your playstyle and adapt as the game progresses. Perimeter has immense replayability and is an excellent experience overall.
The standalone expansion, Emperor's Testament, is also worth getting. It adds a fantastic new story arc and some new gameplay mechanics to keep you going.

Giant pyramid city-colonies towering over energy-conducing spikes that shoot laser shields to the sky.
Terramorfing robots shape the world around them and then merge to become one powerful unit, maybe several smaller ones.
Desperate nomad civilizations traveling through wormholes and using transhumanist superpowers.
It's not like anything before it, and there's nothing like it, probably because it's too weird for imitation.
It hasn't aged as fine wine does and is hardly the best RTS around, but Perimeter will leave a mark on your soul.

Let me get three paragraphs out of the way real fast.. This game's pretty old, and I'm pretty sure it was experimental at the time. I got it when I was a kid in an age where online multiplayer was flaky at best, and downloadable games of this scale were unfathomable.
As a result, I had few "big" games and played the few that I had *constantly*. I've become relatively good at Perimeter, but it took months since I had absolutely no help from anyone else.
What people say about the tutorial is true; it's enough to tell you that you can click things, and that's basically it. You're really on your own and need to be able to handle adventure games without Googling to be able to cope with this RTS.
If you're all good with that, then we can go on to specifics!
So, Perimeter basically has no real story. A "modern" gamer probably won't enjoy this title. The game was designed during the golden years of RTS games, so all of the attention is geared towards the actual gameplay and graphics. The gameplay is fairly unique; less-so today, but especially unique for when it came out: It's about 33% territory control and 66% Poker. I don't know what the missing 1% is, but I'm sure it's nifty!
In a typical game of Perimeter, normal "battles" will last under 5 minutes per enemy. Decisions are fast and unforgiving. Against a computer it's easy to hold out for an indefinite amount of time, but another player will typically make it impossible to keep things at a stalemate. The campaign stuff might last longer, but that's primarily because they keep throwing new wrenches into things.
Territory control isn't usually what makes someone /win/, but it sure causes people to /lose/. The "Poker" element comes in by having all units be made of three basic units, and being able to morph between other units at will. The "mix" of units in a morph isn't shown to your opponents, so "hiding" units in other units can be helpy.
All in all, this is a quirky, unique, and (for me) very addictive RTS from when RTS games were *awesome*. "Perimeter 2" is absolute trash in comparison and a very poor attempt to bring a golden age RTS into more modern times; truly, Perimeter will only appeal to a very small subset of RTS fans. The game's not even $5 if memory serves, so if you think you're the kind of person who likes this stuff, give it a shot!

Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is a 2D, 8 bit retro style 'torture' platformer. After a brief tutorial level to kickoff the game, it opens up to eight selectable levels. A few are far easier than others. There is a lot of parody going on here. Levels reminiscent of old Nintendo games like Castlevania, Metroid, Super Mario Bros 2 and Zelda 2. You'll even find an 8 bit parody of dirty Atari games. Once you complete those eight, then the final LJN style level gets revealed. It is all based on the comedy from the Angry Video Game Nerd web series that has been around for a decade. Its a good game that doesn't offer any unique features that aren't found in other Nintendo games. If you're looking for something fresh and original gameplay wise, you won't find it here.
The game plays a lot like Mega Man. Jump, shoot (with no autofire), duck and use a special item. The only difference is there is 8 way shooting like Contra. You can even hold the trigger to plant your feet so you don't walk as you aim diagonal. The items are few and far between. The tutorial level will walk you through all them. Glitch gremlin that I think kills everything killable on screen? Seven hours into the game and I still don't know for sure. Super Mecha Death Christ definitely kills everything on screen. Things like a rock that do little to no damage. Its just in the game so the Nerd can make a joke. The Nerd can even pick up a superscope weapon that does more damage, but one hit and you've lost it. A lot of times you'll find it in areas with unkillable enemies.
Even as a torture platformer, the game isn't that difficult. Timing is key. More than missing a jump, its missing a jump at the wrong time might get you hit and you'll fall in a pit. Each level is around 10 minutes. You have health measured in beer. Pick up a beer to restore your health. On easy you can walk into enemies with no regard for your life. Normal difficulty and up you have to have skills to not die from health loss. Each enemy causes you to get knocked back which becomes deadly if a pit is around. With that being said, the majority of deaths come from death blocks. Mega Man 2 had spikes, AVGN has deathblocks. These are everywhere! Some are in the ground. Somme are moving. Some are on and off with a timer. Some appear only when you get close to them. If you're not paying attention, to where you step, you're dead!
Nin-Toasters get used as checkpoints. These are pretty frequent. When you die, you respawn, but not after seeing a death screen with a randomly generated death phrase that usually involves an animal, a fluid and an body hole. You cannot turn off these death screens. It could be to hide a loading screen. You need to see it for a few seconds before pushing jump to get back to the action. Most torture platformers just drop you right back into the action.
Each level is pretty straight forward, but still allows for exploration here and there. You'll even find three extra characters to play as. Each has their own style and can be toggled on the fly with the shoulder bumpers. Mike has a high Luigi jump and can use a short range light sabre to break through walls that get highlighted as you draw near. He also makes invisible platforms appear. Couch Guy has a wave attack from his guitar that will go through blocks when the Nerd's gun can't. His jump is short, so he's better for SHMUP sections of the game. Finally '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' has a double jump and a short range arced attack, but can't jump as high as the Nerd. He's good for accessing different areas. For the most part, these extra characters are only used for finding secret areas, that have cameos from other ScrewAttack friends along with plenty of beer and 1-ups.
The enemies feel diverse, but there isn't a huge variety. Each level swaps out enemy sprites. High bouncing enemies, enemies that attract to you, wave pattern enemies, floor spikes that shoot up, hovering enemies, circular flying unkillable fireballs and so on. Each level has its own unique big enemies. Snowmen that belch giant snowballs. Giant turd balls that spit dookie at you in Hell. Axe throwers in the Castlevania level. Each enemy's death had particle effects that felt satisfying. At the end of each level is of course a boss, straight from AVGN's history of evil. Jason Vorhees, Satan, Dr. Jekyll / Mister Hyde, General Custer and so on. Most of the bosses just fly in a figure eight pattern.
Unlike most torture platformers, there was dynamic gameplay. Going from a platformer to a sidescrolling SHMUP. Riding down a hill one a dead corpse, streaking blood behind you. Hopping on a giant laser shark and tearing through lava. These were all a lot of fun to break up the levels. Even with each level having its own theme, there were things gimmick wise to make them stand out. The Castlevania level has a series of timed on and off death blocks. The dirty Atari level has bouncing platforms under your feet. The snow level had ice to slide on. The Zelda 2 level had keys to unlock doors. The haunted level has moving block platforms like Super Mario World and darkness outside of a short illumination around the Nerd. The Mega Man future level had timed laser beams and timed on / off platforms. It was able to keep the challenges dynamic.
It is no doubt a good game for fans that like Mega Man's gameplay. There are just little things that get in the way. The text box at the bottom of the screen with the Nerd talking is a distraction and obscures the action. In fact, the entire game is just a distraction. There are laser lights panning through some levels. Things flying everywhere. Even a vomit inducing waterfall ala Super Mario Bros 2. Half a dozen fireballs flying in a circle, bouncing on platforms, while enemies float toward you! Its all very busy, but that's probably to keep your eyes off the death blocks! The comedy also misses its mark, but I feel a lot of comedy games aren't that funny. Maybe its lacking the Nerd's delivery. Its just not as funny in text form when I'm too busy playing the game to read it.
Playing normal mode first took 2 hours for the first 8 levels and 4 hours for the final level. I sank around 100 lives just for the final boss. Then I discovered how to plant my feet by holding the trigger to shoot diagonal without walking. Normal difficulty gives you unlimited continues and 30 lives. I felt the intensity when I had died 10 times on a boss and I was coming to my final life to beat him. Easy difficulty gives you more health and unlimited lives ensuring you'll get through the game. There are higher difficulties, but normal was enough for me. I have a feeling you can complete easy difficulty in under 2 hours.
To summarize, its the best AVGN game you could hope for. Easy difficulty makes it so everyone can complete the game. If it wasn't for easy difficulty I wouldn't recommend it. I'd recommend it more for fans of old Nintendo games than AVGN fans. If you're into 8-bit Nintendo games, especially Mega Man. Get it. Also take note that 50% of players have the 100 deaths achievement. So does that mean on easy mode they beat it in under 100 lives or did they just give up and not complete it?

As a long time fan of the angry video game nerd I was naturally excited by the announcement of this game.
At its core AVGN adventures is a platformer that specializes around satirizing other games. All of the levels in this game are parodies of old school late 80's early 90's platformer games. And with titles like "Dungeons and Dickholes"
and "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Vania" how could you not help but chuckle.
Though the novelty wears off soon after you've played through all the stages it's still a fun time to be had by platformer game fans. What I mean is the game may be fun at first glance, but after you've played all the levels, they start to feel very similar. Sure one stage may have more death traps then another, and some stages have a more colourful pallet to them, they all basically function the same. Each level has invincible enemies that rotate around in a certain pattern. These enemies can be spike balls, ghosts, fireballs, and just about anything that typically would appear in a platform game. The games biggest offender would have to be the insta kill blocks that kill you instantly. These skull marked boxes often appear out of nowhere and it can be extremely difficult to see where they are in dimply lit stages such as a haunted house themed stage.
I know that platform games are supposed to be about trial and error, but here it feel like it's more about luck then skill most of the times. Also since it's release the game has been a bit glitchy, there was a moment that my character was frozen in place forcing me to exit the level and restart the stage because the options menu doesn't just let you restart from a checkpoint, instead you have to exit the level in its entirety.
This only happened to me once, but I have seen videos of people complaining about this happening constantly, as well as steam forums demanding that this be fixed. So until a patch is released you will just have to settle with a game that occasionally glitches up.
Since this is a game based on a character who makes skits about games as well as other topics you can expect to see a lot of references to James Rolfe's work and his friends make cameo appearances as well. Some of witch are playable characters. Kyle Justin the Guitar guy can shoot sound waves through walls to hit switches and enemies that would normally be inaccessible to other characters. Mike Matei can jump higher than other playable characters, see cracks in certain walls and break them to reveal hidden objects. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t man ( Yes that's his name) has the power to double jump allowing you to get to areas that would other wise be inaccessible.
While the novelty of playing as these characters is a guilty pleasure non of them are necessary because the nerd (Your default character) is the only one you need to beat the game. It would have been nice to see a secret stage that required the powers of all 4 playable characters to progress through. However whenever you are fighting bosses, or have just aquired a gun power up the nerd is the best character to use. He is the only one who can shoot in multiple directions, and since almost all the games bosses float around the screen in a figure 8 pattern the nerd is the only one who has the ability to inflict damage most often. Also I'm not sure if this was intentional, but every time I pick up a gun upgrade with the nerd, and then switch to another character and back the upgrade he acquired was gone.
This doesn't happen with any of the other upgrades that I got so it makes me wonder if this was just something the developers overlooked. I can understand getting hit causing you to loose a power up, but switching characters? As far as the power ups go their are rocks that are pretty much useless and only there so that the nerd can make fun of them, there's the game glitch gremlin that freezes all the enemies in place, and Super Mecha death christ 2000 B.C. 4.0 beta that acts as a screen nuke and kills all small enemies in your line of sight. The game also occasionally suffers from poor level design. Outside of insta kill death boxes there was one time when I tried to grab a beer ( Beers are health in this game) while walls with spikes were closing in on me making it impossible to get the beer without getting hurt yourself. The nerd even makes fun of this stating "who the hell put a beer over their are you really expecting me to get that." This is a reference to one of his earlier reviews for teenage mutant ninja turtles. I got the reference because I'm a fan but non fans will just see this as bad level design. Also in one level when I went down a latter I instantly fell down to my death into a pit of sharks, spikes and just about every other hazard there was. I can understand that this was a reference to his Pitfall harry review, but what's the point of having all these references if the only people who will understand this are fanatics of his show. I get that they wanted to put references in the game, but weren't all the cameos enough? Farcry 3 blood dragon proved that you don't need to make a game's level design bad in order to make fun of itself. And separated itself from games that I like to call "Bad games that think that they can get away with being bad by making fun of their obvious flaws genre" Games such as the simpsons game, Duke Nukem Forever, and the fairly recent deadpool game all fall into this category. Angry Video Game Nerd adventures manages to stay just shy of being placed into that genre due to its solid level design great sense of challenge, and awesome set pieces ( What other game lets you fly on top of the back of a gigantic lava shark that shoots laser beams out of its eyes while you are surfing on lava.)
AVGN Adventures is a mix of old school level design, cooky nonsense some comedic elements and the nerd we all love. 6.5/10

Did you enjoy playing Mega Man on the NES as a kid? Then you'll love AVGN Adventures. This game is hard, but by no means unfair - there is always a path through the level; it's up to you to find it! And of course there are the references to classic games, like the Quickman lasers and space jellyfish in the "Future 2010" stage. (Don't worry, you don't need an ice beam to beat the jellyfish!)

To each their own.  You're entitled to your opinion as I am to mine.  But let me share a bit more of my thoughts on this game:
Seeing as there's no tutorial, the game is only semi-openworld, had terrible handling, didn't have proper controller support, and most of the functions either don't work or are completely non-user friendly, so I'd say I gave it a decent run through.  If a game doesn't grab the player's interest in the first 20 minutes of gameplay, then it's not a good game.  That's the approach I have to games and it's what I use to judge them.  This game just falls into the same category as "Woodcutting Simulator 20XX" where they don't have a polished and user-friendly product and are putting it out anyway.  Other games like Farm Sim, ETS2, and even Construction Simulator 2015 have a decent engine with a fair amount of gameplay but most importantly, they made it user-friendly to make it enjoyable.  This game felt like work.  I'd rather not have to work to enjoy a game.  Which is disappointing, because I would like to find a good police sim...
And if you think that those other sims just got it right the first time:  ETS2 evolved to where it is today, from some really bad truck sims.  Farm sim was a mediocre sim in the early years, but was boosted by community addons.  The problem with the "Autobahn Police Simulator" is it's the same company/producers that keep putting one cookie cutter sim after another, and they don't evolve and improve their engine.  They also put very little effort into their userability.
Hopefully that clarifies my findings a bit more.  I won't say I'm not biased, because it was fairly apparent what this game was likely going to be like, but I did give it a fair shot to draw me in and it failed to do so.

F.E.A.R 2 is honestly an odd sort of game. I first learned about the series from a friend, and what I could read about online. I bought it instantly when I saw it was on sale.
Regardless, my first impressions were...a bit jumbled and confused. Hell, they still are. I was expecting a hardcore blood and guts horror game, and while it does deliver, it takes a while.
However, if you are like me, and kind of mindlessly jumped into the second game without playing the first, there is one thing you need to know.
The game, while very entertaining, and possessing pretty decent graphics, seems to have a hard time deciding on what kind of game it will be. One moment, the game revolved around powering your way through waves of enemies in high tech armor, the next you are creeping down a dim hallway as nightmare fuel tries to tear you to shreds. Right after that, you go right back to mowing down mechs. Oh yeah, and also add that creepy chick from "The Ring" into the mix.
Now this isn't actualy a bad thing, and is actualy pretty cool, but it can be jarring if you don't expect it
Aside from that, the game has the usual shooter mechanics. Not much new is brought to the table. Over all the game is pretty good. It's not a master piece, and it has its share of shortcomings, the game tries, and for the majority of the time, succeeds at providing a unnerving narrative, and a good amount of entertainment.

I recommend this game if you really liked the first one since it is almost the exact same game, just with better graphics.  FEAR 2 is easier by leaps and bounds, since health and armor can be found everywhere.  Its worth a playthrough if you catch it on sale.

The really weird FEAR of the three. I was overjoyed of finally having varied environments, but apparently the change in the level's layout borderline killed the AI. It's so incredibly dumb after the first game, enemies tipping over tables for blockade then hiding at the side of it (being a clear shot) or just running towards you. So this is a letdown.
The biggest plus of the second game that single-handedly made it my favourite: they learned how to tell a story. Having meaningful cutscenes, finding data logs, puzzling together so much more about the story than we knew made the game  really enjoyable for me, despite I could not take the shooting really seriously because of the AI. Though about shootings: weapons are quite nice to handle, granades are powerful and you're able to cook them so you can modify where they'll blow up, and their throw is *really* consistant - it's a fantasticly well working feature.
If you can get past that the first FEAR is the "most FEAR" game, and treat the second as a less horror, more action and more story game in the first one's world, then you're in for a treat. I had low expectations but got utterly surprised how much I enjoyed it. (Huge thanks for the granades, really, if you play the game, don't forget about them! :D )

There are some complaints I have but they are pretty minor, if you wanna build a town of identical sheeple (seriously, they only differentiate themselves when you give them a job, and even then only by changing shirts) but at least they are there, and are animated fairly well (even if they don't move their torso's and their arm/leg movements remind me of wacky arm flailing inflatable tubemen, which is rather impressive to get such fluid motions when animating things)
Some Itemized good things
-Performance is muuuuch better now (4x fps increase on my laptop)
-Game is starting to get some depth
-More decoration options (yay carpets)
-New Monster types are pretty easy to identify
-Devs actively read reviews and care what people think about the game (which is amazing especially with how the Steam store has gotten as of late)
Now then onto the 'downers'
-For some reason 'shadows' cast between vertical stacks of blocks that are adjacent to other verticle blocks (walls casting shadows on themselves)
-A number of the things for science are ONLY used for science making it feel like an extra step just to keep advancing
-Would be nice to have a 'your looking at blah' type deal if only to tell what ores I'm looking at so I can better identify some of them without having to destroy the block (and to tell if flax is full grown)
-A thing to assign beds based on colonist or job would be nice (why are my berry pickers pathing around my base, going down into the mines to sleep)
-Pathing can bork if your building something and the ai tries to go through there
-Miners have a 'facing arrow' now, which comes across as how it works for the guards, when they still only mine the block they are standing moitionlessly on, the 'facing' for them is just which direction their souless eyes, and featureless faces look while they do so
-Noticed the 'crafter' colonists seem to ignore the amounts you have set and kind of do whatever, would also be nice to be able to set a priority on what order they should focus on building things in
-Sometimes when you go to hop up a block you 'float' into it some which is easy enough to fix by backing up till you 'slide out' of the block

Her Story is less a game and more of an interactive movie, that is told through 271 short video segments where the protagonist is giving interviews at a police station.
The only gameplay involved is trying to work around the purposeful limitations of the video archive tool. You are only able to view up to 5 videos at a time, and the videos are searchable by keywords. The 5 videos you can view are always chronological, so the oldest always shows up first. The gameplay is you basically fighting this mechanic by using ever more specific keywords to narrow the search scope down to 5 or less videos so that you can see the new ones. Once you see a new video it's just a matter of entering your own keywords so that you can catalog and pull it up at will , like numbering each video 1-271. That's the game. There is nothing outside of the video segments. The video playback has no pause or any video editing functionality (i.e. you cannot tag a certain point in a video for quick reference later). You do get a "User Session" for dumping video files for easy reference, but you can only add, not remove. This means if you are pursuing a specific line of investigation and want to view a few videos back-to-back, you can put them in your User Session. Problem is, once they're there, you can never get rid of them, sort them, or move them around. None of what I've just described qualifies as gameplay.
The majority of the time is spent trying to view all the video segments and catalog them using permutations of keywords (or use the BLANK workaround). Ex.: MURDER, MURDERER, MURDERED, I DID NOT MURDER, etc... Once you've done that you can easily pull them up and begin cross-examining the statements, if you still have the will. This amount of tedium wasn't for me and quickly made me uninterested in the story. Unfortunately if you've seen movies like The Prestige, Identity, Fight Club, etc... you can guess what's coming pretty early in the game, so the tedium doesn't pay off with any mind-blowing moments.
I applaud the developer for trying something new, but honestly, if I were a police detective that had to use that video archive software, I might think twice about solving a murder case too.

The central mechanic of this game is something quite unique - searching key words and watching video snippets of a series of interviews to gain more clues to a murder. The story is engaging and the mystery will keep you hooked to the end. Only a couple of hours long but well worth the experience. This is a great example of a game experimenting with interesting storytelling mechanics.

I recently found time to sit down and finally play Guacamelee! and I'm glad that I did.  A huge platformer fan, Guacamelee! was a treat, bringing me back to the days of classics like Metroid and Castlevania (I was not expecting a 'Metroidvania' game when I started, so I was pleasantly surprised that it was *and* it was well-executed).  Guacamelee! is challenging, yet provides enough breadth that newer platformer fans will enjoy the game (though it might be tough for the brand-new), while the more hardened among us will still find a challenge (the game is very forgiving in death, its biggest 'flaw' if you're looking for that style of intensity--nonetheless there are pretty tricky areas, side-quests and Inferno challenges that left me feeling pretty badass when I got through).  The art style is quirky and unique, and numerous 'hidden' video-game references are peppered throughout, which adds a fun touch of nostalgia (the Chozo statues were perhaps a bit heavy-handed, but I won't lie, I smiled!).  I did find myself losing track of where to go next in the game, though that may have been a consequence of having to play over multiple play sessions for lack of time (as well as a serious case of "oh, look, squirrel!").
Overall I would recommend this game if you are platforming fan.  Don't expect the hardest platformer ever (especially the core game), but there should be more than enough for a fun experience and no regrets!

It's a budget game made by unknown Russian developers. Also, it's not the Cannon Fodder sequel anyone has been waiting for. However, I have very high tolerate for budget games made by unknown developers so I decided to try it anyway.
I found the game interesting enough to play it for 10 hours until I completed it. The game was OK, for £4 I paid it was good enough. It is a typical budget game. Voice acting is terrible, music is the most generic electro guitar tune on repeat, controls are bad (use WASD and mouse together!), story incoherent and ridiculous, graphics are OK but soldiers look truly hideous with small bodies and huge ugly heads. Oh, and the game literally calls you "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" in few missions... However, that did now surprise me as I knew to expect no better from this game. On the other hand if you can look past all this its OK little shooter. Gameplay is simple, repetitive yet somehow addictive. Its fun killing waves of enemies making huge chain explosions. Difficulty level is just right. Original Cannon Fodder was tough as nails but this one is much easier which I appreciate. There are some vehicles some levels and its quite fun driving those. Suppose you just got back from work. You are quite tired and don't have energy to play something demanding on your brain. You just want to veg-out and pass some time playing something really simple. This game is perfect for that!
Finally, do I recommend it? It depends. Is the game on sale and less than fiver and can you tolerate budget games? Have you already played Cannon Fodder I & II and Tiny Troopers? If the answer to all these questions is yes then sure go for it. Otherwise, you will be disappointed.

Take all the criticism with a grain of salt, this game is truly a lot of fun.
F.E.A.R 2 is a solid Fps that builds upon the first and provides more pros than cons to justify a recommend. Sure they stripped away the lean feature, dual pistols, shortened the campaign by an hour and a half (8 hrs on first playthrough), nerfed the A.I for consoles and dramatically changed the artstyle, but it's not much of a deterrent.
On the hardest difficulty the A.I can be quite a challenge, you can now carry 4 weapons at a time, slo-mo lasts longer (is this a bad thing or a good thing) and the worldbuilding benifits extremely from the expanded story. One of the major antagonists, Colonel Vanek, comes to mind. Also the weapon roster, npc variety, pacing and level design is definitely a step up. From your weaponless encounters with Alma, to a very tense standoff when first introduced to replica soldiers or the moment you breach the surface to witness the devestation on the Auburn district and its inhabitants.
F.E.A.R 1 is like no other game, F.E.A.R 2 is like lots of other games, but it still manages to retain its own identity. And i respect that.

So this is what it feels like shifting through interrogation tapes of a single case that's all cut up and not in order.

For a game that is all about the story, with almost no fancy art direction or compelling gameplay features, Her Story fails spectacularly in that department the most. The non-linear story telling through a police database is a really innovative idea, but the story told through that story telling mechanism borders on the line between bad and cringeworthily unbelievable. The fact that this was heralded as game of the year and a masterpeice goes to show that sometimes pretentious game journalists searching for "innovation" get lost in the idea and forget the details that fall completely all over themselves.

Many will find this title off-putting as it essentially acts as a series of short videos where you, the player, hunt down the hidden truths of the Murder of <Her> husband; with little gameplay other than a simple single-word finder. If this doesn't detract from the title, know that for a title with mechanics as simple as this, it features some really detailed characters and thought provoking narrative points that makes you truly feel like a Detetive nearing the end of a case, something that many AAA titles seem to miss and simply replace with areas of gunplay or action sequences.
The title pushes you to the right direction using adaptive soundtracks and dynamic audio techniques such as positive chords to show you're onto something big, or silence and static if you're thinking about things the wrong way-- often leading to a eureka moment once you've realised something and found the right thing to "ask her"; prompting a flash of an image to make you feel tense and discover more from the new content discovered.
The case definitely feels like one of the best FMV and crime games you can find, where there are little-to-no moments where you should feel completely lost during the search. That said, the ending conclusion
, leaving the user to simply dive into the title and try complete the database for more information to discuss with another player- however at this point, the "eureka moments", flashes and discovery chimes no longer occur, and you're left there in silence with nothing more to see, or start from scratch with your newfound knowledge.
It's a worthy title that shows many big project narratives how to build character, but sadly doesn't offer much replay value. Regardless, for it's price, and game length- it's definitely worth the purchase.

Bought this game second-hand at a used video game store ~10 years ago for $5. First time I played, it, I had no idea wtf I was doing. I lost the third campaign mission more times than I care to recount, then I quit the game. About a year later, I came back to it with a clearer mind and figured it out, peice by peice. Each part of this RTS is unique and great.
Resources:
You have one resource, energy. The main source in the beginning of the game is by having an area of space filled with your "Perimeter" (hence the name of the game). Not by the NUMBER of energy producing buildings you have, like I first thought when I played this game, but by the amount of terraformed AREA covered by them.
Terraforming:
You have to terraform the land to be able to construct buildings, which allow you to make different turrets and units. Buildings that are on ground that was previously terraformed but is now damaged, either by earthquakes, or other units' effects, they start to take damage. Also, damaged terraformed ground cannot support your "Perimeter" so you lose that amount of energy production.
Units:
One of the most important aspects of the game to learn quickly. To start off, there are three types of units. These units in and of themselves are pratically useless, they do very little damage and have very little health. However, through the act of combining them, you can transform them into vastly different more powerful units. Some shoot lasers, some launch missles, some hurl rocks, and some even tunnel underground. Each of these larger units takes a certain number of the smaller units.
Buildings:
There are 3 main types of buildings: energy related, research, and turrets. Energy related include the energy producing building, which also can generate a sheild (for a substantial amount of energy), and energy storage buildings. Research buildings allow you to building bigger and better units and turrets; all you have to do is upgrade them to the proper level and the unit/turret unlocks. Turrets are turrets, they shoot stuff.
The important thing about the buildings is that they can be captured. In order for a building to be considered "yours" it has to be connected to your HQ building, either directly or through relays or the energy producing building. So, if your chain of relays on the way to the building from your HQ is broken, then the building loses power, becomes neutral, and is up for grabs. I love this in games! You can capture your enemy's labs so you don't have to make them yourself, and you can get labs your race can't even build!
This is a very different and unique RTS. Requires a huge amount of testing to figure out the best units and best strategies to use and which labs to get first and where to put your defenses and the ratio of building production to terraforming speed and the amount of energy you need and everything! My god this is a complicated game and I love it! This game is well worth it if you're willing to muddle through the non-informative campaign and figure things out for yourself.
P.S.

It has a very simplistic "make dis den upgrade dat and you wins" strategy. Just spam energy producing buildings and you'll never run out of energy. More of a puzzle game than an RTS. I used to play this game way before it came to steam and I enjoyed it now, after many years. The concept is cool and unique and the campaign is pretty fun indeed.
There are several problems with the game though:
- Repetitive soundtrack and voiceacting. There is 3 factions in the game and like... 2 tracks per faction in total. So, I would recommend listening to your own music.
- Game has no widescreen options and doesn't support multiple monitors properly, so your mouse is going to fly out of the screen if you happen to have multiple monitors.
- No online multiplayer. You can still play LAN though and the campaign is good.
- There are definitely some balance issues with the game - After playing this game for a while I found that Harkback's Scrourge Shark units are pretty darn OP :D Although it is not a real issue if you are going to play the campaing.
On the other side this game has:
- Fun terraforming and combat. The goal is to not destroy the buildings but destroy the terraing that these buildings are standing on. Really unique gameplay.
- Interesting squad morphing mechanics. The idea is that you can transform your army into entirely different units right on the battlefield.
- Good variety of different units: land, air and underground.
- Interesting but sometimes stupid mission objectives. You will see what I mean.
Overall this game is worth a purchase. This is not a strategy for everyone, but at this price you most definitely should give it a try.

Gameplay is pretty fun. Knocking one enemy into another will force them off their feet (provided no shield), which often makes many fights trivial if you juggle the enemies into each other, giving you reasonably large intervals (for a 2D fighter), where no attacks are coming your way. An enemy who has been knocked down can be supplexed across the screen, essentially every enemy is a projectile used to knock down other enemies, combining this mechanic with juggling makes you feel like a true deity though the resulting gameplay presents little threat.
Unlocking new skills throughout the course of the game is done in a Metroidvania-esque manner, though from memory none of the 'backtracking' (hub aside) is required to complete the game. The difficulty ramps up slowly over the game, enemies towards the end of the game usually require one or two specific skills to 'pop' a recharging shield before they can be hurt, in addition they are mure numerous + more damage. However this is largely an artificial increase in difficulty throughout the game, using the knock-back mechanic is less useful in these situations, forcing the Luchador to focus on one target at a time while breaking shields, and trying to combo those enemies into each other before the shield recharges, it makes you feel like much less of a badass chasing one of 8 foes around a screen instead of bringing pain to all 8 at the same time.
Audio is pretty pleasing to listen to, while I'm personally out-of-touch with the genre/nationality vibe they where going for, it seems to fit the pacing of movement throughout the levels pretty well, I could probably listen to this music for a reasonably longer length of time due to the lack of this style in more media today.
Visuals are pretty nice and colourful. Simple larger sprites make everything super-easy to tell friend-from foe, including yourself when things get a little hectic with more enemies. I think this refined/simple look suits the world of the Luchador quite well, bright colours + striking shapes rather than many complex details/patterns. Makes it really easy to pick out which enemies (or pieces of environment) need which skills to break them.
The only negative about this game, is that some of the side-challenges in an optional areas of the game require nigh on pixel-perfect execution of skill sequencing to pull off a combo/maintain hit-streak. In this regard the game feels very much like a Capcom fighter, finding the sweetspot so that you're skills will juggle the enemy correctly. This level of precision is needed nowhere else in the game so it feels more than a little superfluous. Granted Challenges in games are designed to present situations more complex/difficult than the main game (albeit in smaller packets), so probably not solid grounds to complain about.
Overall this game is pretty baller. For fans of other 2D & 3D beat-em-ups It's pretty much a necessity on the list, it may not not cater to the more experienced 2D fighters in the same way it does to the general populus, as overall the game is fairly easy. Its unique setting definately warrants a look when compared with the dark/gritty beat-em-ups we see more often today.

I never leave reviews on games, almost ever, doesn't matter what the game does wrong/right. But I feel like I have to leave a review on this one. If you asked me if you should get this game, I would say absolutely, yes! It has so much potential I wish I could skip into the future solely to see where this game went. However, it is still in early access, which means bugs and emptiness. What I mean by emptiness is, this game has very little content currently, and I would like to make a few suggestions to the creators.
Enemies:
There should definitely be more enemy types. Maybe after a certain amount of nights a ranged type appears that can deal with your archers easier? Or maybe just another type of zombie that can run fast or jump high, or at least survive more than one hit. There should also be some kind of boss, maybe after you reach 200-300 colonists, a super monster appears that can break blocks, has lots of health, and can reach your archers easier.
Colonists:
For this game to have variety, there needs to be much more jobs. The creators have an amazing concept with this and they need to take a hold of it and use it to its most. I suggest making more types of guards (melee, cavalry, maybe some kind of AOE attacker?) and also, more domestic jobs. The one I would like to see most is a builder. Maybe make it possible for you to make an outline of something like you do with farming, set the materials, set the hight, and tell them to go make it. Another idea would be to make something, and then select it and use the builders as a type of copy/paste, tell them where to build, and then have them build a copy of what you built. This would be amazing and would allow you to make huge kingdoms much faster.
Player Character:
There definitely needs to be some kind of tier system. Probably with armor and weapons, a bit like Minecraft, you know, having armor and weapons made out of different materials that are stronger/weaker than just your normal bow. You could also find rare types of materials from monster drops that can be crafted into multiple different things. Also, for controls, please add a way to crouch so that you can go to the edge of a block without accidentally falling off to you death while your building a tower. Also, I've noticed that sometimes when you go to the edge of a block, you kind of get stuck, and aren't able to walk back to the middle. I'm still not sure if this is an attempt at achieving what I was just talking about or simply is a bug.
Blocks/Materials:
This is also extremely important. There needs to be many more blocks. Glass, stairs, sloped blocks, and all different shapes and sizes should be added. This alone would make the game seem much bigger and more developed. I'm assuming gypsum will be used sometime in the future? Can't wait to see it (unless I just haven't reached the point where you use it.)
I know that many of you potential buyers might be put off by this list of things that the game still needs, but seriously, it is a great game and you should get now, not only because it will shoot up in price and popularity, but because even with such little content, it is an extremely good game that can keep you occupied for many many hours.
Bugs: Also, the most noticable bug that I have found is, if you dig a straight staircase into the ground and don't make extra room above your head, when you climb back up it, you will glitch through the ground and are able to fly extremely fast under the surface, before popping back out of the ground wherever you want (I actually found this one quite useful).
Thank you for reading, I can't wait to see this game's future!
Edit:
So, after writing this I remembered a few more things. First off, there is already multiplayer where each player in the server gets their own colony, so you know what needs to be added next... COLONY WARS!!! This would be absolutely amazing. The second thing I wanted to say is, I built a huge wall around my colony, it worked, kept a bunch of the zombies out, but I ran out of space to expand so I figured I would make another layer, named them Wall Rose and Wall Maria. However, once I made the second layer, I realised that the zombies simply spawned inside of it, and I think my time may have been wasted on this endeavor. I'm not sure what the requirements are for a zombie to spawn (darkness, trees, etc) but could you please make it possible to build a huge wall to protect your colony?

For full disclosure: I LOVE rail shooter games since they ever first came out in arcades.
Now, normally I have bent over backwards to make railshooters from consoles or MAME games work using my wiimote and some emulator on my PC.  Why?  Because Rail shooters do not show up on personal computers because people do not find great thrills in mouse clicking people to death or using a thumb controller to do the same.
Blue Estate is a happy middle between Time Crisis & House of the Dead Overkill on the Wii.  The graphics are outstanding and the developers are also on board to help anyone who wants to use other devices to play the game besides a mouse or controller.
I of course, as I am hopefully more famous for, use Mic's wiimoteoncod9.exe (see our group page).  It runs perfect and the game does have varying degrees of difficulty.  The stages are rife with cut scenes but thankfully they are not that long or interrupt the gameplay too much.
It plays perfectly like an arcade shooter, which is what it SHOULD DO.  It doesn't pretend to be anything else.
Here is some good wiimoteoncod9 video of play:
For who is this game for?  Enthusiasts who are willing to do a little more effort to use this game on PC with something that looks like a gun.  It is also for old school arcade gamers.  It is also for people who like the genre of noir with a fat slice of silly.
I recommend this game, it is really cheap(seriously 12 bucks) and please support the developers.  Because if they do well, they'll make more and maybe next time with dedicated IR support :D

Based upon Viktor Kalvachev's graphic novels, "Blue Estate" oozes pulp aesthetic from every pore! It's essentially a Tarantino flick gone on-rails shooter, and a glowing love letter to the heydays of arcade shooters like "Time Crisis" and "The House of the Dead". The console release got a lot of slack by major review outlets for its alleged racism, misogyny and overall 'tasteless' humor (I'm looking at you, IGN...) -- which led to review scores mainly reflecting the authors' disapproval of the game's cynical tone rather than its actual gameplay qualities. However, while "Blue Estate" might present its whimsical world and d-o-u-c-h-e-bag delinquents in a crass manner, I wouldn't deem any of its content overtly offensive -- particularly not when compared to other politically-incorrect games like GTAV or Saints Row.
The visuals, utilizing the tried-and-true Unreal 3 Engine, are splendid and perfectly capture the title's comic roots. It's not a particularly 'next-gen' looking game in terms of textures and effects, but its sleek, vibrant look, somewhere along the lines of "The Darkness II" and "Saints Row 2", greatly intertwines with the comic-stills footage.
The story is nothing to write home about, just all your mafia film cliches in a nutshell, really (one-man army vs. cannon fodder, la familia is law, shoot first etc.). Yet it's delivered in an exaggerated and charmingly whacky way that makes for a jolly good time. Protagonist Tony Luciano is a complete m-o-r-o-n as well as a psychopath, but you'll grow fond of him eventually as the silly plot unfolds.
The KB+mouse controls are spot-on, and, most importantly for an on-rails shooter, the locations are varied and colorful while the enemy/boss encounters needn't shy away from any free-roaming FPS. Even the QTE segments, which prompt you to either use directional buttons or your mouse, are fun since the game is surprisingly responsive to your inputs/motions.
Ultimately, your enjoyment of "Blue Estate" might hinge on whether you can appreciate its deliberately cheesy, self-aware humor and stereotyped characters. Political/social white knights will likely find no value in it.
But, merely judged on its (niche) genre merits, it's a near-flawless experience, and arguably the best on-rails shooter since "The House of the Dead: Overkill".
Here's to hoping we'll see a sequel.

And the world(s) are expansive. Set 3960 years before the Battle of Yavin IV (end of Episode IV), this game deals with the Jedi Civil War, the conflict that started after the great Jedi heroes Revan and Malak chased rumors of dark forces behind the Mandalorian Wars they had just won for the Republic. A year later, they returned... changed... and at the head of a force of fallen Jedi and Sith.
Now Revan is missing, thought killed by Malak in an act of betrayal. And Darth Malak's forces are now hunting the last Jedi to extinction. And proving that Darth Revan's reign was quite nice compared to his...
You are a new warrior. Soldier, scout, or scoundrel you are aboard the ship Endar Spire over Taris when Malak attacks. You escape and now need to track down the missing Bastila Shan, a Jedi Knight with a great power. Soon, you will discover your place in galactic events. And change history for the better... or the worse.
This game is the first glimpse of Revan, the larger-than-life Jedi Master and Sith Lord. One who had a great impact on Galactic History. And as part of the distant past... still possibly a part of the history in the new canon. It also is the first time you meet HK-47, one of the most iconic droids in Star Wars lore. Also one of the funniest, considering it is an assassin droid.
One note: Juhani, one of the companions in-game is likely the earliest BioWare character that has an... interest in their own gender.
Cannot recommend this game enough.

This review is easy. Battleborn is an incredible game that is suffering a lack of playerbase.
Some compare it to Overwatch, but that's a shame, really, because they can't be directly compared. While Battleborn does have a similar First-Person MOBA aspect, it also has an entire story mode, a set of stand-alone missions, and a deep and satisfying achievement/lore system. All modes can be completed solo, as a pre-made team, or with random players.
Throughout all of its modes, the real strength of Battleborn is its incredible amount of detail, polish. and stunningly perfect voice acting. For instance, each of the 7 Story Mode maps have at least 4 or 5 completely different sets of dialogue, and certain Battleborn, if you or a teammate is playing them, have their own set of dialog that adds into each base map dialog. And, of course, the game is steeped in the same Borderlands-style humor.
The issue is the playerbase. There just aren't enough people playing to support such a large game. It's sad really, but most of the regulars are hoping they release a free-to-play mode to attract more players.
Although I love Battleborn, it's difficult to recommend it right now unless you're OK with a mostly single-player experience, or have a group of friends to play with. If Gearbox does manage to solve the playerbase problem, I would change my recommendation to an unwavering recommendation.

The only downside is that right now, there really isn't a lot of content because the game is early access. You will have explored everything the game has to offer only a few hours in--but so far I've been playing for several days with the same old content and it's STILL NOT STALE! Sure, there isn't a whole lot of diverse stuff to do and explore just yet, but the colony mechanics are so simple and fun that you never get tired of them. The creativity and diversity comes from the players!!! I've seen people build sky bases, underground caverns, and good old fashioned castles. Everyone's colony playstyle is different--some people like to have as many colonists as possible, while others want to build the most fantastic base. The fun of this game is in the wacky civilizations you can contrive!
Also--unlike Minecraft, there are very few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s in multiplayer. When I first started playing multiplayer, I would get a stab of fear every time a new player joined because, having experienced Minecraft, I thought they'd immediately begin destroying everything and trolling. But so far, they never have.
This game can only get better from here. 7/10 as it is (early access), 10/10 when looking excitedly to the future.

Cross-Dimensional-Suplex. That's one of the many things you can do in this game. You can beat up a skeleton in the world of the living, pick it up, then switch to the world of the dead and suplex it there. This game lets you do that.
But in all seriousness, this is an amazing game, which I enjoyed enough to completely complete, the combat and platforming mesh together seemlessly in a way which makes combat so very satisfying. When you have all of the special moves, you get so much mobility in fight; and this mixes fantastically with the dodge mechanic of the game (which is really damn good, it's pretty much the gold standard of 2D dodging if you ask me). The things you can do in the fights in this game feel amazing; when you clear out a room of blokes without being hit and piledrive a conquistador skeleton into an Aztec skeleton, you feel like some kind of Luchador god.
Also the story's real nice. I don't want to go too much into it, but it's a real nice, quite minimal story which really completements the game without getting in the way.
So that's pretty much it, I enjoyed this game enough to do everything it had to offer, and considering it wasn't very expensive, I more that got my moneys worth from it.

Guacamelee! Gold Edition is an action, adventure, 2D, indie platformer that has strong Spanish/Mexican themes. Not only that, but there are hilarious cross-game-references. The game play is fun, fast paced, and dynamic. I greatly enjoyed this game, and recommend it to anyone who enjoys indie adventure-type games.
You are Juan, you are trying to save el presidente’s daughter (whom everyone tells you that you’ve had a crush on since you were little. Everyone knows but me?) The villain Calaca has taken her and Juan must master his powers as a Lunchador to save not only el presidente’s daughter, but to also save both the world of the living and the dead.
Guacamelee! Gold Edition starts out extremely basic with controls, but after 30 minutes into the game you will have unlocked several new abilities. Eventually I started to wonder “how can there be more moves for me to unlock?” But sure enough there was consistently new abilities every new zone.
The puzzles grow more elaborate and complex the father you get through the game, it doesn’t slow down and the game gets progressively more difficult as you unlock new abilities, and have new monsters thrown at you every new area.
All in all, I really enjoyed the game play, this game was always making me work harder to fight or platform, but the game did it in certain way that made me think “okay, this time I’ll make the jump for sure”. There were some spots where I would spend hours trying to get past it, but those were extra’s and my own fault for wanting to get them.
I’ve played 16 hours of this game, most of those hours were spent either on challenges or trying to complete every area 100% I decided to do a majority of the achievements the old fashion way, I only had to look up one or two really difficult achievements (that were often times very simple; gotta love over thinking something.)
A majority of the achievements will be unlocked on your first play through; the rest will need to be hard earned platforming with the abilities you unlock. Good news about that; even if you beat the last boss, you can continue from your original save. Instead of bracing yourself for a redo like I do for most games I play. You can beat Calaca and continue and go backwards to keep going with clearing the world. (or after beating the game, switch to hard mode, where you need to do it all again)
Guacamelee! Gold Edition costs $14.99, since I played 16 hours (and still need to put in a few more to complete hard mode) that is easily over a dollar an hour. In my book that is a good quality game. I recommend purchasing this game on sale, or watching for a humble bundle (where I purchased my edition)

First of all, I just want to say this game has no gameplay at all. It is all about the story. If you only play games for the gameplay, you will not like this game. For anyone who wants a good story though, I can safely say that her story is one of the best stories videogames has to offer. Her Story is unlike anything I’ve ever played.
The game is an interactive story, where you’ll have to watch hundreds of interview clips to solve a murder. The police have interviewed this woman, who is the main suspect of the murder. The ‘gameplay’ comes from listening to what she says, and looking for interesting words or sentences she mentions. for example, at some point she mentions Simon. You have this search bar, and if you search for simon, the first five clips that mentions Simon shows up. Not all of them, since then it would be really easy to solve the murder. You continue doing this, looking for more names or words that might lead to more information. That is pretty much all you do in this game. If this sound boring, you won’t enjoy the game. I really liked it! It made figuring out what happened really fun! My only criticism is that in the late game, it can be really hard to find more information. You don’t have to find all the clips though. I unlocked the ‘ending’ about halfway through.
While there aren’t multiple endings, and everyone will get the same story, the way you will discover what happened will probably be completely different to how I did it. The story is not linear at all! I don’t know how they managed to do it, but it really works! The most interesting part of the game is the woman. What you think about her will change a lot throughout the game. Figuring out her story (see what I did there?) is really interesting! Once I finished the game, I thought I knew what was going on. But then I searched up a summary of the story, and it turned out I missed a small detail which changes my entire view on the game! SPOILER:
Her Story is the best detective story told in a videogame, and I love it!
Her Story kept surprising me to the very end. It is one of the reasons why I find videogames to be the superior media to tell stories with. I loved the game so much that I’ll give it a:
It is certainly not for everyone. But for the ones who find this game to sound interesting, I can safely say you haven’t played anything like Her Story. It's also really cheap! I really love this game, and would recommend it to anyone who is looking for a great detective story!

Her story is an investigation game which doesn't spoil the answer by listing player options, proposing solutions or even asking a question in the first place. Think about it, what game does this? It's amazing!
It is one of the cleverest examples in game design I have seen in a very long time, and possibly the only piece of media that truly made me experience the “eureka I solved it” feelings.
I would recommend this to pretty much everybody, even non-gamers.

A unique form of storytelling, driven purely by a search for information. One second you'll think you understand, the next you won't know what to believe. If you like to dig down and uncover the truth, this game will be worth your time.

I've been a long time fan of the RCT franchise since RCT1. I was very excited about the RCTW project ever since I first heard the news that there was finally going to be a sequel. RCTW delivers everything you would expect in a modern RCT game. The greatest improvement of all is the absence of the grid. Everything in RCTW is placed and manipulated in a real time 3D environment. The Coaster Editor is the next biggest improvement. Gone are the days of piece-by-piece track building. In it's place, we have a powerful spline editor that makes creating coasters more advanced than ever before. It's entirely possible to build a track piece at any angle imaginable. And thirdly, we have an sphosticated UGC system in place to guarantee that players can create, share, and place virtually any kind of scenery object right into the game. I feel that my top needs have been met so far by RCTW and the project has a very hopeful future ahead. I'm very pleased to be a part of the experience and I'm excited to see this project carry on the legacy of my favorite theme park sim franchise.
Think of it as a night of something different. Try to uncover the truth of a murder situation through VHS quality videos. Enjoyable.
