As a fan of Roller Coaster Tycoon through this title, I say to the negative reviews, YOU ARE WRONG!!!
Before my input, I will tell you if it’s worth it. YES! YES! YES! BUY IT NOW THEN READ MY REVIEW!
That being settled. The review:
I waited forever for this game to release because of the negative reviews. They were going to release it many months ago and I was EXCITED! Then due to negative feedback, they decided to wait for release until they fix and add stuff to the game. THANKS A LOT NEGATIVE PEOPLE! >:( Then they released it and yeah, it has some issues, but it's still EARLY ACCESS! How about shut up already! Cons:

I would have to say I was a bit nervous purchasing this game. Seeing as basically every review is a thumbs down, spending $50 was a large "gulp" in my throat. However, I am very happy with this purchase and I'll tell you why.
I've been playing RCT all my life. Still to this day, I play RCT1, and make my wonderful parks. I probably got the game in a cereal box, I can't remember; but it's incredible. I also own RCT2 and RCT3, and being a huge fan of the franchicise in general, I bit the $50 and went with this game.
The first complain I see from a lot of people is about lag. Either those claims are overdramatized, or some of the later updates have fixed the issues. Don't get me wrong, it IS a graphically intense game. Running medium settings with an R9 390 (I also have an I5-4460) gives me less than 30FPS. I still have yet to try low settings, but my point is that this game is completely playable for any modern day system with a medium to high end graphics card. If you have a cheaper GPU, you might want to upgrade for a more playable experience.
We don't expect a game like RCT to be this way, but we have to realize that it is worth it in the end. Yes, RCT1 and RCT2 were programmed on a 1995 engine so efficiently than the weakest systems back in the day could run them at ease. RCT3 also was not bad, I ran that thing on an integrated GPU in a laptop. But RCT World is different. The graphics, for one thing, are better, so this is why it is more intense. Will there be future optimizations? Of course there will. Plus, Atari will probably add DirectX12 support, which should ease the game's frame rates and enhance graphical quality even more.
A major plus of this game is the 1.2GB download size. I'm tired of 50GB games, this is a very nice download size. Once you are in the game and get the hang of stuff, you start to realize how much potential it has. The coaster editor is very nice. It may be more difficult to use than the old RCT games, but that's because it has so many more capabilities. The curved paths are another nice feature.
If I had a complaint, it would be that there needs to be more and more scenary and rides! The more the merrier. But the truth is we all know this stuff IS coming. Atari will keep adding more content. Another pro is the peeps look really nice, good graphical detail to them for there being hundreds in the park. Also, did I mention there are recycle bins now? And you can place bins either on the path or off to the side. You'll notice nice little features like that. With some touchups, this game will be rocking and rolling!

This is the greatest game BioWare has ever produced. Perhaps even the greatest game of all time. The plot is beautiful (and full of at least one big surprise). The characters are wonderful. And the world(s) are expansive. Set 3960 years before the Battle of Yavin IV (end of Episode IV), this game deals with the Jedi Civil War, the conflict that started after the great Jedi heroes Revan and Malak chased rumors of dark forces behind the Mandalorian Wars they had just won for the Republic. A year later, they returned... changed... and at the head of a force of fallen Jedi and Sith.
Now Revan is missing, thought killed by Malak in an act of betrayal. And Darth Malak's forces are now hunting the last Jedi to extinction. And proving that Darth Revan's reign was quite nice compared to his...
You are a new warrior. Soldier, scout, or scoundrel you are aboard the ship Endar Spire over Taris when Malak attacks. You escape and now need to track down the missing Bastila Shan, a Jedi Knight with a great power. Soon, you will discover your place in galactic events. And change history for the better... or the worse.
This game is the first glimpse of Revan, the larger-than-life Jedi Master and Sith Lord. One who had a great impact on Galactic History. And as part of the distant past... still possibly a part of the history in the new canon. It also is the first time you meet HK-47, one of the most iconic droids in Star Wars lore. Also one of the funniest, considering it is an assassin droid.
One note: Juhani, one of the companions in-game is likely the earliest BioWare character that has an... interest in their own gender.
Cannot recommend this game enough.

One of the best RPG's ever made. Even if you don't particularly like Star Wars or Sci-Fi in general, you cannot deny the amount of effort, detail and story telling this game has to offer.
This game is HUGE. It has an expansive series of main quests that span over several planets and explore many aspects of the Star Wars universe. As well as that, it also has many side quests to add to an already massive game.
The story is great. Although the main plot in itself isn't the most original piece of fiction ever written, it is the characters, the dialogue and the personality that make this game so damn good.  It has so much personality, everything feels original and the amount of locations and characters truly make this game feel alive.
The customization, in terms of appearance, is not very expansive. You can choose between five or so character templates and choose their gender. You do, however, get a whole of a lot of clothing and weapons throughout the game to make your character feel more unique.
This is YOUR game in a sense. You choose who your character is, if they are good or bad. It makes the story feel less cliche than a lot of the other games in the genre are.
You can explore planets as you please with a party of characters that all add something different to the game. Some are stealth based, some are more aggressive, and some favour certain weapons over others.
The game is not too difficult, providing you level up smartly. Some encounters/segments can be challenging but the game in itself is not very hard. You often have a choice in how you approach quests. You can be stealthy, go in guns blazing or use the force to dispose of your foes.
That's another thing - the force. You can upgrade your character with force powers, good or bad. This allows you to choose whether you are a Jedi or a Sith warrior. Using sith powers doesn't necesarily mean you have to be sith, though. It adds depth to your character.
Overall this game is phenomenal. Easily in the top 10 best RPGs made (so far) and it is definitely in my top 50 games of all time. If you like Stars Wars then this is essential. If you like good games in general then this is also a must buy.
10/10

Having played the original Cannon Fodder to death on an old 486 PC, I can barely believe the people that made this game have any clue what made the original so much fun.  I poured hours into mastering the original's levels, so that I could make it through with my entire squad alive, taking Jools, Jops, et al as far as I could.  Grenades and rockets were a valued commodity, and placing them just right on enemy buildings made combat an almost puzzle-like experience.  None of that was present in what little portion of this game I was willing to suffer through before quitting.  Originally excited to see that this was being made; then disappointed that I heard it wasn't good enough to spend $20 on; then excited to find it on sale for $1; and now, back to disappointed.

Got this game in a sale for mere pence, thinking it's surely worth that, right? Wrong. If you've got any nostalgia for the original at all, you will be disappointed with this.
The low-rent intro sequence kicks things off and before you know it, you're awkardly shifting your troops around to an ill-concieved metal soundtrack while taking orders from a general who is clearly voiced by a British man sitting in a biscuit tin occasionally doing an American accent.
When he's not talking, all you hear are your soldier's footsteps that always sound like they are walking through hospital corridors no matter what the terrain. Even the misison script is written by someone who must've left school when they were 12. Example: "There are six mission crates hidden in the area! See if you can find it!"
Not to mention the multiplayer is Gamespy, which is no longer even active.
Cannon Fodder is easy to get right, but somehow these developers managed to get it so, so wrong. Presumably because they made it for a bag of chips, as that's the only excuse I can see for the poor production value. Making it in Flash would've been better.

This is a pretty great game, one of the best of the early access, but I do have some complaints.
Rules. Why are there so many rules? You can't attach this to that. You can't change the angle of that. Its like the game was designed to work the way Leonardo DaVinci expected his parts to work and I'm expected to use the parts in ways that he would have used them. The result is if I want to attach an extra length of propeller to a piece of propeller I can't. If I want to attach a block to a wheel and wings to the wheel and then twist the wings so they can grab the air and lift something, I can't do that. The wings can be horizantal or vertical. That's it. I'm always running into these unnecessary restrictions.
Then there's the case of the catapult that relies on you playing your keyboard to launch one bomb like you're Stravinsky or something. Tighten the coils with L. Release the decoupler with something else and then release the grabber with something else. There should be a way to make all these instructions one key or button temporarily so I don't have to search for keys.
I can't attach the camera to the bomb. I want to watch the bomb fly. It'd be nice for the camera to track it and record it from catapult to impact. I don't think I can do that. I can attach the camera in a fixed position to some framing, but it won't track anything. Maybe the camera can be programmed to switch to different cameras during the flight of the bomb so that on impact for example, it could switch to directly above the target and looking straight down. Automatically slow down time too.
I wish there were more extensive notes and messages on the game screen while I have some workshop thing downloaded and I'm playing with it. Its great to have instructions at the point where I'm going to download but I need to see them while I'm playing with the creation too. And a lot of these workshop things are incredible too.
Its great the way you can modify your play style while you're playing. You can slow down time. You can make the machine indestructible, turn on the "light a fire by touching it" thing and several others. These all add a lot to the gameplay. I do think a lot of the fanciest of the workshop require things that a beginner might not know to do so including some instruction during the game (hideable) would be nice.

This game has a lot going for it. The most obvious thing would probably be the interesting artstyle that makes the game very unique and helps it stand out from its rogue-lite competition.
However there is a bit more to the game than just repeating similar procedually generated environments over and over again. Most rogue-likes I have seen so far, do not have a really indepht combat system, but RE:IS is one of the rare exceptions to that. The turn-based strategical combat system has an asounding amount of depth, even though it is relatively easy to explain and get started in, really getting the hang of the system and using it to its fullest potential takes time, but esspecially on the higher difficulties you will not be able to succeed unless you make use of every possibility you have. I will not lie, the game is not easy and there are random elements at basically every corner, but one thing the game is very clear about is always showing you exactly how high your chance of succeeding is and in most cases bowing out of the risky challanges is an option aswell.
The game is centered around repeating playthroughs, each time starting of with a new crew. This of course means that there is mostly no influence from your previous playthroughs, except your own increase in skill and understanding. Even though different team compositions will generally result in different playthroughs, even playing the same team can give you a different experience as there are slight changes made to the events you might encounter each time you start a new campaign. This increases the feeling of never beeing 100% certain what you will find in a certain location, even though you have played through the game several times, which ties nicely into the exploration theme.
Overall this is a really good game that ties tactical combat and FTL style exploration into one neat package.

I bought this on somewhat of a whim yesterday, and I'm not disappointed. I can tell I'm going to get a lot of hours out of this game. Calling it "Banished meets Minecraft" might be simplistic, but it has that feel. If you pay attention and read through the little introduction / help manual (F1), getting started should be fairly simple.
Mechanics so far seem pretty solid. On a decent Win 10 machine (AMD 6x, 8GB ram, GTX 970) I didn't have any crashes or major bugs. I'm happy with the path-finding of the AI. I didn't build anything too crazy at first, but later added a giant tree with a "branch" that held a flax garden, and the villager had no problem navigating up the winding staircase to get to it. The monsters seemed to wander when my colony was smaller and were only a problem when they happened to get near the entrance to my walls, but now at "colony size 3" (30+) they seem a lot more focused on getting in, and there are a lot more.
With the right setup, the game isn't too hard. I have four archers covering a 2x20 "entrance" with a stock of 300 arrows and at 31 villagers, the monsters don't get further in than about 4 blocks, and that's rare. I haven't checked to see if I can change the number of monsters at any time, but the devs have included a "2x monsters" option at map creation.
The downside is that the game is still in EA, which means there are a limited number of things to do. My modest village has 4k food in storage and uses around 150-200 food/day. I have every resource possible, and for the most part a lot of it. That being said, there's a lot of potential here and even in it's current state, I like building and creating in games enough that I'll definitely get my money's worth.

Go into this review knowing that I am a well known Indie-Gamer!
Okay, Guacamelee does what few games have done. It pleasantly blends the beloved Metroidvania genre into a humorous setting. With some rather subtle easter eggs and references to boot. The upgrade to access style of gameplay that Metroid and Castlevania have pioneered is very prevelant in Drink Box's Mexican-Lore filled riot Guacamelee.
Now, onto the art style. The stylistic art that is present within the game makes the gamer sit back and say "Wow! That is beautiful." It flows together so smoothly and never has a dull-colored moment. Every area, character, and bad guy each has their own "Wow" factor about them.
Length? Yes, the game is rather short for the non-completionist gamers out there, but it still has plenty to offer them. If you want an 80 hour campaign, there are games out there for you. But the joy and experience of playing an indie title is that while the campaign may be short, it leaves its mark on you for years to come. *Cough* Bastion! Braid! *Cough*
So what would I give the game if Steam had a scale based review system? 4.5/5, 85%, A-, 8.5/10!
Flippin' awesome game. Crisp graphics, challenging, fun easter eggs, and it's FUN. Buy it!

Sit down, kids.  It's time for a cautionary tale.  Do NOT buy a game on Steam just because it's on sale for $1 and you think it looks cool.  Read reviews first.  Watch gameplay videos first.  Look it up online first.  I didn't do any of those things before I bought Apartment 666, and look at where I am now.  I'll never get back the 30 minutes I wasted playing through this game or the $0.99 I paid to download it.  Truly, it's the tragedy of our time.
Alright, let's break this train wreck of a game down.  It's basically a "horror" walking simulator.  Picture PT but terrible and made by a 14 year old.  That's Apartment 666.  The layout of the apartment looks almost the same as PT, as well; just a right angle.  You play as a 12 year old kid who can't find his parents in an apartment full of locked doors.  When you get to the door at the end of the hallway, you end up in your bedroom again.  Repeat this about 50 times, and that's the game.  There's a little more to it than that, but it all pretty much involves the two doors on either end of the hallway.  Every now and then one of the doors along the hallway will open.  You'll usually have some newspaper clipping to read or some obscure and infuriatingly specific spot you have to stand on to trigger the door to unlock (because of course it closed behind you on its own).  The latter is the part that really killed it for me.  There's one particular part where you're in a "storage room" (although that's TOTALLY a casting couch and the kid just had no idea what his dad did for fun when he and his mom weren't home), and to unlock the door, there's a VERY specific spot in front of the couch that you have to stand on.  It took me 10 minutes to figure that out; that's a third of the time I spent playing the game.
The next problem is the voice acting.  Dear god, the voice acting.  I legitimately think the developer got his 12 year old kid cousin to read lines from a hastily written script one afternoon and called it a done job in one take.  They're not even well written.  It's crap like "I wonder where my mom and my dad are," "I knew that this was a bad idea..." and "I am back in my room again?"  The kind of garbage that sure, you might think in that situation but that even protagonists don't often say aloud, and protagonists never say them in that silted a manner.  Also - and here's the kicker with functionality - the game has three achievements, and one of them is bugged.  All three of them are story achievements; start the game, get like 10% through the game, and finish the game.  The "finish the game" achievement is bugged and won't unlock.  The dev says "Look, 2% of people have unlocked it!  It works!" and we're all like "Bro, you've got a 15 minute game, and you're telling me that only 2% of people who start it finish it?"  All of this in spite of the fact that there are a couple dozen people on the Steam discussions saying "Hey, I finished it, and it's still bugged."
Apartment 666 is garbage, and I'm ashamed of myself for even spending $0.99 on it.  The premise is interesting enough, even if it a blatant copy of PT, and it actually does manage to create a fairly creepy atmosphere early on...until its severe flaws become glaring.  There's no real options menu, and your only graphical settings are to change "quality" between low, medium, and high (with absolutely no discernable difference between medium and high) and to change the resolution.  No brightness setting despite severely needing one; parts of the game are so dark I literally had no idea where I was going and couldn't tell if the game had crashed or just plunged me into pitch black darkness.  I almost wish the game had crashed.  It sucks.  Don't buy it.  Go out and buy Sonic Boom or Chasing Dead before you buy this; both are infinitely more fun.

I, like many, have a Pavlovian weakness for turn-based strategy games. Late into the night, I find myself wondering WHY OH WHY I have been compulsively playing Civilization for hours, when there's hardly a lick of story to care about as you progress and battles are formulaic.
Not so Renowned Explorers! I picked up the game primarily for its adventure-explorer narrative; as a person who named their pet rabbit after the leader of the "Kon-Tiki" expedition, how could I not? The premise is remarkably well done: it's full of tongue-in-cheek humor and bizarre excursions to exotic locales, vying for the renown of the global exploration community.
What really shines about this game for me is the blend of mechanics. First and foremost, the fact that you can choose three different styles of combat for most of your encounters (Friendly, Devious, Aggressive) provides a fun and engaging challenge. Part of the reason I love RPGs is because they offer alternative options to combat such as talking your way out of trouble. Renowned Explorers pulls these approaches into its combat scenarios by providing characters with separate stats for physical combat and "speech" combat. Balancing the different strengths of your crew in each encounter makes it more nuanced than just having the biggest guns in the game.
In addition to more varied combat options, crew set-ups make this game extremely replayable. You pick three people as your expedition crew, and the characters' different skill sets make each combo play very differently.
Finally, this is an adventure game afterall, so strategy elements, while present, don't take up all your time. You can buy gear, perform research, recruit assistants, and give lectures to earn strategic resources. The options available here are enough to impact your expeditions, but they truly are secondary to them.
I do have two minor complaints. First, each game "ends" before you complete all of your available expeditions. I expect that was done to allow people to complete more playthroughs with different crews and strategies, but it makes the game seem too short and a little incomplete. Yes, you can play the rest of the expeditions on the map after you "win," but you'll be past the point where you can unlock new strategic resources, and a lot of the battles get pretty easy.
My second - and again, minor - complaint, is that the character's speech combat animations don't make much sense and add little to gameplay. If I remember correctly, Ivan's "Terrify" action always produces a speech bubble of a teddy bear. I guess maybe the idea of a character that burly with a little teddy bear is a bit unsettling, but without actual dialogue, it all gets a bit nonsensical.
The annimations for physical combat are much more cohesive. Anna's special attack is particularly cool, and there are 20 other characters with special abilities and differing stats to try out.

Presentation
Blue Estate the Game is packed with fun. With nice voice acting and jokes littering everywhere, it is certainly a game that will make you smile.
Before you say rail gun shooting game is a dying business, Blue Estate could not disagree more than our antagonist Tony himself. Oh, did I just say antagonist?
The graphics here is good and solid. Character facial expressions and voice acting are great. Funny remarks, ironies, metaphors, politics… OK, you name it, they have it.
Headshot is a common thing, but being able to nutshot? That’s awesome!
Gameplay
Taking the role as Tony and Clarence, you are here to wreak havoc. All of this, started with the kidnapping of Tony’s favourite poledancer, Cherry. With intermittent black humor and swipe actions in-between gun fights, explosions, Chihuahua, bullet proof samurai…Oh well, you get the idea.
Blue Estate does have a unique way to separate itself from the other railgun shooters. The thing that keeps you playing is not how the story is unfolding, yet it is all about the funny bits and pieces that are still to come.
This game offers 2 game modes, the story mode comprises of 7 missions and the arcade mode. The arcade mode has a timer and is refreshed every time you killed an enemy. This fast paced version of the game is a test of skill with the humor taken away from it.
For doubling the fun, the game also allows local multiplayer with another person and can be played with various controllers including Xbox Controllers, the Leap Motion controller and light-gun.
However, with all the good being said, this game lacks one of the most important elements in today’s gaming: Character progression and upgrades. There are many things the developer can do to increase the fun, simply by leaving a few tweaks for players to fiddle with. For example, crazy weapon customization, even more stupid looking enemies and may be…well…more Chihuahuas.
Summary,
In summary, this game is a very much enjoyable shooter that is good for not so serious gamers or those that are looking for some relaxing moments with your best friends. As Jin Bong Sik once said: Insolent Missile!

The reason this game will always hold a dear place in my heart is, most of all, the sheer level of over-arching strategy. The strength of this game lies in its sheer replayability. This game is for you if you are the sort who enjoys picking a detailed game in attempt to learn its every nuance and aspect. Every playthrough will play out differently, amongst the choice in captain and team, the choice specialisations, your expedition plan, papers researched. You can only ever hope where you have all of these variables so thoroughly mastered that you might change one of them, and intuitively be able to bend the rest to compensate

A game that has so many events, character combinations, and challenges that its bound to give you at least 8 hours of gameplay just in trying to finish each mission alone. There is even more replaybility in choosing different crews to take on the expedition and challenging each mission with a different disposition. The dispositions are made up of Friendly, Agressive, and Devious which create a Rock-Paper-Scissors style of strengths and weaknesses and different crew members have different abilities that affect a certain disposition. Even deeper into the encounters is a mood system which gives debuffs or buffs based on the person's mood and also affect a general positive negative balance. This is barely scraping the surface of the encounters and not all events lead to encounters and most tend to rely on percentage chances based on crew skills and stats. Inbetween missions you get to allocate resources towards improvement of your crew and your ability to gain more resources. The goal is to collect treasures (i.e. the collectibles) in an attempt to beat your rival in popularity but you must carefully balance this with crew resolve and supplies to avoid a game over.  The game is a great pick-up if you are a fan of XCOM or Banner Saga style games but also provides a bit of everything to satisfy anyone

I want to like Guacamelee. I really do. The Developers did almost everything right. The art style, animations, soundtrack, sound effects, and humor are all top notch. But there are a couple of major problems that hold this game back. The lesser of the two evils is the level design. For the most part, the side puzzles are clever, and the rewards for completing them make them feel worth the effort. However, I can't say the same for the required puzzles.
Much of the later half of the game is vertically oriented, and eventually the game seems to degenerate into a very sloppy platformer. There are few things more frustrating than almost making it to the top of a series of very tiny platforms, only to have one of the many enemies that have started chasing you (as there's no room to fight them) hit you, resulting in knockback the likes of which hasn't been seen since the original NES Castlevania games, and send you all the way back down to the bottom.
This brings me to the more dire of the game's issues: the controls. As another reviewer mentioned, the game starts off with very tight, responsive, and just generally great controls. But as your move pool increases, you increasingly feel like you're in the game. And by that, I mean that it feels like you're wrestling your controller. There are a pretty decent amount of moves at your disposal by the end of the game, and as which move you use depends on which direction you're moving the control stick, pulling off the right move while moving and trying to dodge can be a hassle.
Also, a quick, slightly-spoilery, albeit non-specific complaint about the story:
And now for the good parts:
Despite my criticisms, the first half of the game is one of the best metroidvania games I've seen in a long time. The amount of hidden collectibles is incredible, and as I've stated before, the optional puzzles are incredible! And it has the benefit of having something that very, very few PC games seem to include these days: local multiplayer. With steam increasingly pushing Big Picture mode and couch gaming on PCs, Guacamelee is finally giving those of us PC gamers with a social life something we've been longing for for a very long time: a game we can play with friends in the same room (without forcing them to drag their rigs over to our houses). Playing with a friend can reduce the frustration caused by the aforementioned problems, and I'll be honest, it's just plain fun!
Overall, despite the control and occasional level design issues, the game is worth playing, especially if it's on sale, and you've got someone to play it with! I might not recommend it at full price, but it's definitly an enjoyable experience.

I know this review is a little late.
has been out for several years. However, I feel the least I can do for this hidden gem is to write a simple review.
doesn't tell its story in one big chunk. Instead, you sit in front of a computer in a police station, looking through the database and trying to piece together what happened in 1994. You don't know who you play as, you don't know how the case is related to you - all that is up to you to figure out. I don't want to spoil much, so I'll move on to another point.
It isn't necessary for you to solve the mystery. There is no cutscene at the end explaining or showing you the truth. That is left for your imagination and detective skills.
is not a long game and will take you around 4-5 hours to complete. But it's the journey that counts. You type "key words" into the database and it displays related videos with "key words" being said in them. E. g. at the start, you are asked to type the word "MURDER" and it displays 5 videos where the word "MURDER" has been said. It's an interesting mechanic but it can get annoying at the end, when you just randomly type any word that you can think of, hoping it displays a new video.
I also have to mention how well each scene is acted. The lead actress, Viva Seifert, puts an incredible performance that won @ The Game Awards 2015 for Best Performance.
+ immersive story
+ lead actress
+ forces you to think outside of the box
- can get boring at the end
8/10
Nonetheless,
is unique and fascinating in its own charming way.

Time for an honest review.
Normally I would not have recommended this game when it first released, but over the past 2 weeks the game has been updated with bug fixes and optimization that has steadily improved the experience. The fact is that this game has a solid base to build off of, and that is what people need to take away from it. I own both Planet Coaster and RCTW, both are hardly finished and both, in my opinion, have a positive future ahead of them. Also, Hats off to Nvizzio for keeping in touch with the community and rolling out updates as quickly as they can. With all of that said, I'll list my pro and cons.
Pros
-Coaster editor/maker in this game is EXCELLENT, Sure its a bit finnicky sometimes, but it's damn good and can only get better, I prefer it to the piece by piece editor in PC, it's one thing I hated about RCT3.
-Decent variety of scenery to start and I'm sure this will be expanded upon
-Solid amount of flat ride content with a new one coming every 2 weeks in Major patches (Yes, I believe them, they have stuck to that schedule so far)
-I'll probably be crucified for this, but after the latest update..graphics have improved markedly, and I'd expect that to continue
-The Management aspect is there, could be better but it's decent for EA.
-Terrain tools are easy to use and effective, need an option for underground building though.
-There is more but I'll leave it at that for now, new update is scheduled to be rolled out Tuesday or Wednesday next week so I'll edit this review at that time
Cons
-Peeps need work (Animations/texture/etc)
-Optimization at this point is a bit shaky, people across a wide array of system are getting mixed results, once the park gets large it really starts to slow down, apparently this is getting addressed in next patch, I'll update if that is the case
-Pathing is shoddy at the moment.
-AI behavior is pretty poor in the current build, mechanics don't always fix rides, janitors are slow, etc.
-Water quality sucks. lol.
-Can't change ingame graphics while in your park. (Seriously guys?)
-Can't place scenery on elevated paths (Again, really guys?)
-Coaster ratings need work, every coaster I make is a vomit comet
-General bugs and such
-Overall, I'd recommend this based on the rate it is improving and the committment Nvizzio has shown to the franchise. I'd expect good things as time goes on.

Now this is a very difficult game to describe. The closer comparison to a prior game, though not perfectly accurate, would be FTL -Faster Than Light- except instead of being in space, you're sent back to the exploration time of the late 1800.
The goal of the game is to become in 5 "expeditions" the most "Renowned Explorers". To do so, you need to select a team of 3 explorers, among 20, with their own stats and skills, and try to gather as much "renown" as possible by collecting treasures during the expeditions.
An expedition is a semi-random map of interconnected nodes containing various ressources and treasures gated behind skill-checks and/or fights, and must be completed by reaching and defeating its associated boss. You have a limited number of free moves or "supplies" to explore the map, with some potential resupply here and there. You can explore beyond these free moves, but doing so will net some random penalties to your crew's stats. Too many penalties and defeating the boss may become impossible!
Between each expeditions, you can spend your hard gained ressources on various improvements: team stats, skills, supplies, amount of ressources or renown obtained etc.
A full run will usually take 2h, or around 30 minutes per expeditions. The first expedition is set (sort of) but you get to decide the next 4 among the 8 available in the base game (10 with the More to Explore DLC). They all come with different difficulties, skill-requirements and themes. The harder they are, the better the rewards.
Of course, a game about exploration wouldn't be complete without a world to discover. Renowned Explorers offers a colorful, lighthearted and witty one. You'll be befriending sheeps, insulting lamas and slapping monkeys (they deserve it) while you visit tropical islands, the deserts of Egypt or the forests of east Europe.
If my 200 hours on the game have not hinted on it yet: I fully recommend this game.

I bought this game on sale a while back because I had fun memories of Supreme Commander 1.
The game feels lackluster compared to Supreme Commander 1. The building system is pretty linear and lack luster and it feels like there's a lack in unit option. In order to build better units they implemented a research system, it's a resource that generates overtime and you can increase the resource generation by building more research stations.
What makes the game incredibly unfun is that it feels like you need to commit to one type of army because of the research system. If you build a land army and commit your research on it but later on you want to add an air army into the mix the air army will be incredibly weak making your overall army weaker.
I bought this for the campaign. In the campaign, the naval army isn't always available to be built in most of the campaign, it's specially important for the Cybrans because their naval army has a research that allows them to walk on land and the ships are pretty overpowered compared to land units. The game only comes with 18 missions, 6 missions per race and all the missions aren't difficult.
The skirmish felt much better in SC1. I enjoyed skirmishes turtling it out against hordes of insane AI armies marching in the door. What makes this less appealing is that only the UEF has a tier 2 defense, plus there aren't any walls you can build.
Overall the game is best defined as meh. If your interested in checking out this RTS, you should buy Supreme Commander 2 first then buy Supreme Commander 1 and Forged Alliance so that you will feel like the gameplay was improved.

I am not good at RTS games. I'm not a good Age OF Empires or C&C player. I am not a veteran. But i think pros of this game are overcoming the cons when compared to most played RTS games.

You can order buildings to produce army even you do not have the resource necessary. When the resource is available, they will automatically start producing. And you can start a loop for a production. You do not have to control all your buildings if they are idle.
Easy to play. Because you can convert resources in this game. Which gives you alternative strategies.
Has nice variety. Because there are naval, land and air units for all the playable factions. And there are different gameplay styles for AI. Rush, balanced, turtle, defence... etc.
What about cons:
Only 3 factions are available to play.

I Rate

Initial thoughts ==========================================================================
All I can say is: FINALLY.
I have been waiting for a game that allows one to be immersed in the creation of a society instead of floating around the top of it telling it what to do. This game is what I have been looking for FOR YEARS. I can not wait to see where it goes.
For people who are looking into buying the game =================================================
It's in early stages, there isn't a whole lot to it yet. But what IS there shows an immense amount of promise.
The lighting engine is gorgeous and the bump map on the block textures is wonderful.
You have a decent selection of building materials for a game that's this early in the process.
There are ragdoll physics (!!) when a colonist or a monster is killed. (it's amusing when a monster ends up pushing a dead monster around until the body despawns)
As far as GAMEPLAY goes, it's got a similar feel to Minecraft. You will start out with some materials so you can get your colony started. Otherwise you just have to mine resources until you can assign a colonist to do the work. At night when everyone goes to sleep, monsters will come out. You just have to make sure they don't attack your colonists! Otherwise the only real goal is to keep getting bigger and bigger and bigger until you have a city!
For the developers ====================================================================
You guys are fantastic. Keep up the incredible work! I will try to be here along the way and I can not wait to see how you and the game will grow. I looked at the roadmap and that's a pretty solid plan. I do have a few questions/thoughts that popped in my head as I played the game.
Will you be adding more materials like glass and various forms of stairs?
Will there be any sort of factory automation aspects to the game? It would be really cool to have some sort of mid to end game  factorization. Like a colonist would be needed to shovel coal into a boiler for a steam turbine. Conveyor belts/pipes used to transport resources.
I also couldn't help thinking about the colonists themselves. I want to build them individual homes but I don't see a point if all they need is a bed. I saw the point about the happiness on the roadmap. Perhaps quality of housing/living arrangements could have an effect on that?
My final thought is families. It would be neat if colonists would develop "feelings" for other colonists and create families so that they all live in a house together. That would also probably require a name feature for the colonists.
==================================================================================
That's all I really have to say haha, food for thought! It's a great game and I really hope it goes far. I wish only the best for the developers.
I hope this was helpful!

A satisfying game. Guacamelee! is not a long game by any means, it took me about 4 or 5 hours to get to the ending on normal difficulty the first time through, collecting about 50% of everything. I feel like I haven't really seen everything there is to see quite yet. I'd suspect that finding everything would take a lot longer, and that the additional challenges found in Gold Edition will make it last longer. Combat feels right, and is much deeper than it initially feels. The game is pretty unforgiving and difficult, especially near the end, so old-school gamers can enjoy that. If you're up the the challenge, Guacamelee! is a great game, filled with dozens of references to other games in an environment that's dripping with personality.
It should be noted as well that the game features local co-op. It's a lot of fun to play with the right friend, but some of the platforming sections feel as though they were designed with a single person in mind and can be difficult to pass with a second player. However, playing alone you'll wish you had a second set of fists against some of the tougher battles. It's all possible alone or with a friend. It's better with someone else overall. Try it both ways.

Nothing really incredible on that side, can be fun to co-op with friends. Sadly, I wasn't able to. With only eight missions available, the story mode isn't the most entertaining nor re-playable part of that game. Very classic, you are destroying different elements, killing enemies for a good 30 minutes before finally getting to the boss. Really, nothing incredible.
Otherwise, the characters are great, funny, have an incredible personality, graphics are comic-fun and the atmosphere remind you of an attempt to be Borderlands2.
One of the fun experience of Battleborn, is leveling up. Every new level, you will be asked to pick an improvement to one of the skill you already possess making you a little stronger everytime. It might go from changing your attack to boosting your stats or variations of the skills to finally unlock an ultimate once lvl 5.
I would say that the FOV is a major issue in this game, your weapon seem to be taking more than 50% of your entire screen, making impossible to see other details or to pay attention to other stuff happening in game. You feel that element especially well in multiplayer.
I believe there is only 3 different kind of map/modes to play multiplayer in Battleborn. A Conquest mode : capturing locations, Incursion (most moba element) : advancing your minions to push lanes, and finally Fusion who takes a big chunk of inspiration from Smite apparently. But I believe the worst part of multiplayer is how weak Battleborn makes you feel. You can crit, head shot, and attack enemies, it is barely worth the effort as they will barely receive any damage.
Overall, I won't make a big description out of the multiplayer for the simple and good reason that, it is not really novative and take elements from Dota, LoL, Smite and so on. Furthermore, it is important to mention that the population of this game is very low, creating queue times that will last forever and resulting in a matchmaking absolutely not balanced (I just lost a game 500-20, I know i'm Unskilled, but still).
Finally I would recommend to buy this game only for dirt-cheap, with a friend to only play the Story in coop mode.

This game follows the Gearbox trend of having wacky, colourful characters and intense RPG-lite first-person action, established in the Borderlands games. It gets compared a lot to Overwatch which is probably unfair, since it isn't trying to just be an arena shooter. There's an arena shooter gameplay mode, sure (though currently there's virtually nobody playing it) but there's also a series of co-op missions that can also be done solo. It's here where I feel Battleborn truly defines itself, as a game that borrows mechanics from the MOBA genre and applies them to PVE content. If you enjoy the gameplay of Smite or Overwatch but are intimidated or otherwise put off by fighting other human beings, as I am, then this game is perfect for you. Not merely a bot-shooting gallery, the story mode has some interesting set pieces and challenging tactical moments, especially on 'Advanced' difficulty. It may be very difficult to find a group at the time of this review, however, unless you have friends who own the game.

Is this a good game: yes.
Should you buy it: yes.
Some problems and bugs on modern systems and my notes on some moments:
- Mod it hard. Not in a "light-sabers with 999 damage" way, in "about 5-7 general patches" way. All patches are easy to install and make the game look better. Though I still encountered some weird textures and tiny bugs. Oh, and don't forget to turn grass off: it may drop framerate below 15 in some locations and make your screen a mess of grey pixels.
- There's no dark side and light side of the Force. There's an "good merciful light" side and "I'm a giant edgy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" side of it. Dark side choises partially consist of killing innocent people just for the sake of it. There are plenty of moments where you can decide, that you are too powerfull to bother with some trivial tasks that stand in your way, and going full sith in this case seems fine, but there are also moments that are just... eh. There is no satisfaction in killing half of the folks you are allowed to kill.
Also top-tier robes is light-side only, and choosing the dark side rewards you in no way equipment-wise and power-wise.
- As I finished the first planet, I was afraid, that my character build was awful, that I've spent some points on skills that are completely useless. My worries have disappeared completely after I CRUSHED several bosses in a row, in sutiations where I was forced to go 1vs1 with the guy. I guess devs were aware of this, because last level consists of Sith being thrown at you every few moments. The only trouble you may have is the final battle, but, with enough buffs and stimpacks, it becomes fairly simple.
As you can see, these are just minor inconveniences. The story is good, as is lore. Gameplay is fun. Graphics are outdated, but this game isn't about a pretty picture.

I know I'm treading on dangerous territory by saying I recommend this game but do hear me out.
First of all it's not worth buying for 3€/$ as it's really short and has some bugs. I got it on the Humble store for a lot lot less and supported charity at the same time so I don't regret buying this.
The game itself is very obviously strongly inspired by P.T. Which isn't a bad thing, especially for people like me who were never able to play actual P.T. May it rip in pieces, it was so good but never popped up in the PS store where I live. Anyway back to apartment 666.
It's a walking simulator. It's not as scary as one might expect from the title, but the atmosphere was enough to give me some creeps. It's definitely a good choice for people who want a bit of a scare but can't handle horror well.
Problems...
We all know at this point that there are many. The devs seem to be aware but don't seem to be able (or willing?) to fix it.
The game is really dark (as it should) but that makes it difficult to spot stuff you need to find to progress. You get a flashlight in one section, then it's gone but it would be good to have it more often, especially in that part where you are locked in the bedroom and need to see a newspaper on the bed that's basically invisible in the darkness of the room.
Sometimes you need to stand in places to unlock things and it's not clear why. Fortunately the community guides help with that.
Ah also don't expect to get the third achievement. It's not real even though the dev says otherwise.
Oh and while the story is pretty interesting there's not enough of it. And the ending is quite sudden and anticlimactic. It feels like the start of a different type of game if you know what I mean. Hehe
And despite all this I'm recommending it?
Yes. Because maybe, just maybe if it gets a bit of positive feedback the dev will decide to give it another try. Maybe the achievement will get fixed, maybe they'll add a few more spooks and clues as to how progress in confusing parts. Maybe there'll be more monster moments. Maybe more parts where you're in a seemingly endless corridor with super creepy singing (my favorite part btw.). Maybe. I don't expect it but one can hope and wish, even if it's for naught.
So that's my review done. Cheers people and no need to tell me you disagree. I know. And I don't blame you at all. I feel your frustration, trust me.

This is such a charming and fascinating game. It combines many gameplay elements including turn based strategy, RPG, roguelike, and storytelling into a very tight and balanced package. The game is fairly short but emphasizes replayability like most roguelikes. The adventures and stories varied and have multiple results so you end up seeing something new every time you play. RNG is used pretty extensively but it feels suprisingly fair.
The multi layered rock, paper, scissor combat system is very unique and adds so much to the charm you could easily confuse it for a Nintendo game. The story telling is light hearted and silly that it's hard not to smile. The secrets and collection elements are very rewarding as well. The game is challenging but beatable even on the hardest difficulties. There's a large number of difficulty settings so it's even playable If you want to adventure with your kids or just want to experience the stories.
The best part of this game is the community. The developers have encouraged community driven weekly challenge events that have brought together the most positive gaming community that I have ever seen. The players are constructive and the deleopers are responsive to feedback. It's easy to get advice from the pros and trolls are delt with in a calm manner.
This game is great and the only complaints that I have seen are in regards to the length. If you don't like playing roguelikes that favor replayability then this may not be the game for you. It's also pretty silly so you should consider staying away if you prefer your games violent and grim.

It's a great little tactics game in which you gather a band of 3 explorers to travel to different countries and find riches and fame. In each place, you'll progress by going from one encounter to the next (similar to FTL) until you reach the final encounter in which you can gain the main treasure of the place. During all this you have to manage your resources (food) and the progression of your characters to get strong enough for the specific encounters. If it comes to a fight, you'll be thrown into a turn-based tactics game with pretty strong mechanics (despite the harmless look).
One playthrough takes only about 1-2 hours and you are encouraged to try different locations or a different set of adventurers. That said, all in all, I'd like to see a bit more variety and more options, especially when it comes to the locations.
All this is set in a lovely and fun scenery with a great art style and a cute sense of humour. I can only heartily recommend this little gem of a game.

This is a very fun game, you can do many things and you may do whatever you would like without too many limitations.
You can hunt 8 different areas including the Southern-Central-Northern Rockies, where you are bound to have successful hunts of many different species. The Southwest, where you can hunt desert animals in the hot, dry cactus filled valleys. The South Central Plains, where the dry weather with beating sun will dwell you into a world of hunting successfully many animals, from deer to bison. The Upper Midwest, where the biggest bucks around can be hunted, mixing with bears and a swath of turkey. The Pacific Northwest, where you can hunt the Western North America and Canada- you're bound to have a nice elk or cougar hunt around these vast lands. Lastly, Africa, where exotic hunts await, hunt Kudu, Lions, Elephants, and Boars, in the hot, dry, arid lands of wild Africa.
You can hunt 16 animals ranging from Wild Turkey to Elephants in the nature-filled maps that are put in front of you. Just remember, some animals you can hunt peacefully and easily, but some may cost you your LIFE, if your movements and actions are wrong to a species.
You are set with a wide variety of weapons to choose from to go on your trips. Remember, choose the right caliber that suits you and the animal for ethical hunting, the weapon you use is up to what you enjoy. The weapons are ranged in types, you are allowed to use bows, handguns, rifles, and shotguns- all the weapons you can enjoy while setting foot in the dirt of the woods.
But now, we unfortunately have to go with the flaws.
First off, the repetitive, yet annoying walking sound is just terrible, just ignore that. What's worse is the painly slow walking that does not resemble anything close to a human's average walking speed.
Second, physics are a bit wonky- with the vehicles you sometimes just randomly fly all over unrealisticly. Also, when you take down an animal with your weapon(s), the animal just stops abruptly and falls over on it's side. Bullet physics are finely realistic though.
Third, I don't know if this happened to anybody else, but- after about 18 hours of gameplay everytime I hit the, "Play" button, and I get a message saying, "Corrupt Installation| [missing config file]". I tried deleting and re-downloading the game, but it still doesn't work. This is very annoying for me, I have been dying to play for a while, if you have a solution, please reply. I use a Windows 8 PC, a fast one, too, by the way.
But I don't think that will stop me from recommending this game, this is an awesome game. I recommend it for people like me who want fun during their times, but I DON'T recommend it for die-hard hunters looking for an ENTIRELY realistic hunting game. If you want some of the most accurate hunting games, I recommend theHunter and Deer Hunter 2005, although this is a pretty accurate game.

Based on the legendary online reviewer by the same name, created and played by James Rolfe, AVGN Adventures is a delightfully retro 2D romp. Clearly, this game was designed to appeal to casual gamers as well as AVGN fans. The controls are very responsive and easy to pick up (I would argue, for all its simplicity, it's some of the best controls I've ever used), and, despite what many have said, the difficulty is balanced fairly, sitting on that line between easy and frustratingly hard to provide healthy challenge. Compare this to say, Worms Revolution or Pokemon Battle Revolution (nominal similaraties purely coincidental), where much of the challenge comes from how unfairly rigged the game and the AI are against you, and you can appreciate how good a game this is. As a fan of the Nerd myself, I also enjoyed the sheer volume of references and characters crammed into the game, and the many cameos from other reviewers (though no JonTron, Spoony, Yahtzee or Nostalgia Critic? REALLY?). The music is also fun to listen to and has a lot of variety. The main complaint I have with this game is also a warning: if you miss a level-specific achievement, you can't replay a level you've already completed or start a new game to go back and do it without your old file being erased. This caused some frustration and anger with me when I started a new game to complete the "No, you listen!" achievement in the tutorial level, only to then realise that the game had replaced my old save file. Given the simplicity of the game, a better saving system really wouldn't have been difficult to do. As a final note, gamers who aren't followers of the Nerd won't get the references (then again, would you really buy this game is you weren't a fan?). A great game, and very addictive.

Well now that that's out of the way, AVGN Adventures is a well-made love letter to all things AVGN. It's filled with all of the things that make the Nerd the Nerd. He complains about various design choices along the way, and when you die you're given a randomly-generated complicatedly vulgar insult about how much he hates the game. Levels, enemies, bosses, and even the pause menu music are based on games he's reviewed. There are plenty of cameos from the Nerd's fellow Internet personalities, and various characters that have been on the show. And the final level and final boss are exactly what and who they
be.
Plus, you know, the level design's pretty darn good, too.
AVGNA is designed to delight through the frustration. It's not I Wanna Be the Guy hard, but it's a tough-as-nails platformer. And what would you expect, considering that this is not only an homage to the Nerd, but also to the frustratingly difficult and poorly-designed games that he's played over the years. But therein lies the mastery in this game. A good parody should include the things that made the subject awful, but without actually being awful itself. It's a challenge, but AVGNA pulls it off without breaking stride.
I mean, it's not perfect. Most of the stages contain a number of the same enemies, only reskinned to suit that stage. Which, of course, is all part of the big parody. But the invincible things that fly in infinite circles start to get pretty tired by the end.
Also, the final boss will rock your world. Difficulty is gradual in the game. You can play the stages in any order you want (and can revisit completed ones, if you so choose), but if you play them in the order they appears on the stage select screen, you will find a pleasant steady increase in difficulty as you go. That said, the final boss was much tougher than anything else I faced. I got him eventually. But man did that take FAR more tries than any obstacle before it.
The music is great, and whatever you hear perfectly suits the situation you're hearing it over. The game is visually appealing and colorful. Controls are responsive, which is a must. The Nerd shoots as fast as you can tap the button, meaning speedier button mashers will have an easier time with most of the bosses (if I had just gotten two more taps in, I could have killed the first boss during his very first vulnerable period). The four different characters (three of whom must be unlocked) each have their uses, and I found myself using each one in different situations over the course of the game. There could be more powerups. By my count, there are four, and one of those can ONLY be used by the Nerd himself.

At the checkpoint/store you can unlock grappling techniques to vary it's effect, costumes to change stats, and access the Steam Workshop costumes you've downloaded. It is also where you can change between the male and female luchadores.
There's (local only) two player co-op, but the game doesn't seem to make itself any harder to compensate. There aren't many side quests, but it never bothered me much.
I give this game a 10/10. (It'd be a 9/10 if I wasn't biased.)

Perfection while it lasts, a bit empty after it's over.  Guacamelee may be short but there are no wasted elements here.  Every screen is expertly laid out to make it a contender for the best Metroidvania of all time.
The platforming, fighting, and even puzzles seemlessly mesh the same mechanics to deliver enjoyably deep 2D gaming that's simple to pick up.  It has learned well from the classics taking elements from Mega Man X and its spin-offs, mixed with the dodging and grappling from modern character action titles, and making you think outside the box to maneuver through varied environments.  The obstacles constantly demand creative applications but the difficulty curve is so smooth, there is never a brick wall.  The system has so much freedom, mashing buttons can deliver satisfying combos while extra challenges and a harder difficulty await those who want to put their precision to the test.  It is almost frightening how much Guacamelee gets right and at $15 might be one of the best gaming purchases you'll make.
I could bury this review in paragraphs of praise, but I do want to point out the game's one shortcoming.  The dazzling world is full of secrets to discover and clever references to recognize, presented in a unique and vibrant art style.  But plot-wise, few of your accomplishments leave a lasting impression or feel like they have made a difference in this world.  As satisfying as overcoming the in-game's challenges is, the sense is fleeting as are the impressions of its cast.  As far as problems go, this affects none of the gameplay and is negligible at worst.  But with so much dialogue, some touch-ups could have given its world a more memorable identity to rival the likes of Zelda and Okami's.  As it is, the memes and references are great but something more emotionally involved could have made it stay with players long after they've set it down.  That is one of the only reasons I can think of that Guacamelee is not talked about more.

Luchadors unite! I'm not a big brawler fan. Most of my experiences in this genre are games that require painstaking trial-and-error to figure all the moves and combos. Guacamelee was able to break that mold because the best part of the games for me wasn't the combat aspects, but actually the way the game trained me to use each skill along the journey through superior level design. And I thought this game was pretty hard, but mastering the moves became second nature because it forced me to use specific skills throughout each level, so by the time the final boss came around it was a piece of cake.
But it's not just the training that made the game fun. There's also the transition between the living and dead worlds which adds a very difficult twist to platforming and combat. Even though the fighting moves are pretty basic, it makes combos reasonably easy to pull off and thus doesn't frustrate. Plus it's always fun to throw enemies around, transform into a chicken and peck them to death, or goat fly across the screen through a horde.
One word describes Guacamelee--FUN.

This game follows the Gearbox trend of having wacky, colourful characters and intense RPG-lite first-person action, established in the Borderlands games. There's an arena shooter gameplay mode, sure (though currently there's virtually nobody playing it) but there's also a series of co-op missions that can also be done solo. It's here where I feel Battleborn truly defines itself, as a game that borrows mechanics from the MOBA genre and applies them to PVE content. If you enjoy the gameplay of Smite or Overwatch but are intimidated or otherwise put off by fighting other human beings, as I am, then this game is perfect for you. Not merely a bot-shooting gallery, the story mode has some interesting set pieces and challenging tactical moments, especially on 'Advanced' difficulty. It may be very difficult to find a group at the time of this review, however, unless you have friends who own the game.

Where to even begin with this one...
The game has as much replayability as you'd expect from a sandbox-style game. The tools they give you to build your creations are certainly robust; allowing you to create anything from a horrible spike-y mess of wood and wheels to a complex pain-train capable of mass destruction–but it's up to you to decide what form it takes on. Replaying levels with the extra tools, workshop content, etc. can add countless hours to the (currently) relatively short game, but as much as I'd love to say this game is "Really Great!," it does have some glaring flaws...
Currently, the game is pretty short, and while I don't wish to fault the developers to this end, the responsibility to create a longer gaming experience rests on their shoulders. I've been playing on-and-off for a long time now, and the changes I see are not very great over a long period of time. Until they add more to this game, this complaint remains valid. Another problem I notice is that the construction of vehicles in this game is a bit... confusing, to say the least. That's not to say that the difficulty curve is anything too bad, I did find myself stumped as to how to make a vehicle that could rotate the first time I picked the game up. While, of course, you could just look up how to do that, it feels like that should not be a complicated thing. Good sandbox games should have easy, user friendly features that should be able to be picked up without a tutorial. (I'm not saying tutorials shouldn't be used, but instead that something as simple as vehicle rotation should just be simple to understand.)
All in all, this game has always had great potential, and it's good to see that that potential is not wasted. To that end, this recieves an "It-could-use-some-work" 7/10.

This is a fun little game of strategy, planning, and story telling.  What stands out to me most is the way the personality of the characters comes through not just in the obvious "story moments", but in the way that you can get small bonuses for resolving conflicts in a way that jives with the characters you picked for your party.
The tactical element in combat is a little light, but it's still there.  Most of the strategy is wrapped up in the larger game of collecting points, not in the smaller combat mode.

Renowned Explorers is a rogue-like exploration game with turn-based combat. After selecting a team from different roles (Speakers, Scouts, Scientists, and Fighters), you go out into the world to find treasures and meet new characters to become the most renowned explorers. Every team composition has the ability to be great at Fighting, being Devious, or being Friendly to your enemies, and how to end each encounter (Aggressive, Devious, or Friendly) has the potential to grant extra rewards... or extra hardships.
The game's unique battle system puts phyiscal and verbal combat together into one unique system that works so well. Each side has an attitude that creates an overall mood in the battle that can give your characters unique buffs or debuffs depending on the rock-paper-scissors style attitude system: Being Aggressive beats being Friendly, being Friendly beats being Devious, and being Devious beats being Aggressive. Adjusting your battle styles will change the moods and attitudes of the battle, granting boons to your side and more favorable end battle results. The battles can be very hard, and you typically are out-numbered, so mastering the mood system and how to coordinate all of your attacks together will help you overcome the difficult encounters ahead.
The game awards you with tokens that grant you money, research, renown, or status that you can spend to improve each character and your crew as a whole. The tokens have some RNG associated with their values, but depending on the outcomes and choices you make in the game, those values can increase, leading to very potent rewards if you decide to focus one or the other. The beauty of this game is how you are able to even pick the same team and go to the same locations but still do something completely different each playthrough. You can focus on one reward type over another or try to balance all of them.
The game overall does have a somewhat steep learning curve, but if you are able to master all of the different systems inside the game, you'll be able to go into the higher levels with relative ease. Also, each game session tends to be somewhat short (~2 hours, give or take), but the game is meant to be replayed... a lot. Try out new teams, new paths, new areas, new combinations, new research... the replayability of this game is incredible.

Back in the day I played lots of platformers, and it seems like Guacamelee has taken all the best features from those games, and thrown in some fun new stuff. The platforming and melee fighting seem a bit simple and even quite easy at first, but once you learn all the special moves and attacks, things suddenly get a whole lot more complicated. I suspect that the game might be a little bit on the easy side for some hardcore gamer, but for me the difficulty was just perfect - some of the areas were very tricky and frustrating, but never too frustrating, and while most areas won't cause anyone too much trouble, the game never gets too easy either. The combat system feels really good once you get used to it and the melee fights are fun, especially the boss fights.
What I love just as much as the actual gameplay though, is the art design and music of Guacamelee. The whole Mexican theme with some totally ridiculous stuff (crazy special moves such as Rooster Uppercut or Goat Fly, a special ability called Pollo Power that turns you into a chicken, etc...), thrown in is simply awesome. The funny little details and some of the silly dialogue actually made me laugh, I love the humour in Guacamelee.
It's not a very long game, even with the DLC and the Hard Mode. According to Steam it took me 30 hours to find all the treasures and secrets and to finish the game in normal difficulty, and then another time in Hard Mode. And thus Guacamelee became the first and only (and probably the last) game ever where I've unlocked all the achievements!
Guacamelee! is also the winner of the prestigious Tomiboo's GOTY 2013 award!

Spoiler Warning: contains spoilers.
This game is fun, but the battle system sucks.
As I see it, these are the problems with the battle system:
Status effect moves are practically unusable--want to silence, poison, stun or blind an enemy?  Good luck, it never works.
Spells you learn do not become more powerful with leveling up.  Rather, the  spells you learn at higher levels are more powerful.  This is really annoying.  It means that flamberge you learned at level 10 won't be doing much damage at level forty.
Enemies don't have elemental weaknesses unless you give them one!  This is so annoying.  Although its supposed to be why you have the Tiarna on your team (She can give elemental weaknesses to enemies) good luck keeping her alive long enough to use her.  She's really weak.  And, as far as I've leveled her up, she doesn't learn any elemental spells herself.  So you also have to keep alive your valmerian mage/conjurer or pair her with magus in order to use her effectively.  It would be nice if some enemies had elemental weaknesses already built in.  Most don't.  As a player, this can be really confusing.  (you constantly have to guess what random spell is going to be effective against a boss, for example.) I don't think a game should give you all the answers, but a working elemental system is something to be expected from an rpg game.  I defeated a lot of enemies just by striking, which gets tiresome.
Enemy variety: although there are a lot of enemies in this game, the variety in each stage is really repetitive.
Victory message variety: there isn't much!  If I had a dollar for every time I heard Nightshade complain about potions I'm pretty sure I'd be a millionaire.
Other problems:
No sidequests.  I was really hoping for some.  Having multiple places (more than two) to go on any given map would make the game a lot more fun.  The overworld maps are huge, but there's almost nothing on them.
You almost NEVER pick up armor.  It would be nice to at least pick some up so you don't have to buy it at every shop.
There's no downtime between battles.  Believe me, defeating Lord Anto's first form and then not getting a save?  Oh. My. God.
Still, there are a lot of positives.  As you go along, you get more and more attached to the characters and you want them to win.  (Although Magus is a complete slimeball at points).
The developer's room is clever.
I'm not even sure what to think of the game over screen.  It is....unique.
Would I recommend?  Yes, if you need a game to keep you occupied.  I wish the large team of developers on this game had focused on making the battle system better, though.

Most of the positive reviews of this game are getting down voted out of existence, so I am going to try and be as fair as possible.  Most of the negativity surrounding this game is based on how overwhelmingly buggy it is right now.  That is 100% true.  But it’s still an awesome game.
I can already feel all those negative fingers twitching over their keyboards waiting to drown me in hateful comments, but let me explain my reasoning first.  I agree: THE BUGS ARE EVERYWHERE.  Early access may even be a little misleading in this one.  When I hear early access, the first thing that comes to my mind is one of those new indie games that’s totally functional, but needs a lot more content.  This is not that.  This is early early access… This game is Super ****ing Mega early access.  We are basically alpha testing this bad boy.  If you are not willing to occasionally fight through bugs or lose a coaster once or twice, don’t buy this game.  The fact that they are still charging full price for something so incomplete is my biggest issue with the game right now.  Almost every aspect of this game has at least one significant issue that needs to be worked out.
However, I ended up giving this a thumbs up because all of the problems are seem to be superficial.  When they are fixed, I am 100% sure this game will be fantastic.  All the bugs, such as, the faulty AI, the wonky EID ratings (excitement/intensity/nausea), the path placing issues, etc. that everybody is complaining about are all very fixable.  I have played many games (early access or otherwise) that were just inherently bad.  Bad concept, bad controls,  un-navigateable menus, bad whatever…  But keep in mind, this game is Super ****ing Mega early access, and the core of the game, the most important part, is rock solid.
And what is the core?  To me, the most important part of any theme park simulator is the coaster editor itself.  I have seen many negative reviews claiming that this one is over complicated and hard to use.  I struggle to even wrap my head around these claims.  When I first started playing this, before reading a single review, my first thought was, “Man, this coaster editor is ****ing amazing! It’s so easy to use!”  I hate to step on people’s toes, so I’ll stomp them instead.  If you put any actual effort into figuring out how to use to use the editor instead of giving up after 5 minutes, anyone in their right mind would be forced to agree that this is by far the most elegant and free form coaster editor yet.  There are practically no limits to what you can do.  Besides, even if the node editor somehow isn’t for you, the prefab piece editor is still present and works just fine.  Although I encourage you to take all other complaints and reviews you read seriously, it is important to me that everyone laugh in the face of any person that says the coaster editor is hard to use ;).  Kidding…  By the way.  But, seriously the coaster editor is awesome.
Since the other reviewers have so completely covered the specifics of the many bugs, I don’t feel compelled to cover them in my review.  In any case, I am confident that given time, they will all be fixed.
CONCLUSION
This game is not even close to being done and full price is fairly unreasonable.  DO NOT UNDER ANY CIRCUMSTANCES BUY THIS GAME IF YOU WANT SOMETHING FULLY FUNCTIONAL.  Give it more time, it’ll get there.  But if you’re like me and you get a kick out of seeing a game in its early stages and watch it fill in, give it a go.  If you want to give a game a negative review because its buggy while in early access, maybe don’t buy early access games in the future…  You clearly don’t appreciate the development process.  (people complaining about the bugginess to price ratio excluded)

First of all, I’m a pretty big fan of roguelikes, I don’t enjoy the punishing difficulty that usually accompanies them; but, I do love the anything-can-happen feeling that they provide. Oftentimes, a sharp, well-tuned “little” game can outshine most triple-A titles. This is one of those times.
hits on a lot of levels for me, I love Indiana Jones, roguelikes, upbeat humor, and pop art. If any of those things don’t interest you, this might not be your game irrespective of anything I have to say. If you’re still interested, lets hit some pros-and-cons.
More Fun(ny) than a Barrel of Colloquialisms
Fantastic Art that Complements the Experience and Conveys the Characters
Replay Value that is Actually Worth Replaying™
Deep Combat Strategy and Dozens of Characterful Combinations
An Ever-Faithful Adherent of the All-Wonderful, All-Good RNG (long may he reign)
Cons were a lot tougher to come up with, and so I’ve written a bit more than word-bites for them, but it is important to recognize flaws in even those things that we love.
I don’t much care for 1000% voice acted titles, Morrowind had plenty enough of the talky-talky for me. Plus, you will always be able to tell more story with the written word, and that’s really what we want... more story, more game. This particular game’s sound is pretty good, but in a game that punches this far above its weight, the sound becomes a key weakness in an overall above-and-beyond style title.
Remember that deep strategy? It comes at something of a price, the emotional rock-paper-scissors that carries the strategy behind this gameplay can break your party without even asking nicely (it’s a hazard of roguelikes but can hit out of the blue like few other titles I’ve seen), and remembering what’s-good-for-you-and-bad-for-those-guys can become burdensome after a few back-to-back playthroughs.
I understand that it’s more roguelike and only RPG-lite...but I will always complain about not-robust-enough RPG features. If character build and customization options are absent, I’m angry; if they’re limited, I’m mad; and if they’re as-robust-as-all-hell with a side of Grim Dawn meets Skyrim… I’m still mildly annoyed. For the record, this game only makes me mad.
My conclusion is that this game is nearly as good (and better in some ways) than FTL; it perfectly captures what a roguelike should be, brilliantly evokes a setting often overlooked, and manages to inject a heavy dose of that good old fashioned just-one-more-turn. So, my hat’s off to you Abbey Games, the modest game you’ve made is nothing less than a modern masterpiece.
tl;dr: If I could only pick five games to play--for the rest of my life--this would be one of those games.
