At the current state of the game, I would not recommend this game to anyone wanting a fulfilling experience. I would, however, recommend this game to anyone who's wanted to be the architect in a Sim City game.
Two features that were not mentioned by the devs as upcoming but really need to be in the game is some sort of blueprint/builder system letting you assign unemployed citizens to build out blueprints you've saved, and another would be an excavator or a deeper mining system than what is present. As is it is far too time-consuming digging out new sections and being able to mark out a specific area to be leveled is much needed.
The biggest con I see is the graphics: they're too good. The lighting is beyond annoying and makes the blocks look like plastic pieces that
have been slobbered on. A secondary worry is how unexplained the zombie spawn system is. I've had multiple neighborhoods flooded with torches, and Zombies will manage to just pop into existence in seemingly lit walled in areas. This became a headache as I would spend every night not excavating a nearby hill but instead running from neighborhood to neighborhood making sure my factory workers weren't getting killed in their sleep.
Overall this game is a great concept and if you'll like to fund the developer's moving forward buy this game and enjoy a good week or so of content.

I think the one problem I had with this game is that it took a while to figure out what I was doing wrong, and it came to that the food situation is a bit confusing as in the top right there is information on how much food your group consumes a day (so for example 600 / Per Day) it also says how much food you have (6000 Food) it takes 2 nights for crops to grow and each crop is 0.5 Food, a couple of crops together is a bread which is 3 Food... so there is a bit of mathematics to make sure your colonists aren't going to starve, I measured with my little group that if they consume 600 food per day, they would need 1200 food altogether before they would have access to any more food, so initially I needed to make sure I had the food to survive the two days to be able to get more food to be able to increase the number of colonists, and as I was getting into the 1000's I just had to check every 2 days that it was vaguely staying at the same amount. I have always wanted a game were you can build a kingdom from the ground up in first-person and Colony Survival seems to be the game to finally scratch that itch.
Pretty impressive graphics for a voxel based game and the villager A.I. seems to be competent enough. The U.I. is a bit confusing but once you figure it out it is not an issue. I had a lot of fun building my small kingdom and managing the villagers.
But the game isn't without some issues. There isn't much to do in the initial Early Access build and the building options seem pretty anemic. I know this is common for a Early Access game but $20 seems a little much for what is there right now. The most glaring issue right now is that the Zombie Sieges, which are one of the main draws of the game, can be easily thwarted (I just dug a two-block deep ditch around the village, thus securing my kingdom from undead invaders.)
But overall, I am exicted to see what additions they bring to the game. What is here right now isn't much but it is stable so I have high hopes for the game. I recommend supporting this game and I hope the developers see the project through to the end.

In response to the developer "updating" the game, I repurchased at the lower price point and will re-review the game...
It's still a mess.
I'm aware that the Dev is 17 years old, and that this person hopes that I will do a more "relevant" review, by which I assume they mean showering praises upon them. So sure, I'll start with some positives:
It's a real undertaking to make a game, even one as short as this, and for a 17 year old to pull this off, well, I'm impressed. Like I said before, the sound design is much better than some indies out there, and the paintings (repetetive though they may be) look phenomenal, and the wobble while walking was executed very well!
That being said, I purposely put myself through the experience again in order to see whether the "significant changes" were really that, or not... and unfortunately, they were not...
The new narrations have very good voice acting, but sadly do not blend well in the game. It was better with no talking because it let the immagination run wild. The very few spoops I got the first time around were due to the silence and my immagination, but this second time around, nothing.
The door at the start still opens inwards and breaks immersion, there are spots where you can see pieces of the level that do not connect (ceiling mostly), there are still weird invisible walls that make navigation tedious and chore-like, the newspaper sound is literally 5 seconds long of chip bag crunching sound and fades out (newspapers don't do that), where the floor and walls meet could use some moulding so it doesn't look like the building was set on a flat expanse of wood flooring, etc.
The one thing that frustrated me more than anything was the looping mechanic not being seamless. I could have forgiven alot of the other stuff if it wasn't for that specific thing. I was hoping that this would have been fixed and that the "fade to black/ wake up in bed"  thing would have been nixed in favor of the hallways endlessly looping (except for death and a few select story moments where it would make sense to start back in the first bedroom.
I'm trying to be honest about this game, and AM NOT attacking the Developer personally, nor do I condone others using foul language towards the dev, even though I understand peoples' frustration at the "quick cash grab PT clones" that saturate the market these days. The developer clearly spent some time on this game, and what was essentially a few people working on this, it is a completely coherent experience which is rare in the age of games getting cancelled left and right. I salute the Dev for their hard work so far!
It is still priced too high though. This is still a dollar game masquerading as a 5 dollar game. If you see this for a buck or .50 cents, then by all means pick it up. It is a mildly entertaining 15 minutes of gameplay.
I'm leaving my original review up, as it still stands. The "significant update" was 1 new hallway and some narration from the main character. Considering that it was updated overninght, I'm assuming it was content that was already built and got added back in, which is fine, but ulitmately, the "update" didn't really fix any of the problems.
I really hate to write negative reviews, but this experience was poor, and the initial handling of the release (and pricing) were not done professionally. I do hope the Dev takes this as constructive criticism and not bashing, and uses it towards making a new game that builds upon the experience that this game has provided them, or in truly polishing this game.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
It pains me to write this, as I'm a big fan of short horror experiences...
This is a .99 cent game that is being passed off as an $11 game...
For experiences like these, reviewing them as "games" is a bit difficult because they are more akin to interactive film, so I will be judging from that perspective.
As a "filmic" experience, this game is NOT one...
MINOR SPOILERS:
The story itself is thinly laid out in a series of newspaper clippings that are essentially the SAME asset with a headline changed each time, accompanied by the most ungodly crunching noise that goes on, and on, and on. Apparently, you play as a child who may or may not have experienced something not so savory at a park one time, and a bunch of people died, etc.
At the beginning, you awake in a bedroom, and you go through a hallway until opening a door, and...FADE TO BLACK...(Loading...)
You wake up in the same bedroom, go back through the same hallway, spoop happens, and you once again open a door and...FADE TO BLACK...(Loading...)
Lather, rinse, repeat...
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now I love a good abstract story, minimal gameplay, and "photorealistic" graphics as much as the next chap, but unfortunately in this case, all three were executed amateurly.
I encountered multiple visual bugs, weird invisible walls that kept me from advancing, and even a strange moment where I couldn't discern whether there was a puzzle built out of purposeful visual bugs, or if there was a timer on the door unlocking allowing me back out into the main hallway. It just felt like a "game-jam" game, and not a polished piece of horror.
Graphically, this game is subpar by a few miles, maybe more...maybe light years... Some assets looked good (read: paintings), and some assets looked terrible (read: everything else), but the one thing the dev truly nailed was the light wobble when walking. Visually, it was the best thing in the game, because even the flashlight (which magically appears for a loop, and then disappears just as quickly) looks...bad...
Speaking of unpolished; the loop mechanic was aggravating because it's essentially a load screen at the end of the hallway, and then you wake up at the beginning, with no ryhme or reason. In fact, there really wasnt much reasoning going on here; and geez dev, would it kill you to make the first door open into the hallway rather than the bedroom? It really kills the immersion when I have to keep clipping through the door...
The reason PT was a jewel was polish, polish, and more polish. This game (Apt. 999 or whatever...) could very well have been used as a prototype to pitch a game that would end up polished after many years of hard work.
The one positive I can give about the game was the sound design. It was decent. Even then, the newspaper noise is ridiculous (sounds like someone slowly crumpling a bag of chips right next to your ear), re-using the same lightbulb pop over and over wasn't great either, and these were just some of the ones I noticed due to their "cringey" (Is that a word? It is now...) repetition.
I wont say anything specific about the ending so as to not spoil it for anyone who really wants to pay $11 bucks for this game, but lets just say that I was extemely unimpressed with how it was executed.
Also, it's literally a 30 min experience if even, and that was mostly due to the horribly confusing "puzzles" which kept me locked in an area until I looked at something, or read something. So yeah, all in all, bad news bears. Stay away unless you're a friend of the developer and want to show them support, which I believe everyone deserves. It's just that this game shouldn't be on Steam, and if it had to be, then it should have been a free to play experience. (Maybe a Patreon option somewhere for the developer, you know, because "Peace and Love" and helping your fellow humans....)
If you've read this far, I salute your determination. I really, truly am sorry that I cannot recommend this game, but I just can't...

Hitman: Blood Money is generally regarded as the best game in the series and definitely lives up to its reputation. Previous games had been plagued by bugs, poor design decisions, and overall unfair situations. This time around, the developers seem to have taken note of what went wrong with previous installations of the series and as a result they have produced a highly polished and well executed hitman game.
As per the Hitman formula, most missions require a few trial runs to learn all the necessary elements such as guard positions, entry points, and target vulnerabilities required to perform the necessary executions with maximum efficiency and stealth. In order to get the best rating, it is almost mandatory to study each level in depth to see where your targets will be at their weakest.
One thing I noticed with this installment of the series is the introduction of well-handled crowd elements. This feature really shines in the “Murder of Crows” mission where you have to wade through crowds of revelers during Mardi Gras in order to track and eliminate several targets. Other new entries to the series include notoriety which can increase upon being spotted (yellow) or from CCTV sightings, which can be rectified through securing security tapes. There is also the addition of a new execution technique (strangulation) that can be done via elevator hatch above a target.
The only downside to this game, and this seems to be a trend for what it’s worth, is the final mission. All of a sudden, despite having done a majority of the game almost entirely in stealth, you are required to gun down an entire area full of trigger happy NPCs. I found it to be entirely inappropriate to the overall storyline not to mention my preferred style of play (silent assassin). Nevertheless, I managed to find a way to take a human shield and plow through the finale. If it were not for that final mission, I would consider Blood Money to be a perfect game. Regardless, it still lives up to its reputation and will likely live on to be the best that Hitman has to offer.

The highlight of the series, being immensely open-ended with a ton of different options for taking down your target, while having a better coat of polish than the other highlight, Silent Assassin. It's relatively easy to beat the game, but the fun comes from experimenting and figuring out just the many, many ways of finishing each mission, and working towards perfection in your final rating. It's not just a question of stealth versus frontal assault, it's poison versus bomb, sniper rifle versus falling chandelier, rigged fireworks versus chloroformed panties.
It's got a dark, noiry style without the grindhouse cheese of Absolution, taking itself seriously even while it lets you do ridiculous things. Even now, having played through more than once, I find myself wanting to go back to try to screw around and finish the missions in new ways or perfect my old plans. I sincerely hope the new Hitman game can even come close to capturing the fun to be had here.

After playing this game some more and mysteriously having my key revoked without a refund, I have decided that this game is the biggest heap of♥♥♥♥♥♥to ever enter Steam since Rome 2 Total War.
Growing up on RCT2 and RCT3 (yes, I am that young), which were both incredible games, my expectations for this game were extremely high.
It was fraught with problems. At first I forgave them, because it was in Early Access.
Let's start with the positives (of which there are few), though. We have to give this game a chance, right?
Good things:
-Snazzy new coaster builder
-Snazzy new paths builder
-I REALLY like the new restaurants which replace basic food stands
-Cars in coaster trains can be different colours
-The new water tool isn't efficient at all but it's top banter
That's it.
Anyway, back to the negatives (of which there are many):
Not only did I learn that this game was not made by the original developers, but I also noticed more and more things that are catastrophically wrong with this game. For a start, it's massively overpriced.
Then you get into the rollercoaster ratings. I simply cannot get anywhere in the campaigns because rollercoasters are rated as high intensity WAYYYY too easily, and in order to make a 'coaster that is exciting at all, it needs to have pretty much ultra-extreme intensity... so nobody rides it and you just lost 20,000 monies, pal.
You only have a small amount of music choices, and they are just variations of exactly the same tune in a depressingly low quality, which drives you bloody insane in five minutes.
Sometimes when you place custom tracks using the snazzy new spline coaster builder, you cannot add another section because the new secton has to be a pre-built track. This is probably hard to understand, and we face a dilemma because in order to properly understand you need to play the game, but that is something you absolutely do not want to do.
I thought I could deal with the supports problem but it is SO common that it is UNFORGIVEABLE. It is so infuriating to have a nice creation utterly ruined and the immersion completely shattered by a track support going through the middle of your loop.
But BY FAR THE WORST PROBLEM is the optimisation. Having spent £960 on a computer, which I have to say is a very good one, you'd expect to get good performance on this game. Right?
NOOOO!
On the very lowest settings on a flat map with a couple of rollercoasters, my computer struggles to reach 20fps. On a map with varied terrain and many rollercoasters, I might as well be watching a slideshow.
I will now proceed to wait impatiently for Planet Coaster, after learning that it was actually made by the developers of RCT3 and it's not just a cheap knockoff of the RCT series. You want to know what a cheap knockoff of the RCT series is?
This game.

I wanted to get back into the FMV genre - I have fond memories of a few games from the 90s - so I took a look around to see what was available. Her Story was the first game I actually bought to see where the genre is now, a couple decades later.
This game is not groundbreaking or life-changing. But it does scratch a very particular kind of itch. I was expecting an interactive choice-driven story, but instead this plays more like an old school detective game. You gather clues and they lead you to the next set of clues (or you make a lucky guess) and on and on until you're satisfied you know what happened.
I wanted there to be a bit more to the meta game, along with more closure and a bigger wrap up for the finale. What's there does answer most of the questions - it just does it piecemeal, and thus left me feeling somewhat underwhelmed at the end.
I think most people would probably be bored by Her Story, but if you want to dig through some video clips to piece together a crime then it's an interesting experiment to be a part of.

Lara Croft GO is amazingly good for what was originally a smartphone game.
To start off, I'd like to say that this game offers a curiously relaxing experience, with its chill music and beautiful, stylized environments. And that's what sets this game apart, really. It gives off a very comfortable atmosphere.
The gameplay is about going through different stages while managing Lara's position to avoid enemies and environmental traps, all the while manipulating contraptions or making use of the unique characteristics of each stage to be able to progress. The level of challenge is just right since the game carefully introduces new mechanics in easy levels, then develops them in harder ones.
It's "turn based" in the sense that the world only moves forward when Lara moves forward, giving you as much time as you need to think things through.
There are also some collectibles hidden in the stages if you wanna go pixel hunting to unlock new clothes for Lara. If you find a golden vase hidden anywhere, you click it to discover a relic or a gem. It's a neat little bonus.
Recommended for anyone who wants a simple, relaxing and extremely well crafted experience.

For me writing reviews for a game after its stopped being supported and/or a sequel has been released. So let's look at:
I feel for games which have a sequel presently and a planned third game in the series, I feel as if a comparison is
most important thing to do.
Some people say that Payday 2 is a 'bag simulator' however if thats the case, PAYDAY is a 'drill simulator' the waiting times for just one drill is often
than 200 seconds, and
heists, of which there is there is 7 in the base game, but 9 with the Wolf DLC.
The gameplay and weapon variety in Payday 2 is predominately better, however, the gunplay is suprisingly tight here, with guns feeling very different, even holding up for todays standards.
The UI however, may be one of
most compex ive ever seen. It displays your current objective in small text in the top right, but underneath
displays your COMPLETED objectives! This makes progression extremely difficult in levels and needlessly complicated. Speaking of levels, this is where my main problem with this game comes in.
I feel like, technically, if your skilled enough, you should be able to beat the whole game on the toughest difficulty to begin with. I can understand why games sometimes gate off the highest levels so plays HAVE to get used to the difficulty and gameplay and quirks of the 'hard' mode to begin with.
HOWEVER, you SHOULD NOT need to farm ONE heist on EASY mode over and over and OVER again when you start a new game, not because your terrible but because YOUR NOT HIGH ENOUGH LEVEL AND DONT HAVE THE EQUIPMENT! And I dont mind farming inherantly however, when there's only 7 levels and you will have to play one over and over and over again, AND THEN once you've unlocked the next heist you will be playing that and the previous ones on a SLIGHTLY higher difficulty until youve unlocked the next time.
In addition to this XP is earned through money, which hearing this, doesnt sound like a bad idea. However, you cannot earn XP unless you win the heist. So you can completely waste 15/20 mins with no gain. There is ONE way you can gain XP in heists, and thats through 'challenges' they start off fairly simple, but by level 20 or so its more of a 'just keep playing' not promoting skill or anything really differing.
Playing this game is such a chore and discovering the new heists, which are actually fairly interesting, especially the dialogue in the loading screens, you will feel alot more close to the characters and their personalities shine through alot more here however, but I simply cannot say its worth it for the obscene amounts of farming to reach these very small parts of enjoyment.

Pixel Gladiator is a 2D, pixelated, base defense game where you control this little space marine and you are tasked with defending your base from the vicous alien life that live on that planet.
The game is an action, rouge-like, defense game where you can upgrade your defenses for your base or buy yourself some weapons to stand a better chance at taking on the alien onslaught. There is a number of weapons and defenses you can buy such as assault rifles, turrets, armor, etc. There are two game modes: Survival, self explanitory but you have to hold out for as long as you can, and Arena, where you take on a set number of waves of enemies.
The game is a really good time killer if you want a quick and easy fix if you're craving a game focused purely on defense and shooting aliens in the face. The alien life is very hostile so if you go in thinking it'll be a walk in the park you will be in for a rather nasty surprise as the enimies are relentless and unforgiving. One wrong move could mean the difference between life and death. You are given a regular pistol and a basic base at the beginning of every mode.
Much like any game of this nature, there is some getting used to. The controls are really clunky at first and unfortunatly there isn't any setting to remap controls. The game has a money system where you have to kill enemies to get money. Unfortunately, you for whatever reason have to be near the enemy you kill in order for you to get the money. Now i know it doesn't sound bad at first, but when you have turrets on your base that kill enemies without earning you any money you might as well be doing it yourself.

I don't think I've ever bought a game faster on steam. Reason being is this is the game I thought Minecraft was going to become. I've been playing Minecraft since it was in Alpha, and all through it's development I was hoping it would turn into a game like this. Where you start by building up your own armor and weapons, then have other humans join you and eventually you can build up towns and even cities. Which you'd have to defend from harder and harder monsters.
At the moment this game DOES NOT have all that. But I can see that being it's potential future. At the moment this game is very reminiscent of a Minecraft mod called SIM-U-Kraft. Which was basically the same premise as this game (Workers need to be paid wages and kept safe and they mine, farm and build for you).
This game IS very bare bones so far, but a couple things I saw that need improvement are:
-Menu Sounds. They are obnoxiously loud at default volume. Luckily you can change that volume
-AI reaction time. I've had archers not fire on Zombies until the zombies were nearly on top of them.
A feature I would also like to reccomend to the Devs is extensive modding support. It's the one thing Minecraft never did and should have done. But I believe in modding support for games like this because it allows players to make the game into what they want it to be. And as an early access game, having players develop their own content has shown (In games like ARK, minecraft, space engineers) to be beneficial .
On a final note: I see a lot of reviews saying this isn't worth the price at the moment. This, I feel, is a very selfish viewpoint. When you purchase an early access game, you're not always buying something with the immediate value assigned to it (which "what is 20 dollars worth of fun" is a totally subjective view anyway). Rather you are making an investment to help a game be worth that price point in the future. It's different from, just naming games here, NO MAN'S SKY not being worth it's 60 dollar price point since it released as a full package and not an early access deal. But you have to view an early access game's potential and not it's current state, before deciding to invest. That's why I invested in this game. I feel it has potential, and I can't wait to see how it grows from here!

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. What an awesome game.
Story
One word- GREAT. Overall it is a story about good versus evil and how everyone can change if with the help of your friends and some self discipline. I will not get into the details of the story because most of you people probably played the game allready and I don't want to spoil it for the new players. Your every action puts a twist on the further story development and the development of your character. Talking, talking and talking IT IS VERY IMPORTANT!!! Collecting clues and subtile little hints from NPC's that you run into is very important if you wish to advance in the game and expirience it in its fullnes.
Characters
Your character is how you make it but let me tell you something-if you don't know how to make a good character it is going to be a challenging game, specially thowards the end and fighting the main bad guy. If you make a charecter only on "recomended" features it is not some bad♥♥♥♥♥mofo. It is a character that is going to take you to the end of the game but you are going to have a tough time fighting the main bad guy. So reading up on skills, force powers and being smart with your points on level ups is crutial to make a good, well balanced charecter. One thing that left me in awe is your team. You get a human jedi girl, humand jedi guy, human soldier, Mandalorian merc, Twi'lek girl, a Wookie, Two droids and a Catharian jedi girl. Every single one of them has an interesting personality and a back story. I loved to talk to them. Voice acting is very well done and you really get the feeling that you are a head of the team and that you are among friends. I really grew to like each and every of the charecters that I played with. As with their personalities each have special sets of skills that you can use in your quests. Offcourse you can not bring all of them to battle. You can bring only two but if one of these characters skills is really neaded in the mission the game tells you that him/her have to be a part of your team. I will not go into the deatails of the characters because I could uncover a lot of the story.
Graphic/gameplay:
Graphics and the worlds (yes worlds) look great. Action takes place on  the planets Tatooine, Dantooine, Kashyyyk, Korriban, Manaan, Rakata Prime, and Taris, and each looks beutifull. Each one has a town to explore and you get from one to the other by your own space ship...you'll see. All in all good looking game. In some places it could be better but it is good.
Now for not so fun stuff. First of all- the game is unstable on Win7. I found it chrashing on me very often specially in cutscenes. Well, it is not really chrashing, rather minimizing and returning you to the desktop. You can klick on the little icon on the task bar and it will get you back in the game....most of the time. Why is that ? I don't know. From the stuff I red on-line it is eaven worse on Win10 (to the point of not working at all). There are a cuple of fixes available that you can do yourself and you can read up on them in Steam Community but those only partially solve the issue. From what I know there are no patches available. I'm not one for solitaire or Candy Crush clones, but sometimes I still want a game I can play for fifteen to twenty minutes at a time. With some grand strategy games, that's barely enough time for a single round of play.
Renowned Explorers is just the game I needed. It's easy to pick up and easy to put down. The game play is deep enough to keep me interested as long as I want it to, but I can also quit when I need to without any fuss. The missions are small enough and the campaigns short enough that I can pick up where I left off without spending a great deal of time trying to recall my plans.
Essentially, this is a board game about risk management. There are three attack types with a sort of Paper, Rock, Scissors relationship: Friendly, Devious, and Agressive (yes, friendliness is a form of attack in this game); however, the rewards for each encounter vary depending upon which of the three you favor. Choosing a party that specializes in only one of these attacks can make victory more likely, but may leave you resolving some encounters with little or nothing to show for it. Similarly, your players can level up in a number of skills that increase their chances of winning rewards in the wheel-spinning challenges scattered throughout each mission. Focusing on a small number of skills can make winning the challenges that need them much more likely, but you will be extremely unlikely to win challenges that call for skills you lack.
The tactical combat is interesting, but the real meat of the game is in strategic decisions like these. Play it safe and you'll most likely retire an unremarkable explorer; risk it all and you'll almost certainly face humiliating defeat; find the right balance and you might just become...

So I wrote a review for Abbey Games last project Reus and gave it a negative review. It wasn't a bad game but it was underwhelming and I found it boring. This game however, gets my hearty reccomendation.
Reus and Renowned Explorers actually have some similarities, altough it may not appear that way. The setting, concept and aesthetics for each game is very different but both games are based on fairly simple systems and concepts, and the gameplay is centered around the player exploring the variations and nuances in those systems.
The thing is in Reus, I had no desire to explore those variations, because I found it incredibly boring, but in Renowned Explorers I love it.
The concept of Renowned Explorers is a Saturday Morning Cartoons-looking bunch of people are part of a society of explorers and adventurers in the age before colonialism stopped being fashionable.
You lead this band of explorers across various landscapes looking for treasure, fame, and science.
The game is played in two phases, the world map phase and the expedition phase. The world map is where you can manage resources, supplies, build up your team and perform odd jobs. It is also from the world map that you can select where to adventure next.
While you're in the expedition phase you lead your party across a map in a specific region, like Mali, Hungary, The Andes, etc. You have a specific goal in each region but there's also a fair bit of random encounters and treasure to gather and explore. You can't always find everything because you're limited by the amount of supplies you have but that in itself encourages replayability.
The game is fairly rogue-like, in the sense that you are not meant to do everything in a single playthrough, and when you do fail or reach a certain point, you are encouraged to just start over with different characters and a different approach.
The game is also interesting because although "battles" happen in a turn-based tactical layout, the game gives you the option to solve these encounters with diplomacy or manipulation as well as straight-up combat.
I've been seeing trends like this a lot lately. I wonder if the influence of Undertale is to blame.
I liked the idea of having options to my battles, but the thing is, the most successful I've been so far, is with a team of explorers focused on a friendly diplomatic playstyle. In my opinion the game seems to push somewhat towards that sort of playstyle, which I find a bit annoying, as my aggressive playthroughs have been the least successful so far.
Overall, if you're in for a rogue-lite experience and like the aesthetics and concept, this game is a lot of fun.
One of the things that I hope more developers realize in the future, is that story can act as a reward for the player. The reason why exploring this game's depths and variations, even if they're relatively minute, is because I was always excited to see how the game rewarded me with the story elements involved. I wanted to know about the places I was visiting and the characters I was playing as or meeting.
This is a really fun game, and although I think Abbey Games has stopped support on it, I would love it if more content was released for it down the line, or perhaps if they expand on the concept in a sequel.

Fun tower defence game with many other genres added in it, all of them in perfect harmony. With lots of weapons and armory, imaginative enemies and bosses, Pixel Gladiator will entertain you for hours. If you won't get frustrated by the bosses' incredible strongness. 7/10
:
+Very simple layout, you will be in arena in 2 seconds
+Lots and lots of weapons, you can try different ones every round
+Smooth, reliable controls.
+Pixelated graphics beat 3D on this game, their art style looks amazing.
-Unfair, overpowered bosses. When I died to the first boss for the 6th time and the arena started over, playing the game turned into working, not playing. This is a major Con. The rounds with normal enemies are perfection though.

Critical analysis of RollerCoaster Tycoon World by Chipgt
Introduction:
I have always been a fan of the RollerCoaster Tycoon (RCT) Series. Like many I have been following this games progress from the beginning. However, this is my first review. I have been looking through some of the steam reviews of the game and felt that many people have been writing review very one sided reviews based on other games. What you must understand is that this review will in no way talk about another game. I feel that from a gamer's point of view you should NOT talk about how another game is better when writing about a current game. Since the early access has launched a week ago the developer has released 5 large updates in response to what their users have been saying. This is awesome, because many of the changes have been based on user feed back. So without anymore delay I will discuss what I like and would like to see changed.
Delete tool:
OK, Of all the things in this game the delete tool by far needs to be one of them. With the added features of bushes, flowers, trees, and more in the random terrain generator there is more that the users must delete in order to build a ride. Currently as of the 5th update you must individually delete one thing at a time. This is extremely annoying. In game time it took me a year to delete a small area to build a ride. I would like to see a delete tool that allows the user to delete more than one object at a time. Or an option were when you hold down the mouse button you can paint away (delete) just dragging over something.
Road/ Paths
So when compared to RCT3 this has come a long way in a good direction. However I have found that there are issues when trying to connect a new section to an old in the transition form large path to small. For example, If I plop a store on a long path, and then want to make an intersection in a different place I am ofter forced to connect it adjacent to a store. In other cases I found areas where I wasn't allowed to build a path and there was nothing there blocking it. Over all I like how it works I just would like to see these restrictions addressed. Other times I want to delete a small section and redo it and I can't. I would also like to have the option to change the theme of a path that is already plopped. This would be a nice tool for theme while building new or modifying old sections.
Coaster builder:
This has by far had the most critiques by many people and I have to say this tool actually is good. I'm not saying its the best, but it is good. I have used other coaster simulators in the past with NO limits and there are a few features that I would really like to see come to RTC world for example, multi view builder. I found that when building a coaster I am moving my view everywhere. It would be nice to have a top down separate view in a remade construction GUI would be nice. This would make building coaster easier.
Building builder:
I love new new buildings. However, I would really like to have tools to build my own. Something that would be scale to the new restaurants would be very nice.
Conclusion:
RCTW is still in early access, the game series has come a long way, and will only continue to get better as it gets closer to official release. It will take users and any gamer who is interested in this series to provide continuous input as new updates come out. I for one will continue to add to my review until official release. THanks for reading.
-Chipgt

I picked this up a day or two after going into Early Access, so if your reading this months down the line, keep in mind I’m writing this Review from that point.
First, I’ll say the game is very bare bones. It’s got a very good foundation for an amazing game, but that’s all it is for now, a foundation. What’s here works well and is fun, all the art is crisp and clean, the mechanics are nice and enjoyable, but you quickly run out of things to do.
The potential for this game is extremely high. If the Devs add a dozen more NPC jobs, and resources being needed for many things and a half dozen more monster types then this game would be awesome.
So, what is there to do now?
-Buildings are just a few simple block types, no slopes, no doors, no stairs. Only cubes. In reality, you don’t even need to make a building, just a giant wall around your crops and beds/ crafting stations clustered up on the grass.
-Harvest is just Wheat for food, and trees for planks.
-Mining is rather sad, Just dig down about 30 blocks and you hit bedrock and all the minerals are on the bedrock level, carve out a square and you will probably find all 4-5 ore types in that small square. Assign some miners and then forget about it. No need to keep tunneling or exploring. Half the Ores I never even used because they just make a couple decorative blocks and I had already built everything I needed out of Stone and wood.
-Zombie Attacks can be rather fun, more of a constant drizzle of them every night than an attack though. Just stack archers at the gate, make sure you have arrows, and you’re good. No fear of zombies breaking yours walls anywhere else.
-The Landscape is nice, mostly flat with some mountains and lakes. Maybe oceans, but I never saw. Of course, none of that is useful. Nothing to do with mountains or sand or water. Just pick a flat area and build.
In conclusion I enjoyed it, but once id built everything and had enough archers that nothing got through my gate there wasn’t much more to do beyond the 6 hours Id played this map. As is, this games not worth the money, but if the Developers build on the potential of the game then I wont regret the money spent. I’ll wait and see how it goes and check in again after some updates.

Absolutely awesome, my favourite entry in SqEnix's GO series!
From the way the main menu is designed to the mechanics and even unlockable costumes, you can really tell the devs were big fans of the original Core Design Tomb Raider games.
If you like the GO games mechanics or like Tomb Raider, I would definitely get it.
Some of the puzzles are a bit easy, some I've spent quite some time on (especially the recent new free campaign), but if you're impatient you can always use hints. Compared to other games in the series it also doesn't have the "complete the level in under 15 turns" challenges which I disliked and the environment aesthetics are gorgeous.
Regarding how it plays on PC - I own both Hitman and Deus Ex GOs on my phone and I actually prefer having a bigger screen for these games. You have to click and drag to move Lara around on PC though but you get used to it pretty quickly.
The only complaint is that I would love to see more levels, 100%'d the game in two sittings and now there's not much to do, sadly.
Well worth the full price, imo.

FEAR 1, simply put, is one of my favorite shooters, not necessarily because of great level design or compelling encounter design, but rather the feel of the combat is phenomenal. FEAR 1 felt like an explosive orgy of boom-booms and men turning into paste while losing limbs and screaming out in agony and fear.
So yeah, it was popping off.
FEAR 2, in comparison, is a very limp donger, it is a sodden♥♥♥♥♥♥ it is a miserable experience.
The first thing you'll notice is the blinding bloom, a lot of people act like FEAR 2 is graphically better than FEAR 3, but I don't think an obnoxious lighting engine that blasts primary colors into your face is "good graphics." It follows the late 00s trend of using fierce bloom and excessive colored lighting to hide the fact that the models and textures are mediocre pap.
The combat feels lose and weak, while FEAR 1 was a little clunky in its heaviness, and FEAR 2 certainly feels more snappy, you're switching out meaty, impactful combat for what feels like little pop guns weakly penetrating fleshy enemies that seem to melt like popsicles when they're dismembered, rather than the brutal mutilations in the original game.
Guns are quiet and feel like mush, enemies glow for some strange reason (enemies weren't difficult to find in FEAR 1, and FEAR 3 does fine without the glowing as well, I don't understand the reasoning for this mechanic) and even though they maintain the aggression of the AI from the original game, they're just less effective, they don't hurt as much, they don't really feel like a real threat, and the enemy variety is still crap.
While enemies will now tumble over cover and are generally mobile, they just don't feel satisfying to fight, everyone has some kind of pathetic nerd voice compared to the rumbling, distorted communications in the original game, and the voice acting for them is just flat, it's just not as fun hearing them freak out like it was in the first game.
They also took out the lean function, and instead replaced it with the ability to flip over cover, but it's rather pointless, there's absolutely no reason to use cover in this game, enemies hit like hotdogs smacking your face so most of the time you just slo-mo (and by the way the meter is absolutely tiny, even with the reflex boosters, compared to the first game) and headshot, that's it, there's even less reason to use grenades in this game than the last.
The absolute biggest disappointments are the shotguns. In FEAR 1 it was easily the most satisfying weapon, here they can't hit worth a damn, do absolutely no damage when they do impact, and feel like someone is mushing ground beef through a sausage maker.
What is this weak nonsense?
I can go on about the idiotic story, the worthless characters, the annoying melee enemies that add absolutely nothing to the game resembling fun, crappy boss encounters that aren't entertaining in the least, and repeating, samey levels that are either massacres of bloom or dark and dingey crap. FEAR 1 didn't have the greatest environmental design, but I expect a greater improvement than spattering color everywhere.
The elementary school is alright, but that's about it.
Even the linear mech segments suck and feel unsatisfying, because the weapons for those blow too, the enemies look goofy instead of cool as they did before (what happened to the sweet heavies with the insect eyes from the first game), and the dismemberment is super lame and reminds me of Fallout 3 where body parts just seem to glide off like enemies are made out of wet newspaper.
This game is mediocre beyond belief, everything about it is an exercise in misery, it's too easy, feels weak, looks like a complete mess that just wants to stab your eyes with bright lights, sounds like crap, plays like crap, what the hell went wrong?
If you can get through it all, somehow, it casts a magical spell on you, basically making you forget everything that happened in the last craptastic 6 hours, since there's literally nothing worth remembering in this absolute turd of a game. Hell, I only recall vaguely being angry at a certain unfun part of the game, and I can't even place it now. I usually remember things that♥♥♥♥♥♥me off very, very well, but FEAR 2 is such a powerful wizard it somehow even manages to wipe clean whatever atrocity it committed upon me.
Even FEAR 3 is better than this abysmal excuse for a game, avoid this junk.

Clever. Frustrating. Interesting. Ridiculous. A lot of games cast you as an unstoppable killing machine, but Hitman: Blood Money eschews the usual action-packed power fantasy in favor of a puzzle game built on the intricate clockwork of its levels. It's more like a point-and-click adventure than anything else, and how much you care for those will likely reflect how much you enjoy it.
Blood Money - as a hitman (or Hitman) game should - moves breezily between contracts, each set in a delightfully diverse stages jam-packed with fun flourishes and quirks. You might be scuttling a terrorist deal in a casino, eliminating an FBI-protected witness at his suburban home barbecue, or interrupting a (heavily armed) redneck wedding. And while you can kick down doors and gun down everyone in sight, it's not really that kind of game. Rather, the joy of Blood Money is in unearthing the idiosyncrasies of each level to put together Rube Goldberg-like murder machines. Even if you do ultimately decide to simply shoot your target in the head, you'll often do so by taking part in a winery tour, ducking around a corner along the way, disguising yourself as a chef, and freely entering the premises via the service entrance to reach your prey. The path of least resistance always involves a few chicken suits and Santa hats, and there's a tremendous joy in fitting those puzzle pieces together.
But if that's the game's biggest strength, it's also its curse. Familiarizing yourself with level designs, guard patrols, and available disguises takes time and patience, and you'll spend a lot of time wondering how you're supposed to combine a sausage with a toolbox to get a dead senator. You're going to fail a hundred times before everything clicks into place… and then you're in a new level and the process starts over. If you can get over that initial hump, there's a lot to love here, but you need to put in quite a bit before getting much out.

Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is a satire platformer shooter game that requires near perfection and patience.  You start out the game going through an opening level that isn't too hard.  Finishing this intro level unlocks eight different worlds all offering semi unique backgrounds, but all share most of the same elements.  Defeating the eight levels unlocks the tenth level, which does require absolute perfection.  Fans of games that require perfection may like the challenge, but most gamers will probably just be satisfied watching the YouTube videos of James ranting about bad games.
If you are looking for challenging and unforgiving platformers, this is definitely one of them.  If you want something challenging without being completely unforgiving, I recommend Eversion instead.

Pixel Gladiator is a blend of shootemup and tower defense. It is currently in early access but the game is fun and looks complete feature-wise.
There is a statement on the Steam store page though saying that content may still be added to the game!
Gameplay:
Your character has a base with a reactor in the center to protect. Enemies come in waves from both sides (left/right) and you need to kill them before they reach the reactor.
The reactor also serves as an upgrade shop where you can buy weapons and gadjets, available only in between waves. The left and right sides of the base can be built with wall defenses that mount turrets. Both of these can be upgraded.
Enemies come in two height sizes. The top turrets can not shoot the smaller enemies while the bottom ones shoot both. Not sure if there are flying enemies as I did not manage to survive a big number of waves (yet :P) but I imagine it would only make sense to introduce them later on and them being unreachable with the bottom turrets.
There are also boss enemies that appear who are much larger and require different strategies. The first one, that I reached and managed to kill, was a huge wormlike creature (Dune comes to mind) that was moving allover the place. I had to shoot it while avoiding contact and the base turrets did not target it.
From what I have seen so far, what makes the game difficult or easy depends on what you choose to upgrade and when. As in how you spend your money and when. My initial strategy of building defenses on one side of the map and handling the other side myself proved very effective until I started getting overrun on the side I was handling myself. At that moment I realized I should not have bought those rocket boots yet! :)
When you think the game is easy, it proves you wrong by showing you that you underestimated it and you need to plan your upgrades better.
Controls are classic WASD for movement and spacebar for things like entering the upgrade shop or building/upgrading defenses.
Graphics:
The game opts in for retro style graphics, which works very well and what is certainly worth mentioning is that it takes a whooping 9MB of drive space!
Music/Sound Design:
The music is electronic and fits the theme/mood perfectly. It is also reminiscenet of the 8bit era!
The sound effects are also in this style as you would probably expect.
Pros:
-Great blend of shootemup and tower defense.
-Simple controls
-Great sound
-Upgrades!
-Game may look very easy at some points but will punish you once you stop planning carefully!
-9MB size. Something that can be run anywhere, even your very slow, out of space, netbook!
Neutral:
-Retro style graphics are not everyone's cup of tea.
-Game is still in Early Access but is fully playable and I did not encounter any bugs.
Cons:
-The tower defense part looks rather simple. Maybe more options are available later on, I can't be sure as I have not even reached the second boss yet. If not, it should be considered as something to be implemented before it comes out of Early Access. Still the game is not easy or simple due to the lack of more turret options etc. It is much fun as it is.
Conclusion:
A fun little game! And little is not an understatement here as it's only 9MB heh! If you like retro style games, shootemups, tower defense games or any combination of these, you should try it!

Colony Survival is a very simplistic, yet somewhat challenging survival mangement game. For more information about the game and development team, visit this link (
)
The game has been a blast in this early stage of development. If you are more into gameplay, mechanics, systems than glorified graphics....then this game juts might interest you!
Ill try to keep it short and sweet, but if you are looking for a more drawn out review with every tiny detail about my experience, you may want to move on to the next review! With that said, Ill jump right in!
Gameplay is fun! Once you get the hang of how things work, you get a lot more time to focus on a very elaborate blueprint of how you want to build your colonies base! The title for the most part isnt that complicated, however, you do have to watch how you recruit, grow, mine, construct, etc..... it does take planning!
There is a few options when playing Colony Survival. There is MP (still in development and working on features to enhance MP play, so patience with the MP portion is required. You can play with others, but sharing reosurces, etc, isnt implemented yet. However, being able to speak with one another and building a community is in fulll swing.)
You also have a choice for a Single Player experience! There are a couple of options for SP that will allow you to play without monsters, having monster invade constantly and doubling the ammount of monsters that invade....
I choose to play without monsters till I could get the hang of the game and even in this "build only" type option, its still a blast to play and survival and mangement is still needed! Pro Tip: If you want to build up a lot of resources for the game before recruiting any AI, simply do not plop down your towns flag and you can pretty much go at it alone performing your own tasks till you feel ready to experiment with AI....however, it is limited and some features will require you do have AI to play ( unable to bake your own bread, for instance! AI only function for the time being! ).
Theres a lot planned for the game to bring it to a fuller experience and the developers roadmap can be checked out at their main website.....A lot will be going into the title during development. The devs have been nice to take in suggestions as well and have been really responsive and answering even the toughest of questions about the game.
Price Tag....A lot of people complaining about the price and are constantly complaiming 24/7, threatening of never buying or trying to persuade the devs to lower the price. Its a very simple matter when it comes to price....1. Dont buy it if it doesnt fit your budget. 2. Wait for a major sale. ( But you maybe waiting a very, very long time! ) 3. Get a job? 4. better get it while its at this price, once new content is added and more fetaures included, the price will surely go up! You might see a half price sale sometime next year, but I wouldnt hold my breath. The price will surely be more than $20 at release.
The last time I checked, I paid around $20 to see a movie, including the price of a soda, and got 2 hrs of entertainemt out of it.....thats it. Im able to replay the game as much as I want, therefore the price of the entertainment is justified, afaic!
As for how the game runs? I cant tell you when it comes to MP. Im currently playing SP and I have had no bugs that I have experienced as of yet. It has been a solid title so far in this stage of development! Pathing seems to be on point and AI reactions to tasks has been smooth. FPS is no problem with everything turned up....even for potatoes!
Overall, its not graphically exciting, very minecraft. However, the systems, mechanics and gameplay has made the game, so far, very fun to play and replay and replay! If you are offset by the price, then I would suggest find another bargain bin game to buy....the game, imo, has been worth the price.
A lot of streamers has enjoyed this title as much as me! Check out the "lets play" vids on youtube if you are still on the fence about purchasing!

The puzzles are easy to pick up but very enjoyable to complete, the low-poly graphics are beautiful, the lo-fi ambient electronic music completes the atmosphere, and everything is presented with an impressive finish.
The game itself is a series of turn-based movement puzzles on a grid. As long as you stand still nothing happens; when you move a square enemies and traps respond. Different enemies have different behaviors like chess pieces, and new puzzle mechanics and modifiers are gradually introduced. There's also some pixel hunting for treasures that unlock special outfits for Lara (most of them from the classic games.)
The main campaign is relatively short and easy, but fun all the way through, and some of the later levels are pretty satisfying when you figure them out. They even managed to do a clever boss fight which is kind of impressive for a puzzle game. The two additional chapters are significantly more challenging and without using hints took me a lot longer to complete than the base game.
All in all Lara Croft GO is an enjoyable puzzler with great production values well worth the time.

This game is smooth yet overly-simplistic. You will realise eventually that it revolves around 9 mythical cards for each character class (plus minus a couple of epic/elite cards). These cards are extremely rare and you can either hit it by luck or try a gambling game that costs you gold. While it may appear to be free-to-play good model, this is truly applicable until you cross level60 onwards, when the main "Mentality" skill kicks in.
Mentality is the single game changer skill in this (yet again, overly simplistic) game. It allows you to pack 4 of the same cards, and of course - must be the mythical cards, so Mentality+1 gives allowance for 4, Mentality+2 gives allowance for 5, and so on...until Mentality+5. Mentality skill is extremely expensive, not to mention all the gold you have to gamble to get a chance to win a mythical card. So this is the way how the game evolves into higher level as time goes on and if you want to win any fights soon enough, you will have to buy gold with real money, grinding well you can take forever.
There are no player base to speak of in this game, which is not surprising when I find out the facts. All the ranking leaderboards you see are in the past created by all these multiple accounts, some of them the same users still sticking around with their main "prime" high level heroes. The developer himself knows as guilty as himself can be as he discriminately allows those who support him by virtue of those developing higher level heroes (>70, 80,90 level), while he ban/suspend those accounts in the mid-levels(level 30-60) if they are around for too long, since it doesn't fit into "his gameplan".
So enjoy a simple game if you can and start from beginning until you near level60. Observe carefully the skill tree - look at mainly the 3 skills: Mentality, Tactics, and Tactics Mastery. The amount of gold it costs. You will understand what I mean. Do not use real cash to purchase credits(which are used to buy gold) into your account. This guy will indiscriminately ban you and you lose access to your entire account.

Lara Croft GO is a turn based puzzle game based on the Tomb Raider franchise. Each level is divided into a grid, and you move Lara one space at a time. You’ll need to pull levers and push stone pillars to weigh down pressure plates to trigger moving platforms and open doors, while avoiding giant spiders and snakes, crumbling floor tiles, boulders and arrow traps.
The good
-	Most of the puzzles are intelligently designed. Solving them gave me that “I’m the smartest guy in the world!” feeling.
-	The last couple of chapters get quite complex and challenging, without feeling frustrating.
-	The game does a good job of teaching the player the rules.
-	Every level has hidden gems and relics to find.
-	It took me 8 hours to finish each level and find about 80% of the hidden loot, which represents good value for money.
-	I didn’t suffer from any bugs or crashes.
The bad
-	Occasionally the puzzle mechanics don’t make sense with real world logic. You aren’t allowed to simply wait or stand still for a turn, which has an impact on some of the later puzzles that have a timed element. Also, Lara’s guns can only be used in very specific situations (you can’t shoot an enemy that is more than 1 tile away). Sometimes you can’t move to a tile that is next to the one you’re standing on, just because there’s no line on the floor connecting them. Of course there’s always a solution, but you have to be willing to accept that you can’t do the obvious thing and find a way to work within the limitations of the game’s rules.
-	I would have really liked an undo move option. Sometimes I’d get almost to the end of the level and realise I’d made one simple mistake which made the level unbeatable, and I’d have to start again from the beginning.
-	If you get totally stuck, there is an option for a “hint”, but this actually tells you the solution to the entire puzzle rather than giving you a small clue.
-	No story or dialogue. I need more Camilla Luddington!
-	Keyboard and mouse controls are horrible. You move by clicking and dragging, which is probably an attempt to recreate the feel of a mobile phone touch screen. You can’t use wasd or arrows or any other keys to move. After a couple of levels of that abomination, I switched to using my 360 controller, which actually controls how you’d expect a game to control (push the stick to move in a direction, use A/X/Y to interact with objects).
The recommendation
If you enjoyed the puzzle solving aspects of main franchise games like Anniversary and Underworld, and you own a gamepad, you should enjoy Lara Croft GO.

Let me start by saying I love the theme and idea of this game, where you are tasked with becoming a 19th century explorer in a cartoony world full of angry nuns, pirates, ghosts, wolves, etc., who love to bring your expeditions to an early end. With that being said, however, there is a lot to bother the would-be explorer.
For starters, don't be fooled by the cartoony, zany exterior, this game plays hard, even for a rogue-like. I don't mind permadeath, per se, as long as it feels fair. On normal to classic difficulty in adventure mode this game will whip your♥♥♥♥♥ I found that playing on normal in discovery mode (more forgiving) was much more fun over all. The gamemakers love to tout that you have to master the mechanics, but honestly the game isn't really that deep over all. Attacks only fall in three categories and there are only a handful of emotions. The deepness of the game is questionable, the cheapness of it at times is not.
Now, after getting that big huge dump on the game out of the way, what is good about it? Is it worth buying? I say it is worth buying, but only at a discount of 50% or more. There is fun to be had in this one, especially in exploring the different lands. Still exploration only runs so deep, you can see all the areas in a 2-3 hours, probably even less time if you're real good. For most, discovery will stop there. A couple of things that may keep folks coming back is the plethora of different characters and all the treasures to find. The game is only really randomized to a certain extent, so for many I would guess that a playthrough or two is going to be where folks check out.
Warts and all, I have a lot of respect for this scrappy game company. I would love to see how they might improve on a next iteration of this game, because like I said I really enjoyed the theme.

This was a surprising one.
Found this game in my feed, and was immediately interested by its colorful art and the promise of travelling (as a country-bound American, I fix my travelling bug by books or other media). With a Fire Emblem-like combat system, if a bit more complicated, it is reminiscent of that series if you're a fan, with a rock-paper-scissors combat mechanic and turn-based combat; however, it operated on hexagons as opposed to squares.
Renowned Explorers is extremely quirky and sets out a number of different ways to resolve any conflict, and it's entirely possible to do so without spilling blood (tears are still a distinct possibility however.) There is one boss fight where my crew complemented and hugged their way from the grips of a vengeful ghost pirate and convinced him to abandon his vendetta. At the same time, there were instances when poor Tibetan demons that just wanted to tease and blow raspberries at you got their fair share of mutilation from my crew, which had low speech defense and needed to get rid of them ASAP. This game is also surprisingly deep, with an intricate combat system with an aforementioned rock-paper-scissors mechanic that can be buff or debuff your team depending on how you behave during the fight by "Moods", which will give you different opportunities or force you to rethink strategy. For example, it could give you -25 speech defense, or it could make physical attacks +50% more effective. To beat the game you have to learn how to manipulate these moods.
It has art style that is pleasing to the eye, is surprisingly esoteric, a bit of history thrown in, and best of all, your arch nemesis is a pompous, cheating Frenchman which you must best to beat the game in time.
This game is a hidden gem, I highly recommend.

First KOTOR aged well in regards to graphics, but in other technical aspects it really lacks. Game crashes here and there, and on Mac you can't even use PC-only hacks to get widescreen mode working.
This game is very old-school, don't expect any quest-markers on map or fluid action combat. What you can expect though, is one of the greatest stories Star Wars universe has to offer - there's a reason why Darth Revan is such a fan favorite amongst hardcore fans. In fact, if you give most hardcore Star Wars fans option to bring back one thing into modern Canon, there's high chance it's going to be original KOTOR story and Darth Revan (before they IMHO messed it up in SWTOR). Darth Revan is so highly regarded they almost made his ghost appear in Star Wars The Clone Wars TV series, up until to the point when George Lucas dismissed that idea purely because Sith shouldn't be allowed to become one with the Force. At least that's the way new Canon works.
Besides Revan, most other characters are very memorable too - HK47 and Bastila being my personal favorites... and while some planets can be a bit more boring than others (Korriban, Taris and Tatooine are EPIC), in general game holds onto solid pace despite very ancient combat system that feels like playing MMORPG with 1000ms ping. Sure it may be based on tactical approach, but after certain point, once your character is powerful enough, it's mostly just spamming optimal rotations.
Ending of the game might seem a bit rushed, it almost feels as if developers were running out of time, but even then it takes nothing away from the entire experience that KOTOR is.
Both KOTOR games are a must for Star Wars fans, or RPG fans in general. On pure gaming perspective it might be debatable whether this actually is one of the greatest games of all time, as the game certainly has some issues,... but considering it's impact on Star Wars as a whole, and the story it tells... 10/10.
Oh how I wish for this game to get remaster update similar to KOTOR 2.

This is a cool game! A really cool game! It doesn't really look pretty from all the screenshots, but the story is so engrossing that you quickly forget all that and get lost in it. gameplay mechanic is: there are 250+ short video clips for you to search for and play through about a murder, and you gotta use the search bar to pick up and watch all of them, and like, in your head piece together what's happening.
it's super interesting to see how the type of search terms you choose evolve during the game by sheer progress. like, for me, it started off with the obvious words, then it got to basic plot words, then it got to basically anything i could think of, and after that..... i went straight for words that reflected the central themes of the game. which made things poignant.
genre is murder-mystery in the form of recorded interviews at a police station. like other reviewers mention, the story-telling is non-linear and anachronistic (because you never know what video clips will come up for different search terms). i thought i'd be SO confused because that's how i am.., but i really wasn't. i kind of found myself hooked as the plot twisted and turned and i was frantically trying to fill in the gaps by scambling for more video clips. it's cool because you always feel like you've got a lot of control over the story-telling and the rate at which you're being fed the plot, but you also feel like so much is left up to chance because you never know what a search term is gonna yield. to figure out what happened, you've also gotta figure out where the lies are and some important clues are given about that if you're observant, but ultimately, you never get fed the real answers for sure. it's a nice balance.
even after you pick up all video clips, the story still leaves so many connections for you to try and figure out yourself. like, some search terms will bring up two completely different videos, but then you kind of wonder...... are they actually connected? there's a lot of theory discussion on this stuff online.
other things that have already been praised: the acting (fab), soundrtrack (serviceable), script (incredibly natural).

This game has a fascinating narrative structure. Unlike most story-based games, I don't think I could have replicated the experience by watching a let's-play video or reading a transcript. It's all about the questions the nonlinear video fragments raised in my mind, and what searches I chose to answer them, as I tried to gather evidence for one theory or another of what happened.
It's beautifully, carefully crafted, with many simple but precise details, and I'm still thinking about it days after finding and watching all the clips, and then rewatching them all in order.

Telling someone an amazing story is difficult to do on its own. It has to be believable, has to engage the audience, and has to make people want to find out more about the characters and the world. It is hard to have a good story like that told to a player through audio visual engagement. Not only is this game able to do just that, it is able to tell its story without actually telling you anything. This game does not have a definite beginning, or ending but is rather, limited only by how much the player wants to know. An incredible form of symbolism found in this game (not a spoiler) is an othello game. Much like this game, othello isn't technically over until all the pieces are on the board, and there isn't ever a definite strategy that you can use to win. This "game" (which is really more of an interactive movie) is spectacular and makes you want to know everything. Even after you know everything. You will still be left wanting to know more.

I've played this game for many many years since it's first inception into the gaming market. In the beginning it was a great game with a lot to offer. It had lots of PvE and PvP content. Nothing more fun than Vampires vs. Slayers killing each other all over the place. It didn't really have much story wise or character building wise, but it did have a lot of monsters, lots of loot, lots of small details and lots of battle mechanics.
After a time it went downhill. It died little by little because hackers got into it. They created tons of hacks and cheats for the game. Infinite HP, infinite MP, massive damage on skills, speed hacks, etc. It got so bad that at one point the hackers were running the server. They could do a rollback on all characters on a particular server and destroy hours and hours of hard work. Shame.
The game shut down not long after. It was picked up by another publisher. The same thing happened. It got shut down. Got picked up by another publisher. Same thing happened. It got shut down. Got picked up by another publisher... rinse and repeat... You get where I am going with this...
While the game itself is fun and I had lots and lots of fond memories and many hours of enjoyment, I don't really think anyone should be playing this the way it is. The software and client are so old that anyone can hack it. Their hack/defense systems don't really do much. You can go online and find hacks for this game by just typing it in. It won't be long before this game gets overrun by hackers too. That is, IF this game still has a market for players, which I highly doubt.
So, in finalizing, it's not that I am saying you SHOULD NOT play this game, it's just that being a veteran player since it first came out and watching how many publishers picked it up and watch it die over and over again for the SAME exact reasons, I'd just felt compelled to let you know what you were in store for and hopefully you'll spend your energy elsewhere like on one of those 100+ Steam games you haven't touched yet. :P!
No hard feelings to the Publisher but this is a walking dead game. Don't waste your time.

Dark Eden is and has always been a free to play MMORPG,
. The game may have not aged that well, but please, it's a classic and should be treated as such. It doesn't deserve all the bad ratings it has here on Steam.

Once you open the game, adjust your video and game options (will be applied when you restart the game), and to  create your account just click on the button once inside the login menu of the game - it will forward you to their website via Steam. I actually didn't have any problem at all running this game, neither any of my friends.
The game still feels and plays just like any other old school game of this genre, such as Ultima, etc. I was happy and suprised to find some of the cities and even training zones with an interesting amount of people walking around there and interacting with each other.
Dark Eden went through ups and downs and some dubious updates, while some people complained that things are too easy now, others like my brother and I just loved the fact that the game will hook you up with some goodies from the start, and interesting dungeon zones to level up and fight with other races.
In the end, it's still an weird old atmosphere and enjoyable F2P game. And to all my dear Steam friends, please be honest with your reviews - if you don't like games of this old style, why are you playing it on the first place? This game has done nothing wrong to deserve such a bad rating.

A game I'd wholeheartedly recommend. For me, this was the best Hitman game of them all. Contracts were interesting, maps were good but tidy, methods of dispatch were variable.
Unlike Absolution (which had far too many levels involving running around, fleeing from assailants, and generally felt like a continous line of being hunted), Blood Money is built around each level at a time. You start the level with your equipment, and then you're left to figure out what you want to do. Do you go in guns blazing? Do you sneak around and set up traps? Do you take out a few potential threats and then wait in ambush for your target? All of it feels like here's the map, there's the target, go play.
I will say the models are fairly dated now. All NPCs pretty much the same model but with some colouration differences. If you can look passed that, you'll find a decent assassination game.
The demo is a poor representation of the full game.

Honestly - a better Hitman than the more recent titles. This was the one to have, that did its franchise the best.
If Grand Theft Auto is a sandbox game, Hitman was the modern sandbox assasin game. It had a multitude of ways to get the job done, varying from actually being an assassin to gunning down a neighbourhood dressed in a clown suit. Both have increasingly tougher restrictions ("it's harder and harder to be the perfect assassin" vs "there's way too many armed FBI agents to rambo as Big Bird in the open" kind of deal). It struggled, though, with some wonky controls pitted against tough, sometimes unforgiving, level design. That's important knowledge to evaluate #3, Blood Money.
H:BM took the crappy combat system and polished it, heavily, to the point you can really enjoy a good firefight and be a badass. As opposed to retreating to a room and gunning the door until the entire level was clear. The Early Warning System lets you know full well when you're blowing your cover in advance, giving you the heads-up alerts that, in Hitman 1, you literally had to discover by screwing up and restarting. Finally, it remans very, very Hitman - Fat, shy, girls do not exist, levels are wacky, stealth is awesome, guns are awesomer, RAGDOLL PHYSICS ARE LOLZ.
Graphically, this game still works without hurting your eyes, and I'd recommend a try

If you guys want an honest review, away from these others or the troll reviews then here it is.
For the most part I played battleborn through its first week of release, we encountered zero mechanical glitches or errors however there was a few issues to come to fruition.
First of all the large unskippable cutscenes that were at first impressive but quickly became tedious and almost as if they were tacked on loosely to remind us all that we're played Battleborn.
Secondly the god awful frame-rate, now whether this has been improved on or will be improved on is another matter but generally a game of this size and stature should be able to hold a solid 60FPS given the nature of the current market.
Finally, THIS IS NOT OVERWATCH, although many elements may seem 'similar' to overwatch, this game has many features that make it individual, for example the single or co-op story mode, its own full selection of original characters with personalities that are both believable and entertaining and a multiplayer mode that stands out from the standard multiplayer found in most other MOBA / FPS cross-overs.
Unfortunately due to the times of release and the stature of 2k compared to Blizzard entertainment this game was destined to fall by the wayside due to a much more refined product (Overwatch).
That does not take away from the fact that for the hours I put into this game I thoroughly enjoyed the experience and am more than happy to return to the game periodically however there hasn't been too much going on to pull me back to battleborn; (lack of decent marketing maybe?)
