Unfortunately there are a few problems with this game that force my hand in not recommending it. The character collision is maddening. I get hung up on my hommes a lot and it usually turns into both of us getting gibbed. I like that some of the characters feel clunky and slow but it isn't done well and getting hooked on elements of the map like bushes and overhead rock pieces that are off FOV is not fun.
They need to implement a comeback mechanic. Winning the game requires that you stray further away from your base and closer to the enemy base so survive-abiliy (which is mostly based on level) becomes more of a factor as the game goes on. I would have liked to see soft comeback mechanics like better design in choke points where good play and positioning can keep you from getting flanked (not currently possible) like TF2 does with one way doors. Another option would be hard-coded comeback mechanics like Heroes of The Storm does where the experience gained from getting a kill is scaled with the level of the enemy. It makes sense that when you kill a big scary monster boss you should get a big reward and if you are Godzilla you should get fewer points for stepping on people who are 6 levels behind you. It is kind of an idea from PVE which wold fit perfectly in this game trying to straddle a campaign and multiplayer. Think lvl 70 in WOW farming boars for XP. As it stands, if a player can 1v1 another player they can just hunt that one until they power spike and can 1v1 the next worst player. Then they hunt those two until they can safely 1v1 the next worst player. Contribute to the team fight/push on the front line while constantly babysitting your worst players defending backstabs is fun but it is only one type of gameplay and all multiplayer modes feel the same for this reason. Match making doesn't balance this out.
I have optimization problems on my machine but beyond that the GUI has issues. Jumping in and out of cut scenes during loading was not smooth and the character selection screen is rendered in a different aspect ratio from the rest of the game so the characters look small and choppy/distorted. A little more than two thirds of the pixels on my screen are being utilized and there is a big black border around this view like I'm watching an old VHS on a widescreen TV.
Buttons are not consistent throughout the GUI so sometimes a button like escape or X will do one thing and sometimes it will do another. Parts of the interface can only be used with the mouse and other parts only with the arrow keys. I also found rookie UI selection errors in the inventory screen that causes strange selection behavior that can result in selling/salvaging the previously selected item instead of the currently selected item. I thought this was just launchy hiccups but the problems are still there months and months later.
Items are rad but there are too few to find. I was on TeamSpeak with my friends and we all had found the same stuff but with random stat rolls. Grinding for items basically turned into trying to find a slightly better version of things we already found and balancing the stats against their higher cost. Do you want to equip a better item, later in the game or a worse item, earlier in the game? The trade off is cool but the loot grinding is unsatisfying. Item/loadout selection is one of the worst implemented systems int he game. Players quickly select their loadouts BEFORE seeing the enemy team and viewing the item stats in the loadout isn't possible. Each loadout is represented by a square filled with three icons. since there are only a few types of items, all of your loadouts will have three very similar icons like Boot or Goggles. What do they do? How much do they cost to equip? Well you have to just remember. Ok what if I pick an all magic defense loadout and load into a game against an all mele physical team? You lose. Lastly the time allotted to pick this loadout is the time you didn't use when selecting your character. A team that is working together to build a good team with a tank and a healer etc. then has just a few seconds to slam a loadout on the character. I would have liked to see a default loadout on each character that can be hot-swapped with a few floating general loadouts during the team loading screen for some kind of counter picking against team comps and maps As it stands now you can't counterpick characters or items.
I wanted this to be a Must Buy with unique mechanics and a new world to dive into but all the cool world building and character design is buried under the sloppy implementation of an unbalanced game.
SMITE beats this game in every respect playstyle options, level design, cosmetics, patch/support, graphical optimization, character kit synergy, tool tip clarity, etc. SMITE is free.

Yes it is Early Access. However, if an EA title is ready to charge money, it's ready to be criticized. I will make quick observations in the usual categories to help you decide if this title is something you'd be interested in:
I think we've all built our own cities in Minecraft, and hoped that the AI that accompanied pre-built villages would do more than just wander aimlessly and occupy a house at night. This game does exactly that, by focusing heavily on the AI elements that heavily lacked in other voxel-based games. It's especially great if you're like me, and not a huge fan of the multiplayer elements in survival games due to the amounts of trolling, toxicity, and the general attitude of "kill first, never ask questions". This game allows you build whatever you like, while adding a survival purpose to it ala 7 Days to Die.
The game itself is currently lacking, but still fun. You get the basics so far, with wood, stone, and various metals to build and craft with. Other than that, here are the current available jobs: wheat farmer, flax farmer, forester, baker, smith, and guard. This gives you everything you need to have fun for a while, but after a quick time playing you will become profitable and self-reliant. Then the only point to continue is to build whatever you like, or to just grow your town to as high of a number as possible. There is currently only one weapon as well: the bow.

The sound is lacking currently in this build. There is no background music, but there are sound effects for every action in the game so far. This is passable for me, as it's Early Access, and I'd rather see more content added than music currently.

High definition voxels. Bloom that makes for amazing sunrises and sunsets. Depth-of-field. It's as modern as Voxel-based games can be, in terms of visuals.

This game comes in a small 100+ MB package, but looks amazing. In it's current state, it runs easily at 60 FPS and doesn't require a high-tier setup to accomplish this. It's nowhere near being feature-complete though. However for the price, it's already a very competent Early Access title. I would recommend it if building a functional Minecraft city sounds appealing, as that is already possible. If you're a bit hestitant due to the lack of features, I would advise adding this to your Wishlist and watching it for a while. The updates seem to be fairly constant for now, and the dev is engaging and diligent, so I'm willing to put my money down.

What a gem of a game!
A bit daunting at first, because there are a lot of systems to learn, currencies etc. But it hs some real depth to it and it's a great theme - not just a skin on a dungeon crawler, but part of its core. Don't let the accessible graphics fool you, this is no toy.
It does suffer from the same issue I have with similar roguelikes, in that you can end up spending a lot of time developing your character/s, and end up losing the game pretty suddenly and brutally. But the development works so well in this game that it can't be a complaint - and it gives you enugh difficulty options that you can negate that to some extent anyway.
Looks great, very polished, well written.
Definitely recommend, and it's a bargain at full price.

Interesting Tactical RPG.
I played through the campaign about 6-7 times, and my most fun playthrough was probably the 3rd or 4th time. It took me some time to understand all the mechanics, which were fun and interesting, but also hard to synergize in a party IMO.
The down side to this game is probably just the lack of places to explore. All of the locations are random generated, but the stories are always the same. So you find yourself repeating the same stuff over and over. When I finally realized this, the game became stale. I played it out a few more times, so I could unlock characters to be leaders, but in the end the replayability is pretty bad.
In the end I still recommend this game, because it is fun the first few times through, and I think that's worth the On Sale Price.
I wouldn't recommend it at its full price though.

A classic RPG with what I believe to be one of the best stories in the Star Wars universe. The combat is old school dice rolling mechanics, which can potnetially throw people off as you simply click what you wish for your action to be before the game does it and tells you the outcome. That is not to say it is a turn based game like Final Fantasy, but it's limitations do take some time to get over, especially for those new to RPGs, or are a fan of new age RPGs like Mass Effect and Skyrim. The amount of customization is limited to cosmetics, as armor for the most part looks the same and there are only really about 5 or 6 faces to choose from, but the real customization is in the feats and abilities you get leveling up. You can tailor your character to group cohesion with feats that, for instance add +2 to hit on any opponent an ally is currently attacking,, thus making the strategy all of the party attacking a singular guy, or you can go full commando and have your abilities tailored to being the center of attention (tanking) such as having +2 on all saving throws against enemies you are in combat with. You can be a healer, a sabotuer, a synergist, really anything at all. The level of customization on feats may seem straightforward the firt time, but once you begin to understand what all the terms mean, and how your character fits into the party, you will see how much variety and usefulness the ability tree is.

If Grand Theft Auto is a sandbox game, Hitman was the modern sandbox assasin game. It had a multitude of ways to get the job done, varying from actually being an assassin to gunning down a neighbourhood dressed in a clown suit. Both have increasingly tougher restrictions ("it's harder and harder to be the perfect assassin" vs "there's way too many armed FBI agents to rambo as Big Bird in the open" kind of deal). It struggled, though, with some wonky controls pitted against tough, sometimes unforgiving, level design. That's important knowledge to evaluate #3, Blood Money.
H:BM took the crappy combat system and polished it, heavily, to the point you can really enjoy a good firefight and be a badass. As opposed to retreating to a room and gunning the door until the entire level was clear. The Early Warning System lets you know full well when you're blowing your cover in advance, giving you the heads-up alerts that, in Hitman 1, you literally had to discover by screwing up and restarting. Finally, it remans very, very Hitman - Fat, shy, girls do not exist, levels are wacky, stealth is awesome, guns are awesomer, RAGDOLL PHYSICS ARE LOLZ.

Her Story is an short but interesting game. Well, less of a "game" and more of a collection of cutscenes of various length that you see out of order and the whole "game" is trying to find the cutscenes and figure out what the overall story is. It's a fun little puzzle/mystery and a rather unique way to present it through gameplay and I highly recommend playing through, especially if you see it on sale (though it's already cheap as is, the short play time can put you off paying full price).
You are a person using an old archive computer to look up clips of a woman being questioned about the disappearance of a man.  These clips are taken from her interviews and interrogations, which have been completely transcribed and subtitled. You can use the old search engine on the computer to search for words and phrases, and it will return up to 5 results that have those search terms in their transcripts. As you watch and listen to the video clips you'll find new names and phrases that will give you hints of what to search next and allow you discover more clips and help you unravel the whole story.
Her Story is interesting and unique. You feel like a detective, shifting through evidence to try and find that new and interesting clip that's hidden in the vast and dated archive system of the computer. Some of the clips are worthless, or just repeats of the same general information, but once in a while a new name or character will be referenced and send you deeper down the rabbit hole on a new lead.
The gameplay has some flaws though. It doesn't feel like it has a real 'ending' and the story is very much open to interpretation. It's difficult to find every clip, as some consist of very obscure words and are very short (only a few seconds long) and difficult to find. The good news? You don't have to find every clip to end the game! The bad news? You'll still feel like you're missing something. The game is satisfying and fun when you're guessing at the story and what's actually happening/happened, but once you have a good idea then there's little point to continuing to look for clips except for the achievements and feeling of completion. It will almost all be a retread of the same information and moments.
That being said, I still recommend this game highly. If you're into mysteries, narrative driven games, or you just want a game that puzzles you in a unique way, give Her Story a try. I rate it 4/5
Oh, and there's a "clear session" button that deletes all of your game data but seems more like a reset for search terms and saved videos from the archive. If you do play this game, don't make my mistake and press it after an hour. It own't clear your user interface, it will make you restart.

Her Story is a unique experience; for me at least, it was a breath of fresh air after a spate of MMOs, FPSs and maybe just a little bit too much Minecraft! The premise is seemingly straightforward, with the game granting the player access to an old, relegated computer and its police database, where they must sift through a mess of video clips from a series of seven interviews. The initial query has already been entered in the search bar- murder.
The story is set in 1994, and the UI is appropriately old school in appearance, complete with major screen glare, though this can be turned off! The interviews have and date stamps and it is clear they took place over June and July of the same year and range from 1-2 minutes to a mere 3 seconds in length.
The one woman cast consists of Viva Seifert, a talented actress, who I felt did a great job of portraying a really ambiguous character and maintaining the mystery. The character was believable, even though at times I didn’t know if I could believe what she was saying! She manages to evoke sympathy whilst also seeming untrustworthy, adding to the confusion presented by the story itself.
The way the story is ‘told’ couldn’t be less linear; autonomy is placed entirely in the hands of the player, controlled and limited by what search terms, and combinations thereof, that are chosen. I shunned the pre-set first search, deleted ‘murder’ and instead searched for ‘death’, I then proceeded with a further 68 successful searches, including things such as ‘body’, ‘blood’ and even ‘fennel’!
I’d be lying if I said I didn’t get confused playing this game. A few times I thought I had pieced things together only to stumble upon some new information that blew my theory to smithereens! On reflection, the overall story and sequence of events being recounted is much clearer (though certainly not definitive) but the interviews are intentionally broken into clips that lend themselves the uncertainty and key details are scattered throughout.
Her Story tackles some heavy themes in its own way and can get pretty dark at times, with some sinister twists and turns that will have you questioning the motives and morals of a good portion of the characters!
All in, I spent a little under 4.5 hours playing, saw 100% of the clips, got 12/13 Steam achievements and managed to reach a conclusion, albeit one that is intentionally open to interpretation. For the more than reasonable price of £4.99 I’d definitely recommend Her Story, just don’t expect high octane, action-packed gameplay! For anyone that enjoys it, I’d also recommend researching fan theories, it was fascinating to see how others interpreted the game – but only AFTER you’ve played!

One of the best Star Wars experiences you could ever have. Knights of the old Republic is an RPG that was made to be on computers. Its controls may seem archaic now but they were a massive step above the original Xbox release. As an RPG there's a lot of depth not only in mechanics but decision making as well. Two of the games strongest features are open ended but linear levels and its moral system.
Kotor is a linear game, but it hides this so well through its level design. Each place you travel too feels like its own small world, full of quests and characters to meet. You can spend hours exploring each one of them. The moral system adds weight to your choices and the direction of the story. Other characters in your team may even be influenced by your decisions and affects what force powers you can equip.
Its a fantastic game, which admitedly falls apart near the end. Difficulty spikes in the final area end up creating a frustrating experience rather than a fulfilling one. But the journey there is more than worth it. Its one of the great PC classics and as a star wars fan or as a newcomer you can't go wrong here.

OK, so this game does not define a new genre, make you re-evaluate your place in the multiverse, give you 40 years of replayability, or make you cry/laugh out loud.  Yes, it was obviously designed as a mobile game. It' just a really nicely done puzzle game.
Now that we have that out of the way... Why do you play games? I play games for enjoyment, and I really enjoyed this game.
The art and sound is very well done. I think overall the puzzle design, art and animation is pretty true to the world of Lara Croft even if it is a lot more stylized and simple than the jaw-dropping art in Tomb Raider. I played with a controller on my couch through my steam link and it was a great way to unwind for a little while. The controls were good overall, although there were a couple of times I got sloppy with the thumbstick and went the wrong direction. I'm pretty sure it was 96% user error.
The puzzles are hard enough to be interesting, but not too hard  (and there are solutions out there if you get stuck). You need to realize that you're expected to die sometimes to figure out how things work. There's no penalty, so go ahead and just try that crazy idea to see what happens. The achievements aren't too onerous - I only had to retrace my steps a couple of times. The save points are well placed for the most part so you don't have to do too much tedious repetition to make it through (there was only one annoying level I can think of). I thought the optional "hidden object" part of the game where you click vases to unlock outfits and get achievements was a nice way to add a little more to the game without over-complicating it.
I just finished the Mirror of Spirits and really enjoyed that as well. The chapter added two new mechanics that made the new puzzles pretty interesting. No new achievements, but you do get a new outfit to unlock.

I previously gave Dwelvers a thumbs down due to the fact that development seemed to have stopped. The developer has since resurfaced (as you can also see from the comments on this review). As far as I understand it, the dev has bought himself free of his contract with the previous publishers. To me, that suggests a level of personal and financial commitment that might yet see Dwelvers become the game it always had the potential to be.
I've played Dwelvers again recently after an absence of a year or two. While I haven't yet finished a game, I have had a lot of fun playing around once I remembered how everything worked.
It's obviously heavily reminiscent of Dungeon Keeper, but with a couple of interesting twists. For a start, there are multiple levels to the dungeon, so you can dig downwards and climb upwards. This allows you to create lines of defence by making areas inaccessible, allows you to dig down to find resources, and brings the risks of a massive cave in every now and then. There is also an overworld that I have somewhat razed and pillaged. The creatures are also different (well the imps are still imps I guess).
Now there are a few things that are still rough around the edges here. For a start, there's no tutorial at the moment (there was one ages ago, but it's been disabled). Even if you've played DK, there's a few things that are just different enough here to throw you at the start. There's no campaign of any sort, you just build and defend your dungeon and pillage the overworld. If you need a campaign to enjoy this sort of thing, I'd definitely wait. If you are more like me and enjoy building a base, then you'll probably have fun now if you enjoyed DK.
The feedback you get when things aren't working is also lacking, and there's a bunch of confusing status icons that appear intermittently, where I have to be honest and say I don't know what they mean. The UI used to equip your minions is poorly thought out and feels like a prototype to me.
Thankfully these are not particularly crucial elements to enjoying the game, although I would hope they will be improved at some point.
I've got my money's worth out of Dwelvers already. It's thoroughly playable in its current state, but also most definitely not finished.
Abondoneware. Stay away.

First off let me say, please ignore the negative reviews, I have read through them and fail to see a reason for a negative review when 100% of their reasons are technical in nature, not game based.
I have been playing this game on and off since 2008.  Once it launched on steam, I clicked to download the game, once downloaded, launched the game, clicked at the bottom "new id" a page appears to enter your email, check it, then add a password and verify your password and bam, your in the game.
Ok so about the game and why would anyone want to play something created back in 2006 or so.  Well first off there is nothing else like it on the internet, nothing.  Imagine a game where  there are three races locked into an eternal conflict.  You can choose to be a vampire, a slayer, or an ouster.
Vampires are creatures powered by darkness.  They can weild strong magic, powerful melee attacks, and drain their prey of blood to restore the vampires health.  They are very strong solo players, but work well in a group also.
Slayers are humans with varried classes.  You have the two handed sworder called a Blader.  There is the sword and board class called a Sworder.  A modern weapon master using shotguns, sub machine guns, Assault rifles, and Sniper rifles called a Gunner.  Then you have a magic using Healer able to call down powerfull light based magic to crush your enemies and also resurect your fallen commrads.  Last but not least is the Enchanter, a character that uses powerful light based magic to crush, capture,  and destory its enemies.  The Slayer race is not as powerful solo as the other races, but in a group, it is the most powerful race in the game.
Ousters are a faiiry like race of all females.  They are magical creatures of nature.  They can choose to master the power of the elements to harness very powerful magical attacks or to be a master of combat,tempering your attacks with the power of the elements.
These three races live in a time of constant battle with each other.  There are many different wars that occur on a daily basis now.  Some wars pit every race against each other, and other wars that make temporary allies of one of the races to unite against the third race.  There is an in depth quest line to advance your character to stronger and higher stages.  There are also many other quests to keep any role player busy.  You have the ability on all races to capture, raise, modify and blend alot of different pets.  Pets add attributes to your character, they can assist you in combat, and race specific pets will actually help you fight your enemies.
You can enchant the gear you find, and use Articles to create even more powerful items.  There are alot of bosses to hunt in the game, but bring your friends, because they can be very deadly.  There always seems to be some kind of event going on, giving you free items to help you build your character.
Even though this game has been around since 2006 or so, this game is still seeing new content added.  At the time of this review new content was added just yesterday.
In summary if your looking for a unique free to play game, where fantasy is the catch word, and you dont mind older yet unique graphics, give it a try.  What do you have to loose, its a f2p.
I hope this was helpful and that we see you in game some time.

Time to Edit my review! FIRST OF ALL:
DON'T PAY ATTENTION TO ALL THE NEGATIVE REVIEWERS!
They are compaining about little nitpicky things that can all be solved by asking a simple question or two, or asking for help in general when it's needed.
DarkEden is a horror based MMORPG set in the fictional European country of Eslania, which is caught up in a massive, three-way war between Vampires, Vampire Hunters (Slayers), and Half-Human/Half-Vampire hybrids (Ousters). It's a click-to-move old school styled game complete with 2D isometric graphics and everything - but don't let that fool you; it has many features of a modern MMO (party system, guild system, etc) and has been receiving regular updates for the almost 20 years it's been out.
This game is one of those "I always end up coming back to it" games; I have played dozens and dozens of different MMOs and this one is the one I can never fully quit. The gameplay and style of the game itself has always stood out to me as something that I have never been able to find anywhere else, and it is actually really well balanced end-game. But enough about that.. let me give you some of the details
Three Races You can choose between Slayers, Vampires, and Ousters. Without going too much into the lore, these three factions strive for nothing more than the complete and total destruction of the other two. Each race has distinct leveling and skill system, and the classes found within each race are pretty unique as well. A quick run-down of the three races:
Slayers: Slayers can be one of five classes: Blade, Sword, Gun, Enchant, and Heal. Blade/Sword are two different twists on your melee classes. First one hits heavy and hard, the other hits lighter and more quickly. Gunners are your best DPS class (you can choose between different types of guns ranging from SMGs to Sniper Rifles). Enchant is your magic DPS + buff class. Healer should be self explanatory.
Vampires: Vampires are segmented into two main classes: melee (combat) and magic. Melee/combat vampires get up close and personal and absolutely decimate anything within range. Magic vampires employ a variety of different classes of magic (poison, curses, acid, and blood) to beat down and render their opponent defenseless and useless before they get beaten down.
Ousters: Ousters can be one of four classes: Fire, Water, Earth, and Combat. Fire ousters have some of the highest DPS in the game across all races. Water ousters are the healers for the ouster race, utilizing water magic to restore and buff allies. Earth ousters are the crowd control/buff class and a good earth on any team will make them vastly harder to kill. Combats are your melee class and pull from the three elemental schools - fire, water, and earth - to apply bonus effects and damage to their skills.
One of the great things about this game is that each and every class available is 100% viable in both PvP and PvE. Even the support classes can handle themselves. While characters always work better in a group, soloing is possible if you need/want to do it.
The game is PvP focused, with there only being about 2-3 safezones for each race in the entire game -- everywhere else is PvP enabled with no restrictions. There are also a variety of events and dungeons that take place that encourage PvP between the races. One of the most iconic events is Bible War: twice a week, all three races duke it out across 10 different maps (including two castles for each race) to take control of Blood Bibles, which are equippable buffs with huge benefits. I have never really found any sort of war system in an MMO quite like Bible War on DarkEden. There are also guild seige wars, base occupation wars, wars out in field maps, capture the flag events, and a variety of dungeons and lairs that players can attend. Most of those encourage PvP and will only activate once a single race occupies it; others require the races to work together to defeat a common enemy.
The item and enchanting system is simple to grab the basics of but can get really in-depth if you want to get the most out of your set. The highest levels of gear and equipment can only be obtained by participating in end-game dungeons and events. There is a pretty complex pet system as well. In this game, pets do not help you kill things - they simply give you stats. The stats that you get depend on both the pet and its tier/level; the upgrade system for pets has just recently been updated and there's a lot that goes into it. Much like the item enchanting system, it's easy to get the basics of, but if you really want the most out of your pet you have to work at it.
The number of dungeons, PvP events, regular world PvP in and of itself, the enchantment system, and other stuff I didn't mention are just some of the really cool things about this game. And while I have seen similar mechanics in other MMOs, nothing really has ever been able to top this game. Quite a number of people I've met on the server so far are people who played ~10 years ago and couldn't get over the game - they had to come back.
The Steam revies are mixed at the moment, and that is a combination of some slight technical issues with the client (have to run it in 16 bit color mode on certain configurations of win7/10) and the fact that there are not a lot of English guides for this game - however, over at the Discord channel for this game we are in the process of putting out guides for everything, as well as answering any questions someone might have. And a number of us are working on a complete and total guide for the game itself, so it's only a matter of time.
I'm pretty confident that if this sort of game sounds good to you, you won't be able to quit either. If you have any questions about the game before you try it, please feel free to stop by the Discord channel listed below or comment/PM me on here!

I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes RPGs and CCGs. It merges the two amazingly well.
I love it that you can play a match wihout creating an account, so you are really free to decide if you like it or not, and then take the next step. The tutorial is helpful, the game can be understood easily. It is a bit overwhelming, but after you realize that you can level up faster by playing some multiplayer games (even if you lose, you get lots of XP), you can get the Energy Points required to make strategic, in-depth moves, even with the limited collection and play area you have.
I absolutely love the level up system, basically you decide how you want to play the game. Would you like more Health or more Energy? Do you want to expand your Hand or make your Buff area bigger? Do you want to get more gold and XP for each win? Or are you going for a huge Collector's Deck? You decide.
The card art is very nice, and the multiple combos you can pull with almost all cards is an excellent idea. You can turn any weak attack into some serious pain with the combos, which makes it so that no card is really worthless.
Collecting cards is really easy, you don't have to buy any packs. You just play the game, and as you draw cards, you always get to keep the ones you played. These cards go into your Stash, out of which you can pick multiple ones and put them in your Collector Deck, which will accompany you on future matches. It also makes you think more strategically in the beginning, as well: do you want to play your regular cards for a guaranteed effect, or do you want to spend more Energy on playing that Rare/Elite/Epic card you pulled, so you can add it to your collection?
All in all, it's a very good game with a somewhat dwindling population (sadly), but I was able to find human opponents whenever I really wanted to. Even if you can't/don't want to, there's a nice Campaign and Quest mode, where you can just play and collect cards.

Although this game is currently in 'early access' i'm not going to be too lenient on it as I originally pre-ordered it to come out in December 2015. For me, it has recreated the old 'Rollercoaster Tycoon' games but just removed the fun.
Pros:
- Despite what some people say, the rollercoaster builder is actually quite nice to use and I was able to create some good designs with it.
- The ride cameras can sometimes be fun (if the framerate keeps up enough!)
Cons (Where do I even start?):
- Such a simple task of building paths is such a pain.. the game is so fussy about what connects where, and even with grid and snapping, I was unable to create a simple straight path system
- The ride a building placement is equally as unpredictable, refusing to allow buildings to be placed in open areas next to paths, also not automatically joining to a path when placed directly next to one.
- The staffing system has been 'dumbed down' and the janitors walk off and do what they want. You find yourself constantly building new staff buildings as the staff have seemingly disappeared and I cannot find a way to track them individually.
- There is little to no customization on certain rides (especially pre-built ones).. Again, this removes a large portion of the fun.
- The game seems to include food and souvineer stands from 4 set themes, limiting your creativity.
- Only 3 maps that you can start from scratch on.
- No autosave feature, so I lost over an hours work due to a power cut. In 2016 I would have thought this would be a standard feature?
- Now for probably the biggest con.. graphics and performance... For a game that was supposedly meant to be 'retail ready' by December 2015, its appauling. The graphics look like a mobile phone game, or a PC game from 2004. Also the performance on highest settings is really bad. On my GTX 970, I can get around 30-40fps scrolling round my park. When I zoom in to watch the customers glitch around the footpaths and disappear into rides, however, i get as low as 15fps. The framerate is also very unpredictable when using the ride cams.
I could go on and on about how I am disappointed by this game, but I'll cut the review here. I was looking forward to this so much last year that I didnt cancel my pre-order when I heard about the beta. I also eagerly downloaded it the minute I saw it was avaliable. I tried to enjoy the game and ignored the criticism, but all it did was make me want to play 'Rollercoaster Tycoon 2'!

What is it?
Renowned Explorers is a glorified board game. There are plenty of BoardGames that currently have a large amount of these mechanics, that this game has. The only difference is the computer tracks all the information, no 1+ hour worth of setting up the game, no need to do a ton of math to determine your end game score.
How much is this game like a board game?
(1) The combat
(2) The traveling
(3) The random encounters
(4) The skill tree character building
(5) The limited type of currencies
(6) The end game scoring system
And More.
All of these and more are almost the exact same mechanics I have found in board games that I have played.
You essentially pick/create a team & you explorer. You have random encounters, random events, obtain random currency, of course your options are limited as to what you can & cannot do.
There is a small learning curve to the game.

I've originally played the first FEAR on one of my older computers back then and never really finished it because I was too scared. I've also played the rather short-lived Free-To-Play, FEAR Online. Coming over to FEAR 2, there's a lot of things that can be said over game story that show its age compared to most shooters now, but here's a few points that I think needs to be made that stands out from others.
What I like about this game:
1. This game aesthetically feels like a downgraded Fallout 4; You get plenty of weapons / gear, you get to be in a giant mech and wreck face, there's feral ghouls otherwise known as the replica soldiers. And of course, ragdolls.
2. You can literally flip tables.
3. You can slow down time. Yes, it's toggleable.
4. You get to see all the horror tropes come before your very eyes.
5. Turn off Film Grain and keep on Head Bob to keep things realistic. Turning off Headbob lets you levitate.
What I dislike about this game:
1. The level design almost feels labyrinthian; if you come back for another session, you'll forget where you have to go
2. Lack of Sound. Granted, this is likely for an atmospheric feel, but really drops the immersion from 1st gripe.
3. The AI; I can't recall if the original had smarter AI, but these guys literally run at you.

FEAR 2 isn't perfect, but it's certainly something special.  I simply can't see a reason why you wouldn't want to give it a chance-- unless you haven't played FEAR 1, of course, in which case you need to throw all your credit cards at the screen immediately and get that game.  Think Half-Life with crazy effects, slow-motion, a crazy conspiratorial plot, and Alma getting up in your grill to give you the spooks.  It has a few shortcomings compared to its predecessor, but also has the same great design and mechanics of the first game while subtly building on the established setup.
Just like the first game, FEAR is a horror game told from the perspective of a mute John Wu.  It's terrifying, it's dark, it's atmospheric... but you're John Wu.  It's a fantastic game with Half-Life style storytelling and great writing, not to mention fantastic combat.  But...
That Ending.  Just... that ending.

Dismissing
several times as some sort of shallow spinoff game using the Tomb Raider popularity, a cash grab at worst or lacking content at best, Steam Store was persistent to keep recommending this. With a healthy dose of scepticism I decided to give it a try .. several hours later it had me completely hooked!
Easing you in with simple puzzles & tasks, it continues to build on its foundations. Introducing new mechanics, new enemies, larger maps, combining what you have previously learned & adding more & more layers to it. Granted, I found the puzzles for the first half of the game to be fairly straight forward, most still offered enough of a challenge to have to replay a couple times as you discover the nuances designed into each puzzle. Although these earlier levels are quick, there are a decent number of them to complete.
While working your way through each level, there are also hidden items to find. Clicking on these will collect them, but as the camera is fixed, so they may only be visible from certain squares. Finding some of these offered more challenge than the earlier puzzles! Collect a set & it will unlock other outfits for Lara. Was a good addition to the main puzzle mechanics along with the few interesting achievements to unlock which are some mini puzzles within themselves. Both offer a reasonable amount of replayablity.
The automatic camera direction gives scope/depth to the levels even when small. Graphically, the retro low-poly art design looks really good, even if some of the animations are a bit basic.
Moving on to the later levels, especially the last location of
, really upped the challenge. I probably spent more time there that all the other five combined, evening resorting to the
hint after getting stumped for way too long
The complexity of these later puzzles was impressive, & not was I expected from a small mobile game. Leaves me really looking forward to the next Chapter,
coming soon ... & for free!
One thing I was less impressed with was the control translation. Using an analog stick on a controller, I found the movement to be very sensitive to small movements. This often resulted in accidental miss-steps. Using Steam's built-in controller customisation I was able to reduce this sensitivity to a degree, but I do not know how many times I had to restart a puzzle due to a double step or wrong direction.
It could have benefited from some more attention to translate the touch style interface into a more precise mapping with a controller. Works fine, if you are somewhat careful but could be better in my view.
plays to its strengths & doesn't pretend to be anything it is not. For the price, there is a plentiful amount of content, some replayability & a decent challenge to be had. This is one of those rare mobile ports that is actually worth playing & certainly worth a recommendation!

Each player has an amount of energy points, these are used to play cards. Each card has a energy cost and there are cards that can affect your or your enemy's energy.
Each round consists of 5 phases
Players take turn playing out the phases, ie. first player goes through draw, equip, attack and discard phase, then the other player goes through draw, equip, defense and discard phase (while seeing the other players attack cards laid out). Then the battle commences.
: In this phase you draw cards from either the random deck or from your collector deck. Either player can draw from the random deck. Your hand can have at most 5 cards, and you can draw at most 3 cards at a time.
: During this phase you can use equipment cards from your deck. They give different bonuses to stats such as; +damage, +defense, -enemy energy, etc.
works as follows; the damage, defense and healing of each players cards are summed up, then the reduce damage, reduce defense, etc. of each players cards are subtracted, and what's left is the damage caused to each player.
When a match is over, the cards that you've played from the random deck are added to your card stash and then you can choose to transfer them to your collector deck. This is one way to acquire cards.
Simple enough, right?
When you start playing the game you get to create a character by choosing one of the three races; human, orc or elf.

This is a very simple CCG; but what does that mean?

The only real difference between cards are the energy points they cost to play and the amount they affect a stat.

I will write a more thorough and thoughtful review for this game in the future, but seeing as it is having a sale, I wanted to write a quick review to any one I know considering getting it.
This is definitely one of the most fun strategy roguelike games I have played. Imagine the same consideration and thoughtfulness of FTL's roguelike strategy and throw it into a 19th century world of exploration and treasure hunting. You lead 3 person bands of explorers as they try to make their mark on history by getting as much fame, fortune, or even scientific discovery as possible. I highly recommend this game and the expansion. It has been one of the best new indie games I have had the pleasure of discovering.

This is a great game. I see it's on sale, if you don't have it and you're considering getting it do so.  If you like turn-based combat or boardgames then you should be right at home. The game has a humorous, upbeat style and likeable charactes. Interactions are all text based, there isn't really anything grim or dark if that's your thing, but it's a good time and mixing and matching your crew of adventurers while devising new strategies is a lot of fun. To me at least.
I saw this game was on sale, I had previously played it and liked it enough that I thought I should give it a recommendation for anyone on the fence. It plays a lot like a board game, with rpg and strategy elements. You pick a crew of three adventurers (who all have their own personalities, perks and skills that will help in various challenges), you travel around an adventure board, encountering combat and dialogue challenges, leveling your characters up, collecting treasures and moving on to the next adventure which you pick from a world map.
Between adventures you return to the Society headquarters where you can buy various specialists that either grant a benefit or make the game play slightly differently and place research points into a civilization like tech tree that does the same. You can also buy items for your characters here that do everything from simply adding attack and armor to adding new perks and skills. There are a lot of different ways to win the game, and there's dice rolls on everything that you can weigh in your favor with specialities, treasures and craftable/salvageable toolkits.
The devs are still supporting the game with new content and tweaks so things are still changing all the time. If any of this appeals to you, you might like renowned explorers. I recommend the game and you can easily find out within the return period if it's for you so what's stopping you, try it!

Part boardgame, part party management RPG, part tactical strategy, part (optional) roguelike, and all of these elements (which mesh extremely well) wrapped in a charming and effective artstyle with clever writing. Your combat and adventure approaches will be dictated by your party makeup, which is chosen prior to the start of the game from a variety of options. Depending on the skills of each, your approach will differ each game, making for a highly replayable game. Want to seduce every enemy that comes your way instead of shooting/ clubbing them? There are options for that. This game also has a large and diverse set of achievements, which I personally like.
I also recommend the expansions, but if you want to test the base game first you can always add it for an additional playthrough (which you will want to have several of just to see the additional content.) This one is worth taking a risk on, even at full price.

It's an indie trading card game with role-playing elements build in - and it's great.
You "collect" cards from a random stack while battling. The cards in the random stack is based on your race and class. You can keep cards (only ones you have used) in a seperate stack of cards to be used in battle along side the random stack, so you can keep all your most powerful cards at hand when you really need them.
Your actual hero is customizable every time you level up - life regen, more energy, or hitpoints, etc. Furthermore, later on you can train your hero skills that effect the battle in certain ways. These, as far as I can tell, can all be done without paying any money. A booster pack of new cards cost 1,500 gold. You can earn about 2,000 gold free every day from daily missions, not including any dueling or campaign mission rewards.
So far, I would totally recommend this game over any other TCG I've played.
The ONLY downside that I've noticed is the actual user-interface and menu navigation is sometimes confusing. Just stick with it, and I'm sure you'll enjoy your time

We're sad that we have to give this a thumbs down. My husband & I have been Atari fans since we got our first Atari Game System back in like 1981. Anybody remember Pong? Yeah...we're old...
We bought the Deluxe version of this back in Nov thinking the release date would be Dec 10th.  We aren't upset about spending that money, however, we're shocked at what this has turned out to be so far.
The Pro's
1.) Early Access- good on Atari to recognize that they needed to put something out there.
2.) Performance- we have a great computer that my husband built, so no performance issues like others have had.   Occasional choppiness, but hey, it's a computer game.
3.) Graphics-the parks actually look really pretty.
4.) Coaster builder- far from perfect, but we actually made several cool coasters & each one took less & less time. The problem is that both the coasters & the pieces to build with are disproportionately large & the test stats are way off. (What exactly is the safety rating about, does anyone know?) I hope some of this is fixable & being worked on.
The Con's
1.) Navigation- we shouldn't have to use the keyboard to scroll around the park. It's not 1989. And can I please have an Undo button? I make a lot of mistakes!
2.) Music- I know Matt said they're working on the custom music, but can we please put a rush on that before my head explodes? The music from RCT3 was so superb, I'd love to be able to import that into this game. Does anyone know if that's possible?
3.) The Vomit- really? Every peep pukes coming off every ride? And now they pee on the path if they can't make it to the rest room? Sorry, but it's disgusting & childish.
4.) Paths- we don't even know what to make of this. Very cumbersome. And we can't place buildings right on the main path. Not liking that at all.
5.) The Peeps- it's like Night of the Living Dead went to a porn flick. What's with the weird moaning? And can someone please make the kid stop crying? I think my ears are bleeding. The peeps have no personality at all. They don't appear to be happy, sad or anything in between.
6.) Rides- again, many seem disproportionately large. It just seems as if things aren't properly scaled. The fact that we can't move the entrances & exits is very odd. Why not? Also, the rides seem pricey, so why do we have to purchase the sign going over the ride?
7.) Complaining- there's too much of it. It appears as if you all have taken a page from the first Zoo Tycoon, & not a good page. The animals were great in that game, but the peeps made me stop playing because of the constant complaining about things you couldn't even fix. Please don't make that same mistake with this game.
8.) Buildings- way too many restaurants & the builings are huge. Seriously, who goes to an amusement park thinking, "Gee, I hope I can get a great Moo Goo Gai Pan while I'm here!" And if you eat sushi, then get on a roller coaster, you're an idiot. No wonder there's puke everywhere. Don't get me started on the huge, ugly, unnecessary employee buildings. I hate this idea. But the Dev Blog dated April 1st states they will also be adding an admin building. And where are we supposed to place that? We have no room left in the park to place a rolller coaster, and with the park entrance being so huge, can't we just pretend that's where the employees go to rest? It's just a game, it doesn't have to be that realistic, it just has to make sense.
9.) Breakdowns-is it just me or did the rides start breaking down as soon as I opened the park?
10.) Entertainers- Oh. My. God. This is the worst thing of all to me.  The Dev Blog dated April 1st said the entertainers will amuse guests while they're queuing. I mean no disrespect, but did you guys actually play this game? I watched one exit their building, walk down a path, enter a queu, interact with exactly no one, turn around & go right back to his building. I told you those employee buildings were a bad idea! And I'm sorry, but that huge, hulking, ominous, predatory owl looking thing is just scary. Remember the shark entertainer from RCT3? My husband & I still love that guy. We named him Jerry. We would turn the game to its lowest speed so we could watch the kiddies laugh & jump up & down as he tried to bite their heads off, then he would joyfully skip away, with his little red sneakers on! So cute. Yeah, that's all gone, along with all the charm, cuteness & personality that was RCT3.
We don't know what this game is, but we do know that it isn't RollerCoaster Tycoon. We have nothing but faith in Atari to make this right. We will continue to play, for what it's worth, and will amend our review as we see fit. Thanks for listening!
PS- I'm not kidding, can I please have Jerry the Shark back???
4/7/16-So, after today's update, still awful. Oh sure, the peeps LOOK better while they're peeing on my path right in front of the rest room, but my janitors are still ineffective. I do think the mechanics are working faster & I do appreciate the flat map. They have a long way to go before this review comes out of the thumbs down status!
5/24/16-So I went in the game today for the first time in weeks. Sorry-still awful! It's not even interesting enough or fun enough to waste another minute playing. RIP, RCT.
11/28/16- Holy crap, they took this thing out of early accesss??? Yikes, sorry to have wasted $60.00 on this. My husband & I are done with you, Atari. Considering we have been fans since you first started in 1974 & we were just kids, you can imagine our disappointment. Funny enough, we also own Planet Coaster & aren't impressed with that one either, although it's better than this nonsense. At least they weren't ridiculous enough to have peeps♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on the path. Shame on you, Atari. Good luck digging yourselves out of this one.

So I decided to play longer then a few hours before writing a review. I'm clocking a little over 20 hours in this game at the moment and all in all I am not to positive about it.
I loved RCT 1 and 2. I played 3 shortly but never got around to actually properly playing it. I have also never been good at building coasters and actually don't quite enjoy doing that. I just put down pre-made coasters and try to get the goals I need to get. So for me as a very casual gamer it all just needs to be simple.
This game can be simple if you give it a chance.
Suprisingly I am actually attempting to build coasters. The builder is a little confusing at first and it took me a while to properly understand the controls and how it all works but I feel that I sort of got the hang of it. They're not the most awesome coasters but I actually enjoyed making them and trying to get them to work and not crash. However some parts are still confusing to me when I try to build and especially with the add-ons like twists and loopings and they give me an error and I cannot continue to build. So I avoid adding those which is immidiatly what does dissapoint me about this builder. I should be able to just add these things. The fact that there is very little explaination as you first start building doesn't help either and for some odd reason I cannot get the tutorials to work so I'm stuck on that.
Overall the coaster builder is not bad.
Now for everything else. I like the designs of the flat rides but at the same time I wish I could edit them. Because I like the size and how they made it I would like to be able to change the colours and such. I miss that. I also feel like there aren't enough rides or even pre-made coasters. I assume thats where the steam workshop comes into play but I haven't quite gotten around to looking at that. I mostly miss water rides. There is a few that have water around them which makes them look cool but no actual water rides. But I miss the monorail type rides the most of all. I don't quite understand why those are not in here.
The shops also miss customizing but I do like the variety in them. Especially the restaurants though it would also be great if peeps stopped saying they're hungry while I built all of them and there is a place to eat every few steps. I'm not quite sure how you can be hungry then.
Paths....those are just bad. Atleast to connect paths is just not fun at all. I don't quite understand why I cannot connect a path from a restaurant to the main path the way I want it placed. I don't want some odd kink in it. I don't want to have to lenght it further just so it will connect to a certain piece of the main path. Since when does path making have to be so frusterating? Because that is just what it is. Frusterating.
Scenery. I am missing so many things in here. All my parks start to look the same because there simply isn't enough variety. Not to mention that I cannot place things on the path 85% of the time! Why can't I just place a simple bench on the path? Also bridges. I cannot place anything on path bridges so no wonder those are a mess since I cannot even put trash cans on them. Scenery needs severe improving.
Workers. In one of the loading screens it tells me that I can adjust things in the building screen for my workers...I have yet to figure this out. I cannot assign workers to certain areas. Picking them up makes my screen flicker so that doesn't help and I simply cannot adjust anything about any of my workers. Not work clothes, not areas they walk or who does what.
The land tool. I like my lands flat. I have yet to learn how to work with the flatten tool as it just does weird stuff. It doesn't flatten that I do know. It would be a great improvement if you can just click on the area you want flattened and it instantly does so.
So far I do not have any issues with the game completely crashing and only once has it become super slow (most likely due to taking up too much memory but these are things I know nothing about).
So all in all I would not recommend this game right now. If it improves then yes as this game has a lot of potential for both casual gamers and more die hard gamers who love to built stuff.

Welcome gamers of all genders, races and species to my review of Star Wars - Knights of the Old Republic. I'll be looking into the pros and cons of the game itself as well as going into the many facets of why this game irks me storywise, but we will get to that later.
For now, let's take a look at how this game plays:
The best parts of this game definitely have to be the tense encounters with enemy kind. Most of the game I found myself to get bored of the many talking portions, but the action bits had be glued to my seat. Don't get me wrong, I liked some of the roleplaying elements outside of the combat but I felt like they could have sprinkled in some more fighting along the way. Gun play is solid, sword play is excellent, laser play is sub par but still good. Boss encounters could use some work but overall I felt like they were a fun experience.
This is where I have to get serious for a bit. Let me just get these things out of the way first: inventory management sucks, the voice acting sucks, I have carpal tunnel because of all the dialogue skips I've had to endure and I think I may be going blind because of this game's uncapped FPS. So with that out of the way I want to address the big nasty elephant in the room and that is the lore. The original trilogy (4,5,6) established a firm but fair canon for the rest of the series to build off of, but for some reason this game and its god awful sequel decided to take ideas straight from the 2000's era attempt at rebooting the franchise, something that real star wars fans would never stand for. For that reason alone I cannot stand by as people falsely praise this game, because not only is it a mediocre RPG at best, it spits on everything the Star Wars fandom built and was one of the final straws in toppling the TRUE Star Wars fandom.
Do not buy this game if you are looking for something to satisfy your Star Wars gaming needs. You should also avoid this if you're looking for a decent RPG to play. The only time I would suggest buying this if it was really cheap on sale and it would satisfy your curiosity to try it out.
Thanks for reading my review!

Welcome to the wonderful world of Renowned Explorers : International Society, best described as a very warm and charming take on "The Curious Expedition" but do not confuse that for "Simple or shallow", no. Nonono. This game is, underneath the big fluffy cuddly exterior, much like a house cat, and like any house cat, it has paws made up of TEENY TINY KNIVES which will dig their way in and cause much horrible pain if you're not paying attention to the various mechanics at work.
If you've never had the joy of living with a house cat, it's the most wonderful experience, and they'll slowly destroy everything you own, but you'll never be able to get upset with them, because they're made of fur, and wuv. Even when it comes to cleaning their ears and they rake nice red lines into your forearm so you look like you've been on a self harm trip.
This game is very much like a house cat, you don't own it. It owns you. Often as a matter of fact. I've played the better end of hm, fifty attempts, often getting to 4* or 5* difficulty expeditions and then it all goes horribly horribly wrong. Oh it's call cute and cuddly in the beginning with nice scottish highlands and pirates treasure out in the carribean but just you wait, wait until you're knee deep in Transylvania, hungry wolves and digging into the legends of one Mr. Dracul who turns out to be a real charmer with the speech and can WRECK a diplomatically inclined team in seconds because as it turns out, your strength just became a phenomenal weakness.
Okay, let's pull the camera back and do a breakdown of the game. It runs in three distinct "beats", first and foremost is the World Map, this serves as your transition between various adventures, it's where you kit out your explorers, spend insight and convert that into "Useful materials" for expeditions ahead, and then spend gold, status, and research on "Things that will help" such as equipment upgrades (armour helps a LOT, so do trinkets), your entourage (who acts as a force multiplier and offers special conditions in the case of the named entourage members), and unlocking areas of the research tree that yields additional supplies, and other useful benefits, again, making the ride through the game that much smoother. It's your HQ in effect, but there's a lot to do between adventures, and a lot of discrete choices to make as to how you want to "build your team", so it's not like a case of "Click click done".
Second beat comes in the form of the "local adventure" map, which once you've selected WHERE you want to go, is then a zoomed up version of the location, say, an area of land or an island, part fogged in and part visible depending on how much terrain you've covered, each map has points of interest (think FTL) and the idea is you move around the points of interest, solving challenges.
Most of these are "Roll" challenges where a % chance to succeed is based on the skills of the team, more skills mean more prizes, in some cases simply having ENOUGH skills in a specific tree will unlock whole new options, which are coloured in and take you down new routes with additional rewards. The limit on simply being able to clean the map is "Supplies", the cap is soft, you can go below zero, but each point that you do, imposes a very steep penalty on your ability to fight. You can get away with one or two points, but more than this is just -begging- for a game over.
The stories for each area are well written and the narrative is cohesive, it's good enough that you'll be able to get a feel for what goes on in each area and you'll pay some attention to the choices presented (there's usually clues in the text as to what's a good choice and what's a bad one), sometimes you'll end up with a case of "Best of the worst" options which can be a tad irritating but that's RNG for you when you don't know what you're going to draw from the story deck for a given area.
Finally, there's the turn based fighting sequence, which kicks in on an encounter. This is not just a case of move and shoot. You have three options, one agressive, one devious, one friendly, the game KINDA works like rock paper scissors, however, there's more than just the fight atmosphere to consider, because if you want the optimal rewards you may have to finish a fight in a specific manner.
In other cases you may face opponents who change their own approach when you munchkin the game mechanics (in other words, attempt to game the boss and the boss games YOU), and each of the RE:IS members have their own specific strengths and weaknesses meaning some just don't work out that well for a specific strategy in one way, but are great when used in a different approach. Using a one dimensional "Oh I am gonna stack the board with speakers" seems great in principle, but then Mr. Dracul comes along and "OH GOD I'M GOING TO GET MY FACE TORN OFF", so it's not always the greatest plan to put all the eggs in one basket.
In fact you'll probably have so much fun with the various boss encounters and the foes like the Smuggler Boss (who you can reduce to tears) and Mr. Dracul that the real goal, beating the obnoxious champion of the International Society will take the back seat as the moment to moment stories you find yourself in matter more, Riveleaux can wait, I've a vampire to convince.
So here's the big question "Curious Expedition" or "Renowned explorers" - Me? I'd say both. They're wonderful games both of them, but if I had to make a choice? I'd take the house cat over the darker sibling, and ONLY JUST. Because it's the house cat, and it's "Heartwarming" (and yes, that's something you can DO to your foes in this game).
I love my cats. I love this game so very dearly. Get it.

You probably have a good idea of what Guacamelee is by now. A Metroidvania with a Mexican Wrestler/Luchador theme, where the stamina-draining moves you learn are what unlock new areas. This is mainly done through colored blocks that require a specific skill in order to be broken. And that's the extent of the Metroidvania.
It's simple enough and proves to be a lot of fun in the largest portion of the game.
However, several things in the end come together to create a frustrating experience unless you're the sort of player who's perfectly accustomed to every trick in the brawler book. And in fact, die-hard brawler fans are the only people I would really recommend this game to, at least to completion.
In the near-end game, you run into enemies and a few bosses that like to 'shield' themselves. A bubble fitting their shape that can only be broken by a specific stamina attack, which uses the same color coding as the aforementioned blocks. This actually starts out as a great idea as it throws around the way you think and need to approach a combat situation.
But therein lies the first problem: The 'yellow' attack, being headbutt, requires you to stand still and press the B button (on the controller).
However, it takes about half a second before the game apparently registers you standing still, meaning you're spamming B while nothing happens but you standing there.
Obviously, in a high pace brawler, this means you are immediately punished for it by being attacked.
This headbutt lag only becomes more frustrating when you are going up against bosses that constantly change their type of shield. So whenever headbutt is required, you can count on it that you are going to get punished for it. It requires a compensation the likes where you feel like you are compensating for a bug.
Another technique that you must master in order to progress is the art of blocking. In the beginning, that's only required to jump through thorn vines. But eventually you will run into situations where the amount of melee and ranged enemies make it short of change of perspective to make it a bullet hell. Blocking is essential, period.
And this is where another problem sets in. As someone trained by 'Witch time' in Bayonetta, I expect my blocking in a brawler to be instant. Many are the times where I had blocked a moment before being hit, yet it did not register. Frustrating.
But the biggest issue are the 'gauntlets' you are forced to partake in. These are single rooms where you are shut in and are forced to beat all the enemies that spawn. Most of the time these are pretty fun, if not challenging. But every now and then you find a gauntlet that simply does not belong in the game. In one, you were forced to constantly pop the appearing timed 'balloons' because otherwise, upon exploding, you receive significant damage. In the middle is an obstruction that has a hazard on top. And the balloons constantly appear on opposite sides of the room, AND you have to deal with other spawning enemies. Meaning you not only have to run like mad at each timed balloon, but you need to dodge any other ranged attacks and then survive the other enemies.
One other that I vividly remember is being forced to fight enemies that like to throw columns of light at you, and for some reason their AI likes to constantly throw these in sync where the distance between both columns is too great to overcome with one dodge/block, meaning you get hit regardless. But the biggest sinner is the gauntlet is the one where you have to kill a series of instakill exploding balloons with the moves they're obviously lined up for. But this brings another shortcoming: The special moves have a deceptively shorter range than they appear to have.
But my biggest gripe with these gauntlets is that they are non-optional. You have to do them, no matter how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t they are. There's no going around them, meaning you have to suffer their punishment for as long as it takes for you to master whatever (usually pointless) lesson it wants to impart. Because I can guarantee you, most lessons you will take from these will not help in boss battles.
Not to mention that the throwing-invincibility frames are deceptive as well, there's no telling in a split second when you are vulnerable at the end of your throw. Yet at the final boss, this is exactly whats required to know.
All in all, the game likes to maximise the abuse out of your weakness, even when they are being forced on you by the game itself. It's unfair and harsh and maybe that's why it's not the sort of game for me. I can take difficult games, very difficult games. Games like Bayonetta (when going for Platinum), Super Meat Boy (A+'ing everything) and Ninja Gaiden (because, game) all are enjoyable for me because their responsiveness is perfect. Any mistake you make in those games are your fault alone. Failing because of an uncontrollable contender, however, makes for something very frustrating. Which is exactly the thing this game sins to.
Storywise... it's cheesy. But what do you expect? The game itself likes throwing joke after joke at you, referencing many things that are Gaming related. It doesn't take itself too serious and neither should you. It's okay.
But with me having a bunch of frustrations with this game, I can't get myself to collect the other hidden mask pieces for the 'Good' ending or even replay the game.
Yes, I have to say the game is pretty good at what it's trying to do. Nowhere near the best, especially with me having so many irks around responsiveness. But if you can get over the gripes I have (or somehow manage to not experience them at all as a rare few do) then yeah... maybe you'll enjoy it. It won't be easy, even on Normal, so make sure you bring some alcohol to mellow you out. Because this game won't let you off the hook that easy.

Lara Croft GO, much like Hitman GO, is a reinterpretation of the Tomb Raider game series as a puzzle game. In this turn-based stylized cell-shaded isometric 3D platform game, you'll have to think, try and retry to find the right path. Enemies move and traps activate only when you move and there is no time limit here, so you can take your time and you can retry indefinitely (or bail and use the hint system).
Lara Croft had already embarked on a journey through puzzle-adventure games with the Guardian of Light and Temple of Osiris. Here the logic is taken to the extreme by stripping away all the action... and yet somehow part of the feel of the franchise remains. At times, this game reminded me of the first Tomb Raider more than the rebooted Tomb Raider franchise. To me, it felt more like an answer to the question "What if the first Tomb Raider had actually been a puzzle game?" than to "What other genre can we put Lara Croft into?"
If you're a fan of Lara Croft or if you enjoy relaxing brain teasers, you'd do yourself a disservice to avoid this game.
However if all you've ever appreciated in Tomb Raider games is their action, if you despise their puzzle and platform mechanics, stay away.

If you're considering picking up Battleborn, the best advice I can offer is to forget any Overwatch vs Battleborn information you've heard. They are two completely different games that are both a ton of fun in their own way.
Battleborn offers a fantastic coop campaign that is full of humour (I challenge anyone to resist loving Geoff the Spider King) and can be extremely challenging requiring good teamwork to complete, especially when if you're aiming to complete challenges or get gold medals.
The online side takes the form of a MOBA with multiple game modes and maps. Unlike standard MOBAs where you buy gear to alter your build during the game, in Battleborn you unlock gear through the coop campaign or from gear boxes and choose 3 pieces to take with you into the MP match. You then have to buy these pieces during the match using shards that are a resource also used to build turrets and such.
The main downside of the multiplayer side at the moment is that due to the number of players when first joining there is a large chance that you will get matched against high ranked players, don't let this put you off though, as long as you've gone through coop missions first you should have some decent gear so the only difference will be skill and experience, which is super easy to overcome....right? right??

Strategic freedom all over the place. Plan your own kills, complete the levels on your own terms, and when all that fails (which it will) improvise (although improvising usually comes in the form of whipping out a gun and mowing down anyone who stands in your way)...
Seriously, though. Hitman: Blood Money allows you to do everything your way. It throws you into a big level filled with a load of NPCs and then lets you off your leash. You'll usually have no idea what you're doing at first, but killing your target is still pretty easy.
Then, you go back through the game, this time trying to achieve Silent Assassin ranking on every level and suddenly you have to piece together some detailed plans and try to kill your target in the most secretive of ways.
My main complaint about this game is really just the fact that weapons lack bass. It sounds like you're shooting a pellet gun. Other than that, it wins in pretty much every aspect.
It's also extremely satisfying to exploit the system. For example, a mission involved me taking the disguise of a delivery boy and then delivering a case of diamonds to my target. Directly after the case is delivered, a security guard in the room with me will escort me out of the building, taking me away from my target. This was intended from the beginning, but with a little bit of ingenuity you can devise a plan so simple that it's brilliant. All I have to do is merely close the door on the way out of the room and whilst the security guard can't see me, hide behind the door. Now he opens it and has lost sight of me, so I throw a coin into the corner of the room so that he'll walk towards it, then descend upon him and sedate him.
Now, suddenly, nobody is keeping watch over me. My genius plan has worked and I'm in the building unharmed. Now I can simply walk right back into the room where I left down the diamond case and shoot my target with a silenced pistol. Simple as that.
That right there is just one tiny example of the kind of plans you have to form to get a high ranking in a level. It grows much bigger, from taking the disguise a priest at a wedding and then whipping out your Silverballers mid-marriage to blow the groom away, from dropping a chandelier onto a moving target using an explosive, the game has some brilliant strategic freedom for you to indulge in.
Get this. Now.

Before people get angry, yes I like AVGN, I like challenging platformers, I like chiptune music and 8-bit grapichs, etc. and I really really wanted to like this game.
However, I am also of the opinion that if you are parodying something by doing the same thing ironically and then charging money for it, you are still doing the same thing as the thing you parody, and there lies the real problem: strip away the funny presentation and this is the very type of game that James Rolfe makes fun of in his videos, a game filled with fake difficulty to artificially pad out the play time.
Yes, I get it, it's meta jokes, and the jokes are fun... the first time, then comes the major grind to actually beat the levels with insane unfair difficulty. The levels are fairly well designed in of themselves and are amusingly parodying many of the games reviewed on the show, but the platforming controls are rather stiff, hitboxes are often bigger/smaller than they look and obviously the game does everything to kill you as much as possible, though not in a funny "invisible block near a pit" kind of way which would give it a bit of a puzzle element, here it's just by throwing a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥at you at once and having you deal with it through sheer pressure.
Also while other fake difficulty parody games like I Wanna Be That Guy at least have the decensy to not throw you back to the beginning unless you pick the higher difficulties when you die, here it does just that on everything but Easy when running out of extra lives which I find to be a major flaw from a modern perspective, no matter how retro or thematically appropriate it is. And before you say "just go play on Easy then", I would if it didn't give me more HP than normal, make bosses stupidly easy to beat and lock off several achivements, which obviously isn't very enjoyable, and it still doesn't fix the hitbox and stiff controller issue.
Ignoring the difficulty, the game is also rather short. If you get good at this I could imagine you would be able to beat the entire thing in 2-3 hours, though it does have a fair ammount of hidden secrets and replay value for the really really hardcore crowd when you unlock the truly ridicolous difficulty levels, so it's not that big of a problem, but still worth noting.
Basically, if you don't mind NES games that beat your♥♥♥♥♥with fake difficulty to the max and aren't affraid to start from the beginning of a stage (or the game itself) every time you die, you will probably love this game. Fans of AVGN may also appreciate the referencial humor to both the show itself and the games that he have played. However, the game still isn't up to modern standards in many respects, and it is rather hypocritical, and therefor I cannot recommend it to everyone. It's basically an extremely niche title with a (relatively) mass appeal brand attached to it, but if you don't fall into that niche it might not be worth the frustration no matter how much you like AVGN. If Steam had a "middle" option I would have picked that, but for now I am sad to say I will have to give it a thumbs down personally.
Also, I think James did a disadvantage to the game by reviewing it himself and showing off all the best bits in the video, made playing the actual thing feel a bit less special.
