Renowned Explorers is the 2nd game of Abbey Games, creators of REUS which I also love and played a good amount. It is a roguelike exploration game similar to FTL which you create a party of three explorers from a good amount of available ones and hunt for treasures across the world while beating challenges game throws at you with various skills of your explorers and occasional combat. But don't think you just beat everyone opposing you when I say combat, because in REIS words can be sharper than a sword from time to time. Insults or compliments can be more than enough to discourage someone from fighting you and can be a better solution.
What makes REIS shine though is its' insane replayability; your crew and captain selection changing how you play and your winning strategy completely, random generated maps and each map having tons of different events which you need to play a map over and over again to see all of them, highscore chart and weekly challenges. Another thing is Abbey still supports the game with adding new events and treasures, even after being nearly a year since its' release. A great thing when they could just move on and start to work on their next project.
Even after playing this much I still didn't see many events in the game and there is still lots of treasures I couldn't manage to get. There is lots of strategies I still didn't try. And I don't do weekly challenge's even because I couldn't find time to work on them yet. That's a good enough example of game's depth and replayability I think. And as a last note its dlc, More to Explore is a great addition to the game. It's new maps are great and it's campfire system adds a whole new strategic layer to the game, giving you new choices you can tinker on. So don't worry, it worths that price tag easily.
Renowned Explorers is one of the best games I played in last years and easily worths its price. It has excellent storytelling, humor and art, great replayability and strategic depth and it is tons of fun to play. It is a must get if you are a fan of roguelikes or Indiana Jones style adventures.

The game has so much good (and potential) in it, that it almost hurts to not recommend it.
But basically the game falls down in one crucial area: The combat. The combat that was supposed to be the one thing that gives the game it's edge. Despite all the hype, the combat isn't as complicated as one would think at first. Whenever I see an incoming combat on the map, my first reaction is the save and quit. The combat is too sluggish and takes too long, not to mention several other things I personally disliked, but are irrelevant here. And the system of different attack types isn't as good as advertised.
And the maps are always the same. Period.
"Procedurally generated" IS a straight out lie. The maps are always the same, that always have the same key places in them. Some less meaningful places change places and content, but those things are too irrelevant to matter.
Character customisation is almost non-existent. You may be able to buy a few items for your team here and there, but they really don't seem to matter all that much. Buying items for the tank is pointless, since all the enemies (almost) always spawns around your team and they always ignore the tank completely and run straight at your glasscannons. And buying more dmg for these glasscannons is pointless, because then bosses will one hit them.
The game has one of the best, if not the best in-game manuals that I ever rememeber seeing (which is awesome, since I hate browsing through wikis to be able to play a game). And as I originally said, the game has so much good things going in it, but they all become irrelevant when the combat takes all the fun out of it.
The negative tone here is probably due to me not being the correct audience for the game, at least considering the amount of positive reviews it has (I bought this after playing FTL, I'm guessing I was expecting a bit too much).

Renowned Explorers is a unique blend of exploration and turn based/hexagonal combat. The game is designed to be replayed multiple times, offering 2 game modes and 4 difficulties. The goal is to be the top explorer and beat the present #1 - a task that I couldn’t achieve even on normal difficulty. To be at the top you have 5 expeditions to rack up more Renown than the top explorer (2500). Expeditions get harder towards the end with the last one being super hard to beat. Expedition maps are procedurally generated so every replay is different, and so can be your approach since there are multiple ways you can choose to take your playthrough. Focusing mostly on Research, Status or Gold or choosing a combination of heroes that focus on different playstyles.
But the combat is where it’s at. It takes a different approach than any other turn based game out there. There are 3 ways to beat your opponents - Aggressive, Devious or Friendly. You choose your approach based on your opponents mood since one mood is advantageous to the other.
So becoming a top explorer is not an easy task when you have all of these things to worry about and find the perfect blend. I personally enjoyed the first 2 playthroughs but then got bored of it. I would still recommend it for the fans of the genre since the game is unique in some aspects.

Dwelvers is the spiritual successor to the Dungeon Keeper series, and keeps the feel very much alive even in its early state.  I'm in fact writing this review because of some negativity I've been reading regarding its pre-release quirks(the tutorials not quite catching, occasional unit bug, etc.), and I'd like to balance that out.  Yes, it's a little rough around the edges, but this is not a finished product.  The developers are very upfront with this little tidbit, so anyone that thinks the game is terrible based on its current state is very sad, as the game is quite fun.
You start with a single room, where your units spawn, and must dig out areas for your soon-to-grow brood.  Each combat unit has different needs that require satisfying, giving the planning stage some variety.  Beds, a kitchen, a farm, a well, all these and more you'll place down to keep your minions satisfied, and ready to wreak havoc on those around them.  There are random monsters inhabiting the underground, lending variety to what could have been a boring excavation phase.  As you expand, you'll find pathways leading to the surface, where the game starts to get more interesting.
Exploring outside of the subterranean world leads to new issues, namely, humans.  Once they're aware of your existence, they want nothing more than to put you down.  Then you can make all kinds of nasty traps in your maze of tunnels and caves that is your personal lair.  Whether using ambushes or the hydraulic mechanics(or both), it's fun taking down the invaders, monster or human.
All in all, the game is a pre-release and that does shine through occasionally.  Does that detract from the fun? Absolutely not, as I've sunk a lot of offline hours into this game already.  The potential here is massive, and the game just oozes character.  If any of this sparked your imagination, just grab the game, and get digging.  You'll be glad you did.

The worst part of the game is the port quality and how unintuitive the controls are at the start of the game, I thought my game was broken and with no control menu you’d have to look it up online how to actually play the game. I figured out the click and drag controls by sheer coincidence. The game could have been perfect puzzle game if they put effort into the port and made the controls more intuitive and given a hotkey for restarting levels.

F.E.A.R. 2 Project Origin is the sequel to the “classic” F.E.A.R. and I don't have much to say in the way of a traditional review. Its a shooter, its kind of cookie cutter but a kind of weird shaped one that is sort of intriguing so you play with it a bit.
This game continues the story from one but it doesn't really add much to me. Its sort of blasé. I didn't find myself engaged with it really at all. The horror elements are also lackluster. I don't recall a single moment where I felt much tension. In fact there was an area clearly designed to be scary in which the lights flashed on and off while apparitions bombarded the room only occasionally doing damage. In this cacophony of confusion I was not frightened, nor did I feel tension. The enemies had become a nuisance and I was unable to easily distinguish a path let alone the correct one.
As far as hallway shooters go.. its fine. The guns feel good. People die. Slow motion will always be awesome. There are more modern touches for this game than the first with iron sights. However older elements like leaning have been removed.
I feel like this game has suffered the proverbial “consolization” process. I feel as though it has lost its soul. As in the developers had their original vision in F.E.A.R. 1 made the game they wanted and are now forced to take that vision and pull on and stretch it to create more content. I feel very strongly about Crysis 1 compared to Crysis 2 and the reason I bring this up is that I feel the same thing has happened here. Both sequels took away what made the original games so unique in exchange for a standard cookie cutter hallway shooter.
And I get it. From a business standpoint no one is ever going to say throw away what makes a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of money for something more creative and unique. Unless the formula really has gotten stale and a new IP actually is the better risk assessment for staying in business. I understand that businesses need to make a profit in order to take risks.
At the end of the day I still recommend this game because it is fun. Its mindless and I hate to repeat myself but shooting people in the face in slow motion is really fun. There are also some mech and turret sequences with some really ironic music playing in the background that are sort of qwerky in an endearing way.
It just feels a little soulless.

First off, this game is firmly in the category of interactive fiction.  If you don't like interactive fiction, and want actual gameplay, move on now.  As a lover of crime dramas and investigations I found this game to be extremely unique and highly enjoyable.  The entire gameplay loop is typing words in a 1990s style search box and seeing what videos pop up. The fun is in taking bits of pieces from a single woman's side of police interviews and searching for more layers, slowly peeling back some semblance of truth as to what really happened.  The story's quite gripping, and I was very excited to dig deeper.  The actress playing the woman was great, her mood and gestures giving all sorts of hints as to if she was lying or hiding something.  I definitely recommend this one on the cheap, as there's no replay value and its very short.  I got it as part of a Humble Bundle and the experience was definitely worth it!

Battleborn, dispite being panned by most in favor of Overwatch, is a very fun game. While the matchmaking may take awhile, since player numbers are low, the PvE story mode, which can be played solo at any time, is well worth it, and with the varying dialogue, challenges, and, to an extent, enemy patterns, missions can still be fun after multiple playthroughs. This even extends to the DLC, in which both maps so far have 10 different dialogue sets that each reveal bits of the DLC's lore.
The cast is also extensive. With 29, soon to be 30 playable characters, each with their own weapons, abilities, passives and ults, there's plenty to experiment with. From melee characters like Boldur and Attikus, to more traditional characters like Oscar Mike and Marquis, to even more outlandish characters like ISIC and Orendi, there's sure to be a character for anyone to enjoy.
The game does have its faults though. Some areas are poorly optimized and require a higher-quality machine to run well. Matchmaking takes ages due to low player numbers, and may pit you against high level opponents as a result. Level geometry can sometimes get in the way, such as getting caught on an edge and such.
Overall, however, I personally believe the games' pros outweigh its cons. On top of that, if you want a game that you can sink as many hours into as you did dollars, then Battleborn may be the game for you, especially if you are a PvE kind of guy.

In the end I would definately recommend this game, If you are someone that doesnt like replaying games wait for a sale, are you a completionist this game is an absolute steal even for its current price.

I bought the game a little after release and have put 13 hours in it already (its 12:30 am the morning after).  Theres your review :D.
I absolutely love it.   Its got its quirks; early access and all.  Ive had a couple crashes, but your progress seems to be saved constantly.  When you load in, even after a crash, you are exactly where you left off.
There isnt "a lot" of content right now, as some people have mentioned, buuuttt that doesnt really matter at the moment.  After 13 hours I am still thinking about what I'm going to be building next.  So many plans :D!!  What is here is plenty for many many hours of enjoyment.  I'm sure that I will have plenty to do until the dev's start adding things.  I mean, I've "got" everything in the game as of right now (minus some snow, lol) but that doesnt have any real impact on what I am able to do with the game.  The only real limit for "value" is yourself (imo).  If you wont have fun in a sandbox, the game isnt for you.  If youre looking for a hardcore survival sim, this game isnt for you.  This is a relaxed colony management sim and a builders canvas.
It must be said that the graphics are actually beautiful.  The depth of field and "dynamic eye adaptation" work wonders.  Depth of field is usually the first setting in a game I turn off, but I really enjoy it here.  The textures are quite good as well!  This is not a simple box game. And the lighting....man, the lighting looks simply amazing sometimes.
The difficulty is on the easy side for sure, as of right now.  Ive got a colony of 62 with a 7k+ surplus of food and a bounty of everything else.  The hordes are def increasing in size, I actually lost my first colonists about 10 hours in when I expanded my village without properly considering all the paths the monsters may take.  But if you build smart, place defenses accordingly, and secure your food situation, the game really lets you do whatever it is you want to do.
Loving it! I cant wait to see what these devs do with the game.

Yup, it's early access, but man it's doing it for me.
Do you wish for Minecraft reborn as a resource management / tower defense game?  That's what this is.
No, you won't be digging through miles of stone looking for ores or looking awestruck at majestic caverns.  The terrain isn't all that deep and the ores are plentiful and each instance is infinite.  What that means is that you can build a nice little home for your coal miner - he'll dutifully roam between his bed, his coal block and his crate, dropping off the ore into the common stockpile on each trip.
I personally feel that the blockish aesthetic has run it's course - sure it's a voxel game, and that's fine, but couldn't we still have some round bodies and heads?  Please?  Surely there's a balance between cubes and AAA shooters.  Here's hoping.  Even with the voxels though, there's some great work with alpha and normal mapping here; the rock looks rough, and guards' mail glints in the sunlight.
There's not a whole lot here, yet - Staggering archers along a few funnel paths to the town center is simple enough, but I think that's a good thing.  It allows room to breathe, plan your next colonist's home, and expand when the time is right.  It's early access, and I've had a couple hiccups, but man it's still fun.  It's closer to what I wanted Timber & Stone to be, even at this early point.
Yes, it's a touch pricy for such early access fare, especially given the rash of cash grabs out there, but I'm satisfied with the GAMEPLAY, which seems all too often to be an afterthought.  YMMV.

Platforming in this open world relies on the use of an ever expanding list of new methods to get a little bit more movement from special attacks, thus allowing further progress into new zones or back into secret treasures hidden in hard to get too places. Failure rarely ever sets you back very far, usually one or two jumps back in most places, but in some more rare and almost always optional content places a mistimed jump or incorrect sequence of joystick motions and button presses can net a frustrating loss of work. A gamepad is really suggested. The brawling elements are pretty fun, combos and special powers are nice and fun to use, but attack button mashing plus the use of throws is all that is needed for most fights early in the game. Overall difficulty is pretty good, and not too hard for all the necessary plot content, with the most difficult jumping puzzles and fights (other than boss battles) being left purely for the got a have it all collectable and achievement hunters.

There's a reason why I nominated this game for the "I Wish This Game Was Alive" award. It's because I do. I honestly, sincerely do wish it was still alive.
And yet, I still recommend it because the co-op element is still pretty damn great, and there's still some players, very dedicated, that'd love to play with or against you. It's dead, but it can still be revived.
The marketing ♥♥♥♥ed it, Overwatch ♥♥♥♥ed it, the bad optimization ♥♥♥♥ed it, the monetization before ANY balance change it sorely needed ♥♥♥♥ it, the lack of PVP tutorial / entry-level ease ♥♥♥♥ed it. And it's still badly optimized, the monetization is still dubious and getting into PVP is still confusing, at BEST. Not to mention the marketing is still skewered and Overwatch is ever so more popular.
And yet, there's still a beautiful gem inside it. A portmentaeu of lavish game design that conjoins the intrinsic feel of a MOBA, the minute pacing and smart level design of L4D and the aesthethic and stylistic choices of Borderlands.
Sure, the writing feels amateurish frequently (but just as frequently pretty damn funny), but the characterization and inter-relationships are handled almost expertly, with almost every aspect of the game's world positively reinforcing that every personality, and every character was handled with care, from mechanics to personality to backstory.
If you can look past the issues, if you can look past the unecessary hate this game gets, if you can get past the cringe the great, genuinely well-made parts of the game might win you over. And with enough people won over, it might still live.
It's dead, but it can be revived.
I just hope it's not too late.

Hitman: Blood Money is pretty cool, I guess.
You play as Agent 47, a genetically engineered super assassin created solely to take out the trash. And by trash, I mean murder. The game takes place through various points in Agent 47's life, going from location to location and drowning as many people in their toilets as physically possible. While all this is going on, a reporter is getting a story on Agent 47 from a mysterious man describes his toilet-drowning life.
The game is a stealth game but not like you'd suspect. You don't hide in the shadows or repeat the last persons sentence in the form of a question. Instead you're out in the open, blending into society the best way a man can with a barcode on the back of his big beautiful bald head. Get use to it, because you're gonna be staring at it for awhile, not just because you can play the game in third person, but because it's beautiful. I mean, look at it, it's so shiny.
Each mission you are given the task of murdering someone who probably has it coming, you do this by planning out an attack, playing dress up like I used to with Polly Pocket because my mom refused to buy me any G.I. Joes because they would encourage  meto be a strong male role model for children. Thanks mom.
Now, with the right equipment and the perfect shade of underwear, you go on the attack, soloing out people at their most vulernable and promptly drowning them in a toilet. Way to go!
You'd think that this whole murder shtick would get boring after awhile considering it's all you do, but surprise! It doesn't. THe new locations, difficulty of your target, and unique ways you end up drowning others in toilets keeps the game fresh. It's by no means an easy game, unless you're me. Then it's super easy because you're super good and I have a history of drowning others in toilets.
Keep that last bit to yourself.
But when drowning others in toilets isn't an option or you're just a complete chump, the game gives you a plethora of weapons to go on a murderous rampage with. These include Agent 47's iconic handguns, the silver ballers. They are baller. See what I did there?  While the shooting is nothing special, the guns have just enough OOMF to be entertaining to fire, especially when you send people out doing back flips with hand gun bullets.
But surely there's a punishment for going crazy, right? There is, and it digs deep. Not only will the game detract money you can use on new weapons and upgrades, it will also call you a total loser. After each hit, you get a newspaper describing the incident where you're called anything from a Silent Assassins, to a ghost, to a skulking man who drowns people in toilets. The more damage you do and the less inconspicuous you are, the less money you have to spend on yourself. So no new Xbox for poor Agent 47, you horrible person.
But should you play Hitman: Blood Money?
I will admit, this is probably the last Hitman game you'll play that feels like an honest Hitman game. While it does seem odd for an angry looking man in a bird suit to not look suspicious, the disguise mechanics is what gave the game that flavor it needed to stand out from its competitors like Thief or Splinter Cell. It's fun, it makes you feel like a badass when you succesfully pull off the perfect hit, and it's easy to look over it's problems just by how fun the game is on it's own.

After his Mother’s passing, your character Phillip, receives a letter from his supposed dead Father and sets out on a journey to Greenland in search for answers. If you’re are a fan of first person survival horror games and puzzles this is a must try, especially if you enjoyed Amnesia: The Dark Descent (same developers). Overture does a good job of drawing you into the story and although a lot of it is presented in notes found throughout the game (reading can put some people off) i still found it interesting. The characters, although not that many, are very well voiced and the character red is the star of the show and you really connect with him by the end of the game.
Overture has a similar feel gameplay wise to The Dark Descent, just a lot less refined which is understandable being frictional games’ first full title. That being said it is still fun exploring the abandoned mine and avoiding the threats. The puzzles in this game were great and i think were just challenging enough without being frustrating and it really shows off what the HPL engine can do with the physics and controls. One criticism of the game is the combat and how clunky it is. And i’d have to agree. I think it was purposely bad to encourage you to avoid enemies but it just shouldn’t have been included to start with. When you start the game you won’t be able to hit anything but after some practise it becomes too easy and you can kill everything and it takes away some of the tension.
That being said, Overture does a great job with the soundtrack. Credit Mikko Tarmia. All his work with frictional is fantastic. If you choose the stealth option the game can be quite tense and give you some frights. Despite some flaws its still a really fun game that i’ve played through 4 times and definitely worth picking up especially in a sale it goes silly cheap.

This is a rather simple and casual CCG with pretty much no complexity. You don't really have to strain your brain on this one, game requires very minimal thinking due to the lack of card effects, but more so on that later.
Once you beat the tutorial you'll have to create a character (you have to pay real money if you want to have more then one character). You can pick between 3 different races (Orcs, Humans, Elves). Orcs have only one class which is Warrior, Humans have Knight and Rogue while Elves have Archer and Mage. Each class has different stats and different class-specific cards it can use.
The main problem in this game is the previously mentioned lack of complexity. Pretty much all cards will do one of the following: Deal damage to enemy, Increase your defense, Decrease enemy defense, Heal you, Increase your energy (mana),  Decrease enemy damage. The only difference between those cards is the energy cost and the numeric value of their effect and the fact that some of them will do multiple of those effects. Due to that there's very minimal amount of strategy and thinking involved with this game.
In the match, you'll have Random Deck and Collector Deck. You can draw cards from either of them during the Draw Phase. Once the match is over the cards that you used from Random Deck are added to your Stash and you can then transfer cards from Stash to your Collector Deck. You can only have 10 cards in your collector deck when your character is level one, but you gain more slots in collector deck as you level your character up.
When your character levels up you can increase his HP, Energy, Regeneration (heal per turn), Might (extra damage) or Resistance (extra defense). This is an interesting feature, but if you get matched against enemy who's level is higher then yours you'll be at disadvantage (I haven't played enough to know how good is their match making system).
Now would I recommend this game? I don't know really. I wish the game had more complexity to it but maybe it will have in the future. I'd say if you're a fan of CCG's or are interested in them and what you've read in this review didn't make you not want to ever try this game, then do give it a try. After all it's free and only about 100 MB to download so if nothing else it's worth giving a try. Just do keep in mind you're likely to find it boring if you're not into casual games.

As far as futuristic robot RTS games go, this one is my all time favorite.  For anyone who loves robots and RTS games, this is one I can highly recommend.  It is just one of those games I have always loved, every once in a while I'll launch the game and spend a little time playing skirmishes.  I played the first version of the game for a while but stopped when I got a new computer.  I installed SC2 on my new computer and have really had a lot of fun with the game. I really wish that someday they make another addition to the series, because it really is a great RTS series.
Performance of the game I would say is pretty good overall.  I've played it on my older computers and it always seemed to run fairly well, which used to be really impressive to me to see so many units doing so much at once.  Now on my more modern computer it is kind of to be expected it will run butter smooth.
I really like the camera in the game in that you can easily zoom very far away to a satellite view.  It reminds me very much of how the camera worked in homeworld, and I loved that effect where it transitions to a different UI as you zoom.  On the downside, the camera control when zooming in close and attempting to rotate in 3D space is not that special.  You can rotate the view and get some angles, but it could be so much better if it was done in a similar fashion to Total War's recent games.  In the Total War games I love that you get such a cinematic feeling with the camera, and this game could use this as well to great effect.
I think I tried to get through the campaign, but it wasn't really that interesting to me I guess, or I would probably remember it better.  I also rarely find any interest in playing against others online, in my experience with other games it's often like playing against super hard AI and I don't like it when games are too hard that they frustrate me.  I do love setting up skirmish games though and playing those, and totally destroying the AI.  I like to set the AI to a low custom so they are easy to destroy, but it can be fun to play against harder AI ocassionally.  It can be very challenging!  A decent amount of maps for skirmish make me happy enough.  I do find I play the same maps over and over, and would like more.
I'm not a hard core RTS gamer, I don't memorize all the units and worry too much about specific strengths.  I just like building a base, building a huge army, and sending my enemy some hurt.  Each team has some awesome super units, but I like the UEF and Cybran factions the most.  I also love that you can build nukes and blow the crap out of the enemy eventually.
The game is pretty well balanced I think.  If I were to think of what I would like improved about this game...
- A ton more units and super weapons, different factions, etc.
The game already has plenty, but it makes you addicted to wanting more and more fun toys to destroy the enemy with.
- Maybe some better graphics?
The game is kind of old now, but it still looks good to me. Most of the time you are seeing units from pretty far away so it's not that it matter too much.  It would be cool though if when you do get close there is even more effects and detail, like the Total War games where there is DOF and a lot of unit detail.

Released in 2009, four long years after the first title, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is the follow-up sequel to the highly successful First Encounter Assault Recon. Players will once again take on the role of a Special Force operative, although this time you're no nameless "point man" peon; you're Sergent Michael Becket, and Alma has a very special connection with you. This game takes place mere minutes prior to the blast that was unleashed during the end of F.E.A.R., and proceeds to play out through events that happened before, during, and after it.
Unlike the first game, Monolith missed absolutely no opportunities to spoil gamers with buckets of gore and moments of horror that seem to last a small eternity. From hallways drenched in blood, random mutilated corpses littering the environment, even more intense fight sequences, and ambient lighting that sets the mood just right, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin has everything that players were left wishing for from the original. The game has a brilliant balance of action versus horror, sometimes the two are intermingled, which is something that Capcom could really take notes on when it comes to recent Resident Evil titles. There is zero downtime in the game from start to finish; either you're about to get a shiver sent up your spine, or you're going to be blasting the brains out of an enemy.
This title reveals even more about the origins of Alma Wade, and the reason for her wrathful vengeance. As Sergent Michael Beckett, you start off on what seems to be an ordinary, routine mission; until the blast is felt from the other F.E.A.R. team. From there, things begin to go haywire, and you start experiencing what are mild hallucinations at first. As time goes on, and Alma gets closer, your hallucinations become even more frightful, and down right disturbing. Some of your other crew members are affected as well, although none as intensely as you. Your ultimate goal becomes to stop Alma, and seal her away for good; of course, she doesn't want any of that.
Above being a wonderful horror title, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is hands down one of the greatest shooters of the last decade. The guns are balanced, and the variety within is plentiful; action shotguns, combat shotguns, assault rifles, sub-machine guns, lasers, pulse rifles... the list goes on. It's very satisfying when you down an enemy, and the hit detection is spot on; whenever you miss, it's nobody's fault but yours. At a few points, you even get to control a mech! The A.I. is dialed down a little from its predecessor, although not by much as the foes are still quite smart, and will flip environmental objects for cover to their advantage. Thankfully, this time around the flashlight is not limited and you can keep it on for the whole game if you like, even though it does cause a nasty reflection when zoomed in on some optical sights.
It's stunning how well this game has aged over the last seven years, not only in terms of gameplay but also in graphics. In retrospect, comparing F.E.A.R. to F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin, it's crazy to see how far graphics had come within a four year span. The game is on par with Metro 2033, prior to its redux of course, and it was released over a year prior to the aforementioned title. The environments are richly detailed, and as always the lighting plays an incredibly important role in visual immersion. As well, F.E.A.R 2: Project Origin comes with a soundtrack that, astonishingly, outdoes its former counterpart by a landslide. I wish that Monolith or Warner Brothers would've released it as a paid download, or perhaps even free DLC, as it's one of the most enjoyable horror and FPS scores to grace the ears of gamers.
F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin can be enjoyed without having played the original title; in fact, I recommend this game over the previous installment. The story is much easier to grasp, and all of the holes are filled in with easy-to-find intel scattered about the levels. Not to mention, the game clocks in at a longer lifespan; between 7-9 hours, as opposed to 4-6. It's in every way better than the original, which is not something that can be said for many sequels. For an older release, the game is worth every penny of its current price tag, but if you can grab it on sale that's even better. This is not an experience to be missed.

I started this game expecting something great. Being a big fan of Sam Barlow's work in Silent Hill: Shattered Memories, I knew the story won't disappoint me. And it didn't, though it was certainly not as engaging. But the way the game made me experience it almost ruined the effect.
The story of the game is told through a set of VCR-quality interrogation clips in the form of a documentary. The videos are nicely acted, the story is interesting and vivid, leaving some food for thought even after you watch it from start to finish. The game imitates the experience of sitting in front of a CRT display with Windows-like interface, using a search bar to find new clips by keywords or phrases that you can type in freely just like you would in any other search bar. You're supposed to watch videos and get some clues, important words or ideas out of them regarding where the conversation might go or where it might have originated from, search for those and find more videos this way. In the end you're supposed to try and piece everything you've found together to get the full picture and solve the mystery or, rather, figure the story out. And that's it.
The concept itself is nice, and the interaction helps to enhance the immersion. The problem, however, lies with the way the videos are structured within the plot. Thing is, the story, despite being told through a series of seemingly self-contained interrogation clips, is created in such a way that it has a clear beginning and an ending, and thus you can easily stumble upon a video from the very end and hear a major spoiler as a result. The interrogation clips are also not as self-contained as they may seem. One video often follows the logic or thought found in the previous video, and watching them out of context that happens 99% of the time is rather pointless.
Imagine having an already ambiguous movie split into 30-second clips, the clips scrambled, and being offered to watch this movie by randomly (or following any kind of logic you can come up with) picking those clips and trying to make up a coherent story out of them, given the role of a character who does that within the story itself. That's how Her Story plays, and this is the first time when I can say that such interaction not only adds nothing the story, but completely messes up its flow and almost ruins the impact it makes on the player.
Even after you've found all the pieces you will still end up going to the game's installation folder to watch all the clips in their chronological order, as the game doesn't allow you to easily do even that. Doing so made me appreciate the story more, and that says a lot about the gameplay.
If only the interrogation clips were more self-contained, the logical links between them a little more obvious, and the flow of the story was linked to the logical choices the player makes with their search queries, such gameplay would've made much more sense. As it stands though, I can only recommend Her Story for the narration, the style and the nostalgia. The gameplay may entertain you for a while, but soon you'll realize that here it's nothing more than a gimmick that stands in the way of you experiencing the story the way you want to experience it.

An enormously enjoyable strategy/RPG/roguelike thing that's surprisingly hard to explain. Choose a crew, each with unique talents, send them on expeditions filled with randomized content where they attempt to solve mysteries, pass skill checks, engage in entertaining conversations, and fight in a wildly unusual turn based combat system built around the interplay of global and character moods and skills. Then go back to your home base and spend your assorted gains to enhance your characters, publish research to give yourselves bonuses, buy equipment, and collect a retinue of followers. While you're at it, give lectures to turn your fame into yet more bonuses of your choice. Then, go out again, with the ultimate goal being to amass enough renown to win the game.
It's deep, rewarding, and wholly unique in my experience. It's also amazingly replayable, with a diversity of expeditions each of which plays differently every time depending on both luck and the particular skills of your crew. Charming art, clever writing, and an appropriately absurd atmosphere add to the fun.  All in all it's great fun, and I'd highly recommend it for any fan of strategy and/or RPG's.

So in conclusion, I would recommend the game to all my friends and surely say, it would be a great purchase and you will have tons of fun and will keep you active for a good time !

Before people blow up the comments on this review, I played this game before it was on Steam which is why my playtime is practically nonexistent.
Details of gameplay are mentioned as applicable to each section.
PROS:
+ Simpler gameplay than MMDoC, MtG, or Hearthstone might appeal to those who find such games too complicated. There are currently no effects (poison, lifesteal, retaliation, etc.) At its core, BoE has damage (as well as bonus damage, which is added to damage only if it's dealt), defense, and healing. Defense is subtracted from damage for each player and the net total is applied. Healing then heals any missing health. That's all there is to it.
+ Novel and not P2W card system--gameplay works like this: The game generates a random deck of cards for you in each game, depending on skill levels and other factors. Initially, you will draw all your cards from here. At the end of a match, any cards you played get added to your "Stash". Cards in your stash can then be added to a "Collector's Deck" (which is an alternate deck you can choose to draw from during a match) or can be converted to gold (used to buy other cards). Therefore it's sometimes recommended to avoid playing a beneficial card in order to save enough energy/mana to play a rare card just so you can keep it.
+ Some RPG-like elements. Levelling gives you stat points which you can apply to your hero in order to increase things like energy, hitpoints, regeneration, etc. This helps reduce some of the RNGsus-ness from the game as you'll have a noticeably easier time defeating certain opponents if you've applied your points in a constructive way.
+ Nice music
+ A developer/company rep is currently active in the forums. Currently there are only a few posts there so I don't know how long that'll last but it's always nice to see someone around and feel like you're being heard.
CONS:
- That simple gameplay feels redundant after a while and may not be appealing to more experienced TCG players.
- Less variety than other games. In terms of playable classes, MMDoc has six factions, MtG has five, and Hearthstone has nine. This game has three, and they form sort of a rock-paper-scissors triangle. In terms of card variation, the lack of game mechanics more complicated than direct damage means practically every card either heals, adds mana, does damage, or adds defense.
- There's very little room for strategy formation or planning. A turn consists of drawing cards (until you have five), equipping a card (an ongoing spell, if you will), playing two cards, and then discarding zero or one card. There are no permanents; most equipped cards last 4-6 turns before disappearing. Where BoE deviates from most other games is in the combat. You don't have creatures that exist on the battlefield so much as you have cards that deal damage for a turn (occasionally two or rarely three) and are then discarded. Therefore, the only real planning takes place when deciding when to play a card that lingers for more than a turn. For example, you might have a card that deals bonus damage and last two turns and another card that deals normal damage but only lasts one turn. If you don't have enough mana to play both, you'd have to play the bonus damage first (it wouldn't do anything without normal damage to add to) and play the normal damage card the next turn, at which point the bonus damage would take effect once before disappearing. That's really all there is for strategy though; the main goals in this game are keeping your health up (so your opponent can't one-hit you) and making sure you have enough cards that deal normal damage (since there's quite an abundance of cards that deal bonus damage and you never seem to have enough cards you can use them with).
- You can only play as one class. If you'd like to try either of the other two, you need to pay real money. This is frustrating since it means you'll have to play on various guest accounts to really test out strategies and get a feel for which hero is for you.
- Some balance issues exist
Overall rating: 6.5/10, it's worth giving it a shot if you're not typically a TCG player. For the rest of us though, Battlegrounds of Eldhelm feels wanting of more complex gameplay.

I wanted to write a review on a variety of features of the game!  So far, I'm very much enjoying this with 18.5 hours played.
I like these.  It is fun to have a pre-built park and take on different challenges. I hope they add more to this or even allowing players to create their own scenarios that other people can play.  Campaign and Sandbox mode also available.
Easy to use and get other player's or friends rollercoaster creations in my game.  Amazing how talented some are with their custom rollercoasters.
When I first started I went right into the game.  There were a few things I was annoyed that I couldn't do well, like how shops or rides were placed.  Once I took the time to actually go through the tutorial, I solved most of the issues I was having.  Take the time to go through the tutorial, it will help you and you can open any of the various tutorials at anytime in the options.  Like I didn't have snapping on at first until I realized I needed to turn it on by pressing N once to set it on.
I found it difficult at first and it definately can use some work still.  The more you use it, the better you will get.  I'm sure this will be a feature that is heavily worked on throughout early access.
A nice diverse bunch of peeps are within the game.  They give plenty of info of what they like and don't like.  As well as a number of variables depending on what they are doing in your park, eating, etc.  I found peeps to be the most buggy aspect of the game and the developers will need to improve them.  They graphically glitch out often like on ride cameras or sliding around when walking.
I saw a lot of reviews saying they were having issues and listing beasty specs.  I have an average PC and I had no problems, minus frame drops here and there.  The frame drops seem to increase with the more peeps in the park or possibly just the park getting larger.  The developers will need to optimize, but it is still playable.  Make sure to look into the graphics settings where there are a variety of options.  There is one where you can favor fps and some others depending on what you are looking for.
They do seem to be taking feedback seriously and giving updates.  Let's hope they keep that up as it is vital to most early access projects.
The menus look fantastic!  Icons are easy to understand.  The second you get into the game,  you will understand what options are for what.
Good.  The zoom in and out with the mouse wheel is sensitive until you get use to it.  I'd like to see edge-scrolling available like on the Sims.  Maybe there was an option for it, but I don't think I saw it.
Yes!  They are available.  It sucks to get an early access title and those aren't available yet.  Luckily, they are here.
Paths are slightly tricky at first, but you will get better at them the more you play.  I think the developers can do some slight adjustments, but overall, the paths are decent.  The textures are attractive as well.
There is a good amount of rides, coasters, buildings, and objects available with a variety of themes (also consider Steam Workshop).  Coasters sometimes seem to freeze and stop running, but it usually corrects itself after a while.  The developers will want to look into that.  I was happy with the ride variety currently in the game.
This is an enjoyable game and I wanted to keep playing it and growing my park.  There is tons of potential here to grow what is already a decent base for an early access title.  There is clearly some specific graphical bugs that can look silly and the developers will want to get on that as well as further optimization on a variety of features.
I would recommend RollerCoaster Tycoon World and I'm rather surprised by the amount of very negative reviews.  Many with little time played.  Again, as I said above, I was a little annoyed at first when I started, but going through the tutorial solved many issues that I thought the game had.  The issue was that I though I could jump right in with no problems.  Take your time to learn how everything works and you will have fun!

Alright after reading through some reviews that were negative and searching for the positive ones to no real good avail I have decided to write my review. YES this game has the Roller Coaster Tycoon title but does it really feel like the RCT we know and love? Not really to be completely honest. I was so excited for this game to release and my s/o was generous enough to buy it for me when it was available for purchase so I didnt really spend my OWN money on it. But I do feel for those who did pay for it themselves with their OWN money. I have enjoyed the game so far to a point but I have run into a few issues and these are kind of major ones.
Coaster Customizations:
This is a big one for me! I absolutely love building and designing my own coasters and I figured this point to point style system of building would lead to some REALLY cool coasters. And although it is a very useful thing its a bit confusing at first to use. But what I was really disappointed in is that there is a lack of pre-set parts for the coasters such as loops, corkscrews and twists. Yes they have some but then when you do use them they seem to have messed with the coaster a bit and changes the way it works entirely.
Another complaint with the coaster builder that has REALLY frusterated me is how the BRAKES SYSTEM doesnt seem to WORK PROPERLY (at least for me) now it may be something that I am doing wrong but I get to a point where I want to have the "Block Breaks" so I can add a stop point for a second coaster to pause at while the other coaster is at the station. Ive done it in 2 and 3 plenty of times. But when I test the coaster it seems to give me the error that the "Coaster did not complete its circut" and then the second caoster never takes off? This is really weird to me and would like a bit of an easier block break system.
The final thing with the coasters and really the rides overall is that you cant really customize them too much. Like for example; you can change the colors of the tracks but you cant really fully customize the train cars, you have preset trains available. But I would like to see the ability to add patterns and change individual colors on the trians. Maybe instead of the individual color boxes you can choose, try implementing a COLOR WHEEL with ALL the RGB colors on them?
Scenery options are a bit of a disappointment not much able to mess with there.
ALSO THE BIGGEST ISSUE I AM HAVING IS A HUGE ISSUE WITH MY MEMORY RUNNING LOW WHILE PLAYING THE GAME FOR MORE THAN AN HOUR!!
I have 8GB of Corsair Vengance RAM DDR3 1600MHz and IDK WHY I am getting the error that my computer is running out of memory....
Thats really all the issues I have with this game. I like it when it works, but it needs some fixing. I would recommend the game but not at this current time.

Okay, I hear a lot that it wasn't as good as the first. And with sequels, its a general rule of thumb to compare them to their predecessors.
After playing the base game (ignore playtime, I played offline as well) and the Reborn expansion pack I have mixed feelings.
Storywise? It doesn't quite live up to its parent (or its E-packs). The story works, covers the basics and doesn't make it a random, COD-inspired, shoot everywhere kind of game.......But it isn't better than the first F.E.A.R. and it should be. I won't go into the stories of the base game or its E-pack, its better if you learn on the way.
Gameplay? Brilliant. They didn't step down from the challenge at all and delivered refreshing mechanics wrapped up in solid gunplay. An impressive, expanded arsenal adds more variation, strategical advantage and capability on the virtual battleground. You can use melee combos but if you have a shotgun (as you usually do) then its pretty useless.
Also: Mechs.
The enemies aren't stupid (remember how old the game is though) and there are an impressive array of them. They're not particularly easy either.
Like the first, the game is completely linear with no open world features other than a health pack 10 feet from the given path that you may need later on.
The only qualm I have with it is the unrealistic head motion, its hard to describe but you'll know what I mean. After a few minutes you get used to it but it can cause confusion on occasion. I just turned the sensitivity down,
Speaking of settings, some of the default controls are unique and therefore confusing. Rebind them for a more familiar feel.
In respect to this game's age, the visuals are nothing to cry about, the audio has no issues either. The soundtrack fits the action and the voice acting is minimal.
Overall, I do recommend this game.
But I recommend its predecessor more.
The expansion pack: Reborn is everything the same except the story. Its just about worth the money. You may as well get it with the game. On the plus side, it comes with a different style of HUD that I found infinitely more useful than ANY of its predecessors.

PAYDAY: The Heist is a first-person shooter developed by Overkill Software and published by Sony Online Entertainment (now Daybreak Game Company). It was originally set to be released on October 4, 2011, but due to development issues, it was pushed back to October 18. The game was released in North America on that date via the PlayStation Network, and on November 2, 2011, in Europe. It was released worldwide for PC on October 21, 2011, via Steam.
PAYDAY: The Heist features dynamic environments and enemy spawns. Teamwork is the key to the game, as players will have to work together and assume different roles. Players can play online, alongside up to three teammates; or offline, with or without AI-controlled teammates. While players go by their screen names online, the player characters do have names: Dallas, Hoxton, Wolf, and Chains.
The game's successor, PAYDAY 2, was released on 13th August, 2013.
The game was made available as a free download for one day during the CrimeFest 3 year anniversary event on 16th October, 2014.

Lara Croft GO is a concise and enjoyable turn-based puzzle game that carefully integrates some basic traits from the Tomb Raider franchise. The environmental hazards, position-based puzzles, and deadly spiders are just some of those thematic changes. Square Enix Montreal's turned-based recipe, which was a fraction more effective in Hitman GO, is flexible enough to provide clever puzzles even when new tools change the rules. With about three hours of satisfying challenges—and two more in the harder bonus tomb—this is a puzzler that can be played in short or long sessions. Lara Croft GO demonstrates that, when it comes to porting franchises to different genres, Square Enix Montreal are taking the right steps.

I can honestly say that Her Story had one of the most intriguing game premises I had ever heard of. I wasn't around for the FMV craze when it first came around, but even aside from that the idea of putting all of the pieces together through the medium of an old computer was a level of meta that is unusual in games, and makes for a great plot device in a mystery game. Ultimately that's what the game is: a mystery waiting to be solved.
Having a good idea of what I was getting into, I kept a handy document for taking notes throughout my playthrough, which saw extensive use and consultation. This game gives you a lot of clues in a jumbled up and confused manner and frankly even with my notes it was difficult to keep them straight; I don't know what I would have done if I'd tried to rely on memory. I highly recommend any other player does the same.
As for the content of the game itself, I could only describe it as a slow burn. It was a low-key adventure, a cold foray into the mind of a disturbed individual. Viva Seifert does a remarkable job. I cannot adequately describe the cold chills of anticipation and anxiety I felt after stumbling upon the first really revelatory clip of my play after putting in a supposedly innocuous word. It was not nearly enough to explain what really happened, but it opened up so many new possibilities and sent me tearing down a new line of questioning. Ultimately that lead went nowhere and I had to try something different, but I really felt like I had a bigger piece of the puzzle than before. As I continued on I found my opinions warping continuously, confusedly, as I found all kinds of things that I slowly pieced together. As I learned more about the events of the story, and also of the subject's past, I felt sympathy, anger, dread, and wonder, and sometimes a feeling of surrealism about the whole affair. When I finally put all of the pieces together, I still had more questions than answers, and those questions remain now. I have opinions and inclinations, but nothing certain, and that's how it's going to stay. Despite all of that, I feel quite satisfied with the end of my journey into the mind of... whomever I was speaking with at the end.

Her story is a game that's unfortunately very difficult to review, as it isn't really one. I'm not being pretentious here with bull like "It's not a game, it's an
", it's more like a film played in the wrong order. In Her Story, you look thorugh a police department's interview video database, watching segments of a woman being interviewed in any order you choose.
So, how do you get a game, or a
, out of what is basically the chapter select screen on a DVD? How do you build suspense, foreshadow major plotpoints, and not immediately play the last scene when all the power rests in the player? To put it simply, you can't. Not 100% of the time, anyway. I was only 10 minutes in before I watched a video that revealed a major twist that I didn't even realise was a twist because I was never told the opposite, and only halfway through the database before I searched the two phrases that bring up the most important scene, and the last scene. (The phrases were, and of course major spoiler warning before you see them
)
You may be wondering now, "If that's his opinion on it, why is he reccomending it?", and the answer to that is that I thoroughly enjoyed the 2 hours in which I played the game, how ever short it was. The acting throughout was phenomenal, Viva Seifert is a brilliant actress, and genuinely made me feel as if I was watching actual police interview tapes. The writing is also as remarkable, creating a working non-linear narrative even though the player sits in the editing booth. The twists and turns of the plot still work even if you've seen the twists before the setup, as when you do see the setup, you put all your information together then, and sit back for a couple of minutes as you try to comprehend what had just happened.
Quick note that some might take as a spoiler so proceed with caution, it's only a minor spoiler but a spoiler anyway -
Overall, I'd say that "Her Story" is an extraordinarily well written and performed game that is unfortunately, and quite ironically, bounded by its freedom. If I hadn't searched those terms mentioned earlier, I could have perhaps have had an experience ten times as good as the one I did, however the gameplay mechanics are too experimental and too limitless to work to the narrative's fullest potential.

Blood Money is commonly regarded by fans as the pinnacle of the series. Polishing the gameplay set by previous entries, this masterpiece delivers some of the most unique stealth gameplay available. Hitman is the series that pioneered social stealth, the ability to “hide in plain sight”. The disguise system in Blood Money works great and it’s fun to try different disguises to figure out what works best for certain situations. There are so many memorable levels in Blood Money, and I still manage to find new ways to perform assassinations. Levels like A New Life, Curtains Down, and The House of Cards are works of art. In this game, there are many creative ways to dispatch your targets, more so than any other Hitman game. You can rig a piano to fall on someone’s head, you can blow up a photoshoot with some well placed mines while dressed as Santa Claus, you can silently garrote your target while disguised as a birthday clown. Those who played Absolution and are looking for a taste of what the old games were like should look no further than Blood Money. For its current price, this game is a steal. Without a doubt, this is the best stealth game I have ever played.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

A good first attempt by Frictional Games.  Pretty rough (ruff) around the edges, but I enjoyed playing it well enough.  The story isn't bad, though the gameplay mechanics leave a lot to be desired.  Here's what it boils down to in my mind; if a game makes something you could easily do IRL overly difficult, then it's doing something wrong, and will just frustrate the hell out of people.  Take swinging a pickaxe at an infected dog or giant spider for example.  The spiders in particular drove me crazy, I mean, how hard would it be to step on one of those suckers, or pelt it with rocks, and do you really mean to tell me that it takes two hits from a pick-axe to kill a spider, but four to kill a dog, and you can’t harm the dog during its “getting up” animation?  That, and how the game freezes whenever you examine something, but doesn’t actually pause the gameplay (like when you’re being chased down by blood-thirsty hounds).  Other than that, the puzzles were engaging and I enjoyed the horror elements.  I wouldn’t buy the package now for $10, particularly ten years after its release, but it’s certainly worth $0.99 for a horror classic.  Just keep in mind, Requiem is really just a collection of puzzles; it doesn't really contribute to the plot in any meaningful way and was mostly just tedious to me.

Penumbra Overture is a first person survival horror game with focus on puzzles. Because the game has been developed by a small team I will try no to be too harsh with them. First of all this is an adventure game with an interesting story about a 30 year old man, named Philip, that goes in a solo expedition in Greenland to look for signs of his dead father that he never knew. This story intro seems a bit unrealistic for me, I mean who will go alone in the middle of an icy desert to search for someone he never met, simply because of curiosity ? Based on the first episode impressions, I would have preferred a plane or a boat accident.
Anyway the graphics look quite well for a low budget game (I recommend using very low brigtness & gamma for best experience) and the sound is great, even though it's a bit repetitive at times. The game uses an autosave system which can sometimes make you miss some dialogue if you were doing other stuff at the same time. The bad thing about Penumbra Overture is the AI, is basically s**t, on hard difficulty the only difference is a two hit kill, but the rest is the same. There are also some bugs/exploits that you can use to beat the AI on hard and remove any need to sneak (hint: climb a box a kill everyone).
In conclusion Penumbra Overture is a good game with an exciting ending that makes you buy the second episode right away. I only wish the make the AI better for a more immersive experience.

To be very clear - you might not like the game.
However, I spent £0.49 on it, and I've had my monies worth after 20 minutes. I didn't expect it to be good, and it is not great, but it is good (for me). It has been witty, funny, clever, and made me really smile at moments.
It has a jerky type of movement that reminds me of the old games before smooth animation was invented. However, it feels responsive, and the character moves where I tell it. So the jerky movement is a great recreation, spot-on in fact. The artwork is a mix of acceptable bad mixed with some pretty good art for a top-down game. The sound effects ... or rather the voices and vocal recordings are exceptional. There is a lot of speech involved which adds a lot to the simple experience.
What attracted me to the game was the price of course. However, I thought the ranting discussion threads created by people with nothing better to do than find an object to attack (love the internet!!), were too drama-like to ignore.
I bought the game to see what the fuss was about (bearing in mind most of the ranters might not have actually played the game). And they were wrong. It is not a bad game. It is not a great game. A great game would be the original GTA, Or other top-downs like Prison Architect. However, is it worth supporting an indie with £0.49 of my money? Yeah, I am happy. If the ranters keep publicising the game I reckon the devs will be very happy too!!

Game is visually designed to resemble classical 8bit games of Nintendo era. It succeeds in that very well. The graphics are simple, yet there are many little things mixed in the background.

Game consists of several levels and a hidden final level, which appears after finishing every other level. Levels are mostly basic sidescroller which vary occasionally into faster sideshooters. There are also other playable characters hidden in the game, which you can unlock by finding them. The hidden characters have different abilities compared to each other.
I played the game with keyboard and had no difficulties, although it seems to be designed to be played with a controller. The controls are very fluent and you feel like you are in
of your character. There are some parts which are harder with some of the playable characters. Luckily you can swap between them freely in the middle of the game.
The game is notorious for its difficulty. Nothing in it is impossible of course and since you have unlimited continues, you can keep on playing. It is just frustrating enough to make you want to finish the stage you started, even if you have been stuck on a difficult part for some time.
Overall a decent and fun platformer game. I would recommend it to anyone who likes classic sidescrollers and/or The AVGN.

1: Obviously this is a port of a mobile game, and apparantly it is much cheaper in that format. So I guess if that's an option for you, go that rout instead of picking it up on steam.
2: The puzzles were a lot of fun, although far too simple early on. I realize that's just common game design, teaching you the rules before letting you dive in fully. But in truth, it takes a large chunk of the entire main campaign before they really let loose with any tricky stuff.
2.5: The fifth "new adventure" chapter is definitely where the best puzzling is, and where about 3.5 of my 8 hours(for full 100% achievements) was spent... though a huge chunk of that was spent hugely overthinking two specific puzzles.  I've seen another reviewer mention their length to be around 5 hours, and that sounds about right for anyone who "gets it" right off the bat(and does everything there is to do without looking anything up... 3: I'm sure the aesthetic is going to be hit or miss for a lot of people, but I personally found it to be gorgeous. The music was also perfectly atmospheric. While every aspect of the gameplay is pure puzzling, the game is designed(and more importantly presented) in such a way that it definitely still gives  a strong feeling of thrills and action. Especially towards the end of the main campaign.
Honestly, this game felt like the perfect minimalist companion to the old school Tomb Raider games... and without any of those damn swimming levels to boot. Again, I recognize that it can be found cheaper elseware, but I in know way felt cheated by the 8$ I spent on it. And if you wait for an epic steam sale, it's absolutely 100% worth whatever pittance you'll end up paying for it.

Game Mechanics
Fun game with decent replayability.

A fun roguelike game where you plan expeditions and find treasures across the world. With multiple aproaches on how to confront others and a wide variety of characters to play as and even more resources to unlock during your adventures it offers decent replayability.

In RE:IS, you take a trio of intrepid explorers, chosen from a set of 25 characters across 4 classes with varied skills, on an adventure to seek glory and renown. It's fun and whimsical, with attractive, colourful, cartoonish graphics. It's simple to learn, difficult to master, and endlessly replayable. Four main factors ensure that no two adventures are ever the same:
- Goals: Do you seek fame and glory, untold riches, or scientific advancement?
- Attitudes: How does your team handle conflict? Friendly, winning foes over with your charms? Devious, playing with their heads and breaking their spirits? Or Aggressive, shooting first and (maybe) asking questions later?
- Classes: There are Scientists, Scouts, Fighters, and Speakers. Each class brings something unique to the table, and the 5 characters within each class are all wildly different from each other.
- Areas: There are 11 in all (plus an additional 2 in the More to Explore expansion), but you can only explore 5 in a single run-through. Different characters will be better equipped to deal with different challenges, and each map will also be slightly different every time you go through it.
I only have a couple of complaints, and they are very minor ones. First, I can only imagine how difficult it must be to proofread such an immense, complex, branching script thoroughly, but I have found quite a number of typos and grammatical errors throughout. None have yet affected clarity, though.
Second, there are a few sidequests in each area, with clues peppered about the map to help you solve them. However, because the maps are generated in a mostly random fashion, it is entirely possible (and often not especially difficult) to solve a sidequest before encountering its associated clues. When this happens, the script/NPCs will still give you the clue, not acknowledging that you don't really need it anymore. If the developers had found a way to acknowledge when a player has completed events out of sequence, and adjust the script accordingly, it would make the game seem that much more polished. It isn't game-breaking, nor even really a problem at all, just a missed opportunity.
Bottom line, if you like lighthearted RPG/strategy/adventure games, I highly recommend Renowned Explorers. I've probably done 8 or 10 run-throughs as of this writing, and I still don't think I've uncovered even half of what there is to see in this game. Every campaign leaves me wanting more, and thinking about what I'll do differently next time. I have not yet played the More to Explore expansion, but I just downloaded it and I'm excited to try it. I may update this review after playing it a bit.

Definitely better than the previous entry of the series "Contracts" but not as good as "Hitman 2: Silent Assassin" for sure.
The original hitman idea ("Codename 47", "Silent Assassin" and "Contracts") was all about trying not to kill anyone but your targets and as silently as possible while this game, offering you extremely cheap progress solutions involving killing and/or sedating people, encourages you not to go for SA. I'm not saying there is no "silent assassin" in there, because, well, there is and being able to kill with SA grade is usually quite fun but the game discourages to do that.
Another thing I missed on my hits was planning. Being able to see blueprints BEFORE starting the mission (as in "Hitman 2: Silent Assassin") you could plan your hits, taking appropriate weapons, checking escape routes and fixing the map on your head being able to move much better during the hit. On "Hitman: Blood Money" you blindly step into your mission without any kind of knowledge (on mission start you can buy hints... another quite dumb thing in my opinion).
This "new" 47 can be seen on cutscenes/plot too (killing witnesses and actually having them in the first place, not being 1 step ahead his enemies, etc). Plot then was far better in "Hitman 2: Silent Assassin", far better.
On the technical compartment, audio and video are good, surprisingly good actually, I enjoyed both visuals (often stopped during a mission to look at the environment) and audio. Controls are quite good too once you get used to the changes from previous 2 installments (action button split in 3 different action buttons).
In the end I'd say this game was definitely fun and well made but not enough to beat the enjoyment that "Hitman 2: Silent Assassin" gave me back then.

The early part of this game is colorful, charming, and highly enjoyable.  The music is great, the references are quirky and it briskly evolves into a fun and comedic metroid/castlevania with a intricate combat system and satisfying level design with purposeful rooms that teach you more about your repitoire of available actions.  Then just before the final world, it becomes a convuluted version of Super Meat Boy, with an sudden and jarring spike in difficulty, twitch reaction based trial and error sequences, and unforgiving checkpoints.
You know, to put it simply, the reason why Super Meat Boy works and this game does not is that SMB's controls only require that you jump at the right place and at the right time.  In Guacamelee, you not only need to jump at the right place and at the right time, but also in the right dimension while dashing, power punching, double jumping, wall running, and goat flying. Logicstically, the puzzles aren't even hard to solve, they're just borderline impossible to execute on the first 20 tries.   As a result, a game that started with the promise of having fun in a colorful world of Mexican towns and countrysides becomes a frustrating excercise of piloting my awkwardly moving avatar from one abstract platform surrounded by sawblades to another abstract platform surrounded by spikes... the sudden twist is alarming and if it's something this studio doesn't realize, or are unwilling to admit, they're next title will be a scary proposition.
It's a unnerving choice in game design to lock away the "best ending" behind the hardest machinations of the game, and provide a "regular ending' that so morose and completely unexpected that it clashes with the light-hearted tone established in the other 99% of the the game prior.  When a player doesn't even know that he or she has to collect secret orbs that are well hidden in the game it makes the default ending provide absolutely no pay off for the player's actions up to that point.  "I know we promised you cake, but here's a dirty boot instead!"  The default ending really destroyed my morale to continue further in the game.  And the "true" ending serves as no substantial improvement in resolving the remaining storylines presented in the game.
I mean, who was the Guardian of the mask?  Why did the villians have more personality and background than any of the good main characters?  What happened to all of the unresolved story lines: did the devil stay as a chicken?  What happened to the Jaguar Man? Even if we saved the girlfriend in distress is the world of the living/dead still threatened with evil spirits and skeletons? At best we only see a kiss and then the credits roll at the end, as if that solved all of the major world issues.  For the amazing writing and world up to that point, I expected better.
What's even worse is that the either ending of the game is wholly irrelevant when considering that the main character can freely travel between the world of the living and the dead.  The sullen ending provided by the default ending is absolutely ludicrous given that if the hero just pressed LB, he'd immediately be in the world of the dead and be reunited with his childhood love interest.
No wait, LB makes you dodge, I meant RB.  Wait, what was RB for again... goat run?  Belly flop?  Turn into a chicken?
Great music, colorful world, charming casts of antagonists, but ultimately a large mistep in game design puts pressure on the mechanics of Guacamelee turning it from a silly and inspired romp into a frustrating tedious platformer.
