This is an attempt to make a spoiler free review from a modern perspective for people unsure as to whether to purchase the game and are unfamiliar with it, but it is, of course, my own opinion, and an informed consumer should look at multiple reviews before buying.
Gameplay: The game follows a D&D style turn based combat system, which can either be fun or needlessly boring depending on your preference. It is not a very difficult game to beat, either. Most enemies are there for the sake of being there to slow you down and/or give you something to do. Difficult fights that require you to scratch your head and mix up your approach are few and far between. Don't get me wrong, that does not necessarily make this an unenjoyable experience, but those who wish for a challenge will be dissapointed. In between combat you will focus mostly on dialogue (WARNING: there is A LOT of dialogue in this game; if you are not a fan of listening or reading lots of text, it is unlikely that you will appreciate this game very much), though you will probably also be doing quite a bit of inventory management and min-maxing of equipment, too. Skills in this game are usually used to aid in combat or dialogue (i.e. repairing droids to help in fights, using persuade to get more money out of a quest that you were given, etc...) Apart from that there are several optional mini-games but that about sums up what you actually do.
NOTE: It's very useful if you go into this game knowing how basic D&D or D20 RPG systems operate so you understand what all the stats mean. You might have some trouble getting a grasp of the systems without knowing anything about that.
IMPORTANT NOTE: This game has difficulty running on anything newer than Windows XP. It's probable you'll have to do some troubleshooting to fix issues playing the game, especially with cutscenes.
Story and Quests: The main story in KOTOR is good,  but is unlikely to be that life-changing or awe inspiring for anyone, and its big twist can be seen coming for some time if the player has been paying close enough attention to all the dialogue and story thus far. The main plot also begins rather slowly and takes quite a bit of time to develop. This is not the game for the impatient and easily bored. Sidequests typically are, again, good, but not great. There are some real gems in there, though. I mean, it's a Bioware game. Perhaps the biggest strike against it is the binary morality system. You tend to either be the nicest and most compassionate person in the galaxy, or be a psychotic space Hitler. That being said, the game is classic Star Wars in design, so it's likely that is purposeful, but you should still be aware you are unlikely to be morally or ethically challenged or questioned in any way during this game (very much unlike its sequel, KOTOR 2).
Characters: I'm giving this its own section because I feel like it deserves it. Optional party member quests and dialogue are a large part of this games overall story. Most party members in KOTOR are not particularly interesting, and it's likely you'll only do the backstories for characters you do find interesting. But most of this is entirely optional, so it doesn't really count as a strike against the game, and is a nice addition.
Sound: Music is by Jeremy Soule so of course it's good. It is not classic John Williams, however. Take that as you will. It can either be good or bad.
Graphics: Very dated. I don't feel the urge to go into greater detail as you can just look at screenshots above.
Aesthetic: It is mostly bright and colorful without overdoing it. Nothing particularly stands out here. It's vibrant where it wants to be vibrant and dark where it wants to be dark. I don't really have anything to compare it to. Again, I recommend just looking at screenshots.
Conclusion: It's a very good game, and definitely worth playing if you enjoy this style of combat and are patient enough with the story. You don't even need to be into Star Wars to have a lot of fun with this game.
TL;DR: It's a quintessential Star Wars story (albeit a very slow paced one) mixed with D&D style gameplay and sidequests. If that sounds like something you'd like, you will probably enjoy this game. Be aware that if you try to run it on anything newer than Windows XP you can have problems, especially with the cutscenes. You may have to do some troubleshooting to get it to work.

I did really enjoy this while it lasted, and the main actress really pulls it off, and the story is quite interesting.  However, I managed to figure out what was going on in under 2 hours, and ultimately I felt like this should have been part of a wider gameplay experience.  Like, maybe the interview tapes was only one part of a bigger detective game, where perhaps you also had to interview people, search the crime scene for evidence etc.  Now that would be cool.

it may look like minecraft on first glance, but it definitely isn't.
don't believe me? lemme explain:
of course you could run around and gather stuff. but why would you do manual labor if you can hire people to do it for you? food farming, wood and stone gathering, ore mining, smelting, crafting... all of the boring tasks of a survival game are being done by your own private workforce!
of course, people aren't cheap, as they require food and beds. but both of them can be automatically produced. and the process ofthat is simple, yet rewarding.
of course, these people 'could' use houses, but that's not necessary. you don't need to be a good builder for this game. just place some beds on the ground and dig some trenches to protect your little settlement.
if you do want to build nicely, but aren't  talented, as of now, you can easily let your dudes build stuff for you! you can even download blueprints from the workshop!
but if you somehow wall in your flag (the centerpiece of your colony), a siege mode starts, in which the game gets much harder.
having a ton of people attracts monsters too, but that is also no problem, as you can hire guards to deal with monsters easily. just place them strategically - or spam them, if you have a giant city.
this game also has far better graphics as minecraft, because blocks aren't just simple cubes: they're shaped, they have depth, they refract light. it's like minecraft on HD-steroids, just with a much better performance!

Let me start off by saying I just got this game. I was one who fell head over heels for Overwatch, and like many people looked at this game as an inferior and too similar of game. I kept putting it off, but I finally found it on sale and decided to pick it up and give it a go. Granted, I haven't thrown a lot of hours into it, but I'd have gladly payed more for it for what enjoyment I've already received.
Now, the question a lot of people want to know is....how similar is this to Overwatch? Well, it isn't. The way the characters handle can feel like Overwatch, especially with your abilities but that's where the similarities end. I haven't played PVP so I can't weigh in on that yet, but for the PVE I'd liken it to a cross between Overwatch and Destiny gameplay, with Borderlands style comedy. Granted, it doesn't beat any of those games in a specific category...(Overwatch has better characters with abilities, Destiny had a more open world and better gunplay, Borderlands was funnier)....it's the fact that this game is able to blend those together so well, and it doesn't fail in any category.
All in all, it could use a little polish here and there, but overall this is definitely worth picking up. Especially if you're not paying full price. I'd probably give it a 7/10-7.5/10 on any other website, but on Steam I'll have to settle for a YES I'd recommend this.

A delightful gem of a game that got off to a slow start due to a bad release time and low marketing visability. While there are legitimate issues with the game at present (queue times being the biggest drawback for me) I can't help but love this game despite it's flaws.
Pros:
1-5 player story mode with entertaining levels and writing (This game comes from the developers of the Borderlands series)
A well designed 5v5 Competitive PVP with 4 game modes
Very likeable and diverse roster of 29 (will be 30) characters to play, with unlockable lore challenges that help you learn to play each one and tells you more about the character and the universe they live in
A supportive community willing to help new players learn
A responsive dev team (most concerns raised by the community have been addressed in a timely fashion)
Plans for new content (some of which has already been delivered)
Cons:
Small playerbase compared to similar games
Long queue times for matchmaking (mainly due to the first con)
Some performance issues on a few levels (devs have made it much better than it used to be, but the issue persists)
Steep learning curve (ask someone to show you the ropes or look up tips on the forums) MOBA players and FPS players alike will find things they are unfamiliar with. Knowing the unique mechanics of the game will go a long way to help you improve.
I've had a blast playing this game with friends and I'd recommend it as long as you are aware of the cons. Chances are if you've played and like any of the Borderlands games you will enjoy Battleborn. The PVE alone would be worth buying the game on a sale.

Get this game if:
1) You're a fan of Dungeon Keeper and/or The Settlers series (or any clone thereof, such as Knights & Merchants, Cultures, The Nations, etc).
2) You like god sims.
3) You like to play as the "bad guys".
If you meet all three criteria, well... it's a must-get.

There is another DK clone around, but this one looks great! Especially I like that developers want to incorporate the idea of overworld - that certainly is a good idea. I hope they will develop it further.

Comparisons between this and War For The Overworld are, of course, inevitable. The fact is, however, that despite the basis of both games on Dungeon Keeper they are very different beasts and I heartily recomend both games to anyone looking for a Dungeon Keepers sequel.
WftO is a much more traditional Dungeon Keeper sequel type affair, despite that fact the the (lovely) devs on that team were legally obliged to shout at me whenever I mention that particular EA franchise in relation to their game. They're still great guys, though! :)
But Dwelvers is what we're here for so as well as just saying it's a great game I guess I should describe it a little and highlight the differences between this and Dungeon Keeper/WftO.
Bottom line? Dwelvers is more in depth and complicated in terms of management of your creatures.
A bit more in-depth is to say that it takes the dungeon building of the original and expands upon it in a somewhat Minecraft-feeling type of way. You don't just mine outwards to expand your dungeon, you can also mine up and down and the massive levels very quickly become truly huge, with overland access points and monster rooms scattered here and there, as well as resource points and The Maze.
As well as the addition of the third dimension in terms of exploring, there is also a lot more to do to keep your creatures happy, fed, and equipped. Gone is the gold of the original which would fuel an automated chicken farm. Now you have to carefully manage your crops, mills, kitchen, fishers, brewers, and ensure there's enough space for everyone to get to the table laden with food. It makes it feel more engaging than the original and adds a big dimension that makes it feel like a living dungeon rather than a ... I dunno ... Almost like a franchise in the original? You threw gold alone at it and it worked however much you messed up your layout. This is a different beast and you should really be prepared to deal with the layout problems that will inevitably crop up.
Defending your dungeon is quite aa lot more in depth than the original as well. Or it can/will be at least. As well as your indirectly controlled creatures you also have your delightful array of traps which is where things get deliciously sadistic. As with Minecraft's redstone circuits, gone are the days of a line of automated cannons and it has been replaced with a potentially massively complicated hydraulics system.
Potentially? Yep. You can have a pressure pad which makes a cannon fire or a wall squish someone very easily, but you can also push the boat out and use the already impressive array of hydraulic systems to make gob-smackingly complex trap systems on mulitple levels doing all sorts of terrible things to your enemies. Blowing them up and squishing them are just the start, if you want to put the time and imagination in.
So, verdict?
This game is in alpha. It shows in the rough menus and UI elements, particularly the missing tooltips on some windows, but it's already lightyears ahead of Dungeon Keeper and a very different beast to War For The Overworld - If you're looking for a traditional DK then I'd point you toward WftO but if you're looking for something that builds on the original in terms of management and building complexity, Dwelvers is definitely for you.

Most of the negative reviews of this game are completely unwarranted. I've been a fan of this franchise since the very first game, and this has the potential to be the best one yet, even though it does need a lot of work. Most of the people who seem to hate it either seem to ignore the fact that it's an incomplete early release, or simply didn't have the patience to actually learn how to play it. Finally, I think it does measure up to it's main competitor, Planet Coaster.
First, let me say that if you're expecting an easy-to-play, piece-by-piece builder like the previous two where everything always comes out perfectly square and symmetrical with complete ease, you're going to be disappointed. The node-based coaster builder can be tricky, and it takes some work to get parallel tracks or symmetrical scenery arrangements. However, most of the people complaining about this seem to have completely ignored the snap and grid options. Once you learn to use it, I actually find these elements superior to analogous elements in other simulators like Cities:Skylines. It does take a while to learn to and optimize the path building, scenary placement, and coaster-building features, and it's a bit more difficult to use, but the trade off in difficulty pays off with the high level of freedom you have.
Now, something very negative about this game, it is EXTREMELY buggy in its current state. It crashes a lot, the frame rate is really low, a number of the features (such as the coaster's physics engine) are woefully incomplete, and the AI in guests and maintainence needs a lot of work, but it is important to remember this is an incomplete game. It's probably more buggy than most games that are called beta or early access, but that's more the fault of Atari's marketing than the game itself. If they work out these bugs, it has the potential to be a really good game.
The best feature of the game by far is the coaster builder. Judging by other comments and You Tube videos, most of the people complaining about it seem to have absolutely no clue what they are doing and haven't even tried to learn how to use it. It is in my opinion the best coaster builder out there right now. It's less complex than No Limits, and gives you way more freedom than the builders in the first three or the current version of Planet Coaster. Granted, the physics engine is probably incomplete and what's right now there is probably a place holder (there's very little friction on coasters, the breaks are way to powerful) and there are some bugs with the coaster builder (frame rate slows way down, some features cause it to crash, and there are a number of bugs with the breaks). It's also somewhat difficult to learn how to use (though should come somewhat naturally to those familiar with No Limits), but again what you lose in easiness pays off in what you gain in freedom. Again, don't expect an easy piece-by-piece builder, but do expect to be able to build really realistic coasters. I love the mixture of node and piece-by-piece builders.
Since I also have access to the early bird version of Planet Coaster, I think it's worth doing a point-by-point comparison between the two. Granted, both games are incomplete, so all of this is subject to change, but it's worth mentioning how I think the two stack up against each other.
So far, here's what's better about RCTW:
-Better Coaster Builder with way more freedom than you have in PC, but PC's builder isn't even in alpha yet so this can change.
-Better path builder. PC's path builder is easily the worst part of the game, it's so wonky and very difficult to build decent looking paths.
-UGC. As someone who spent hours looking for and working with CS in RCT3, this is a huge plus. The integration with Steam Workshop is great, and it allows to add elements of piece-by-piece building in RCTW that aren't there yet. Also, it expands the potential for customization in the game in the future way out there.
-Better looking flat rides.
-Better camera controls. Though PC has very similar controls to RCT3, RCTW's controls are more intuitive and don't clash with other controls in the game.
Here's what's better about PC:
-Better overall graphics. Even though some elements in RCTW are more detailed, the lighting, shadows, and such in PC are way superior.
-Better sounds. Sounds like guests on coasters are having sex in RCTW, and coaster sounds in PC are more realistic. Also, it sounds a lot less cluttered.
-Better Scenery builder. Piece-by-piece building allows for a lot more freedom in building buildings and the scenery in general looks better.
-Better AI. Peeps act and move more naturally, and there are fewer bugs. It gets you to think about the layout of your park a lot more.
-Way less buggy, and better optomized overall.
Here's what's neutral/debatable between the two:
-Stalls. The Stalls in RCTW are more realistic, and the feature of walk-in resteraunts is a huge plus. But, the stalls in PC are more customizable.
-Coster stations. Like stalls, they're more realistic in RCTW, but more customizable in PC. Granted, RCTW's devs said they're planning on allowing for blank coaster stations for mor customizations in future updates.
-RCTW has more features, game modes, and such as of now but that's just where it is in its development.
Overall, I slightly prefer RCTW but that's mainly because the main reason I've ever played these games is for coaster building and, as it stands now, RCTW has more features overall, but PC just needs to catch up in development. Both have the potential to be great games.
In conclusion, do not by this game if you're looking for a completely ready-to-play, fully optimized, and easy-to-play game. It still needs a lot of work, and is difficult to learn to master all the controls. Most of the reason why people seem to hate it is a mixture of bad marketing and unrealistic expectations of how complete it would be. For casual gamers new to the genre of theme park simulators, it's definitely not worth the price. But if you truly love simulation games, and have the patience to work through the bugs and actually learn how to play, and want to support the development of a potentially good game, it's definitely worth it.

An interesting 'game' that plays out as a detective story that has brilliant acting and an engagin story, but ultimately is a bit on the short side and left me wanting more.
In Her Story, you are trying to unravel a mystery through searching through police archives of interviews (in FMV).  You can search for different interview segments by text searching for words the interviewee said, but it only ever gives you five segments for any search.  Time to get your Columbo on piece on!
I did really enjoy this while it lasted, and the main actress really pulls it off, and the story is quite interesting.  However, I managed to figure out what was going on in under 2 hours, and ultimately I felt like this should have been part of a wider gameplay experience.  Like, maybe the interview tapes was only one part of a bigger detective game, where perhaps you also had to interview people, search the crime scene for evidence etc.  Now that would be cool.
Still, Her Story is a nice little concept piece, very interesting and unique, and the acting in it is really good.  Just there was more to it...  Will recommend but be aware that you're getting a very good but also very short and unreplayable interactive experience

Everyone will have a different experience opening up the mystery. There's no win/lose condition, you are just left to investigate on your own. It's a good game to experience alone but it's also a good game to play with a group. You find the clips by searching with keywords. From those clips you can pick up on leads and follow them for your next search.
However, only the first 5 results of a search are accessible to you, so you can't just use a broad search term to try and cheese your way through the mystery. Also, there are a few red herrings that will catch you out if you search for things too obvious such as 'Guilty' etc.
It's pretty fun. I wouldn't compare it to an "interactive movie." I'm not a fan of telltale games and such but enjoyed this because it's more of just straight up detective work with no hand holding.
The only con is the obvious lack of replayability, once you've finished the game once, there's not much left except to find every last clip that's left.

This is a very different game from the 1st supreme commander, and bears no resemblance what-so-ever to the glory that was Total Annihilation. Biggest change (for the campaign at least, it's been patched out for skirmish) is that construction must be paid for in advance. You can still queue stuff up but your engineers / factories will sit their twiddling their thumbs until the mass is in the bank. This coupled with the fact that they'll all try and grab it as soon as it hits their minimum means a single factory can basically halt production for everybody else.
Other changes are the tech-tree, which is now navigated using research points generated by research stations. I don't personally dislike this, but combined with the fact that enemy patrols are invariably small and frequent, the temptation to sit behind a few shield generators and wait out the tech tree is ever present. Additionally the number and variety of different units has been vastly reduced, mission maps are small, restrictive and heavily scripted. The rock-paper-scissors effect has been ramped upto 10, with the rather notable exception of mobile anti-air being absolutely useless, even en-mass.
There are also some glaring quality control issues, path-finding is terrible, you'll often find construction halted because a single unit is trying and failing to move out the way, the AI will repeat the same attacks, at the same time and in the same place for the duration of the game, offering no real challenge, to the extent that wrecks will stack up in nice neat rows. The only times missions are remotely difficult is if you get constantly hammered in the first 3 minutes, anything longer than that and you've had time to set up multiple overlapping shielded defences and can basically sit anything out.
So in short its small, claustrophobic, and in RTS terms practically on rails. There are probably enough of the old TA/SC staples to stop it being considered entirely generic but it is far and away the worst entry into the franchise.

Playing through
has severely diminished my impression of its spiritual successor,
. They are both created by Frictional Games and share an almost uncanny amount of similarities in regards to art style, narrative, story, level design, gameplay, and puzzles - although the A.I. of the enemies in Penumbra is much worse. It's as if
was a practice run in preparation for Friction Games' magnum opus.
There are an excessive amount of red herrings and redundancy in regards to inventory items and world objects.
contains many useless inventory items such as the flashlight and glowstick that never need to be used due to how bright the game is overall, especially when crouching will also increase the brightness of the area around the player. This makes stealth incredibly overpowered; there is no disincentive to leave the comfort of darkness and to only crouch walk everywhere in order to easily bypass enemies. It would seem that the developers learned their lesson from this exploitative mechanic when they made
as staying in the dark in that game will drain the player's sanity. There is no sanity meter here in
.
The silent protagonist is a tired trope, although there is dialogue in the beginning and some text near the end, the protagonist never speaks throughout the events of the game which makes for a boring experience. The enemies - which contain zombie dogs, spiders, and large worms - are more an annoyance than they are threatening and, while some of them can be easily disabled, others can not be effectively killed. There are a number of chase sequences that break flow of the game, where
moves from a very slow, methodical, and deliberate pacing to a frantic "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom" action platformer.
The engine of
has many problems. I understand that it was first created to support 2D graphics and later adapted to 3D but there are issues that just don't make much sense to me, such as not being able to capture the footage with screen-recording software, graphical errors duplicating the screen as a picture-in-picture overlay, and camera culling where geometry will disappear when it reaches the edges of the camera's field of view. One instance of
winning over
is where the physics are taken more seriously here as objects feel they have real weight, meaning there are no ridiculous instances where I can fling heavy objects across the room with ease.
is filled with puzzles where the solution contradicts everything the player has learned up to that point, requiring the player to unlearn and rebel against the vague rules it has set, such as
when all the other previous barrels in the game can simply be dismissed as filler set pieces.
There are a myriad of grammatical errors present that make it difficult to read certain passages of text. On that note, the tutorial text explaining what keybindings do are presented in a matter-of-fact fashion from the protagonist's perspective: "if I want to grab something I should press LeftMouse" is too jarring and immersion breaking. The text will also often dismiss itself far too early for me to read the entire sentence and, since inspecting items can sometimes not be repeated, means I would miss out on vital information.
Frictional Games suffers from a lack of focus, in which they try to force so many different types of gaming conventions into an adventure horror game (platforming, object physics puzzles, vent crawling, running from danger) it starts to confuse what the game should be and takes away from the story. In regards to the story, Frictional Games also goes over the top with exposition. They are simply unable to contain themselves when it comes to story writing and their need to explain away what makes these types of games, and their mythology, scary - the unknown.
My playthrough of
reflects my time with
, where I began to dislike these games after the mystery and horror elements were replaced with platforming sequences, frustrating enemies, and the fear of the unknown diminished to a laughable level.
The final 10 seconds were the scariest, and most interesting, part of
.

This game does a lot of things well. It has a very unique dual world warping mechanic that is used throughout the entire game, is very intuitive, and meshes well with the other game mechanics and storyline. Unfortunately, it deceives you with one game and replaces it with another. The sound, art style, combat mechanics, and metroidvania ability mechanics are all very well designed, but it also has many flaws. Most important flaw is the use of color-coded puzzles and combat mechanics without a colorblind-friendly mode. This makes the already difficult combat a dice roll for the colorblind.
The game starts off as a very good beat-em-up metroidvania, but at the end it becomes an extremely hard (super meat boy level hard, no exageration) platformer with a few combat sequences in between. Though a lot of the very hard platforming is optional, they are very unforgiving and require godly levels of coordination with very very sparse checkpoints.
The combat at later stages also border on unfair levels of difficulty. Enemies can exist in another world that you can't hurt, but they can hurt you. A lot of later enemies also have unblockable attacks, so you end up with half the screen full of enemies you can't hit or block.  You have to swap worlds to deal with these two types of world enemies, and they can overlap each other and not hit or shoot one another.
Getting hit is also a major punishment as you are knocked out for a fair amount of time. The worse thing, though is being knocked far away from your enemies. Being a melee only character, not being able to get close to enemies who are charging for unblockable attacks is bad. The hit stun is way too long and punishing when there are large numbers of these enemies. Although it's rare, it is also possible to be stunlocked in some arenas that have a large number of enemies.
The DLC shows you just what the developers had in mind for this game as they are all platforming based with little to no combat. This is a puzzle platformer disguised as a combat metroidvania.
If you like supermeatboy type platformers with very difficult combat, then this game is for you. For anyone like me expecting metroid or castlevania style gameplay, you probably won't find this game very fun after the first half.

This is an attempt to make a spoiler free review from a modern perspective for people unsure as to whether to purchase the game and are unfamiliar with it, but it is, of course, my own opinion, and an informed consumer should look at multiple reviews before buying.
Gameplay: The game follows a D&D style turn based combat system, which can either be fun or needlessly boring depending on your preference. It is not a very difficult game to beat, either. Most enemies are there for the sake of being there to slow you down and/or give you something to do. Difficult fights that require you to scratch your head and mix up your approach are few and far between. Don't get me wrong, that does not necessarily make this an unenjoyable experience, but those who wish for a challenge will be dissapointed. In between combat you will focus mostly on dialogue (WARNING: there is A LOT of dialogue in this game; if you are not a fan of listening or reading lots of text, it is unlikely that you will appreciate this game very much), though you will probably also be doing quite a bit of inventory management and min-maxing of equipment, too. Skills in this game are usually used to aid in combat or dialogue (i.e. repairing droids to help in fights, using persuade to get more money out of a quest that you were given, etc...) Apart from that there are several optional mini-games but that about sums up what you actually do.
NOTE: It's very useful if you go into this game knowing how basic D&D or D20 RPG systems operate so you understand what all the stats mean. You might have some trouble getting a grasp of the systems without knowing anything about that.
IMPORTANT NOTE: This game has difficulty running on anything newer than Windows XP. It's probable you'll have to do some troubleshooting to fix issues playing the game, especially with cutscenes.
Story and Quests: The main story in KOTOR is good,  but is unlikely to be that life-changing or awe inspiring for anyone, and its big twist can be seen coming for some time if the player has been paying close enough attention to all the dialogue and story thus far. The main plot also begins rather slowly and takes quite a bit of time to develop. This is not the game for the impatient and easily bored. Sidequests typically are, again, good, but not great. There are some real gems in there, though. I mean, it's a Bioware game. Perhaps the biggest strike against it is the binary morality system. You tend to either be the nicest and most compassionate person in the galaxy, or be a psychotic space Hitler. That being said, the game is classic Star Wars in design, so it's likely that is purposeful, but you should still be aware you are unlikely to be morally or ethically challenged or questioned in any way during this game (very much unlike its sequel, KOTOR 2).
Characters: I'm giving this its own section because I feel like it deserves it. Optional party member quests and dialogue are a large part of this games overall story. Most party members in KOTOR are not particularly interesting, and it's likely you'll only do the backstories for characters you do find interesting. But most of this is entirely optional, so it doesn't really count as a strike against the game, and is a nice addition.
Sound: Music is by Jeremy Soule so of course it's good. It is not classic John Williams, however. Take that as you will. It can either be good or bad.
Graphics: Very dated. I don't feel the urge to go into greater detail as you can just look at screenshots above.
Aesthetic: It is mostly bright and colorful without overdoing it. Nothing particularly stands out here. It's vibrant where it wants to be vibrant and dark where it wants to be dark. I don't really have anything to compare it to. Again, I recommend just looking at screenshots.
Conclusion: It's a very good game, and definitely worth playing if you enjoy this style of combat and are patient enough with the story. You don't even need to be into Star Wars to have a lot of fun with this game.
TL;DR: It's a quintessential Star Wars story (albeit a very slow paced one) mixed with D&D style gameplay and sidequests. If that sounds like something you'd like, you will probably enjoy this game. Be aware that if you try to run it on anything newer than Windows XP you can have problems, especially with the cutscenes. You may have to do some troubleshooting to get it to work.

It's been a long time coming but I owe this game and its successor, KOTOR II, a review out of respect and great love for the series. Years after I finished both games, a decade after the initial release, I can't help but to look back on what can be considered the greatest Star War games and the best the RPG genre has to offer. I entered the Star Wars scene only recently, after avoiding the franchise for so long, and these are the games that made me want to saturate myself in its lore and history.
This in itself is a feat considering how outdated these games are. Needless to say, the graphics are
. I'd put them on par with games like Fallout: New Vegas, which is a similarly ageless classic that survived the test of time. I'd also say that the graphics here are somewhat better than New Vegas' in terms of lighting and color, and if I had to guess it's because of KOTOR's liberal of black and cleaner, darker color schemes. Regardless, the worth of a video game is not determined solely by its appearance or budget and that is not why either franchise is so spectacular.
Enter the KOTOR realm of sci-fi fantasy, space-opera RPG goodness, with a complex universe, spades of history, and a plot that not only manages to pull everything off, but ultimately be coherent and fulfilling. Have you played a recent open-world RPG that promises to deliver freedom and a good time worth the money, yet feels somehow... lacking? Or even disappointing? The KOTOR games give all and more - and what I mean by this is that the story, character arcs and world are so complete that there's nothing that you can change about them. Others may disagree and say that's exaggerating, but it's clear that whoever wrote these games wrote them to its maximum potential, which is something sorely lacking in modern games, especially ones based off popular franchises. At least on a personal level, having played reknowned games like Skyrim and GTAV, this game is up there on the "most brilliant games I'll never forget" list.
Like a true RPG, KOTOR is deeply ingrained with choices that matter. Your character matters. Your relationships matter, your words matter. Anyone who knows anything about Star Wars knows that a person's choices can lead them down the path of light or the fall to the Dark side. You can decide to be a Jedi, a Sith, or someone in between and all those around you will
and react and that affects the story. And I mean this in the literal sense that the story, scenes, and ending differ vastly upon the path you choose, not just some ending cutscene tailored to a few dialogue options in the game.
Gameplay, like the graphics, is simplistic but in the end you just can't deny that double-sided lightsabers are awesome. More than the fighting, I enjoyed the exploration, though I hesitate to call it open-world. KOTOR is all about travelling from planet to planet and learning what each world has in store for you and your character.
I was particularly impressed by the scope of history and design woven into these worlds, and perhaps this is because Star Wars is based on an amalgation of human cultures. The universe feels grounded, and that includes intergalatic space travel, special powers, and aliens. It's not in the science and realism of its universe, but the deeply human, emotional connections that are shared across the KOTOR and Star Wars saga among its many species. That's why this game is so highly rated. I can only compare this to universes such as Tolkein's - extensive and relatable even through its most fantasic moments - that you could make another ten movies or games of it and you'd still have material to spare.
I played KOTOR II before the first one, and looking back I'm not sure why, but I actually recommend playing it in that order - KOTOR I has a (slightly) more linear story but features a certain plot event that I feel is the proper climax of both games.
In any case, if you love Star Wars, or if you don't care about Star Wars but love science fiction (the games are nothing like the movie trilogies btw), if you love intense story-driven games that put you in charge of the story-telling, or if you just plain love a fantasic game, this is a game to remember. And what a fantasic game it is. Much love to Bioware and Obsidian, you are the creators of miracles and legends.

tl;dr, Improved mechanics over FEAR 1 and a move towards action over horror.
While the first game (and it's DLC's) strove to find a balance between spooks and shoots, the sequel aims towards action over horror. There are still spooks abound in the sequel, but the lean towards action can make or break the game for players. That being said, (almost) everything from the first game carries over and is improved. Guns handle much better than they did in the first one, they also do more damage. The flashlight and Slo-Mo are both much better this time around as well. The cover is the (for the time) standard crouch behind objects, and the weapons are somewhat balanced.
Also, the slide kick (Dash forward and press melee) is awesomely broken. Unfortunately, as is often the case with 2nd games in a horror franchise, this game is a transitional game between the spooks of the first game and the action of the third game.
I also never played the multi-player so I have no opinion on it.
+
Much improved mechanics in every aspect
The action parts are done much better than the first
You mostly no longer need an entire clip to kill one guy
The horror is still intact
-
The scares are much less frequent
The levels are much more linear
The game is (much) shorter than the first one
Fear 3 does the action better
Fear 1 does the scares better
7/10

This game may be older, but it is considered a cult classic to this day. The Hitman titles before this one are the perfect brew of quirky, challenging stealth and humor. However, this one is regarded as the best in the franchise because it not only had the elements of the first couple games, but implemented a disguise system, upgraded accident system and above all: unleashed the freedom of sandbox gameplay (something the newest title "Absolution" did not particularily have).
Basic Overview: You are one of the world's best assassins who was created in a laboratory as a killing machine, plain and simple. Your alias: 47. You work for a smoke and mirrors agency under a mysterious woman named "Diana" who provides you with targets and mission details. The targets are larger than life, often rediculous and have prices on their heads that can set any average joe up for the rest of his days. The cleaner the hit, the more money in it for you. Your shady bosses have some international pull so weapons and certain things can be planted on the job site to make your work easier. Other than that, you do how you see fit. You can go in there gunning if you think you're strong enough to overpower your target's security. If you don't fancy getting shot, you can sneak in wearing a disguise, infiltrate your mark's hideout, then give them the drop when nobody's looking. There's also the option of say, rigging a chandeliear to fall on somebody's noggin slap-stick style or making someone have an "unfortunate accident" by falling over a railing. The possibilities are endless! However, whatever inconspicous things you do such as leaving evidence, getting seen by witnesses or getting your cover blown can effect how easily you're detected in future missions. You aren't the only one in the Blood Money game either, any job could be a set up! Are you willing to risk the odds for the payout?
Cons: The controls seem rather "stiff" and not fluid, especially when moving slowly or pivoting on the spot. There are sometimes annoying glitches such as people falling through floors/doors/walls when pushed and alerting your enemies. The AI can be extremely unintelligent and rag-doll glitchy which can bring some comedy into the gameplay, however, they are crack shots and can be extremely unforgiving, especially when glitched within a close proximity to 47s character. This game is sometimes not compatible in default settings with certain hardware/Windows versions and may crash/not run at all, but a simple patch and or resolution change often fixes these issues. Some level design may seem lazy in parts, but it's still nice to explore your whole environment, which is part of the Hitman experience.
Overall: I give this game an 8.5/10 given it is one of the funest games I have ever played and I still play it from time to time. I reccomend this game if you like stealth games, but you want a hint of free rome and added options in there. If you like linear stealth action, I would recommend the next title in the franchise "Absolution". The next game, simply called "Hitman" boasts it will bring the sandbox element back into its gameplay. I think anything like Absolution's systems with Blood Money's freedom it would be a win/win! Fingers crossed!

A fantastic gem of a game.
The aim of the game is relatively simple, take a crew of three and discover as much as possible and become the world's most renowned explorer. How you achieve this is up to you. Do you want to be known as a devious researcher, a prized fighter or perhaps you simply want to bask in your own glory. There are several different ways to play, with various different expansions giving the game hours of replayability.
Encounters are relatively simple, yet also fun and engaging. Buffs and debuffs become very important and the mood of the battlefield has consequences. Trying to be friendly to an aggressive opponent for instance, would put you at a disadvantage.
Each team has a cptain that offers various perks to the expeditions and can help boost your final score significantly. Each character (16 in total) has their own perk. As you play the game, you can unlock more captains to add more variey. Crew members also have a set of skills that will assist you in finding treasures, not every treasure you find on the map will be yours; you need the right people for the job. The skills are further developed and acquired as you progress in the game. Certain characters traits, being mean, guillable or even hating coffee even come into play with additional dialogue options or events in certain places.
The actual exploration at first is amazing, while the number of expeditions is static, the maps are somewhat random and certain things don't always spawn. Lategame, this can also be quite frustrating when you're trying to farm that one treasure you don't have. This will take quite some time to achieve, though.
There's also quite a bit of humour in here, which adds to an amusing experience. The art specifically is fantastic and some of the faces the crewmembers pull really tickles me.
All in all a highly enjoyable experience that I can't recommend enough. I've been playing the game for over 100 hours and I'm still discovering things!

This is an excellent, simple puzzle game. I love the minimalist aesthetics. I originally bought this game for my iPhone, then bought it again when it was released on the Windows store, and now bought it a third time on Steam. The Steam release removes the in app purchases (hints are now free) and also adds controller support, which is fantastic.
The game distils the Tomb Raider format down to its essence: you'll play through a large number of small(ish) linear levels, where you will have to shoot wild animals, dodge others, and solve puzzles to reach the end and progress to the next level. The game is essentially turn-based, with enemies moving only when you make your move. You can also hunt around (using the right stick on the controller) for vases that contain items, which is great for your inner hunter-gatherer.
It's a small game that you'll probably finish in a few hours or so, but it's a pleasant experience, with great visual design, and a few fun puzzles along the way. It's an excellent way to waste a few hours and I couldn't recommend it highly enough. I, for one, will play through the entire game yet again and am more than eager to do so.

I'll keep this short because its still very much an Alpha. Overall, I've enjoyed my first play and I would encourage others to get behind this game so that it can be made amazing because the potential is there.
I've left this "review" just as much for the developer as anything.
Pros
======
1)Even at this stage the whole feel of the game is enticing and really made me want to delve into things. Thats a big draw for both DK fans and newcomers.
2) The humour is dark/ sarcastic/ pratchett-eque enough, without being its own clique thing.
3) The production chains make sense.
Cons
======
1) I Initially felt a little out-of-control of what was going on, of my minions and dungeon, whereas in the DK games you feel more responsible for the whole upkeep of the dungeon.
2) The tutorial needs to be more idiot-proof (ie me proof, as I was left a little at sea in certain circumstances)...easy fix.
3) I felt the icons weren't as clear and intuitive as they could have been.
4) Some sounds need a major replace...pickaxe digging for example.

If you've been waiting for a true successor to Dungeon Keeper, as I have, then I think you've found it. Certainly shows the most promise out of all the games inspired by DK that I've tried over the years. The 3D dungeons are awesome, although some way of building over pits would be welcome.
Resources come in more types than in DK2 (Which only had gold, iirc). Here you must actually manage production lines as well as mine the appropriate resources. You can also make resource trades with the surface world, which makes things a bit easier if you end with an overabundance of some resources -although the available trades are limited. Traps require a lot more planning than in DK - pressure plates and wires rather than self-activated when something appears in range.
Can't wait to see how it develops, with more rooms, more creatures (Friendly and not) and several other things (there's a list on their forums)

The premise of this game is fine. It's a fairly effective short-term turn-based strategy game with a few good mechanics to make it function. But that's it. It has all the basic parts needed and not a single bit more.
There needs to be at least one more skill tree line / unit type to really give the game something above the most shallow level of mechanics. There also needs to be something that makes different games more varied than just map types. Unique units/upgrades/buffs/debuffs tied to different thief types would go a long way to improving the non-existent replayability (i had assumed there was some sort of bonus to the different thieves i was playing as through the campaign but, it's all the same). As is one game isnt really any different from the next, so it gets old quickly.
If this game was in alpha I could see it becoming good. As is, I can't recommend it unless it's on sale for 5 bucks and you've got 5 hours to kill.

Although Dwelvers adds a few new mechanics to this genre, such as resources instead of gold and being able to dig downwards, it is in too early of a stage to be worth buying unless you just want to support the development.

When I first saw this, i thought it was a lame ripoff of the dungeon keeper games, or even their younger estranged step-sister, the Dungeons games.  Since the dungeon keeper sort of genera is incredibly difficult to nail correctly, i had absolutely no hope for this game.  So I picked up the free demo on their website ((which steam does not have yet,)) and gave it a shot to see how badly it failed.  45 minutes later, i was purchasing the full game.  Or rather, the pre-alpha.  Even as a pre-alpha game that is no where near complete, it is a LOT of fun with only one minor visual bug that i've found so far.  I just spent roughly...7 hours i believe playing the sandbox in a single play.   The game is a little difficult at the beginning.  There is a minotaur maze in the game that I had wandered into on accident intended as your end game challenge.  I was slaughtered, barely managing to block off the minotaurs before retreating.  But the next 5 hours of my game play was a satisfying mix of raiding smaller groups of weaker enemies and looking for new armor and weapons I could give to my fighters, and developing infrastructure to support my rapidly growing horde.  every complaint I have about this game is due purely to the fact that it is in alpha.  Resources are a bit imbalanced with wood being painfully difficult to get ((but a good incentive to leave your base and explore the underworld)) and stone far far too plentiful with massive piles of it stacking up in my store rooms.  ((this gave me incentive to construct more rooms and find more resources))  There was a single broken texture having to do with placing a skull candle in a prison cell breaking the texture of the wall below it.  However, this will not stop me from playing much much more of this game!  About 7 hours into the game and only on easy, so I cant wait to amp up the difficulty!
TL;DR This game is freakin sweet and an incredible reboot of the dungeon master genera of game.  I highly recommend playing it and beg you to forgive the slightly off balancing issue, as it is still in alpha and will be fixed soon, I am sure.  Play the demo to see if you like the genera and if you do, BUY IT!

This game is a shameless copycat of Dungeon Keeper with some additions/changes. Borrowing or totally copying the great grandmaster is no shame though. Why reinvent the wheel when it already works perfect?
So, the good things first:
- It's a shameless copycat of Dungeon Keeper with some additions/changes :-)
- The major addition is: 3D. You not only build a 2D-Maze, you build it up and down too.
- Considering the early access: It works! No crashes/big bugs in my whole playtime yet (sadly this has become a "good" point. Should be default, but as Dylan said: The times, they are a changing...)
- It's cute and cuddly, if you consider that a "plus" :)
- Trading routes seem like a nice idea. Could need a little work in the details though.
- The UI looks well thought out. You can acces most things with two clicks or two keys. As a keyboard-user that suits me well
And here're the downfalls:
- The music is annoying. Just after some minutes i just wanted to punch it in the face. With a brick. Multiple times. Maybe just a matter of taste
- The whole 3D-Maze could get a little frustrating. It get's bigger and bigger, deeper and deeper and if building on multiple places i always loose oversight. Maybe you're smarter :-)
- Not that much rooms yet. After some minutes you're done with the basics, from there on you're "just" exploring, leveling, killing.
So far it makes a solid impression for an early-access-title. If you're into Dungeon Keeper or similar games, go get it! It's fairly priced too! If there will be more rooms added, it will definately be a keeper (no pun intended).
If you're not sure if you'd buy this one or War For The Overworld: This one is the "cute" sister with some things different than WFTO which tries to be Dungeon Keeper 3 (which is totally ok!).

Guacamelee is another one of those action platformers set in quirky colorful world with an over the top story and a silly sense of humor. If you are like me and you are sick and tired of this genre I sincerely recommend you to try out Guacamelee.
At the first glance Guacamelee really seams just like any other game from this genre. What saves it from the awful fate of mediocrity is it's gameplay. While most games concentrate on one or two unique mechanics, in Guacamelee you have a wide variety of special moves that are use both for combat and traversing the environment, and sometimes for both tings at once. Which is cool, but isn't the thing that made me love this game. The awesome bit is that while the platforming is simple at first and requires you to use only one or two special abilities at once, later on you'll need to be able to preform very complex  combinations of you abilities. The satisfaction of pulling off some of the more challenging platforming segments is wonderful. And the same goes for combat. The only thing I didn't like about it is the pace at which you acquire new abilities. It's slow. I didn't notice the first time I played trough the game, but on my second run on hard mode in the beginning of the game I felt handicapped. Another thing I noticed only ind hard mode is that the boss hit boxes aren't all that grate. Every now and again fighting a boss I got hit by it's attack when the animation of that attack had already played out. If the game had been more combat oriented this had really been a big problem for me, but since I only noticed it a couple times on hard mode it's only a minor annoyance.
And wile the games artstyle doesn't  set it apart from all the other indie games, you can't deny that it looks quite nice. Simplified blocky shapes and the bold color pallet works well together. Wen it comes to the visual part of the game I only have tow criticisms. First - I have no idea why would anyone think that it's necessary to have a thick black line always present on the top of the screen. There definitely  has to be an more ascetically pleasing way to make the health and stamina meter always visible. Also there is no reason to have pause button prompt always be displayed at the top of the screen. Second - every now and again there ware situations when the color of a particular enemy matched the backgrounds color which made identifying their attacks difficult at times. And wile for the most of the game it's a non issue since health enemies aren't that strong and give a lot of health orbs once killed, if you are fighting a boss on hard mode where it can kill you in 5 or 6 hits it's a bit annoying not to be able to see it.
When it comes to the games story I really can't tell you anything. I read just the first four or five dialogs, realized that I absolutely didn't care and stopped reading. I really hope that there will come a day when indie devs will realize that many people don't care about the story in a game like this and will start to put in options that allow to skip story at faster pace. Because in Guacamelee you have to press a button for every line a characters says. It takes ages to click trough some of the more lengthier dialogs. And it absolutely enrages me when there is a conversation before a boss fight that is repeated every time that you try to defeat the boss. STOP THAT! No one wants to click trough that♥♥♥♥♥♥again and again. Good thing this game only has four instances of this.
All in all it's a surprisingly competent action platformer. It may lack the design elegance of games like Super Meat Boy, but it's grate no the less.

The choices presented in this game are morally very complicated. If you go through the game determined to always make the light side choice or always the dark, you'll be missing out on a lot of what makes this game great. Instead, try to articulate to yourself exactly why the choice you're making is rationally right.
For example, your first choice is how to respond to a spoiled brat in a cantina who thinks you're her waiter. If you embarass her by pointing out that you're not her waiter, she will later ambush you with two thugs and you'll have to kill them. If you care about preserving life, you have to adopt a servile attitude and let the brat believe that you're her waiter, which is just so... undignified... maybe even dishonorable. After all, that which can be destroyed by the truth should be. But her thugs would be destroyed by her irrationality. Maybe the thugs are evil and killing them would improve the world, but that's not known. I chose the truth. The world does not bend to accomodate one's irrationality, and neither do I. That spoiled brat's attitude is going to get people killed sooner or later, better to have her cross me now and learn her lesson, than to let her go on murdering people on a whim until something else stops her. There's really no way to avoid someone dying here.
Another example, drunk men start a fight with you, do you kill them and take their stuff? They started it, but their judgment is impaired. You can intimidate them to leave you alone, and then they'll probably find someone weaker to pick on. I intimidated them, because I didn't want to kill people over being belligerent drunks.
Another example, you witness bounty hunters about to drag away a merchant who owes money to a local corrupt businessman. What's the right thing to do? Intervene and kill the bounty hunters? Why? Is what they're doing wrong or do you just dislike their attitude? Are they evil or just doing a dirty job? Later on in the game you have the option of collecting a bounty on another man who defaulted on his loan (identical situation), do you kill him, give him money to pay his dept, or just let him keep hiding? Why?
The game is basically a series of moral puzzles. Just don't get sucked into thinking of morality in the game's terms (light vs dark side). There are several different motives and principles involved that I've been able to identify so far:
1. Fighting for the good (killing evil people improves the world)
2. Saving lives (people are capable of redemption)
3. Consent (non-initiation of force)
4. Curiosity
5. Honor
6. Wholesomeness
7. Power
None of these principles or motives are in complete agreement. Some compromise between them must be found in every situation.

I'm honestly shocked at how much I'm enjoying this game.
This was one of THOSE games. You know what I'm talking about- one of the games you get in a bundle, add to your account, and then kinda forget about it.
Abbey Games made another title I enjoyed a lot, Reus. And while I had throughly enjoyed that game, this one kinda flew under the radar. So much so that I failed to realize they were made by the same folks (art style was a dead give away, shame on me for not noticing).
REGARDLESS, the game.
If you were to hold a gun to my head and ask me to tell you what games it was like, I'd say
"Hey, woha, whats with the gun?! I'd tell you regardless, jeez!"
And if you were a normal person and ask me to tell you what games this was like, I'd have to say it's like...Fire Emblem with elements of Civilization 5?
Fire Emblem in the sense of the tactical movement of your characters, the RPS style of combat. Civ 5 for the very simplified map movement, discovering new resources, upgrading and progressing through tech trees, etc.
Gameplay starts off by assembling a team of exploreres. First you pick a captain, then two crew members to round out the team (usually in ways that compliment the captains strengths/weaknesses). Then you set off across the globe to look for treasure and adventure!
The game offers multiple encounters and choices based off who you have in your crew, what you've chosen to level up for those characters, their equipment, and previous interactions during your adventure, So it really begs for multiple play throughs to see what combinations yeild the most interesting results.
The game is exceptionally fun, and I highly reccomend it, especially to those that enjoy rouge-lites, tactical RPGs, and management games.
At it's current price point (21.99 CDN), I'd say it's well worth full price.

Okay, let's start with a simple statement about Battleborn: Battleborn is a game rife with marketing issues and inconvenient circumstances that, at its core, is a very fun and entertaining game that has only increased my respect for Gearbox.
Battleborn is a hero shooter/MOBA, which differs from multiple similar games like Overwatch and Paladins because it has universal mechanics for characters that are used to fight, and unique mechanics designated to maybe one or two characters in the roster. You pick one character at the beginning of a match or mission, and then you are stuck playing them for the rest of the match. This leaves a lot more competitive potential to the game than its charisma and PvE system will let on, but we'll touch on that later.
The game has more competitive capacity than most hero shooters I've seen due to its somewhat complex gear system and its restrictive idea of team composition. Now, that said, the best part about battleborn is that the game introduced a system called the Helix System, which from my experience, allows one player to potentially fill two roles if they orient themselve for one or another. The Helix system provides you two choices of upgrades per level, allowing you to pick one only. For example, you can play someone and be provided with the option to increase your maximum shield capacity or be given 30% more damage for your auto attacks... But then again, I suppose you're not here for the tutorial anyways.
The PvE scene is amazingly, not low-effort. The dialogue is funny, if not a bit cheesy at times, and the characters all have a unique charm about them that feels signature to a Gearbox IP (which you'll definitely see if you've played Borderlands), Allowing for a lot of bold and charismatic characters to come together with a decent amount of lore behind them to explain it as well-- provided some suspension of disbelief-- as any good story-oriented game does. Every character has a good reason to be there, and, while granted, it's not exactly a novel-quality work, they even have lore explaining things down to the PvP. If you liked games like Borderlands and you like a game that has decent story around it, this is a great choice, and unlike most games that have a mix of Campaign and Competitive Multiplayer, neither side feels really tacked on.
They have the trademark Capture-Point gamemode and a gamemode akin to most minion-oriented lane push games a la DotA or League, but the game encourages high action and map control off the bat by not allowing you to have passive income for your in-match currency. Instead, deposits of the currency are found across the map and are just as much an objective as the camps that summon additional minions for your team. The bad thing about this, is that it leaves a game entirely open to stomping, and if you get your first sentry (tower) destroyed, it's likely you'll lose due to their massively increased pressure. The good thing about this is the fact that it more or less requires you to play out your early game well, and you learn how to spend your in-match currency wisely. Right now, the gear system is in a really good position where, the better your gear is, the more it costs, and the worse off it is, the less it costs, even reaching no-cost prices if it's a piece of common gear with an additional negative stat on top of the original stat. If you don't have any gear, PVP offers an option to keep you relevant by allowing you to level faster by spending your money on structures that help defend or push out minion waves, providing experience.
Now, for the nitty-gritty of what everyone needs to know: This game is suffering. It's suffering from a low playerbase and sorely missing a few crucial things that I think would lead to not only a healthier, but a more enjoyable game. The game so desperately needs either an in-game block list to prevent matchmaking with traditional pubstompers queueing in 5s, or it needs an option to change the queue's mmr search system. Right now, there are so few people playing on PvP that while, admittedly, I'm max Command rank, I still get matched up against people of a depressingly higher skill than me. I can understand a game's mmr system screwing up, as I've even seen it this year with League, but the game also lacks a LeaverBuster system, which can lead to a somewhat toxic culture of either forcing a surrender as early as possible, ot leaving with no punishment. And I think the worst thing about this game's negative points is that it suffers from bad publishing and bad marketing.
2K dug this game in a hole by claiming they had no idea how to market it, when-- if we're being absolutely honest-- They have no idea how to market ANY game. Borderlands got popular off of its own reputation and word of mouth before BL2 came out, and the only games beyond Gearbox games that they ever tried to market were already successful, already popular, low-risk series. 2K has an uncanny property of choking the life out of new and independent IPs before they even reach the shelves, and I believe that this game isn't the only one that can testify to that (looking at you, Evolve). 2K rushed the game out to compete with Overwatch, knowing that Blizzard was a far larger and more dominant company that was already prepared to stomp any game that even barely used a similar set of mechanics into bargain-bin dust, even going so far as to take up 50% of TOTAL online adspace for any games at one point in time, and rushing most of their work to compete with any hero shooters being developed at the time. The game came out unpolished, compared to a game it really wasn't all that similar to, and was amassed with hatred from die-hard Overwatch fans simply for being there in the presence of Overwatch.
At its core, Battleborn is a good game that suffered severely from trashy, uninvolved marketing, almost monopoly-level competitive mindsets, and a publisher that cared so little for the game post-launch that they were willing to stab it in the back and bury it in the woods as a last-ditch effort.
But the developers care. The developers have been more interactive and personable than any I've seen at most companies or even indie groups. They're usually out streaming updates every time they happen or talking to people in their forums, and some of them even play pretty regularly. And if what Battleborn Day had to offer doesn't stand as a testament to how these developers will reach out and serve a community that's passionate about the product they created, then I don't know what will. The community here is passionate about the game, and goes out of their way to make their own community events, where people will guide new players and try to teach them anything they want to learn.
And it really hurts to see that go unnoticed simply because business took its course as usual.

is a light worker placement game where you play the head of a thief guild set in a world echoing Oliver Twist.

Each stage your guild competes against another organization on a grid map of several city blocks.
The goal of most stages is to earn some number of points. Whichever team first earns that many points is the winner.
There are two forms of currency: Coins and Lanterns.
Coins are used to hire henchman into your guild.
Lanterns are used to expand your tech tree.
At the beginning of each stage, you begin with just yourself and can take 2 actions (which you can increase via the tech tree). As the master thief, your player character is responsible for clearing fog of war, robbing buildings, and killing enemies.
There are several kinds of henchmen you can hire, though each must be unlocked via the tech tree:
- Urchin: sent to control key buildings. Different buildings give different benefits depending on the number of Urchins. For example, a Bank gives 1 Gold for 1 Urchin and 3 Gold for 3 Urchins.
- Thug: Can block a space for 2 turns
- Gang: Can attack other units or evict enemy Urchins. Starts with 2 hearts, which you can increase by 1 for each Thug you add to it.
- Saboteur: Places a trap in one of the buildings you control that lasts for 2 turns. Any enemy character attempting to infiltrate the building will get stunned.
- Truant Officer: Can evict all Urchins at a single location.
- Assassin: one-time use. Does 6 damage
Points are earned several ways:
- Assassination Contracts:  Kill some character that spawns on the map. After each target, the next target has 1 more heart.
- Blackmail:  Placing (and keeping) 3 Urchins in a Church
- Bribe: paying 5 lanterns, an amount that increases by 1 after each Bribe
- Other: Some stages have alternative ways to score points.
+ Good artwork.
+ Some variance across stages
Several of the stages have special rules or features, which keeps the game fresher.
+ Game explains mechanics well
+ Three difficulty levels (Easy, Normal, Hard)
I've only played Normal so far. Normal may be a little too easy? I only lost once throughout the campaign and that was when first starting out.
+ Appropriate campaign length
Any longer and the game would have started to really drag
* Gameplay is straightforward and offers a few different strategies, but is probably a little too simple.
- Unremarkable story, setting, and characters
I'm happy there's a story. The setting successfully invokes an Oliver Twist-ian feel.
But, there's nothing new or interesting.
Characters are never really developed.
- Watching the enemy's turn takes too long. You can skip it entirely, but you then lose potentially important information about what the enemy had done.  I wish they had a speed-up option.
- Emma seems too young to fulfill her role. Or maybe the artwork just makes her look too young?

Penumbra Overture might be the scariest game I have ever played. Not because things are jumping out at you from the dark, or because there are rivers of blood everywhere you look, but because there is none of that and you are just alone in the dark. There is a constant feeling of peril and you don't quite know what to be afraid of, or what form the next threat will take. Yet you know it is there, somewhere around the corner, waiting for you. So you crawl through the shadows, afraid to turn on the flashlight, listening to blood hurling snarls of feral dogs nearby, knowing that if you are discovered, the pickaxe in your hand will do little to protect you. And even when all is quiet and you know it is just you, that mere thought becomes your new tormentor as the walls close in and the darkness becomes unbearable, because every evidence suggests that many people found themselves here before you and none of them ever left. And just when you think your nerves are at their limits, you find yourself in an adrenaline-fueled sprint, desperately clawing for your life, trying to lose your pursuers.
I hope that by now it is clear that the atmosphere in Penumbra is superb. Graphics are somewhat dated, but you can easily run the game in any modern resolution simply by editing the configuration file. The way you swing tools such as pickaxes and hammers by actually moving the mouse back and forth is a unique idea and sets this game apart from the rest. I guess, I only have two complaints. First, the game eventually becomes quite predictable as you learn that most scares are triggered by picking up story items. And second, most of the items like flashlight batteries, flares, painkillers, and beef jerky are useless, or rather I have never found a use for them since the character can see perfectly well in the dark and heals on his own over time. There is also a lock you pick up in the beginning and a broom later on that I never figured out what to do with. These items left me puzzled, unlike the actual puzzles you will need to solve throughout the game to progress, which are very simple, with the solution usually in the very same room as the obstacle. If you played Amnesia... this is much better.

Okay, time to burn through the review for another game that I haven't played in literally years but still feel entitled to sharing my opinion on. Like most of what I write, this is based on very vague memories coupled with absolutely no additional research or refreshers on what the game was like.
Penumbra Overture is definitely the weakest game that Frictional has ever released, unless they did something prior to Penumbra that I'm just not aware of. The decision to include combat was a huge misstep for the series, since the AI in this game is actually fairly exploitable if you can kill your enemies. In most Frictional games (or any of the dozens of other Amnesia clones about playing hide-and-shriek), I tend to spend a minute or so hiding in one place when a monster is around before slowly stalking it and determinign the patrol route so I can sneak on by. In Overture, my first instinct whenever I enter a new area is to find where the crates are that I can hide on top of, then goad dogs into running over so I can leap to safely and bash their skulls in. Once I have a pile of dog corpses I can just explore the room at my leisure, removing the tension that should be consistent throughout titles like these. Debatably I could just not exploit the system and use combat as the last resort it was probably designed to be, but a big part of horror is not having these kind of options open to you. It would be hard to really get into the spirit of fear if in the back of my mind I knew that I could just bash some skulls in.
Dog fights aside, the puzzles are exactly what you would expect from a Frictional title: mostly inventory-based point-and-click adventure style puzzles with occasional environmental puzzles to break up the tedium. If I remember correctly there are also spiders sometimes, as well as a big worm at one point? I seem to recall the worm being a highlight, but it's all kind of a blur.
The story is, as always, as there as it needs to be in these titles, even if the writing for Red seemed a little inconsistent and try-hard crazy. Ultimately I would still suggest that people play it, especially if they want to get the full Penumbra experience.

Penumbra Overture is one of the first games released by Frictional and while it is far from as well rounded as their other games it is atmospheric enough to set up the story for the Penumbra series without beign too dull. Besides Outlast, this is one amazing horror game for several reasons.
Story Rich: I've watched and played lots of horror games and about 80% of them have the same thing, just run away from monsters and don't get killed. However, this game does have the same aspect, but has more to it. Every stage or "chapter" you complete allows the story to become more clear and you become more interested about what will happen next.
Characters: The personality for each character makes the story a little more "light-hearted" as time goes on. Instead of the game feeling completely dark and terrifying, you might get some jokes to reassure yourself that these are people, not robots. The main character and "Red" were a great mixture to show how a game's plot can really be.
Mixture of puzzles and horror: Puzzles and horror are wierd genres to blend with each other, but for this game they did it perfectly. This is a game that forces you to be brave because you have to focus solving puzzles while also trying to hide from monsters in the shadows, which makes it scarier.
Music: During certain points if the story you hear different music throughout the game. Some for puzzles, some for hiding. Music can give people unsettling feelings in certain situations and this game did it fantastically from start to finish.
Graphics: For a game made in 2007 the graphics are actually pretty good. Not much to say about this part, like if graphics are good they're good.
Hope you try this game out and enjoy this review.

This game has much to offer - quality animation style, bright colours, and a quirky combat system. The game doesn't have much in the way of story, but it doesn't need it. It follows the traditional platformer style - love interest has been captured by some bad guy, good guy pursues bad guy to save love interest - you know how it goes.
Anyway, the game starts with baby steps. It can feel slightly frustrating when you first play it, but when you learn all the different "moves/concepts" of the combat system, you appreciate why they started so slowly. This combat system is, quite frankly, fantastic. When the enemies start gaining shields that you have to break, or they go into another dimension that you can't attack, you have to think quickly and act accordingly - button-mashing only gets you so far in this game.
The difficulty mark-up is erratic, though. It starts fairly easy, and then the last part of the game is wincingly hard. It almost killed the experience entirely as it was so needlessly hard - I like difficult games, but this game's difficulty can offer you little by way of dodging/returning damage. Sometimes, you just get ♥♥♥♥ed over without doing anything wrong. I eventually triumphed, but only after a fair few tries.
I'd recommend this game to anyone. It's fast, colourful, funny and challenging. What more can you ask for?
