A fantastic game that has suffered a string of bad luck since shortly after release. While virtually all of the problems have been addressed (balance changes still happen regularly, graphical issues have been addressed) and plenty of new high quality content has been added (with more coming), the only real problem that I can admit to is a small player base: if you try to find matches purely through public matchmaking, you're probably going to be disappointed. However, the existing community is extremely loyal and active.
When you start playing, check out the official forums and join the official unofficial Discord channel to find people to group with and help you learn the various mechanics, maps, and other initially daunting elements that prevent people from enjoying a truly stellar game: for one thing, the level of character customization is significantly higher than for other similar games (characters level up in matches/missions, allowing you to choose helix options to change how they play; you also create your own gear loadout from a wide number of gear choices that you collect to further tweak your stats). With the population where it is now, you're basically refusing to give it a chance if you try to do public matchmaking.
Gameplay-wise, the thing that most separates BB from the pack, in my opinion, is the PvE. It's well written, fun, appropriately challenging, and thoroughly replayable (especially the new operations), and it's something that none of its competitors has, afaik. They really should be pushing the game's PvE elements more rather than trying to make it out to be some PvP-centric game with a smattering of PvE for when you can't find people.

Dwelvers has a lot of potential.  The tutorial is a bit lacking in certain areas but makes up for it with its humor and light-hearted nature.  Being a fan of "Dungeons" and "A Game of Dwarves", I was able to dive into this without too much trouble.  For those of you not familiar with games of this genre, you'll have resources that you'll need to collect and resource chains that you'll have to construct in order to grow your base.  You can dig out blocks in order to make rooms and then seed these rooms with various objects.  I'm anxious to see what else the game will offer once it officially launches.

Just recently found this game and preordered it before it came to steam.  So even though its not showing I have a lot of play time I have been playing the game for about 2 weeks.  In my opinion this game is moving the direction that I would think that dungeon keeper would have gone if it was still being made.
War for the overworld is great when it works which is almost never for me but when it does work its got nothing on Dwelvers at all.  There is more fun and always something to do in Dwelvers.  You get most all the good things from Dungeon Keeper, though you cant slap your imps... However a bunch more resources to handle, and you have to keep your creatures happy.  I tried the other day to see what would happen if I didnt make beer for my orcs and well I thought nothing to bad would happen however my orcs got really mad and started killing off my other creatures.  And thats just one of the many things you have to take care of in this game.  You have actual production chains for farming and feeding your people.  You can setup your rooms however you like instead of just dragging an area and its all automatic from there.  I like the ability to customize my rooms and even add some decorations to them.  Being able to build a fireplace in my bedrooms or barrels in the walls in my cookery room.  These little touches gives the game something extra on top of the dig rooms and fight puny humans.  The cyclotaurs are a nice thing that when you defeat them for now its kinda the end of the game, but they are harder to defeat than it looks or sounds.
You also can trade with the overworld for resources, once you find a ladder up, and eventually we will be able to go above ground and do stuff up there.  For now the above ground stuff is just a preview button but you can at least get kinda an idea.  You also have to craft weapons and armor that unlock as you find them so you can equip your creatures with stuff to make them better in fights as well as training them up to do better.
For such an early build of the game there is tons of content and for the moment it seems to be bug free.  However since I have had the game there were bugs but with help from the community they were found and squashed really really really fast.  When 0.8 came out originally I downloaded it noticed a bug and then 4 hours later it was fixed and the updated version was released to the public.  The Developer Rasmus is really on top of everything, I am seriously impressed.  He also is very friendly and you can tell that he really cares about this game and the players.
Overall the game has been a great experience so far with everything and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an actual game that improves on dungeon keeper

+ MANY different ways to play through the game: Combinations of locations and heroes and different strategies allow some serious replayability, espeically considering the amount of outcomes and side-adventures possible for each location.
+ A deep and highly interactive 'combat' system: The way you fight in this game is truly unique: Very similar to a regular tactics RPG in some respects, but completely different in others. Difficult to describe in a short review, but very fun and very satisfying to say the least.

+ Game is priced affordably. Content rich expansion 10 months after release is priced very reasonably, and really adds some goodness.

It's a digital boardgame with the goal to beat a certain highscore. At the beginning you pick 3 units out of 4 categories to make up your party. At the beginning there are only 1 units per category unlocked.
The game consists of four parts in two phases. You can try 5 levels to reach the highscore, each having different properties.
Within the levels you have the discovery part, wherein you navigate a graph which has fog of war, with a vision distance of 1.
You can see what possibly awaits you at next nodes and movement is limited by a resource. (I've seen this in a similar game with a similar name.)
The level's exit is marked at the beginning and running out of fuel makes it so every move reduces the party's stats for the level, so you wanna avoid running out of fuel.
Nodes have stat checks, where you pick one party member and roll the dice. You see the percentage chance before rolling so you just pick the highest.
The other part in this phase is combat. It's turn based combat on a hex grid. There are 3 types of attacks which complement each other (we've seen this in many RPGs). The prevalence of a type determines the type of combat (which can frequently fluctuate) which changes stats. The different types of attacks also have buffs and debuffs. The game tries to bash "violence" and so one of the 3 types is aggression, which often results in fewer resources after the fight and has it's own stats, whereas the other two types, being verbal violence and compliments, sharing their stats, making it easier to gear up for them. The "non-violent" attacks work exactly the same, they just have a different presentation. A very superficial change. You cannot gain inforrmation on enemy units and you cannot tell by their looks if they have ranged attacks, since those can be "verbal". This makes combat rather frustrating as you can get easily surrounded and gangbanged by enemies whom you thought were out of range.
At the end of a level, there is the second phase on the world map. Here you can spend your 3 resources. Purchase gear with gold. Unlock general bonuses with resarch. Increase resource acquisition with reputation. Then pick the next level.
The whole game has an adventure/indiana jones theme.
These kind of boardgames are fun at the beginning and rather random when you play them more often.
I liked that the game let me skip the tutorial completely.
I disliked that the game literally told me to "Stop being so entitled!" and to "Check your privilege!".
The hamfisted denigration of physical violence by slapping on a veneer of verbal violence and "pacifism" was pretty meh.

This game is thouroughly enjoyable for the fans of an FTL-like experience. A charming, challenging and innovative strategy game that depends a bit on luck, but has enough depth to encourage multiple playthroughs.
Stand Out Feature: A rock/paper/scissors combat mechanic which causes moves (both yours and your opponents) to set a "tone" for the encounter, which in turn will setup future moves to become more or less powerful.  In conjunction with being able to design your party fairly freely (either maximized to exploit one of these tones, balanced to handle whatever the enemy throws at you, or anywhere in between those two extremes), this encourages experimentation during combat and creates scenarios in which careful considerations must be made.  In addition to tones, both players and opponents might be put into certain moods by moves used upon them (Excited, Furious, Sadness, etc) which function as a conditional status effect that makes certain moves more or less powerful, adding more calcuations into the decision making process during the player's turn.
Pros: Endearing art style.  Multiple challenge tiers to provide a tailored difficulty.  A large enough cast of characters (all with their own individual skillsets and level paths) and scenarios to choose from to foster replayability.
Cons: Animations become repetitive quickly.  Many non-combat encounters resolved by a % die roll that's not always clearly defined stat wise and will heavily influence your success or failure regarding the overarching goal.
Would Recommend To: Anyone whose a fan of turn based strategy games.  Anyone bored of traditional turn based strategy games looking for a twist on the formula.  Lovers of indie games with solid production value or good price/gameplay content ratios.

Having played Amnesia and SOMA, I needed to go back and play the Penumbra games. While certainly not as crisp or well-rounded as either of those games, Penumbra: Overture is still a great game. Although it's now ten years old, it holds up well and accomplishes more than some games do today.
The strength of Penumbra and relies on its atmosphere. The world you are thrust into is creepy and unsettling. While this first game is not nearly as scary as other games made by Frictional Games, Penumbra: Overture holds its own and is still a solid addition to the horror genre. It feels more like an adventure game with horror elements, though, so it lacks some of the feel of other popular horror titles.
The gameplay is mostly solid throughout and utilizes an inventory system where you pick up necessary items needed to advance the storyline. You also have to solve several puzzles throughout the game, some of these being a little more frustrating than challenging. The biggest flaw in gameplay is immediately noticeable when you encounter an enemy. Unlike other games made by Frictional Games, you do have the option to fight enemies in this game. However, due to the clunky combat controls, this is mostly just frustrating, and nearly impossible versus the spiders in the game. In addition to the difficulty of combat, the inclusion of it in the game detracts from the scariness of it all, ultimately lowering the impact of the game. While engaging in combat is not necessary to progress through the game, it does feel highly out of place here.
Overall, Penumbra: Overture is a solid game. Not as scary as you might expect from a horror game, but still worth picking up and playing through.

It's profoundly derivative, and stuffed with callout after callout to its predecessors - but the execution is tight, the design is very easy on the eyes, and the challenge level is enough to make you feel like you're learning but not so much that it gets frustrating (other than in a few small areas.)

There's a lot to do here and the adventure is fairly challenging (especially on hard mode; oh, Jaguar Javier, you were a worthy opponent). So if you are into Metroidvania formula and not afraid of dying a couple of (hundred) times you should definitely try Guacamelee.

Okay...
My opinion regarding SupCom2 is a little...neutral. The game itself is okay and adds an interesting twist to the SupCom universe. However, it isn't the TRUE successor to the original SupCom game.
For one, the resource system. It just seems...eh. It changed from the positive/negative income and moved to building/unit pricing where you need X amount of resources to buy Y. Doesn't exactly endear me.
Another point is the research tree and research points. Why?! I was perfectly okay with going through three techs. T1, T2, T3. Simple. Easy to understand. But now, I've been given a third resource. I'm a casual gamer, I don't do competitive stuff very often. Rant at me if you wish, but getting a third resource was a pain in the carping♥♥♥♥♥ When I tried to move to focus on one thing, something else suffers. Honestly, I would forget about research and then half way through the match, remember I can upgrade my stuff. So, meh. Not enthused.
I do have a pet peeve. Why can't I order engineers to assist in building something? In SupCom original, build time could be cut down if you assigned an engineer to work on it, of course at the cost of using more resources. But it's gone now. I'm not pleased by the lack of that mechanic, but I can live with it. I guess...
Now, I HAVE to bring up the naming. Seriously, take a moment and look at the Aeon Illuminate unit names. The 'Weedoboth' fighter/bomber? The 'Sooprizer' Experimental Gunship? The 'Fistoosh' Mobile Missile Launcher? I'm mildly amused. And I'm also questioning the alcohol content the designers possessed when they named these. That, or sleep deprivation. Or it could be they had only a week before release. I unno.
One last thing. When I first played SupCom, I was blown away by this 'epic' feeling. The units and their attacks held a kind of weight to them, as if a single shot from a T3 Aeon Battleship could conceivably oneshot most structures and units. Now, these units in SupCom2 just feel dinky and unrefined, even when at maximum upgrade sometimes. Sure, it doesn't hold true to all units, but it's present in most. The build time is also shortened. When you went to build a Tech3 artillery piece on SupCom original, you EARNED it. It took an hour to build that thing, you deserve it and its firepower. In SupCom2, you have TWENTY heavy artys, maybe more. You can spam them for days and don't get me started on the nukes. I'm not even gonna step in that territory of rant. I've done enough for tonight.
Long story short, if you want a sequel to SupCom original, go get Forged Alliance.

Amazing game. Great level design, a good soundtrack, creativity in target execution and an interesting story are most of what made this game really fun for me.
As a new player, remember to save a lot (on rookie difficulty) and experiment while loading the save if something goes wrong. Be prepared to spend some time repeating parts of some contracts just to get that silent assassin score, because things won't always go the way you want them to. This isn't exactly a fast-paced game, so don't buy it expecting it to be one. The gunplay is not really there, because it isn't required if you're attempting to be a silent assassin. You CAN go guns blazing, but the game isn't exactly built around that. Things like how the player is positioned in relation to the camera, make it a bit annoying (if not hard sometimes) to go in and kill everything. That said, you shouldn't really be playing it that way, as there are other games that are meant for fast-paced pew pew action and they do it much better.
You definitely do not need any past experience with Hitman games to play this, but there is a learning curve. To those who played Absolution first: This game is nothing like Absolution, it is a completely different genre.

It's an interesting game with a set of unusual puzzles - using mirror and prism obelisks to bend light rays around to trigger runes so you can go through a pyramid.
The story portion of the game is ... odd.  I appreciate that the writers gave the main character a backstory, but the information comes up in jagged bits as he enters each new chamber.  "Hey, I figured out the chamber.  If only my wife hadn't left me and taken the kids with her."  After a few chambers, you uncover a god who likes to dole out bits of the pharoah's story in an omnious voice.  The sequence is: wander in to a room, get a random thought from the "hero", solve the scarab part of the chamber, get a foreboding sentence or two from the god, then solve the rest of the chamber.  Lather, rinse, repeat.  The two sets of dialog don't mesh that well together, so it comes across as a mash-up of 2 incredible disparate Twitter feeds.
Overall I liked the puzzle play, but there are a few glaring problems.
1)  You can't zoom out all the way to see the entire puzzle chamber.  After the first few rooms, you have to pan around to see all the parts of the chamber.  Not only is this annoying and unnecessary for game play, but it's very easy to accidentally reposition an obelisk instead of moving the camera.  With some of the obelisks requiring very precise positioning, having them get bumped around is monitor-punching frustration.
2)  The game mechanics aren't well explained.  Most of it is pretty intuitive.  The scarabs, though, are not.  I thought the scarabs had to be destroyed when lining up the light ray to the exit.  They don't.  They do need to be destroyed by the blue light, all three at once, but the light ray doesn't need to be accomplishing any thing else during that time.  I wasted a stupid amount of time trying to nuke them while opening the exit from the chamber.
Despite the flaws,  it's a fun game that most people should find challenging with a story that is unintentionally amusing.

Khaba is a very short but fun puzzle game. Most of the puzzles are pretty simple up until the last couple (Khaba Steam screenshots section will help if you need it).  Story is pretty thin, you can see the regular ending coming for most of the game.  There appears to be a second ending if you manage to collect all the green scarabs on each level, however I can't say for certain and though the puzzles were okay, I wasn't a big enough fan to spend my time trying for the scarabs.
Game is fun for the most part, however for at most 5 or 6 hours of gameplay tops and no replayability I would recommend waiting for a sale.

An enjoyable experience, maybe an 8/10.  The voice acting was good, and there was a bit of a story.  But actually, I really appreciated the stripped-down nature of this game.  It's only a series of laser-and-mirror puzzles.  Almost all of the levels are challenging, and some are very difficult.  I'd say each level stands alone, unlike in many games with environmental puzzles, where you learn a trick at one point and reuse it later.
The controls are slightly imprecise, perhaps because this is a mobile port.  It's easy to accidentally bump one of the mirror-type things out of alignment and have to redo parts of the puzzle as a result.  I would have also liked to be able to zoom out just a little bit further.  But overall, this is a good, solid puzzler.

A fantastic game that has suffered a string of bad luck since shortly after release. While virtually all of the problems have been addressed (balance changes still happen regularly, graphical issues have been addressed) and plenty of new high quality content has been added (with more coming), the only real problem that I can admit to is a small player base: if you try to find matches purely through public matchmaking, you're probably going to be disappointed. However, the existing community is extremely loyal and active.
When you start playing, check out the official forums and join the official unofficial Discord channel to find people to group with and help you learn the various mechanics, maps, and other initially daunting elements that prevent people from enjoying a truly stellar game: for one thing, the level of character customization is significantly higher than for other similar games (characters level up in matches/missions, allowing you to choose helix options to change how they play; you also create your own gear loadout from a wide number of gear choices that you collect to further tweak your stats). With the population where it is now, you're basically refusing to give it a chance if you try to do public matchmaking.
Gameplay-wise, the thing that most separates BB from the pack, in my opinion, is the PvE. It's well written, fun, appropriately challenging, and thoroughly replayable (especially the new operations), and it's something that none of its competitors has, afaik. They really should be pushing the game's PvE elements more rather than trying to make it out to be some PvP-centric game with a smattering of PvE for when you can't find people.

Her Story sat in my library unplayed for over a year as, while it had rave reviews, I simply didn't understand the game nor my goal in it. Once my task was clarified as simply "uncover/play all the videos in a search-restricted database" I got to work. This is when the meat of the game slowly hooked me.
Years of detective games have programmed me to expect something more linear, leading, and "breadcrumb-like;" with an end goal of tagging a suspect and winning/failing based on my final conclusion.
Her Story has no grand finale or capture. It's strength is delivered through an unfolding story of a possible murder; all told over a series of recorded interviews. The mystery, intrigue, twists/turns, all come naturally through this simple mechanic of discovery.
Play it, you'll enjoy exploring and the resulting revelations.

Dwelvers is a top-down Dungeonkeeper-style game with inspiration from the settlers
this games focus seems to be on creating an efficient production line in order to keep your minions happy and well armed, to do this, you must build a farm to create flour, then a cookery in order to create bread with the flour and water, as well as beer for your minions to drink, then you need a bar in order to give your minions somewhere to consume these products
one thing that is very different from Dungeonkeeper and this game is that, instead of having all furniture and such be automaticly created upon room construction, you have to build these yourself, which means that the rooms you create are going to be more expensive than you may first expect
the game also seems to be very stable to me, as i also played on the apparent untested "multi-threading" option and have yet to experiance a crash
I really like the graphics too, as well as the music, the graphics has kind of a "a game of dwarfs" feel to them for me, and the music is fantastic.
another thing is that you can individualy equip your minions with equipment that you can create, trade for or just find in a chest somewhere on the map, which i really like
a gripe with the game though is that the AI needs to be worked on, as of now, it seems to be doing alot of idling when there is work to do, and may just stand on a tile where something is supposted to be build just waiting on the required resources to be deliverd to them, which is annoying to say the least, and hopefully they will go to fix this problem ASAP
another, although more minor, is the apparent lack of minion variery, as so i have only seen about 4 different types, though from the look of it it seems that they will include more as the head, leg and boots slots of the equipment screen are never used
all in all, i think this game has alot of potential to become a really great game, and i'm excited to see what is next

We see a lot of games advertised as a Dungeon Keeper sequel. It keeps happening, but we get things like "Dungeons" (dungeon theme-park) or EA's recent "Dungeon Keeper" (please insert micro-transaction) game.
Dwelvers is actually, legitimately, really like Dungeon Keeper.
Gameplay consists of cube terrain chunks you can mine out or build upon. You can dig rooms out, construct farms, dining rooms, kitchens, prisons, and other things a dungeon should have. The game is also 3d in a sense. While you cannot built a multiple layer dungeon where one room is on top of another room, there is a limit to how steep of a wall a creature can climb. This means impassible cliffs are a thing.
Maps are randomly generated. You can select difficulty level and input a seed number (or accept the random number offered to you), so there's infinite replay in the game.
Your minions have needs. They need sleep, food, and booze. If their needs are not met they will become unhappy. If they get too unhappy they will rebel against you and attack your other minions.
Everything costs resources to build. The resource system is much like Settlers. Rooms can process resources (a kitchen can turn flour, water, and wood into bread) into other resources. There is also a trade system in game where you can send out trade caravans to exchange one resource for another. This trade system is nearly identical to Settlers.
Traps are a thing. Ever play Evil Genius? If you haven't, you should. Evil Genius was Dungeon Keeper meets Austin Powers combined with a hefty dose of creative trap components which you had to assemble into an overly complex, excessively slowly moving death machine that gave plenty of time for secret agents to escape from. Dwelvers has trap components you can construct any number of death machines from. Excessive complexity optional.
And on top of all of this, you have to of course defend your dungeon against various heroes and other monsters who will try to ruin your day. If you lose your Dungeon Heart, its game over man. Defend the Dungeon Heart at all costs.
One thing to keep in mind is that this game is early access. The core gameplay is there, but the game is not yet finished. Not by a longshot. The number of rooms, furniture items, and monsters is limited. The game isn't remotely balanced when it comes to defending your dungeon. You can be wiped out by the very first enemy you encounter in the first 30 seconds of the game if you're unlucky. There is also a surface world. You can see the surface world but you cannot yet interact with the surface world. Presumably there will be interaction between your underground realm and the surface world at a later point in the game, but as this is early access this is not yet implemented.
The game has all of the core pieces in place and functional. The game is stable, enjoyable, and entertaining. But because the game is early access it is still incomplete. Players may run out of things to do after a few hours of gameplay. Once you build up your dungeon, construct all of the rooms, and have the basic food supply chain going you've beaten the game and experienced all content in the game.
My verdict:
The game is an enjoyable and fun sandbox style dungeon builder, but you're going to run through all in-game content within a few hours. This is not due to a fault in the game, but rather its early stage in development. Presumably there will be more stuff to do implemented later on in the development cycle. More monsters, more rooms, more pieces of furniture, more enemies, and more challenges.
The game's art style is really unique and it has decent gameplay for an alpha. It's still got a long way to go, but so far it's a fun game to play.

Sooo I purchased the bundle with all three Penumbra games.. and as you may have guessed i ran into a BIG problem.... The game crashed, ALWAYS. Although i found a way around this problem. I'm running on WIndows 10 (Official). First of all locate the games Main Folder (right click the game in Steam Library-Properties-Local Files-Browse Local Files). Then search the folders for Penumbra.exe(or Requiem.exe, 'cause i got all three games in one bundle) and then right click the .exe file. Go to Properties again (all the way down) and then search for the Compatibility Tab. Then just run the Search for Compatibility Issiues (always on top). Let it do it's job and there you go, you'll be good to go :). Oh AND DONT FORGET to right click the .exe file and Send it to Desktop (Creates a Shortcut of it) .
P.S. NEVER RUN THE GAME THROUGH STEAM.

I recently finished this game after having it in my backlog for quite a while, definitely wish I played this right after finishing the first instead of waiting.
Performance/graphics:
At this point you probably have hardware moden enough to max this game out and play at 60fps stable(or higher) without frame drops. There are tons of options for video/advanced settings and also has settings like headbobbing available. Graphics wise it's very similar to the first but definitely updated. If you got through F.E.A.R.'s graphics then you'll definitely appreciate F.E.A.R. 2's graphics.
Extra content/DLC:
The "Reborn DLC" is just more backstory, not exactly related to F.E.A.R. 2 in the slightest. Definitely worth picking up if you can get it on sale with F.E.A.R. 2, but not needed to enjoy the main story.
Combat:
Pretty much exactly like the first. Fluid weapon combat, four weapon slots, multiple grenade types to switch between, slow-mo(bullet time), but now you can commandeer vehicles! I found vehicle combat to be a very nice addition to the game and definitely made the game feel more open and expanded.
Atmosphere:
Same as the first, great horror aspect and definitely a no lights, middle of the night, wear headphones experience. There are a bit of jumpscares/scenes that will make you react even if you're expecting it.
Story:
Continues on from the main story of the first F.E.A.R., so if you enjoyed F.E.A.R. then I can 100% recommend F.E.A.R. 2 based on the story alone.
Price:
I picked up F.E.A.R. 2 for $3.74 and the Reborn DLC for $2.50. F.E.A.R. 2 is worth it for $14.99, but if you're a bit on edge totally wait for it to be $9.99 and definitely pick it up at $4.99 or less. The DLC I would wait for it to be $4.99 or less, it adds a bit more backstory, but not enough to warrant a $9.99 price point in my opinion.

Honest review incoming if you want seriousness.
I really wanted to give it a thumbs up...
The game is enjoyable, not great... but enjoyable. Unfortunately, yes there a ton of issues which are making it feel hardly worth 20$ even. They give you a warning that says it's early access and to expect some issues, but there's more than "some" if you will. I'll break down some basic pros and cons (I have not played RCT3, my last was RCT2 if that helps judge any of you guys looking to possibly jump back into this franchise.)
Pros:
- You still get to make a theme park and make rollercoasters.
- Menus seem pretty clean and pretty easily navigated.
- Some of the customizable options for paths and such are cool.
- Probably couldn't be stated enough, the spline with coasters has so much potential and upside if it works, but still seems a bit too frustrating at the moment.
- UGC could make this insanely awesome once implemented.
Cons: (Yes, there's quite a lot, but it's just things I honestly think they could improve on and make this game much much better.)
- Lag... This is arguably one of the most frustrating issues noted. Switching around in the menus seems to just not sit right at all with the game. There's so many points in the game that lag becomes an issue that as much as I'm trying to ACTUALLY play the game with a positive outlook, I physically can't...
- Very minimal customization options. (Mostly scenery things, but a few others)
- Path creation is quite annoying, putting a stand or booth down or whatever non-ride hut you put down.. if it doesn't form a line you should have the option to automatically have it connect to the path at the easiest and shortest route. Creating a super small path 1 inch away from the building and not being able to connect it gets very frustrating. (I'm sure they already know this.)
- Coaster creation again. I can't even make a basic loop on a coaster anymore. Some of the prebuilt pieces offer some neat designs/ideas but they ultimately feel kind of lame. I figured they'd have an option to add a "loop" and then you can choose the metrics on it.. but you have to do some funky spline work that right when you think it looks good and you budge just a hair, the whole piece you just spent messing with is all messed up. Adding a straight track with spline feels ridiculously hard when it shouldn't be.. They need to have some snap options or something to help the building process of coasters. Simplicity honestly goes so far if it works (which I know it has in previous games). Honestly, I could explain so much more.. but I'm just assuming they're working on trying to fix the relatively poor custom coaster design process. Such a good concept so poorly executed. :(
- Pre-made coasters feel half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and that's being generous..... Not even going to get into that.
- Not sure the bigger park staff huts works any better. (I could just be confused one how it works..?) I had a small mechanic hut near some rides with 1 employee, switched it to 3 and it felt HARDLY any better to fixing the rides. I finally get to the bigger mechanic building, employee 10, and I literally feel like it's producing 0 work. It'll have like 1 ride repaired when 5+ are broken down right next to it. Not sure again if I'm dumb or if that's just not working. Eventually rides get fixed, but it takes much longer than I think it's supposed to be.
- Campaign has some very bad issues. If you want someone who hasn't played your game before to really get into it, you have to give some better direction and descriptions. ie... you don't get all coaster style options right away, you should be able to highlight over the items you don't have and it tells you how to obtain them. One of the biggest issues, though, is the freezing/"GG games over" pretty much after you get so far. My buddy and I both bought 2 expansions of land to our parks and that seems to be the sweet spot that you have permanent game issues. His saved game in campaign no longer loads, and mine takes about 3-4 minutes to load my park and then another 2-3 to become functional as the screen is froze trying to load it. (I have a very good computer and internet connection, as does he). Once I finally get in, it's just consant issues, to the point I can't play the game.
- Deleting is a nightmare. If you ever get that feeling in your stomach trying to do something super simple but it's beyond frustrating... prepare to get that feeling.. a lot. You give the delete a bulldozer emblem... make it a bulldozer, let us just cruise over those trees and bushes with ease... Obviously we want confirmations on deleting our rides and such.. but don't make it take 40 minutes trying to clear some land.
- I actually tried the music for some of the rides. C'mon...
TL:DR review, should you buy?
I want to say yes.. buy, but I don't feel comfortable doing that. The game has SO much potential.. it's 2016, right? It has a lot of issues, and if they're open to ACTUALLY reading reviews, I think they can knock this game out of the park.
Unfortunately, everyone knows a game is defined by it's launch (sad but true). And this one failed pretty hard. It's labeled early access, but I've played much less developed games in early access that ran better.
BUT!!!! Don't give up on this game. Give them some time, enjoy older RCT games. Companies typically respond pretty well to issues, we'll assume they'll do the same. I'll continue to attempt to play the game and keep up with some updates, but for anyone looking to invest... wishlist it and let the game get to at least a playable state.

I see Khaba as a mix between God of Light and the puzzle aspect of Deadfall Adventures. With a top down view, you refelct a light beam to open passages, doorways and secrets, with a main goal of guiding the light beam to the last door. The game does get pretty tricky once you start advancing in levels, but it also has a repetitive feel like most games ported from tablet. I'm not saying its bad, I just feel like I'm doing the same thing I was doing the previous level, just in a different way. Pretty much just a game to pass some quick time, like you would on a phone or tablet as you're waiting at the DMV or something. The game also has a story line that goes with it. You take the place of Michael, an explorer looking for the secret treasure from the Dark Pyramid in Khaba. He gets trapped and must use the light beam to open doors. This is where the game really takes the feel of God of Light, which is also a tablet game. The story is also accompanied with voice acting, which I really like to see in games. I'm not one for reading the story so that was a plus.
If you like puzzle games like these then I would recommend picking it up, but I would honestly wait for a sale. The $10 price tag is a way high in my opinion, considering you can pick it up on Android for $0.99

While exploring the ancient pyramid of 'Khaba', Michael gets trapped inside leaving only a light source to use as the escape plan. Bouncing the light source between orbs and mirrors, Khaba is a puzzle game that will quickly suck you in to a false sense of security. Levels do appear quite simple at first, but gradually introduce new mechanics that will quickly have your brain melting, more so if you try and collect all the green scarabs that unravel some of the secrets contained within the tomb and Michaels past history.

At the time of this review I have played through the campaign and played a single match online. Based on those two experiences, I can easily say that this is one of the best games I have played this year.
At its core, you control a Thieves Guild, along with its main character: The Master Thief.
The Master Thief is primarily used to scout the city and burgle neighbourhoods in order to steal coins. You'll also get to upgrade your Guild so as to get access to other types of units, which include, for example, the Thug, the Gang and Urchins. These are hired with said stolen coins and are sent into the city to infiltrate businesses, block your opponent from doing any infiltrating, and to attack your opponent's units.
Your opponent is - of course - doing the exact same thing during his or her round.
The game thus becomes a sort of chessgame during which you both try to get the upper hand, althewhile trying to block the other. Resources are necessary not only for getting more units in the field, but also for pursuing those tasks that grant you victory points. These tasks vary from using urchins to take control of a church, assassinating wandering targets, spending resources on bribes, etc.
Whoever accumulates the necessary victory points first (which vary depending on the map) wins the game.
If you enjoy tactical thinking, set in a Dickens-setting, then you'll enjoy this game.

This game turned out to be a lot more than I was expecting. Its cheerful and cartoony, but has very tactically fulfilling and difficult gameplay. The more I play the game, the more depth I discover in manipulating the emotion systems. The larger strategic elements- the planning and preparation between expeditions, and the actual exploration- also do not disappoint.
The adventure mode ends after five expeditions, which is just at that sweet spot where its not so short I feel like I only just started to get rolling, and not so long that I'm discouraged from replaying or restarting after mistakes wipe out my expedition. Theres a good variety in the expeditions, but obviously I'm hoping they continue to release more support or DLC for the game.
Speaking of which, I whole-heartedly endorse the More to Explore expansion. The campfire element, which reminds me of Darkest Dungeon, and the character stories add a lot more narrative and strategic depth. The additional two expeditions (Andes and Lost Island) are also some of the most entertaining with multiple ways to complete them.
Finally, I really like that the game presents options other than violence for achieving your goals. I mean, you can still stab and shoot your way to riches if you really want to, but you don't have to. Friendliness is just as (if not sometimes more) effective.
I picked this up on a whim, and its quickly become one of my favorite games!

Her Story sat in my library unplayed for over a year as, while it had rave reviews, I simply didn't understand the game nor my goal in it. Once my task was clarified as simply "uncover/play all the videos in a search-restricted database" I got to work. This is when the meat of the game slowly hooked me.
Years of detective games have programmed me to expect something more linear, leading, and "breadcrumb-like;" with an end goal of tagging a suspect and winning/failing based on my final conclusion.
Her Story has no grand finale or capture. It's strength is delivered through an unfolding story of a possible murder; all told over a series of recorded interviews. The mystery, intrigue, twists/turns, all come naturally through this simple mechanic of discovery.
Play it, you'll enjoy exploring and the resulting revelations.

Just like in past challenging games such as limited lives, removing the save feature, and the use of limited continues to replace the save feature if you plan to full play the game in the harder difficulties. So it has replayability.
The Bad: This game is hard to recomend if you're not a fan or never even heard of who the AVGN is. By playing the harder difficulties and the save feature turned off, you can't quit out the game and lose all your game progress. The game is short and can be finished in about 2 hours. The bosses feel somewhat repeatative and can be predictable when most of them move around the screen in a figure 8 pattern.
I don't have a lot to say for this game. But the game will urge you to play it again time to time. You may have a lot of lives. But they will start to run out fast if you're not too careful. The game has to do with a lot of time and patience if you plan to get through it alive. If you try to speed run the game with no thought, you will die so fast before you can say game over. The hidden characters you find and play as can be useful sometimes to get from a point you can't reach, a hidden wall or passage, and help you out getting a few extra lives and power ups. Although you will be using The Nerd more than any other character when it comes to killing mostt to all enemies and bosses. The game maybe hard. But can make you come back just to beat the harder difficulties to prove you can beat them since the game is short, but sweet. The game recomends you get the full experience by playing it using a controler. The game is really unfriendly to those who use a keyboard. You can rebind the keys, but the jump timings can be hindered just by a bit when it comes to key timing. I don't recomend  buying this game at $15 full price. Wait for the game to go on sale. Still, it's a fun game not to pass up. A good game to play for yourself. But the game is much better when The Nerd plays it. Guacamelee does a really good job of being challenging without being frustrating. All of the game's elements are clearly defined, so the player can easily evaluate every room and plan their strategy. This is true for both the puzzle rooms and the enemy fights. Some fights do get a little chaotic, and it feels that sometimes it is impossible to avoid taking some damage. But even in the case of dying, or even missing a platform, the cost of dying is very close to zero. If you mess up a jump, you teleport to the last platform you touched, rather than the start of the room. In boss fights, they do not start all the way over, only partially.
But Guacamelee also offers more challenging rooms that are purely optional. Collecting all the orbs to get the alternate ending is quite the task, but well worth it, since it stays consistent with the game's well defined gameplay parameters. For all of the rooms, it is clear what you have to do, and they are strictly either platforming or fights, never both.
The art is very nice, and has a lot of cute references to internet and gaming culture. And the soundtrack is unbelievable. That is all I'm going to say about that.
It took me about 8-9 hours to find all the orbs and most of the chests and then beat the game. I played with an Xbox 360 controller the whole way through.

This return to the F.E.A.R. series, despite its tossing the stories from Perseus Mandate and Extraction Point out the window, is another great romp thorugh terror and weirdness and lots of shooty. The visual updates show, rather well, what a difference four years can make, and it's interesting to get a take on events from a fresh point of view.
This time around, instead of wrecking house and/or face as the mysterious Point Man, you're filling the boots of a Sgt. Beckett. While not quite the engineered killing machine Point Man is, Beckett's still pretty good at his job, and as it turns out, has more connections to the strange things going on than he realizes. A lot of F.E.A.R. 2 is uncovering backstory behind the events of the first game, as well as laying some groundwork for more F.E.A.R. in the future. This is telegraphed fairly obviously as the game progresses, but it never feels like filler or something they shoved in there to get on to F.E.A.R. 3.
Running around town following the massive wave of destruction unleashed at the end of the first F.E.A.R. makes for a lot of desolate, obliterated territory as the story weaves its way from the outskirts to the epicenter of the blast itself. The somewhat familiar territory provides a nice contrast to the new character and the new coat of paint, as well as new weaponry including mech suits. Yup. Mech suits. Big guns. Pew pew. They're really fun.
Basically goes without saying that if you liked F.E.A.R., you should play F.E.A.R. 2. The scares are a bit dialed back this time around, but the ones that are in there are great.

Verdict: Buy it on sale and strap the hell in!

Having played this game for just over 19 hours I want to give my fair assessment of the game.  There is no denying that this game has been riddled with problems from the start.  That being said, while I was not happy to hear of the "early access label" I definitely support the decision now.  This game is not remotely near full release!
There is no denying that this game has a lot of issues.  The real question is whether or not the game is moving in the right direction.
Pros:
-coaster mechanics have vastly improved from the beta
-looks and feels like Roller Coaster Tycoon series
-a fair selection of aufio and video settings
-farily strong visuals (though nowhere near close to Planet Coaster!)
-a large assortment of props and settings
-a fair selection of options:  campaign, sandbox, etc.
-incredibly fast load times
-an easy to use interface
-the ability to buy more land to expand your park
-easy to use teraforming options
-three types of land/terrain with more coming in future updates
-prompt responses from the developer and a timely update of upcoming changes and additions
-steam workshop creations
Cons:
-the path system is very awkard at times
-manually deleting of every single object (aka no mass delete)
-limited amount and variety of rides, shops and food options (at this time)
-no ability to build structures using idividual pieces (will be added at a later date)
-peeps (they are awful re: visuals, movement, etc.)
-30 second night cycle (I really don't get this one...???)
-maitenance doesn't seem to work and/or is very buggy
-rides break down and often don't get fixed in a tmely manner, or at all
-no ability to place lights and benches on elevated paths
-complete lack of optimization... this game will make your system "work" for it!
-occasional crashes and there is NO Autosave feature
I have faith in this game but I also have many concerns and reservations.  I was tempted to ask for a refund but I made the choice to commit to the game simply because I want the game to be successful.  I had 100's of hours of playing RCT3 and I want this game to deliver so I have decided to support Atari on this one in the hopes that this can turn into something special.  Only time will tell if that is a sound decision.
I also plan to buy Planet Coaster at some point.  However, a big issue with PC is the GPU specs.  Most systems will be able to play Roller Coaster Tycoon World.  The video card requirements for PC are very high at this time and a lot of people will not have the hardware to run the game at optimal levels, if at all.   RCTW can cater to a much larger market at this time and the fact that it's on Steam is huge for me.
For people who want the Roller Coaster Tycoon experience and are willing to put up with a lot of bugs and glitches and minimal content, then I recommend the purchase in order to help out the development team.  If you don't want to put up with all of the hassles of "early access" then I strongly reccomend that you pass on this game for now.  Be very clear that if you buy this game you will be getting a very incomplete experience.  So, do you want to support the developers or do you want to wait and see?
That's my .02c  Take it for what it's worth.

I had a lot of fun with this game. A lot more than I expected to, given that I am not a fan of the original Hitman. This one felt much more polished and easier to understand.
Graphics: For its time, it looks great. The environments look pretty and the character models are quite good. Some of the landscapes, like the Vegas city scape, had me saying "wow", even though the game is nearly 10 years old.
Story: The Hitman games are not known for having incredibly gripping storylines, at least in my experience. The story was better than I expected it to be, but is probably still the weakest part of the game. Fortunately, you can look past it because just about everything else is great.
Level Design: Yes, yes, and yes. This game is everything I've ever wanted out of a sneaking game in terms of level design. The levels are very big, usually containing at least 4 large floors with numerous maps and PLENTY of ways to complete the missions. Some are obvious, and some require a bit of intuition. The game forces you to explore the whole level and figure out how to complete it on your own. It doesn't baby you and tell you what to do. I will admit, I had to resort to walkthroughs at times, but when I managed to complete the level my own way, it was incredibly satisfying.
Gameplay: My issue with every Hitman game has always been clunky controls. This one is no exception. At least the games are consistent in that sense. Absolution has the smoothest controls so far, but it's still not quite on the same level as something like Assassin's Creed. But, obviously, that is an entirely different style of game.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game and would reccommend it to anyone who enjoys badass, intuitive, sneaking based games! 8/10

Hitman series is well known for bringing the feeling of being a professional hired assassin to a whole new level. I would say that Hitman: Blood Money is arguably the best game in the Hitman series, but more on that later on.
The story revolves around Agent 47, a cloned assassin-for-hire whose flawless record places him in high demand among the wealthy and elite. You don't know much about him or his past. Only thing you are certain of is that he is best in the business. You're thrown into an open world. You're given targets that you must kill and in some instances, objectives to complete. The rest is up to you.
Graphics are okay for the time that the game was released and that's the only outdated thing. Gameplay still holds up the fun factor. Stealth can be a little too easy in my opinion, but there are moments that can still be challenging. You choose how you play the game and that's the biggest part of it. If you're thinking of picking this game for the first time beware, you will find yourself spending lots of time doing trial and error to find the best ways to kill your target.
If you enjoy a sandbox stealth experience, Hitman: Blood Money is for you. If you enjoy more linear games with story and character progression, avoid it.

This game is like a puzzle rather than a straight out-and-out murder simulator. You plan your hit as you go, take note of points of interest, then attempt to execute the plan in as tight a timing as you can manage with as literal collateral and evidence possible. Get in, subdue the guards, strangle the target to death, then plant the barbell over his neck so it seems like he died when working out. Why did the guards get KO'd? They won't know, or care.
But on your way out of the room containing the dead target and his unconscious guards, you're spotted by an obese, elderly southern woman who starts screaming bloody murder, waving her arms and stomping her feet like it's the running of the bald, and suddenly you're in a hardcore chase simulator where you -have- to catch up to the tubbo and snap her neck before tossing her over a railing lest she lose you the coveted Silent Assassin rating.
As you manage to pull a kitchen knife -- wait, a kitchen knife? Right. You picked up a kitchen knife for the melee unlock at the end of the level.. only you remember that's only in Contracts. Either way, you pull out a kitchen knife by mistake instead of the fibre wire, and you end up slitting the poor woman's throat and watching her slowly tumble to her knees and cover the walls in her ragu as you contemplate what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are.
As this happens, you realize the clown and the caterer have seen the entire chase and murderer, and are now making their way to the Secret Service van positioned outside to keep an eye on the witness you were dispatched to.. dispatch. Pulling your pistol out of your coat, you put a round into the backs of their heads with expert precision and wipe sweat from your shiny bald plate as you manage to sprint to the exit before the guards can find the brutal murder-trail you've left behind.
At the ending stats screen you realize that you left your suit and a customized gun behind alongside killing three innocents, so you don't get a Silent Assassin rating and have to spend a whole chunk of your assassination fee to clean up after the ♥♥♥♥ing carnage you've caused.
And that's Hitman: Blood Money. And it is fantastic.

Well what can I say? Another amazing Hitman game....
Game has the same concept as the previous titles but;
-Weapon Customization: All ICA weapons can be customized with various attachments.
-Notoriety ratings: After completing a mission, depending on how well you cover your tracks you will either gain or stay hidden in the publics' eye. There is a newspaper after the mission that describes how the assassination played out(weapons used, how many killed, how many witnesses. Be sloppy and miss? The editors will say you are a shotty marksman. Kill the target, and make it an accident? The editors will disclose it how you made it seem. etc.
-Money system: Depending on your rating you will be awarded a sum of cash. Failure to retrieve your iconic suit, or weapons will result in a loss in the final income.
Now onto the general stuff;
There aren't as many missions like Hitman 2, but since there are so many ways to kill in this game, there is some replay value. You can also play the many difficulties if you want a challenege once beating it on easier difficulties. The graphics have been enhanced and the level design is fluid, there is no more "dead ends" like in Hitman 2 USSR levels. The soundtrack is done by the amazing Jesper Kyd and does not dissapoint. Each level has their own unique ambient music which sets the mood every time. They have added melee combat in this game which is a plus, you can now disarm enemies and take their gun/knock them out(makes a lot of noise so use only when you have to).
With all the nice said and done onto the problems. Sometimes there are annoying glitches that send guards running in the room you are in when you silently kill your target, I don't know if this is intentional for scripted reasons or an error in the patrol coding. It happens sometimes but not enough to be bothersome unless you are trying to get SA everytime, just hit restart and try again. There are some clipping errors, or times civilians are walking in eachother.
Other than that this is the same cookie cutter formula for a Hitman game, just additional content and ways to kill!
I would recommend this game if you are a fan of the Hitman series.

SUMMARY:  This is a pretty good casual game if that's what you want and if you don't pay full price.  (Luckily I got it on sale, but even at half off retail I think I paid too much and am disappointed.)
This game has a lot going for it, but it's terribly important to know certain things about it before spending money on it.  With that in mind, I'm putting the CONS list first.
CONS:
... Staggeringly short.  I tend to take my time, but in less than 10 hours I've started four playthroughs and beaten the game twice on the standard difficulty (classic difficulty, no saves, permadeath).  You get to go on 5 expeditions, most of which are limited by supplies to about 10-12 moves.  (I'm generalizing; there are ways to make individual expeditions last SLIGHTLY longer.)  The first of the five is chosen for you, and is also shorter than the rest (about 7 moves).
... Repetitive.  There are very few expedition options.  They prompt you what sort of things you can expect to face and find, and it frequently happens that there are no good options for a party's strengths or an expedition's needs.  Also, while each one is partially randomized, the draw pool is small and I got the same "random" scenarios multiple times.  The network of possible moves changes, the rewards change, but the bulk of each expedition stays the same each playthrough.
... Limited.  You pick three explorers from the provided 20.  There's a degree of diversity between them, but most of it is in hidden features that may or may not even matter.  (My wrestler was devout, which mattered in exactly one conversation option.)  My friendly gold obsessed party with the Scout captain was functionally identical to my aggressive research obsessed party with the Scientist captain.  There are obvious gaps, like characters who are glass cannons and fit in a certain sort of party, but without sturdy characters to defend them who also fit in that sort of party.  Each character has a couple of options in encounters, but it's pretty common for disimilar characters to have exactly the same attacks, so everyone plays pretty close to the same.  Each character can also be upgraded slightly (you get one of two options at each level, and I commonly finished with character at level 4), but a lot of the options are minor and there's no way to level up in the field.  There's a research tree with six small branches, but you can only choose from two of them at first, so most of the "options" won't have time to affect much, assuming you devote enough time to Research to unlock any of them at all.  There's equipment to buy, and its very important, but there aren't real choices about it, so gold is mostly the illusion of a mechanic.  There are followers to hire, but they do minor things that you may not even notice unless you invest a lot in them, at which point they only provide their marginal effect on your last expedition.  In short, so much of the game felt like discovering that a lake is really a puddle.  It's broad and looks refreshing, but it's too shallow to do much in.
...Vague.  A lot of information could be useful, but isn't available anywhere.  Monster attacks are the most typical example of this.  Fights involve a lot of splashy (and whimsical) pictures that mean nearly nothing, combined with wildly unpredictable attack strength and a bevy of ignorably irrelevant status effects.  Perks are similar.  It isn't uncommon that you'll get to choose new perks, not knowing if or how those perks will help you.  My favorite is choosing between two perks of the same type, each with a stylish but vapid name.  How are they different?  They probably aren't.
PROS:
... Interesting concept implemented well.  I really liked the entire exploration idea, and the game is built on it from top to bottom.  Everything works together to point back to that central conceit: stepping out on adventures into the mysterious unknown.
... Interesting mechanics.  The game has some really unique combat mechanics--(attack types, approach types, moods, feelings)--which are challenging but rewarding to manage.  The best of these is the encounter outcomes, trying to resolve an encounter in a friendly, devious, or aggressive manner to achieve different rewards.
... Solid platform.  I haven't encountered a single bug.
... Whimsical atmosphere.  Everything from the art design to the quests is pretty lighthearted.

I really wanted to like this game. I've been waiting all of my childhood for this game. The two things that ruins it for me is that to make a rollercoaster, the primary element of this game, you need to spend hours tweaking and fixing the coaster because for some reason, coasters enjoy crashing themselves. After 2 hours, I gave up. The second thing is that this game is poorly optimized, and even on low settings, I get around 30 FPS on my decent computer.
tl;dr It kills me to say this, but don't play this game, even if it is tempting.

I wouldn't recommend this for anyone who is expecting a perfect game. Rollercoaster Tycoon World is far from perfect, and it certainly isn't ready for anybody who isn't willing to deal with bugs. This game has them. Some are game-breaking (like, I can't launch scenarios without my game crashing entirely, in one case requiring a complete reboot of my ROG laptop) and some aren't (my favorite thus far are the horrible animations on the giant slide - I laughed at that for far too long). However, I feel the game is fun, and it has a lot of potential.
Some people are also experiencing issues with RAM leaks; I am one that can say that I haven't had that issue on any of the devices that I have played RCTW on. All were laptops with good graphics cards, a quad-core proc, and 16GB of RAM. I can also say that I haven't run into anything particularly problematic yet, except the scenario-issue I mentioned earlier.
And for those complaining about graphics: there's a setting that you have to disable. When we got Beta weekend 1, everyone was locked to the highest graphics possible, without any FPS prioritization. The game now adjusts automatically for the specs that it thinks the computer can handle. However, it also has an FPS prioritization setting. That  needs to be disabled to get the full quality of the game. Thankfully, my laptop (970 Geforce GTX) can handle that. Not everyone can.
If you don't have the minimum specs, the game won't run well. Period.
If you don't have the recommended specs, it will run better than not meeting minimum, but you still want recommended. The game is demanding, even with some optimizing.
For those that don't meet recommended - wait for further optimization unless you are patient.

Very good game. It is a turn-based RPG that is essentially a very unique spin on Fire Emblem. There are three ways to combat your opponents in fights: Attacking, Friendliness, and Bullying. It sounds rather dumb but it's pretty charming to play with. The amount of times you do these actions can change their effectiveness as well as the other 2's in battle, implementing a Pokemon-esque weakness system that is dynamic. You assemble a crew of 3 people (remind you of a certain space-themed RPG?) and set out to explore interesting areas in a competition to become the world's most Renowned Explorer. In your travels there will be decision making (some of which activates a slot-machine type thing where there is a chance that you can fail/suceed), random events, and many other interesting occasions that will make every expedition charming and eventful.
TL;DR this game takes Fire Emblem and adds on great elements from other RPGs such as Pokemon, FTL, Fallout (decision-making), and many more. An interesting, charming, replayable, polished, wonderful game and a must-buy for any Strategy/RPG fan.

If you're looking for a fun strategy game that doesn't ask for more time than you're willing to spend, and yet still has the potential to be played for hours on end; Antihero is the way to go. The game itself offers a fresh perspective for the strategy genre, as well as an endearing art style. Although an extension of the campaign would be great, this game is engaging and enjoyable in all modes.

It's a fun game. It has many board-game elements, but makes good use of being a video game - such as using stealth which doesn't really work in board games. AI is reasonably tough, and multiplayer is fun. I recommend this game for people who enjoy board games.

Antihero is a nice turn-based strategy board game. Perfect for people who want to chill out from other complex or action-heavy games.
You control your hero - a thief - and summon other NPCs in order to capture points of interest on the map and fight one opponent for set amount of victory points. There are multiple ways of achieving victory and some maps add special objectives for a twist. Each turn you manage your resources - gold and lanterns - by entering house squares, placing NPCs into buildings and attacking neutral/enemy NPCs on the map. Your hero also has a talent tree, where you can choose between learning a new skill or earning free gold/lanterns. Maps for each game are randomized - buildings of interest spawn at different squares and NPC movements are also random, which is a plus.
This game has three game modes:
- Campaign (also doubles as a Tutorial)
- Skirmish, where you can play against AI or against another player at your PC
- Multiplayer, where you can play against other people online through Steam
I finished the campaign on hard difficulty under 6 hours of game time, so it felt rather short. However, if you enjoy the game during the short campaign, skirmishes and online play can last you for a while. The game is quite easy to learn and offers enough depth to keep you invested. Finally, the graphics, animations, sounds and music are great and they perfectly match the theme of the game.
If you like board games and you want to play this game against other players online, get it. If you're not interested in online play, the price tag 14,99€ feels a little too high for the play time this game offers, so you're better off waiting for a discount.

When I looked at the first few screenshots of Magrunner, I thought it would be a neat-looking Portal-like with good gameplay. What I got instead was a horror game with badly-designed puzzles thrown into it, with way too many cutscenes in between the few-and-far-between puzzles.
The main mechanic of Magrunner is that you can change the magnetic polarity of objects into either red, green, or white. White objects aren't affected, but two objects that are the same polarity will attract, while two objects of different polarities will repel.
The first problem here is that this is the exact opposite of how we've been taught magnets work when growing up. This on its own wouldn't be too bad, truth be told, and it could actually spawn a good puzzle game where this is the core mechanic.
Except in this game, it's often not easy to determine the outcome of what happens when you have three or more different magnets, some red and some green, all trying to act on each other but moving in very constrained ways.
Further, I'm pretty sure the physics engine in this game isn't well-made. I mean, stacking two cubes one on top of another (the game snaps them into place for you) and making them repel will actually send the top one *at an angle*, not straight up! And when a number of puzzles require you to jump on top of these tiny tiny cubes and stay atop them while you fire yourself up, then jump off at the peak onto a narrow platform, one can't help but get frustrated at this game.
Puzzle-wise, things aren't very good either. Many key pieces of the puzzles are tucked away high up on a shelf that's easily missed if you're not careful enough. One early example gave you two cubes at the start of the level, and a switch that you could almost, but not quite, reach with the two cubes. As well as a platform that seemed like it'd lead to the exit. What that platform *actually* leads to is a third cube, but you'd have no way of knowing that unless you actually expended the effort to go up there. Glass exists in this game; why not just put the third cube up there on a glass platform, instead of tucking it behind a curved bend in an alcove in the wall?!
Indeed, the architecture of the levels doesn't feel like it fits a testing facility. You have all these brightly-coloured walls with weird beveled bits that do nothing; small decorations jutting out into the passageway, and giant one-off structures and curvy passages that don't look modular at all (which is what you would expect from a testing facility). It broke immersion quite frequently. Indeed, Portal, going the opposite direction, by making the test chambers all regular and blocky, was better in this respect since you could easily believe that this was how a test chamber would look.
And don't get me started on the bloody cutscenes. By the time I'd finished the second level, I'd already spent 10 minutes playing the game. Of which 8 minutes was from watching three (yes, THREE!) cutscenes in the two levels.
THREE CUTSCENES. TWO LEVELS.
That's ridiculous.
Other stupid stuff in the game includes:
* All levels before a particular level having the very bottom floor be safe, then that level having the bottom floor be instadeath without it being properly signposted. (A previous level's voiceover suggests that the floor *IS* safe.) Contrast this to Portal, where the first level that has goo has GLaDOS telling you "The floor here will kill you. Try to avoid it.".
* The cutscenes. There are a lot of them.
* Putting a hatch into a lower floor underneath a platform. You can't see the hatch and it isn't indicated at all.
* The cutscenes. They're before and after every single level. Sometimes even DURING levels.
* A launcher that launches you straight into the edge of a platform you can't move prior to it. There's no way to--
* The cutscenes. They're really annoying and long and just people talking while you're in an elevator. Or the screen cutting to black with voices when you're in the middle of solving a level. Which idiot thought it was a good idea to INTERRUPT THE PLAYER'S GAMEPLAY the same way I'm interrupting you reading my review right now?!
* --know beforehand where the launchers take you (unlike in Portal where it's indicated).
* The cutscenes. They're mainly just useless boring banter about corrupted corporate image.
* Walking speed is REALLY REALLY SLOW and you can't speed it up. This one should really have been at the top of the list, actually. Oh well, no matter, it's still a stupid thing in the game.
* The cutscenes. Shut up already, Kram!
* The "change the polarity of the cube you can't get to to bring it to you instead" mechanic isn't introduced well.
* The cutscenes. Did I mention those? I just want to play the damn game; is it THAT hard to let me do that?!
It's as if the people making this game didn't take any courses on puzzle design. Or get anyone to test their game (which is ironic considering that their game is about someone getting 7 people to test their system).
By the time I ragequit an hour into the game, I was having far more fun jumping around in the bloodsplatter of someone who'd been freshly eaten than actually solving the puzzle in the room containing the bloodsplatter. That's honestly a grim outlook for the rest of the game.
(Also, the game doesn't have antialiasing and had a lot of visual tearing on my machine. This is even after I set the game to use the NVIDIA graphics card and anti-alias the game. Prepare to see blocky blocks.)
* The cutscenes. Yes, there are just that many of them.
If you're looking for a puzzle game, you should actively avoid this monstrosity and play Portal instead for a Portal-like. Or maybe Polarity, because that one's quite good.
If you're looking for a horror game, consider trying something else (because it takes quite a while before the horror bit shows up).
While this game isn't as bad as Soko Match or Rolling Shapes, it's still an abomination, and one I'd want a refund for. But alas, I bought this thing over two years ago, so that's money I'll never get back.
* The cutscenes. Come on, you knew this last one was coming.

Supreme Commander 2 is a worthy sequel to Supreme Commander and Forged Alliance; however they do scale back a few features that will upset fans of the original. Some design decisions don't make too much sense, either.
The graphics are slightly better but not enough for a sequel, in my opinion. Though the models in game look pretty good, the UEF especially looks like factory production and cargo crates, a step backward from their sturdy designs in the first game. Cybrans and Aeon still look pretty good, though. However, in the campaign, somehow the character models look a lot worse and more uncanny, with lip sync quite a bit off. The interface is rather simplified and annoyingly all unit and building descriptions are gone, with just one sentence like "Experimental Assault Block". It rarely tells you all you need to know, especially with the more specialised units.
The gameplay has changed from the slower methodical pace to a faster one where getting high tech units is easier, but said units aren't anywhere near as powerful as they used to be. The Collossus for example is still very powerful but goes down very fast when it has no support. There are far less buildings and units to build now, as the process has been streamlined. Instead of having tech 1, 2 and 3 units, all units are unique and are upgradeable, so I think this is a good change. I do miss the massive fusion reactors now, though. Thankfully, unit ai is improved and now move much better as a group. However, for some strange reason you can't build anything when you have more than 1 engineer selected, which baffles me.
The new research system is both good and bad. Research is a new resource that is constantly generated, and building research stations increases the rate at which you get research points. This new system is mostly a positive change, as it allows basic units to become quite useful later one (such as adding AA to ground attackers) and has pathways to different experimental units. It's also easier to access, which saves on time. However, if you don't get much research you're pretty much screwed as you can't get the essentials like shield generators or air transports, which is part of the negative change.
The story... well there isn't much. We have three characters from each faction to play as to beat a bad guy. Very little makes sense past dialogue like "I will annihilate everything" so the gameplay in each mission is far superior to dialogue or writing. It's nice that you get rated at the end of each mission based on your performance, so this increases replayability a little bit.
I haven't tried much multiplayer. as I haven't been able to find a game within a minute or so. Joining a steam group or community for this might be needed if you're looking for that.
Overall, a solid sequel and great RTS. Not as mind blowing as Forged Alliance but still worth buying if you're a fan of Supreme Commander or RTS games in general.

Penumbra:  Overture Review
It's all right.  I wouldn't call it a horror game however, as it's more of an adventure/exploring game with spooky stuff rather than horror.  The story is interesting enough to keep you engaged, although you're gonna have to play all three games.  You play as some dude who gets caught up in some mysterious family drama and ends up in an abandoned mine somewhere in the middle of nowhere.  It's been overrun by mutated animals, giant spiders (of course) and worms big enough to rival the Alaskan Bull Worm from Spongebob.
As you progress you'll do the typical look-around, combine items, solve situational puzzles, kill a few enemies, etc.  The game basically plays as one big map instead of levels, so unless you know exactly where you're going you're gonna get lost and frustrated.  Certain things won't even activate until you do something else in a completely different area and you won't exactly get a hint.  I used a walkthrough most of the playthrough which helped tremendously, and I didn't feel that it took away from the experience, in fact it was kind of fun for whatever reason to play with the walkthrough.
You'll collect notes strewn about that range from diary entries to data logs and such; they give you a sense of what happened in the mine and you'll quickly realize that something went very wrong.  You'll also (after getting a radio) get these messages from a guy named Red who is evidently trapped somwhere in the mine.  He will lead you throughout the game until its end.  I should also mention that this game is rather short.  Don't be fooled by my playtime hours as I've played it across two computers (got halfway and reset).  So I do recommend it, and although it markets itself as a horror game don't expect too much horror, just enjoy the experience casually.
