It's a bit weird considering that I came to know the franchise I played the most by 2016, by pirating it's very first game.
Payday: The Heist.
And when I paid my due (buying the original), it's because this game is just pure awesome!
I'm still not of the hook yet, as when Payday 2 came along, I pirated it first until like 10-20 update the game have released, that's when I decide to just buy the original for good to make the enjoyment of the game unhindered by searching the pirated update (it still exist though, iirc)
PDTH shines in it's cinematic heist flow and solid gun play, compared to Payday 2 which offer diverse playstyle and ever increasing arsenal and heist location. But Payday The Heist still holds its own as a classic throwback on the game that spark the genre of heisting-with-your-friend.
One feature I would surely miss from the recent iteration is the character interaction during heisting. Every heist have some kind of story between the character as it progresses. I hope Payday 2 can aim higher on that department.
Sadly, PDTH is bogged down on a number of element.
The Heist is more-or-less static, you can only do it one way or a mix of 2 with still the major way basically the same with every heist released in PDTH.
Progression system to unlock arsenal, equipment and passive skill is grindy at best. You won't reach the end growth if not clocking more than 50 hour doing the hardest heist getting all objective and loot. So it might turn off some people.
There's only 1 game mode, which is heisting. Don't compare it to Left 4 Dead series which have mutator, scavenge, etc. But PDTH relief this by having the heist objective a new and different on each heist. Basically making the heist's objective on the same level with L4D various game mode if I say so.
For those of you who came to know Payday 2 first, you won't regret buying this game that spark the genre. It might server as a break from your 1000th hour of Payday 2. It'll feel fresh, trust me.
Even better if you can get your other heisting partner in Payday 2 to play along in this.
Discount is really generous when it comes to sale.
Getting DLC for this is more lucrative, since it ties also to existing Payday 2 DLC, buy 1 to get 2 so to speak.
Get ready to begin the story of the original Payday crew
And it'll not be as easy as Payday 2.

Amazing game that fell prey to some tragic marketing and competition.
If you enjoy MOBAs and FPS titles, this is the perfect fusion you have been dreaming of.  The game mechanics are awesome, with extremely interesting and diverse skillsets and leveling options for each character, the combat is fast paced and tight, and if you appreciate the humor of Borderlands titles the story/characters are epic.
However; the launch of this game was spectacularly botched.  Blizzard "happened" to launch their hero shooter simultaneously, which deeply ate into the player base.  Then you must consider Battleborn was released at AAA title price, but the various characters were locked from the beginning except for 5.  This was done to gradually introduce players to the characters, but people associated it with free to play rosters in such games as DOTA2 and League of Legends, so this decision displeased many.
Furthermore there were initially massive graphical optimization problems on ATI cards, these didn't show up in the extensive beta/ technical test because they only occured on one specific map type not present in those tests.  In the first several weeks there were some very large balance problems as well.
All of these factors led to the vast majority of the intended audience for this game giving it the cold shoulder.  This creates a further problem we are now dealing with, in that the small group of people who have stuck around have put a lot of time into the game and are now very competent.  So whenever completely new players pick up the game, they predominately play against people with hundreds of hours of playtime, get stomped, and give up.
So if you have a good group of friends and go into this together, you can have a great time.  As a solo public grouper... Overwatch is a lot less intimidating :D

Okay. When I first made a review for this game, I just did standard criticizing. However, the game has updated since and deserves a fair review, as they have fixed many things. I will break this game up into parts and review each one seperetely.
Interface:
By interface, I mean the translucent, white bar at the bottom of the screen ingame. It is, well, okay. It gives you what you need, but it does not do it efficently. It seperates rides from rollercoasters, but that is just small nitpick I have. I really hate how stall types are merged into 4 small sections with only 2 being useful. It is okay, but you cannot search for stalls as a whole. There have been many times I have wanted sci-fi/western/normal/adventure theme only and had to look thouroughly to even find the stall itself. In tries to go for a more modern look by making everything unocolored, line drawn icons. It only makes things harder to pick out. It also is inneficent in other ways. In one tab, there is a whole entire area dedicated to facades. It, however, contains barely anything. Instead of trying to make more, they just created a tab of them and put a few dumb things in to make it look complete. Not to mention that I usually go there looking for terrain coloring and clicking on it (because it is a spray can). Maybe I want to look for a roller coaster and click on rides? Though that, itself, is a small issue, it is still ANNOYING and easy to prevent. The interface does have it's pros though. It moved on from RCT3's circle interface that was literally everywhere and hard to navigate across and instead had a normal interface at the bottom of the screen. It also does look nice. I would just rather functionality over design. I give it a 4/10.
scenarios:
I have to be honest, I hate the new scenarios. I had true fun playing the sceanarios in RCT3. I have no fun with the new scenarios, and I knew I would hate them all when I played the first. Instead of being put in a well established park that has a lot of room for improvement, I was put in a nearly 100% complete park and told to make new stuff with a predefined pathway (yes, I know I could change it if I wanted to) in 12 months. It already had about every resturaunt, and it had no "Discovery" feature that would let me unlock new stuff as time went on. I do like the return of the scenario creator, however. I have no dabbled in it that much yet (I will explain why later), but I love that they have reintroduced one great feature in the series. While I like that scenarios are included and applaud the developers for taking the time to make what would otherwise be a sanbox game into a game that you can actually PLAY for a reason. While I hate the scenarios, I do appreciate the scenario editor and that the developers even added them in. Therefore, I give this feature a 7.5/10
sandbox:
This is the true reason (and in my opinion one of the only reasons) to buy this game. While limitations do still apply, I still love the ability to be able to create the theme park of my dreams. I have had hours of fun in sandbox mode and have even spent a whole day working on my park at one time. It was a mess, but it was fun. I do, however, not like the restrictions that are applied. I will, however, get into that in a later area. I really do like the sandboxes of othger games better though. This one is good, but it is not the best. It lacks features that those ones have, but it is FUN, and that is what mainly matters. Though this area is short, that is because I really do not have that much negativity for it. Therefore, I give the sandbox mode an 8.5/10. It is mainly good, but I have see better.
Items:
By items, I mean stalls, decorations, and paths. Let's start out with stalls. I like the new twist on the game by adding buildings as a bigger form of stalls, but I am dissapointed with smaller stalls and am indifferent on the choice to add staff buidlings. The small stalls are pretty bad. There are small things, like ketchup and mustard bottles on sci-fi souveneir stores (which is just outright laziness), but there are alsobig things. I really hate the lack of stall types. There are many, yes, but explain to me why the only small stall that has a drink is the soda stall. That is PURE laziness. It is hard to be creative with stalls when I have already placed every single one in a small park 3 times already. Now, staff buildings are OKAY. It is cool to have a building with workers that makes it where you don't have to spam the hire button, but it makes staff take up so much space. It is outright annoying. Even bathrooms (which are not staff, I know) take up a ton of space. I like the new bathrooms, ya, but the developer's were too lazy to implement the tiny, dirty stalls that is so common in theme parks It is just annoying. I rate this third of this section 4.5/10. I will now be moving onto decoraqtions. Theya re what really spice upthe park, and I have mostly postive words to say about them. They look nice, and even trees are randomized. I will rather be criticizing what is NOT added. There is one big thing missing, buidling materials! How can you make a good aprk when you cannot even add a wall! Parkitect and Planet Coaster do this so well, so why does Roller Coaster Tycoon World fail? Onlt the developer's know. I like the return of UGC and the new addition of using the Workshop to find and apply it easily. I, however, don't like how they are just lifeless statues. In RCT3, I had a poorly made McDonalds stall that actually worked! In RCTW, I have a giant building with incredible detail... that does nothing. Atari really messed up here. I can only hop that they will fix this. I really liek the decorations, but I hate what they don;t have. Therefore, I am giving them a 7/10. Next, we have paths.I have a sort of love hate relationship with the paths. They are good, yes. However, they are such a pain to use! They give them dumb rules, like "You can only expand this path if you delete this one then put it back in the exact same place after you are done." That is so dumb. Curved paths, while being a nice addtion, are impossible to use! I ill struugle and struggle with them,a nd I usyually give up on REGULAR paths! Plus, if you don't use grid or snap, they will be all wonky and off center! They could try to reintroduce path blocks, but I don't think they will. I do, however, really like them with grid/snap. It makes using them so much easier! I just don't like that they are basically required! Because of these mixed views, I give paths a 7/10. Therefore, my overall rating for these 3 are 6.2/10. I wish I could have given them a better rating.
Terrain:
Terrain sculpting is really nice, but I don't have many words to say about it. The only real things I would change are the lack of the ability to make caves and the fact that I want more terrain colors in the paint tab. I do wish that they fixed placing items of bridges, however. They will just fall through (not when I place them but I literally cannot place them on the path) , and no one ikes that. I give terrain an 8/10.
Fun:
This game is actually REALLY fun. It is not great to any extent, but I like it. There is not that much more to say besides that it is fun, and that is what makes a game good. I give this an 8.5/10
DLC:
I liek the DLC, ya. I however wish it added a bit more. We get the classic mascot, 2 new themes, and a gold park entrance on those 2 themes. There is not much in this section because there is not much with DLC! It is good, but it is dissapointing. 7/10
FInal Thoughts:
Roller Coaster Tycoon World is a good game, but do I recommend it? To be honest, I really want to, but I don't. It just is not good compared to Parkitect and Planet Coaster, the 2 rollercoaster games of 2015-16 I absolutely love. Overall, I give RCTW an 8.1/10.

One word - awesome.
Let's start with things that I didn't like:
Campaing seems to be short. I am almost done with it, and it only took a few hours on normal.
There is quite a lot of handholding in the beginning. In first two-three missions - many of your moves will be predetirmend. Not my favorite way of learning, to be honest.
Okay, that was a short list.
Now things I do like:
Art style - chraming an hilarious.
Depth that comes with multiple playstyles, objectives, and, ultimately - human opponents.
Awesome selection of multiplayer modes - hotseat, asycnchronous and synchronous online modes. Love it.
Making house rules - genious. If you feel like game is poorly balanced - you have tools to make it how you think it should be. You can tweak a lot of things related to  victory points and prices. This is generally is such a great and rare thing to see - despite that I don't think I would change anything. Maybe I will experiment with reduction of price on Thugs and increase in price of Bands, but game is enjoyable as it is.
Dynamic gameplay - I am no game designer, but it seems that many mecahnics (increasing price on multiple units, upgrades, high cost of thugs) were made in a way that facilitates easier catch-ups and combacks, which is great for a multiplayer game. Overall, it seems that game is balanced in a way that favors not establishing dominance and gaining more and more agvantage over your opponent, but in a way that favors leveraging advantages you have at the moment into earning victory points.
In conclusion - try this game. It is great.

This game just works. This, in spite of being maligned as not even a game - less than you can do in a youtube session - is a game by someone who knows how to make them.
Interrogations, despite being abundant in video games, can be some of the worst gaming experiences. You can't follow your intuition, you can't ask the questions you want to, and any kind of urgency spoils rather than enhances the experience. Her Story cuts through all that by already answering all of the relevant questions and handing you the reigns to use your intuition to find those answers. Small tweaks in the old database system set just enough roadblocks in your way to keep you working at the mystery without distracting your attention, and often while adding to the 90s PC ambience.
Its hands-off approach and ambiguity set up a game which ends simply when you feel satisfied. Perhaps you will feel satisfied because you finally know her story. But maybe you won't! Playing this together with a friend lead to a great discussion on the crafting of the game's systems, but also to neither of us being certain about what we thought had happened. Perhaps instead, like us, you'll leave satisfied in the mechanics that lead you to wonder about it.
This is not a game where you can see any one of the clips and have the answer. As the picture you see expands, you have to look at it differently.
It's some weird♥♥♥♥♥♥ but not too shabby. Just make sure you go in order with the video clips.
Okami, Metal Gear Solid(1998), Half-Life, these are very different games from the regular ones. Well 'Her Story' is also in that league. A must play.

The core mechanic (jumping on a physics-controlled jelly floor) is only fun in a sort of experimental sense - it makes a terrible foundation for a platformer. The height of any given jump is unpredictable. If you are in a safe spot, you can repeatedly perform the same jump until you get the height you want. If need to jump while running... well, you can just hope (and probably fail, then replay the level the exact same way and hope you get a better unpredictable jump height next time).
Some other, more tolerable issues:
- Same old "unique surprise" at the end
- No gamepad support
- Occasional glitches (stuck in a wall, physics launching characters unpredictably, stuck in a perpetual-death loop, etc.)
- Meandering overworld maps without any real purpose/content, just meandering

Fear 2: Project Origin tells the story of psychic soldiers, crazy little girls, secrets and coverups. There are some cutscenes and readable backstory but seriously, that's not why we are here. We are here for some good old ultra violence. So let's look into that.
The game tries to be cinematic with it's slow-mo combat but now in the year 2015 it fails. The effects that maybe once were cutting edge are now average at best. To get as much sparks in the air as possible there needs to be a lot of bullets flying and what this means is that all weapons are horribly inaccurate and ineffective. Single headshot with assault rifle does nothing, you need 2-3. Spraying at a distance of say 15 meters you can be sure that you need atleast 20-30 smg rounds to kill an enemy. The sniper rifle is the players best friend even indoors.
Project Origin is new enough to have physics modeling but it basically only applies to corpses. Throw a grenade into an office full of desks, books etc. and very little moves. So no redeeming factors there either. Bullet spongy enemies without a proper fireworks display gets old fast. The game has few sections where the player gets to pilot a mech and in those you can destroy a decent amount of the scenery. Why it's restricted only to these levels is beyond me.
What suprised me most though was how powerless the sound design is. The weapon sounds and explosions are really weak. The design is also weird: For example if you stand next to and look at something that makes noise (machine, person talking, burning corpse etc.) you hear the sound it makes. Turn 180 and the sound almost disappears. Face the object again and it returns. When that is added to the lackluster visuals there really isn't much for the senses. Needless to say, on a modern machine Fear 2 runs without problems. On top of that it does have a wide range of graphical options to choose from.
Fear in this game translates into jump scares and they really are not scary. Some of the most gory parts are ghastly but there is no sense of threat. It's just blood and gore. Levels are made of grey facilities or ruins of a city so no wild set design here. At one part of the game the player has to navigate through a literal monster closet factory which was just silly.
Fortunately the AI is really aggressive and they will run after the player like bloodhounds and throw grenades like they have boxes full of them on hand. Only problem is that they tend to come at you one or two at a time so it's rarely overwhelming. I think Guacamelee is a very unique platformer, and you could easily have fun or at least SOME fun playing this game.
Looking at the gameplay first, as that's supposed to be the strong poing in such games, Guacamelee has the traditional gameplay expected from platformers but adds many new, irregular and original ideas to the concept, therefore making it sensible to call it an indie game as well.
It's fun and interesting, yes, but here comes a but... and it's a big BUT I'd say, the game becomes rather difficult, maybe a bit more than you'd want it to be, even on normal difficulty. About halfway through the game or even before you may reach the realization you're gonna need more than you're mere two hands to play this game properly with a keyboard. There's some crazy platforming going there, and you may quit it quickly if you lack the patience and dexterity the game would require at some stages. Another thing is that the boss levels feel quite unfair in my opinion, as the bosses would have MANY advantages over you, I somehow managed to get through it on the normal settings, but I guess I'll never be able to do the same on Harder difficulties...
I'd say that's like 7\10 for gameplay.
With all that said, the game is not too long. You could play through the main story within 6-7 hours or less. There's also a replayability value as there are many secret areas, some mini-quests and an alternative ending. But still, even as a completist I believe it's possible to finish it all within 8-10 hours.
That's 6.5\10 for length and 9\10 for replayability.
As I said, gameplay is overly alright. What about the rest? here the game fails a bit in my opinion.
Guacamelee is revolving around a mexican style... which it does perfectly, but perhaps I just couldn't get to it. Graphics were sweet, nothing too special but very sweet indeed.
The music I found annoying most of the time, until I learned to just completely ignore it. There were lots of moments where the music reminded me the old Pokemon games. And that's Not a good thing.
And, eventually, the story - that's the weakest point in the game in my opinion. Without telling too much (and there's not too much to tell) it's a pretty typical save-the-princess kind of story. Pretty dull, nothing too good or special.
So, bottom line, I'd say it's 6\10 for graphics, 4\10 for music, 2\10 for story.
That's kind of a shame because personally I pay a lot of attention to music\story\graphics in video games, and here they just don't suffice in order to make it a truly memorable platformer.
While I do recommend giving this game a shot, as I did enjoy it and play it to its (one) ending, I don't think I'll ever return to finish this game completly and find out all of the secrets, as I usually don't like those video games which make my hands hurt. Somehow, there are simpler platformers such as Rayman which I felt were much more memorable and enjoyable.
If there's ever going to be a Guacamelee 2, I'd like to see the original gameplay and concept stay, with some more thought when it comes to everything that revolves around the game itself.

Penumbra: Overture is the first game released by Frictional Games, using their proprietary HPL Engine. It's a very dated game, since it was released ten years ago, and you need to keep this is mind if you decide to give it a shot.
You'll be exploring an old decaying iron mine which hides some secrets in its depths. The story is interesting but the gameplay falls a bit short after a while, because it gets boring to explore labyrinth-like corridors and to evade the enemies roaming around. The combat is original yet VERY flawed, I never managed to land a single hit with the weapons I found, but an empty oil drum got the work done. That's where the HPL Engine is cool: to whack enemies with whatever stuff you find laying around.
The game makes a very clever use of the items you'll be finding around to proceed exploring the mine and the puzzles are fun to solve as well.
The graphics aren't anything worth mentioning, other than the excellent dynamic lightning (for 2007 standards) and the atmosphere it manages to set together with the sound effects. I must be getting used to these horror games because I can't say that I was scared at all, but Penumbra can be very unsettling at certain times.
Grab it in sale to enjoy how much Frictional has evolved over time.
I'll be starting Penumbra Black Plague now and I hope it is as interesting as Overture.

Great game.  So much nostalgia from my childhood.  Been needing a change from playing Kerbal Space Program and Age of Empires all the time, so I finally decided to play this game again.  Was sad to find out upon launching the game...
INSTABILITY ON WINDOWS 10 (I found a solution; keep reading)!!!  The game allowed me to select new game and create a character, but as soon as I launched the gameplay, it would instantly crash.
Was able to get the game to work though.  Hope this helps someone:
My solution:
1.  Go to the game directory for KOTOR (C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\swkotor)...for most people; exceptions for example, all my games are saved to HHD on drive F.  Right click on the executable for the game (.exe file) and select Properties.  Go to the Compatibility tab, and check the box which says "Run this program in compatibility mode for:".  I selected Windows 8 from the drop down menu; if you finish these procedures and it still doesn't work, stry Vista or XP (The Windows 10 instability seems to also affect Windows 7).  Hit OK.
3.  Once in game, got to Options and then Graphics.  Deselect Shadows and Grass.  I chose to run the game in 1024 x 768 at 75 Hz refresh for screen resolution (1280 x 1024 was just too small for me).
4. Select Advanced Options.  The setting on this page that seemed to make the game crash on me was Frame Buffer Effects.  Deselect this.  I was able to run at High graphics, 8 sample AA (Anti-aliasing), Anisotropy at 16%, and enable V-sunc.
These are all the changes I made.  The game appeared stable for the intro scenario and didn't crash.  I will update if this changes as I play farther into the game.
Another recommendation I had been given was editing the .ini file to run in windowed instead of full screen mode, but I didn't have to do this to get the game stable (I think) but it's something to keep in mind if your mileage varies from mine.
Just in case, here are the instructions I was given for windowed mode:
1. Go to swkotor.ini file and open it with Notepad (or Notepad++, etc). This should be located in the game directory.
2a. Locate the following line: Fullscreen=1
b. and change it to: Fullscreen=0.
3. In the [Graphic Options] section add the following line: AllowWindowedMode=1
4. Save the file and exit.
5. Launch game from directory .exe.  Launching through steam client or steam desktop shortcut will revert changes to this file.
Good luck!

Hitmang: Blood Money is the beautifully crafted story of an adolescent boy growing up trying to figure out what life is all about. In the game you encounter unique moments that are iconic to a young man's life - ranging from killing your first victim to hiding your first cold, lifeless body. Hitmane: Blood Monet is a great game, but it does have it's cons:
-Controls are sort of funky
-Optimization for PC is just not there
-Very violent for an E+ rated game (this
surprised me)
-Levels feel very boxed in, and it often feels like there is nowhere to go, and going about most situations is very one-sided.
Other than that, the game is sure to provide some quality entertainment. Now for some pros.
+Physics engine is pretty good. It can be a bit too realitic sometimes, but that's ok
+Graphics are fantastic, especially for when the game was released. They may not be up to par today, but the game is still just as enjoyable.
+The story is very rich with drama, romance, comedy, and especially blood - which is just essential for any Hotman game.
+Has an E+ rating, so many different types of age groups can enjoy it.
Overall, Hit and Run: Brood Mother is a pretty great game! I give it a 9.5/10. Thanks for reading!

Amazing game that fell prey to some tragic marketing and competition.
If you enjoy MOBAs and FPS titles, this is the perfect fusion you have been dreaming of.  The game mechanics are awesome, with extremely interesting and diverse skillsets and leveling options for each character, the combat is fast paced and tight, and if you appreciate the humor of Borderlands titles the story/characters are epic.
However; the launch of this game was spectacularly botched.  Blizzard "happened" to launch their hero shooter simultaneously, which deeply ate into the player base.  Then you must consider Battleborn was released at AAA title price, but the various characters were locked from the beginning except for 5.  This was done to gradually introduce players to the characters, but people associated it with free to play rosters in such games as DOTA2 and League of Legends, so this decision displeased many.
Furthermore there were initially massive graphical optimization problems on ATI cards, these didn't show up in the extensive beta/ technical test because they only occured on one specific map type not present in those tests.  In the first several weeks there were some very large balance problems as well.
All of these factors led to the vast majority of the intended audience for this game giving it the cold shoulder.  This creates a further problem we are now dealing with, in that the small group of people who have stuck around have put a lot of time into the game and are now very competent.  So whenever completely new players pick up the game, they predominately play against people with hundreds of hours of playtime, get stomped, and give up.
So if you have a good group of friends and go into this together, you can have a great time.  As a solo public grouper... Overwatch is a lot less intimidating :D

This is not a review. This is meant to be informative.
I have put a lot of time in this game and I have enjoyed it. With that said, I can not recommend this game. Regardless of the type of gamer you are, this cant be recommended to anyone considering the price. Whether you want a PVP or PVE experience, this game was made to focus heavily on PVP.
Campaign
The story mode consist of 8 stages (called episodes) and a prologue. The prologue takes about 20 minutes and the rest of the levels are around 40 minutes. This is around a 5-6 hour campaign. Replaying stages is sometimes fun because most of the dialogue changes. Each boss and mini boss has a chance to drop a legendary item. Each level (except prologue) can be played with 1-5 players. Each player increases the difficulty and loot drop rate.
Versus
Multiplayer consists of 4 game modes.
Incursion: Your traditional MOBA mode.
Meltdown: Usher minions down the lane to be sacrificed.
Capture: Capture and hold 3 points for as long as possible.
Face-off: Collect masks from killed minions (Veresia) and deposit them.
Operations (DLC)
This is a PVE mode. Currently there are 2 of 5 operations available, each sold for $5 (US) or included in the season pass. These are shorter than the story missions, about 30 minutes. You have to play each operation multiple times to gain the whole story. They can be played with a total of 3 players.
The problem with this game is the size of the player base. On a good day, there are around 300 peak players but most of the time the game struggles to reach even 200 peak players. There is a spike when DLC is released but this only last the weekend. A week ago the community decided to have an event called ‘Battleborn Day’. This actually pulled in over 700 peak players. Only a few days after and its back down to barely pushing 200. The game is dead and people are refusing to admit it. The small amount of people still playing are mostly High Ranked players. While they say that Command Rank means nothing and that people can be just as good, this is a lie. All the Hero s play very differently. While being new doesn't mean you suck, it does mean you lack experience. Almost all new players start out with Miko (The Mushroom) and always are at the front of the group attacking. Miko is a healer. Almost everything he does is focused on healing. Many have begged for this to go Free to Play. THIS WILL NOT SAVE IT. Just because its free doesn't mean everyone will play this. Games have tried this before and only a few make it. This year alone, around 10 games shut down.
If this isnt a problem for you then keep in mind this game is always online. You cant even see the main menu unless you are signed into steam and connected to the SHIFT servers. Once they decide not to do anything with it anymore and they shut it down, you wont be able to play. This also means you can lag while in single player. If you are disconnected from the server in a single player game, the server will close meaning you have to start the level from the beginning.
If you can get this for around $5 or maybe a little more if you can get a group together then it would be worth it. If not, you are taking a huge risk.

How the game works:
1.) Map
The map consists of rectangular tiles which are covered in fog of war. These tiles can be either streets or houseblocks. Streets can be used to move units. Houseblocks can be burgled for money and research currency (lamps).
Houseblock also contain one of several infiltratable buildings which give different bonuses like more money, lamps or discounts on units.
2.) Exploration
Each turn, the active player gets a character which has a certain number of actions per turn. The number of actions depends on certain skills in the research trees.
An action can be:
- Get rid of up to 3 tiles fog of war at streets
- Attack an NPC / enemy player unit
- Scout a houseblock und burgle the building you entered the housblock through.
- Burgle a building of an already discovered houseblock
After all your actions with this character are used, you can't explore further. (with one excpetion)
3.) Builder Placement
Each turn the active player can spend gold to hire henchman. These are:
-Urchin (can infiltrate buildings to give the player boni)
-Thug (can block streets and disappear after 2 turn(doesn't count for gangs))
-Gang (can attack NPC / enemy player units, gets an upgrade for each kill(8 total), gets life by "devour" Thugs)
-Saboteur (places traps in buildings for 2 turns. Unit which attacks a trapped building is stunned for 1 turn and loses all actionpoints. Also scouts buildings)
-Officer (clears an entire building from urchins. Disappears after 1 use)
-Assassin (Deals massive damage. Disappears after 1 use)
4.) Research
Each turn, the active player can buy upgrades from 3 tech trees for lamps. these upgrades give several bonuses like more advanced henchman or more action points for the temporary character.
Campaign:
The campaign consists of 11 levels with different objectives.
The first 3 levels are more or less the tutorial, where the game guides you through its mechanics. But, the third level is by far the most difficult one in the entire game.
The rest plays like a normal skirmish with some cool ideas to change the objectives (don't wanna spoiler something here).
In my opinion its the strongest part of the game, despite its length.
I still have to criticise the 3rd level as to hard, not just in terms of an normal level, but also as an follow up, to the first 2 really easy and guided missions.
Skirmish:
Skirmish games are games for victory points against the AI.
You can choose to play on 4 different maps. 3 of them already known through the campaign.
You can also choose the difficulty of the bots from 3 different difficulties.
To make a long story short, you play through the above mentioned steps (How the game works) and fight for victorypoints.
After some matches you get a spin on how things work and this mode brings you no challenge anymore.
Multiplayer:
The Multiplayer is split into 2 options, which play out like skirmish matches, but against a real opponent.
1.) Live Match
The are literally skirmish matches against a human player.
The big downside is, you can't choose a map (its random) and you just can see the scenario info in loadscreens
2.) Casual
Casual matches play out as skirmishes too, but not synchronous like a live match. The match is hosted on a server, so you can actually leave the game for your opponents turn.
You get an email when your turn begins.
The problem with this is, even, when you stay ingame, everytime your turn starts, you get an email. It is possible to disable this in the options. But i would prefer a simple
query if the player is still taking part in the actual game. If not send a email, if he is, dont send one.
In this mode you're actualy able to use the scenario info outside of the loading screen.
And now the criticism:
These are mostly aimed on the multiplayer part of the game
1. First turn advantage
After a developer answered to this post, that they took measurements to prevent this, I played some more games against a friend.
Every time, the player, who started first won the map. You really get some extra lamp on your first turn, and our experience may be just unlucky, but at least for me, this is a thing.
2. Maps aren't randomized itself, but how the ressources are distributed is.
This is a big problem. Especially in the early game. A fairly legit tactic is to rush to the enemy base, research thugs and spam his base. This forces the player to develop gangs and let them stay out in the open, so they can be killed.
If you also have no gold generating buildings, you have to kill the Thugs with your main character, which costs you an action and also the only attack for a round. On the other side, the other player still has his freedom,
can expand faster and snowball out of this.
I dont wanna have a mirrored map or something like this, but I think a money generating building at the start area should be added.
3. Victory points are randomized over the map.
I.)Churches spawn in different locations with different distances to the player
II.)assasinationtargets / NPC targets spawn random through all of the map (despite buildings)
It can happen, that a Target is spawning in front of a playerbase, which means the other player has some big problems, like:
- the other player hasn't lifted the fog of war yet.
- the "lucky player" will kill the other players gang for getting the target (which brings the other player into a hughe disadvantage)
- the "lucky player" can train his gangs with addspawn from the target.
-the "lucky player" also can have some disadvantages by this spawn too.
This targets block paths, so one player can trap the enemy inside of his spawn very easy and also spawnkilling new gangs without having any risk.
4. Insufficient Visibility for Victorycontions
Victoryconditions are just visible through a button in the menu (through the gear symbol) or the loadscreen before a match.
In live matches the button in the menu is not clickable.
I would like to see a button in the actual game (in the UI, not in the menu) which shows you the victorycondition of the current map when pressed.
After playing some more games and also played the campaign, i can understand why many people recommend this game. But I still have my concerns especially
on the PVP side of the game and can't change my decision with good conscience.
I will look into later patches and update this review if neccessary.
I hope the team behind this will keep it up and take this as its meant to be, constructive criticism from someone, who appreciates and likes the idea behind the game.

At first, this game may seem enjoyable and the art style is nice. Playing on normal difficulty where the AI uses questionable strategies, you'll enjoy it for a few hours.
However - against hard difficulty AI or any competent player, the game becomes a long and grating war of attrition. This is not fun at all. To add to that, there is an element of RNG involved - if one of the players spawns near better resources, that player is clearly going to have an advantage.
So in all, the game doesn't have much replay value once you've completed the story. It works much better as a short, single player game instead of a long, grindy multiplayer where both players come to a stalemate after gathering the map's resources.

Have you ever experienced the beauty of a "fine" game? Let me elaborate: What I mean is a game that is not utterly awesome, but still does everything right. A game you pick up for a second playthrough knowing you will get nothing innovative or mind-blowing, but in spite of this, you'll still enjoy every second. Hell, after finishing, you won't rule out a third run happening in the future.
FEAR 2 is this kind of game.
Sure, FEAR brought some really impressive new stuff to the table, like mixing horror themes into an FPS setting, clever AI and FPS bullet time. But those were achievements introduced by the first game, and thus, FEAR 2 cannot claim them as its own. Actually, there is really nothing new in the sequel (with one notable exception, but more on that later), and stripped of the hallmarks of the series, Project Origin is a pretty standard FPS:
...which is what makes it so great.
A big part of why it succeeds is its pacing. FEAR 1 is a great game, without any need for great improvements. But what it lacked was proper pacing, a deficit also found in Condemned 1, another Monolith game. Many sections dragged oooon and ooooon without much variation. It was warehouse after warehouse after warehouse, and later bureau complex floor after bure- you get the point. Its scenarios simply didn't know when they wore out their welcome.
FEAR 2 eliminates that weakness. Its pacing is just great. Just when a setting tends to get tedious, it switches to a new one or offers a new enemy or a nice set piece to spice things up. It never, ever gets boring, in my opinion. What's also great is that the graphics still are very good. It's a bit more colorful, but not to the excess of FEAR 3, hitting the sweet spot between the drab first game and the overkill of the third. It's another example of this "just fine" mentality I mentioned in the beginning.
No, FEAR 2 won't blow you away with a great story. No, your jaw won't drop to the floor every five minutes. No, you won't marvel at game-changing innovations. Will you have a good time all the way through? Hell, yes.
...but my review would not be complete without addressing the one awesome new feature the game DOES introduce. You probably guessed it: Exosuit battles. There are only two sections in the campaign, but boy, are they fun! Nothing beats the feeling of gleefully raining down destruction with your gatling guns and missile launchers. Also, what could have basically have been just an overpowered reskin of the normal on-foot sections -and strictly gamplay-wise, it is - is helped so much by its presentation. You feel every step of the hulking mech when its lumbering steps shake your view, and the vision has a slight oversaturation combined with grain that completely sell the experience, A part of me wishes there would have been more of this, but on the other hand, its restrained use is another example of FEAR 2's pitch-perfect pacing.

As far as fictional trope genres go, horror is a close number two to my love for scifi (sorry fantasy).  Anything from slasher to paranormal usually gets me excited and interested, and one genre of horror I've always been in general orbit around is Lovecraftian.  Due to a lack of bandwidth or maybe just poor choices on my own part, I've only dabbled in this area of horror, but have a pretty good idea of how some of the more popular concepts and characters work (spawning all KINDS of shoggoths in Super Scribblenauts back on the Nintendo DS!).
Magrunner: Dark Pulse starts out as the gleaming, pretty, Mirror's Edge style universe, with nods to Tesla and Facebook all over the place, that after the first hour or so quickly devolves into this grimy, rusted, supernatural, Lovecraftian romp.  I almost kind of wish they hadn't peeled away the fancy futurist style so quickly, because aside from the early and late chapters, you're left with this rust tinted, more decayed set of maps.  The futurist stuff was probably the prettiest part graphically, and using it so minimally just didn't do the assets justice.  The level designers could have taken some more nods from the Portal series and slowly peeled back those layers (remember how crazy those last few levels of Portal were?).  The final levels are just crazy and wild and nonsensical, and will tickle anyone's Cthulu curiosity if only briefly.
Speaking of Portal, as a first person puzzle game with different rooms/puzzles/chambers/situations for each level, there will always be a lot of comparisons to what many will argue is the best benchmark for this type of genre.  Mechanically speaking, the idea of using attracting and repelling magnetic fields on props in the map sounds like a simple binary solution mechanic you find in the Portal series (blue and orange portals vs red and blue magnetic fields), but Magrunner's difficulty curve turns it up to 11 as the narrative proceeds, so if you're looking for a challenge: Have. At. It.  Magrunner actually implements the one thing I always craved in a Portal game though, in that there are levels where you have to outwit enemy AI and cause their untimely demise using your magnetic glove and props on the map.  This is a lot different from the stationary turrets of Portal-land, and can be a lot more intense when the oogie-boogie is trying to grab you relentlessly if you miss that jump.
The story has a basic setup for why the protagonist is doing what he's doing, and dives into the "what the heck even?" of being thrown into the mix with a Cthulu-death-cult that comes as the standard reaction for anyone who hasn't been exposed to this sort of stuff.  There's nothing outstanding about the narrative, the cut scenes in between acts are told via animated paintings and get the jist of the basic plot across in small bite-sized pieces, while virtual interactions with NPC's do the rest of the heavy lifting in that regard.  The universe itself has some interesting pieces that never quite get explained, like why magnets to do what the Zuckerberg anagrammed benefactor aims to do?  Or what's the deal with mutants in this society?  What happened to the other testing candidates? And what even happened to put Earth into the state its in (to avoid spoilers) after the last level for the epilogues final cut scene?  Maybe if I was more up and up on Cthulu stuff the ending would make more sense, but I've become used to accepting the wtf endings that horror narratives provide so I'll leave it.
If you're big on Lovecraftian themes, or are looking for a challenging first person puzzle game with a unique and challenging set of puzzle mechanics, be sure to give this a look when its on sale.  If you're only here for the story you'd be better served looking elsewhere.  As it stands, I can't hold any of the games flaws against it TOO hard, since it does most of what its trying to do competently, and it has a really weird mix of genres in a single place I wasn't expecting to find in the first place.

OH, I hated to give this game a thumbs down. The first part if fantastic!
Let me explain. The first part of the game is a Puzzle Game and the second part is an arcade game.
For those of you that don't know the difference, I'll explain.
A Puzzle game (PUZZLE) gives you a situation that is placed in front of you to solve. You have all of the information that you need up front and you can take your time to intellectualy solve the puzzle.
A simple example are the kinds of puzzles on MillerWorldInc.
An Arcade game on the other hand is a puzzle of sort BUT it doesn't give you all of the information up front. They were designed to make people keep putting quarters into a video game machine to "Keep Trying Things Over and Over" in order to figure out what the Software Designer wanted you to do.
Does the Mario Brothers ring a bell?
And OVER and OVER is the key word here.
The second part of what could have been a fantastic game is reduced to the repetitive Trial and Error crap that was designed into the arcade machines of the past who's main function was to keep you putting quarters into the machine to learn just a little more each time before you were killed by whatever.
And this is where Magrunner falls Very Short for puzzle solving people.
Like I said, in the beginning you are presented with puzzles for your mind to solve.
By the end it unfortunately just turns into an adolescent arcade game.
BUT>>>For the few bucks that they are asking, I would still advise PUZZLE PEOPLE to buy the game and just play it until it turns into an arcade game because I think you will still enjoy the beginning which will bring you hours of entertainment.

I'm going to state my opinion of Magrunner's Gameplay, Story, and other miscellaneous bits that I feel are worth mentioning.
The story show promise for the first few hours. An introduction with beautiful art illustrates our main characters, and also delivers a bit of back-story on what today's hottest events are about. The first area the story fails to grab with is by not giving enough character to the characters. They show emotions, and say words, but it doesn't feel like what anyone says is important to more than moving the story forward. To put it loosely: it's not enjoyable to hear.
Cthulhu enters scene, and he proceeds to step on a stone and fall on his face. Honestly, why couldn't the developer/publisher just have left Cthulhu out of it until we found it out in the story.
Promotional screenshots, trailers, literally the first sentence of the store description informs the buyer/player that the Cthulu Mythos is revelent to this game. WHY? It makes the actual reveal lackluster.
However, for a positive on the story, when we do start to leave the facility, and hints of Cthulu, and the unknown are present; the setting is truly un-nerving because it's that contrast of hell and high-class facility that keeps you on edge for a while.
I also found the third act having been devoid of dialogue a bit sad. Though the mad scientist was fun to see! Crazy buggard.
The gameplay is something I would call rough. The ideas are all there. The puzzle have a lot of thought put into them, and the challenge is pretty high, and unlike some I liked the wide/big enviroments, because the art/designs of many of the rooms were pretty rad.
The mechanics are cool for the first half of the game. They involve using a reverse magnetism with like polarities attracting, and opposites going away from one another
(They most likely did this so if you wanted to connect more than two objects there wouldn't be any conflicting issues with two objects being the same, and one being opposite, and everything flies everywhere)
There's a lot of pieces that are involved in solving the puzzles, like: platforms, pendulems, boxes, smaller boxes, and what I'd consider the worst addition to puzzle solving: the entrance of Dex's dog Newton. All puzzles until the introduction of this dog had you using boxes and platforms in your environment. And also by changing their polarities and locations to then reach an end. This dog however changes everything. It lets you place either polarity basically anywhere. It's like if in Portal you could place a white-portal-placing-wall anywhere for solving puzzles. It would be a nightmare.
Speaking of nightmares, I don't remember the name of the level now, but I skipped the entire level by falling off an edge and onto the environment. I did so out of pure frustration for the amount of "things" present for the puzzle. similarly the rock design of space created a lot of situations where I could be stuck, or just shimmy around the environment, like it felt as if I shouldn't be allowed to go to those areas.
Last bits on gameplay: The puzzle difficulty really ramps up around the middle, and some of the latter puzzles are downright evil in design, and left me wondering if the developer just thought we'd know that we should carry boxes on the under-belly of platforms that are transfered from another platform.
I really do love the graphics on this one. Just because it's unreal from 2013 doesn't mean it doesn't look good. I'd love more non-sense effects like depth of field (present for a short while after entering a room) motion blur, better anti-aliasing, and bloom (please don't shoot me if these are actually present) As it doesn't seem to have that 110% C I N E M A T I C presentation of a 2016 game, because it isn't one.
But, act 1's clean facilities are a beaut to see, and the design put on show would be breathe-taking to actually see in person. the second act feels a bit to old and rustic without much change over 3 hours, but that was probably the intention. And, by act 3 we hit full space-on-Cthulhu action, and some of the locals in this act are pretty dang-on fine.
The animations are a mix of great, and iffy: The human's movements are great, and add what little character the characters need into place, but the animation on The Old Ones doesn't feel weighty enough. It kinda looks like someone did a mo-cap for it, and didn't edit it afterwards.
The models look great. From Gamaji's multiple appendages flying about, to Xander's blood soaked face in the third act; All the models are of high quality, and look like actual people.
textures could be better.
-Cthulhu is hinted far to early, and too obvious, as the transmission in the subtitles clearly shows the first and second part of the name cthulhu with the sentence shown.
-Second also is that we see Xander once or twice, and the reveal of him being mad doesn't have enough punch because of it. Maybe a bit more interaction with the main character, would've benefited the development.
-More tips. Maybe it's because I was on an SSD, but I only saw 2-3 tips that were barely relevent to solving puzzles. mostly just on the basic controls. So, more text-boxes or explanations on the physics of the game would've made the second and third act ride on smoother.
-Sometimes the physics work, and sometimes they don't. A lot of it relies on calculations, and numbers that we as players literally cannot see in the code. It's infuriating for a platform to fall down, down, down because it was a hair away from connecting WITH THAT DAMN DOG.
An interesting gameplay mechanic, thrown in with Cthulhu, but ultimately both pieces are on the rough side. So, I give it an average 5/10

The game features a man following in the footsteps of his father who left him a mysterious letter from apparently before his birth, telling his son not to follow him. Having limited info about his fathers wherabouts and life, his curiosity got the best of him and he went off to find out what happened to him by going to a mine/military bunker in icy Greenland, pointed out to him in the letter.
From there, you play as a fit, but not strong man, exploring a dark, and abandoned mine network solving relatively simple puzzles, sneaking around strange monsters, and out running even stranger monsters. The majority of your inventory use will be light sources (flares, flashlights, glowsticks) and puzzle items and keys, Penumbra hardly has combat, you can find a hammer, pickaxe and broom, but they will be used mostly to deal with easily breakable planks and barrels, and rarely if ever for combat. Attacking enemies never served me well, and I always found myself better off running away and somewhat exploiting the dog AI. Apparently you can kill spiders, but the "attack" mechanic is so clunky that its never worth it when it only takes two hits to be killed and the fast enemies are hard to hit. The dog like enemies has funky AI, which sometimes you can run away from if they "Kind of detect you" or sometimes detect you from really far away when they haven't before. The same dogs are also fooled by you jumping on a chest high box, and sometimes go away after you run in to a "steam cage" in the later portion of the game. (You can probably kill or subdue them here, but it has never worked out for me). You can use beef Jerky to distract them if you stay out of sight, but I found it better to learn their patterns and walk behind them.
The gameplay is physics based and "Mouse-motion control based", so you have to swing your mouse to attack and drag your mouse to pull levers, twist valves, and open doors. Most players will either hate this for being needlessly cumbersome, or love it for the tension it brings. I found it good tension for opening doors and not knowing what to expect behind the door or when being chased, but was annoying otherwise. Thankfully, most "inventory puzzles" work like classic adventure games where you either combine items or place one over something in the environment.
You'll eventually recieve communication from a character that has gone mad from living isolated in a small area of the mines for weeks and assists you in your journey. I grew a disdain for this character, as well as the lack of reaction from the PC for the way he treats him. The player character eventually has an opinion of him that I oppose, and I feel many other players will feel the same. To be as spoiler free as possible, the ending was unceremonius, abrupt, and a set up for the sequel.

Wow!  Just beat this game and that's about all I can say is wow.  It was awesome!  I just glanced at the first couple of reviews and noticed they're negative reviews complaining about the combat style and I guess non-intuitiveness? of the control scheme, and I have to say, I do agree if you're playing it on a traditional monitor/screen.  But I just played the whole game on my Oculus CV1 thanks to the VR mod and it's truly amazing.  The genius modder, Joseph Delgado, definitely deserves props for this one!  Some notes on the VR mod:  It fully supports Oculus Touch (even though he wrote it for and with the HTC Vive in mind), however, it does require a 360 degree setup (3 sensors) because there is no turning mechanism (snap turning or otherwise).  But with 3 sensors in 360 setup, it's nothing short of fantastic.  The only issue is Philip doesn't jump as high or far in the VR mod since the modder did something kind of screwy with the gravity I believe.  I didn't actually play the game in 2D before I jumped into VR so I didn't know any better until I found 2 spots in the game where it was completely unpassable in the VR mod due to not being able to jump far enough.  Once I realized I just played those 2 parts on my desktop real quick and once it gave me a save point, I went back to VR and it only happened twice.
So for the rest of my review on the game, I want to point out that these devs really knew how to make a great game.  It has everything from compelling story, crazy atmospheric gameplay, sounds, and the list goes on.  This is a gem of a game.  I'm kind of torn on whether I should play the next Penumbra game since there is no VR mod for it, or just wait for the source code to be released so another fine soul can add VR support.  Hell, even though this is an old game by now, it might prove a good idea for the original devs to add VR support for this series and gain some recognition and reputation for a future game/series hopefully built for VR as well.  Just food for though.  Anyway, 2 Thumbs Up!

While Hitman: Blood Money kind of has an odd start (I'm pretty sure the tutorial was more focused on showing you how cool they are for adding new features instead of actually teaching you the features), I think it definitely turns out to be a great game. I wouldn't say the game is very hard, but it does take strong attention-to-detail and overall good observation of people's walking movings and general behaviors to even reach your enemy. I currently haven't played any of the other games except Absolution, so I will just give pros and cons for a new person to the series rather than a Hitman veteran.
Pros:
- Solid execution that makes this game still fun 10 years later without feeling dated.
- Great level design which gives you a choice in playstyle; it could be possible to beat one level 20 times, based on what traps, weapons, and disguises you use.
- Fun levels which almost make you excited or scared based on your situation; all levels are truly entertaining.
- Great introduction of storyline -- The game's story takes place in the present, tells you a little more about the story and Agent 47, and sends you in a non-linear flashback of one of Agent 47's hits. This allows you understand the gameplay and story easily, and learn about Agent 47's life.
- Changes future difficulty of levels with Notoriety. Obviously, in real life, if you shot up a drug lord's factory, it would be all over the news, and people would eventually find out an idea of the guy who did it. Because this is in the game, people will eventually figure out who keeps killing these people, so you'll end up being hostile to guards before you even really start the mission. It makes you have to understand how to limit witnesses and having your cover blown. Luckily, you can reset things like this for paying money to fix it, but it's still a pain in the butt and would be easier to just stealth.
- On another note, the game encourages you to do things in a somewhat subtle way, unlike the notoriety.  If you drop your weapons or leave your suit behind, this can not only change notoriety a bit, but it costs money for the Agency to retrieve it, so you have to pay a fee. On top of this, killing civilians with no witnesses also costs a fee for obvious reasons.
- Intelligent AI during missions. So many games I've played where AI ignore key things like blood trails that humans would clearly follow, but Hitman: Blood Money pretty much has it to where AI act as intelligent human beings.
Cons:
- Unfortunately, there are some weak points of the pros I described. A problem in the AI is that they ignore weapons dropped on the floor, this becomes really obvious in the "Flatline" mission when you place your guns down.
- The tutorial is pretty bad.
- This being a game from 2006, there are parts that really make this game show its age and feels frustratingly dated, and kills a lot of the immersion. However, these parts I could count on one hand, and are very rare.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game, as I had a lot of fun and really experience something I hadn't felt before. This is a really nice concept and I played it constantly for a while. This is the best Hitman game in the series, and if you're looking for a good stealth game to get immersed into, this is a great game to start with, or even try if you're a stealth expert. No matter your experience with stealth or Hitman, this is a great game to play and you'll definitely have a lot of fun with it.

Disappointing game of tug-of-war between sparse gameplay mechanics and lackluster story.
To explain that opinion dump in the previous sentence, I need to at least briefly summarize Her Story's premise and ideas. The game is, by and large, an investigation game, where you are tasked with figuring out what happened using little bits of recorded interviews with the woman arrested for murder. You are acquiring those files by typing words into the search engine that yield results depending on what woman said on the record. Use clues and keywords discovered to finish that puzzle and figure out what happened.
Sounds kinda unique and interesting right? If you read the positive reviews, you can see people enjoying putting the story together. I could agree that on the basic level there is something satisfying in figuring things on your own without any handholding, but the overall experience was tarnished by the disappointment that is the core story. Not only the plot presented, when examined from A to B, ends out outrageously outlandish, cliché and nonsensical, but it also doesn't mesh well with the gameplay ideas on which Her Story was founded on.
Since you are only limited to the small clips of random answers, everything you find should provide information that could be used to advance. This makes most of the clips artificially foreshadowy or obvious red herrings that are needless fluff that won't add anything substantial to the table. In those filler parts themes and arc words are repeated ad nauseum, making it look like a attempt at planting more
interpretations of the story that fails miserably. Additionally, since you can type anything into the search, you can discover the main
extremely quickly, by simply following some particular clues. I use the quotation marks since said big, grandiose revelation ends up being extremely bizarre, if not outright stupid. It absolutely tarnishes the credibility of the plot. Her Story after that becomes low-stakes hunt for the few remaining blanks very fast, forcing you to ask questions like
. Finally, the limit of 5 oldest videos as a search results, was supposedly put in there to slow down your progress, but in the end it becomes more of the hindrance that makes you question, who in-universe would create such broken and unusable database system.
Her Story was engineered in the way that it could be explained in two or three different interpretations of the events. It's good that the games sometimes don't offer straight answers and you as a player, are welcomed to make your own judgments. Unfortunately this only works if at least one of the ideas for what actually happened felt plausible and didn't rely on absolute stupidity of the entire cast or bullet-proof suspension of disbelief of the player's side.
When you are ready to wrap it up, the game itself ask you as a player/in-game character are they are satisfied with the outcome. The only way to "officially" end the game is to agree with this statement. I find this bit extremely arrogant on the developer's part, since it assumes that the player finished the game happy what they saw and learned, which ultimately isn't a case in my view. Her Story ends up without fanfare, both in the literal and figurative speech, leaving the feeling of disappointingly hallow experience not worth the hype. It's a experiment at some quite original mechanics that ultimately fails. Too many compromises. I had high hopes that those 25+ awards on the sidebar will mean something and game will truly succeed on bringing something revolutionary and refreshing for the industry.
...I was wrong.

Her Story is for people who like to spy on others, solve mysteries, and explore databases. It feeds into the human inclination to watch other people, combined with the excitement of discovering secrets. Great for dopamine junkies. There's a fair bit of typing, and you'll want volume for this (although subtitles are an option).
Also, you'll want a pen and a piece of paper to take notes; by the end of the game, my scratchpad looked like I was playing a really dark and creepy word search puzzle. I think I ended up writing down about 150 keywords with which to search the video database.
My biggest complaint is that the music that plays while you're between videos (in the interface proper) is wildly out of place, and cannot be turned off.
Pros:
+ amazing, complex story.
+ great acting.
+ clever interface.
+ feels very realistic.
+ really, the story is incredible.
+ has a windowed mode.
+ subtitles.
+ achievements.
+ trading cards.
Cons:
- jumping back and forth between mouse and keyboard.
- extreme difficulty in getting all the achievements.
- the music wasn't really necessary, and rather distracting.
- no option to turn off the music.
Ephy Rating: 8/10
Summary: If you enjoy people-watching, spying on the neighbours, or true crime, you'll probably enjoy this experience. Definitely recommended.

I wanted to like this game. I enjoy a good mystery quite a bit. But this one...well, I don't know. I figured out one of the core conceits of this one in pretty short order, and it struck me as kind of a bad cliche, and one that rather strained credulity. And, contrary to the experience of other reviewers, I didn't find that there were dozens of twists and turns after this; there's really just that one "big twist," and once you've uncovered that, it's just a matter of figuring out what topics the interviews cover that are only tangentially relevant.
I gather from the other reviews that I'm in the extreme minority in having this reaction to the game, and that others found the story well-written and engaging. But I found it pat and trite.
To put it another way, there are a lot of people whose reviews say something along the lines of "it would never work as a movie you watched straight through." My experience agreed with this, but didn't find that the interface did anything to fix that.
Editing to add: there are people who disagree with the conclusion I reached, and have concluded that the reason the story is so implausible is that it is false. Unfortunately, this requires a level of planning on the part of the interviewee which is similarly implausible, and would put it squarely in the idiom of The Usual Suspects, or The Interview (1997). There is a third interpretation which also relies on a cliched trope, but a different cliched trope. None of these really strikes me as an interpretation which puts the story in a better light, however, so I stand by my review.

I got this game a few weeks ago, when it was on sale for ~$30 USD. I got the PC version, and have already sunk around 40 hours into this game. I really enjoy it!
Here are some pros:
Here are some cons:
Overall review: I think that this is a great game that recognizes the fact that it's doing a lot of MOBA-styled gameplay (like PvP mode Incursion, or having abilities with cooldowns and damage that can be augmented as the character levels up each game) in a first-person shooter, and it
that fact! There's a ton of variety of characters, playstyles, and loadouts, so every person that plays this game can play it in the way that they find most fun. There are characters with rocket launchers, all sorts of guns, grenade launchers, laser guns, and a slew of melee characters!  Personally, I've really enjoyed just single-player Story mode, but there's something for just about everybody! Although $60 may be a high price tag, I think that I easily got $30 of content, which is what I paid for this game. Although it's not as fast-paced as some other FPS games (each Story mission taking anywhere from 20-30 minutes if you're rushing through or up to an hour if you're farming XP and coins, like I was) some of the PvP matches can be over in about 10 minutes! The tanks feel tanky, the assassins feel deadly, and the supports can do way more than just healing or shielding!
Things that this game could do to improve: change how much money that it's being sold for when not on sale. It'd be great if you could either play the base game for $20 or less and then have the current amount of microtransactions, or pay the full $60 and then
would be unlocked except the DLC Ops modes. That means your gear bank expansions, skins, and taunts would all be purchased using in-game currency, and you wouldn't have to spend another penny to get everything unlocked in the base game. If the first option is chosen, hopefully more people will buy the game and the playerbase will increase, helping to negate some of the downsides in the game right now.
Wait for it to go on sale for about $30, and then buy it. Worst case scenario: you play it, don't like it, and still get your $30 worth of content. Best case scenario: you play it, fall in love with it, and then you've gotten a game with tons of variety, replayability, and customization.
would recommend. -1.25 for high price and microstransactions at the same time, and -.25 for a few bugs that are still in the game.

Paper Monsters Recut is a 2.5D platformer where the world has a charming paper Mache look to it. We play as an unnamed robot looking fellow on a quest to stop an evil dinosaur. To accomplish this we will jump on the heads of our enemies Mario style and make our way through an over-world full of levels as well as secrets. Unlocking new levels require us to collect golden paper clips which there are 3 of in each level. You can either walk all the way to the area you want or you can simply teleport there. It's a really pretty looking over-world but it can be a bit poorly designed on some spots making it difficult to go to your destination.
This is a friendly and simple game that feels like it is centered for children. It is an easy game, perfect for those just starting out with video games. It can be quite boring in fact if you have even a bit of experience with platformers though on the other hand it can also be relaxing. Along with the paper clips scattered around each level there is a golden button that unlocks a few mini-games if you collect enough. Most of the secrets are extremely easy to find so it wouldn't be abnormal if you finish the game with everything collected.
Controls feel a bit funky at first though it didn't take long to get used to them. For most of the levels the most you can do is simply jump and run your way through obstacles. Annoyingly enough the jumping sound effects are very out of place and sounds like you are playing as a squishy blob. You can double jump and take three hits from your enemies before biting the dust and being sent back to a checkpoint. It's not much of a punishment since you keep everything that you have collected and they give out extra lives like candy. Your enemies range from dinosaurs, cacti and sombrero wearing spiders.
They don't chase you or actively try to harm you, they just walk around a preset route and randomly attack at nothing. Jumping on enemies is not always a way to defeat them since as you may guess jumping right onto a cactus is not the best of ideas. At the end of each area there is a boss to fight that all require different methods to take down but are incredibly easy. Defeating one will get you a golden key which unlocks a new area for you to conquer. From time to time they throw in some neat gimmicks to spice things up such as sledding down a snowy mountain or commandeering a submarine. You'll also have access to a jetpack in one area which also gives you a laser gun to defend yourself with.
Defeating enemies is not satisfying since there is a ton of delay from the moment you jump on them to the moment they flatten that just made it feel glitchy in my opinion. The mini games you can unlock are an endless vehicle section and a Runner type of game. It is a very per the rules type of game and there is nothing you haven't seen before or any unique ideas other than the artstyle. But wow, is the game pretty to look at and there are quite a few themes to go through. Levels are usually only a few minutes long and you can blast through this game in just a few hours. There is no real replay value unless you missed a few things or simply want to play it again for the sake of it.
Story is paper thin (no pun intended) and barely something worth mentioning. There a few characters that are in the over-world but are just there to serve as breathing tutorials whose role could have easily been replaced by a sticky note. Music on the other hand is pretty stellar and a joy to listen to. There are “Super-Secret Levels” hidden around the over-world that have you collecting 20 pieces of candy though each one of the is mostly the same and are pretty boring. All in all Paper Monsters is a good game for children or those of us looking for a game to relax with but other than the artstyle there isn't anything else that separates it from the rest of the genre and as such may be less than stellar for those looking for a remarkable platformer.

I cannot recommend this game. I want to, I really do, but it is unbalanced in a few, yet crucial, ways that transforms a charming and novel experience with a lot of promise into sheer frustration, or, more frequently, shock and disbelief. Make sure you've made your sacrifices to the random number generator gods before playing this one. There are (at least) two things that need to be re-worked: 1) the Resolve mechanic, and 2) the attack power of minions. You start each expedition with barely enough Resolve to survive it. The early expeditions are easy enough, but then sometimes you die on the first encounter of your first expedition. Even hardcore rogue-likes are more balanced than that. Failure is often so unavoidable mainly because Resolve is reduced for each character that falls, and once you hit zero Resolve, it's 'game over'. This is also due to minions doing nearly as much "damage" as bosses, and respawning at a considerable rate with no perceivable limit to their quantity. Because some encounters railroad you into certain strategies, and because your party might only be really good at other strategies, you can end up with a highly skilled and decked-out party who is just up♥♥♥♥♥♥creek in some encounters. And that wouldn't be so bad occasionally, but since the result is 'game over' and you really had no chance, it's more than a little confusing and frustrating. So to save yourself from this fate, you'll find yourself just doing whatever your party is best at, regardless of whether it's appropriate to the situation.
IMO, the worst kind of gaming experience you can have is really wanting to like a game that has some genuinely great ideas and a lot of potential, but not being able to because of the despair it engenders via meaningless "are you feaking kidding me?" and "I'm not even mad anymore, this is just ridiculous" moments, in spite of your level of mastery. That's what happens here w/ RE:IS. Maybe it's worth a purchase on sale, but not at full price.

The developer, Ian Snyder, must have thought it would get boring after about an hour so he changed it, removed it actually.  There is no narrative so there is no explanation of why this happens and it becomes a constant struggle against the physics, which worked well only minutes before.  The final levels of the game felt as if I only completed them out of luck and patience.  I'm not trying to bash on the game for only being about two hours, but more levels with just the base mechanics would have been fine, but the ending completely ruins the fun and leaves me with anger and frustration.
During most of the game though the music is soft and relaxing, a bit atmosphereic in some areas even.  The sound design is nice and precise with no audio delays.  But the smooth music is ditched during the end of the game as well and leaves an almost hollow and unsettling sound, but not scary, more of an "if the gameplay is bad so as well be the music."
I would not reccomend this game unless you can get it for free, even the $1.99 I payed I felt was not worth spending because of the fight I put up with against the game itslef at the end and was relieved to see the credits and be done with it.
