I usually dislike turn-based RPG's with complex management systems, and this game is certainly that. However, the charm and wittiness of how combat works actually draws me in more than I'd like to admit. If you want to call it that, as it draws more inspiration from ace attorney and Faster Than Light than your standard "here are a dozen similar-but-different ways to harm an opponent"-RPG.
Aside from that, the game certainly does a lot with very little (most encounters are but text, a few bitmap images and some quirky sounds). The wheel of fortune is great, encounters are interesting and the writing is top-notch.
I'm still absolutely not sold on this type of game. But Renowned explorers is certainly unique enough to warrant a look even for those who usually skip traditional RPG's.

It's a decent game, if a bit on the repetitive side. Even swtiching up your team and strategy doesn't help as much as you might think, as you're playing through the same scenarios (randomized to an extent, but the same core events at each location) with variations on the same kinds of attacks and defenses.
Visually, there is nothing to complain about. It looks great, and it plays snappy. There's a decent amount of humor, and it's entertainingly written. I've only encountered a handful of weird UI things, and no bugs worth mentioning.
As a starting point for a bigger game experience -- updates, DLC and the like -- it's good. If there were dozens of adventures and more gameplay variety, I could see giving this a whole-hearted "Buy it. Play it. Love it." review. It's not there yet.

This is a game which features randomly generated maps (but the encounters are mostly the same on the same type of map), a hub world and RPG elements,
The jewel of this game is the interesting combat system which features 3 types of attack types which counter one another (friendly>aggressive>devious>friendly) and special modifiers that apply on the whole battlefield depending on you and your enemy's mood. I would really enjoy seeing this system adapted into different games as it is quite tactical, forcing you to choose your actions carefully and make compromises.
The encounters require you selecting different options which might have a different impact on your current adventure, or pretty much rolling the dice using your best characters in order to pass your current obstacle.
The hub world is mostly a place where you upgrade your items, stats and resource gain, not much is really to be said about it. I suppose it is a nice addition that offers a bit more strategy in your games.
You will probably end up going trough most of the content in about 10-15 hours. Personally, after I  went trough all the encounters I do not feel to try out different character combinations or am I willing to play the game again. Yes, small variations will happen now and then but the incentive isnt all that big after you've been trough the encounter a couple of times already.
Overall this is a great game, and I would definetely recommend it if it were in the 10 eur price range.

Just... one more.... expedition!
Sid Meier said a game is a ''series of interesting decisions''. Never has this been more true than for Renowned Explorers. Assemble a team, weigh up their pros and cons, and start making meaningful, important choices.
I feel like some may bounce off Renowned Explorers due to its unusual and unique ''combat'' system. It's really more of an ''encounter'' system, where you're looking at the emotional mood of the encounter and weighing up how to approach it advantageously.  These african villagers are being friendly? Let's be aggressive and exploit their weaknesses! These Caribbean pirates have us at gunpoint? A devious approach will disarm them! You get the idea.
With a choice of 16 playable characters, I'm still discovering new combinations to exploit, new configurations of teams that work well in certain situations. Each character has their own unique abilities, strengths and weaknesses. It's up to you to decide which combination fits your play style.
This play style extends to the ''overworld'' where your expedition stakes a path across whatever far-flung wilderness you've found yourself in. Supplies are limited, so the choice lies with you as to how to proceed. The game is generous with information, and makes clear the risks you might be getting yourself into. A 98% chance is still a chance. And sometimes everything will go south on you. Wonderfully though, it never feels unfair. You knew the risks!
I can't wait to play again.

Ultimately this is a very repetitive cooridor shooter.  Where the original FEAR brought cutting edge AI and slow-mo mechanics to the FPS genre, FEAR2 offers very little innovation.  It feels like wasted potential because the gunplay is satisfying, and is probably what kept me playing.  However, the AI is extremely dim witted.  They are supposed to be highly trained mercenaries or clone soldiers yet they charge into your machinegun and shotgun blasts.  The cycle gets pretty tedious.  Walk into a room, enemies come in, kill them all, regen your health and ammo, move onto the next shooting gallery.  The horror elements manage to elevate the game a little higher as they are genuinely unnerving.  The story is also severely lacking in its presentation.  First starting with its characters, which are so uninteresting and serve only to radio in exposition as the game goes along.  Because of these weak characters I never cared what was happening.  FEAR2 also suffers the same problem where NPCs never do anything interesting, and conveinently find a way to fail to meet up with you or fight along side you.  In the end the game is very monotone and is an average shooter.  5/10.

I rate the game FEAR 2: Project Origin 3.5/5. Pretty good.
But...it has a few problems. The ending leaves you hanging and the overall game is not nearly as scary as the original, trading the quiet, creeping terror of the original for a broad and bloody spectrum of horror.
+Better graphics than the original with lots of little visual flourishes (which somehow detract from the feeling of quiet, still creepiness unfortunately)
+Extremely, blatantly horrific gameplay. The mech sections of the game are particularly horrific, making you feel as if you are more some sort of mechanized, manufactured killing machine (or are claustiphobically trapped inside of one) than a person (the sounds for the battle mech are done much better than those of the rest of the game.
+The game ensures that you understand its plot this time around.
+When voice acting occurs the voice acting is good.
+The elementary school section of the game was still really creepy and very well done.
+Outstanding enemy AI.
+Allied AI characters don't get in the way or detract from the experience.
+The general feeling of the environments were palpable and extremely detailed.
-But the better graphics are somehow less clean, more messy and more cartoony causing the game to be less creepy overall.
-Does not support all five buttons on five button mice. Supports 3 buttons only. Given the number of controls this game has this can feel fairly inconvenient sometimes. Fortunately, the keyboard has more than enough buttons to make up for this deficiency in the game.
-Crappy new music and any music this game has which is good came from either the first fear game or its various add-ons (with one exception)
-Mediocre sound. Enemies who are not supposed to be clones of one another often die with the exact same scream. Enemies do not scream enough (ande sometimes not at all) when set on fire.
-More of the game should have been more open-ended battle mech sections. Indeed, this engine would allow for a great mechwarrior or warhammer 40k other battle mech game to be created.
-Highly linear, relatively short gameplay with only one cliff-hanger ending.
-Voice mails have been replaced with silly little email things
-Somewhat generic characters throughout.
-Bullet time special effects still aren't spectacular.
-Oddly fast pacing for a horror game.
-More of this game should have been as creepy as the elementary school section of the game.
-Many of the enemies weren't creepy enough but were instead merely horrific but lacking in subtlety.
-Buggy in two particular places. Toward the beginning of the game many surface textures vanished for a short time and toward the ending I fell through a floor and died once.

3. Just the right length of time.  Too many games are too long and you end up feeling like you are running in circles - each level looks and feels the same.
4. Not into cheap scares.  Very few of them.  E.g. enemies do not pop up behind you when you cleared an area.  This lends a strange type of realism to the game which does not match the content.  The game could have done with a few more surprises.

The bad:
6. Does not add much to the first game's story line.
7. Movement around obstacles can be cumbersome.
8. The game signals when, were and what type of enemies are up ahead.
9. Not actually scary.

The ugly:
10. Nothing really, except maybe the gore.

I've played all the Roller Coaster tycoon games over the years. This one is a bit tricky at first. Expect to spend a few hours understanding how to make your first coaster unless you get some tips. This is more of a guide and review at the same time. Here are some tips. :)
Expect a little frustration building your coaster at first. When building your coaster:  Hold down the shift key, and use the mouse wheel to move it higher or lower. After you click on a peice of the track in build mode you can drag out that track and make curves, etc. and press 1, 2, 3, or 4; all these numbers do different things. Then you use your mouse wheel and to adjust. One of the numbers lifts up the track on one side for example (press 2, and then use your mouse wheel for example).
Also the camera is a bit quirky. You can go into options in the game, general, turn off auto focus coaster when building (so it doesn't jump everytime you click on the track), turn off auto zoom out camera if object is to large, and change your camera field of view if you like.
Also the graphics can be improved; changing them is a bit quircky. This is done by pressing escape, options, graphics, turn off better fps over graphics.. This makes the graphics settings go lower for some reason though. You then need to adjust higher the other settings AFTER you select this.
Placing a ride or object: Hold down the shift key, and use your mouse wheel to turn it around before you place it.
Adjusting the size of the map: Click modify terrain, and you'll find the option to expand there.
Also when you place a janitors building for example each building is used to hire the number of janitors for that building; differnent than RCT3.
This is a great game, but I think the issue is most people aren't taking the time to go through the tutorial. In addition to that the coaster building is a bit advanced; you can do a lot with it, but the key will be the first few hours.For beginners it's a bit tricky.
Is it fun? Yes it's a lot of fun to play. I'm enjoying my park the more and mroe I play it. The more I play, the more I want to play. It starts out slow and grows on you once you figure out what your doing. It's also fun to decorate/improve the park.
The graphics are pretty nice as well. I'm looing forward to this game growing, but as for now it's a good game if your willing to read a guide like this one and others you'll be fine. :) Also if you enjoy a challenge on coaster building you'll like this game. Expect a lot of crashes during testing, but it's gratifying and realistic.. You adjust angles of track to compensate, etc. It just feels nice, and it's a good sandbox style game.
There are a good amount of rides, and park finances.
Why are there bad reviews section: Most people don't understand the options they have at their disposal, and haven't read the tips/guides on controls. Changing the graphic options, and adjusting the camera are all fairly easy to do once you have read these trips.
I have experienced some crashes for example when making a huge roller coaster with lots of turns, etc. I'd say save every so often in case, but the coaster build is pretty fun once you get the hang of it. The game is itself seems to run pretty smooth though on my system; a 980 GTX, 16 gigs ram, and a 3.4 ghz quad.
The problem is if people didn't get it within 1-2 hours many immediately went for the bad review/refund option, but this one is worth digging deeper and playing imo. :)

The game should really appeal to anyone who likes the AVGN videos and maybe only them. People who don't like the comedy style of AVGN or don't know him will probably just get annoyed with the game and the story as a whole. There is swearing everywhere but its just text, there is no voice in this game and the story is told via text boxes with drawn art cards depicting scenes at the start of the game and the end. Honestly, story is negligible and really isn't to the concern of the player in these sorts of games. Its all about gameplay.
You play as the nerd or one of four characters you can find. You can hot swap between these characters and some may make situations easier but in all honesty all you need to beat the game is the Nerd and Guitar Guy. The nerd being perfectly fine with all situations aside from those the Guitar Guy is required. Each character has their own special stats/move so you can have some choice about how you accomplish a goal. But for the most part their is really only one way to get by most obstructions. Jump a second to soon or late and you die or get hit. This is to be expected with this type of game but it does get annoying as you progress and insta death blocks become more and more common.
Oh yeah, insta death blocks. Some of the biggest bs to ever grace this game and they are everywhere. I mean EVERYWHERE. They are just plain overused, like the dev couldn't figure out how to give a fair new challenge to the player so they just tossed insta death blocks in everywhere they could which is especially painfull as you get more and more stuff on screen and you have to pay attention to all of it to keep from getting hit. Once you figure out when to jump, run, or whatever it stops being such a challenge unless a glitch or so messes you up.
What I found is the game has really strange hit detection. Sometimes things that clip into your character don't hit you (enemy attacks or insta death stuff) but sometimes you can be not even near it seemingly and it kills you. Exactly how close you can be to something before it kills you is something I still havn't figured out. It just seems like luck that you live or die, especially in the last insta death dissappearing and reappearing block puzzle. You just have to keep trying over and over until it lets you through. Of course skill does come into play but I can't tell you how many times I thought I was in the clear only to have the blocks appear and instakill me although I know I was clear of them. Its complete bull. This same problem can happen with platforms but it seems to be limited to falling platforms I think. You can jump and get stuck on the corner and then the platform falls.
Bouncing is a game of luck aswell. You can try and get good at it but even when you think you have it down your character desides to take a suicide dive straight into insta death. Its like playing with fire while soaked in gas, you have to have the patience of a saint and a surgeon in one to do it right.
Controls are solid aside from the bouncing mechanic which is like the wheel of misfortune. Your character controls very smoothly and solidly aside from times when you need to do jumps perfectly on a single block with an instadeath right beside your intended jump spot. At times like that its easy to overjump and die or under and fall to your demise but this maybe also something to do with the weird hit detection. I really wish I would have recorded it in slow motion to see exactly what was up.
Bosses are a pleasant challenge and once you figure out there pattern they are pretty easy, but thats after you die a good number of times though. Fred Fuchs, the final boss, is an absolute pain in the rear as he is right after the most horrible level in the game. Once you get past beginners traps and turtle your way to the end you will have no lives, but even with knowing the level well you might only get to him with 20 lives and let me tell you that you'll probably need them. What I did was crouch on the lowest right platform and when I could I would jump up and shoot him as he flew up until  he brought out his balls. When hes got his balls out (hehe) crouch on the left side of the platform when hes flying to the left side of the screen, and when he flies to the right side of the screen get on the left sideof the middle platform and crouch. When he starts crapping on you you have to pause the game to see if he is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥above you, then you have time to react and dodge him. I would advise shooting at him while hes above you then pausing fast as you can when under him. It seems like cheating, but honestly since the crap is random its fair in my opinion. When he brings out his wrecking balls or chain balls (whatever the heck you call them) get on the two platforms farthest to the left.
There you go, Freds dead baby!
Powerups are fairly rare and and theres only 4 types, beer for health, the SNES gun, mecha jesus, and the glitch gremlin. The gun sucks because in one hit you lose it, and the gremlin is mostly useless as it only stops enemies and fire balls and similiar dangers like that from moving. It dousn't make them stop damaging you so its pretty useless aside from points where you get lucky and you line everything up so you can run through an area without getting hit at all. Mecha jesus kills everything on screen and is only really used around where he can be picked up.

The main focuses of AntiHero are tactics and map domination. Each map is different and neighborhoods seem to be randomly assigned. I love the variety of characters and play styles that the game allows, and how the characters and upgrades fit into the theme of the game. The only one I'd say might not fit as well as the others is the assassin, but it's obvious once you start making headway through the campaign that a character like this is needed to keep other character advantages balanced.
There are so many possibilities and potential strategies and I absolutely love that. It's not a typical tactics game where you calculate your move radius and go after the enemies. It's also not a typical map domination game where you move units and battle your opponents units for territory. Every house can be burgled, every establishment infiltrated. How you play is truly and entirely up to you. This is what makes the online play, in particular, so exciting.
After seeing the gameplay trailer I knew I wanted to try this game. After trying the game, I knew I wanted to 100% it, something that very rarely happens. After beating the campaign on regular difficulty, and now being one level away from completing it on hard, I want everybody else to play it. The graphics are charming, the characters are memorable, and the structure feels right.
I look forward to seeing what else is done with this game.

Antihero doesn't feel all that fast-paced. I'm writing this review after playing for 1.8 hours, but it feels like I've been playing much longer. The game is a slog to play through. I have enjoyed this game for the majority of the time i played it. Which implies it is not perfect.
I started this game up after watching a bit of gameplay and finding the art style quite nice which is very personal preference regarding art style.
Like many others i decided to play the campaign first which does a good job of showing you the ropes and providing 10 varied levels but none of them (aside from lvl 6 which was a pain) gave me a huge challenge even though i played on hard difficulty.
But the meat of the game is not the campaign despite telling a nice little story. The meat of the game is the multiplayer which is a very different experience from the single player.
So what makes the meat of the game worth your money?
- The different maps you have seen throughout the campaign make each map feel unique.
- The very varied strategies people use online compared to offline means you have to adapt to the situation you are given every single game.
-  Online also has 2 ways for you to play
1. Active game which essentially is the normal way to play the game
2. play by email which means every time you have done your turn you can exit the match and come back a day later if you want assuming your opponent has taken his turn by then.
- Randomized location for every special building in each map so even if you get the same map twice, it won't have the exact same special buildings in the exact same spot.
- Almost chess like strategy which means you will learn to think multiple moves ahead
So overall, i enjoy the game and the devs seem to be eager to improve on the game to add features and balance the game which is greatly appreciated.
Pros:
- Solid multiplayer with ongoing balance changes and features planned to be added
- Art style (very personal)
- Story
- Variation in levels
- Campaign has easy, normal and hard difficulty
- Fitting soundtrack (may seem weird but to me this is important)
Cons:
- Campaign is more of a story / tutorial than a challenge to keep you busy for hours
- Balance issues
- Uncertain but i believe there are only 5 maps in the multiplayer and i have had multiple games in a row end up on the exact same map.
- Some animations are very long.

Magrunner is similar to Portal, in that both are puzzle platformers with one central game mechanic that is used both to get through levels and (occasionally) defeat or avoid enemies.  But that's where the similiarites end.  Magrunners is set in an interesting future utopia (or dystopia, depending on your point of view).  It's early visuals are appropriately bright and cheerful for the setting.   However, as the game progresses this  gives way to horrific landscapes and an unsettling atmosphere.  Magrunner delves fairly deeply into tropes of the Cthulhu mythos, but combining it's cultists and nightmare creatures with a futuristic setting and puzzle platforming creates something fresh.  The art direction is fantastic, and the Lovecraft inspired creatures and settings are appropriately unsettling and awe-inspiring.  The few characters you interact with are interesting, and their voice acting is fairly good.   That being said, your interactions with these characters are  fairly limited.  Magrunner creates an interesting world and characters, but it feels like you barely scratch the surface of exploring either.  On the birght side, that leaves lots of material for a sequel.
All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed the game.  I reccomend it to any fans of puzzle games, platformers, or HP Lovecraft.

This is a great Portal-like game that uses magnets. Who doesn't like magnets, right? A fun and innocent puzzle platformer with magnets, what could possibly go wrong?
Mwuhahahaha!!!
Seriously, though, this was a very enjoyable game. Each new level adds a new twist on the game mechanics and requires you to keep thinking in new ways to solve the puzzles. Just when you start thinking,
, that is when Cthulhuthian horror starts creeping in to give the levels an extra sharp, terrifying edge. By the time you reach Act III, you just want to crawl under a warm blanket until the voices stop.
For those of you unfamiliar with the Cthulhu mythos, it is nothing like typical horror which can be both dull and disgusting with its mindless, rampaging zombies or masked, knife-wielding weirdoes and an excess of pointless gore. The literature of H. P. Lovecraft doesn't try to gross you into fright, it strikes at the underpinnings of your very concept of reality, leaving your sanity to tumble helplessly into an endless abyss. Just thought you ought to know...
Anyway, although the physics system is good, the portrayal of magnetism is not accurate. I hate to be nitpicky, but as an engineer, I can't help noticing that the game objects act more like they are electrically charged than magnetically polarized, except that I've never heard of a cylindrical electrical field. It is possible to create a cylindrical magnetic field, but only if there is an electrical current at the center, which the game frequently omits. If you can work past these inaccuracies, you will surely enjoy the harmonic motion mechanics and application of chaos theory.
The story behind the game is a bit light, and the voice acting is second rate, but it is enough to set the creepy tone for the later chapters. The ending is quite odd, but what else can you expect from a game inspired by the works of H.P. Lovecraft. Overall, the creative gameplay and unnerving atmosphere more than make up for the game's weak points, and I can recommend this game for anyone who enjoys puzzles or things that go bump in the night.
Whatever you do, don't look!

First of all, let me start off by saying this "no" recommendation is at the full price, because this game is definitely not worth $10. On sale for a dollar or two, it's definitely worth checking out.
So let's start with the positives. This game is full of ingenuity and really interesting mechanic ideas. Most levels have some kind of unique gimmick to them, which are then fully explored over the course of the area.
Most of these work pretty well. They add an interesting wrinkle to the gameplay and some of them change up the playstyle substantially. My personal favorite was the water level- each stage is half covered by water, which essentially acts as a flipped gravity zone. This gave each level a great deal of verticality, and I think it was the best showcase of the game's physics.
Speaking of which, the physics are mostly pretty good. The jelly floors react satisfyingly to your movements and jumps, and although they can lead to some frustration with precision (more on that later), overall it's a fun concept. You can bounce all over the place, and the jelly physics are used in some interesting ways.
The music and aesthetics are top-notch. It is a surprisingly atmospheric game, and always pretty to look at.
And now, we must move on to the game's problems. First of all, a lot of people are reporting major bugs with the game. Personally I didn't encounter anything game-breaking, but it seems to be widespread so be warned.
The biggest problem with the game lies in the level design. Early in the game, it feels great to move around the levels. However, the control scheme and movement physics were clearly designed with wide open spaces in mind, as the player character blasts around the screen absurdly fast. The level design is completely out of sync with this engine, however, as later levels rely very heavily on precision platforming on narrow platforms or through narrow spaces. The speed at which the player character moves is completely incompatible with the level of precision the game expects from you, which leads to immense frustration, especially in the second half of the game.
The other big flaw with the level design comes from the jelly physics. The fun of the game comes from bouncing around the gamespace and using the jelly physics to propel yourself to new heights and the like. Why, then, does the game insist on having so many extremely narrow corridors? It doesn't make any sense and due to the bounciness these corridors are frustrating to navigate. This is even more true when you have to make a jump near a corner; the corner will always propel you diagonally away, making starting a wall climb impossible. Which wouldn't be so bad, except the game regularly forces you into this kind of position.
My other main gripe with the game is the abomination of a final level (I'll keep this as spoiler free as possible). The first half isn't frustrating so much as it is tedious; you're forced to navigate extremely large levels with haphazardly placed obstacles, often being forced to take completely blind leaps and falls. The second half takes the established mechanics of the game and changes them up in tons of different ways. I won't lie, it's creative, but it makes for absolutely horrendous and frustrating gameplay. It takes the already difficult precision platforming and adds an element of near complete randomness to the equation, to the point where you just have to get a few lucky jumps to have any hope of succeeding.
Overall, The Floor is Jelly is a game with a lot of great ideas, but the game never comes together to feel like a complete vision. The level design is totally at odds with the mechanics of the game, and that's a shame. It's definitely worth checking out if you pick it up at a sale price, but it's absolutely not worth the $10 price tag.

I think a certain skeleton said it best:
"i know your type. you're, uh, very determined, aren't you? you'll never give up, even if there's, uh... absolutely NO benefit to persevering whatsoever. if i can make that clear. no matter what, you'll just keep going. not out of any desire for good or evil... but just because you think you can. and because you 'can'... you 'have to.'"
That is exactly how I felt when I played this game. No matter what kind of obstacles this game threw at me, no matter how much the clumsy controls infuriated me, no matter how many times I was afraid the game would break, I kept pushing forward.
In all honesty, the graphics and music are fantastic, but the fast-paced and precise nature of the platforming betrays both of them. In the beginning, the platforming isn't too bad. The concept of floors and walls reacting like jelly to your movements is a really good concept, and on certain levels, it was executed pretty well. Some of the platforming elements within that concept worked pretty well, too, at least in the beginning. During the later stages, however, the platforming just got frustrating. At one point, I even got stuck in the floor, making me have to restart the whole level. I also found myself having to make several leaps of faith in a series of counterintuitive trial-and-error hurdles.
The ending levels seemed to have absolutely no rhyme or reason to them; they just existed solely to seem trippy. It felt like a steaming pile of rejected ideas that were snuck into some levels by a bitter level designer who was fired from this job. Oh, and did I mention the controls were awful? Because they are terrible. In the first few stages, it's not too bad, but when the platforming gets more complex, it becomes all the more frustrating. If you so much as blow on one of the arrow keys, your character moves at a ridiculous speed, and the areas can get pretty cramped later on, making the whole thing almost unmanageable. Yet, in spite of these issues, I still wanted to keep going forward, because the game was a relatively fun experience. In the end, though, it just wasn't worth it. I beat the game in a single session (2-3 hours, because I was offline for the rest of the session); it is certainly not worth $10.
5/10 It's a decent game with some great ideas, but is severely flawed.

As a follow-up to
,
simply doesn't cut it. It seems that Acquire couldn't be bothered with crafting a compelling storyline and cast of characters. Every mission is a variation of "kill all the baddies", and fights rarely deviate from repetitive 3v3 brawls. There's no real strategy to the combat either. As long as players continually upgrade their equipment and remember to spam special attacks, then there's nothing to worry about. Before long, the entire ordeal devolves into a mindless cacophany of button-mashing. Maybe the hero will decide to a cast a spell, perhaps they'll run away to avoid getting surrounded, and that is the extent of the game's variety.
Still, I'd be remiss to ignore the crowd that actually *wants* a mindless hack & slash adventure game, especially one that's frequently on sale for less than a dollar. Is
capable of delivering at least a couple hours worth of entertainment? I'm afraid to say it, but no, not in the slightest. The controls have a muddy feel to them, and hits never seem to connect in a satisfying manner. It's hard to explain, but whenever I kill an enemy in this game, my immediate thought isn't "I killed another foe!" It's more along the lines of "Oh... They're dead? Oh okay." In the midst of a conflict involving various edged weapons, death is expected. However, I still found myself mildly surprised whenever I killed someone. It's these moments of confusion that keep the game from being enjoyable, even at the most basic level.
Then there's the online mode. I played a few cooperative missions, which were amusing only in how quickly my partners and I were able to stomp the opposition. Thanks to issues such as lag and input delay, this game, which already suffers from an absence of anything resembling nuance, becomes a total joke. As long as buttons are being pressed, then good things will happen. Enemies will bleed out and fall over, and players will bathe in miniscule equipment upgrades, as well as enjoy practically insignificant bonuses to their special skills. If another trip on the hamster wheel sounds at all appealing, then consider downloading one of those F2P MMOs, at least they're guaranteed to be easier on the eyes.
In short, consider investing your money elsewhere, such as on a pack of gum. Get something that'll keep your breath minty fresh, which is far more pleasant a feeling than anything this game could ever provide.

"What's in a name?" is the main downfall for Supreme Commander 2.
The game is a very potent RTS, streamlined and easier to understand, and for many aspects, it's a good thing!  The economy is more straight-forward, there's a good tech tree, and matches are action-packed!
But, do I recommend this game?  NO.
It suffers the same problems as almost any RTS sequel.  To improve on a series, you iron wrinkles out of your previous game, make it easier to learn, to understand, to play, and ultimately to enjoy for as many people as you can.  The same changes happened with Lord of the Rings : The Battle for Middle-Earth II, in my opinion:  Solid game, loved by many and in many ways, superior to the first game.  But as for SupCom2, it lost its soul.  They are maybe better games in the end, but also more generic experiences that they once were.
So, SupCom2, great game, but bland.  It needed to be named something else, because this isn't Supreme Commander.

The game's great!  It's a very fun stealth-action game.  I've enjoyed carrying out missions a bunch of different way.  The levels are open and huge.  With the customizable and collectible weapons, there are plenty of ways to kill your targets, including with objects in the environment. The story is pretty good, and it was able to keep me going through the game.  However, the freedom within the gameplay is what makes this game intriguing.
The game would be much shorter if you knew how you'd want to carry out a mission from the start (there's no one correct way to do a mission), so try to start playing without the help of the internet or your friends too much if you want to put hours into the game before finishing it.  You'll never complete a mission on your first try, trust me. You'll pretty much be improvising from the very start.
For those who never played a Hitman title, I strongly recommend doing your first play-through on the "rookie" or "normal" difficulty.  These difficulties give you the help you will definitely need within the viewable (<probably misspelled) map, such as " ! " icons to show you areas of interest, and other things that you wouldn't see on Expert or Professional difficulties.  On the harder difficulties, you are given less information about your surroundings within the map.  Therefore, in order to be able to play, and even really enjoy the harder difficulties, is to play on "Normal" or "Rookie" first.
The tutorial level is completely different from how the other levels are since it's more linear due to the fact it just teaches you the controls and how to play. After that mission, you'll need to reply on your weapons, map, and your thinking ability to help you understand what you can do within each of the other settings.  You'll also need to manage the money you earn after each mission when it comes to unlocking your guns' attachments, your equipment, etc.

This is a great game, and it seems that the ones before this one are great as well.  I plan on playing the other Hitman titles.  All of the ones before "Hitman: Absolution" (currently the newest one available) (Blood Money is the fourth game, Absolution is the fifth) seem to be at very reasonable prices.  I got this game for 9 bucks, I believe.  Absolution is, I think, close to 20 bucks, which isn't so bad.  But these older titles are cheaper, and are in fact more open within the levels.  Absolution was a bit more linear within the levels.  Still fun though, but it was different, I suppose to capture more of an audience for this brilliant video game franchise.
This game, Hitman: Blood Money, is a classic, and is considered to be one of the best Hitman games ever made.  The sixth title has already been announced, and it's been confirmed by IOInterative that this next title will bring back the open and "sandbox" variety, and the freedom, that the older games have.  This game here is proof of this franchise's brilliance.  It's a good taste of the past, and a good idea of what's to come in the future.
Therefore, I recommend this game to those who are willing to take a challenge.  This is a hard game if you haven't played it before.  Blood Money encourages you to take a "Silent Assassin" approach to your missions (only killing your targets, not killing, sedating, or doing other suspicious acts in front of possible witnesses, making your kills look like accidents, using silenced weapons, etc.), which is exactly what I challenge many of you to do.  This franchise is one of a kind, and this game is just the icing on the cake.  It is a must buy.
So, yes, I recommend this game.
Buy it, play it with an open mind, and please consider the other titles.
I'm looking forward to the unreleased sixth title.  But in the meanwhile, I believe I have some catching up to do with the other games in the series.

This is an amazing game. You have complete freedom to complete the levels however you would like. You can go in with a mission and immediately start shooting, or you can take the approach I favor, and go in and never get seen. In this game, you become agent 47, a bald, elite Hitman clone. The goal of every mission is to take out a target or sometimes several. Sometimes, you must protect your target. Other times you must retrieve suitcases full of diamonds as well. You do all this by sneaking around, taking disguises, and silently taking everyone in your way out. The gameplay is awesome.
However, the graphics leave a little to be desired, and the Glacier engine is infamous for being difficult to mod.
Other things I liked: you are able to modify your weapons. This means buying nicer scopes, silencers, lockpicks, and larger clips. I also liked how funny some of the 'easter eggs' are. The gameplay is fun, the characters interesting, the game modes themselves are excellent. But the game is entirely broken in terms of matchmaking and lack of player base. In order to play the game, you need to find other players. There are no players. You join your matchmaking queue for an "Average" wait time, and spend the next five to ten minutes waiting for another player to be linked to you and your game lobby, before being placed in the server, alone. There isn't even an option to wait for a minimum time so you can at least begin playing, nor a minimum number of players so that when a single other person, like you, bumps into each other briefly, the game will allow you to play it. There's not even a drop-in selection to join a game partway through. This game has a lot of promise and potential, but fails to deliver any satisfaction. The only way to really play the story is Solo, or to drag in another person in the barren wilds of Matchmaking.
I said at the time I first wrote a review, that: "Maybe someday this game will be playable, and I eagerly await that day, but for now, Battleborn has been a Battleblunder."
And now that Battleborn is Free-to-play for the Versus modes, there may yet be hope for at least a little bit of PVP action, though for those of you looking for a cooperative experience, this is not the game for you.

I genuinely love this game. Clearly, so does Gearbox, because they are constantly tweaking and balancing things, changing up the matchmaking, improving the flow of gameplay, changing the boss fights up so an enemy you faced ten times before suddenly busts out a new special move and you need to change up your strategy, adding new characters, and balancing, balancing, balancing. With the addition of the Story Operations (Attikus and the Thrall Rebellion is as hilarious as it is replayable, it's a giant loot pinata and at $5 offers top-tier entertainment at bargain-basement prices!
The only problem is the dwindling active community. They're all great, it just makes finding a match take longer sometimes. Sometimes they make a patch that fixes this. Other times the patch throws it off again for sake of a balanced match. In either case, you can help alleviate this problem by buying this game and encouraging all your friends who stopped playing to log back in and help you get gud!
tl;dr It's a good game that's only getting better. Play it so the queues go by quicker with better balancing.
P.S. Just becayse someone's lvl 100 doesn't mean they're good. Skill matters a lot in this game.

I used to see this game advertised on Steam and think it couldn't be any good. Boy, was I wrong.

My favourite genre is probably the Metroid-vania type of games.
Mostly because they have just the right amount of combat, action oriented gameplay, and then also some necessary exploration!
Seeing Guacamelee, it interested me greatly, both because of its genre, and also because it "draws from Mexican culture". Why make it all up when we have cultures full of interesting folklore already?
So, I was pumped. And I now stand really impressed. This game blew all of my expectations out of the window, and here's why.
First off, the presentation.
The game looks gorgeous and unique. Enemy and character design overall was very detailed, and it looks really great. Everything else isn't anything to sneeze at either, it looks pretty good overall, although the characters were what stood up for me. Some parts of it can look to same-y, but it has a bunch of different areas to keep things interesting.
The music wasn't something that I'd listen to out of the game, or is stuck in my head. But it fits the setting really well. and makes the experience more atmospheric.
Another note on the presentation: there are tons of stylized references to multiple videogames, specially in the form of posters in town. Those are all "revamped" to fit the setting, but anyone can see who/what they're referencing. And the most important thing: those weren't just references because "it's cool". One can clearly see that they've seen what made those games great, and they've managed to put most of those aspects in their own game. More on that later.
So, gameplay.
In Guacamelee, you have a lot of combat and platforming, and they both behave very closely to one another, because the special moves you use in combat, you'll also need to platforming, be it to reach an higher platform, to stand in place until a platform moves, etc. And platforming scales really well, starting out pretty easy, and getting more and more difficult as you progress. The same with the combat, and here's my biggest complaint: the game was way too easy. The harder parts were actually "optional" as part of secrets, and exploration.
I'll explain it in more detail further.
As you progress the game, you gain several abilities (by breaking Metroid-like statues) and those will help you in both combat and platforming. Combat was surprisingly good, as the player could pull some really long combos, and it wasn't too hard to make. And the combat never felt like a button-masher, and dodging is also an essential part of it.
The Boss Fights were also impressing. Each Boss has several phases with different pattern that the player should memorize. Unfortunately, once more, they were way too easy and didn't provide much of a challenge, despite the fight being enjoyable in itself.
Also, the last Boss fight had a weird hitbox that messed it up a little bit. Nothing game breaking though, it just felt weird.
To keep going forward, besides unlocking new abilities, the player should also explore to find Money (to buy Costumes for different playstyles), Health and Stamina (what is used for special abilities) around the world. These are the sections that usually provide the biggest challenge in terms of platforming, and they were really enjoyable!
These require the best use of all the abilities the player had learned up to that point.
And this is what mesmerized me: this game does a lot of things right! Platforming, Combat, Exploration, the World, and I could go on. They've taken some of the best aspects of previous game and made it their own, and they've done an amazing job here!
They've taken a similar respawning system as in Super Meat Boy for the hardest platforming sections, and a Metroid-like transformation to reach tighter places, just for two very obvious examples. The point is, the references are there not just as a nice poster, but also deep in the mechanics of the game, and I'll applaud the developers for that. Great job!
On the exploration side, there are also some mysterious "Orbs" that are very well hidden, and present the most hardcore platforming in the game. Nothing is told to the player about what they're in the game for, and it made me go all in to find them. Some of these challenges could get somewhat frustrating, but it's good that they're there! Some challenge, at long last!
Well, unfortunately, I only went to find them after I had 100% each zone, and the reward wasn't very useful to me. So, I won't spoil it, but you should try to find all of them right away. The last one you can only obtain after defeating the last Boss.
All in all, they were worth it.
The DLC provides 17 challenges that are also very enjoyable, ranging from combat to platforming and rancing. They were all well done and provide additional challenge and add new suits with different attributes which is always nice to keep things fresh!
So, overall, I really enjoyed all of my time spent with the game, and have found explored 100% of the game's areas, and it was all worth it. The sidequests all had character to it and were pretty amusing, adding a bit to the world and setting of the game.
It did more things right than it had the right too, which was impressive! Sometimes, it felt too ambitious with it, but those feeling were far minor compared with the positive aspects of it.
Now, I'll get on with the bad parts.
The first one is one I don't understand, and almost despise.
They've decided not to include Hard Mode until the player finished the game. And there was no NewGame+ option. What the hell? Why? Seeing as the developers went deep into many games to see what they did and didn't do right, how did they reach this conclusion?
Normal Mode was by far too easy! I barely felt challenged at any point, and it highly detracted from the experience, specially after seeing "You've unlock Hard Mode!"... It's not very enjoyable repeting the whole game, specially from the 0! If there were a NG+, I might've done it, because I still needed to unlock some Suits and Explore part of the world. But having to do everything all over again just harded didn't really feel very nice... So, I've done almost everything to do in the game, with the exception of playing the game in Hard Mode. A game that I've found too easy...
I don't understand this decision, honestly. I just hoped the developers realize this mistake and don't make it in future games, because I sure look forward to them now! If I'm the one missing something with this, feel free to reply and tell me, but I really hate to have to repeat the whole thing to play the game as it was intended.
Another thing, is the fact that the exploration isn't all that rewarding, since the player doesn't really need to upgrade to beat the game. And, specially after the end of it, exploration was mostly there for the achievements (except for the SideQuests, which were genuinely amusing, and some optional secrets along the way).
I'd also like to make 2 constructive critics.
One of them is about the Map System. It was pretty good, letting the player know where previously encountered coloured blocks were in the map (these were areas blocked until the player gained X ability), but some areas were not as direct or evident and easy to see by looking at the map. As such, a nice addition would be a sort of "Note" system in which the player could right Notes and a certain point in the map for further reference.
Another one, is about certain achievements. There were some for beating the Bosses or Arenas on certain conditions. These made the fights harder, and more interesting, which is a plus! But there was no way of knowing about them without browsing the achievements. many players probably missed enjoyable content because of that. So, a cool addition would be to add a Tab for Optional Objectives so that the player always knows what can be done.
Well, that's all from me.
I loved this game and I certainly recommend it to everyone who likes the genre! Cheers!

Your ability to combo and throw enemies is pretty satisfying at the start of the game, and it's like "Oh yeah I get it, I'm totally a luchador."  But it does a great job of building upon this with mobility and access powers.  These take the form of fighting moves, as opposed to different energy beams (a la Metroid), and so at first they feel a little dry (as in, oh this block can only be broken with a certain punch I just got, but not my other punch... OK?).  However, I really appreciate how well they compliment the game's melee-combat focus and double up as ways to dramatically improve your character's mobility.  The game is most fun to play near the end, and you start to feel like a superhero luchador, which is just something I had never considered.  My only complaint is that the combat is a bit unforgiving.  It's hard, which is actually nice, but if you take a hit, it takes an excruciatingly long time to get back up, and on the last boss your timing has to just be incredibly perfect, so that got frustrating.
I would definitely recommend Guacamelee.  Also it has co-op.  Go play it with your other friend who is also good at games.

The first thing you have to know about Magrunner:Dark Pulse is that it falls into the 'First person puzzle-platformer, with a twist' category that has become so popular since the release of Portal. I'm talkin' Antichamber, QUBE, Quantum Conundrum, Twin Sector... the list goes on. If you aren't a fan of that style of game, I doubt you'll enjoy this.
That being said, Magrunner is an extrodinarily impressive take on the puzzle genre. The core 5-10 hours of gameplay revolve around using a special glove to influence objects through magnetic-like properties. You have red and green charges (or red and blue if you choose). Same-charged objects attract, while different-colored objects repel. So basically the opposite of actual magnetism. Surprisingly, there are an impressive number of interesting, brain-busting puzzles you can create with this simple mechanic.
Beyond that, much like Portal, there's an overarching story that unfolds beyond the simple test chamber in which you begin your story. That's where the similarities to Portal start to decline, to its detriment. Whereas in Portal, humor and intrigue act in tandem between segments of puzzle-solving, Magrunner focuses primarily on intrigue through Lovecraftian horror, feeding you bits of the unfolding story while you work from one area to the next. While this
work in a story with a number of twists and turns, the plot isn't
deep, so it can be a little boring when you're working between sections of the game. The voice acting itself is a little flat at parts, and the music (if there was any) was so forgettable that I legitimately can't remember if there
music. It also can be a bit buggy, such as when the final boss just stood there pointing at a block half-way through the battle, leaving me to wreck everything unopposed. Oh, and achievement hunters? Most of 'em are easy pickings, but there's one achievement that is REALLY hard to complete. You'll know it when you see it.
Point is, if you're a fan of the puzzle-platforming genre, and perhaps a fan of Lovecraft, you'll find quite a bit to enjoy about this game. I'd almost say grab it at full price, but maybe wait for a bit of a discount.

Okay so a few things about this game...
While it does have its downfalls, it is a pretty good game when you take it for what it really is. A 3v3 deathmatch game.
Combat in this game is very Dark Soulsish. You can block, parry, dodge, plus a few interesting things (high/low/medium attack). I haven't tried multiplayer yet (bought two copies for my friends) but I'm sure it would make for a very interesting experience. You get punished for missing a parry, or attacking when you shouldn't be, which is even more reason why someone should play. (No easy mode here.)
Reasons why I would recommend this game:
-Interesting combat system.
-Challenging AI on higher difficulties. Really.
-You can dual wield shields. Or if that isn't your preference, dual wield helmets.
-Loot system is nice.
-Large selection of weapons to pick from.
-Upgrade system is pretty okay too.
The ONLY problems I have with this game are:
-Unable to tell your AI to focus on an enemy. Many times I had 1v3 situation while my "Allied AI" are busy looting shields.
-No fluent transitions/combos between the different types of attacks (low/medium/high).
-No explaination on WHY a piece of armor increases or decreases a specific stat.
-That heaping price tag. Get it on sale for 70% off or something.

There are a few big qualifiers to my recommendation

1.5) I didn't buy any of the DLC. None of it seemed to matter very much, unless you just want more character slots or something.

In Brief:  An interesting take on turn-based tactics with rogue-lite elements.
Renowned Explorers is one of those titles I picked up during the holidays because I needed something fun and light to do during the massively gray Wisconsin winters.  I was happy to find that the board game elements that you see in the trailer video are not just window dressing for the game, but evidence of some definite knowledge by the designers of some of the best trends in current hobby tabletop games.
If you are a board gamer like me, then think of this as a "Solo Co-Op Adventure Game", the kind that is in the vein of Pandemic.  If you are not the sort of person that goes really old school and game at a table with dice/cards/pieces, then this game is best thought of as a cousin to games like FTL.
Play focuses on managing supplies as you explore a random mixed map, with conflicts mostly taking place in turn based combat where you position yourselves and attack with character qualities like "Friendly Compliments", "Ranged Combat", or "Personal Insults".  Characters have different strengths and weaknesses in combat, as well as areas of expertise that help you gain advantage from non-combat encounters.  Make your way to the designated goal on the map and try and use any accumulated bonuses from the search to complete the final challenge.
The adventuring is broken up by periods of downtime where you can spend money, research, and prestige for new advantages and abilities.  All of this is framed in a theme of an idealized early 20th/late 19th century where diversity is celebrated and the baddies are easily recognized.
So, who would like this sort of game?  It's the kind of title I think would be good for a parent looking to have something to play with a child who is already into games like Minecraft or reading Jules Vern or Harry Potter.  It's also a solid game for anyone who likes to play for 2-3 hours and then be done to do something else.
I wouldn't recommend it for tactics gamers who focus on the 4X style games or military tactics exclusively, as the combat is focused most on relatively quick resolutions and a lot of elements are abstracted for the sake of flow.  Also if you get turned off by the idea of winning through the forging of friendships or pulling sneaky Scooby-Doo style tricks to fool your opponents, then the tone and theme here will not be for you.
In the end, I enjoy it because it has a lot in common with board games I enjoy with my friends, it's a good break when I just need something different, and there's legitimate challenge in winning a game without feeling like I can only get to the end by finding every exploit possible or just because of a few lucky rolls of the virtual dice.

I honestly do not know why this game gets bad reviews as it does from some people. But i absolutely love it. Actually i like it better then Forged Alliance. I for one like that instead of random plots of land. Other things i am sad to see go were the Support Armored Command Units. They were very useful but i wont that ruin my gameplay fun!

If you're looking for an assassination sim, then this is THE game to play.
For starters, the game gives you practically limitless freedom in every mission (except in the final mission of course, but no one likes that mission) and the game has tons of variety from mission to mission, in terms of both settings and the enviromental kills you can use.
The sheer size of the levels will complete overwhelm you intially; making success seem almost impossible. But through countless restarts, you'll slowly piece together a plan to kill your targets in the most effective way possible, making the game feel like a puzzle game at times.
What's more, the levels are highly replayable thanks to a scoring system that encourages you to be as discreet as possible; meaning you'll have a few late nights trying to get the highest rank on a particular mission- and it's extremely fun to do.
Other than having a linear tutorial and the aforementioned awful final mission, this game has very few flaws. It also runs well on mediocre gaming PCs, which is also a plus.
Overall, if games like Assassin's Creed are a little to "loud" for your liking, then this is the game for you.

A few caveats, though: the game has no definitive end. You will likely just know when you solved the mystery, but there's no credits roll to punctuate it. It's also rather short, and offers little replay value, so think of it as an interactive, pretty good movie.

This is a 1v1 "competitive" board game. With no real online community to play with. As of now only about 10% of players who played the game have won an online match only 1% stuck around long enough to win 10.
The strategy and gameplay lack any real depth. Its a very simple game and one that is not balanced or adjusted for competitive play. The biggest problem is this game has very few options for "strategies" and even fewer instances of weighing pros and cons and making decisions.
It seems like "rank" is just flat wins so 10W 100L is the same same as 10W 0L
The only guide on the game reads regarding one of the limited maps in the matchmaking pool:
"The first guard should spawn on the first players second turn. Giving them the gang advantage and the ability to bully from the start, because of the close proximity of the guilds. First turn player also has the benefit of spawning and naturally scouting tiles that gives access to 2-3 blocks without going out of their way. "
Here we see just one of the many examples of bizarre game design decisions for a competive 1v1 board game.
To start you should balance the maps, in a stalemate dont let random event decide the winner, rank needs to be + for wins - for losses not just how many wins.
Balance random maps like having some special buildings not start right next to either player but instead tend toward the neutral zone.
You need to think hard and come up with a way to make the game fun to play. The cascade of who gets the first slay that sorta just keeps playing out in an endless exchange is anathema to fun. A stop gap fix is to reduce animation time and then look at fundemental design choices and see what you can do.
Another option would be to up the number of players and pitch it less as a competitive game and more as a party and political board game. Id still shorten animations if you went this route and fix the endgame but it could be a quick way to solve many of the other issues the game has.

I bought into first access  so I have been following and playing this game for a long time.
An interactive turn-based strategy board game. You play one on one vs a real or AI opponent. The entire map is fogged so you are unable to initially see what your opponent is doing. You start with a master thief. You use that thief to scout the map (remove the fog) and steal one of two resources (gold or lanterns) from buildings. Lanterns enable you to upgrade your thiefs abilities, with 3 talent trees to chose from, and unlock units. Gold allows you to purchase unlocked units. Units interact with the board in special ways to benefit you or hinder your opponent. There are special buildings on the map which once controlled, can generate resources, reduce unit costs and give other unit benefits. Ultimately the goal is to gain enough control of the board's special buildings to amass enough resources to earn 5/6 victory points. Vicotry points can be bribes (purchased with lanterns), contract kills (NPC's murdered by your master thief or another unit), blackmail (earned by gaining full control of a church (an aformentioned special building)), or through specialised map specific win conditions.
THE POSITIVES
- Has a single player campaign (4 hoursish) which does a good job of teaching the games mechanics and contains a decent story as well.
- Good voice acting and music.
- Great art style (I find it very Don't Starve).
- The game is well balanced.
- Different play styles are viable and the best players alter their strategy in game based on their opponents and RNG elements (NPC spawns, building spawns etc.)
- Has a number of different maps which varies gameplay.
- Options for live play (one constant game) or casual play (no turn timers, players can take their turn and log out while their opponent plays).
- A basic ranking system exists.
- Short wait times for games, never had to wait more than a couple of minutes.
- A very friendly development team that is active in the community.
- A charming game that you can tell was a labour of love.
Overall a game that is simple to understand and hard to master. After completing the campaign (4ish hours) most people should understand all the games mechanics. However, since the game has come to steam I have played 5 minute games against newer oppoents and hour long games against experienced opponents. The game contains lots of depth with each player trying to maximise turn efficiency and slight errors allowing the game to swing in an instant.
THE NEGATIVES
- The ranking system is currently based on wins and nothing else, losses are not taken into account, hopefully will be changed in the future.
- The campaign isn't long enough to justify the price if mutliplayer does not interest you.
- Although rare, and good players will be able to adapt in most situations, there is the potential to get unfavourable RNG which can make winning more difficult. It won't cause you to flat out lose like in card games but it can certainly be a factor at times.
CONCLUSION
If you are a fan of strategy games, board games, multiplayer games or any combination of those you will probably enjoy this game, as it is a well executed game that incorporates all of those aspects.
This simply has too little content for the price.  As other reviews have mentioned, if this were to cost $5 it probably would be worth it.

I just cannot recommend this game.
Sure, the "Gangs of New York" + "Oliver Twist" theme is nice and the campaign provides 10 varied levels, BUT it's a problem of value for your money. If you can get it for 5$ or less, then yeah, maybe, but otherwise there are infinitely better strategy games out there.
I finished the campaign in 4 hours, and these 4 hours felt longer than they should have been. This is in part because the game's animations and sequence of events are artificially long, but mostly because
. After the first 3-4 levels (out of 10), I had enough mastery over the simple systems that finishing a level was just a matter of going through the motions and waiting for the predictible conclusion. It is quite easy to figure out what to do and which options are the best. There is not much granularity in gameplay, not a lot of small decisions that can make a difference down the line. I can't imagine different players using very different routes to victory. And you can feel that from the get-go, with a tutorial that does not allow the player to develop his style or experiment.
After finishing the campaign, the game wants you to play online versus real opponents, but frankly, I cannot see how online play might take off. The depth is just not there for a strategy game, and I don't know how most games will avoid degenerating into mirror matches with no obvious way out of the inevitable stalemate. I'm not bothering to find out, anyways.
Another unfortunate aspect of this game is the lack of thematic coherence. The promise of backstabbing, assassinating and blackmailing does not translate into anything at all. These are just words and images glued over game mechanics that have nothing to do with them. There is no stealth, no guild member management, no lies, no scheming ... nothing that you would expect from a game that sells a thieve's guild fantasy. Gameplay-wise, the game is an abstract resource management game with a very simple combat system, all rolled into a 1v1 turn-based strategy structure.  It feels like the art department wanted to do a thieves guild game, while the game design guys decided they wanted 30-minute strategy duels. Not to mention the music which absolutely does not fit the theme whatsoever (although it's a nice music if you like Pachelbel's Canon, which I think it is based on). What a mix ...
Now this game is not all bad. The art is competent, there are no noteworthy technical issues (in the off-line campaign at least), the devs put a very nice effort into varying the gameplay across levels, the learning curve is smooth. A shame that the pros get overshadowed by the cons.

It's obvious that this game was only playtested by the developers.  Outside of the very basic mechanics (magnetic attraction and repulsion), very few are adequately explained as they are introduced to the players: mirrors are introduced with just a cryptic image, block-powered magnetic fields aren't at all.  Unlike in, say, Portal or Quantum Conundrum, the environments are very visually busy, meaning that when something new is introduced, it's very easy to mistake as just part of the set dressing.  And overall, the game just isn't very fun to play.  You move infuriatingly slowly, meaning that when you inevitably need to backtrack to retreive a block you accidentally sent flying, the time you are in transit is longer than the actual time it takes to solve the puzzle.  The story seemed interesting, from the part I saw, and the voice talent was pretty good.  But my interest in how the story played out was swiftly outmatched by boredom and frustration.

The Good:
Decently programmed and moderately difficult magnetic puzzles
Feels like Portal without portals
Vaguely interesting plot twists
The Bad:
Some of the worst voice-acting you'll witness
Color scheme is "customizable" between two horrid options
You will never care about the story

I waited forever for this game to go on sale. When that never happened, I bought it straight up... Bad idea. I trusted the game as a followup to Gladiator Begins on the PSP, which I had a lot of fun with, but this game is missing a lot of the already limited features that game brought to the table. There's just not a lot of content for what you're paying for. You'll spend a lot of time fighting nearly identical skeletons. Whereas, in Gladiator Begins, you see your character rise from a slave to a hero and it's all rather gratifying, this game is really just a slog with little story to get invested in.
One of the best parts about Gladiator Begins was getting in and out of close scrapes with the enemies, having your armor knocked off, running over to retrieve it, and re-engaging. For whatever reason, that doesn't happen here. Instead, you'll find most fights are either you successfully luring the enemy into one on one engagements or you being smashed from multiple sides. In general, it feels too easy, but more importantly, it just isn't as exciting as Gladiator Begins was, since you're rarely worrying about losing and retrieving your armor and weapons.
All in all, I'm a big fan of the developer, but there isn't enough content in this one to justify the purchase. The online mode isn't worth mentioning since you will never find anyone to play with. I'd just avoid the game altogether.

This game is 1 step forward and 2 steps back.
Let's compare this to the previous game in the series, "Gladiator: Begins".
First of all this game does have a story and a story mode, but the story is as barebones as you can possibly get, it's literally just some text before each mission. Meanwhile every previous game in the series has had a full blown story mode with interesting characters, and while usually a basic plot, it was interesting enough to keep you interested in what was going on. Hell GB had branching paths and multiple endings, this game has 0 variation in story.
Combat wise it's again 1 step forward and 2 steps back
The combat controls a lot nicer than on PSP, especially the camera controls. It adds in a dodge roll which is pretty nice, and combat feels a bit more fast paced than before. But then you realize that there's no longer health for individual body parts, meaning that you can no longer break arms making their weapons unusable and the like, so it just becomes whoever targets the weakest spot first and goes to town on it.
They've removed the shield style and mixed it in with the single sword fighting style. There are no longer different stances for each style, so everyone using the same weapons fights the same. That being said they added a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of passive abilities that you can equip to customize your dude, but 90% of them are "X skill has 30% shorter cooldown" or "you do X more damage"
The graphics certainly look a lot nicer but customization has really gone down the toilet. They advertise TONS OF CUSTOMIZATION! but what they mean is customization combinations which is basically nothing. In GB you had nearly 20 faces and 20 hair styles to choose from, which isn't an amazing amount but it was enough to be good. This game has 4-5 hair styles for each race, and they are all the exact same hair just on a different model with 1 unique hair per race. Each race is gender locked, each race has 3 faces to choose from that are nearly identical, there's face tattoos, but again identical for each race and all pretty lame.
You no longer level up as you progress and have to rely on upgrading equipment for all of your stats, which I guess is a gameplay style choice, but it was a pretty big change, IMHO I wasn't a fan.

I have always enjoyed a medieval setting when it comes to video games whether it is a strategy title or RPG. Perhaps it’s because of the cool armor and weapons themselves that I find it so much more engrossing than a modern or sci-fi setting (with one or two exceptions). So right away I was interested when I heard about Clan of Champions and that it happened to be an action fighting game.
The game’s story is rather simple. The Kingdom of Ematrias and the Al-waav Urban Allied Forces have been at war for some time only to have turned their gaze towards a forgotten castle town. A place that, legend says, once held the secrets to technology that gave them the ability to create powerful weapons. It was discovered that such weapons still existed in this town. Now these warring nations are trying to gain the advantage by hiring experienced mercenaries.
And that is where I came in. As one of these mercenaries it was my job to find these relics. So I started with the customization screen where the game boasts over 10,000 combinations. Sadly it isn’t as great as it sounds. It isn’t that there are only three races that I could choose from: humans, elves, and orcs. Rather it was that the number three seemed to be the operative word for the character customization. There were three voices, three head types, three facial types, and three hair types that I could choose from. The only things I could really change were the color of hair and skin for my character to black or blonde or even fuchsia if I could find the right combination.
Major disappointment on my part.

I came from playing Battlecruiser Millenium Gold, and I found that most of the changes to Universal Combat seem to be cosmetic with improved graphics and a slightly modified interface, although there may be more substantial improvements internally as well such as support for modern joysticks. Regardless, it plays essentially the same with only a few keystroke command changes, and in my view it is still a fantastic game.
Let me start by stating the obvious: this game is not for everyone, not by a long shot. First off, you need to read the extensive manual. There are just no shortcuts here to be had as you have to invest the time to learn the commands and various interfaces, preferably while having the game running in front of you so you can try out what you learn. And even then you will likely frequently refer back to the manual for the more esoteric stuff. It is a complex game with a steep learning curve, but for a reason, which is that you get to control every facet of your ship and its assets, down to the location of each crew member and their various assignments. You are truly the captain of your ship, and the better you know her the more enjoyment you will get out of the game. On top of that, there are a lot of addtional things you can do like first person piloting of a fighter, shuttle, or rover, or even walk on the surface of a planet and engage in exploration or combat. You can  create concerted attacks on planetary bases by marines on the ground with close air support from fighters and tactical bombing from orbit. You can mine planets to collect valuable minerals for trading in space ports. Or you can just roam the galaxy on a 5 year mission to explore new worlds and new civilizations :) To put it another way, a vivid imagination is a pre-requisite as well as a willingness to immerse yourself in the experience. With time, you will develop a fondness for your crew and an attachment to your ship, the hallmark of a true captain...

Now for the detractors out there, this game plays just as advertised. I have yet to experience a serious bug with it and it delivers what it promises. The impression I get from reading many of the negative reviews is that either the reviewers have not taken the time to really learn the game because of its apparent initial complexity or were more suited for different types of games such as Elite Dangerous or its ilk.
Universal Combat (and its predecessors) is a monumetal achievement that has no equal in its breadth and capabilities, and for under $10 it is a total steal. Nonetheless, if you prefer to try the game first, then Battlecruiser Millenium Gold is available as freeware and will run perfectly under Win 7 to Win 10 as long as it is set to Win 98 compatibility.
And if you are still hesitant, consider reading the Starcarrier SF series from Ian Douglas, as it will give a real feel of what this game is all about.

I hated every moment I played this game.
To start off with, this game is meant to be primarily humorous, if you buy this game, it's because it's going to be something that amuses you and makes you laugh. However, if your sense of humor is anything like mine, then you're not going to laugh, and all you're left with is a tedious, badly designed game.
It plays like snake. You know the one, the old atari snake, where you're moving on a 4 directional plane with a tail behind you. If you've played snake, you've played this game, only I prefer snake. There are obstacles to avoid, and different events which all play out the same way every time across all three "campaigns", only increasingly difficult.
It has so little to do with GTAV that it's kind of skeevy how they used its likeness to get attention and purchases. The only aspects of this game in common with GTAV is you play as 3 seperate characters, the word 'heist' is shoehorned in, and.. that's it really.
The humor is largely political and social, and I'm under the assumption that the political humor is largely related to a specific event and person over in the UK, so if you're an American like me, or really any other place that isn't the UK or you're not versed on world politics, you're not going to get those jokes.
The social humor is predictable and dumb.
Every campaign goes the same way... you run some things over, then the next phase is running away from something, then you run over something specific, then theres another phase of running away from something, then there's a "heist" where you go top down over the chracter within a room and grab items of some kind while either avoiding or slaughtering the other people in the room depending on if you took the Stealthy or Brutal route. This process is only made slightly harder across the other campaigns, but its mostly just reskinned.
There's also some hardcore mode difficulty which I haven't and am unlikely to ever play.
The art style I think is supposed to be quirky or deliberately trashy looking, but it ends up just coming off as lazy. The crayon drawing equivalent art and scanned handrawn work patched together into vague animation does not appeal to me, and I grew quickly tired of looking at it.
The voice acting is maybe decent on its own, but the dialogue I found to be wretched. It's also repeated.. constantly. Constantly you will hear the same f**king dialogue spouted, and it gets so old so fast that at certain points I had to take off my headset.
All in all, if this games style of humor appeals to you, it's worth the 74 cents my friend paid for it. But if you don't like the jokes, then there's nothing about this game that is worth the money.
Recommended if you like the humor. Not recommended if you don't.

NotGTAV is an action RPG shooter drawing from the best elements of games such as Assassin's Creed 2, snake, and of course GTAV. As a pastiche of many types of games is it succcessful as a game in its own right or is your money better spent elsewhere?
