Unlike GTAV, a game which NotGTAV itself claims is "immeasurably superior" (notably, not a qualified statement), I could run this game on max settings with no fps lags. This in itself is a remarkable achievement considering I am running the game on a low end laptop, but the graphics themselves are independently fantastic. The accuracy of the Lidl Swindon is far greater than GTAV's relative accuracy of Los Santos (which is based on Los Angeles of course): having been to Swindon and many Lidl's I can say that the game conveys their shitness very accurately, whereas having been to LA, GTAV does not portray the shitness of Los Angeles very well at all.
The gameplay is fast paced and thrilling, and the pacing of the story is excellent. At no point is one bored of the current task, nor do you ever feel that the story has lulled in its development. Playing 3 characters and their own stories in parralel is reminiscent of Pulp Fiction and is done in a far superior manner compared to GTAV. Rockstar could learn a lot about storytelling from Notgames, considering the trite that they came up with for GTAV's "story" mode.
The radio feature is also far superior to that of GTAV. Changing the stations is quick and easy, and the selection of music is much, much better.
Unfortunately, not every game is perfect, but this one comes pretty darn close. The only negative I can think of is the voice of David Cameron - while the game portrays the shitness of other aspects tackled by the game, the voice actor here does not do a very good job of portraying the shitness of David Cameron.
Nonetheless this is a solid entry in what I hope is a long series, and I wholeheartedly recommend this game, while eagerly awaiting the release of NotGTAV 2!

TL,DR version at the bottom for your convenience. (~.^)
First, let me get something gigantic out of the way. Something huge. Something that could indeed be described as the "Elephant in the room". "What is this 'elephant'?" you ask? Well, it is an imposed one forced down your throat by nearly every living Blizzard fan. Or, to be more precise, Overwatch fan. Allow me to explain as fast as I can cause it's 2016, and we all have ADD lol.
First, There are curently THREE "hero FPS" games on the market that essentially use the Team Fortress 2 model as thier foundation in one way or another. You choose a character (Hero), with a special "kit", personality and playstyle, and you go from there with match making and such. Much like you would normally do in any FPS....but with more character, personality, individuality, etc.. Thus adding to the fun of the game. They play like MOBAs to some degree and are generally team-based, complete with tanks, offense and support classes. These are known as "Hero-Shooters". Now you know...
But what are the three? Overwatch (Blizzard), Battleborn (Gearbox), and a little gem known as Paladins (Hi-Rez). Why should you know this? Because Overwatch fans will destroy you if you even mention the other two games. This is common with Blizzard fans for some reason. As if Overwatch was the first hero-shooter ever made, but it wasnt. Much like how WoW wasn't the first MMO ever made, even though they acted like it was. Same thing happened to "Section 8" when it was attacked by Halo fans, even though S8 is STILL better than Halo five. But W/E. So let's boil a few things down real quick (too late) so that you know what's actually happening here with each game and where you should go from there.....
-Overwatch is Blizzard's take on TF2. Simple as that, really. You choose a character. They have abilities that you use to help you win the match with your "friends". You capture objectives and... well... that's kinda it. However, Overwatch has the best character designs I have ever seen in just about any game. The lore behind them and the story that you are technically taking part in is incredible, and you can't help but feel attached to them in one way or another. In THIS regard, Overwatch has no equal. Overwatch puts you into it's world like no other. And that's technically it.
-Paladins is Hi-Rez's take on the hero-shooter as well. Still in beta, but shows great promise and is actually better than Overwatch if you're looking for more depth in your hero-shooter. This is because Paladins has a loadout system that you can make to specialize your hero to your liking, as apposed to just being stuck with whatever default kit the hero has. Want more booster fuel for your rocket-shooting dragon? You can do that. Enemy team focusing on tanking? Buy in-battle "cards" to punish them for it. This allows more strategy and depth than Overwatch currently offers and, with a bit of tweeking, this system will only get better. No need to change your hero. Characters are pretty good, but not Overwatch good. Not yet at least. Paladins is also incredibly lite on your system and will run smooth as silk on a toaster if need be. Did I mention it's completely Free to play? Yeah, that's a thing.
-Battleborn.... Ah yes. Believe it or not, this is essentially the BEST hero-shooter out there for TONS of reasons. And I was sure, even back when both Battleborn and Overwatch were simply advertising that this was going to win out. Sadly, a poor launch, unjust hate, Odd technical problems and stupid choices by the devs threw Batleborn to the low-end QUITE fast. Which is a terrible shame. Characters are fun, in-battle hero customization is very deep, more game modes, hero peronality almost that of Overwatch, SINGLE PLAYER STORY with optional co-op, loot system (which acts similar to Paladins loadout system), tons of unlockables, is gorgeaous and focuses on the FPS/MOBA aspect more than any of the other two shooters. Seriously, this would be our default hero-shooter, and still can be. They just have to make it run MUCH better, give actual skins, not re-colors (BAD MOVE #1), and maybe even make it free to play.
But to be more precise, what does Battleborn offer you? Why should you play it instead of Overwatch or Paladins? Allow me to summarize.
1)- Personality we've come to expect from the Borderlands franchise is off the charts. And that's something unique this title brings with it. The characters, love 'em or hate 'em, are wonderfully voiced and full of themselves. Honestly, even the characters I don't like I actually STILL like playing. There's soemthing to be said about that
2)- Single Player mode with optional co-op. Don't feel like PvP but still want to enjoy the game and the lore behind it? No problem! Just hop in, choose your toon, and let the hilarity begin. Bring a friend, and some crack, for added fun IF YOU WISH. You can solo just about anything if you're careful and have the time to spare.
3)- Multible VS game-modes. Not just everyone fighting for the payload for the millionth time. You, the player, have options as to what mode you want. Remember those days?
4)- The Helix System. Essentially an in-game character talent tree, of sorts, that makes your hero better at what you want them to be better at. When you level in-game you get a point to spend in this talent tree in real-time. And believe me, there's A LOT to consider when choosing these "talents".
5)- Loadout System. You know those single player games you danced around in last night? Odds are you got some gear from bosses and mobs and such. Why does this matter? Cause you can make a loadout from that gear which helps you be a better you for both PvE and PvP alike. But you can't benefit from said laodout without investing in-battle currency to activate a piece of it. Which leave you with a deep choice of whether or not to upgrade yourself via the gear, OR upgrade defensive structures throughout the PvE/PvP maps that help you a lot in diffferent ways. Again, more depth and choice.
6)- Flashy, over-the-top abilities and effects all over the place. Very colorful world! Can sometimes be too much, but you get used to it.
7)- Balanced. There will always be a balance problem in some way or another, but honestly I have yet to truly say something is terribly OP or not, as opposed to Overwatch constantly complaining about who's the OP hero of the week. Kinda reminds me of Demigod in turms of balancing.
8) - You live a bit longer. Just cause someone got the first shot on you doesn't mean you will die by default. Your hero can take a few hits. Just enough to make a comeback, in fact. I like this a lot and adds to more enjoyable battles.
And there be my long-winded lecture on the matter. In short, in terms of raw content Battleborn wins hands down. Even in it's current state. There's simply MORE to do! With Paladins and Overwatch sharing second place. All are great games and all should be tried.
-Want it simpler? Play Overwatch.
-Want Overwatch with customization? Play Paladins.
-Want both and even more content? Battleborn is your choice. Just be sure to have the right specs. it's a resource hog for some odd reason.... lol
As ever, I hope this "review" has assisted you in your choosing to support this game. I have been gaming all my life, and I know a gem when I find one. This is it. If the price is a bit too high, you can do what I did and head on over to Gee 2 A dot com and get it for dirt cheap. More you support the game, the more it will grow and the more fun yee shall have. Simple, right? And if it doesn't work out you still have a lovely single-player game with tons of character and flashy things. What's not to like?
TL, DR? Battleborn for raw content. Paladins if you like Overwatch with hero customization. Overwatch for Blizzard's version of TF2 with insane character design. Simple. Enjoy :)

So Battleborn, the oh-so critically acclaimed "bad game"... well, hopefully this Review helps encourage people to try out this foreshadowed Gem Masterpiece
So what is Battleborn?
Battleborn is an awesome Co-Op / Versus by Gearbox (makers of Borderlands) set thousands of years in the future, where the universe has 1 star left. A bunch of groups are defending it and keeping the last light on, while the Jennerit, a race from the planet Tempest, are set to see it destroyed (they're basically Vampires honestly :v) You, a Battleborn, are sent on a quest to stop their plan, and let nothing in your path hold you down before taking them down.
Or of course, do Versus and have some 5v5 Battleborn orgy action by ripping into other players and emerging on top!
Its... quite absurd, but its from the heads behind Borderlands, so its expected to be absurd honestly!
How would I rate the game? Well:
- Good length Campaign, which also extends with the Operations DLC's (all in Season Pass)
- Very worth while Season Pass: with way more content then you'd expect for what you pay
- Absolutely fantastic humour. Literally laughing my♥♥♥♥♥off at some of the lines even still
- Large hero roster. Over 25 Battleborn, and all very unique from one-another, and great personalities to boot.
- Great ranking / leveling system: You actually feel like you've accomplished alot by leveling a Battleborn
- Endless variety of skill building with 100's of different pieces of Gear to equip and activate
- 100's of Challenges and Lore to achieve / unlock. Gives ALOT of replayability
- A fairly small variety of enemy types to fight. (Can have same enemies / combinations) on alot of levels
- Random frame drops in certain areas. (Probably just particle effects, but yeah, idk)
- Small variety of BGM. Could definitely use an expanded soundtrack
- Some minor terrain / environment clipping. Pretty hard to find, but it does happen
Well, thats all I gotta say for Battleborn.
Would I recommend it? ♥♥♥♥ YEAH I WOULD!
The game has waaaaaaaaaay less people playing then it SHOULD! We could always use more Battleborn! You up for the challenge? I hope so.
Overall Rating: 9/10

I wanted to like this game but it's... absolutely stubborn about making me dislike it. It's fun in theory, but in execution it's just a more physics heavy Portal with less cleverly designed/more tedious puzzles.
First off, the story. Is way too instrusive. In acts 1 and 2 you have elevator segments between a large portion of the levels that takes up a loading screen for essentially a cutscene... that is the same every time, just with a different person talking to you. The plot actually affects the gameplay very little in the first two acts, other than to make things take longer. All characters communicate via a hologram popping up over the magnet gun, but don't actually do anything. Sure, the scenery gradually degrades more and more, but that's about all that happens plotwise that is the slightest bit relevant to gameplay. Well until the third act when monsters start appearing.
Another issue is the tedium in the puzzles; there's a lot of waiting around for things to be in the right place and making mistakes can sometimes set you back quite a bit even if you don't die. On top of that there's a lot of trial and error involved (far far more than Portal) because of the physics engine, which is unfortunately not perfect enough for this kind of game. There's inconsistencies in how objects behave on occasion and it's often hard to predict what will happen until you test it. Some of the puzzle rooms are pretty big as well while also lacking in direction, leading to confusion not even part of the puzzle. The game also doesn't have a large enough variety in obstacles to keep things fresh; at some point things stop evolving (aside from the monster segments) and the puzzles start to get rather repetitious. Maybe digging deeper into a concept explored previously but it's not fresh enough to hold the interest. The game probably could've benefitted from being shorter, especially in the second act; that segment of the game took up probably 60-70% of my initial run playtime on its own.
The monster segments are also entirely out of place; they're alright when you know what to do but until you do they're largely trial and error, often almost expecting you to know what to do if you want to survive at all. There's not a large number of them and they're all confined to the end of the game, but they still really aren't a good fit for the formula. The final boss especially, since it is entirely possible to have the game autosave mere fractions of a second before you die, forcing a level restart. Plus there's a needlessly difficult platform hop involved. I thought we agreed that first person games and intense platforming are a combination that really has to be fine-tuned or excluded period. It's only a single hop done twice but it's a pretty fast moving platform and failure means death, soooo.
The game's on the whole not terrible, it's an interesting concept and there are some good puzzle designs here but there are far more bad puzzles than good and I wouldn't recommend it over its peers.

There are things you need to collect every now and then to open up new doors, but there are no sign posts to guide you. A lot of the game is exploration. The other main part is puzzle solving. Slowly, they begin adding new mechanics, never explaining them to you but giving you a safe(ish) place to experiment with them until you figure out how to manipulate your mechanics and environment. There is a bit of simple(ish) puzzle solving in order to unlock your goals at times, which adds another bump in the interest curve since, as usual, you have no indication what the puzzle is or how to solve it. This start getting crazy at the end, adding in mechanics like low gravity, high gravity, permanent deformation of the floor, the penultimate "the floor is spazzing out", and the final "the floor is NOT jelly."
Pros:
+Lots of variations of tasks, mechanics, puzzles, etc. Everything stays fresh and nothing wears out its welcome.
+Very atmospheric music. Music reflects surrounds and is ultra soothing. Do yoga to this, honestly.
+Great art. Minimalist with lost of variations of color in the levels. Wintry white and blue, beautiful sunsets, bluish wetlands, warm pinks and oranges, etc.
+Nice level of difficulty. Not simplistic or trivial, but not frustratingly annoying. I felt challenged without feeling stupid, and I'm really terrible at platformers, so it's good for different skill levels.
Cons:
-Short. My total runtime was 3 hours.
-Last few levels hurt my brain, not because of the difficulty level but because the platforms seriously start spazzing out and take over the whole screen. (No, not a glitch, it's one of the mechanics introduced.)
Overall: 10/10. Super fun puzzle-platformer. Would bounce again.

This is going to be a hard review. I wish I could be neutral about it, but due to Steams review mechanics I will have to reach a verdict at the end. Oh boy. Please read carefully, especially my conclusion!
Lets talk about the atmospheric, story-driven experience you are going to get out of this first. Though graphically not top-notch given the year the game was released it sets up a great, intimidating and believable atmosphere with a mysterious touch to it. Great sound assest, brilliant light effects and decent level design regarding maze-like interiors. Aesthetically everything falls into place when you consider the fact that you are
going
to find secrets
left behind. The story, while a little bit predictable, is told very well and involves the player in it.
Mechanics. It is Frictional Games' first game which set a milestone in story telling gaming, which is wonderful. Not so wonderful is the fighting system, which is forced upon you
. It is not like in Games like Half-Life where you bash your enemies' heads in with your crowbar while still being able to evade their attacks - no! You have to swing your melee weapons with your mouse and you control it directionally, meaning that you can swing either side: left, right, or direct push. Problem is, that your screen locks when you try to swing, so you are unable to move. This is obviously not a good idea and you might think, that it encourages sneaking. And yes, at first that is the case - but soon you are not able to avoid encounters and you will have to brawl your way through, which is frustrating in a great way. This is a big negative, since it is practically forced upon the player and you have almost no way of avoiding it or finding a way around fighting - and you will come across those situations regularly.
Other mechanics work quite well. Puzzle solving is a bit tricky at times given the dated graphics, especially texture quality. For example: You find a key and don't know where to put it? It might be that pixely black mess of a texture on a control panel! This makes it quite complicated and it could use some sort of indicator, but well, it works somehow. Certainly, patience is required.
IF, only if you can withstand a large amount of depressing forced and flawed combat (I guarantee you that you will shut your game off multiple times!) and live for excellent atmosphere in every aspect, I can recommend this game. This game shows you why Amnesia was/is such a big success as THE atmospherically overwhelming and best written game up to this day (haven't played SOMA yet). Play Penumbra and - if you played later games of FG like Amnesia - you will experience an immersive adventure putting you through a relentless environment.
Recommendation? I shouldn't, because it forces those combat sequences on you like crazy. But I have to considering the artistic part of the game, which takes a greater part than combat.
If you really have doubts about the ever returning bad combat system, just read up on the plot and continue with the second game without playing this one. That's basically the workaround.

Penumbra Overture is a great little horror game. It is plain to see that it is a predecessor of Amnesia: The Dark Descent. There are many similarities within the imagery, gameplay and storytelling. For Amnesia fans seeking more content, this series is definitely worth playing.
The setting, an underground mine, allows for a certain amount of isolation and otherworldliness. I am not claustrophobic at all and didn't find the envrionments particularly scary, but I can appreciate that it is an eerie setting. I enjoyed the feeling of being deep within the ground.
At times the game reminded me of John Carpenter's The Thing, one of my favorite films.
The game would have benefited from far fewer enemies. They can be easily killed but the controls make it time consuming and frustrating. Killing enemies became repetitive and felt like a chore, but it was a necessary evil... it didn't make any sense to waste time sneaking back and forth repeatedly in the hub environments when the enemies are so easily killed.
The storytelling was very well done. Most information is gathered through found writings. The writings were extremely effective at building the world and adding tension to the game. Generally I was excited to find a new note to read, with a morbid curiosity of what information I would discover.
The controls are somewhat clunky and finicky. For the most part it doesn't affect gameplay because you can explore at your leisure. Perhaps it adds to the fear when you are fumbling around in a hurry.
There are scripted sequences where it becomes a problem. This is because a certain amount of precision is required and the clumsy controls don't allow for that easily. Add to that a healthy dose of guesswork. I was disappointed when I had to replay scripted sequences 4-5 times trial-and-error style. That type of frustration is the fastest way to break immersion and remove all fear from the situation.
There is no manual save and the auto-saves are far apart considering how easy it is to die. I have been spoiled by newer games, but it was really annoying the few times I died and lost a bunch of progress. Minor gripe!
I came to the Penumbra series as a fan of The Dark Descent, looking for a similar horror experience. Overture is obviously not as polished as The Dark Descent but it is well worth playing. I am glad I was able to do a blind playthrough and have another great experience courtesy of Frictional Games.
Replay value is not really there for me. This is only due to the controls and the repetitive enemy encounters. The game itself isn't something I will soon forget. Great ending! I'm looking forward to the next game, Black Plague. From what I hear it's even better than Overture.

I honestly enjoyed most of this game, which is why giving it a negative review bites. The problem is, the back chunk of the game is atrocious. You're suddenly going from what I referred to a couple of friends as "Hard-Mode Portal" (same 'solve the puzzle room' gameplay, with two-button controls, even if it's opposing magnetic polarities rather than holes in time/space) into a terrible action title.
I was going to recommend this with a caveat of "By the end, some puzzles become irritating due to the checkpoint system, where you may have to restart chunks of stage if you mistime a polarity swap or make a slight field mistake on some items", but no, when you suddenly have to begin juggling explosives to kill massive sahaguin and all sorts of tentacled beasties* whereas you were previously free to take time and puzzle things out? Ick. Do i recommand this game? Maybe!
It took me 10 hours to finish the game, a third of that is playing, another third is thinking, and the last third is dying.
This game is a « portal » copycat, with magnetism as game engine, but the physics are often imprecise.
It remembers me another game, bad rats, when you think the solution correctly, you build the solution correctly, but it may fail just because of some pixels offset, or even worse, won't do the same result between two identical simulation!
A puzzle game can be hard and challenging, it's not the problem, but it shall not be « hard » to build the solution, it's just annoying and not enjoyable.
I give three situations you will encounter in the game:
- Sometimes you need many tries ( deaths ) just because the timing of platforms or cubes ( how hard is it to detect the peak altitude of a cube when you are riding it and then perform the correct imprecise jump!).
- Often (very often), and despite of the zoom feature, you will send your « newton » (a castable magnetic point) instead of setting the magnetism of a device, because we are talking about pixel aiming here...
- Sometimes, with the exact same configuration between two tries and when 3 or more magnetic points are involved, the result will differ, making you think your solution was bad at first. It's even worse when it happens on « catapults » because the cubes are snapped to the same precise position, so it's not even a targetting problem.
When i play a puzzle game, i don't wan't to be blocked because a piece don't fit well, i don't call that a hard puzzle but a glitched puzzle.
Anyway, the physics are also almost realist, it means when you expect to « capture » a charged object by using another object in vinicity, it will or not work depending of the momentum and the distance of the moving object, wich means some situations are complex but previsible, and added to the pre-existing points, you will be able and will need to place your own point (one at time) on almost any surface . In term of complexity, it worth the speed and direction conservation you have to master in portal when you use big falls to make big or long jumps ^^ This was the feature that made me go on to see what challenging puzzle was waiting for me in the next level, despite of the « glitches » i mentioned before.
The graphims are okay, and clear enough to focus on activable objects.
The story is a joke and the Cthulhu background is just a pretext to glue the puzzles together, don't expect epic fights ( there are only 2 kind of monsters, and they basically just walk towards you and you die on contact... the screenshoot are kind of lying btw. i suspect in early versions they just planned to use a countdown to add some stress) or deep story, everything is incoherent and not fun ( opposite to portal story), and the cutscenes are unskippable! ( remember i said you will die often not because you are not clever, but because of the unfair difficulty to build the solution, expect to see the same cutscenes often ). You will feel alone till the end.
There is a decent chance you won't finish the game because you won't enjoy it till the end, or even because it's too hard.
You may enjoy it if you don't mind loosing half of your play time because of the game and not because of you, the other half will show you how clever you are.

First of all I would like to get the big elephant in the room out of the way.
Many people will tell you that this is a reinterpretaion of Portal, and while I can see where they are coming from I disagree.  This is strongly inspired by Portal 2, and to me that is a big difference.  In Portal one it was a puzzle game that gave you flexability to solve the room puzzles creatively, with some solutions being better, faster, or more fun.  In one case the devs even purposely left in a clever shortcut to practically skip one room through a very clever trick.  In Portal 2 the puzzles are set with one solution, sometimes letting you do parts of that solution in a diffrent order, but essentially only one solution will pass the room.  This is the puzzle design in Magrunner.  It doesn't make it bad, but in my opinion, like Portal 2, it scores lower than it would.
Unlike Portal, which has AMAZING voice acting and writing, MagRunner has Good or OK Voice Acting and Writing.  The script could have used allot of work, but is not bad or terrible.  If you can suspend your disbelief it is still entertaining.
The Art style is sometimes very unique and at other times looks like a mod to turn another game into Portal 2.  Soem examples of content inspired by other things is the "Mag Glove" your character uses, which is inspired by the demon summoning glove Rasputin wielded in the first Hellboy Movie.  Another is the catpults from Portal 2.
The puzzle design, a bit poor in some places, was fun and diffrent enogh from "Thinking with Portals" that at my  first sitting I was finding myself wanting to do room after room.
There will be solutions that will make you groan, sometimes in a good way, and sometimes in a bad way.

An important clue that a game is good? That it's fun even when you're losing at it. Antihero is so great, you'll have a ball even as you're learning the ropes and having skilled players (or savvy AI) kick your butt. Seriously - this is one of the most unique, fun, cool-looking games I've played in a while.

Overall I'd give the game 6/10, The Main issue is the single player mode truthfully is just an in depth tutorial, that explores each aspect of the game individually. The Game itself has it's own atmosphere which is a beautiful blend of dark and goofy, with the characters being very original with their own personalities, which are expressed very easily. Game-play by itself warrants a 9/10 playing the game felt smooth, and the mechanics are fresh and creative, the only caveat is i feel there is plenty of space for further growth into further forms of game-play, where exactly i am not entirely sure but based on how unique this game was i am sure the dev's are up to the task if it comes to that. I have played a few multiplayer games now and found a common theme, people that are playing the game at the current moment try to jump into multiplayer without knowing the intricacies of the varying strategies and being someone who has mostly mastered this game i feels unfair, and the opponent will often quit after realizing i am way ahead. The game is worth buying even if only to play multiplayer.
Quick Tips: your economy is the most important thing early game, the game always starts you right next to a source of lamps and you should spend as many actions as necessary to take it first thing. then attempt to find a source of gold, as an early source of income (such as an upgraded bank) can assure you victory.
Don't forget certain points can be fought over, like the bribe; it's worth getting early because then your opponent can't get the first one requiring a larger pool of resources to gain the 2nd one putting them farther behind.
Try to focus on two or three sources of income, because if you take the time to build them they are attractive weak points to attack wasting your resources to keep retaking them

This game is basically a singleplayer / multiplayer turn- based board game with fog of war.
The graphics are charming, the art style consistent and sound and music fit the theme nicely. It supports 21:9,  though the UI does not make use of it much and some people complain about resolution proplems. Devs are looking into that atm of this review.
If you play on multiple devices, be aware that the game has no cloud save. Your save files are hidden well in %appdata% under "com.timconkling.aciv"
The single player campaign is an extended tutorial across 10 levels that tells a side story that you will not be able to remember in a week from now.
When you start the game, it seems that it has lots of depth and choices, but after 2 hours you have basically seen almost all the game has to offer.
Campaign is fun, but nothing breath taking. You need to be aware of your early game choices so you do not fall behind and from there build on your strategy.
For me, there are not a lot of winning conditions, as most of your choices are quite connected: establish a well rounded economy and play aggressive. That's it.
You can play games asynchronous, like in Frozen Synapse, where you do a turn and then your enemy does his, when he has time. You can receive a notification in order to see that your turn is up, which is nice. Or you play in a real time environment, where you have to watch your enemies moves, which I guess, might be a little tiresome after a while.
I can see this game as a substitute for playing board games with friends, when you all live apart. Or maybe you enjoy competing on leaderboards. Given the simple nature of the game and its indie origin, I doubt that many people will compete, though.
2v2 and FFA game modes are planned for the future, as well as new maps.
I can see the game get quite repetetive in the long run.
Wether or not this game is a recommendation for you, depends on how much you enjoy the multiplayer part. I will give it a recommendation, as I can see that the devs put a lot of love into it, but I would wait for a sale. Right now I would say, this game is above average but still not great.
Hope this helped you to have an overview.

"A rather superb single and multiplayer turn-based strategy game for the discerning gamer, in which you outsmart and out-steal your opponents. Indulge in a little bribery, blackmail, and assassination to rise to the top!" - With this, the game of Antihero is introduced on the website. Bribery, blackmail and assassination, combined with a wonderful art style, make this a must get, isn't it? Well, here is my impression!
 
Installation of the game over Steam goes swiftly and a few minutes after clicking the install button, the game is ready to play. It takes up about 125 megabytes of your storage - almost impossible to believe in days where a patch of your regular run-of-of-the-mill game can easily come at a gigabyte or two. Then again, this is not
a game, is it?
Firing up the game, it presents itself in windowed mode, which is quickly changed in the setting to get the full-screen experience. The settings panel is very light - it allows you to set audio levels, graphics resolution and there is a full-screen toggle and that is about it. No complex key-mappings, controller support or other complex settings. Very minimalist, so I can quickly focus on the game itself.
Your goal in the game is to guide a master thief to achieve supremacy over a town by scoring victory points. There are various methods to earn those points: you may assassinate targets, blackmail city officials or use some other tactic. You are not the only master thief trying to do this, so there is a scoring system where you can see who has more points. Whoever reaches the required amount of victory points first, wins.
The game can be played in the single-user campaign, where you battle your way through various parts of the city, following an superbly narrated story line. The early missions, called chapters, are focused on teaching the game mechanics, with increasingly difficult tasks. The later chapters expect that you know what you are doing and give you access to more resources, while also increasing the complexity of the task at hand.
You start a chapter by scouting the city around you with your master thief. If the opportunity offers itself, you may visit a house or two and collect gold or lanterns, the two currencies in the game. Those currencies can be used to either upgrade the skills and abilities of your thieves guild, or to hire staff into your organization. The staff to hire consists of various types, ranging from urchins to assassins. Each has a different skill set, and a rising cost. Urchins are for example used to infiltrate buildings, giving you specific advantages. An assassin can take out most of the hostile characters in one turn, but disappears after that. Managing the two currencies in the game, coins and lanterns, is key to winning the game.
The game consists of various chapters with increasing difficulty, different objectives and a range of characters that you meet. While the early chapters tend to be finished after a few minutes, later chapters take increasingly more time. The difficulty setting is an obvious factor in the duration of the chapter.
With the description of the game done, we now turn our attention to our impressions of the various aspects of the game:
It's Portal if the antagonist were C'thulu. It's really cool. I recommend this wholeheartedly.

If you liked the puzzles in Portal, you'll probably like the puzzles here. I had a fair bit of fun solving them over ~8 hours of gameplay.
Don't buy this expecting the personality that Portal has, though. No real humor. The plot makes no sense at all, and the script is pretty corny. Suprisingly, the voice acting wasn't bad, if melodromatic.
All in all, a pretty good puzzle game. The Cthuluesque theme really didn't come into play until near the end of the game. It felt tacked on for 2/3, and then in the final 1/3, finally actually became a little more relevant as monsters were introduced. They were a reasonably difficult challenge, as you had to be quick in your reactions.
*story rich* wish it was longer though

This is an interactive story more than a game. Don't expect a game here. That said, I completely enjoyed listening to all these videos to understand the story. One thing I especially like is that the hints are very subtle and the surprises keep coming at a steady pace.

While Planet coaster is vastly superior in terms of graphics, object placement, freeform coaster building, ride and peep animations, terrain, bugs/crashes, and a charming atmosphere even at its alpha stage, we still have to wait until the end of the year for a game with any sense of challenge or park management.
In the meantime we have to hope that RCTW improves to satisfy our park management cravings while we wait.
These pros and cons are against other major FINISHED park management games like RCT 1, 2 and 3.
PROS (THINGS THAT ARE BETTER THAN THEY WERE 12 YEARS AGO):
-There are curved paths.
-You can build a truly freeform coaster if you have the patience of a saint.
-The water dynamics are so impressive that I assume that they were already part of the Unity Engine and not the RCTW developers.
-There is a car park at the entrance. I like this
CONS (THINGS THAT ARE WORSE THAN THEY WERE 12 YEARS AGO):
GRAPHICS AND UI
-If there were no curved paths in this game, it would almost be GRAPHICALLY IDENTICAL to RCT3 (2004!)
- I get memory leaks where the game eats up to 26GB of my RAM. I am guessing not all players have 32GB ram to deal with this issue!
-The interface looks VERY bland. I am not asking for candy crush but I’ve seen accounting software that looks more exciting than this.
PERFORMANCE ISSUES
-My FPS is actually fine for the first 1000 peeps on max graphics. As soon as I get over 1500 peeps (easily achievable with 2 of the 9 park tiles), my game becomes unusable. The game freezes for 5 seconds every 30 seconds, crashes around every 15 minutes, and takes over 2 minutes to save the game (no joke).
(I have i7 3930K, GTX 970, 32GB RAM, SSD)
-Once my park starts to be a decent size (3 tiles or 2000 peeps) the game can no longer save or open it without freezing.
-I have not heard anyone with over 2000 peeps in their park claim that it is running smoothly.
How can I be motivated to spend time building something that I can no longer use once it starts to get interesting?
PATHS
-Building paths can be a pain when connecting to other paths or building up or near hills.
-Changing the path material means destroying anything connected to those paths (LIKE SHOPS) as the game will not allow you to place the path directly next to them again.
To fix: Add a material paint brush tool in the path menu and avoid the issue altogether.
-The game is SO PICKY when it comes to snapping benches, bins and shops to paths. They won't snap to positions that look perfectly acceptable and by default they seem to want to snap off the path onto the grass.
To fix: Allow intersecting geometry and free placement of path scenery and allow shops to be freely placed much closer to the paths. Let your users judge what is intersecting and what looks good for them.
PEEPS & STAFF
-The peeps animations are very wooden and they don't walk as families or groups like they did 12 years ago.
-Peeps sometimes stop walking in queue lines and hold up the entire queue for a few minutes.
-From birds-eye level the peeps stutter around the park at 2fps
-Sometimes all the peeps in the park disappear all at once and gradually start spilling in through the entrance.
-Staff are often seen sliding around the park without moving their legs like ghosts.
-Staff are often seen walking adjacent to the paths, phasing through all the scenery like ghosts.
-Mechanics are often seen congregating at ride exits, phasing through each other like ghosts.
I am pretty sure the staff are ghosts.
RIDES
-THERE ARE NO LOG FLUMES
-THERE ARE NO TRANSPORT RIDES, how hard can it be?
-While you can build rollercoasters piece-by-piece like you could in RCT3, parts like helix sections, loops and barrel rolls are missing.
-Coasters built or edited with freeform tools lead to a very un-smooth ride when finished. Something as simple as a descending helix can be a nightmare to build smoothly.
-Adding a lift-chain is way harder than it needs to be.
-It is not yet possible to change the colours of shops and non-coaster rides.
-The pre-built coaster stations are much larger and more realistic than RCT3 but you cannot choose where to put the entrance and exits.
-Tweaking an existing coaster can be dangerous. Clicking on a section of track to make a banked curve sometimes causes the camera to move which causes that piece of track to move way out of place. You then have to spend ages putting it back into place to avoid an unwelcome s-bend in your coaster.
To fix: GIVE US AN UNDO OPTION! Alternatively, allow us to lock certain axis’ when needed.
-Deleting parts of a coaster can be very tiresome after it has been built.
-Building pre-built coasters from the menu is an absolute nightmare in any park that is not perfectly flat and barren.
To fix: Give us an option to snap lowest part to terrain height and automatically bulldoze any scenery that would get in the way. At the very least allow us to see the ride supports during placement so we can see how ridiculously high off the ground the base of the coaster is going to be.
-Pre-built coasters do not display any excitement/nausea stats.
-All my coasters have ridiculously high nausea ratings while I think it looks quite safe.
To fix: allow us to see that nausea heatmap on our ride while we are building it if we want. At the very least, give the guests time to visit a toilet at the ride exit before puking everywhere. There are never any staff nearby to mop it all up.
TERRAIN
-Adjusting terrain under rides or roller-coaster supports is totally forbidden
-There are very few terrain materials available. This is like an hour’s job for a texture artist.
-There are no waterfalls like there were 12 years ago
-You cannot build tunnels like you could 12 years ago
SCENERY
-No building blocks/wall sections like in RCT2&3. I don’t want to have to trust an amateur Maya modeller for well-optimised and decent looking models without ridiculous stats from the steam workshop every time I want to build architecture. I want to design things myself. Look at what planet coaster lets you do!
-Selecting scenery items freezes the game for up to 5 seconds each, and occasionally CRASHES THE GAME ENTIRELY
To fix: if you don’t have budget to optimise your game any further, at least allow autosave.
If you can bear these problems for a few hours, zoom out and look at your park from above with all of its curvy paths and freeform coasters it can actually look quite realistic.
The fully working park management aspect is a fun challenge and is just as addictive as the original games.
Since no other title can claim both of these points at the same time yet, yes I would recommend this game to keep you busy until Planet Coaster comes out at the end of the year, after which, you will probably never touch this game again.
However, as I am unable to open saved parks (loading screen crash)  and experience memory leaks after they start to get big I cannot yet recommend this game.

I have rather mixed feelings about this game. The graphics and music are pretty good, and the challenge of trying to use bouncy jelly to reach the end is a novel one, compared to many other platformers where the world is totally solid. The game falls down in some key areas though:
No map. This game requires a lot of jumping through doors that lead to adjoining areas. Unfortunately, this makes it very easy to get lost, or go in loops. A map that updated new levels as you found them would have solved this, and without it things can get very frustrating.
The jelly physics isn't consistent. Most of the time you can count on the jelly to interact in a certain way, and that's fine once you learn how it works. But there will come times when the jelly just refuses to act the way it did before, and you will randomly get thrown off a wall into the void, or find yourself completely unable to jump up. Given that is the whole point of the game, I find it very frustrating that this issue existed. [This issue gets more pronounced later in the game].
The controls require a keyboard, and I just found it very difficult to play this way. I feel this game would have benefited greatly from controller support, so you may want to look into a keyboard-xinput mapper if you want to play it.

I had little expectations when I started playing F.E.A.R. 2, but i had thought the series sounded interesting and wanted to play the first game when it came out. Playing this game was still a disappointment. The levels were dull and uninteresting in design and layout. The characters all dull and two-dimensional, not to mention very stereotypical. What could be claimed as a plot and setting were poorly presented, badly paced and left me wanting it over not even half-way through. There was no scariness, no tension. Jump scares were continually accompanied by violin screeches, and were ineffective. The ending was disturbing, and didn't make much sense until I looked at some videos on youtube after about it. Even then it feels like it was mostly disconnected from the rest of the game. The possible attempt at adding atmosphere by having the HUD flicker was very annoying, bothered my eyes and since it didn't extend to anything besides the player's HUD and flashlight it felt like it was meant to punish the player more than be atmospheric.
Playing through on normal difficulty I found there were more than enough health and armor pickups to almost be constantly at full health. Weapons were frustrating because of the number found in game, the limit to the number able to be carried and their blandness, none really stood out for power or accuracy or usefulness beyond what ammo was most plentiful. At least one weapon had no other ammo besides the 5 shots it had when given. Grenades felt weak and mostly useless. (shock grenades were the only type consistently useful).
The boss fights were moderately interesting. The AI was interesting, the use of cover was fine, but the randomly running between cover spots, or the often indecisive movement of the AI trying to choose a spot to run to for cover were a pain. The powered armor sequences were even more linear and dull, and there was a greater tempation to not use the armor when available to try and give myself something challenging. I also went through most of the game without using the bullet-time ability very much. It didn't really seem needed for very much. There is also only about 6-7 different types of enemies, most of which are similar soldier types.

Renowned Explorers captures the feel of pulpy adventure serials through an appropriate soundtrack, charming character designs, and decent animation, all the while providing an interesting set of systems for hex-based "combats," social maneuverings, and between-mission downtime sessions.  The "combats" themselves aren't necessarily solvable by violence alone, however, and may be won through feel-good diplomacy or psychological cruelty, and is reflected in a rock-paper-scissors approach to each units' three base abilities - one each for aggression, deviousness, and friendliness.  Overall, this results in an engaging experience which can be enjoyed in around two hours of playtime per session.
Reaching the 2500 points required to win is a little tricky, especially with the old research trees being overhauled and replaced, but adjustable difficulty settings make this a tad more manageable task.

"97% chance of success to get a legendary treasure? AND YOU BOTCH IT! Go home you Russian ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I am never picking you for my Explorer team again!"
10/10, would pick Russian guy for my team again.

So much of the game is about building up your team, but the game will be over before you finish leveling them up or get an opportunity to benefit from much of the skills and bonuses that you accumulate. The Friendly/Devious/Aggressive system of resolution is interesting in theory but the execution leaves a lot to be desired, since their end effects are hardly distinguishable. Moving around in each campaign feels less like exploration and more like playing a slot machine with a very limited number of quarters. It often does not feel like you have very much control over how much of the game's victory point resource you get, and so ultimately it comes down more to luck than anything else whether you can even approach winning or not. The music and encounters are extremely repetitive after a few playthroughs, with enemy types, map types, and win conditions having little to no variation.

Despite being part of the 0.5% of people who have actually beaten all the standard levels in Colour Bind, I still don't know how to feel about Colour Bind. The game looks nice enough, and I enjoy the simple graphics, but I can't deny they are incredibly simple and are probably not an enticing factor for most people. The music that's there is also quite alright, but is nothing special. Of course, this is a platform-puzzle game, and the most important factors are the platforming and puzzling. So, how are these factors?
Well... like everything else, it's a bag of mix. The game has 50 standard levels, with a fair amount of other levels and cooperative levels in the game as well. These levels, at the very least, can take a few seconds to complete. If you're good, 30 seconds for most of the later ones. Most people will only experience a small portion of the 50 for reasons I will elaborate on. Each of the games levels are quite clearly either a primarily puzzle level, or a primarily platforming level. You can easily tell this from first glance, though there is some mixing of the 2, generally, it's one or the other.
The puzzles are... poor. I hate to sound so negative, but they really are poor. They are hardly puzzles at all. There isn't really any thought required on how to solve these puzzles. As soon as you see the level, it becomes pretty clear how to solve it. On occasion there is a puzzle that may stump you a bit, but it becomes clear how to solve it very soon. The problem is solving it, which brings me to the platforming.
The platforming, oh man... well, the platforming isn't actually bad. I mean, the little 2 wheel car vehicle thing you drive feels good to drive. It makes a satisfying clicking noise while you drive, and by pressing space, the wheels expand, which makes you jump. The physics work quite well I feel, and all this combined makes it quite fun to move around. It's just a shame the rest of the game isn't made for this sort of control in the slightest.
You see, the game is made for you to constantly make tight jumps, land on small or precise areas while in low gravity, and navigate areas where a single slip up can easily make you restart the entire area. Now, this may not sound that bad, and it wouldn't be, if it wasn't for one small issue. Once you've "jumped", you can't control where your car goes. You can't control yourself in the air at all! See, you pressing your arrow keys only move the wheels of the car clockwise or counter clockwise. This tiny little thing makes so much of the game harder than it would usually be. Every single jump in this platform puzzle game needs to be thought about greatly in advance, and even after thinking about it and deciding the best place to start committing to a jump, the game still contains a rather moderate amount of randomization from the physics. One second, you could find the perfect place to start a jump, but if you try it again a second time, you could easily only end up bouncing half as high and sideways. It seems like this shouldn't be possible, but it is, and it happens a lot.
So, you have a game where the puzzles are not actually difficult to figure out, but because of the way your vehicle controls, it becomes impossible to actually do most of the puzzles without losing numerous times on them. The game is like a test of patience in a way. Think of super meat boy, but instead of every level revolving around skill, it feels like every level here revolves around luck, and I'm talking about the kind of luck that you get once you've broken 50 mirrors while walking under ladders while crossing numerous black cats. In short, you feel like the game is constantly working against you. You know what you want to do, but you can't seem to make it work.
And yet... even after all this negative criticism, I like this game. It's well made, the visuals and sound are nice, and doing stuff still feels good. It's clear effort went into this, and though some things could be improved, the game is still rather charming in its own way. Kind of like, a separate reality. I suppose you just have to take it for what it is really, and what it is, is neat. I don't think you would be missing much by not buying it, but I recommend that you do, at least when it's cheap.
There is a single person on youtube who has actually managed to speedrun the game, so I guess it must be possible to become good. But as mentioned before, the vast majority of people who buy this game will never reach the final level. Quite literally 99.5% of people in fact, so I suppose beating this game could be seen as a reasonable achievement, and the final level is actually rather neat. I won't spoil it, but it really does change your view on the game and the developer as a person, and will make you appreciate the game a lot more.
So yeah, fun game, but one that only a minority of people will really enjoy for what it is.

*Mein Eindruck:
Anfangs war Battleborn bei mir auf der *kein interesse* liste. Dann habe ich erfahren dass Battleborn von den Borderlands  machern ist, also wollte ich dann doch mal rein schauen.
*Der Prolog*
Der schlimmste Prolog jemals. 0815 rapmusik, einem Prolog Video welches sich nicht zwischen 3D, Comic und 3D-Comic entscheiden kann. Wobei die "nur Comic" version wirklich so schlecht ist das man nicht weiß ob das wirklich ernst gemeint ist.
Nein wirklich der gesamte Prolog + das Erste level welches dazu gehört ist wirklich katastrophal.
Das Gesamte spiel ist etwas Chaotisch, ganz nach der Borderlands manier. Wärend das Gameplay selbst aber sehr abweicht.
*Gameplay*
Willst du ne runde Battleborn spielen, musst du online nach Random mitspielern suchen, bzw. Steam Freunde einladen. Abgesehen vom Prolog gibt es keine Singleplayer möglichkeit. Also meldet man sich an zum PvP oder Öffentliche Storry Modus an. Es dauert ein wenig. Das Spiel ist nicht sehr bewandert dennoch ist die Wartezeit ok. Und man muss nicht warten bis die Gruppe voll ist, sondern es kann schon mit einem mitspieler los gehen. Wenn das Spiel entschieden hat das 2 Spieler ausreichen, geht es dann auch los. Ein kleiner LvL Prolog den man glücklicherweise Skippen kann. Und man gelangt in die (ich sags mal so:) Champion auswahl.Dort wählt man einen von veilen Chaoten aus, die meisten muss man noch freispielen und dan gehts auch schon los.
*Die PvE* Level Bestehen meistens aus ettapen gemixt mit Halten verteidigen, eskortieren oder stupides durch ballern.
Jedes Level wird von einer kleinen geschichte mit Synchronstimme begleitet das ist ganz angenehm weil da schon Borderlands typisch, merkwüdige Persönlichkeiten zum vorschein kommen.
*PvP* habe ich noch nicht wirklich ausbrobiert.
*Die Charactere* Machen alle wirklich spaß. Sie sind selbsterklärend dennoch interesant durch das interaktive Skillsystem und sie können halt was was sie heldenhaft von jedem anderen Character Unterscheidet. Das ist so League of Legends Mäßig könnte man sagen.
Je öfter ein Character gespielt wird desto höher kommt man im Level mit diesem Character. So kann  jeder sehen wie erfahren du mit diesem Character bist.
Charactäre können durch Punkte erspielt werden oder durch erfüllte mission oder erfolge im spiel freigeschaltet werden.
Man kann sie mit 3 Items vor spielbegin ausrüsten die spezielle Boni geben.
Flamer gibt es nicht, dafür einen Voicechat wo selten irgend jemand redet, Geschrei, oder Geflame habe ich noch nicht erlebt. Das spiel ist taktisch auch nicht so anspruchsvoll das man dazu gezungen ist mit seinen Teamkollegen zu Komunizieren so das es auch eher nicht zu verbalen auseinandersetzungen mit anderen mitspielern kommt. auserdem ist in dem spiel zu viel Action als das man zeit für eine taktische übersicht hätte.

TL:DR This is a great turn based strategy game with a flavorful setting. You're a thief running a thieves guild and trying to own the town! Feels like a board game but utilises nifty computer things like Fog of War to enhance the experience.
In Antihero you play as a thieves guild master trying to own the town. There are multiple gamemodes which will make you think twice about how to play the game. It is a turn based strategy game with multiple paths to victory. Will you kill your way to the top? Perhaps you will blackmail officials to be the master of the town....or will you bribe your way to victory?
In Antihero you go about this in several ways with several characters. Your master thief is the character you will be giving most orders. He will scout for you and burgle houses/estates for currency. Your street urchins will infiltrate buildings to give you more influence (mechanic wise it will give you more currencies to spend). In the game you have gold to hire characters and lanterns for upgrades. There are 3 different upgrade paths for you to choose to customise your playstyle.
Is this game any good? Currently there isn't a giant campaign but the 11 missions or so do a terrific job of explaibning the various gameplay mechanics of maps and different characters. There are multiple master thief skins for you to choose in online mode and the 4 different map modes will keep you on your toes in online matches.
The developers seem really active on the steam disccusion forum and there is a roadmap that shows they are exploring the ideas of more maps, more unique map mechanics, a 2v2 or Free for all mode (as there is currently only 1v1 for PvP).
The game is great in its current state and it can only grow from here on out. My suggestion? Get it now! :)

Ok, first of all, I have 2 complaints. Firest, there is no gamepad support, and that is very odd for a game like this since it would be quite enjoyable as a couch game. Second, there is a level where you can become stuck and have to restart your save. I was fortunate enough to encounter this level early (you can do some levels in any order) and it can be avoided if you know what to look for or have a bit of forethought but it is still a problem.
Aside from that, the game is short, but memorable. What story it tells isn't unique in this age but that doesn't make it less charming and the graphics and music compliment each other very well. Having a stringed instrument accompany a jiggly world was a good idea.
The last level is very frustrating and intended to be completed in unconventional ways - as far as the rest of the game is concerned anyway - but it's not necessarily a flaw. it is nonetheless challenging in a different way than the rest of the game but the rest of the game makes up for it.
The levels themselves are varied and keep the experience interesting. My personal favorite level was the rain level. I also think all the levels, with the exception of the last one, are of acceptable length; I never felt like I was in one for too short a time to appreciate it or too long to become bored. This is definitely a game I can see myself replaying in the future.
It's definitely worth your time. If nothing else, at least buy the soundtrack. You can find it on Bandcamp, on Disasterpiece's page.

I've played all of the battlecrusier games for many years. After the learning curve, the game is very engaging. It is now mid 2016 and I have YET to find a game with this much depth and freedom.
This is a game where you have to think in order to suirvive.
With all the 4x space games out there now, and all the FPS out there now, this is the one game where you can create your own playstyle. You can go from taking over a starstation to invading a planetary defense system. You can steal enemy craft and even use their own air defense against them. You can be a sniper or have a crew of snipers watch your back as you lead a team of 40 marines into battle. Of course you have close air support knocking down everyting in the sky or any tanks on land that are a threat. And I'm just scratching the surface.
You captain a capital ship with up to 8 fighters at your disposal. These fighters increase their skills as they fly missions. Then of course there's shuttles that your AI can take to either drop off mining drones to mine valuable minerals on planets or sent them to tow abandoned or damaged ships including your cap ship. OR you can cripple an enemy ship and send your crew out to tow it to the nearest friendly starport for a nice reward and experience points.  And I'm just scratching the surface.
You can leave your command chair and hop in one of your fighters to get in the fray while your flight officer, combat officer, and other staff will continue to pilot the cap ship and keep her on course to her destination. You can have up to 7 AI fighters as your wingmen to help you attack several enemy targets. Or you can have your cap ship engage in multiple targets with powerful beam weapons or fire and forget missles to engage multiple hostile fighters. Or you can command a fleet of cap ships as a supreme commander to completely overwhelm any opposing forces. And I'm just scratching the surface.
You can have your cap ship orbit a planet and target a military base below. You can then lauch a space to surface missle to destroy sensitive installations or destroy an entire base... all while you're on the planet watching the mushroom plum from miles away. Or you can setup a strike teamy, just outside their early warning system, order a couple of fighters to 'soften' the targets. take out the early warning system, knock out their barracks and air to surface units... then come in with your best marines, tanks and ATV's take over the base... and of course, you can pilot any of the vehicles, or just sit on a distant hill and watch it all unfold through powerful binoculars. You can even take a reserve crew and have one of your shuttles drop them quietly behind enemy lines for a sneak attack while the ememy is focused on your main attack. And if you ever find yourself stranded on a planet or somewhere in space, you can always call for one of your shuttles to come and tow you back to your cap. OR if you're near a friendly base, 'borrow' one of their shuttles and fly back home. AND I'M JUST SCRATCHING THE SURFACE.
I didn't even mention the management, repair and upgrades of your vehicles, the leveling up of troops, dealing with intruders attempting to sabotage or steal your assets, trading, hiring.... the list goes on.
Now, if anyone can find a game, past present or future that is able to pull this off, I'll gladly pay top dollar to add it to my library. But I must warn you. You will be hard pressed to find such a Gem.

Penumbra: Overture is a solid survival horror from Frictional Games. Everyone knows frictional games from the massively successful and terrifying Amnesia: The dark desecent. While I have played some Amnesia I personally really enjoyed Penumbra. While the graphics are dated, and Amnesia is overall a better experience, Penumbra delivers scares and is a really good starting point for the studio. It's cheap and short, and it is 100& worth it, even if you are going back to it. It's a great game.

Penumbra: Overture represents the first of three episodes in the Penumbra series. The game offers an immersive horror atmosphere with interesting puzzles and a very strong storyline, which continues straight into the sequel Penumbra: Black Plague.
The only disadvantage of the game is the stiff and sometimes frustrating combat system. Therefore, stealth should be prioritized over combat.
The game has no Steam achievements.

First chapter of the Penumbra Series.
After a mysterious note from his passed away dad, containing clues. Philip (protagonist) sets out to Northern Greenland to find out more about this mystery and the past of his father. I like the fact that the game takes place in Greenland. Deep down in a long abandoned mine. A very unique choice for a location. Being a with snow covered uninhabited place makes a perfect set for a horror game.
The beginning of the game got me right on spot. The story started off rather sad but had me curious about what was next. Was rather vague at first but piece by piece it started to connect. Not to forget that this is part 1 and part 2 will give even more depth to the story.
Every level has a couple rooms that contain valuable information and/or objects that you require to venture further. In between these rooms there are dark halls and corridors with danger lurking around every corner.  Some levels have some very difficult puzzles that took me a while to figure out. It felt like an accomplishment each time I managed to solve a clue and make progress.
According to the developers, playing in the middle of the night with headphones will grant you a full immersive experience. I did as they say and it sucked me right in. Psychological horror at its finest. Not a lot of jumpscares to freak but mostly the atmosphere. And spiders. :) Have fun

This is one of the game I have the most mixed feeling about. Being one of the game I was most hyped for, having the main character being one of my favorite video-maker on the internet and one of the pioneer of modern video-format video game reviews, but does the qualities of the game finishes there?
First of, the gameplay. The nerd, being a player of old school games, had to have something resembling this in his own game. So, the gameplay is a mix of multiple games, but mainly from 2D shooters like Megaman. You're able to shoot (with the nerd) in eight directions and can jump. That's about it.
During the game, you can find other characters that can help you during your adventure, three of them being even playable. The first one is The Guitar Guy, who is the creator of AVGN's theme song. His weapon of choice is his trusty guitar that shoots waves of sounds that passes through wall, making some parts in some level easier to complete.
Next, we have Mike, James Rolfe's friend and the 'co-founder' of AVGN. His weapon is a lightsaber that only attacks at melee range, but is the fastest weapon. He also jumps higher than any character and has the power to see special blocks that can be destroyed with his saber to reveal items, like in Castlevania.
Finally, we have... Bullsh*t Man. For this review, I'll just call him BSM. BSM is a strange case, being a character from another sere run by
, James' website. His power is the 'sh*tdouken' where he throws a poop projectile that suffers from gravity, making some kind of arc. His main ability, however, is a fart jump, allowing to jump in mid-air to make platform parts easier.
For the gameplay, we also have collectibles. You can collect beer bottles for health, Nerd heads for lives and a Super Scope for a temporary power boost. You can also find the Nerd's friend that will give you tons of power ups while saying funny stuff. They are well hidden and make it worth to get off the main track to explore a bit.
To finish with the collectibles, we have the special powerups. There is the 'rock' which is... a rock. This is a reference to Friday the 13th on the NES. It's literally the worst weapon in the game. Next, we have the glitch goblin that freezes any enemies or obstacles to pass them easily. And we have Super Mecha Death Christ, which is a fully loaded Jesus that kills everything on the screen.
Sadly, even with the amount of collectibles you can get, the gameplay stops there. Sure, you have some sections where you ride either Santa Claus or a fire shark, but the game doesn't really change much. Not that it's a bad thing, but it might get stale for some players.
This game, however, has a different meaning for the word fun. "The best part of a journey is the travel, not the destination", this game make it so you wish there was no travel. You are a god (or too young to play) if you don't swear at least once during the game. This piece of software sh*t is made to make you suffer.
The difficulty, however, was expected. There is different difficulty option that changes the lives and beer bottle count, but even at easy, it can be hell to some players. Which this game is challenging and fun, the replayability is kind of non-existant. Sure, you unlock some new difficulties, but the experience doesn't change. Then, the art department, namely the graphics and sound. From the mouth of the developpers : "We tried to stick to some kind of 10-bit display. 8-bit didn't have enough details while 16-bit wasn't enough old school." This statement make it so that this game has a style of its own and it really shows how much you can do with it. The appearance of the game is really good and each level has a different theme, making the backgrounds vibrant and ever-changing.
The soundtrack is simply awesome. For a game about a swearing nerd, the music really sets the mood for some balls to the walls action. Some of those tracks could make it to my music player if I wouldn't be so lazy. The sound effects, for the most part, are pretty good. Each sounds are different enough so that it doesn't sound like recycled bleeps and bloops and it sounds like it could belong on an old console.
This game is obviously a gift to the fans of the nerd. It's a challenging game, but that's about it. Both for fans and non-fans, you shouldn't buy it at full price (15$) and wait for a promotion, which happens very often. Even then, I think that only fans could really enjoy this experience due to the sheer amount of easter eggs related to the f*cking nerd there is hidden in this.

When I look back on KOTOR now, I think classic Bioware mechanics, classic Star Wars story. The merging of two formulaic entities to create something that is certainly standard fair for Bioware nowadays and probably hammered to death in the Star Wars universe. That said, I think about the experience when this game actually came out and it's hard to deny that there is something special that happened here. From a plot and story perspective; A true Ode to Star Wars that encapsulates the feeling of the first movies (4,5 and 6) so truly that it's hard to fault them on the story being so familiar. If you've played Bioware games since, you will also be familiar with what's going on under the hood as it plays very similar to other Bioware RPG's (Jade Empire, Dragon Age, etc) but again when this beast first came out a lot of these features were new and still exciting and that would probably be considered a strength instead of an overused format.
All other things aside, this is a game created by Bioware when it was in my opinion, at it's best and what Bioware did best was write engaging stories with characters that were filled with genuine humanity. So even though the format might seem tired now, the story and the characters are truly one of a kind and if you're playing through for the first time I would bet that some of your favorite moments you experience in this game would likely become some of your fondest memories that you have in the Star Wars universe as a whole.

Overall whilst F.E.A.R 2 may not have been as good as the first game and its expansions, it did a great job of continuing the F.E.A.R storyline along.
Now let's take a look at the pros and cons!
Pros
1. Excellent combat and gore added to this game, i think the gore even tops the first game!
2. The campaign length was fairly decent and even managed to overtake the original game in length! (6-8 hours.) Whereas the first one could be clocked in 4-5 hours.
3. Included a nice change of scenery in comparrison to the old game, going from indoor factories, to an abandoned school and walking through deserted towns.
4. The game pieces together the characters only mentioned from the original game very well, well enough for you to have a clear understanding of where they slot in the story!
Cons
1. Combat wasn't as fun. The hand to hand combat was a bit brought down in my opinion and the enemies had better rag doll and physics, seeing as the orginal included a "John Woo fighting style."
2. The DLC or expansion F.E.A.R 2 Reborn was a bit disappointing. Whilst the story was pretty good it was no where near the same length as the original games expansions, or as fun for that matter.
3. The story wasnt as interesting as the original for obvious reasons... (No Pointman mentioned or Fettel)
4. In a lot of instances the textures from the original still seem superior to this game as the replicas look better and the textures are more smooth!
Overall whilst i may prefer the original, this game has still given me just as much fun as the original and makes a great addition to the series. For $15 you really can't go wrong with the purchase and it wont let you down!

This game is selling for $60 more than it is worth and then tacks on microtransactions to add insult to injury. Gearbox and/or 2K intended for this game to be F2P from the beginning and decided to charge players to help them beta-test it before mass release.
Battleborn has sold nearly 300,000 copies yet the average player count at any given time is only 300. The vast majority of people who bought the game no longer play it. I tried playing the newly released DLC last night and it took 15 minutes to find a single player and we were stuck with a 2 person team instead of the nominal 3 person team. The actual mission took 30 minutes to complete. If you buy this game, expect to spend ~33% of your play time in queues. I highly suspect that the reason that the new DLC uses only 3 players instead of 5 is to reduce queueing times.
I consider the core co-op gameplay solid but horribly diluted by the incessant drive to collect "loot" from containers scattered around the level in inconvenient nooks and cranny holes. If you want to achieve a high score and optimize your level progression, it's impossible to focus on simply killing the enemies and completing objectives. It's often incentivized for players to ignore objectives to the detriment of their team in pursuit of claiming loot for themselves and I have lost many games because of it. The items gained from the loot serve mainly to take up space in a horribly undersized inventory with less storage space than a 1970s floppy disk. Gearbox badly needs to examine loot systems in other games that do not distract from core gameplay and appropriately complement player progression.
Beware the few hangers-on who still play regularly and have developed Stockholm syndrome from Gearbox's abusive and exploitative practices. They brigade these reviews and fill them with misinformation. There are Reddit threads where they desperately coordinate to keep the positive review ratio above 50% to deceive others into sharing their misery.
It's a competitive marketplace and there are many similar games that offer a far superior value proposition than Battleborn.
Don't waste your money.

"I think I just solved the problem on my PC. First time I ran the game it went 60fps and then the 2nd time it started running like crap (3-5fps).
I ran process monitor and saw that the game was looking in the registry for calibration settings for every gamepad I ever connected to my PC (I have 2 I use regularly), and it was checking every 50 milliseconds. Obviously this is something that would have to be fixed with a patch but if you have every gamepad you've ever connected to your PC plugged in while you run the game, it should fix the lag.

When a developer artificially increases the difficulty in their physics-based puzzle game by skewing the physics and creating an unfair layout, then that is a bad developer and they should feel bad. It's a case of difficult for the sake of being difficult. Rather than implementing clever game design to benefit the experience, such as Portal or Antichamber, Colour Bind instead derives its difficulty from the fact that the physics are wonky and the levels work against you. This game requires precision and timing but, unlike Super Meat Boy or Dustforce, it fails to apply its mechanics in a rational way.
In the first five levels I experienced such frustration that I have no desire to return back to the game. If this was intentional, kudos. I won't be recommending it to any sane individual, though. The only thing going for this game is that Colour Bind has options to aid those who are colour blind. It took me far too long to realise the game wasn't actually titled Colour Blind...

This is a weak recommendation.
The concept is interesting and discovering the first clue that things weren't adding up (
) was a great feeling! The in-game ReadMe made me think I was building a case and submitting evidence to court. It turned out to be more of a narrative experience than a game with an achievable goal.
The story is intriguing and engaging, but it is gated by a very tedious mechanic - typing keywords into a search bar and sifting through videos, which are nonsensically capped at 5 results to artificially create a progression. There is no way to arrange a timeline, nor are transcripts available to you. I ended up taking 20,000 characters worth of notes to alleviate these shortcomings. You have no way of knowing how important information in a video is, before uncovering it, so by the end you'll be typing almost any word mentioned anywhere, in the hopes of discovering the last few clips. After hundreds of keywords I was able to uncover everything but 10 clips, which are near impossible to get without looking them up. Frustratingly they also contained zero relevant information. It took me about 8 hours to thoroughly exhaust the game. I see little replay value.
The narrative is carefully crafted and has some clever bits and twists, but I would have liked unlocking a chronological version in the end (if possible even with the detective's parts which are weirdly cut out through-out the game) to rewatch it all with my new knowledge to spot the tells and foreshadowing. I didn't like how the story took quite a few turns into the absurd and poetic, making it more of a fairy tale (as referenced even in-game) than a documentary. For what it's worth, it did make me think about the implications afterwards.
If you like stories and if you can pick this up cheaply (on sale or via a Humble bundle), you won't regret it, but don't expect too much. At full price I'd pass. It's a one-trick pony and not a flawless one.
