If you like Amnesia, this is the developer's first game and it lays the foundation for what came later. It shows in a lot of ways, but it is by no means a terrible game.
For starters, this is the only game Frictional Games has made that feature weapons and combat. This is a good thing, as Overture's combat is clunky and broken. Swinging requires you hold left click, pull to the left or right to prepare a swing, and then swing in the opposite direction to hit. The hit detection is very short-range and the swing area is small. However, the most commonly encountered enemies (dogs) are easy to kill as you can use boxes to stand out of reach of their attacks and simply stun-lock them with your weapon until they die.
The atmosphere is creepy, but all of the story is through notes and you never really encounter anybody else. Aside from some rare jump scares, there's nothing terribly scary because the combat AI is so laughably easy to manipulate. There are spiders in this game, which might make you freak out if you have arachnophobia.
Luckily, the game is puzzle-oriented and there are only a handful of areas full of enemies. Most of the puzzles are figuring out a process of doing something such as turning on a generator or determining a four-number door lock by translating it through Morse code. The Morse Code puzzle is probably the most difficult out of the bunch and merely requires a pen and paper (or notepad) to write down possible combinations; all other puzzles involve manipulating objects in your environment and following some written instructions.
The story ends on a cliffhanger in Overture, so it's recommended you ALSO play Black Plague, which plays much more like Amnesia: The Dark Descent and has much better story presentation. Requiem is technically the third game in the series but is only tangentially related to the other two.
So if you're looking for a horror game that involves atmosphere and puzzles rather than focusing on combat like Condemned or Resident Evil, this is a good place to start. It runs on just about anything at a respectable framerate.

Antihero exists because Civ 5 and being a♥♥♥♥♥♥is fun. The game takes place on a little game board. You have street tiles and building tiles. On every map theres a couple districts that you can steal from. At the beginning of the game only the thieves guild and the street in front of it is explored. The main character can use their moves to explore streets or buildings. When you steal from a building in a hidden district the district building is revealed. The district buildings can give you special buffs or collect resources after you steal from them. To get these buffs and resources you need to send street urchins to infiltrate the building. Along with street urchins you can also build gangs, thugs, assassins, and other units to control as much of the map as you can while denying resources to enemies. There are two resources. Money and Lamps. Lamps are used to buy upgrades to get new units and abilities. Money is used to buy units. There are several assassination targets around the map as well. Along with their little guard guys they make up the npc faction in the game. If you kill any of the targets you get a victory point. You can also get blackmail points from certain buildings and you can buy bribes with lamps. If you get all the victory points before your opponent, you win. There are a couple game modes with different rulesets but thats the basic gist. The ai is pretty smart and is able to deny you resources and collect resources pretty well. It also thinks a couple steps ahead and tries to predict your moves. The ai faction with the assassination targets is pretty smart as well. As far as I can see they try to troll you by blocking passages and teleporting the target around. This is either a smart ai or i'm just unlucky. As for multiplayer capabilities you have a local hotseat and two online multiplayer modes. Asynchronous multiplayer and a live match. The hotseat mode isn't all that great. Since my friend could see what I was doing he didn't have to scout me to check. It was like stream ghosting but without the stream. The game is pretty fun for a couple of hours and definitely worth 15 bucks. The depth is a bit of an issue though since theres not that many units and upgrades. But im sure in high level play it's all about the mindgames instead of all about the units. The game seemed to miss that "one more turn" effect that Civ games have because the games are too short. This made me get kinda worn out after a couple levels because I got bored of setting up the same starting base over and over again.

The campaign serves as a tutorial, followed by a series of increasingly unfair scenarios, involving more victory conditions for you and/or better starting conditions for the opponent. For skirmish games against the AI or online play (featuring both real-time and asynchronous games), only a handful of map layouts are available, but specific business locations are randomized for more replay value. The goal is to earn a specific number of victory points, earned by blackmailing churches, bribing guilds (both of which simply involve having the maximum number of units inside), or assassinating neutral characters (plus other alternative methods depending on the map). There are two resources in the game: gold, earned from buildings and burglary, is used to purchase units, while lanterns (from different buildings) are used to purchase technology upgrades. Units include the master thief, used to scout and burgle houses, the urchin to infiltrate businesses, the thug to block paths, the gang to attack enemies, the saboteur to plant traps on buildings, the assassin to instantly kill any unit, and the truant officer to evict all urchins in an enemy building. There are multiple strategies you can employ towards victory, and ways to counter each plan as well. The AI is generally a good player (which makes the concessions it's granted in the campaign unnecessary), choosing a varied strategy each game. Antihero is an approachable turn-based strategy game with a unique setting and compelling gameplay mechanics.

I'll let you in on a little secret: my favourite game is Metroid Prime. Prime 2 and 3 probably rank second and third respectively, but before I get longwinded: I love Metroid games.
As such I also have the poor habit of buying Super Metroid every time Nintendo rehashes it just to get some more of that sweet exploration action. Consequentially, I also love the Castlevania series...basically for being Metroid. Enter Guacamelee, an indie game that basically is Metroidvania, but dipped in taco sauce and smothered in chili's. Along the way he learns new moves from peculiar looking statues and supplexes baddies into the ground to save the woman he, supposedly, loves. An interesting turn-based digital board game with a really nice aesthetic. You play as a leader of a thieves' guild, hiring street urchins, gangs and thugs, and even assassins to explore, burgle and take over the Victorian themed city.
Pros:
+Campaign - although not very long there is a story-driven campaign to help you learn the game. The story is not particularly ground breaking but the various scenarios you face on each map provide interesting venues to explore your strategies. On one map part of your victory conditions is to eliminate three gangs a la Gangs of New York. On another you will be trying to infiltrate and protect a ship carrying precious cargo, in order to have your urchins carry the goods back to your hideout.
+AI - the AI seems to be pretty decent, pursuing victory conditions and trying to double cross you whenever possible. You need to play efficiently and agressively pursue the victory conditions yourself if you want to stand a chance.
+Local and Online Multiplayer - you can play against humain opponents both online and via Hot Seat, with customizable rulesets.
Replayability - while the maps seem to be premade layouts the districts containing building are randomized each game. This means even if you are playing the same map twice you will find buildings and enemies in different places each time (this includes the campaign missions). THere are also 3 upgrade trees, allowing for different approach.
Aesthetics - the map and characters are nicely drawn and animated. There are clear inspirations from other media, like the criminal gang being lead by a character resembling Daniel Day-Lewis' from Gangs of New York, or the assassin looking similar to Evie Frye from Assasin's Creed: Syndicate.
Neutral:
+/-Music - the soundtrack fits the setting and does an OK jub, but is otherwise unremarkable. I expect most people would get bored by it sonner than later and would switch to something else.
+/-Game modes - currently it seems the only game mode is 1v1. It is designed very well for this mode and it's difficult to say whether other ones would be equally enjoyable. If you are however looking for a game with groups of friends there is currently no mode for that.
Cons:
-UI While mostly clear and understandable there are some minor issues. Since the map is being viewed in an isometric view, including the characters I've had several moments where it was difficult to select the character/building I wanted to interact with. I would also appreciate it if it showed what the effects of interacting with buildings are while hovering over them. Some of the icons are also a bit larger than necessary.
Summary: A pretty solid board game that is fun in its current state, with some minor issues that could get ironed out and good base for future expansion. Definitely recommended if you are a fan of the genre.

Guacamelee! Is based on four concepts:
- a Metroid-vania style of gameplay
- a semi-complicated fighting system
- luchadores portrayed in a cartoonish way
- jokes based on modern internet popculture
It seems that there is pretty much nothing you could dislike. Indeed the first half of the game was very enjoyable for me. Some dialogs are written really clever, and the gameplay itself is enough to keep you playing.
But then it all falls in to pieces. The more powers you unlock the more difficult it is to play on a computer keyboard. Soon it becomes unplayable and confusing... and this is the part when someone tells me I should use a gamepad (like the authors told me on the beginning of the game). Well I tried... I have three gamepads and none of them worked... oooohhhh.... it needs an XBOX controller?
So now I should pay because the authors are xbox fanboys or because they sold their souls to MS? Not a chance.
Releasing this game on a PC (an also Linux for god's sake!) is a mockery.
The keyboard and mouse are basic PC controllers , so a game released on WINDOWS/MAC/LINUX should be designed to work with them, or at least allow ANY gamepad to work with it on all operating systems it is available for (I use Linux all the time, and never once had a problem with any of my gamepads in a game that allowed them).
There is also something else, that happens after the first half of the game – all the creativity of the authors just vanish (and the jokes from the first half began to stop being funny in the context also):
„Erm... I don't know how to make this game actually, so... hmm... let's make it incredibly difficult, and fill it with irritating enemies, internet memes redrawn to look mexican and references to other games!”
Give me a break...
This is unfortunately a trend in modern indie games .
„Don't have an idea to make the gameplay interesting? Make it freakishly difficult.”
„Don't have an interesting story? Make it a parody. A parody with a very difficult gameplay!”
„We don't know how to balance the gameplay? Let's give the player every ability we can think of! And make her/him use them simultaneously during a very difficult gameplay!”
I bet at some point of the development, the creators of games like that think they are smart, and creative. Throwing every idea for a gameplay element in to the final product, redrawing jokes made by others and making obvious references to other games...
P.S.
Of course the level of difficulty is not only to be blamed on the controller. The game is literally unfair. Exactly like playing a badly designed NES game. UNFAIR. The projectiles thrown by enemies go right through every element of the environment, every enemy and stop only at the player. Every enemy attack is impossible to block and usually it has priority over your attack even if it is a combo, or a special move. Also, some actions work in some cases, and don't work in other (in which logic tells you, they should). The controls feel very awkward generaly, and most actions are hard to trigger.

One of the types of game that is missing on Steam in a big way, is asynchronous multiplayer games. These are the games that you can play a turn, and then move on with your day, knowing that eventually your opponent will play theirs and you can come back to it later.
Antihero is a perfect example of one of those kinds of games and it does a very good job of presenting a solid lobby system for matches. While the option exists to play a synchronous real time game as well, the asynchronousity is really where the game stands out.
This is a solid strategy game, with enough options that you're planning out the future, but not enough to be overwhelming to strategy novices. A perfect entry game (if you're just starting into strategy), you'll be charmed by the well-done graphics, the theme, and the play.
To put the finishing touch on the game, is a campaign that's long enough to show you how to do most  things, without sticking around too long and boring you. The game is designed as a multiplayer game, but you can tell that this campaign has been given a lot of love as well.
If you want to just play the single player campaign, I'd say that there's still enough content at this price point to jump on the wagon. If you think you might dip your toe in the multiplayer scene as well, it's a no-brainer. Also, if you're looking for a multiplayer game with no toxicity, then this is it, because other than the actual gameplay, there is no interaction with the other people that you're playing with.

This one is 1 vs 1 either in campaign, online or local hot-seat. I imagine playing against other human players would be quite fun. I do wish there was more than 1 vs 1 though, I would have liked this game as a 4 person game I think a bit more than 1 vs 1, but it is fun.
In this game the maps are all slightly different and affect the way you play with different win conditions. It's a neat idea.
One thing that I found to be questionable is possibly the A.I.
I have no idea why but I can't get past the 3rd campaign level, nor can I beat any skirmish games vs the computer. I am not sure if the A.I. player is extremely overpowered but they definitely seem to be. No matter what I do the computer player beats the crap out of me and counters every strategy I use. Nothing I do seems to work in my favor.
Either it's a way too difficult A.I. player or the game does not explain the how or why well enough in regards to what the player is supposed to be doing. I have no idea what I'm doing that's not working. Nothing I do seems to be good enough to defeat the computer player either on normal or easy.
On top of that, the game has a "fog of war" type of thing. You have to scout certain areas in order to reveal whats under them. That's fine, except that all of your opponents moves are essentially hidden due to this, making it even harder to tell what I am doing wrong. I also am suspicious that the computer character was cheating in campaign level 3 but because I am not able to see what they are doing I can't confirm or deny, but it definitely feels that way.
Obviously these games are most fun when played against other humans and that's where I expect the most fun to come from with this title. Again though, it can be quite frustrating because it's very hard to tell what you are doing wrong when you lose and the fact that you can't really see what your opponent is doing makes you question the fairness of it all. Like I said before, I'm convinced that the computer player cheats in campaign level 3 but I don't know for certain because I can't see what they are doing most of the time.
First Impressions Gameplay Video
Would I recommend this? I want to say yes, but I think I have to be more specific.
If you want this to play the campaign and skirmishes against the computer, I would have to say no.
If you want this to play specifically against other human players or your friends either online or local hot-set style, I would say yes - BUT - only after checking out some sort of tutorial videos. Interesting concept but boring and predictable plot twist.
In Her Story you have access to the partial records of what happens to be the interrogation of a woman who might or might not have commited a crime. The player types keywords to navigate those videos and reconstruct the narrative of what happened.
Her Story is one of those games that is more of an interactive experience than a game, although the classic line is getting blurrier and blurrier. Caveat Emptor.

It was tough to come to a decision as to whether or not I would recommend Her Story. The game is very short (100% in just over four hours) and offers no replay value. With that in mind, the four hours of content would have to provide something of very high quality to bring me to recommend the game to others.
After the initial hour or two of playing, I was loving it. The idea is different from anything I've ever played, and the acting/story/music all come together nicely. I steadily uncovered interesting plot points and twists in the story which were exciting to find due to the way you progress.
Unfortunately, although you do have a few flash points of excitement and interest, there is no real conclusion or end game. It feels more like a proof of concept, waiting for someone to extend on the idea and provide more of a finished product. While at the start the discoveries you make are down to your intuition and insight, the last third or so ended up in me resorting to complete guesswork, which made it repetitive when trying to find more information and not very rewarding when I did.
There is no real end. It's very much left up to the player to interpret things and as much as don't mind a certain degree of openness in terms of endings, I felt like there had to be something more. I enjoy open-ended games, but usually, these at least provide a beginning and an end, with everything in-between up to the player. Due to the random nature of Her Story, you can find the most interesting plot points in the first 5 minutes and then be left with many clips that don't provide anything new for the story throughout the remainder of your play time.
It's a real shame because I've been wanting to check this game out since the first time I heard about it. Fantastic concept and the story is interesting, but the execution just falls short. I'd say if you see it as part of a bundle then it's worth having a look at, mainly due to the unique approach. I cannot recommend Her Story at any kind of regular price, four hours of gameplay just isn't enough to justify the price unless the experience provides something exceptional.

An underrated indie gem. Derek Smart deserves credit for sticking to his guns, and sticking with this game. Universal Combat isn't pretty, easy or intuitive. But it's still an unmatched capital ship simulator with an unforgiving '90s-style attitude.
This game will not hold your hand (tip: read the manual) or tuck you into bed at night. It's definitely not for everybody. It's about outer space and it wants to kill you. It's a sandbox with the complexity of hardcore naval sims such as Silent Hunter.
It's about logistics, space battles, crew management, reactor meltdowns and nuking cities from orbit. You will be boarded, ransacked and the perpetrators will escape in a stolen shuttlecraft.
Your ship will be set adrift while on fire.
I didn't discover this game until recently. I've known about Smart since the early 2000s, but dismissed him and didn't give him a chance. He was a joke, a crank, his games were bad. That's what I thought, but in reality I didn't understand him.
Now I do ... I think.
Smart is foremost an engineer, as this game reflects an engineer's mindset. It's about spaceships, but it's really about complex systems, taking things apart and figuring out how they work. This has its downsides: Engineers are not celebrated for their empathy and they don't make for great artists.
But engineers do make great systems.

Her Story is a mystery game where you go through short video clips and take keywords from those clips to search and find new clips. You can only see the top 5 results from any search, so you have to wade through the clips and piece the stories together to figure out what the next keyword is. The clips are done in the style of police interviews, with the overarching goal being to try to find out who committed a murder. Along the way you learn the intricacies of the woman being interviewed. To top it off, the game has a great ending that gives you more insight into what was going on.
Onto the value of the game. The game is $6 USD and took me about 2 hours to complete. I dislike judging a game just by how long it takes, but that is pretty short. If the game looks interesting to you I'd say it's worth it at full price, and if not just wait for a sale. Also keep an eye on the Humble Bundle store, as the game goes on sale quite frequently on there.
If you plan to play this game do yourself a favor and don't look up any gameplay. The less you know going into it the more you're enjoy it.

Possibly the best choose-your-own adventure game I've ever played.
Lots of text and static art, but its all really good text and art. In "combat" there are very simple animations and each character has their own sounds they make, most of them really funny and/or cute. But that's about as far as it goes, there's a lotta reading to be done. Not as much as say Sunless Sea, or really a large number of other similar games, but still a lot if you don't often do this kinda thing.
The mood-combat mechanic is funny, interesting, and different approaches often yield different outcomes. Other times, they simply flavor the same outcome, but if you can get into a game like this then that's really just as good as dsitinctly different outcomes.
It gets compared to FTL apparently, I KINDA see it but ehhhhh honestly I think its better not to have such a pre-conceived notion about a game like this before playing it, since so much of the game is about how YOU play it; it does share some DNA with FTL, but they're more like distant cousins than brother and sister. For example, if you get totally destroyed in an encounter, you don't necessarily lose the game, you lose what is essentially a life, which is by far your most limited resource (and I call it a resource because it can be traded as though its a real thing for other things in some encounters).  Sometimes your capacity for supplies - essentially your "fuel" - imposes a really harsh limitation on you, but there are ways of dealing with that, particularly after finishing a couple expeditions.
Also, as an aside, I love Anna. I want to marry her, and after I kiss the bride, I want her to let out that awesome mad scientist laugh <3 <3 <3 (she's also incredibly useful in almost any group). Each character, while some abilities are shared, are unique in fun ways and often a specific character's mere presence will open up unique options (usually to bypass what amount to skill checks in this game).
I love it.
Fun and different, recommended.

Defeated an Abbey full of Nuns by seducing them with an Argentinian bombshell.
Hows that for an attention grabbing headline? Of course a sword swinging Greek 'Michonne' and an unhinged scientist obsessed with electricity helped.
Renowned Explorers is what would happen if you filmed the next Indiana Jones movie with a cartoon effect camera and then made a video game based off that movie using FTL, (Faster then light) Austin Powers and X-Com as inspiration.
One minute you will be befriending Sheep, launching daring hostage rescue missions in the bowels of a pirate ship, fighting ghosts, cracking safes in a tree house or writing research papers.
And the next you will be trying to convince a group of villages that you came to their island riding a giant flying fish and because you are so awesome they should give you all their treasure and food.
Just like in just about every game, ever, there are times where your expedition of explorers will be attacked by slavering wolves, the horror!
How do you deal with these brutes? Well shooting, stabbing, punching, laser beams and odd chemical concoctions do the trick. As does throwing the canines a party, hurling insults about how they smell like fish or the age old art of seduction. All valid, depending on the skills and capabilities of your party.
The game is outrageous, fun, challenging, fresh and just like X-com, sometimes 95% chances just aren't good enough.
There is a huge amount of depth and customisation in how you approach the game, with the sole aim of first earning more fame than a certain Frenchman, and then trying to beat your previous scores and find new treasures!
Do I recommend it? Indeed I do, it's worth grabbing even when not on sale.

This game is actually incredible. Reus, the previous game from the same developers, was one of my favourites despite finding god games in general to be hit and miss. I loved the intricate systems of Reus, with a ton of different resources, strategy, depth and complexity, because it was handled in an intuitive way through tooltips and fun tutorials that never dragged the game to a screeching halt. Unlike some strategy games where you have no idea what resources go where to build whatever while advisors badger you incessantly, Reus gave you the notes and tips you needed to understand every system, but never shoved it into your face. Really, it was the pinnacle god game for me.
RE:IS is like Reus, but instead of being a perfect game in a so-so genre for me, it's a perfect game that's also a mashup of my favourite mechanics, genres and themes. It's like this game was tailor made for me.
Renowned Explorers: International Society is sort of a roguelike, but there's a lot more to it. It has the overland mechanics of a good old fashioned D&D hexcrawl, the battle systems and trinities of a Fire Emblem, random written events and challenges a la Eighty Days or Tales of the Arabian Nights (the best board game ever), Civ-like research trees, time management, RPG loot. Throw in a steampunky Indiana Jones aesthetic, and I'm so very very sold. It's so good.
Better yet, like Reus there are a ton of different systems. A elemental trinity of physical, diplomatic and taunting attacks. Status effects based on how cranky or cocky you are. Twenty unique characters to pull from. Tons and tons of traits and subtraits. A dozen tokens and currencies, each with a different purpose.
But also like Reus, the intricate web of synergy is completely demystified by the tooltops and the UI. Forget what a Discovery token does? Highlight over it, and it will break down the numbers based on your current stats and upgrades. Need a referesher on status effects in battle? Hover over the icon and get informed. Forget what to do between expeditions? The concise in game manual is only a click away. Combined with tutorials that a) don't treat you like a moron and b) are done within five minutes, RE:IS strikes the perfect balance between providing information and beating you over the head with it.
One great example is the way unlocks are done. In Sunless Sea, which is a fairly similar texty roguelike mashup I quite enjoy, you get thrown in the deep end with a ton of traits and unlocks and places to go and stats to pick from before you have any idea what they do. RE:IS purposely keeps your pool of captains small; every other character is unlocked, but only as a secondary assistant. They explain abilities, they suggest synergies, they outline strategies your captain excel at. But as you play, you get a better grasp on the rules, and your most used secondary characters are soon unlocked as new captains complete with their own traits and strategies.
And despite all the tooltips and synergy help, it's still a challenge. I've yet to win on the classic difficulty, but it's never felt unfair when I've died. There are setbacks from dice rolls, sure, but I'm always in control and they always give me the odds, so it's up to me to build a better team and make better investments next time. And a complete game is five expeditions, which only takes two or three hours, so it's closer to a short game of Civ than, say, a long haul XCOM campaign.
One last point: when rolling percentile chances, your characters spin a giant Price is Right wheel. I don't know why I find this so deeply satisfying, but it blows the hell out of simulated dice rolls.

If the Star Wars Galaxy represented the old canon, the EU would be the Outer Rim. Unstable, conflicting, weird and somehow able to be amazing or downright terrible at times, the Old EU always has been a "Wild West", Outer-Rim of sorts where content quality was in the hands of outside contributors, many of them with no other reason than to make a few quick credits by flashing some yellow crawl text and John Williams fanfare before the drivel that they push out.
bringing law and order to the far reaches of the galaxy with its crack team of licensing and merchandising agents, reining back in the Star Wars creative universe with a heavily copyrighted iron fist. Now, with the scum of the galaxy flushed out of the airlock, and the original trilogy hoisted again upon a pedestal, supported by the raging hard nerdboners of millions of OT fanboys, we have peace.
Knights of The old Republic, along with other works such as The Zahn trilogy felt like unessecary casualties of an overzealous purge by Disney. Although many absolute stinkers deserved to be booted from the canon, some of them were legitimately worthy of taking on the Star Wars name as extensions of the stories told in the movies.
motifs and plot points that repeat and echo throughout the whole saga. It's like poetry, y'know. They rhyme. KOTOR is no stranger to that. On the surface, its story is the story of Star Wars, of a chosen one destined to bring balance to the force, defeat the baddies, get the girl and save the day!
Having never played any of Bioware's older rpgs, I found the gameplay to be really dated which lessens the fun somewhat. Case in point, the only direct player actions in combat are basically selecting a target and queuing up your attack orders or force powers, everything else being a dice roll. The user interface is clunky, with too much data hidden behind too many buttons and menu screens that draws the player away from the game.
However, I cannot fault the game for simply being old, spoiled as I have by more polished and refined mechanics from newer titles.
Being a Bioware RPG, you start from a central hub, first a planet, later your starship, where you can select your party and choose to travel to different locations. You can pursue the main story by visiting any number of different planets, all of them giving off the distinct feeling of a unique place in the Star Wars galaxy. The characters that you meet along the way, your party members, all have a story to tell, and the choices you make reflect who you truly are.
the concept of discovering who you are, and what you are versus what you want to be. Every quest decision and interaction with other characters affects not only their perception and relationship with you, but also your own morality. The game employs a meter that starts you off in the middle and every decision you make skews you towards either the light or the dark side. I absolutely love the option of either being a goody-two-lightsabers light side jedi or being a ruthless,
geful Dark Lord.
does it still make sense to get KOTOR today? It's a given that its dated combat, graphics and gameplay cannot hold a candle to later RPGS like The Witcher or even Bioware's own Mass Effect series. However, if you are an avid fan of Star Wars, I would definitely say yes, just for the experience of being a Jedi or Sith, choosing the Light side or the Dark, in hands-down the best story experience ever in a Star Wars game.
Which makes it in my eyes the second-best Star Wars game of all time.

Fantastic game, especially when considering it is nearly a decade old. I had played the first two games long ago and while I always loved the concept of the hitman series, there always seemed to be flaws in the series. Hitman: Blood Money more than the others I have played seems to come closer to the concept of the perfect assassination puzzle game. This is a true open level concept with a myriad ways to accomplish your end goal, a compelling ranking system which names you according to playing style and rewards your success with a clever pay structure built for replay. Add to this the many easter eggs and special scenes and Hitman: BM is a wonderful experience. There are a few flaws in this gem (saving/loading is lousy and the character models are dated) but the overall experience makes this game well worth a play through. 8/10
Pros:
- Open level concept allows for many play-throughs and different play-styles
- Level Design is second to none... even the weaker levels are well thought out and fun to play through
- Reward/Newsprint system is fantastic motivator
- Weapons are diverse and allow for a variety of kills
- Puzzles within each level are fun and challenging
- In-level jokes and hidden references are abundant
- Final level (Requieum) is one of the better endings I've ever played
Cons:
- Save/Load system is awful (the developers tried to enhance difficulty by limiting saves but it just doesn't add to the experience)
- Controls are wonky and stiff compared to newer games (translates to a steeper learning curve)
- Some of the gaurd response zones/pathing is a little too black and white which can, at times, hurt the immersion (i.e. Stand here and you are fine, but two feet to the left will cause a gaurd to shoot you)
- Some of the weaker levels are towards the end of the game so there is less of a build-up then would have been preferred
- Character models and graphics optimization shows the games age (though not as bad as you would expect)

AVGN has been apart of internet culture for quite some time now, so it was a no brainer that the nerd would finally get his own game.
The AVGN is notorious for playing bad games and being rather crude while presenting such games. What I find interesting about the AVGN game is that they actually incorporated these game design flaws and made them into something great. From impossible jumps to unfair design, AVGN Adventures takes these monstrosities of game design and turns it into something fresh, exciting and just fun.
The difficulty on this one is worthy of the title "NES Hard" and the actual game itself plays like a mixture between the original classic Mega Man games and Contra. The music is reminiscient of nostalgic 80s chip tune and brings gamers back to a time where the basics were all you needed. The sprite art is beautifully built from the ground up with some clear inspiration from other titles, again, such as Mega Man.
Many people seem to say that this game has hardly any replay value which I would like to say is complete bogus. There are three different characters to play as in AVGNA, two of which need to be unlocked by finding them hidden throughout the 8 different stages (All based on episodes of the AVGN.) Also, the game can be played in different difficulty settings, allowing for more than one gameplay experience. A true completionist will want to not only beat this game in more than one way, but master AVGNA, much like those of retro gaming tastes do.
The in game dialogue (in text boxes) is crude, filthy, disgusting, and downright hilarious. AVGNA incorporates many of the Nerds' iconic quotes as well as invent new terms that are definetly NSFW.
Overall, this game is definetly worth purchasing and playing through. The difficulty is extreme at times and I would recommend a controller rather than a keyboard. Those with a taste for retro gaming will find this a masterpiece. Even, if you're not into retro gaming, pick this one up when it goes on sale. You won't regret it.

He's gonna take you back to the past...
I'm a huge fan of online critics like the Angry Video Game Nerd, informing many online of the worst games from back in the day, and from the day I saw this game for the first time I was so excited for it.
After weeks upon weeks of waiting, I finally got the game, I played it, and it♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ME OFF!
I'm half-kidding; the graphics are nice, the music is epic, and it can be satisfyingly fun... but it's not perfect.
I have a few big gripes about this game;
1. The Difficulty: I'm a young gamer, so I haven't played on an actual NES or gotten far in it's harder-than-diamond library. But come ooon! There are so many insta-death obstacles like those friggin' Death Blocks and frustrating stages that require pitch-perfect accuracy when jumping. A majority of the cause is probably...
2. The Keyboard Controls: WHAT HAPPENED GUYS? Z and X shoot and jump, and the Arrow keys move, which is pretty crappy; you can rebind them, though.. "But the developer designed it to use a controller!" The people of Steam will say. Well, I can verify that once I got used to the controls on an old third-party controller that I had it was a bit easier, I ask this... WHY PUT IT ON PC IF YOU'RE BEST LUCK IS USING A CONTROLLER?! Why put the game on a platform that's controller isn't the best to use? They should've just put it on Xbox if they were going with the controller thing... or made the keyboard controls bearable.
Those are my biggest complaints, but I found some other things that could've been improved; for a game based on such a funny guy, where's the humor of the game? Most of the humor comes from references to the show and cameos from multiple online comedians, like Egoraptor or Brentalfloss. Some make sense, but others really don't. They had a great opportunity to make some new jokes, but it just falls flat.
Lastly, the enemies are bland; they're typical horizontal/flying enemies reskinned for each stage. The best example of this is the generic vertically-moving fireballs, just changed to match the level's theme with nothing new.
Overall, if you're into games that kick you in the balls and you love the Nerd's show, it's the game for you. If you're just looking for a fair platformer that recalls the glory days and you don't really watch the show or aren't too into it, I don't recommend it.
I give it a 7/10; it's solid, but it could've been a LOT more.
If you a second opinion on it, I recommend checking out James' review of it and some other games based upon his character of the Nerd on YouTube.

Well…I usually don’t bother writing Steam reviews as I often trust in the overall consensus of those that have already done so (what difference would my 2 cents make?).
However this is probably the first time I have found myself in a situation where a game I hold in high regard is otherwise very divided in opinion.
I suppose this is the very essence of what it is to be a “niche” game so the first thing I should probably say in this review is that “Universal Combat” (UC) is not for everyone.
You will come out of it either loving it or hating it, but very unlikely anything in between.
Now much has been said about the need to read the manual before playing and I can appreciate that many gamers nowadays (particularly the younger generation) would consider this requirement (at best) rather quaint in 2015.
Indeed with there being so many free games and demos right there at your fingertips, I can see how the investment of time would be a deal breaker for some.
As such the best I can do is tell you what 3 aspects of UC appeal to me the most, and should you be intrigued, perhaps you might be willing to preserver though the trials of learning how to play it.
* Scale:
The 3D environments for both space and planet side are mind-bogglingly vast and I am not aware of any other space sim that can match it (at least outside of an MMO).
Capital ships dwarf the size of their occupants (you’ll notice this if you decided to go on a space walk outside your ship) and these ships in turn are tiny compared to the celestial scale of the planets & moons within this universe.
If find that UC conveys the enormity of space exceptionally well.
It is a very humbling experience to fly to a plant and watch as it fills up the entirety of the view screen.
*Planetary landings:
Like the space environment, the planet surface is massive (it takes 5 hours in real time to fly around the Earth in a shuttle) and they all have a day/night cycle (some even have weather effects).
But what really sets this apart from every other space sim I’ve known is that it lets you land on any moon or planet you come across and explore it in first person (even a gas giant if you don’t mind dying).
Any on top of that you can land anywhere you like on the planet’s surface rather than being restricted to predefined zones.
However I will admit that the price for this vastness is a great deal of emptiness as the areas outside the city & base zones are pretty much uninhabited.
Nevertheless I feel that the procedural generation works well mixing up the terrain features so it’s not like the surface is uniform and everywhere looks the same (the exception of course being barren moonscapes which are supposed to look samey).
* A.I
I’m the kind of guy that is fascinated by A.I in gaming.
I find it as much fun observing what an A.I does in various situations as I do playing the game.
And Universal Combat has a pretty interesting A.I to observe.
Even as you go about your business in the game there is a hell of a lot going on behind the scenes.
Trade ships are randomly generated which proceed to each star station along a route buying & selling goods. This will affect the inventory a station has to sell as well as the economy in general.
Next you have raiders which are also randomly generated.
They will try to attack the aforementioned trade ships and thus their success/failure also affects inventory & economy of the stations.
You have :
- Criminals being generated, with police being generated to pursue them.
- Diplomats appearing and assassins dispatched to attack them.
- Colonists & workers headed to uninhabited planets to build cities
- Paramedics looking for the distress signals
And of course rival military forces clashing in as chance encounters or as retaliation for some other transgression for which the player never witnessed.
While you're docked in a station getting repairs a whole dammed war could be going on outside and given enough time nations that were allies in the beginning of the game can sometimes become enemies just by one incident that the player may have nothing to do with.
*Overall:
To me Universal Combat is something very special: A vast simulation experiment with a game thrown in.
I have been watching this game’s predecessor (the Battlecruiser series) since 1998 and in all that time I have seen nothing which comes close to it in terms of scope & scale.
UC is a vast improvement on the old Battlecruiser series in every conceivable way and yet here it is being offered for FREE!?...Unbelievable.
However as I said before it is not for everyone.

From the beta, Nvizzio and Atari have definitely improved features and I can confidently say that this is an addictive Rollercoaster Tycoon game, albeit glitchy, rough around the edges, and needing a few improvements. The positives:

- Early Access. Atari/Nvizzio can see what we like, dislike, and improve it before final release.
- Coaster builder is great fun, many improvements have been made since the beta.
- The themes provided in-game are nice; I've enjoyed creating different "zones" in my park. Currently working on a Wild Western area as I type this.
- Ride the rides, returning from RCT3.
- Large variety of decorative pieces for the park, and 3 different maps.
The negatives for me consist of:

Because of this, I can't recommend the game. Not at full price and not as the interesting indie title I thought it was going in.

Overture and Black Plague are two halves of the same game.  Overture is part 1, Black Plague is part 2.  The second part is a direct continuation and has the same game mechanics/gameplay (except a few minor differences) so this review is for both games.
First of all I rate this 9/10.  Part 1 has terrible combat and that's the only reason it's not a 10/10.  Luckily the devs seemed to realize how bad the combat was and completely axed it in part 2, so like Amnesia you must run from or outwit monsters instead of engaging them.
Overture is primarily a puzzle solver.  It's not too scary, but it does have a creepy atmosphere.  What I love about Frictional Games is that their puzzles are very sensible, although there were a few here that had me really confused.  Part of the problem is that you have to destroy your environment sometimes, but there's no indication which objects are destructble and which aren't- and sometimes you have monsters on your heels, so it's hard to look around and search the environment to figure out what to do before you die.
Black Plague is where the game starts to get really interesting.  It has an AMAZING story, and in addition to good puzzles (less environment destroying in this one) the setting is truly horrific.  Amnesia didn't scare me, but this game did.  It doesn't even use cheap pop-ups, (well a few) instead relying on music/sounds and unsettling atmosphere.  Psychological horror at its finest.
The story is intensely engaging.  You will care about the friends/family the protagonist (Phillip) encounters in his journey.  There are many sad moments.  But the true meat of the plot lies in an ancient mystery you will slowly unravel as you discover the many notes, books, and strange artifacts strewn throughout the mining/research facility.  The ending is satisfying in that it gives you the answers you seek and doesn't leave you hanging, although I was somewhat disapointed that you appear to be presented with a choice, yet your character can only make one in the end.

Penumbra: Overture, while originally a mere expansion of a tech demo by Frictional Games, does a decent job of standing as a full-fledged game. While not quite on par with Frictional's later and more famous effort, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, Penumbra fires off a trilogy that's intriguing in its own right, and just as atmospheric.
Starting out in a cabin amidst a frozen waste, you're presented with little motivation beyond trying to uncover the fate of your presumably dead father. After stumbling your way through a howling blizzard, you clamber down a mysterious hatch and find yourself in an extensive cave system and facility that leaves a lot of questions to be answered. It's not long before you realize there may be someone, or something, down there with you that doesn't want you to find those answers.
As Frictional tends to do with their games, the horror in Penumbra: Overture takes the form more of a looming dread than anything particularly scary. Your powerlessness is repeatedly reinforced, as even something as small as one of the wild dogs somehow roaming the underground can end your day. Using your wits, stealth, and remnants left by those inhabiting the caves before your arrival, most of Penumbra relies on solving puzzles to progress. As you get further in, more and more notes and instructions left behind push you even deeper, eventually toward something no one should have known was below.
Visually, Penumbra definitely shows its age, but things look cave-y enough in the caves and lab-y enough in the occasional lab that you get the idea, and you're unlikely to get lost just because of how things look. Interaction with items feels a bit clumsy, as lifting things just makes them hover in front of you, but the ability to throw or use items and giving things weight appropriate to their apparent mass adds to the immersion of the game. Death, when it comes, is often swift and brutal, but the checkpoints are placed as to not make things too much of a hassle to retread. If you can, remember to manually save now and then, just to be safe.
Other than the awkward interactions and a couple of puzzles being a bit difficult to figure out, there's nothing I really found fault in when playing Penumbra: Overture. I highly recommend picking up the follow-ups, Black Plague and Requiem, if you like the first.

I came to this game because I was so impressed by SOMA.
I can say now that the Frictional team are masters at creating an atmosphere of genuine terror and authenticity (when viewed through the lens of 2007 technology), emphasizing story and thinking rather than egregious violence.
However, by any standards, the gameplay is laughably bad at times.  "Combat" is either trivially stupid (tossing a can at a dog 5 times) or impossible (swinging a hammer at a spider).  The puzzles range from simple to impossibly counter-intuitive.  If you find yourself spending more than 5 minutes wondering what to do next, don't hesitate to look it up somewhere.
The story also leaves something to be desired.  There seem to be several subplots woven together, but I saw no real arc or connection between the story's beginning, middle, and end.  Maybe the dots are connected in the sequels?
Enjoy this game if you're interested in seeing the roots of Frictional's more modern work.  There is also something to be said for it's atmospherics, horrific story, and historical value, but not much.  Don't expect too much out of it as a game.  Like SOMA, some elements of the gameplay actually chip away at the value of the overall immersive experience.

Giving this game a thumbs up because the interactive physics engine is spectacular and the first hour of gameplay feels fresh and great. The puzzles are fun to get through because you can pick stuff up and toss things around. It makes the Source engine feel primitive. The sound is also done well-- dissonant soundscapes that make your skin crawl just a little bit. And these shining points are why Penumbra Overture gets a solid "MEH" instead of a dissentful "GARBAGE"; read on.
After the first hour or so, the game gets quite mundane. The game begins in the typical "abandoned mine" game trope, which is one of the worst settings there is, on par with "the water level that's mostly swimming". Nobody likes abandoned mine levels, we all just begrudgingly power through them hoping to get to the next area. Unfortunately there is no next area-- the whole game is in this mine. As a result the level design feels uninspired and boring.. because it is. And the one lake area that adds some dynamic to the world is a total non-sequitor.
As is standard for horror, combat is terrible. We are encouraged to sneak around enemies, which does have novelty for the first hour of gameplay. After that, it's just Outlast before there was Outlast.. I grappled with the poor fighting system until I found a reliable way to exploit it and kill the dogs (almost) every time. Running from enemies doesn't increase tension. It never increases tension. It only breaks momentum. The corridors are too long to backtrack through if one has to stop and wait out the dogs, so the dogs need to be taken out back and axed. Crouch down and time your hitstuns.
The spiders are poorly implemented. They can't be killed in any practical sense, and they can outrun you. It's a matter of trial and error, death and respawn, until you've brute-forced the maze to the point of memorizing the right path. There was an instance where I got check-pointed with spiders right on my tail, thus making the current objective impossible to complete. Player death was unavoidable because I hadn't previously been moving along fast enough for a sufficient head start. I had to reload an older save and use hindsight to briskly run through and make all of the correct turns.
Similarly, boss battles are all one-shot kills and require fast environment interactions to get past. Once again, they're impossible to beat the first go-around. But after enough trial and error you learn where to go and what to press. It takes all the tension out of the prospect of death. Good game design involves giving the player the opportunity to analyze and deconstruct the situation in the middle of the action, but Penumbra punishes the player for slowing to look around despite it being necessary to advance.
My guess is that this game was playtested only by the creators, and knowing the lay of each path, were able to breeze through with little difficulty. Uninitiated players, despite Penumbra Overture being a relatively easy game, will inevitably die at certain points in their playthrough, making death expected, accepted, and anticlimactic.
Nevertheless, I still recommend buying the Penumbra Collectors Pack this Winter Sale because it comes out to only 83 cents for each game. Although most of my review was negative, it's fortunate that the majority of the game is puzzle solving with that neat physics engine. This game is worth the 83 cents, and it was fun to see where Frictional came from before I play Amnesia for the first time.

While the RPG elements may not be deep enough to completely satisfy more diehard players, KOTOR deserves its legendary  status as one of the greatest examples of the genre.
An excellent soundtrack (composed by the renowned Jeremy Soule) compliments what is an exhilarating ride through the Star Wars universe, travelling to numerous planets all with their own visual style, enemies and inhabitants. Along the way you'll meet characters who can join your team and aid you in your bid to save the galaxy. Unlike most games, almost all of these characters are memorable and developed well to the extent where you find yourself considering your choices carefully so as not to alienate your favourite companion(s).
On the subject of choices, KOTOR provides the player with extensive decisions to make, many of which have a significant impact on how the story unfolds. Many of these choices are built around the light side/dark side dichotomy, with each evil decision pushing you towards the dark side of the force and vice versa. These choices influence not only the story, but the effectiveness of equipment and force powers, many of which are affected by how much the player aligns with either the light or dark side of the force.
Last but certainly not least is the plot itself. The narrative that this game weaves is widely considered among the greatest in video game history with a twist that (in my opinion) exceeds the famous "I am your father" scene. Simply put, this game is a must buy for anybody who doesn't have an irrational hatred for anything involving Star Wars.

F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin continues off the time-frame of the first, however this time around you no longer play as Point Man, but instead take on the role of Michael Becket of Delta force squad. The game delves deeper into the uncanny story based around Alma by taking the player all the way back to where it all began, hence the name "Project Origin".
This sequel is a prime example of a hit and miss game. It improves upon some things the original F.E.A.R. lacked, while at the same time taking two steps back on some things it did great.
You can expect more varied level settings, more types of enemies, and more Alma with all the supernatural events she brings along with her. The graphics are vastly improved too.
Like the first, Project Origins presents an unsettling atmosphere, but the horror while there, turns stale rather quickly, because of the abundance and over use of it while also feeling forced for no apparent reason. The gameplay also takes on a more modern generic feel opting out the lean cover mechanic and adds iron sights (ADS) with other various modern gun mechanics.
Overall I would have to recommend Project Origin, if not for its continuation of the intriguing story of Alma despite gameplay feeling disappointing at times.  7/10

Her Story is a mystery game where you go through short video clips and take keywords from those clips to search and find new clips. The clips are done in the style of police interviews, with the overarching goal being to try to find out who committed a murder. Along the way you learn the intricacies of the woman being interviewed. To top it off, the game has a great ending that gives you more insight into what was going on.
Onto the value of the game. The game is $6 USD and took me about 2 hours to complete. I dislike judging a game just by how long it takes, but that is pretty short. If the game looks interesting to you I'd say it's worth it at full price, and if not just wait for a sale. Also keep an eye on the Humble Bundle store, as the game goes on sale quite frequently on there.

Universal Combat is something of a trip in to the past, and anyone playing it needs to realize that. When I first played this way-back-when, it was probably the most absolutely complicated game I had ever attempted to play, and 14-year-old me really liked having to figure everything out as I went along and really learn how to play this thing. And frankly, that's where the satisfaction is. Universal Combat hails from a time when games really didn't tell you how good you were doing. There were no 'atta-boys. The satisfaction came from realizing that you had figured the game out and were getting good at it.
I suggest giving this a try and playing it for at least 6 hours before deciding if you like it or not. I personally enjoy the challenge of not just moment-to-moment ship management, but of the long term planning you can really get in to when determining either a brief patrol of border space or an extended campaign in to enemy territory. What spare parts should I take? Where should I deploy mining drones for resupply? Where can I park for repairs? And I do mean park for repairs; if you make poor choices and take damage, you realistically could be down for hours. It's brutal. But coming through several of those limp-home-and-pray adventures is what builds the narrative in your head and really helps you get in to the game, I think. I might not be able to follow my marine security detail around while they hunt down saboteurs, but damn if I don't stare at the PERSCAN screen and yell obscenities at them anyways.
It's not polished, it's not perfect. You'll have complaints. But if you give it a real chance and keep an open mind, you'll probably never forget playing it, and you'll have a totally different sort of fun with it than you do with Planetside 2 or Smite. And hopefully you'll stick around for Derek's next project, because I have a feeling it should be pretty cool.

Single-player simulation of military spaceship operations, where the player takes the role of commander on the bridge of a big cruiser or carrier in space.
Core features are:
1)capital ship command simulator, with complex equipment, AI onboard crew, and AI or player-controlled fighters and vehicles.
2)the dynamic world, a big sandbox galaxy with seamless 3D space and planetside warfare.
A very good thing about this game is there's no initial grind, because you don't start with a useless piece of junk for a ship like in most other spacesims!
But be advised: this is not a shooter/"ww2 fighters in space" type of game. It's complex, more similar to Eve Online or to a naval sim.  There's a lot to learn that's not presented to you nor obvious.  So if you are into hardcore military sims and have time to put into it, universal combat might be well worth your time.
You can begin your military career either with a mission-based tour of duty('acm'), or start in 'roam' mode where you are free to do whatever you wish in the open world.
Numerous instant action scenarios are also present.
Roam mode especially should be used in a roleplay mindset, so reading the game lore will greatly enhance the experience.
Other than fighting your faction enemies and completing acm missions, your might also venture in the usual trading/mining/salvaging/bountyhunt/pirating businesses.
You'll be able to capture enemy bases in both space and planets, give orders to fleets of AIs, and your own crew AI will improve making them more effective in their duties.

I bought the DLC with the added fixes and campaigns, but this applies to the free version as well since they are fairly similar (well for the moment).
I used to play Battlecruiser Millennium a few years ago yet I still needed to refresh my memory - the interface and controls are not intuitive, but after reading the manual and tutorial, and playing for a few hours, they become functional. Once past that stage, the game can be truly appreciated for its massive scope and the freedom it gives the player as a captain of a huge spaceship. The sense of scale is exceptional  - I sometimes land my 1 km carrier at a planet only to go outside and walk besides it, or go for an EVA near a huge star station and zoom out. This is awesome stuff  (yes even if the first person mode is less than stellar. But then this is mostly a space sim and a unique one at that).
I must say I actually find this game pretty. It is dated, but the lighting, textures and models are very nice and atmospheric (see my screenshots). The design of the ships looks realistic with visible launch bays, bridge, etc. Being mostly a hard core flight simmer I like these small touches.
In the Captain career, being able to manage the crew, the ships resources and smaller crafts (fighters and shuttles) appeals to me a lot and I don't think it can be done at this level in other games. There is plenty of stuff to do in the huge galaxy in roam mode - trading, space combat, mining, planet ops...
I can also say stability has improved since the initial Steam release and it is not an issue anymore. And I have been playing quite a lot lately.
If you like space sims and aren't afraid complex games ignore the bashing and give it a try. Truly highly recommended.
(PS I'm looking forward to the added features of the DLC, especially the 3D bridge - that sounds like a blast).

So, Besiege. This is a really unique game, and I'd really recommend it to a lot of people. If you're deciding whether or not to buy this game, just spend 5 minutes on reading this review.
Who should buy this game
People, who look forward to playing a very fun physics-based sandbox game
Gamers, who are interested in some kind of technic and war contraptions
The creative ones, people who can find a thousand solutions to one task
Why should I buy Besiege?
It's growing very quickly and is not abandoned, unlike a lot of Early Access games
Very cheap as for the content that it gives you

The developers promised to add a multiplayer mode and a multiplayer level editor in late 2017!
Below is a more detailed breakdown.
Gameplay
Gameplay is the main point of Besiege. Just to list a few things off, this game provides you with a nice campaign (even though there are not so many levels yet, but every level has a ton of replayability potential). There are also a couple of sandbox maps. The player is equipped with infinite amounts of different varieties of building blocks and elements. There is literally everything, starting with a simple cube and going right to holders, pistons, different versions of cannons, bombs, wings and a lot of other stuff. The best thing is that anything you will build will work and people have already came up with some really crazy ideas. Ever wanted to create a huge flying carrier? Or a machine that swings a giant hammer around itself, smashing everything to pieces? You can basically do that. Also, slow-motion is epic.
Graphics
I like the graphics. There is not much to say, but the visual style is pretty unique and is just enjoyable. Fire, water, explosions, the machines themselves look great and organic.
Sound
There is some nice ambient music that I really enjoy listening to. The sounds produced by machines and structures are simply great.
Sanbox-iness
This is not some kind of an official criteria, but I just wanted to mention how flexible Besiege really is. First off, in any level (including the campaign ones), you are able to disable the small building box that limits you and build anything. The sky is the limit (and your computers hardware, of course). There are quite a few cheats on the options panel, that can give you something like zero gravity or infinite ammo (most of the weapons fire only once or just can be held on for around 10 seconds). There are 3 large sandbox levels. And, as I've already mentioned, a level editor and a full multiplayer system are coming in 2017 (well, hopefully in 2017. The devs promised at least.)

Up until yesterday before the release, I was only slightly frustrated it was taking so much time for the game to come out (it was originally planned to be released early 2015) as I really wanted the game to be as great as possible and did not mind Atari taking time to make a game that would deserve to be called RCT, especially after I got to play the beta back in November 2015 when I saw that they were very far from having any part of the game finished at all.
But after such a long wait when I finally got to play RCTW yesterday, I went through extreme excitement to denial, followed by disgust and finally ended up laughing nervously in front of my screen.
To make it simple, if RCT3, a 12 years old game was released today, it would still be by very, very, very far a better game.
In RCTW, everything is broken:
- The graphics of the peeps, structures and the land when zoomed are absolutely disgusting and can compete with games like Super Mario 64 released 20 years ago (I am barely exaggerating)
- The roller coaster building system is completely broken and it takes hours to complete one that has many chances to end up not working properly at the end.
- It is very buggy, I mean so so so so so buggy, I had to relaunch the game 3 times in 2 hours I never saw anything like that before.
- Despite the fact that they look like they were made using MS Paint, the peeps will look like either vampires (Vendors at stands with red eyes) or zombies (they walk like zombies when they hold anything), or witches (janitors cleaning vomit with a broom and hovering when moving). Looks like they got the horror theme right at least!
- The non roller coasters rides are not only very few but look worse than the ones on RCT3. The way peeps act while on some of them is completely unnatural and it just hurts so much looking at it.
- Unless I missed something, there is only ONE song that can be played for all the rides. They give you the option to change it depending on the theme but essentially, it is the same song just slightly different! And if you have 2 rides next to each other and play the music on both, the music is not synchronised and I let you imagine what it sounds like!
- Even when I got frustrated and tried to be nasty with my peeps this would not work! The peep picking tool does not work, taking one and putting them at the opposite part of the park teleports them back to their original place after a few seconds, peeps in cars that are ejected from the coaster will be teleported to the exit, and drowning peeps (Yes, I was very annoyed at this point!) by adding water does not work, they either keep walking underwater or may eventually stop moving and start "jumping" in the water indefinitely.
A few extras:
-Most park management options from RCT3 are gone.
-Peeps disappearing, flying, going through walls, queuing the wrong way.
-Female peeps (even male?) make porn sounds.
-Sounds of babies crying all the time or children sounding like they are being tortured.
-Background decors unfinished.
I am stopping here but I could add more, and that is after having played the game only 2 hours!
But I know what some of you may want to say: "it's normal it's an early access!"
Well, before you go any further, here is a thing: Atari had planned to release the game early 2015, and after being postponed multiple times, we got to play the beta in November 2015. More than 4 months later, I cannot see ANY improvement whatsoever that has been made. (I actually think it is even worse as during the beta we did not get the chance to see the monstrosity that are the peeps as they were only "ghosts" back then.)
Atari had multiple chances and a lot of time to improve the game but fact is they just did not care so I cannot see how this game will be any better in the future. I requested a refund of the game and advise everyone not to buy this game.
A very disappointed fan.

PROS
- Coaster Builder: It's always been so easy to create a roller coaster in RCT, and this coaster builder definitely adds a challenge and makes me want to get better at making them. It can get very complicated though, particularly when the supports of (most noticeably) the wooden coaster get in the way and you actually can no longer see what piece you're making. I also found that when you ride the coaster in first person  there's alot of little bumps and mini-twists in the track that I hadn't noticed before, making the roller coaster seem really unnatural.. this may, however, be down to my inexperience with the feature.
- Variety: Not too bad, only about 8 types of roller coaster, such as Stand-up, Hyper, Wooden, Flying etc. I'm sure this list will grow however. Also a few flat rides which, again, will grow in time, but for now it's enough considering it's EA.

- Realism: Everything ACTUALLY looks right and feels real, everything is bigger, MUCH bigger, with realistic, big roller coaster stations, buildings take up way more than one square on the grid.. everything is just BIGGER. The parking lot out the front, the entrance itself.. the scale is just massive and really feels like a real theme park.
Music: Seemingly unimportant but I like it.
CONS
- Not as developed as I was hoping for: I honestly thought the game was WAY more developed than this.. it still feels like a skeleton. Know that I didn't play the beta though, this is a brand new experience of RCTW for me, so I can't compare it to that. I've been following the game since it's announcements but have nothing more to go on than screenshots and trailers. I was a bit gutted when I discovered the game was coming to EA.. Atari really do have no excuse for being this slow, I think they announced the game way too early that now it's annoyed people so much a lot of us WANT it to fail. I'm not one of these people, but I sense from other people's comments that they just want to see this game drow after putting so much hope (and a bit of money, too) into it! So yeah, this far down the line I expected much more meat on the bones.. but alas, it still feels very empty. (This may contradict my PRO for variety, but in that sense I understand the game is EA and will have little variety, despite the fact I wished it was further into development than this)
- Paths: oh my god. Oh my god, oh my god, oh my god. Words cannot describe.. They're the most infuriating thing and I can't explain why.. They've been very lazy with the paths, they don't build right, they mess up all the time.. oh my god, just paths. Sort it, please.. There was nothing wrong with simple click and place in the previous games or, heck, ANY other simulator! The grid also needs revising, I think, nothing seems to fit nicely.
- Visuals, ie menus and HUD: Wooowwww it's hideious. Like, actually hideous.. I don't know if they're going for a Sims 4 kind of minimalistic display in-game, which would look good.. but it just looks so random, maybe like they haven't really focused on that yet. The menus look cheap and Alpha-like.. think Cities:Skylines, just a grey, rounded text box with some words in. Put some effort in, Nvizzio! Get some sort of theme going with the menus, like the blue bubbles in RCT3! It just makes it look.. like a game!?
- Buggy: Yes yes yes, it's EA I knoooww, but considering (again) how long this has supposedly been in development (I get the feeling they just go into the office every Sunday or something to do 2-3 hours worth of actual development on the game) it's a bit odd to se a mechanic floating around and attempt to inspect a ride whilst it's mid-flow, getting kicked in the face multiple times by the flying chairs.. silly. The game just crashed on me for no reason either, to be expected in EA I know, but this far down the line? Not sure.
VERDICT
I want to give this games a thumbs up, just to show them that there IS somebody still rooting for this game. My biggest worry is that all these (overwhelming amount!) negative reviews will make them think "Ah screw it, we're giving up. Nobody cares anymore, we're only going to be slated for everything.." and BOOM, there goes RCTW. I know this won't happen, I trust the developers are passionate about this game and want to make it better.. just please do it, listen to the fans and start righting your wrongs. We WANT to like this game, I want to LOVE this game.. and I will still hold on to the hope that one day, maybe soon, I will. RollerCoaster Tycoon World could be amazing.. just look back at what made the first three games so good, and do it better. I have faith in this game, and when it's at a stage that I can reccomend it to other people.. I most certainly will :)

This is a quick little platformer with a wonderful score. The level design is solid, twisting your brain just a little to do most levels. The floor is indeed jelly-every surface is elastic, meaning you will oftentimes find yourself building up tons of momentum and leaving a jiggle mess of straight-edged surfaces in your wake. It's fun to build up speed, but unfortunately, you rarely get to use it. I can definitely recommend the gameplay to any platformer fans.
This game also features music by Disasterpeace, the artist behind the Fez soundtrack. Which is good. Unfortunately, the game doesn't stop there in its similarities to Fez. There's a distinct "meta" aspect to every scrap of "plot" you reveal while playing the game. There is even a point where the game "breaks" and you play through it (a la Fez's opening/glitch level). There are several secret terminals spread out through the levels, and on them is some code you may or may want to decipher (I didn't). The secrets and the related deciphering is almost completely borrowed from Fez's anti-cube collectables. Furthermore, the game has no enemies, and focuses on exploration. This is not specifically something Fez owns, but it does add to the familiar atmosphere.
Now, I said "unfortunately," but I actually love Fez. What gives? Well...Fez has a semblance of a plot. It has more of a point to "meta" items and hints of a long-forgotten ancient race. The Floor is Jelly has...nothing. There's nothing set-up for you at the outset, there is very little text, and everything tossed in feels just, well, tossed in. It reminds me more of antechamber in how developed its world is than Fez does, by a long shot. So taking elements from Fez just feels out of place.
All this talk of unneeded elements is just a gripe though, something I wanted to point out. Overall, it is a solid game with a solid draw, even if the follow-through is somewhat shallow. I enjoyed my experience. I don't think I'll play it again, but I definitely would tell a friend who likes platformers to try it.

Edit: New Review in light of the winter update, that doesn't just say to get Overwatch
Alright, so let's talk Battleborn. Battleborn is an FPS MOBA made by Gearbox Softwear, and because it was kind of similar, it was always put in direct competition against Overwatch. And well, it's no suprise who won that battle (pun not intended). Battleborn came out on the first day of the Overwatch open beta, after all...
So, is Battleborn really so bad compared to Overwatch? Since the two have been so intrinsically linked, it can be hard to tell sometimes, but I'll try my best to review it as it's own game. I'll start with pros/cons.
Pros:
Character diversity: There is a pretty good character roster, and the winter update finally unlocked all the characters for everyone (fixing one of the biggest mistakes on launch if you ask me).
Stylization: Taking a similar sense of humor from Borderlands, Battleborn pulls of an interesting world, coherent in it's diversity. I was somewhat skeptical until I played the Attikus story op, and now I want to know more about the Thrall Rebellions.
Content: Although the PvP modes are iffy at best, it's made up for with a campaign and story ops. The custimization is pretty decent too, in terms of actually affecting the game over cosmetics.
Price: $30 base price, goes on sale for $7.50. Defenitely worth that much, although the microtransactions are a little frustrating.
(Don't tell anyone, but the game is also g a y)
Cons:
Music: Not stellar. Either distracting to gameplay or the mood.
Player base: Practically no one plays. The concurrent players went up with the update, but they still have more people playing Borderlands 2 on almost any given days. This means queues are hell, and kind of require outside matchmaking (like on r/battleborn). This isn't Gearbox's fault, but it definitely affects the experience.
Balance: It is not. Despite massive changes to characters, some heroes just feel way more powerful than others. I'm looking at you, Alani.
The game leaves me with rather conflicted feelings. At first, I hated it, partially because my terrible laptop could hardly handle the game. But now, with an actual PC,I'm having second thoughts. The two things that tipped me over the edge to positive are the price, and honestly, the player base. Because it's so much smaller, they are a hell of a lot nicer than the overwatch playerbase. It's a lot more welcoming, tight night community, and I like that. I would definitely reccomend you at least give this game a try on sale; it could surprise you.

In the late 90's I published a Call of Cthulhu RPG scenario on Cthonian that resides near a coal mine somewhere in Eastern Europe, so this game has been pretty much a deja vu for me.
Unfortunately, the game itself does not stand the test of time.
Graphics is crude. Plot is decent, but nothing more. It is full of Lovecraftian cliches. The characters (character) you meet  being affected, implausible. The worst part of the game, however, is physics and controls. Interactions with environment tend to be clumsy, using equipment is very unhandy.
How big is the problem? Well, I tend to avoid all creatures not because I was afraid of them (as it should be in horror games), but because I struggle to omit any fight possible. To simply hit an opponent with a pickaxe was a challenge requiring very high skills with mouse and keyboard. At the same time the enemies are plain stupid (attacking until dead in a repetitive manner) and happen to die in weird positions - dogs drop dead 2 ft above ground, or partly in the wall or in the ground. Again, it's a glitch, not a horror element.
All in all, not recommended (says a Lovecraft fan). I had to force myself to finish the game.
