Challenging fights are fun... but I hadn't even really completed a full level (past the tutorial), so it seems like it just ramped up too fast. And while the game is technically a 'tactics' game, in that it has a grid and you walk around, there seemed to be less tactical decisions focused on positioning, movement, cover, etc... and more so just their 'mood' system.
This is a good game, you guys. If you've ever wanted to win over a monkey with flattery or shoot a nun, you need this game.

So, a game of the AVGN at last! I could say that I'm a fan of his work and videos which are ridiculously funny! To see a game made and based on his numerous rage quits is really a great idea! To put it bluntly, this game is like a nostalgic return to the past, playing some truly HARD NES games! There are a few references to his videos and the appearences of popular characters.
The stages have their own themes so you old school gamers, you're in known grounds! Anytime you die, you get a randomly generated outrage from AVGN which is fun when there's a great mix up.
The graphics are as you would expect from a generic platform game. The music is very well done! The controls are for the most part feels very solid although, when I played the game with the XBOX 360 gamepad, I had a hard time being precise with it.
PROS:
+Ridiculously funny!
+Gameplay is as you would expect from an old school platformer.
+Music is well done and catchy!
+Keyboard controls are solid.
CONS:
-Incredibly and blasphemously hard! There is way too many death blocks everywhere. Prepare to retry many times and don't forget to reach that checkpoint!
-Level design is as bad as the games reviewed by the Nerd himself. (Death blocks, hard-to-reach items and areas, frustrating precise jumps).
-At $14,99, I find this action indie game very pricey. Only buy on a discount!
OVERALL:
If it wasn't for these tedious deathblocks, the game would be short as there isn't much variety to the stages other than being lucky enough to avoid deathblocks and occassionally shooting some enemies. They might be the main reason to "make the game" feel longer but the overuses of the deathblocks was and still is very annoying to me.
RECOMMENDATION:
While I haven't finished the whole game yet, I would still recommend this game to old school platformer purists only. If you love AVGN, it is a big bonus and you gotta be prepared to die very often and scream like the Nerd himself! But, buy on discount only!
RATING:
7.0 / 10

This is most certainly the best Hitman game.

The game opens to a simple yet bleak 90s desktop and a directory of clips of interviews conducted by the police. Your job is to search through the library of clips and piece together the story based on the testimony provided by the person who is interviewed. These clips utilize full motion video (FMV) meaning that they utilize prerecorded clips which, in this case, feature an actress.
This game appeals to an audience that is interested in a
. As a result,
relies on its cutscenes to relay its story as opposed to gameplay, so do keep that in mind if you are on the fence about buying this game.
I believe that developer Sam Barlow has created a work that, like Nolan accomplished in the cinematic world with
,
that we are used to seeing in video games. Unlike a film, the player is given the option to choose the order in which he or she watches the clips because the clips lack a proper chronology. The player thus constructs a story that, although is objectively the same for all players, can be interpreted differently among the player base because of the numerous orders in which one can watch the videos (There are a couple disputed theories about what happens in this game within the gaming community.). Think of the game as a visual novel with the pages in completely the wrong order.
However, careful attention has been paid to the presentation of the protagonist's story in order for it to be appropriate with this type of gameplay. In turn, the player must be diligent when watching the clips. The limited interaction just does enough to immerse the player in a detective-like role but also forces you to direct your attention to the visuals and dialogue present within the game. From the actress's (Viva Seifert's) excellent performance to common onscreen actions, every element within the clips aids the narrative as whole.
Unlike most video games out there,
does not spell out everything to the player throughout its playtime. And, in a way, I think that is where the beauty of the game lies. Barlow presents the narrative in its pure, unadulterated form. It is up to the player to find the truth, whatever that may be.

But if you just want a chill coloring game to relax to, and have some spare time, you will enjoy this.

It's an interesting concept that starts with some promise as you begin colouring the world, but boredom sets in as soon as you realize how slowly things progress and how large the world really is.
This has been described somewhat as a Zen game, but unlike other such games such as Flow, etc. there is little sense of progression and the pace is so very, very, slow.  Nudge trees slowly, collect the colour that falls from them, and paint the world until the colour runs out.  Repeat.  It is the very definition of grinding, only with no real goal in sight.
There are some redeeming qualities: it is pretty, and the music is tranquil, fitting with the zen-like feel.  Unfortunately that wears thin quickly as there is precious little actual game-play.  The little bits of text you unlock are simply small statements designed perhaps to evoke deeper thought, but there really isn't much to them and they don't add much to the experience.
Some would say it is art, but to me it is a game without actual gameplay.  Evocative statements and abstract graphics cannot make up for the fact that there is simply little to do, and what there is is so drawn out you would need to grind for hours and hours just to see it.  It simply tries too hard.
The trailer shows all sorts of interesting parts of the game that I suspect are many hours away.  Getting there is simply not that interesting, and takes too long.

Visuals and Graphics: 7/10
Gameplay Mechanics: 2/10
Overall score: 4/10; TLDR
I did not buy this in a bundle. I bought it solo on IndieGameStand for $1 because it looked great.
This interactive screensaver (**not game) is tolerable for $2-3. $5 is too much. To be fair, I did enjoy my zen time in this flawed non-game.
This application is like an alpha concept demo.  LIke wandering through a 1st person shooter with no bullets or melee, you get a good sense of feel of the presentation without any game mechanics implemented.
The gameplay is missing.  Like a small developer who had a beautiful project envisioned which he never had time to finish.  Rather than junk all the work, he/she releases the incomplete alpha app (avoiding the word 'game').  I get it. Developing a game is tough; life moves forward; the author must eat; other priorities overshadow this project.  I think it is a beautiful project.  Sell the Alpha for $1 maybe and perhaps finish it at a later date.
If the author were to finish the game, I envision a bear eating berries and having a transformative effect on the environment.  Or a bee or collection of bees pollinating the neighborhood and effecting change on the makeup of the flora.  (The dev is like a bee--he works very hard, and we gamers come expecting delicious honey for next to nothing $$ and do not care whether the worker starves for his hard work.  I actually applaud what the author started here.)
However, again, there is NO real game mechanic.  I read the reviews that say this app was meant to behave as a tranquil zen sandbox--No, that is a cop-out excuse for a demo released before it had a game built around the concept.
I have extra time on my hands, so I can drop my 12 hours into this game for even Zen foolishness.  Most of you cannot--play 15-30 minutes of this, then Uninstall.  The app is like painting your house with a trimming brush and full set of watercolors.  It takes forever but you end up with a nice kaleidoscope result.  That is all that happens.
The app even mocks you with fake/useless collectibles and makes parallel references to the futility of life.  Why not take this beautiful app as the pollen/seed spreader and tack on a few simple game mechanics.  (ex: Cultivate this red plant in the NE side of the garden.  The Blue plants and ladybugs and animals flourish as you succeed.)  Develop some weak but simple game mechanic by producing/accomplishing a small goal.  Rinse and repeat for a few dozen challenges.  The sandbox all works mostly the same, but my idea gives some reason to play or immersion to polinate/transfer/spread each plant color.
Instead, there are no instructions--nothing accomplished--All the plants, bushes and trees have their own inherent colors that do not change.  Your only action is to paint a hue to the ground/grass beneath them by picking nearby color from a unchangeable plant.  As you paint, there are 100 other bugs slowly painting the areas that you have brought to life--so you have no real control of color.
Instead, you paint the world with a tiny trim brush. You do a little--then do a lot until you realize that your own input is not really having much effect but the world remains grey and incomplete, so one might grind for the futility of a full color completion.  The world needs to be 5 to 10 times smaller because it takes too damn long for no better finished result.
Pursuit of Achievements is a silly set of badges in many games.  There are a plethora of nonsensical achievements.  "Make a swollen and fertile world" 0/50 What?! How would any of this be accomplished? "Sprinkle a modest joy over the world" 0/20. It wants you to cover 20% of the world with Yellow.  Over half of the areas are painted by bugs with a semi-permanent color which the player cannot change.  So, how would I get 20% of the world yellow?  Most of the achievements revolve around a find-a-needle-in-a-haystack subgame.  After walking the whole world around and making small interactions--you will quickly accomplish quite a few nonsense achievement. (Bump into 1 beetle.)
The only controls are WASD (configurable + controller)    Remember I have the luxury of doing nothing but wander for hours WASD, redipping the paintbrush every few feet,  After revealing color to the world 6 hours later, I was about to uninstall the app.  4 of the needles-in-the-haystack are colored runes that go into the useless stacks of Zen sayings, Zen history, Zen coins, Zen jewels, Zen artifacts.  All useless.
SPOILER ALERT that should have been put in the nonexistant instructions/tutorial:
6 hours done, ready to uninstall, it turns out, that if you click the 4 Runes while standing still 6 times, your paintbrush will drop a few paintballs which will bounce around and change a small to medium area around you.  It is random--so you have a new tool which just introduces more randomness into the world.  Not a means to guide the color development.  Now there is a population of little people that walk around with their paintbrushes too.  So, instead of competing with the 300 bugs, you now also compete with 100s of "LittleThings" that also shift the colors of the environment.  No control.  Just beautiful paints wandering the canvas--with your tiny ability to shift the localized colors a bit.  The rest of the world shifts as it wants.
Keep doing that for hours instead crafting the look of the gardens, or making honey, or scaring a competing hive out of the neighborhood, or stinging the brutish humans who trample the gardens.  All of these mechanics are missing.
Beautiful interactive screensaver game though. 4/10.

Okay so I'm revisiting this. It's been a while since I reviewed the game last, got my money back. Decided to re-buy it and give it another chance, I generally try to do so with most games I play.
So, it has changed. First thing I noticed was that they'd obviously changed the graphics up. When I last played (again, so long ago) the game looked older than RCT3. Even when Planet Coaster was in EA it had more going for it than this game did.
The next thing I noticed is I was actually able to build a coaster without the game either exploding on me, the FPS tanking or the coaster just up and decided life was no longer worth living. So this played a fairly big influence in my re-review.
Next I started taking a look at the decorating elements of the game. I wish the controls were more intuitive and less awkward really. But I do like the styles they've chosen really.
A number of bugs I was inundated with when I last played have not shown themselves once, so I'm pretty happy there.
The game still needs polishing. Peeps need fixing, their animations are clunky and awkward. These people are who you see a lot of in game and yet they feel rather unloved. I do like the artistic style though. It all just needs more love.
Moving onto how the game has grown since it first hit steam, It has grown and the dev's have tried. Though I'm concerned by the apparent silence since Post-Release Update 7 a few months back. They're showing some progress and I'd like to see it continue. More developers and publishers need to take responsibility when they balls up and fix what they broke (Yes I'm glaring at you EA and Bioware). So I'm pleased with Atari and Co for their work in trying to fix RCTW. It just needs more. As well as more fixes on bugs and problems that have been repeatedly asked for since Day 1.
Will I recommend it? Well yeah. It is.. an odd situation this game really. It is a neat little game, partially polished but there is evidence they're still doing what they can. It's been a long time since it came out now and it needs the fans and community of RCT to come together to support Atari etc in getting this game on it's feet and standing tall and proud.
I can't guarentee you'll enjoy it. Neither can I guarentee you'll like it or have a bug free experience. That is up to you as an individual. All I can say is that since re-buying it, I've enjoyed myself. I still prefer Planet Coaster, but RCTW brings its own concepts and ideas to the table and it's healthy for the ecosystem for these two games to co-exist.
I wish everyone who buys this game the best of luck.

This game is, quite obviously, in the RTS, or "Real Time Strategy" category. Perhaps less obviously to those who haven't played it yet, it's also, actually a real-time *strategy* game. Unlike pretty much every other game in the genre, it is first and foremost about strategy. Unit-level tactics and micro (think Starcraft II) are *not* the focus of this game. In some ways, I think that giving the same genre label to this game as other "collect resources and build units and fight and win" games does it a disservice. Because it's actually something quite different than most.
Want to build 3 tanks, 2 mobile shield guys, an artillery guy and an anti-air guy, in a never-ending loop? You can. You just queue them up and tell it to loop. It'll keep doing that until you tell it different. Want to destroy your enemy without leaving your base, with long-range artillery or nukes? You can.
Unlike almost every other "RTS" I've ever played, the difference between the winner and the loser in this game is almost never based on the "actions per minute" (how fast you can click on stuff) of each player. It's based on the strategy, and how well that strategy works on that map against your opponnent's strategy.
After a few hundred hours of play, I'm not bored with it, even against enemy AI (which is quite good, and varied from game to game). One of my favorite games of all time.

Supreme Commander 2 (SC2) is much better than Supreme Commander 1 (SC1). Don't believe all the naysayers!
SC1 had tons of different units, 4 tiers and huge maps. The intention behind SC1 apparently was to simulate epic battles. However, it failed at that miserably. The usual multiplayer games didn't last longer than 10 - 20 minutes and ended at tier 1 or tier 2 at most. So you weren't able to use most of the units anyway. No epic battles of several hours (if players played seriously).
SC2 doesn't try to simulate epic battles. SC2 is a very quick game. 1on1 games usually take about 10 minutes. Everything in the game is streamlined for quick games and it never gets boring. The game just makes a lot more sense. Unlike SC1, it doesn't try to be something which it isn't. If you want longer games, play 3vs3 games which can take about 30 minutes.
Cons:
- The online community is practically non-existent. The game is very old after all and most players who play it don't host public games. RTS games in general aren't the most popular games.
Pros:
+ The game isn't expensive. Ask a few friends who like RTS games and play with or against them! IMO, the game is worth its current price of 13€ just for its skirmish mode against AI. There is also a single player campaign for all three factions.
+ There are not tons of different units. Too many units make a RTS too complicated without providing a real benefit. You don't need tons of different units to have a strategic game. Too many types of units just make the game bloated and make it difficult for new players.
+ The size of the maps is just right. No boring wandering around in slow moting in huge maps.
+ The ACU or an engineer can build all buildings. No need to distinguish between T1, T2 and T3 engineers. Better buildings and units are unlocked via the research system. Different tiers of engineers would just have been annoying without providing any strategical depth.
+ Stability. Unlike SC1, SC2 never has crashed on my PC.
+ Easy to pick up, difficult to master. That's what a RTS game should be like. There is a lot of depth in the game, e.g. knowing how to counter which strategy of the enemy.
+ The factions play very differently. Every faction has its own cool things and the balance seems to be very good.
+ Beforehand I was sceptical when I heard that the mass and energy isn't reduced per second when constructing but you have to pay the full amout of mass and energy for buildings and units. In fact it works perfectly. Nothing to miss about the old economy system of SC1 (or Total Annihilation).
+ It is not possible to build a turtle base which withstands everything. Allowing too heavy turtling would only lenghten the game without making it more interesting. In SC2 attacking is the best defense.
+ There is a lot of tension in the game. You always have something to do. There is no time for breaks. Fortunately, a game is short enough to be able to relax *after* the game ;)
Conclusion: SC2 is the result of streamlining SC1. It's not a trivial game like some people may try to make you believe. IMO, the right things were simplified but the developers never oversimplified anything.

Under the lights of moon and gas, skulking in shadows and pilfering unattended coffers, are the downtrodden and forgotten. These Dickensian societal wastes don't let an oppressive government and cruel police force get them down, because at night - they rule. Criminal enterprises scour the street for gold and victory, taking back what's theirs and what wasn't (but is now). Men, women, and even children smirk slyly while moving stealthily to dip their fingers into pockets or their daggers into backs.
In Antihero, you play as a variety of cutthroat criminals who are tired of being told to live a poor life just because of where, and to whom, they were born. Trying to live an "honest" life is more criminal than actually stealing, so they've taken the lesser of two evils and opt to be creatures of the night. You'll build up your gangs and enlist urchins to rough up rival crooks and take over businesses, siphoning off resources to keep the cycle going. Either through murderous skullduggery or stealthy thievery, you'll be able to claim the title of Master Criminal while taking out your competition. Blackmail, bounties, and boat-loads of booty await you on the cobblestone streets in Antihero!
PROS
+ Charming art and fitting music.
+ Simple to learn, difficult to master.
+ Satisfying variety in ways to play and win.
CONS
- Disappointingly short campaign.

So, Besiege. This is a really unique game, and I'd really recommend it to a lot of people. If you're deciding whether or not to buy this game, just spend 5 minutes on reading this review.
Who should buy this game
People, who look forward to playing a very fun physics-based sandbox game
Gamers, who are interested in some kind of technic and war contraptions
The creative ones, people who can find a thousand solutions to one task
Why should I buy Besiege?
It's growing very quickly and is not abandoned, unlike a lot of Early Access games
Very cheap as for the content that it gives you
Enjoyable gameplay and graphics
A ton of space for creativity
The developers promised to add a multiplayer mode and a multiplayer level editor in late 2017!
Below is a more detailed breakdown.
Gameplay
Gameplay is the main point of Besiege. Just to list a few things off, this game provides you with a nice campaign (even though there are not so many levels yet, but every level has a ton of replayability potential). There are also a couple of sandbox maps. The player is equipped with infinite amounts of different varieties of building blocks and elements. There is literally everything, starting with a simple cube and going right to holders, pistons, different versions of cannons, bombs, wings and a lot of other stuff. The best thing is that anything you will build will work and people have already came up with some really crazy ideas. Ever wanted to create a huge flying carrier? Or a machine that swings a giant hammer around itself, smashing everything to pieces? You can basically do that. Also, slow-motion is epic.
Graphics
I like the graphics. There is not much to say, but the visual style is pretty unique and is just enjoyable. Fire, water, explosions, the machines themselves look great and organic.
Sound
There is some nice ambient music that I really enjoy listening to. The sounds produced by machines and structures are simply great.
Sanbox-iness
This is not some kind of an official criteria, but I just wanted to mention how flexible Besiege really is. First off, in any level (including the campaign ones), you are able to disable the small building box that limits you and build anything. The sky is the limit (and your computers hardware, of course). There are quite a few cheats on the options panel, that can give you something like zero gravity or infinite ammo (most of the weapons fire only once or just can be held on for around 10 seconds). Renowned Explorers: International Society (RE:IS) is a turn-based strategy adventure roguelike. Boy is that a mouthful! I have never seen quite a game like this. RE:IS draws aspects from each of its genres and combines them into a unique experience.
Upon first glance at this game it can be somewhat puzzling or appear glaring simple even. You take a team of three explorers, making one of them your captain who gets an extra perk to help you along the way, and conduct 5 expeditions across various regions around the world. Each playthrough will have its own ups and downs and no two will every be alike.
At first glance the game doesnt appear to have much content. But the replayability is so high that after ~80 hours of gameplay I am still finding new treasure or trying out different strategies. There are 20 different characters to choose from. Thats 6,840 different combinations! With over a hundred treasure to collect you will find yourself sinking countless hours and playthrough into this game to master every detail. Plus the devs are constantly improving the game and adding more content!
There is more than one way to play. Combat is its own unique formula utilizing a rock-paper-scissors weakness chart creating different moods that effect your team. But even this gives way to more depth after you master the basics. Perhaps that boss that is easy to defeat deviously gives a different reward if you are friendly, but becareful because friendly abilities only do half damage to him.
The art and the story are both fantastic and the events continue to be amusing even after you've gone through them before. With an active community and weekly challenges there is always more strategies to try and scores to improve.
If you like turn-based strategy and roguelikes this is a game for you.
It quickly became one of my favorite games to play and I am still learning more and more about the secrets of hidden treasures.

It's high adventure in the golden age of exploration, with bright, colorful graphics and a tongue in cheek tone. The gameplay is fun (if challenging at times), and the replay value is great, as in addition to selecting an entirely new crew, you'll find that there are various secrets tucked away in every expedition that'll take multiple attempts to uncover.

Oh boy, this game. Bioware nailed it again.
When I first played it when I was about 10 years old or so I didn't like the fighting system really. The game was available on four different CDs to install. I couldn't finish it back then because of bugged boss fight. Now, around march this year I began playing it and got super hooked and finished it the same month.
When you start you get to create your character with a set of heads different to both genders that you can choose, class, starting statistics and skills that you can hover over or smthng so it'll tell you what they are for, so while this could be overwhelming for some people it's explained well. You play as a soldier and start on Endar Spire cruiser. The action takes place ~4000 years before our canon Star Wars movies. You serve for the republic. You wake up and learn basic gameplay mechanics.
Well about the gameplay because I said I didn't enjoy fighting in this game when I was young: the game has an active pause and it kinda plays like a paper RPG with many different stats rolling your chance to hit a target etc. This can be considered a con if you want something like a Jedi Knight game but it works really well here and makes the gameplay strategic and all of your skill upgrades give you satisfaction when then help you win. You fight with up to 2 partners on your side at once and you can choose skills for them as well, just make sure to disable auto-promotion for them.
You can play melee in this game from the start in the form of vibroblade. I don't want to spoil it to you so I'll just say that there are at least 4 different paths you can take in designing your character and only one of these is gunning people down. I'm not saying that gunning people down is empty and boring: there are also many abilities and weapons for that! When you play you'll understand because if you want to go melee you'll have to chose one of 3 paths.
Now more about this world: Sith soldiers look dope af. Republic soldiers look authentic too. It doesn't look like episode 4 or anything, it's new and fresh but it fits Star Wars theme very well. The planets have quite a lot of story to them and you can talk to many NPCs and get many sidequests. Your choices have some consequence and you can gain light and dark side points depending on your actions. After finishing KOTOR I can safely say that this is the best Star Wars story ever told alongside Original Trilogy (ep. 4-6). Doesn't have none of the Death Star nonsense you and I already got bored of! The plot is very interesting and dialogues with your partners are 10/10. You can spend a lot of time talking to them and sometimes the game will prompt you that something is wrong with one of them and you should talk to them but it's not necessary, however this is the real icing on the cake. This game is kinda like Mass Effect and it's even made by the same guys: Bioware. If you want a good Star Wars story then definetely buy this! However, now let's go into some technical issues...
Knights of the Old Republic II got updated on Steam with new resolutions as far as I'm concerned and - workshop. This one on the other hand requires some outside programs for you to enjoy 1920x1080. Another problem is that cutscenes are prerendered videos that will not play in 1920x1080 res no matter what. It isn't a big issue unless they don't play for you at all... If you don't set up your mods correctly for higher res then it might disable cutscenes, and cutscenes have also some tendency of making setting up your resolution crash the game. After you figure it out though you can get around 50h out of this game in one playthrough.
50 hours is a lot of game time for a game that is all gold. The begining can be a bit of a chore but when you get hooked you will sometimes play 4h straight! This game is such a classic...
Now to music: it's not John Williams, there is some hints to him eg. Bastilla's Theme has some moments sounding like Force Theme. There is a lot of interesting music that you can chill out to in this game or get pumped up. As for graphics they are rather bad but they don't make the game any less enjoyable than if it had Battlefield graphics for me. This is same stuff as Mass Effect 1: it's old but it stands out because of the great, belivable world, your partners and the story in the game.
My visit in this world was great and totally worth the time. The game's stuck in my head ever since March. I'm still waiting for a right time to begin playing the sequel. If you want a good Star Wars story then it's a must-play, if you love Mass Effect then it's a must-play, if you want to play a good RPG then it's a must-fu**ing-play. Don't make the mistake of spoiling yourself this story without first playing it, no need to watch other reviews. Wait for some discount, get it and try it out! If you want to then bother getting higher res with mods, if you don't then play full oldschool mode and swap your monitor with your old one that you still keep in the basement.
Worse than Mass Effect 1 but they don't break the immersion or anything, the world is still very belivable and badass.
Great voice acting, varied languages (as in: you get to listen to alien languages as well). Music is top notch.
Strategic, if you like games with active pause system and paper RPGs you will love it. If you want a fast paced game then it's not for you. Skill upgrades give satisfaction and more than make up for the lack of Jedi Knight-like combat.
Very belivable, you'll get hooked so hard! Best Star Wars story alongside Original Trilogy.
Your partners have a ton of dialogues, a lot more and less scripted than Mass Effect. They're very varied and tell your their point of view on stuff, they'll argue with you but if they see that you have a point they will be sorry later on for being too aggressive. They are very human, as in they act like real, but they aren't all human.
More than a decent amount of weapons & upgrades, the progession system of skills and abilities is very cool! Lots of replay ability in this. Hell, you even get many different grenade types, mines, usables in form of adrenaline. Lots of different armour types that make all game styles viable, different headgears, belts, implants...
Overall the game would get a perfect 100/100 from me but it requires too much hussle to get working properely with AD 2016 standard of resolution and even X years ago when I played it as a little guy there were some bugs, and now there were some bugs too. A bit of odd gameplay decisions in some areas that don't work too well.
The payoff however, is superb! This is a hard choice for me. From the perspective of playing this over half a year ago I want to give this game a perfect score but I remember that there was some negative things in it and I even pointed them out in the review. This game definetely deserves to be a part of the Canon.
I'm gonna give it a score of 99/100. Might've increased the score slightly because of the nostalgia, but ffs: this game is so great now so imagine how great it was back when it was released in 2003! Don't get it spoiled to yourself by watching it on Youtube, IT'S DA*N WORTH PLAYING AND THAT'S IT! There is a reason why I bought it 2 times.

Loads of people say that Silent Assassin was the point in Hitman that it got really good, though I kind of see Blood Money as the Hitman game that got a lot of right. While I love Silent Assassin and Contracts, they were in that time of stealth that couldn't get right on the nail but they still held up to be amazing type of games as long you can look pass a few clunky bits of rules you'd have to follow. Blood Money gets a lot of right with how stealth works through the sneaking and disguises, and gameplay wise pretty solid. From the most I remember from the previous Hitman games you pretty much had to follow simple orders, mostly ranging from "snipe this guy" to "make this look like an accident" while the journey is to which whatever you feel best fits whether be being sneaky and only take out a few guards, or just go guns blazing until to the point where the game will actually need some stealth involved. Blood Money's missions feel that. Such of the mission where you're in the opera pretty much shows how much you can assassinate your targets in many ways to act cleaver, which adds up to re-playability to try out different outcomes with so much you can do. Almost every mission has about a dozen ways to finish off your targets, along with a dozen ways how to get close enough to get there. The game can be short what with there being 12 missions (maybe 13 if you want to count the tutorial mission that doesn't add up to the main and very hard to pull off and SA rank ironically), most missions if done right could may as well end up being as long as twenty minutes tops. That's not so off putting through since there's a lot of re-playability in Blood Money where you can try out different ways to finish the mission, or otherwise try to get perfect Silent Assassin ranks on every mission.
As for a port it's a swell port. Most problems have to do with the default keyboard controls which you probably have to fiddle around with to fit what's best (Right mouse to open inventory is REALLY weird). Especially weird for people who probably has played it on consoles and got used to those more, as I'm one of those that pretty much played Blood Money through on the PS2. I don't think Blood Money has any controller support if you're used to those controls and skip over the keyboard, but that's more of a preference and I prefer KB+M just for better aiming during first-person view. It's optimized well enough, though this is a game that came out of 2006 so don't expect high quality graphics and don't worry about performance. Navigating menus with mouse is tough, which I don't mind using keyboard to speed past them, but could be a problem to others that prefer to use a mouse to navigate the game menus. It's not a perfect port but it's one of the better ports if you're willing to go through the controls options for about five minutes.
Otherwise it's Hitman Blood Money on the PC. To me it's pretty much the best Hitman game for how much you can do, gameplay improvements over the other Hitmans (Hitmen??), stealth actually works well enough that it doesn't feel like you're hoping to work around the limitations and just feels great when a plan comes together. Even if Absolution wasn't a mediocre flashy action game with too much generosity for a stealth game, this was going to a point where Hitman got really good and nine bucks is more than enough to experience that.

There isn't much to like here. The graphics are okay, distinctive and colourful. No voice acting. An okay story, but unremarkable writing. There's local coop if you want to get help in fight segments.
The gameplay is a mish-mash of ideas that other games implement well, but here you have to juggle all of them at once and that's headache-inducing.
Most of those gameplay ideas could have been fun individually, given a lot of testing and fine-tuning. For example, there is a dimension-swapping mechanic. Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams is built around that and does it much better.
There is also a body-swapping mechanic; as a human the character can jump a bit higher (each high jump is a mini-combo that combines multiple buttons pressed in rigid sequence; such as, jump, hold up and immediately press special for an uppercut, then jump again and change direction to land), and as a chicken the character can go through some narrower gaps. Sometimes you need to insert dimension-swapping and wall-jumping into those jump combos.
The combo system is extended in combat, with many enemies having guards such that you need to sustain a high combo to get your punches to land. There is a directional throw mechanic that can disrupt some enemies. In combat, the game forces you to use almost all of your abilities (except maybe the chicken): movement combos, dimension swapping, guard-breaking, throws, plus combat-specific combos, through unreachable enemies, shields that require a specific combo to unlock, enemies in the other dimension, guardable attacks, unguardable attacks, enemies that can only be defeated by their own projectiles, and so on. The platforming is the same; you need to use almost every control, including some movement combos and parades.
As if this wasn't complex enough, combat and some obstacles have knockback and render the controls unresponsive for a few seconds. Worst case, you can spend the whole fight blinking in and out of responsiveness, or getting your combos disrupted and punching empty air. I'm not against games that require practice. The mark of a good game (as in: VVVVVV) is that the player increases in skill until they can tackle challenges that seemed impossible before. As Guacamelee ramps up the complexity, the game never stops feeling fiddly.
There are other sources of needless complexity; some checkpoints are savepoints and some aren't, and you should pay attention to which is which. After a difficult fight, you won't have to do the fight again if you die, but you still need to seek out a savepoint if you want to leave the game. Depending on which you find more challenging, you may be forced to go through a combat sequence to finally save your progress in the game's tricky platforming. The shop system isn't really worth discussing, having three different fracking ways to reduce the stamina cooldown and yet more extra combos.
The overall presentation is metroidvania, which means you traverse a set of maps using platforming and combat, but the game is actually very linear. If you explore the rest of the map you end up frustrated because you haven't unlocked the right combo or ability. The very few side-objectives always require you to advance the main objective; after hours of play I can remember four side-missions and just two that I could finish. Dust: an Elysian Tail is a much better metroidvania in every respect: fast and fluid movement and combat, diverse nonlinear missions, voice acting and so on.
tl;dr don't waste time on this game, it gets unplayable fast. Pick a game that knows what it wants to do and does it well.

This game really came as a surprise to me, and really opened my eyes to how great we have it as PC gamers. I got this game in the HB11, which at the very least, put this game's value at $0.25. This not only made my expectations of the game really low, but it also came as a very nice treat when I played it for the first time and saw its true colors.
The game itself is very well-done, especially when it was one of only three games that Gearbox Studios has developed. It is a Metroid-vania style action-platformer with a hint of Mexican flair. I was not too fond of these kinds of games, but Guacamelee! really opened the door to me as a gamer, and I really enjoyed everything about it. The story was always on the side, but it kept me entertained enough to keep playing through different stages and not get too worn out. The implementation of these wrestling moves as different ways to get around really had me pondering whether or not I would have to come back into an area later in the game or if a certain puzzle was skippable.
The only flaws that I had with the game were the spikes in difficulty at the very end and grinding sessions. Don't get me wrong, the developers did a great job of mixing in platforming with combat, but there were certain areas in the game, such as orb 3 &4, that took me around 45 minutes each. These areas were not Super Meat Boy-esque, but the jump in difficulty suddenly was a huge weight on your shoulders. For both of those areas, along with the last two bosses, I had to look up a strategy online to beat them, as nothing early in the game prepares you for that. On the bright side, though, these acheivements were within grasp, a lot more so than games that put hour limits and nearly impossible missions on the list.
Overall, I had a great time with this game, and would recommend it for anyone, really. The game itself has many great parts to it that any gamer can enjoy, with or without the pain of some optional missions.

Let's get this out right now, this game is complex, definitely NOT for the casual space shooter fan. You may see reviews on here saying there is no tutorial, well there is a tutorial free roam scenario designed to be played along with a written tutorial document included. This is a game from the days when you had to read a whacking great manual and tackle a learning curve that was very steep. Once it is learned, however, it opens up a whole galaxy to explore and a myriad of options and things to do. Want to fly around the galaxy looking for a fight? It's here. Want to land troops on a planet with tanks and fighter planes to assault an enemy stronghold? That's here too. Want to take control of those vehicles on the planet surface and get stuck in yourself? Yep you can! You can even land your huge capital ship on any planet/moon and get out for a stroll around taking in the sights. There's trading and mining here as well as salvage from destroyed ships, towing ships in distress to a star station for help, real time movement of crew around the ship, full control of power distribution to all systems on your ship, teleporter to transport men/cargo down to a planet surface, and evac them from the planet and so much more.
This game has it all from capital ship command to slugging it out on planets or even the hull of your ship in first person mode, naval vessels and space fighters which can also be flown in the planet's atmosphere to support your ground troops.
All this from an indie dev team in the early noughties! The version here on Steam is an overhauled and remastered version of the original 2009 Collectors Edition and to have it here for free is nothing short of amazing. What have you got to lose? Download it now, you won't regret it!!

Lets start with the bottom line.  This game is awesome.  It does have a learning curve, it can get confusing, and if you're afraid of a little light reading, it's probably not for you.  Don't expect to be able to jump in and fumble your way through figuring out what button does what, and be blasting ships out of the cosmos in five minutes.  This isn't Halo.  It's a simulator, and the effort and energy went into allowing you to control and actively manage a huge spaceship, it's crew, and to play with the most dynamic and brilliantly crafted AI I've ever seen.  The graphics and sound effects are not as pretty as others, like Evochron, but despite that, the immersion and enjoyment I personally experience from this game rivals that of GTA 5.  It's an open universe, and you can pretty much do whatever you want.  And though it's not as pretty, there is a lot more of this game to experience than any of it's "competition" in the space sim genre.  If you intend to try this game, which I recommend you do, judge it after you complete the tutorial, and realize that this game is an iceburg.

I feel like this game is a complete letdown and I will explain why:
- First; The Coaster builder is terrible. Yes, they added the familiar piece-by-piece building that we all know form the original games. Which is fine. The spline based coaster builder is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The main issue that I have is that the piece you are forming is attached to the camera. So when I'm building a coaster, have the piece where I want it, and want to check from another angle I can't because the piece will slide along.  Furthermore, I've spend 10 minutes to tweak the brakes in order to make the coaster pass the test. I don't want to spend 10 minutes on tweaking the brakes; in real life if a coaster has it's desired speed it will open the brakes and let the train pass through. The stations are troublesome too as I can't change the length of them. So if I want to have a compact coaster I can't because the station is gicantic. Other strange things will happen to your coaster as well in freeform mode; supports where going straight through the tracks and my axes where inverted at some point so every new piece I placed was all messed up. The experience was just frustrating.
- Realism is not great too. I don't think the developers took any time watching real rides and Roller Coasters, because if they did the game would look completely different. Some rides that are included do not even exist in real life, whereas all of the rides in the previous installments did. Even more, the Roller Coasters look afwul too. They remind me of the toy Coaster Dynamix models, with the supports being constructed by plumbers. I'm a mechanical engineer myself so I know what works and what doesn't. What we're seeing in RCTW doesn't work in real life and that bothers me a lot.
- All rides look more like they belong on a carinval instead of a theme park.
- The lack of water rides. Where are the log flumes, the rapid rivers etc? I mean, come on, those are essential ride in theme parks! Why aren't these in the game?
- The path system is a mess as well. Paths won't connect to the places I want them. In the previous installments you could snap paths together to make a plaza, this isn't possible in this game either. Also the three widthts are way too limited.
- The guests look terrible. Even horror movies are less scarier than these mutants. They can't be drowned as well, but I'm not counting that.
And finally, but most important: The game is missing all the charm that the previous installments had. And I think that is the part where this game really dissapoints me most. A utter shame, luckily I can still play the old versions and I will continue to do so as this piece of empty software is not worth both my time and my attention. I was done with this game within half an hour and I believe that says enough.

The experimental units actually felt experimental, you couldn’t build that many without a massive compromise to your economy. In SC2, you roll them out like normal T3 units, probably with the same build time as well.
I personally was expecting more from this game considering where it came from. I do dislike this game because I really wanted a progression from SC:FA, it was the only one of its kind. I think I wouldn’t have been offending if it didn’t use the title “Supreme Commander”.
Final words, if you are new to this title and want some good ol RTS action, buy it now. If you are a vet from the previous games, just save yourself the disappointment. I’m currently following “Ashes of the singularity”, it appears to be what SC:FA fans wanted. I am a bit concerned with the point control system though. We’ll see how it pans out.

Payday: The Heist
Developer: Overkill Software
Publisher: Sony Online Entertainment
Release date: 18th October of 2011
Genre: First-person shooter
---------------------------------------
Payday: The Heist is a cooperative shooter, that means that you won't be fighting against people but AI, that means the game is an excellent choice for friends. But you are limited to only 4 people, which is not bad, but could be more, but as every other game, this game has seen better days, as in time of this review, there are barely any people left playing, and you can hardly find a lobby with more than 2 people. The game also has a variety of weapons, but not much heists so it will get old quick. In the heists you fight againsts law enforcers and sometimes even gangsters but those are limited to only few missions. There are a few of special units which all can be annoying at times but serve their purpose. There are 4 playable characters, Dallas, Hoxton, Wolf and Chains. Dallas is an american, Hoxton is british, Wolf is swedish and Chains is a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Each of these characters have their own masks, which are range from the iconic clown masks to president masks. Not all are unlocked, so you will have to figure out how to unlock them on your own, or just look up a guide. There si a variety of weapons, but there is a DLC which will be my next review which adds more weapons and heists. The weapons are in three categories, Primary, Secondary and Handguns and in heists you have one of each of these weapons, so you sure aren't short of firepower. Primaries: AMCAR-4 which is an assault rifle, Reinbeck, which is a shotgun, Brenner 21, which is a light machine gun and M308, which is a sniper rifle. Secondaries: Compact-5, which is a submachine gun, Mark 11, which is a submachine gun and Locomotive 12G which is a shotgun. Handguns: Crosskill .45 which is a pistol, B9-S which is a pistol and Bronco .44 which is a revolver. The game also features skill trees where you can upgrade those weapons and gain also more ablities. These skill trees are Assault, Sharpshooter, Support and Technician. The player also has deployables, which can also be upgraded in the skill trees, those deployables are Doctor Bag, Ammo Bag, Trip Mine and a Sentry gun. Those skill trees also include Player upgrades and Crew bonuses which need to be equipped, Player upgrades are Thick Skin, which increases health, Toolkit, which reduces time to complete an action, Extra cable ties, which are used to tie civilians, Extra start-out ammo, which is self-explanatory. Crew bonuses are Sharpshooters, which decreases weapon spread, Agressor, which increases weapon damage, Big game hunters, which increases amount of ammo, Protector, which increases armor, More blood to bleed, which increases bleed out time, Speed reloaders, which decreases weapon reload time, Mr Nice Guy, which increases cash reward and Noob lube, which increases also cash reward. All of these things you equip while joining a lobby, not in the main menu, which is kind of an annoyance, but it isn't too bad. There is not much heists, but for a few hours of fun it will do. The heists are: First World Bank, Panic Room, Diamond Heist, Green Bridge, Heat Street, Slaughterhouse and No Mercy. The gameplay is simple, you shoot cops and complete objectives. If a player gets downed, he will enter bleed out which is a countdown and if the countdown finishes before the player is revived by a teammate, he will enter custody and needs to be traded for a civilian or a dominated law enforcer to respawn. The player has certain amounts of downs, 3 to be exact and if the player gets downed after being down three times, he will enter custody. There are also assault waves, which is a time when you can't trade hostages or dominate cops and there is a ridiculous amount of cop spawns, assault waves normally lasts around a few minutes. There are also the special units, which are cops with special abilities, which are The Shield, which is just a cop with a shield, The Tazer which has the ability to taze a player sending them into a state where they can't move and will fire constantly, if they can't kill the tazer they will be downed. The Bulldozers, which is like a tank, The Sniper which is just a sniper on high buildings which can be seen with his enormous red laser, and at last is the Cloaker, which is a unit that walk slowly and emits a loud screeching sound when it targets a player, when the unit targets a player, it will sprint towards the player and if it makes contact with the player the player will be instantly downed. There are a few difficulties, which are Normal, Hard, Overkill and Overkill 145+. The highest level a player can reach is 145.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall rating: 2/3
Final verdict: Good game, has it's flaws, dead playerbase. If you have 4 friends or 3, buy it, if not, ehhhhh, you can miss out on this game.

This is the first of the Penumbra Series.
I was an avid fan of Amnesia: the Dark Descent, and wanted to try another Frictional Games piece.
This game is somewhat disappointing.
Without giving away too much of the story:
- There is only one or two types of enemies during the entirety of the game, making their patterns highly predictable and once you find a way to exploit their terrible AI, they fail to present any challenges.
-  The story is written as if an edgy teen indie team created it. The story must be intentionally vague, as (SPOILERS) the ending literally finishes with "to be continued." As a player, you never actually know what's going on. Sure, you know where you are and that you want to escape and how you got to where you are: the basics. The more you play, however, the more unanswered questions you end up with.
- I want to give this piece the benefit of the doubt and consider the entire series in my review; perhaps the second and third games answer all of these questions and creates a fantastically crafted story. Unfortunately, the first game alone does not produce that faith in me.
Although the game is an older "classic," the story and mechanics are ridiculously simple, repetitive, and ultimately boring. Perhaps after the other games, I will feel better about the series, but this game is not worth playing alone.
--EDIT--
The remainder of this review is after I have completed the second game - Black Plague
I will reserve my criticism for that specific review, but because the sequel answers many questions and is a good game, Overture is a necessary evil for the means of continuity in the series.
Long story short, Black Plague is far better than this game, but you should play this too for the best effect.

To finish, i really recomend this game if you appreciate a simple game who can give to you a special experience using puzzles and the Survival Horrors mechanisms.

TL;DR:This unique but short FMV game/interactive fiction gave a few hours of gameplay (and deveral more hours pondering what really transpired) and is well worth getting on sale
This is a found-footage puzzle game based on a database of full motion video clips of a British woman being interviewed at a police station. The game play appears to be on a windowed desktop from a late-90's computer system with a CRT monitor. You search the database of video clips using key words. The video clips that you can watch are only those retrieved by the keyword search, so choosing the right keywords is important. Figuring out what is going on in the videos is part of the puzzle. Figuring out *how* to figure this out is another part. There is very little hand-holding here. Be prepared to have a notebook to help keep track of things. Maybe the devs could have added a notebook program in game, but it's no big loss (I just run in windowed mode and keep a notepad window open). All of the lady's dialog is subtitled, so it is no problem to play with the audio off (but you miss her melodious voice).
Even after you think you know what went on, even after you think you've finished the game, you'll find yourself going back several times and changing your mind.
The only downside I can see is the gameplay itself is on the short side -- you spend more time puzzling over everything that transpired.
The actress (Viva Seifert) does a good job with what she has to work with. There is pleasant piano background music as a soundtrack. The game costs a few bucks and periodically goes on sale. Well worth it!
EDIT: I can't stress this enough: when you play the game, keep some notes. The smallest thing might be important. Think of it as old-fashioned detective work. I have a complete index of the videos in the guides section, taken from my gameplay notes.
EDIT2: Lead actress Viva Seifert has a pretty impressive wikipedia page for non-acting stuff, check it out if you're curious.
EDIT3: Whatever you do, don't hit the "Delete Session Data" button unless you want to start the entire game over...(there's a saved game folder mentioned in the pinned discussions, you can transfer your game in progress to another computer this way)

This game brings back memories.  Yes, it had a troubled release back in 1996 but blame Gametek for that one.  There's not another game in existence that creates this kind of immersive world in a fully modeled futuristic starship along with planetary surfaces, planetary bases, space stations, and moons.  I can land my ship, or take a shuttle, or beam down the surface for a leisurely stroll across a beach or I can drop in with my Marines for a full blown assault on an enemy base.
Or I can just hang out on my bridge and "nuke the site from orbit."
And that's the endless possibilities of free roam.  I haven't touched on the scripted campaign which can be tough as nails but incredibly fun and rewarding.  The massive space stations that will blow you to pieces with a burst of their weapons, the fact that I can hop into a fighter and duke it out while my capital ship supports me.
Oh, there's also fleet command and control, trading, capturing starstations, ship to ship combat, trading, mining, powerful artifacts that can turn your ship from kick-butt to kick♥♥♥♥♥♥and-take-names-without-breaking-a-sweat style.
This game is complex and it requires some time investment to learn the concepts and the systems.  If it helps, think of this game as "Falcon 4.0" in space only you aren't flying an F-16 but a half mile long starship with fighters, shuttles, marines, landing craft.  There's a plethora of resources from a well-written manual, tutorial videos, and in game help but make no mistake this is a game that will require some learning but its oh so rewarding.
Don't let my steam playtime fool you, I started playing this game in 1998 with the release of BC3K 2.0 and I can safely say that in the past 17 years no other game has come close to doing what this one does.  If you want to be in command of a futuristic starship (don't think Captain Kirk....this ain't no wimpy Enterprise...more like William Adama) with entire fleets to command and stations to blow up and planetary surfaces to fight on then this game is for you.

So.....this game.
Putting aside any personal isssues with Derek Smart (and let's be honest, a lot of people have issues with him), let's try to be as objective as possible in this review...
What exactly is UC and does it live up to its claims?
It's a 'do anything in space' simulator. You want to command a battlecruiser? Check. You want to be a Marine on a planet shooting stuff? Check. You want to fly from a planet to space and dock with that carrier you see over there? Check.
The problem is...well....the problems are...
One: Excessive micro management: Why for instance, should the commander of a large ship have to manually set power levels? Why can't....say....the crrew AI do that for you and if you want to then alter it, you can? By default, there isnt't enough power to go around and you have to go in and manually set it. Or, say you want to send....I don't know, four Marines and a tank and a pilot to a planet. You have to tell each individual what to do. There's no group option.
Two: HUD issues. The HUD itself isn't intuitive at all, the three MFDs at the bottom of the screen don't easily tell you what they are, the radar is 2d, not 3D and that is confusing as well as you got no clue if the enemy target is above or blow you.
Three: Questionable vehicle physics. Why should a shuttle be able to stop on a dime in space? I can understand tanks or ATVs stopping quickly on a planet, that makes sense, however...a shuttle, in space, you cut the power and it instantly stops? Really? Yes, I'm aware it's explained away as some technical stuff but that's an easy and cheap way to get around the issue.
So what are the good points then given I've laid out some issues with it?
One: You can literally go anywhere and do anything you want to. For instance in a free roaming scenario, I have taken a battlecruiser from Ear to the Moon, landed troops, done exercises, got picked up by the shuttle and flown back, all without cutscenes or scripting.
Two: It's seamless once it loads. Yep that's a big, big plus. You want to go from planet to space? Get above a certain height and push a button, then confirm it (again....micro management issues but....), there's a few seconds worth of animation and you're in space. Same for going to a planet.s, get close, it'll ask establish planetfall, say yes,a nd sit back.
It's pretty. Oh yes it is, it's some of the most atmospheric graphics in a space game....and you feel as if you can actually go to that nebula, or that planet....or even that base and dock there
You are not the hero. Okay, this is  astrange one but....most games are all about the player, right? Well, UC, CE isn't. There's an entire universe going on, things happen regardless of you being around or not. You can be in a system and go off for a few days, come back and find that station you were docked at got attacked and changed hands, or there's a war on a planet that broke out while you were going there.
However....I personally wouldn't recommend it unless you want to spend a LOT of time reading and learning. It's not a simple pick up and play game in the least, it takes time, dedication and (sadly) figuring things out on your own so you don't have to deal with Derek Smart to enjoy it. Don't get me wrong, once you like it, it's definitely good but I do feel many, many people will be put off by Derek Smart and won't even look at it.
If UC was made by somebody else and released on Steam for free, it would get a much, much better reception, I can absolutely say that for certain.
Either way, although this has not recommended at  the top, try try it out. Make up your own mind and be prepared for a lot of reading and learning too.
The scale has always tickled my imagination, and I have come back many times over the years to gawk at the ambition.

It's been a while, but I have to say that I feel some people still aren't giving the game enough credit for what it was--/is/ to this day.
2K screwed the pooch on Battleborn, but its developers are still plugging away at the game, hoping to please whatever crowd they have left. It's dedication, and it's something that's pretty respectable in this day and age with developers abandoning their projects as soon as they're out the door.
Battleborn is a MOBA, plain and simple, but it also possesses a fairly interesting story mode with a new Operation dropping soon (Oct. 13). It's some of the most fun I've ever had in a game like it, and all it needs is a sizable number of people willing to play it.
Recently, an anonymous source tipped off Kotaku and Polygon that there's a chance it's going free to play by the end of the year. Of course, Randy Pitchfork denied this, but . . . when has anything he's ever said been proven to be true? He said that The Pre-Sequel would never, ever, not in a million years go to next gen consoles, but it did. High hopes in that regard. The source also noted that Gearbox wanted it to be free to play to begin with, but 2K "suggested" pricing it for $60 dollars, and in that state, I can't say I recommend it right this second.
I'm cautiously optimistic. If you see it with 40% off, I'd say go for it, but you really might be better off waiting for it to go FTP.

- Heroes always getting Balanced

While somewhat interesting in concept, I can't really recommend this game, as it essentially lacks much of anything of interest to actually *DO*.  You start play plunked down on a gray world full of trees, and are functionally tasked with making it a colorful world by bumping colored trees, rolling over their colorful fruits, and then spreading that color to other trees. Your color fades to gray after a dozen or so moves, so you have to bump another tree.  Rinse and repeat.  And repeat. And repeat. And repeat for hours on end...
As you roll around, you collect random collectables that you collect because you get an achievement for collecting them all.  (Unless they disappear because some random critter activated the object outside your sight range, and then you can never collect 100%.)
The game world is huge, which is something of a negative, because, with gameplay from start to finish basically consisting of just bumping trees and spreading color, I ran out of interest in the game before I could cover the world in color or get any of my completion.  There's a "mystery" to uncover by collecting journal bits, but it just doesn't have enough suspense or reason for players to care to carry the player to the finish line.  Unlike a lot of other reviewers, I actually managed to decypher the language... and was not particularly impressed by the results.  It's a simple symbol-to-letter cypher that is made even easier with each line starting with Roman Numerals, but the need to click through each symbol is *HIGHLY* tedious, yet served as a distraction from a tedious game... No wonder so many people quit with lower hours played than I have.

The Indie Platformer genre is one of my personal favorites so as you might imagine I was excited when I found out that The Floor is Jelly was on sale in the Humble Store. The game looks beautiful from the very beginning and the music, which changes as you progress through each uniquely designed zone, is best described as relaxing. While the controls handle well, it was initially difficult to get used to them due to the nature of the "jelly" floors, walls, and ceilings. The minimal astheitic accompanied by tranquil melodies really does wonders for this platformer.
Now that the positives are out of the way, I can honestly say that I will not be recommending this game at it's ten dollar price point. The options menu, unfortunately, lacks numerous features including the ability to change the resolution and rebind hotkeys. More importantly, it is not worth spending the game's full price tag when you find yourself stuck in a wall after only 11 minutes of gameplay. Common sense tells me that I should be able to open the menu and restart the level. For whatever reason, there is no such option. For a game of this genre, a simple level restart feature that you can bind to a key is a must.
Restarting the game fixed the glitch and respawned me back at my previous checkpoint. After roughly 20 more minutes I stumbled upon another glitch. The new checkpoint where the game had me saved had no ground below it causing me to continuously fall to my death upon each respawn. Restarting the game has no effect as there is no way to switch checkpoints or restart the level. The only solution is to clear my save file and start again from the beginning. Unbelievable.
Evidently, there is a workaround which you can find
that involves 3rd party save editors. However, this should not be necessary for a game with a Metacritic score of 81.
It is unfortunate that my experience with The Floor is Jelly has been a negative one. If you decide to pick this game up, do so when it is on sale and pray that you don't get stuck.

. No title describes what this game developed by Ian Snyder is really about more. This is a platformer game where you control a little tiny human guy and guide him through each level, with each level split up into several rooms connected by windows.
Your little guy can jump around, and can climb up walls by jumping up them like in the
games. It doesn't sound that simple, though. Whereas other platform games took place on
, in
, well, the ground acts exactly like that. As you move around, the ground beneath your feet violently wobbles and jiggles around like a gigantic waterbed. It's not just the ground that flings around, too. Even the walls and ceilings ripples and bounces as you wall jump and hit the ceilings retrospectively. It's not all bad, however. You can take advantage of the wobbly ground by using it as a trampoline, but you'll need to time your jumps right or your bounce may fall flat. It may take you a while to get used to these bouncy castle physics, but soon enough, you'll be bounding around like a pro.
There's no enemies or monsters to fight, but there are plenty of hazards along the way. Each level is strewn with bottomless pits and dark purple spiky blobs, and if you fall or hit them retrospectively, you'll be sent back to the entrance of the room. Thankfully, there's no lives to worry about or anything, and you restart very quickly as well, which is good.
The puzzles are well done as well. For example, very early on in the game, you'll come across a spiky wall which you cannot seemingly pass. You'll have to bounce on the ground next to it and then use the resulting ripples in the ground to quickly run underneath it. Had the world have been solid and not bouncy, this wall would have been outright impossible to get past. Each level also has their own gimmicks as well; two stages have water where your gravity is reversed underneath the surface, and you'll need to utilise the resulting momentum to get through their rooms at times. Another level sees you rotating several structures to let rain water reach white plants while trying to keep 'catflowers' out of the rain at the same time. Another level has platforms that only become solid while you're touching one at a time, allowing you to slide down or walk across into the inside of another platform, which then becomes inverse-solid in which the outside is solid and inside is air. Some levels are less linear than others, these levels require you to explore to find a certain number of 'keys' that will open a portal that leads to the exit.
After reaching the end of the first level, you'll come to an underground cavern which serves as the game's central hub. As you make your way through this bouncy cavern, you'll come across a large locked door, and you'll need to beat the three levels that this cave branches out to in order to unlock it. Through this door is a darker cavern that branches out to three more levels, and after beating them, you'll unlock another door that leads to the final two stages.
The final two stages is where the game starts to get more tedious. In the second-to-last level, you must jump around in low gravity to find three keys at the end of three separate sections to unlock the portal. It sounds simple at first, but then as you grab each key, the way back becomes riddled with... I won't spoil it entirely here, but let's just say 'instakill hazards' on the same lines as spikes. These hazards are erratically placed, and often requires trial and error in knowing where they are, leading to a few deaths. The final stage itself is no better, with most rooms requiring sheer luck rather than skill to get through.
There's also a few secrets hidden around the world as well. There's 31 in total, and each contains a house that contains a terminal. Activating all 31 terminals unlocks a neat secret that's fun to mess around with. However, there's 6 terminals that can be permanently missed in the second-to-last level as you start collecting those three keys, and with no warning or indication that this is the case until it's too late, it's pretty frustrating to have to restart your save file.
The aesthetics here are amazing. The environments are beautiful and dreamlike, the wobbling of the ground is very fluid, and the interactivity is incredible due to the world's bouncy properties. Objects like trees and bushes sway and move with the wobbling ground as you bounce around, and in two of the levels, if you bounce next to a tree or bush, the sudden movement of the tree or bush may scare off any birds nesting in them and then they'll fly off to a more stable tree or bush. There's other neat stuff, too, like frogs making wobbles in the ground as they hop around in the underground hub level, and the rain in the Wetlands level makes the ground constantly jiggle as each raindrop pounds down onto it. The houses in the secret areas are built on stilts, and even wobble around as you jump onto them as well as onto the ground underneath. There's also a neat window effect that let's you see their randomly generated interiors as you get close, but disappointingly, their furniture stays fixed in place, no matter how much the house wobbles. Each level is also accompanied by a beautiful soundtrack, most of which is written by Disasterpeace, known for his work on music in other games like
.
Unfortunately, some effects could cause slowdown at certain times, such when more intricately generated houses are onscreen. The initial Humble Bundle release allowed you to switch to lower quality graphics in the options menu to help eliminate some slowdown, but that option seems to be missing in the Steam release.
Despite it's playful physics and unique platformer gameplay,
is over way too soon. A level editor would have been amazing, with the ability to create our own jelly worlds and share them online, but it's very unlikely we'll see one anytime soon.
Pros:
+ The whole world is bouncy!
+ Varied stages.
+ Soothing music by Disasterpeace.
+ Bouncy worlds!
+ Dreamlike environments.
+ Some well hidden secrets.
+ Some of the bounciest landscapes and caves in videogame history.
+ No lives to run out of, and very quick restarts.
+
wobbling effects on the terrain, and how the background objects wobble and move around with it.
+ Did I mention bouncy worlds? Because the world is bouncy.
Cons:
- Some slowdown in some areas.
- No low quality graphics mode.
- No level editor.
- Secrets in the second-to-last level are permanently missable, with no warning given.
- Final stage relies too much on luck rather than skill most of the time.

Mind you, this is not game breaking, but I'm just peeved the developer wasn't upfront about this and would like to highlight this to others.
So yeah, from the short time I've spent on it, the game is something unique. 2D indie platformers are a dime a dozen, but this can stand tall and distinguish itself from the horde.
UPDATE: Having completed the game, I would say it was disappointing overall, but not outright bad. A lot of nice touches (the visual aesthetic especially) but the game didn't have a hook. It just didn't draw me in. I don't have any problems with the relatively short length, but this was a game that felt...empty. There was no soul here, for me at least. Given I went in with lofty expectations, I naturally come out disappointed. Would still rate it around 6/10, so it still gets a thumbs up from me.
