I tried playing Amnesia multiple times but was terribly bored and not sacred (though I could never last long enough to get to anything that actually happened I guess). I was afraid that Penumbra: Overture would be similar, but luckily it was not.
The graphics are not amazing by any means, but this almost just adds to the creepy atmosphere of the game. In fact, most of the horror elements of the game are just by sheer creep-factor, suspense, and tension alone. The story and atmosphere do most of the work, but they do it pretty well.
Combat is a little difficult - weapons are melee-only and swing pretty slowly. Weapons movements are not very fluid, but once you get used to it it's not terrible.
Overall, it's worth playing, but know that you have to continue on to the next games in the series to get any sort of conclusion to the story (based on having just finished Overture, apparently the first in the series).
One thing though - a lot of the combining inventory items and figuring puzzles out seemed almost impossibly difficult. I don't use walkthroughs very often at all, but I did for the majority of this game, and I have no idea how anyone could get through it without a walkthrough. Maybe I was impatient, but I think I definitely would have simply stopped playing the game if I wasn't 1) brought in by how scary it was and 2) the ability to use a walkthrough - otherwise I definitely would have put the game down and wouldn't have bothered. It's just not the type of game you *want* to spend tons of time on - you just want to play it. Perhaps I should play through Amnesia with a walkthrough...

Penumbra: Overture is the first in a series of horror games released in early 2007. While the developers like to class this as a first person adventure game, I would also say there is quite a lot of elements of survival horror and psychological horror.
The game uses a game engine called Newton Game Dynamics which is known for it's physical and realistic simulations. The adventure portion of the game focused a lot on physics based puzzles as well as a physics based combat system (i'll get more into that later). You can also play a lot of this game as stealthy as possible. The AI in Overture is well coded and respond realistically to noises and light.  There are also no guns or fire arms so your combat mechanics are based around manual weapons such as hammers and pick axes.
The combat system is the one aspect that I disliked to begin with; it is very hard to control as you actually have to swipe your mouse in the movement you would like to hit the enemy. It can sometimes get very confusing and you may end up turning your camera 180° without wanting to, then getting smacked in the back of the head, which at times can be the difference between life and death.  I found I was able to get to grips with the technique eventually, it just took a lot of actual conscious thinking when I needed to use it. It's certainly not a mechanic I would like to see implemented in other games, at least not in this form.
Your main focus when playing is on exploration and classic  adventure game object and item interactions.  Most of the puzzles require searching for keys or other objects which can be placed in another object, such as batteries or motors. All of the puzzles resolution can all be found in the game; there are no wacky puzzles that are really impossible to work out. Clues can be found in books and letters, which again are found all over the game. The game is split into four chapters, each of these chapters has one "big" puzzle which may stump you for a while, they normally involve some sort of maneuvering of some kind, for instance my favorite is a steam pump floor and you have to memorize the pattern in which steam is pumped out of the floor, that puzzle alone takes a ton of thinking and memory skills to progress.
Graphically, Overture looks like a 2007 game, this is not a bad thing - it's just very dated. At the time this would of been a very good looking game. There are however fan made texture mods which make the game look amazing, and if you are confident in installing these type of mods, I would highly recommend giving it a try.
As with most horror games, the music and audio plays a massive role in Penumbra. Like I said at the start, this game has a lot of physiological horror elements. At times there isn't actually anything physically to be scared of, however the music tempo changes and suddenly you start hearing thumping sounds, then all of a sudden you are on the edge of your seat wanting to throw your headset on the floor. Penumbra does the audio side of things brilliantly; in fact if you we to play the game without sound on at all, it wouldn't even be remotely scary.
The story mode of Penumbra took me about four hours to complete, which is a solid amount of time for a adventure game like this and I was ultimately happy with the conclusion. Luckily you don't have to pay for each of the games in the series individually, so the price for all three is very well compromised with the length of the game.
I didn't have any technical issues with the game either, the game runs at a silky smooth 60 fps, and can be played at full higher resolutions which is always nice to see from older games.
If you are a fan of the horror and/or the adventure genre of games, you will certainly find alot of enjoyment in Penumbra. This is certainly a series that I am looking forward to playing the next installments of in the future.

It's not an actual game - in the traditional video gaming sense - but more like an interactive story (which is definitely clear from the cover pic, the previews and the game tags).
Anyhow, I'd seen this title flash by before but I hadn't ever given it much thought, because I was afraid it wouldn't be my thing.
Funny enough, it turned out to be *exactly* my thing. It's the string of themes that were revealed in the interviews that really did it for me.
The actress did an impeccable job at playing her role. She really portrayed the main character well (i.e. the gestures, the facial expressions, tone of voice).
I was not familiar with her before, but I was definitely impressed by her performance (it is what kept me going and going, even though I had - prematurely - discovered a very important bit of the plot due to stumbling upon a video clip that revealed key information in regard to the core plot).
That was quite disappointing, but thanks to the actress, I really felt like continuing nonetheless.
About the character; there is something odd about the way she expresses herself in some of the clips - a certain inconsistency - which at some point becomes obvious why that is (this isn't a game flaw mind you, it's meant to be that way).
At first, the story is scrambled and very confusing. Some video clips don't seem to make sense - what is revealed sounds rather cryptic or just very neutral - and not exactly alarming - because as the player you discover bits and pieces of "her story" by browsing through the local police office's database, in a non-linear fashion.
You type whatever comes to mind (based on the information shared in the videos) and then see where it leads you as you type some keywords (so as to unlock more clips).
And as such, the action in game is limited to typing keywords on a PC screen at the office (and perhaps taking notes on a pad).
It's really too bad there wasn't any interaction outside the PC and the video clips.
After I finished up I did feel satisfied, but then again I have a great sense of imagination, so story-rich content works well for me, without needing all that much action.
The lack of interactivity could pose a problem to players who really do need to be doing something more elaborate in order to feel entertained.
This is really one of those titles that either feels like a hit or a miss. There's no gray area. Either you like it or you don't.
It's quite an interesting experience nonetheless. That's what it's meant to be = an engaging experience (story-wise).
I feel content, but I believe a lot more could have been implemented.
If it wasn't for my natural inclination towards wanting/needing to know stuff to satisfy my curiosity, I wouldn't have enjoyed it as much.
keywords: cycle of life, death, birth, mystery, detective, legacy, intrigue
PS I've heard one of the music tracks in game before, but I cannot remember for the life of me where! There's this melancholic yet hopeful vibe to this tune and I'm trying to remember but I just can't!
It's one of those tunes that was picked from a free music database, that's why.
PPS I finally remembered where I heard one of the in-game soundtracks before: Youtube = Study Music

There's a few points to be made about Her Story; some caveats, if you will.
I have absolutely nothing against non-linear storytelling, or at the very least, has you play it in a nonlinear fashion. I'm a fan of movies like Memento and A Normal Lost Phone has a similar concept and mechanic, and I quite enjoyed that game. The problem is that I felt Her Story's execution was somewhat sloppy.
You primarily, first run, going to get videos through the utilization of keywords. The issue for this is that you lose the concext of when this was said. It doesn't help that there are utterly mundane and irrelevant points that simply serve to confuse things further (I'm all for versimilitude, but utilize it in a way that doesn't hamper my enjoyment, thanks?) And without context, you are going to be flying around collecting disparate information and trying to piece it together. And I simply found that tedious in Her Story's case, particularly since I had to figure out when exactly people were saying what and what was irrelevant and what was just noise.
I disagree that the ending is meaningless, as some critical reviews have claimed, but I do wish that if you're going to have a stinger at the end like that, the character in question had been explored a little more and I had more of a reaction than just "Oh, it's them."
There's games for people and not for others. And I guess Her Story, despite my desire to enjoy it, just wasn't for me.

If you've never played the Hitman games, get this one. If you have played 'em, but haven't played this one, get this one.
Hitman Blood Money is one of those games that people really disliked when it came out, but really pine after years later.
It's a strange old game, and there's a few interesting quirks that you'll quickly notice and probably find funny.
Let's start with the Gameplay, as that's where HBM really shines.
The reason Hitman games are so fun are because of what they require from the player; an inimitable combination of patience, problem solving and timing. HBM is without a doubt the pinnacle of this 'watch, plan, wait, execute' style of gameplay.
The infinitely replayable open-ended structure of each of the levels, the scaled timing of each individual NPC's movements and routines, the strange and often unexpected events that randomly catch you off guard and the peculiar brand of dark humour, subtle social satire and movie cliches that fills the game are what make HBM such a classic.
My favourite way of playing this game is to enter a level, then explore it, sneak through the restricted areas using disguises or distractions, find the target(s) and watch their every move, plan a way of offing them to make it look like an accident, then casually walk to the escape route whilst nobody's any the wiser to your involvement, and the newspapers that 'review' your performance afterward just list an accident as opposed to a murder or a killing spree.
Ah, but i suppose there are a few downsides to the game, and as most players of Hitman know, this comes as no surprise.
The physics engine can be (and has always been in any Hitman game) a bit eccentric; There are times that the limbs of K.O. characters flop about uncontrollably if they're being dragged on uneven ground, and occasionally objects clip through parts of the environment in strange and egregious ways. thankfully none of this is game breaking, merely peculiar.
The AI can also go a bit screwy on occasion; enemies seeing through disguises can every once in a blue moon happen unexpectedly with no underlying cause, enemies can become suspicious of you even when there's no reason to be, or my favourite, security guys opening fire into a crowd of civilians you're suspected of escaping through (oh, wait.. they do that in the new one too :p).
The graphics are nothing to write home about; they were pretty impressive back in 2006, but now they're considered dated and quirky (all the guys have muscles, all the girls have huge implants.. no idea why). HBM should pretty much run on anything of the last 8 or 9 years.. (egad, has it been that long already?)
The Audio is pretty good. The soundtrack is very atmospheric, thanks to Jesper Kyd et al. The SFX are pretty standard and the voice acting is nice'n'hammy, which is just what you want from a Hitman game.
The Storyline is surprisingly good. There are two seperate narrative strands that meet up right at the end for a climactic finish.
To Summarise, if you're the kind of person that wants an immersive, challenging game that involves careful planning, clever distractions and devious, underhanded tactics, then look no further. HBM is a game full of little secrets, subtle jokes and peculiar quirks; it's a game that rewards you for your patience, and lets you play it how you want to.
In HBM you can be the Sam Fisher style assassin sneaking in, doing the dirty deed and leaving, or you can be Chow Yun-Fat running in with your dual pistols and fancy suit, capping every bad guy in sight, but you can also be anything in between (as long as you terminate your targets and don't die! :p)

This is the best Hitman game currently for sale. Obviously some of the controls and gameplay mechanics are a little dated, and the graphics are definitely showing their age, but the level design, options for dealing with each mission, and no-BS mission delivery system are all superb.
The levels are huge, freely roamable, and logical. Stealth is rewarded but if you're just trying to finish the game, outright violence works fine, too. As long as you get the job done.
Free of the goofy cartoonish personalities and faux-dramatic emotional story of Absolution, Blood Money's story takes a backseat to the actual mechanics of hunting people down and killing them. How you complete the job is up to you, as it should be. Plan your own route, choose your equipment, observe and recon before taking action.
The downsides: some of the controls take some getting used to, the AI has some unexpected behaviours (which usually result in them shooting you for some infraction you weren't aware carries the death penalty, such as forgetting to wear a costume to the costume party), and, in my opinion, some of the early-game unmodified weapons are just so poor that they are almost unuseable (the sniper rifle before it is upgraded, for example).
Still, if you like games of patience, skill, and outwitting, plus killing people, this is the purest form of Agent 47 currently available.
I am looking forward to Hitman 5 this year, which promises to undo many of the mistakes of Absolution, but I'll believe it when I see it.

Certainly, this is not the first physics sandbox we've seen, and almost certainly not the last. So what makes besiege different? Well first there's the obvious medieval yet playful theme. Then there's the variety in mission-like challenges set on islands in which you mostly take, destroy, or kill to win the objective. Sounds simple enough, but infact the later challenges get increasingly difficult, as you need to build flying machines and contraptions, catapults that somehow have to fire exactly where you need to, and other hurtles that make this game endless fun.
And if you're not the objective-based mind, there's much other stuff to do. You can go into a sandbox with basically no limitations. You can build things as big as you want at the expense of frames depending on how beefy your computer is (notably a pitfall with very largemachines with many moving parts.) This can luckily be somewhat tamable with the adjustable speed of time, going anything from 0x to 2x as fast on a slider (0x means no time will pass.)
Here is a list of ratings and why:
Creativity (How unique is it): 3/5 , It allows for almost anything especially thanks to the steam workshop, though not an uncommon sandbox/builder theme that has similar competing games.
Errors/bugs (Fixing of errors in-game): 5/5 , all bugs that I have encountered have been fixed well within a few weeks of detection, which makes this game virtually bug-free.
Affordability (Is it worth buying): 5/5 , this game is definitely my money's worth and very affordable for what you get, and all Steam workshop DLC (that I've seen) is also available for free.
Objectives (What to do and how to do it): 4/5 , the objectives are very fun as you need sometimes very specific machines for a certain task, though there are a few tasks that seem very similar to eachother.

Almost two games in one.
Story Mode is like a  "Co-Op First Person Action RPG" (kind of like Borderlands, but with less emphasis and gear/weapons and more on skills) and the Player vs. Player modes are more like DoTA/LoL mixed with an FPS.
Together it reminds me of classic World of Warcraft if you could only play the Dungeons and  Battlegrounds (Alterac Valley/Arathi Basin), but mixed with an FPS.
+ Visually Impressive
+ Variety of fun game-play options
+ Good Re-playability (unlocks, large roster, challenges)
+ Humorous
+ Easy to pick up the basics
+ Community isn’t hard on new players
+ Fun to play with others
+ Not Pay to Win
-Small player base can make for a wait time for matches
-Aren’t allways matched with people your level, or skill in Player Vs Player matches (be prepared to lose if you are a new player)
-"Story Mode" is kind of light on story (DLC is an exception to this)
-Learning curve can seem daunting, especially in multi-player (similar to other MOBAs)
-Not as fun if you are looking for just a PVP game, or just a PVE game, have to play both to get the most out of it
The thing about this game is that it has both Player Vs Environment (like borderlands) and Player Vs Player (Like DoTA or LoL) elements, and these interact with each-other.  You have a command level (which is like player level) which can give you things like badges and titles, and Character Level which lets you unlock additional options (helix mutations) for the character.  The loot you get from Story Mode can be used in the PVP matches. The credits you earn from either can be used to purchase additional characters, more gear storage, or load outs.
Great game. I would recommend this game even at full price if you want both a Co-Op game and a game you can play against other players. If you aren't sure you'll play both, but are still interested pick it up on sale.

FEAR made its mark as one of the best first person shooters of all time, and a monumental achievement in video game horror and storytelling. FEAR 2 barely seemed like it tried to do better, but neither did it try to only be more of the same.
The gameplay took a bit of a turn for the generic, falling into the recent crowd of iron-sight shooters that encourage you to be a lightning-fast bulletstorming hero. The first game had realistically inaccurate weapons, but allowed you to lean from cover, both allowing and forcing you to be more delicate about how you handled each firefight. FEAR 2 has no lean ability, so cover is substantially less useful, as you have to expose half your hitbox to get the crosshairs on your enemy.
Melee and slowmo are still there, hardly changed, except that melee attacks are no longer one-hit kills to common soldiers. Action-heavy sequences such as the giant mech suits essentially act as glorified turret segments, desperately trying to out-bullet your foes.
As far as horror goes, the original FEAR was a little in-your-face with a lot of the scare scenes, but handled the atmosphere with excellent subtlety and sensitivity. The atmosphere in FEAR 2 is far less satisfying, as it is, in turn, much more outrageous. Outdoor segments are often punctuated by blood red skies and outrageous ambience, failing to immerse the player the way the original did. Sections of the game relying on simple, tried and true atmospheric tricks such as low lighting and eerie silence are much more effective.
Some of the enemies tend to be legitimately terrifying as well, often in conjunction with the superior atmospheres of the levels they appear in. Watching the Remnants idly try to act out their lives as they did before they died is deeply unsettling, and sneaking past open cell doors knowing Abominations stalk between the darkest corners slowed me to a stop even on my second and third playthroughs.
Unfortunately, in keeping up with modern action titles, FEAR 2 undermines a lot of its horror by forcing you to escape scripted insta-death events with furious button mashing.
Naturally, the biggest draw to a sequel to FEAR would be the pseudo-'antagonist,' Alma. After FEAR, I was left in eager anticipation to see what she might wreak upon the world. Everything that goes wrong in FEAR 2 is because of Alma. Her character is handled reasonably well in the sequel, even as she is far more apparent and active in trying to get in your way. Her comparatively bi-polar nature is unnerving, as you're never quite sure what she's trying to do to you, though this might instead be confusing to players who struggle to follow this considerably more disjointed plot. A lot of imagination went into furthering Alma's story, but its difficult to decide if that imagination came from the passion of the writers, or their desperation to be more unexpected and outrageous than last time.
Bottom line is, FEAR 2 is not the sequel I hoped it would be, and certainly not a landmark achievement in any of its genres, but it came closer than it could have. Many parts of the game toe the line in terror and storytelling drawn by its predecessor, but it never exceeds it, and fails to maintain that level of quality throughout. It's worth picking up on a sale for anyone who wanted more Alma, more FEAR, and more slow-mo scissor kicks, and if you're like me, largely unsatisfied by the so-called "Vivendi timeline" of Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate.

For whatever odd reason, there's an awful lot of fans of the original F.E.A.R. who consider this game to be inferior.  Personally I find both games to be about equally brilliant, but let's try to analyse the possible reasons for this, shall we, and see what conclusions we come to...

Firstly, F.E.A.R. 2 is absolutely, unapologetically a more blatant "horror" game.  A large part of the charm and uniqueness of the original was the way in which it spent the vast majority of its time being a reasonably straightforward (if thoroughly excellent) first-person shooter, with only sporadic - but thereby highly effective - bits of supernatural horror creeping in; with this sequel the devs decided to turn that balance of action versus horror into a more balanced fifty-fifty split, with all manner of beasties and what-not galore now terrorising the player as well as the expected super-soldiers and giant robots.  Perhaps some naysayers felt this made the series less unique, or made the horror less "psychological" and more, well, downright physical I suppose.  I can see that point of view, honestly I can.  But...I also can't really see how they could have maintained the same super-subtle unpinning of horror without simply REMAKING the original, and this is of course where all manner of "art" / "entertainment" industry follow-ups encounter controversy; not just games, but movies, books, bands, you name it.

How many people bemoan the fact that their favourite band didn't "keep the same sound", and essentially just keep making the EXACT SAME RECORD, over and over again?  How many people believe that Aliens took the stripped-back purity of Alien and ♥♥♥♥ed it right up the pooper-shooter by turning it into a slam-bang, high adrenaline ACTION MOVIE?  Here's the thing: You can't please everybody.  EVER.  Some people want to recapture what they experienced the first time, more or less verbatim, while others want something which is sufficiently different to distinguish itself from the original product, though perhaps with just enough in common that there's some continuity maintained.  I personally belong to the latter category.  I would much rather play F.E.A.R. 2 than F.E.A.R. 1, MARK 2.  There is a difference between these two concepts, after all.

So what one needs to ask themselves, then, is what kind of person they are, or to put it another way...if you enjoyed F.E.A.R. 1 and are wondering if you will also enjoy this one, then perhaps THESE are the questions you need to ask yourself:  Are you the kind of person who enjoyed the first game, in spite of "not normally" being a fan of horror games?  If the answer is yes, then perhaps this one may go too far in the "horror" direction for your liking.  Or are you, like me, someone who actually HUMOURED the original F.E.A.R. on account of it appearing to be something of a horror game, in spite of the fact that most of the screenshots seemed to indicate otherwise?  If so, then you're probably gonna ADORE this one.  And if you're somewhere in-between the two types of people I just described, well...wait for a sale and take a punt anyway.  Why not?  You only live once.

There are other differences between the two games, of course.  This one is arguably a bit "harder", not least of all in the earliest bits where you don't even have the benefit of your slo-mo ability to make up for your♥♥♥♥♥♥poor marksmanship (I felt THAT one, believe me).  Your "health" isn't nearly as generous in this one, either; expect to get more-or-less "insta-killed"...a LOT.  The soldiers also don't tend to be quite as "vocal" as the earlier game...but given that the soldiers in the first game had virtual diarrhea of the mouth and a tendency to give away their location at every possible opportunity, this is arguably an improvement.  You also don't get to shoot two pistols at a time or perform those oh-so-impossible first-person jumps which suggest your character has springs instead of legs (in this one, you actually see your character's hand realistically propel him over obstacles, etc), so overall, a slightly "grittier" level of realism is definitely the order of the day here; and again, it's up to the individual whether they consider this to be a boon or an abomination.

If you ask me, this series didn't really start to go (and even then, only slightly) "downhill" until the third F.E.A.R. game; which I personally also loved to bits, though I would be inclined to agree with anyone who thinks it's the weakest of the three.  But hey, it gets harder and harder to stay "fresh" as a game series progresses, so what do people expect?  If you're happy to live your life in stasis, you have my blessing.  Me, I'll take a pinch of spice in my bowl, thanks.  Then again, I'm the kind of person who doesn't like to stay in the same boring old job for fifty solid years, either.  Each to their own, it takes all kinds to make the world, etc etc...

I had to cook it over a while to decide exactly why I love Renowned Explorers so much. It boils down to two things.
1 - Many roguelike experiences are built around the question, "Will you live to cross the finish line?" It can get really depressing to die and fail over and over again. RE:IS (on its standard difficulties anyway) asks, "How cool will your adventuring career be?" I rarely straight up lose a run, but it isn't about winning or losing. It's about the first time you finish with 2500 Renown. Then 3000. Then 3500. You'll get a little better at squeezing more efficiency out of your runs each time you play, and you won't need an unbreakable spirit to want to keep trying.
2 - Another factor hampering many roguelike experiences is that there's only one paradigm for interaction. The whole game is dungeon crawling. No single gameplay system can entertain you forever. RE:IS has three different types of play: Roleplaying as you travel from node to node and decide how to handle incidents, Combat on a turn based grid with a handful of subsystems that don't overwhelm, and Resource Management as you spend your hard earned gains on things that synergize with your strengths and shore up your weaknesses. You'll constantly rotate between these 3 activities, so none of them ever overstay their welcome.
RE:IS is amazing. I eagerly await and will gladly pay for more DLC.

The game basically has three layers, all of them are very well designed and crafted.
The strategic one is your headquarters in roughly XIX century London, were your spend earned resources and prepare to your next expedition. To be honest, I like this part the least, but its fine and pretty complex as well. In fact, on the first few runs, it might appear overwhelming.
Then, there are expeditions themselves, full of random encounters and adventures and witty dialogues. They're amazing, and so far I can't say that I have become bored even from visiting the same areas. The layout of the expedition changes each time you play, and the special locations present there vary from one run to another, and of course, the outcome of events is often different for different teams and runs.
The third layer is tactical battles. Well, you don't get too much of them to become tired, there is always a final encounter at the end of the expedition, and typically two to four aside of it, depending on whether you are looking for fight. At first, the battle mechanics might appear complex and TERRIFYING, but as you grasp the basics (it takes a few encounters) and become more CONFIDENT, it becomes quite EXCITING. I guess any tactical battle system that operates with terms like 'attitude', 'mood' and 'emotions' is definitely worth giving it a try. Oh, and I like the form of field grid too.
Some people might say that the battle mechanics is not really a big deal and devious and friendly abilities can be replaced with say ice and nature magic, the notion that I don't exactly agree with. Even if technically that might be true, the path you choose to resolve encounters is reflected back onto the adventure level, and affects how your quest continues, which I find pretty cool.
As for drawbacks, the only thing I might think about is the number of available expeditions and well, their tight concentration in just few geographical areas. The game is great, but if it just had even more content it would be even greater.

This is a charming throwback to the early 90s era of SNES JRPGs.  Chronologically, it came on the heels of Final Fantasy IV, the first SNES Final Fantasy game, and the first to come stateside.  This game, however, never saw an original release in 1993, in the US.  It was eventually released on disc with Chrono Trigger as Final Fantasy Anthology for the original PlayStation.  In that release, the graphics were very much alike to Final Fantasy IV.  This Steam release contains the updated graphics, higher-resolution capabilities, and modern character sprites of the iOS release, similar to Final Fantasy VI.  If you have never played the original, then all of that will likely be nice for you; if you were a fan of the old-school purist pixels, you may dislike the updated feel.
If you are a fan of IV and VI, and you've never played FFV, you owe it to yourself to play this one.  While at times the dialog can seem very silly, take into account the era this was originally created in; it's very much of its time, and JRPGs have never been a serious genre when it comes to dialog.  They often play out like anime, one moment serious, the next completely silly, and FFV is no exception to this.
The music is excellent in this game, and very familiar to those who grew up on Squaresoft SNES games.  The Job system, if you aren't familiar with it, is akin to Final Fantasy Tactics.  Any of the 4 main characters can learn and specialize in any "Job" i.e. Class.  Once an ability has been learned by leveling up the Job, it may then be assigned regardless of what other Job the character has taken.  So a Knight can use White Magic, or a Black Mage can Summon.  If you look to Final Fantasy IV for some archetypes, it's easy to see where to go with this.  Edge would have been a Thief/Black Mage.  Rosa would have been an Archer/White Mage.  Cecil would have been a Knight/White Mage.  Rydia would have been a Black Mage/Summoner.  In FFV, you can mold the four heroes into those same archetypes, or you can create any other variety that you want.  Some neat possibilities exist.
I won't comment on the storyline except to say that it has castles, dragons, pirates, and small rural villages in need of your help.  And Crystals.  Always Crystals in the early days!

Final Fantasy V
Developer: Square Enix
Publisher: Square Enix
Steam
2015
The 16-bit step child, the "Lost Boy" of gaming, the, um, leper at Square...well whatever I want to call it, this game received no less than five attempts to localize it through the 90s. Square's excuses for halting the American development was the old "it's too complicated for you redneck, fast food stuffing, xenophobic, superficial, warmongering, ignorant, loud Americans." I am paraphrasing. Seeing as Square at the time thought Mystic Quest was already a handful for our simian minds, they canned the project.  This would become the first Final Fantasy to get a complete fan translation before an official North American release.
Square eventually would release this game for the Playstation, strip out all the beautiful Amano art from packaging and call it a day.
The Steam version you see here is actually a port from the iOS version which is a port from the GBA version. I mean, why waste good code, right?
If I sound particularly cynical, it's because I feel this game got a bad rap in the states. Granted, it's my least favorite for the SNES, which puts it at third, but is still on my top five Final Fantasy games overall. I love the job system, and the strategies you need to pull off boss battles. At least until you get spell blade / rapid strike then strategy just goes out the window in favor of brute♥♥♥♥♥stomping.
Graphically, this version is odd. Not bad, just...odd. I notice a lot of people complain of background clipping and tile lines showing (psst...your lines are showing V) and it's evident, even in the ending you can see it clearly, but I got used to it after a few hours of gameplay.
Another thing that gets people's♥♥♥♥♥♥boiling is the use of the Yoshitaka Amano art. Look, I have never been a fan of the weird CG-faux-chibi art Square barfed up for the Playstation version.  I may be the outlier, but I enjoyed the use of Amano's art as character portraits. It was comical at first to see Bartz look like a white haired prick when he's obviously an angry brunet, but the character portraits grew on me as the game progressed and now, Galuf's is the greatest representation of a cantankerous old man and using anything else is tantamount to blasphemy.  Seeing everyone the way Amano had envisioned it made for a wonderful experience and I looked forward to seeing new characters along the way, just to see what they would end up looking like.
Another thing that makes people go Leopold Slikk at the game is the barrel chested orangutan armed sprites in the game. I don't have much to complain about it, I came to terms with this in Final Fantasy VI for Steam. All these things individually are not bad, As a whole, I can kind of see how people rage on the game, but the overall enjoyment outweighs the negatives.
Another thing that turns good people into screwdriver-wielding madmen may be the music. Regardless, any faux pas of the graphics is more than forgiven by the music. Final Fantasy V has some the of the most memorable tunes in the series, and I will always crank the volume when squaring off with Gilgamesh. Again, some will complain that the music was never remastered and they are nothing more than nice midis, but I never expected a digitally remastered symphonic composition here and shame on you if you did. I mean geez, are you new here, have you seen how Square has treated this game in the past?
Anyways, overall I had an enjoyable experience playing this game and at $10 on sale, I'd say I got my money's worth at 86 hours. This title isn't for everyone, it's changed just enough to anger purists and revisionists alike. If you're not jaded and can look past a few faults, this title is worth the time, especially if you're new to FFV or have a fondness of the GBA version.

It's a solid Final Fantasy game that could have gotten a better port. Overall I enjoyed playing the game.
The updated graphics look pretty good although I have no idea why the character portraits look nothing like the characters in game. I also liked the fact that the SNES music was kept as it still sounds great and adds a lot to the atmosphere of the game.
While the story is rather simple, backtracking to locations does reveal a bit more background of the characters. The story isn't as great as in other Final Fantasy games, but it does work well enough. The job system that adds abilities to your character's repertoire adds a lot of cutomisation to building your party. There's an optinal area that was added for the GBA version that is also in the Steam version which lacks any story and feels rather random.
The main problem with this port in my opinion is that the cursor doesn't work properly. Since encounters are handled partially in real time this becomes a quite big issue. After playing for over 20 hours I slowly started to get the timinig when I could press a button. but often enough I still missed it and had to navigate the menu while enemies were already attacking me. Especially when grinding for level or jobs the unreliable cursor does get on your nerves.
The game is quite difficult and some bosses need a quite specific tactic with the right jobs in your party. Luckily there is a job that makes it much easier to deal with those bosses, but it takes quite a while until it becomes available (and can easily be missed). Finding out how to deal with those bosses can take a bit of time, but I think it actually makes the game more fun to play.
This is a fun JRPG that deserves at least a patch to be more enjoyable, but as it is I'd still recommend to play it.

Definitely pick this game up if you're a fan of platformers, and seriously consider buying the soundtrack.

There's nothing on the main menu that clearly means "start the single-player campaign," so I clicked "resume." That took me to the "create a profile" screen, so I did that and loaded up the "tutorial" scenario. Next I saw a "briefing" screen that gave me no direction other than "rtfm to learn how to play." Already I'm not thrilled with this "update." Next I got dropped into what feels like a cockpit with some pretty familiar-looking HUD elements. Since I recall (from the game's original incarnation) that the tutorial began with a ground mission, I assumed that I'm somehow meant to get myself down to the big red planet that's nearby.
Before too long, I get a message that says "urgent message received." Okay. Where's the message? Let's figure out which one of these buttons leads me to a place where I can read the urgent message. The only thing that seemed remotely useful to that end was "comms," which was within the "command" menu. But the comms screen is really just a log of what messages have already flashed up on screen. So all I see there is "urgent message received."
Okay, whatever that urgent message is will have to wait; I need to get down to this planet. Oh look! A button marked "Shuttles." Surely, that will allow me to command my shuttles. Nope. It just opens a branching menu that lets me load the shuttle with... personnel I guess. I'm not sure, since there was nothing selectable anywhere in the tree. Okay, let's go back to the "command" menu tree. Hey look! Shuttles again! Let's launch a shuttle! Tell it to go to that planet!
Wait. There's nobody on the shuttle because there's nothing to select in the "shuttles" menu.
Then my PC rebooted (which is in no way related to the game).
So... In my experience, a tutorial is something that's meant to teach you how to use something. This doesn't do that. Apparently, this is the scenario that's meant to accompany the 90-something-page tutorial novella.
Okay. All done. Thanks Derek Smart for making me remember that your games are totally counter-intuitive and inaccessible, even to a guy who lives for complicated games that don't suffer from Monkey Syndrome. Admittedly, this game does not. It suffers from the reverse. Everything in this game seems to defy convention, seemingly for no reason but the defiance of convention.
I confess myself pretty disappointed. I was really excited about this game when it was first released in 2004; back when I had the patience to pull it apart and figure it out. Even then I had a hard time with it. I was hoping that a "Collector's Edition" would at least have added a proper tutorial. Pretty disappointed.
If you played this game ten years ago and still remember how it works, I can't imagine you'll be disappointed with this new version. It seems like a really cool game; it's just entirely unapproachable. If you don't feel like reading a 90-something-page tutorial, don't bother with this one.
It's also nice to see Derek Smart is still totally uninsterested in what anyone thinks of his games. He made it for himself, so why should he care if anybody else can figure it out?

Ah, Universal Combat.  Somehow I hoped we had seen the last of Derek Smart.  Don't get me wrong, I don't despise the man, but his snarky, combative attitude in the face of the overwhelming evidence regarding his shortcomings as a developer have left me hoping for the day when he retires from public life; that, and I was one of the foolish who purchased Universal Combat when it came out only to discover it was broken and buggy even after several patches and any attempts to challenge this was met by scorn and insult by Derek Smart himself.
This is not a good game.  It will not be a good game no matter how many times he changes the name.  It IS a very ambitious game, however.  To his credit, Derek Smart tried to make a game that pushed hardware and design boundaries.  The sad reality is that he failed, but rather than accept this and work with critics to address the problems he chose to attack whatever fanbase he had for pointing out the shortcomings of the game,.  Now it is on steam (for free, no less) and that is supposed to diminish your ability to criticise this product, but for those of us who purchased the game when it first came out it just brings back visions of falling through surfaces, user interfaces better suited to spreadsheet software than a game and terrible, game destroying bugs.
I won't address the visuals, which for the time were not bad.  I bought the game originally because of the promise of fps and ship based exploration and combat, and what I ended up with were two halves that never really seemed to fit together or work even on their own.  Attempting to hold the two halves together is an interface that is poorly thought out (see how long it takes you to figure out how quit for a start) and overcomplicated with fields and windows of redundant settings best handled with a single button or accessible from a quick bar.
It's unfortunate (but not surprising) to see that time has not changed Derek at all; looking at the comments on steam he continues to attack naysayers with the same eagerness he did on his own forums once, and that is a shame.  I would have hoped that the years had brought him some wisdom about dealing with critics and fans alike, and that rather than insult their intelligence and rebuff their concerns with snarky comments he would have hired a PR representative who has less of an irrational response to criticism.
You will likely play Universal Combat regardless of my review, and I invite you to do so.  You will also discover that the game has some nebulous design decisions and unresolved bugs that will hamper your enjoyment.  Just do not expect your feedback or criticism to be well received or heeded at all by the game's designer as he has great difficulty accepting flaws in his work, though he will gladly take all of your praise.

Some tips for newbies:
-Disable flight launch if you aren't launching. If you get intruders on board they'll run off with your cargo.. and shuttles/fighters!
-Use perscan when you have marines on board, and assign them accordingly. ALways PREP FOR COMBAT.
-Upgrade your REACTOR before you upgrade your engine.
-Buy at GALCOM and sell at MAJORIS
-Deploy mining drones on seperate moons/planets. Not only does this make it easier for you to keep track of which shuttle is picking up which drone, but also you get a wider variety of minerals. (Sell at Majoris)
-If you see static on your HUD.. CLOAK AND RUN. If you don't have cloak then EMD AND RUN. It's a cloaked enemy ship, possibly fleet, and if they're cloaking it means their AI is probably higher than your crews AI so they WILL get on board or open fire if you don't get out of there. It'll be days, possibly even weeks, before your crew has the skills to take on such an enemy.
-Don't attack starbases without a fleet or without friendly nearby ships also attacking.
-Regularly stock up on RADINE, PLUTONIUM, NUTRIPAKS
-Keep your turrets at 60%, guns at 30% and shields at 25% to conserve energy. Raise shields when enemy is around. Guns should be fine unless you're outnumbered, they're pretty powerful even at those %'s.
-Regularly send out a shuttle with the "Cargosweep" order. They'll sweep your current & surrounding sectors for ejected cargo pods full of goodies. Be careful though, some pods are booby trapped.
-Beam Resnig down onto the most volanic, vile planet you can find.
-Keep playing. This is not a fast-paced game. To see any real progress it will take days, not hours.

Very excited that this game is released for free on Steam. This is one of my favorite game series of all time. Haven is an adventure RPG with a psycho-analytical plot: you have gone insane, and must find a way to regain control of your mind from various psychological structures, which have turned against you.
Game progress is linear and the game takes 4 hours to complete. Battles are varied and interesting, and strategy is useful. Visuals are artsy and weird, but professionally done.
You have a choice of three characters to bring with you as party members for each quest, and you may switch between them, as needed. These characters represent different aspects of your personality, and are entertaining in theory, but lack  emotional depth - their primary function is to participate in constant intellectual banter. As the game progresses, there is an increase in the number of party members you can have.
Each quest consists of a map in which you must make your way to the final boss, while fighting random encounters along the way. There is variety in each level and there are unexpected obstacles to your path that might take a while to solve, but nothing that will really discourage you.
There are waypoints to save your progress, so you can leave the map and not have to start at the beginning. You are allowed at any time to travel back to Haven (your home base), which replenishes all stats. There is also a special room you can access that allows you to buy new skills with currency collected while on missions.
All parts of this game are satisfactory, and the biggest issue to consider for your purchase is whether you appreciate the kooky artwork, and the psycho-analytical content of the narrative.

Released on Steam on August 5th 2016 we have Haven. Developed and Published by Cleril Calamity Studios, Haven is an RPG developed using Enterbrain’s RPG Maker. This isn’t the first RPG Maker game I’ve reviewed, and you can catch the other one here. For transparency, the developer sent me a key to the game for me to review.
In Haven, you play as the poet Cleril, within his mind. Over the course of the game, Cleril is joined by three other denizens of his head and together they fight against his subconscious for control. The game has a very psychological aspect to it and adapts a fairly interesting battle system. But is it any good? Let’s find out in…
[THE GOOD]
The hand drawn artstyle is a good touch. One thing I’ve never been too keen on with RPG Maker games is the reliance on the stock assets or sprite edits of existing assets and Haven’s implementation of having custom assets goes to show the effort made. While a section of the game does have a snippet of the stock assets and the menus absolutely reeking of them, it’s used in a much more creative way, considering the setting is Cleril’s mind. Interaction with objects has been done pretty well, It’s a little impressive that for every stump in the game, there’s different text when you interact with them, then again, I’m pretty weird and you’d have to be in order to interact with every stump in the game.
The game’s battle sequence I thought was a little unique. Cleril and his allies each have a Sanity and Ink meter. Sanity acts like HP while Ink acts like MP. Alongside a standard attack, Cleril and his Allies also possess skills which can use Ink or Sanity, as well as support skills which can be used to replenish them. Each character has unique abilites which you can use to strategize for the battles ahead and new skills can be learned in the Dictionary upon receiving Ink Wells throughout the game. As Cleril’s allies level up, they can also learn skills of their own as well as having a unique skill or ability that Cleril can spend Ink Wells on. Allies each have unique personalities and certainly add to the good aspects of the game. However, with all things good, there’s always…
[THE BAD]
The biggest complaint I really have here is the game is too vague in parts, especially in the story department. Without spoiling too much, we quickly learn that we’re in Cleril’s mind and that Cleril is insane, but why? Why is he insane? How did this all happen? Is there anything else going on in the world around him? The game leaves a lot of unanswered questions which still left me scratching my head once I had completed it. Granted, I did come across a sidequest that hadn’t been implemented into the game yet so I suspect there’s much more to it, but the game isn’t listed as an Early Access title giving me the impression that the game I should be playing is a complete game.
I feel the game was a little misleading with the ‘no handholding’ element. I found the game essentially guided me to just about everything, even telling me that I should save before a certain battle, how to escape battle (though admittedly I never had to), and that to heal, I could return to the main hub, or Haven while I was out of battle though it didn’t always work.
The game also features a couple of frustrating areas which requires a lot of trial and error to bypass. One particular area I found required a lot of reloading due to what’s happening. Encounter rates seem to skyrocket in certain areas with one pretty much setting me up for an encounter each step towards a chest with an Ink Well in it. The game’s lack of items while explainable since we’re inside someone’s mind does force players to play more strategically and use skills to regenerate Sanity and Ink. Asides from that, there isn’t much else to talk about here so we’ll now move on to…
[THE OPINION]
I can’t say I’m a huge fan of RPG Maker games, but don’t get me wrong, there has been some good come out of it (I’m looking at you Corpse Party). I was able to beat the game in a couple of hours with the only real hurdle being the frustrating areas I mentioned earlier. Story was interesting enough and enjoyable, but still quite vague. I do like the setting and the idea of the game taking place inside the mind, as well as your efforts to try and control yourself but I feel execution could have been handled a little better. The game certainly has potential and I think Cleril Calamity Studios has done good on it, but hey, keep at it, I think you can certainly improve.

The game at least succeeds in being atypical where its general approach is concerned, even bending the RPG Maker engine back on itself in order to make some things work. Cleril’s game tells the story of a mad poet named Cleril (which seems to be a more common name then any of us ever imagined) who wages metaphysical war against his own mind. He’s locked in a cell for reasons that we’ll never know, and thus has little else to do. That confinement leaves him plenty of time to focus entirely on inner battles.
Haven is the name of a place Cleril retreats to, inside of his head. He’s fully aware of his escapism. There’s no twist ending about which world is real; Haven’s a mental prison of his own making, a way to escape the physical prison others have made for him. It’s supposed to be idyllic. There are green fields and wispy clouds, all stacked on a lump of earth floating carelessly through the sky. With giant brown eyes scored into the ground that track your movement as you explore. You know, that old chestnut. Cleril lives there with the more agreeable alter-egos that splintered away from his personality. These include The Jester, who represents his sense of humour, and The Bookkeeper, who records his memories.
But something isn’t quite right. Instead of ending up in Haven, Cleril’s latest trip into his own mind takes him to a location that he doesn’t recognise. It’s filled with inky black infants skittering around that both adore and loathe him. They’re "inklings," the manifestation of ideas long abandoned. Some of them are warped, mutated and violent. Others are scared, or furious, or confidently indifferent. And they’re all trapped in this place where ideas come to die, kept in place by a hulking reaper with a double-sided scythe. The problem now is that Cleril is just as trapped as they are. By taking out the guard and claiming his own freedom, he’s essentially allowing his unchecked ideas run riot in his own mind.

Haven is...bizarre but not in a bad way to say the least.  I played a bit of the game while it was in demo and thought it was relatively interesting so I think it was worth paying the five bucks to see how the rest of the game would go. Now whether it was worth my five bucks is kind of the point of this review by a guy with an avatar of Kurisu with a banana. I should note this review might have some mild spoilers.
Haven is a RPGmaker made RPG game about Cleril who is travelling through the various parts of his mind in a war against his own subconscious. The concept in itself is enough to make it a little different from your average RPGmaker fare otherwise I probably wouldn't have considered trying this game at all. Helping Cleril are his alter egos, other figments of his mind who aid him in this war. If you haven't brushed up on your psychoanalysis terms you might want to read the opening chapter of an intro to psychology book but otherwise it's very accessible. That said I think it was really enjoyable getting to explore the mind itself.
While the game isn't a 1080p AAA sexy beyond belief title I wouldn't say it's hideous, especially considering it's a game with a zero dollar budget. The art is fairly nice and hand made but some levels are more memorable than others but I wouldn't call any of them ugly. The characters and enemies designwise are actually pretty memorable parts of the game. I particularly like the design of the Alter Egos and the bosses although Cleril himself is give or take for me.
The gameplay is a variety of clicking on things, solving puzzles, exploring around, and turn based RPG combat. If you're not into RPGs this more than likely won't be the game that suddenly makes you fall in love with the genre. The puzzles range in difficulty and the later puzzles will take more thinking power but most won't leave you absolutely stumped. The only exception to this would be the very first puzzle in the Hippocampus which was stumped the hell out of me. I'm not exactly sure how many sidequests there are but I did play Jester's. The Stranger's was not finished however and a message is even left in the game saying as much which is disappointing.
Combat at first glance runs like any ol' turn based RPG but what makes this different is there is a skill tree system where Cleril and the alter egos can learn new skills and abilities which can change how your playstyle works. Think something like FF10's sphere grid or Digital Devil Saga's skill system but not as large. That said I do think some of the things you can get is very conditional and I never see a real need to ever use them so you'll likely be sticking to only certain skills. This does make experimentation a little interesting though for those who like to try different things. As for difficulty it definitely isn't blistering hard like a SMT title but it isn't♥♥♥♥♥♥easy either. You'll find some of the later bosses especially making you think a bit. There isn't a need to grind though so for those who hate grinding will enjoy this. There's even a button to have the alter egos at the same level as Cleril. You could grind if you really wanted to but I don't see the point.
Haven's music is a very mixed bag. It definitely has a variety of sounds from dubstep to blues to NIN esque industrial but it doesn't always fit every instance in the game to me. I think the music after The Hippocampus tends to be better in general. The lyrics in some of the songs can also be a little distracting. Overall though the music (mostly) does what it's supposed to be doing and I guess it's better than silence.
The writing seems to be one of the main points where the dev prides himself for this game. The story is definitely very philosophy driven and while I didn't necessarily agree with the arguments they were written mostly well but at times I felt like the philosophy talk makes the story confusing at times. For example there's points where all of the characters get philosophical and I find it gets confusing on what they're even talking about. As for conversations between characters they're fairly decent. The Jester ended up being my favorite character but I also came to find the rest interesting enough. That said I never felt a huge connection to any of the characters so I never felt a personal investment. It felt more like I'm an outside observer more than anything.
Earlier I mentioned how The Stranger's sidequest was not complete which leads into perhaps one of my main issues with Haven. The main story is complete but everything else seems to not be. The Stranger's sidequest wasn't done and I honestly have no idea if The Bookkeeper had one and if he did I somehow missed it despite talking to him before every level. There's also a part where you learn about an alter ego that no longer is around called The Flirt that Cleril says he no longer needed. I honestly wish this character was actually in the game though although it was interesting in itself that alter egos can disappear. After battle you'll also notice the victory spoils screen says "This is just to prevent a crash." I would have rather seen the dev make use of this screen somehow either through an item system or just some kind of money system and you could buy unlockables or something.
If you've noticed Haven updating several times part of that was me finding little issues here and there but the dev was extremely quick at fixing these issues. I will definitely give props to the dev for actually making sure to fix these issues so quickly and he's very approachable about any possible issues.
So for all of this long winded writing written is Haven worth it? I would recommend this game. It's definitely not going to get an indie GOTY award from Geoff "Dorito Pope" Keighley but I would say it's a mostly solid title. I wish it had a little more content, achievements would've been nice, and perhaps a bit more polish wouldn't have hurt. Five bucks is fair enough to me but if you're on a budget I wouldn't say you should feel guilty about waiting for a sale. Overall it wasn't a waste of my time, I had fun, and I hope the dev learns from this and only improves from here. Don't believe some weirdo on Steam though, go play it for yourself and give your own review.
Final Score: 7/10

The first game was Supreme Commander, then came Supreme Commande : Forged Alliance, then this.

Which leaves only skirmish and multiplayer, where the gameplay is far shallower and blander than the original game and you'll quickly grow bored of it.
What basically ruined this sequel is basically the same thing that ruins a lot of PC game sequels, a studio has initial success and then they set their eyes on the lucrative console market.
Here's a quote from gamespy reviewing the Xbox 360 version of the first Supreme Commander.
"Cut out about 50% of the units, make the maps smaller and tighten up the bleeding edges to make a new strategic model and we might really have something. The pacing's right, the idea's right, but stuffing the entire PC version of Supreme Commander onto the 360 is just more than the poor machine can handle."
That's pretty much what they did here.
The only thing Supreme Commaner 2 deserves credit for is that on the whole the skirmish A.I is somewhat improved over its predecessors in terms of actually amassing units and launching credible attacks.

A great way to convert console gamers, but as a sequel to the beloved Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance, this really does disappoint.
People say that this game was dumbed down and ruined by consolification. Not quite true, as while it's undoubtedly dumbed down, Supreme Commander also got a console release (can't vouch for Forged Alliance though). I think it's a Square Enix publisher issue. For example, the unit cap was considerable larger in older games, and while it's still large by default, it doesn't live up to the old standard. However, and I think this may be a sign that the devs KNEW this game was worse, you can change your unit cap in a .prefs file in your "Appdata\Local\Gas Powered Games\Supreme Commander 2\" folder. (Only tested up to 1000.) You can also activate the ETA timer in there (another removed feature), so that when you hold SHIFT to queue, you can see a (normally incorrect) ETA. I don't really understand. It's like they added it, but it was turned off, lowered or removed at the last minute, and I can't imagine that's the devs.
It's sad to see SupCom die, really, and this game can be quite a bit of fun with friends, but the campaign is awful too. The gameplay is dumbed down (but you knew that already), and the voice acting sounds like they were bored. If anyone played Spider-Man 2 on PS2, Xbox or Gamecube (but not PC - god not PC) then it's like the citizen voice acting; they sound bored as hell, and slightly underpaid and rushed. The writing is cheesy too, so I don't really know what went on there (although that trailer above really wants to push this 'awesome story').
It's said for me to say I don't recommend this game; it does have it's moments; but I can't understand some of the choices made. Especially when it had such potential - well, I say that, but making games is hard, people have misfires, and while this is a big one (it killed the franchise as far as I'm aware)
TL;DR: Get SC:FA if you want a really good RTS, or get Supreme Commander: Gold Edition or whatever it was called to get both 1 and FA.

This was definitely one of the best games I’ve bought last year. It’s a strategy game with turn-based combat and resource management, great replayability and an active developer to boot, who’s working on a big update at the moment (January 2016).
You assemble a team of three explorers that you send on five expeditions in the quest of becoming the most renowned explorers. To become “renown” you need to find treasures but also resources that enable you to attract an entourage, conduct research, and buy equipment in between the expeditions. And of course, you also need to survive the encounters.
You can play in
; one lets you make saves, the other ends with your death. The latter is the way it is meant to be played and, in my opinion, the only way to play it. If you want to ruin the game for you, use save-scumming.
The first step is to assemble your team. You can choose between
with very unique skills and perks that belong to one of
(scientist, scout, fighter, speaker). The combination of classes, skills and perks that you have in your team can greatly influence your success in the game. There isn’t one character that is just better than the rest, one character can do great in one team and be a bit useless in the next, and depending on the strategy you want to follow during the main part of the game, you might need a different combination of classes anyway. Trying out new teams is a big part of what makes this game so much fun and adds a lot of replayability.
You can choose between a few destinations that all have their unique styles, events, treasures to find, and requirements. The
, you move FTL-style from node to node, using supplies as “fuel”, and are confronted with different events or encounters. There is a big variety of events that are also influenced by which classes and perks you have in your team and the choices you’ve made, so it doesn’t get boring fast. I’ve played over 75 hours by now and I still get events I haven’t seen before and I’ve only found half of the unique treasures in the game, so there is a lot to keep you interested.
Some events require luck, where you have a certain percentage to succeed based on the skills and perks of your characters. There’s also luck involved in the events that you get, some of the rare ones can be great if you find them, although they usually also involve a severe penalty if you fail.
Turn-based combat that reminded me of X-Com. There’s a lot of depth to the combat system, much more than immediately obvious. Your characters and your enemies have
, friendly, devious and aggressive. The type of attack you and your enemies use influence the overall
, e.g. if you are both devious, the mood is tense, if they are friendly and you are aggressive, the mood is brutal.
Some of these moods can be beneficial to you, e.g. give you more defence, while others can be negative. So, manipulating the mood by the attack-types you choose is very important.
Equally important is
. A friendly attack can leave your character in an impressed mood, which lowers your defence against speech attacks. So you might need to use a friendly attack on your own team member to heal them and change their mood to confident, which adds 25% to their aggressive attack. Obviously, you can use the same principle against your enemies, by using attacks that put them in moods which provide debuffs.
And finally, sometimes you want to end the fight in a specific mood because you’ll get a bonus if you do.
All of these effects are explained in
that you can access during the encounter, there are no hidden effects, very little luck is involved and a lot of strategy. Great!
You might “win” the game by just doing your thing and ignoring all these details but on higher difficulty and during the more difficult expeditions you will have a very hard time if you don’t use the moods to your advantage.
During an expedition you earn
that you can exchange for gold, status and research points after the expedition and use to upgrade your equipment, conduct research and hire an entourage.

lets you get more of the resource that you want to focus on, can give you more supplies, can give you extra bonuses if you end fights in a specific mood, etc.
lets you hire an entourage which will let you get more out of your tokens and can also provide you with more perks.
The success of your overall strategy (which destinations do you want to visit, do you want to focus on a specific resource, ...) will be very much influenced by the choices you make here.
: Fun game that requires a lot of strategy and a bit of luck (although it is very rare that you’re getting completely screwed over by RNG), with more depth to it than you’d think. You can easily finish one game in one evening, although if you’re like me you’ll likely want to start a new one immediately.
The only drawback is that there could be more destinations, but as the developers are already working on a big update, I'm hopeful that this will be fixed soon. And as I still haven't seen everything there is to see after 75 hours of gameplay, I can't really complain too much, anyway.

;If you're looking for a short(ish) game that allows you to play through one set of adventures in a few hours, this is perfect.  There are a lot of parallels to FTL, from the semi randomly generated maps, to the resources collected, to the semi random upgrades, but I feel that RE:IS has a lot more depth than FTL does - both are enjoyable in their own way, and both will take a while to master the tactics, but RE:IS just feels like there's more there.  The different combat powers, the way you can affect your crew and the enemy based on mood and how you 'attack' is very nice.  I like the different options you've got for upgrading between expeditions and how there are plenty of different paths to follow.  The game isn't perfect, but it's got plenty of enjoyment in it, and I'm definitely looking forward to more content.
If you're looking for a nice, gentle difficulty curve, it seems like it might be there, if you pick the right crew and know the right order to take the expeditions in, but it seems to win, you're going to have to hit some of those nasty, RNG difficulty spikes and let fate have a big hand in the final decision.  I like the fact that you can 'finish' the game without winning, but there are also situations where you end up in a fight where you very quickly realize you're over your head, and unlike FTL, there's no way to run away and have the chance to lick your wounds, your game is over (assuming you play adventure mode).  This does seem a little harsh, even in a roguelike with permadeath, being locked in a fight where you know you can't win, which will end the game, but you still have plenty of resources if you could run away and try something else is more than a little frustrating.  I wish there was a 'run away!' option from encounters, but that's pretty minor.
If I have any complaints about RE:IS it's that there's very little map content - there only seem to be a few of each 'difficulty' map, and within those maps, the variability is somewhat limited, so you're going to be playing the same mini adventures over and over again.  FTL has so many different encounters, this seems to be less of an issue there.
Additionally, the only ongoing 'unlocks' that you can obtain in RE:IS are getting crew members to the point they can be captains - though this is similar to FTL's unlocking of new ship layouts and new ships, since you start with all the crew, this somehow, to me anyway, feels less like an accomplishment, but it doesn't take anything away from the enjoyability of the game.

As of writing this review, I have something like 40 hours (yes, 40) into this game, and still haven't beaten it. Admittedly, I didn't go for any of those wimpy copout lower difficulties and modes - I went straight for Adventure; Classic.
Here's the thing though, time after time, I may have lost, but I've never really felt like it was unfair, and I've always learned something new about how the game works. I've heard the FTL: Faster Than Light comparison - and there's a lot of similarities - you'll never feel like you've got QUITE enough resources to tackle the curveballs the game sends your way. You'll lose far more often than you win.
Still, where I found FTL to be frustrating, RE:IS is rewarding. Every set of skills is valuable, and will open up paths you never even guessed were going to be there. Most importantly though, this game had me grinning like an idiot even as a crotchety priestess from Scotland whooped my professional hit squad's collective behind. A good purchase.

RE is a great game which combines procedurally generated expeditions with a node based exploration system and an unexpectedly deep turn-based combat system dominated by mood. Between expeditions you can earn resources by lecturing, gain various entourages, research papers for various improvements and buy gear in shops.
1)
– you pick 3 explorers (scientist, scout, fighter or speaker) each with various perks (engineering, diplomacy, survivalist etc.) that have an effect on your chance for success during expeditions. As you level them up they gain more perks and their stats increase
2)
– every place (Mali, Hungary, Egypt etc.) has specific challenges and treasures to be discovered, and certain perks are more beneficial than others depending where you go as are certain styles of combat. There are 5 expeditions per game, so you won’t see them all during one playthrough (2-3 hours).
3)
– there are 3 moods of attack (friendly, devious and aggressive), and each mood has 3 emotions (friendly – you can impress, encourage or excite an enemy or your own unit). There are many types of attack (cone area dmg, ranged etc.) but most inflict dmg and one of those emotions. Furthermore those attacks have an effect on the general combat mood which can give you major buffs/debuffs. So if you are Devious and your enemy is Aggressive you get a big evasion boost and so on. The more you play the game, the more fun it gets.
This game is immediately fun when you start playing. It has a great atmosphere (think Indy 3), is very ‘cheeky’,  many big encounters have unexpected resolutions and it gives many nods and winks along the way. But the sheer number of possible outcomes, expedition combinations, the fact there are even individual (not class based) choices for many of the 20 characters and the great combat system is what keeps you coming back over and over again.
The developers are very active and new content is still being added. There is more to the game I didn’t put in my review and hopefully modding support is on the way. This game is perfect for mods.
Anyway 60 hours in and I like the game so much I wrote my first review. Hope you like it as well.

I DO have some complaints about the gameplay machanics that anyone thinking of buying this should now about, though:
*The combat is clunky and barely responsive. I can see that were going for for a immerisve and substansal feeling system with interaction beyond clicking a button to swing, but it was implemented horribly. It consists of holding the action button to ready yourself, and using the mouse to swing but it takes such broad movements that it's hard to hit anything and good luck lining up enemies when they can simply step out of your hitzone because you obiously can't move the camera while holding the action button.

This review contains minor spoilers, mostly of the beginning of the game.
Penumbra: Overture is a first person horror adventure game and the first part of the Penumbra series. You play as Philip, a physicist who teaches at university. After his mother's death he receives a letter from his supposedly dead father whom he barely remembers at all. The letter contains a key to a safety deposit box as well as the instruction to destroy everything that's in the deposit box. When Philip opens the box he finds several document and maps, some of which he cannot even decipher. The findings point to a location in Greenland though. So, instead of destroying everything Philip packs his things and leaves to follow the traces his father has left behind. After arriving at the location he manages to find an abandoned-looking mine.
Penumbra: Overture plays in first person perspective. The player can manipulate objects by clicking on them and then dragging the mouse accordingly. Doors and drawers are used in the same fashion. This system was later refined and used again in Amnesia: The Dark Descent, so if you have played that one you have a pretty good idea how it works. Many of the puzzles are solved by manipulating objects in the enviroment. It is also possible to pick up various objects and pile them up to briefly block a door or throwing them as a distraction. Philip can also crouch and hide in the darkness - a skill that is very much required. While combat is possible I'd highly advice against it. There are only melee weapons available and those work in the same way as manipulating objects works. You have to actually swing them around using the mouse which is very awkward, difficult and therefore risky. The combat is the one thing I really dislike about the game. Luckily it is avoidable in most cases.
While exploring the mines Philip has to mainly rely on stealth and wits. As already said combat is very dangerous and in most cases not worth the risk. Also, there are certain enemies which are so massive that you cannot possibly hurt them in any meaningful way. So for the majority of the time Philip has to lay low, hide if possible and run if necessary. While staying hidden works most of the time there are some parts of the game where you have to get away as fast as possible. This really helps with spicing things up and making the player feel unsafe. Many of the puzzles revolve around manipulating physics objects but there are also some which revolve around finding information and acting accordingly. So you have to example figure out how to assemble an explosive charge, find all necessary ingredients (or substitutes), assemble the device and use it to clear a cave-in, so you can move on. There are several other puzzles which can only be solved by exploring the environment and gathering the appropriate information. Those are very engaging and reward the player with a true sense of accomplishment after figuring out the solution.
Penumbra: Overture features a really creepy atmosphere. You are all alone in the abandoned mines with no human being around but still it is obvious that people have been there until very recently. Whenever you apparently get really close to meeting another human being that chance is taken away from you, so for a majority of the time you can only rely on yourself and on the voice of a crazy sounding man who contacts you over the radio from time to time. While he sometimes sounds really nice he seems very unstable and probably not the person you want to rely on when it gets serious. Overall Penumbra: Overture does a very good job in emphasizing Philip being isolated in a hostile environment.
Penumbra: Overture is the first half of a two-part game (Penumbra: Requiem is rather a spinoff which does not directly continue the main story). The story continues and reaches its conclusion with Penumbra: Black Plague. Because of that you will not be able to figure out the whole backstory after having played only Penumbra: Overture. There are find several hints to find, though. While I think that Penumbra: Black Plague is even better than Overture, Overture is still a really good game.
If you like horror games and/or engaging puzzles this lesser known gem is something you should really try out.
