This game does not live up to the RCT name. It would take at least twice as much development as it currently has to get anywhere close. If you're crazy about theme park simulation games, you might find some enjoyment from it, but let me go over the good and the bad.
Not limited to a tile system like the previous titles
Coaster builder has piece by piece functionality, although limited
No piece by piece structure building like in previous titles
No water rides, transport rides etc
Coaster builder is extremely challenging to work with
--> It uses your camera's orientation and mouse position to orient new nodes
--> Clicking on a node moves it
--> Often tells you that smoother curves are impossible and forces bad track design
--> View of nodes is obstructed when adjustments are deemed illegal, making it hard to fix
--> No smoothing or straightening track functionality
--> Coasters don't slow down due to friction as much as you would expect
--> Coaster supports are unrealistic and don't reappear if removed
--> Brakes don't work properly, causing coasters to fail
--> Block brakes don't work properly, and multiple trains often cause coasters to stop working
--> Height limit is unrealistically low (80m)
Coaster types
--> Missing kiddie coaster, wild mouse, corkscrew coaster, looping coaster
--> Spinning coaster spins irradically, causing high intensity ratings no matter how realistic
--> Launch coaster catapult is too short and launches to height limit (80m) at slowest setting
Peeps are not properly implemented
--> An unrealistic number of peeps visit your park (300+ with just a carousel)
--> Zooming out causes peeps to turn into a slideshow
--> Zooming in fully does a weird blur thing (fake DOF?) causing peeps to disappear
--> Peeps puke, pee, and litter an unrealistic amount, making parks look like garbage
Paths are difficult to work with and not properly implemented
--> Snaps to nodes at the center of pathways rather than the outside edges
--> Ride queues cannot be curved
--> No stairs
--> Cannot place stalls/rides right next to the path, must create a short path connecting each
--> Elevated pathways often clip through the ground
--> Elevated pathways cannot contain path objects like benches
--> Connecting to other path nodes can be extremely laggy
Theming is more limited than previous titles
--> Restricted to generic, western, sci-fi, adventure
Staff is poorly implemented
--> No staff zoning
--> Staff ignores buildings, fences, etc, preferring to phase through them like ghosts
Deleting is poorly implemented
--> No auto delete for scenery when building coasters/paths
--> Delete tool is extremely laggy when mousing over objects
Filling in parks with rides causes FPS tanking (I went from 60 to 14 after building 4 coasters)
tl;dr there are more cons than pros

I really like this game and highly recommend it to anyone who likes old school PC games and simulations. If you ever dreamed of being in command of a space battleship then you should give this game a try. I spent many nights flying through the galaxy role playing as Captain Julian Augustus, Battlecruiser Commander and I can't wait to get a free weekend or three to give it another go.
This game is very complex and and takes a while to learn to play it. This game is originally from a time when PC games came in a box and included a detailed and lengthy manual. These manuals were often a treat and included background information, cool artwork, a written tutorial, list of commands, etc. I miss those types of manuals.
The tutorial is a PDF file that you print out or read on a tablet while you play through the tutorial scenarios.  I'd recommend doing that. And print out the command reference as well or keep it open on a tablet.
The main thing to understand is that this game is deliberately complex. It is designed for someone who wants to feel like they are commanding a real battleship. To get the most out of this game you have to learn to play it and you have to use your imagination and really get into the role playing and the simulation. If you treat it like an arcade style game you're going to get frustrated.

Im about 10 hours into the game when im writing this, I am a long term FF fan who have finished all releases post FF5, some of the earlier titles I have casually tried but never gotten far so im currently going back to play them all start to finish. This is my first time playing FF5 so I can not compare it to other ports.
I should probably finish the game before writing a review, however, after 10 hours I already have a lot of opinions and feel like I have a fair understanding of the game outside of end game content and the full story. This review is primarily intended to adress the concerns I had myself from reading other reviews before I purchased the game - hopefully someone in a similar position will find it useful! Now onwards!
Story
One thing that held me off from playing FF5 for many years was the thought that the older FF games had very little in terms of story, and the story is in my opinion the number 1 reason to play the franchise. This was further reinforced by constantly hearing how FF5 had the worst story of the bunch (perhaps excluding 1-3), I can tell you that I was WRONG. Whether the story is as good as the others remains to be seen, but it is definitely there, it's engaging and I can't wait to see what happens next. The main difference between FF5's story and FF6's is in the content, you will still get the same amount of story. Cutscenes happen regularly and within the first few hours I have already laughed many times and cried twice. It is definitely a Final Fantasy story.
Graphics
I think most of us (or at least me) who go back to experience the classics want it to be as close to the original as possible, we want to be able to say "FF5? Oh yes, I played that." and that's why im a bit on the fence on the 3D remakes that 3 and 4 has, how different can you make a game before it's a different game entirely? Yet on the flipside the originals are so out dated at this point even for retro fans who don't emphatise the graphics it can become a distraction.
Well, no such problems here! You get the same old 2D designs just sharpened and updated without to many creative liberties and "improvements", which is perfect to me. And let me tell you, the game looks gorgeous, with the HD sprites and beautiful spell effects the game ages so much better than the later 3D installments.
The number 1 complaint you will see about the graphics are the tile seams and yes, they are really bad at certain parts - but unless you are intentionally trying to be a critic, you'll quickly get used to it and not even notice it. The only time I actively thought about it was when I saw a big rock with terrible seams, travelling around flat surfaces like sand, floors, grass there's no problem.
Is this enough not to want to support this release and pick up another? I'll leave that up to you, I am only here to tell you that from a gamers point of view it does not take away any enjoyment.
The thing that bothered me personally the most.. The character portraits look nothing like their ingame sprites! Now the thing that bothers me the most about this is that I want to imagine a character like they are actually supposed to look, when someone mentiones Faris I want to have an image of Faris pop into my head and not some random art that the developers felt like using..
However, from what I understand the portraits are actually made from original concept art for the game - so even though they look different from the sprites, perhaps they actually do look like the character was intended to look? From what I hear many of the ingame sprites will typically look exaggerated because otherwise it would be hard to tell sprites apart in it's original low resolution. Spinning it this way, the idea became acceptable to me and the portrait art isn't bad by any means, personally I think it's beautiful.
In the end there is no real HD content out there to show us what FF5 characters really are supposed to look like in full glory, and there probably never will be.
Post-review addition: I almost forgot, but one issue I had was that the game had a white line across the left and top side of the screen when running full-screen, it was very distracting. I easily solved it by grabbing a program which lets you run borderless windowed mode in full size, basically simulated full-screen and it works like a charm and is very easy to set up. However it does mean running a third party program with your game. Something i personally hate to have to do.
I'd personally not want to play the game with that line, so I highly suggest fixing it the way I did if you do not plan on playing windowed or have an easy time ignoring annoyances like that.
Gameplay
Let me start out with saying this game is BRUTAL in terms of difficulty compared to all the later games in the franchise. Now there are two reasons for this, the first one being that the game is simply designed to be more challenging than the later games - most games from this era was.
Secondly, the way the job system works lets you easily change classes on the fly and as such I think they kind of expect you to change jobs to suit the area you are going to or the boss you are going to take on. But I am the kind of person who likes to make my perfect and well balanced setup that I enjoy and keep it that way, as such I am obviously intentionally making things harder for myself.
Using one example I faced I fire boss who was weak to ice and resistant to physical attacks, obviously this boss would have been a lot easier if I simply made my warriors into spellcasters who could cast ice spells, in not doing so the battle was a lot harder. This is not really a bad thing though, it is just a point for consideration. Personally I really enjoy the added challenge and will keep playing my way - but know that if you do the same and a boss is too hard, there are options availiable to you.
There are many more examples I could give but it all boils down too: The game wants you to switch jobs on the fly, but you don't have to if you like a challenge.
UI/Controls
Not much to say here really, some people don't like the combat menus but I think they look better than the originals. However I will say that the fonts during conversations is way to big, I wish I could change that. It is quite clear that it was designed for handheld devices, it really should be scaleable in the options.
The keyboard controls works great and are entirely customizeable, however they suffer the same issue as most FF ports seem to, that is if you bind your confirm key to a letter, when you type in someones name and press confirm it adds a later, so if for an example like me you have confirm on E, when you confirm Bartz name you will get Bartze. It's annoying but fortunately in this game you only get to name 1 character anyway so you can change the controls and change them back after.
Conclusion
It's a Final Fantasy game, if you enjoyed other classics in the franchise you will certainly enjoy this one. As a game it gets full points and you'll get way more hours of entertainment for your money than most modern games will give you.
Whether or not you should buy it comes down to your feelings on half arsed ports, it has some flaws, however for 15€ (7€ on sale right now) what you get is more than worth the price in my opinion. There is no question the game itself is worth the price, the only thing to consider is whether you want to support this particular port, i'd personally have no problem paying 7€ for HD textures alone so I'd say don't nitpick and go for it.

Oh my God, where do I begin with Haven. I'm aware that RPG Maker games usually have a bad rep because people usually affiliate games made in RPG Maker to be complete trash because (as the traielr for the engine describes) it's so simple that a kid can use it. However I'm always open minded when I go into these titles as there have been true classics made in the engine varying from games like Corpse Party and even the surprise that was The Deed. However Haven fits into the category of what most people tend to think RPG Maker titles are affiliated with, complete trash and then some.
Gameplay in Haven is the typical sort of thing you can expect for a game made in the engine. You walk around, interact with things and get into battles. Now usually the gameplay in RPG Maker games are quite hard to mess up but somehow it's messed up in this particular title. The main issue with this is that you could probably just spam the attack button and win. I remember there was a notice that came up before a boss battle saying "It's best to save here, you're probably gonna die" (litterrally that's what it says, I'll be talking about those messages a bit later.) So I saved and guess what happened? I spammed the attack button and I won. "Designed for RPG veterans" my a*s. Now I also want to talk about the messages. One of the games main promotions that it features is that there's "No handholding" that is compeltely false. This game tells you absolutely everything. It reccommends points where you save, litterrally saying along the lines of "This is a challenging battle, may I reccommend you save." Also not only that, there's a 3rd screen that appears after a battle saying "This is here only to prevent a crash." Usually when this happens in other games, the screen is converted into something else. This is common practicie among huge developers as well, they take a glitch and then make it into it's own unique thing. A great example is the Creeper from MineCraft. The Creeper actually came from a bug when the develoeprs were designing the pig, so instead of covereing the design up saying "Error, this thing wasn't meant to load" they actually converted it into something new for the game. That's what could have easily happened here, you could have added in a new aspect to the gameplay with the menu or you could have made the player obtain loot and that menu could show it. Anything could have done, not just a piece of text saying "This is here to prevent crashes."
The story is both the best and the worst part of the game. For most RPG and Adventure game titles, the story is what carries the game, it gives the player a reason to continue. Now Haven has a pretty good setup for a story but the execution isn't quite there. The story is you are basically playing as the main character called Cleril and you're exploring his psyche and he's trying to explore for something I guess. He's accompanied by other personalities that he has and when put together they make up the actual person when they're actually just divided personalities helping the man actually discover something. In case you didn't realise my complaint when explaining the plot, my main issue is that it's confusing. It let's you in on the plot well enough but the the more you head into the story, it just becomes more confusing. You might be thinking that that's the main point of the story and even though it is, it should be explaining things better because I realised that the main character seemed to be all caught up with everything you needed to be. I feel like if the main plot is to explore the main psyche of a character, I should be exploring it along with him but at the start of the game, he seems to know more than I do.
The graphics are sort of hard to sum up. The graphic style seems inconsistant. Now I wouldn't mind if you just kept with your primary graphic style that you were using for the characters and the environment, even though those in general look sub par, at least it would be consistant. There are these random out of place looking images that look like they were just stuck onto the screen (look at the 4th screenshot for the game as my example.) Now the sound, when the game started the sound seemed pretty good but then it took a turn southwards around 40 mins into the game when there was suddenly lyrics thrown into the music which made the music seem really out of place. If you want an idea of how out of place it seems, just imagine fighting a dragon in Skyrim and instead of having that epic music playing, replace it with the Incy Wincy Spider nursery rhyme being sung by kids. Yeah, that's how out of place it seems.
It's hard to really find much to like about Haven because the majority of it is bad but when there is something good in it, it quickly disregards it and swaps it out for something bad or when there is potential for something it just seems dissappointing when it reaches the pay off.
Pros
+ Potential for a good plot
Cons
- Simplistic gameplay
- Handholding
- Out of place messages
- Confusing plot
- Inconsistant graphics
- Out of place music
Final verdict: 1/10

You know, I really hate when people say certain things aren't games. They're "walking simulators", or "interactive movies" or whathaveyou. It's usually unfair because even though your interactions are limited in some cases, your actions either change the story or there's some sort of gameplay involved.
Her Story is possibly the only game I've ever played where I would at least partially agree, "No, it's not a game." Let me explain why. The entire game consists of typing in keywords and watching videos. There is nothing more to it. There is no reward for watching every single video, and the "ending" is no different if you had given up right away or see it through to the end.
I would compare it to something like Night Trap, that old Sega CD game that became infamous for its lack of gameplay, and "disturbing content". Except, Night Trap gave you far more to do. There were different events you could only see by replaying multiple times, and there were fail states. Not that a game requires a fail state, but there should be some sort of reward or risk for doing things in a certain way or certain order. Here there is none of that. No matter what order you view the videos, whether you quit halfway through or see it to the end nothing really changes.
Her Story is akin to reading a book out of order. For example, you'll skip to chapter 11, read the third paragraph, then jump back to chapter 2 and read paragraph fourteen. There is a certain thrill when you piece something together and get that "Aha!" moment, but it's largely artificial as you didn't really piece togehter anything. You watched a bunch of clips out of context, and put them in the correct sequence in your mind. Not much detective work here.
This wouldn't necessarily be a bad thing if there was more to it. But the game is nothing if not repetitive. You type in a keyword, and watch the videos related to it. Unfortunately, you can only view the first six videos related to that keyword. So after trying all the obvious things like "murder", or "suspect", and every name and object that comes up, you're sort of left grasping at straws throwing out random words like "billards" or supercalliefragillisticexbedosish" in the vain hope that you'll find one of the key videos you're missing. It also doesn't help that the game is very specific in certain instances. (Example: "murdered" is considered the same as "murder",  but "pair" and "pear" are different, as are "married" and "marry" are not.)
In my experience, it's almost impossible to view them all without cheating and looking up the secret to viewing all the videos in chronological order one by one. It's even more unfortunate that a good number of them are nothing but filler, meant to pad out the length of time it takes you to see everything.
But for what the game lacks in gameplay and content surely it makes up for in story right? I'd say no. The story is more concerned with being clever than it is with making sense. I don't want to spoil anything, but needless to say contrivences and coincidences rule the day in this story, and the internal logic begins to break down if you think about certain aspects of it too much. Sure there are a few twists (though you'll likely figure them out ahead of time), but they're not really enough to make this game worth the price of admission.
It also doesn't help that there are a few loose ends that are never tied up. And while I would agree to an extent that "Not everything needs to be solved" in a game that completely revolves around unraveling a mystery, it's a bit unfair to the player to have them try to figure out what happened only in the end to reveal that there are no answers for certain events.
I originally purchased this game because I had heard amazing things about it. That it was truly revolutionary, and one of a kind. You'll never play a game quite like it. Needless to say, it didn't live up to expectations. Not even close. I couldn't recommend anyone pay more than $1 for this. And even at that price, I'd say the cost of admission is too steep.

Battleborn is trying to be a good game by taking a piece from a lot of other popular games, but not making it their own.

I came into this game expecting it to be something Overwatch was - a tight, competitive MOBA style FPS, with lots of characters and a lot of fun PvP.
I can honestly say that is exactly what I got, but that is NOT what is most fun about this game.
The story mode is gorgeous and fun. It's fast paced, has huge bosses, and the set pieces are truly awesome. There was a point during a boss bottle where it transports you into the space void, and I can honestly say I was not expecting it. It reminded me something of a Final Fantasy-style boss battle.
I think that's where this game's strength lies, in its cooperative story, not its competitive PvP. Battleborn just has a really cool aesthetic and feel that Overwatch, in my opinion, can't hold a candle to. I want to read about this world and play RPGs in this world; where Overwatch I just want to fight.
Give us some meat in the story mode. Flesh it out. That's your niche. Don't try to compete against Overwatch, you've already lost. Instead, go a different direction and offer something Overwatch can't - PvE. GOOD PvE. That's what you cut your teeth on, Gearbox, and it really shines through.

Writing my very first review in support of this awesome game.
9/10, best game I've played in a long while.
The graphics and art are great. There are so many animations and so much work put into it. For example, every character you come across, down to the sheep have 9-10 different facial expressions depending on their mood.
The music and sound effects are varied and interesting. Some of the songs I've found myself humming to after stopping playing.
The controls are great. I love games that you can play solely with the mouse.
The atmosphere and story is lighthearted and fun. You play a group of explorers searching the globe for rare artifacts. Think Indiana Jones. The characters (there are 20 of them) are each so unique. Rare in a roguelite game, you actually feel like they have character.
The gameplay, which is the core of any gaming experience, is some of the most original I've seen in years. You have 3/4 different things going on. First you have your character selection. You choose from 3 among 20 characters. There are so many combinations and synergies here it's ridiculous. Then you have the preparation for expeditions, which is akin to X-Com. You manage your crew, giving them jobs, hiring supporters and specialists, outfitting your explorers, then sending them on expeditions. Expeditions follow an FTL-like system of branches, but unlike FTL there's more strategy involved in how you make progress. Each path costs a different amount of supplies, and you have a better idea of what your headed into. Planning your trip becomes a major strategy factor in itself. Most places you go will have branching multiple choice paths. Some of these are very in depth with numerous paths. Depending on your explorers' skills, more opportunities are available to you, making each game very different. Finally, there's the combat which is imo the best part. It's a highly original turn based tactics game where you have a rock paper scissors dynamic of friendly persuasion, devious demoralization, and of course, outright beating the crap out of the enemy. Every character has one basic skill in each of these three, with most being best at one. Then two unique moves. Usually these are very complex with multiple ways to use them. Then 1-2 unique passive moves. Oh yeah, then the passive abilities that the equipment gives you. Oh, I almost forgot, and every character, including enemies, will have different moods which influence their stats. All this combines into a tactical combat system with more depth and variety than just about any other. It's fun as hell.
The only con I would give this game is that I wish there were more expeditions to go on (there's about 10 right now). But this is mitigated by the variety within each one, being randomized each playthrough. This fault is being remedied though, in that even in the short time the game's been out they've added a free one, and have more DLC planned. This is why I'm writing this review, please support this game, I want to see it thrive and expand. It's definitely worth the 20 bucks

You are going to hate
no matter how much enjoyment you gained from playing it. There is one simple reason for this: The moment the credits roll, you’re going to realize you just finished one of the best games ever made. And this can never be undone.
4000 years before the battle of Yavin: You wake up aboard the Endar Spire amid a battle against a Sith-Fleet. Just like you, your character has no idea what the hell just happens and where he is. But behold, there is the unsung hero Trask Ulgo who is kind enough to explain the situation and the basics of the game. This is how the best
game ever created starts.
From a modern point of view,
might seem outdated. Its graphics pale in comparison to recent roleplaying games like the
,
or the
Series (all these titles are great in their own regard). But fancy graphics don't matter.
puts heart and soul into its characters, plot and ultimately its dense atmosphere. And in one swift stroke
pulls off what George Lucas never managed to do with the prequels: To tell a story of grand scale that is nonetheless personal and adventurous. Simply put, it creates a story that lives and breathes the original
.
But you don’t need to be a huge
fan to adore this title as it is a great RPG, too. If you enjoyed
or
,
is for you. The roots of the former titles can be traced back directly to the latter. Elements that were introduced in
were later refined in these games. Your character is mute (just like in original
). Every other character is fully synchronized. Some people are bothered by this and I can fully understand that but it offers the advantage that there are a lot more dialogue options than the recent
-ian triad of “good”, “neutral” and “evil”. And, of course, this helps to bring some of the most memorable characters of video game history to life.
You might’ve guessed it: The characters of this game are just amazingly well written. Every one of them brings something different to party. Every one of them is unique. And every one of them is memorable. I still can recall dialogues with every party member and that is no incident. Conversations are the beating heart of
. Especially the ones with your crewmembers are excellent. Sometimes, they are dramatic. For example the quest that revolves around Bastila Shan’s parents. Other times they are hilariously funny – especially the conversations that involve a certain droid. Even the banter between your party members during missions is well written.
manages to create some of the most beloved characters of the
Universe and with that they shaped the so called “Expanded Universe” for years to come. Credit must also be given to the beautiful voice acting by everyone involved.
Naturally, this is also connected to the excellent storyline which offers one of the most shocking plot twists ever created. But truth to be told: The mission goals might get a bit repetitive during the mid-game. Nevertheless the steps to achieve the goal vary stark due to highly entertaining side-quests and level-design. For instance, during one main quest you are accused of a crime and have to defend yourself. If you do something wrong, they'll sentence you to death. In another mission you have to finish the training to become a Sith. Furthermore your quest leads you to highly diverse planets from the vast deserts of Tatooine to the tightly populated planet of Taris with its urban vibe that is reminiscent of Coruscant. The tremendous score by Jeremy Soule just enhances the experience - he carefully mashes up well-known tracks from John Williams with his own arrangements to create a unique soundtrack, that is deeply rooted in the realm of
compositions and yet highly distinguishable (listen to Bastila Shan's theme for reference).
Besides the old-school-graphics, the gameplay probably discourages most people from picking it up. Admittedly, it’s slow as it is round based. That means you have choose an action your character takes after the enemy “finished his round”. It’s nothing like
where you are actively aiming and shooting. If you want to boost the challenge, you stop using the pause button and choose an action for every party member. You don’t have to, though. The game is not very hard if you just want to enjoy the story. However, some boss fights can be really annoying on the first try.
If you think about playing
, do yourself a favor and just do it. You won’t be disappointed. If you generally like
games or
you should play this as it was a defining game for the former and the latter.
:
combines a cast of great characters, a compelling story with some unpredictable twists and turns with polished gameplay. Conclusion: Play it, meatbag.

As for the game, it is not self contained, meaning that you must read the manual and possibly do the tutorial. This game is an acquired taste and involves a lot of knowledge and study.
This game is not really about you dogfighting, even if you can take a planetary defense fighter and pilot it. The meat of the game is the capital ship. Crew management (it simulates where each crew member is and what they are doing, even if you can't walk inside the ship) and other internal management of a capital ship, including a fighter squadron. You can be boarded, coordinate ground operations, pilot shuttles or fighters of your carrier, use orbital missiles, take over enemy space stations and explore a universe that, while not as large as Elite: Dangerous, will take you a long time to explore.
Multiple races and occupations will change the game dynamic. There are military carriers, science vessels, trade ships, small fighters and more!
As for the Campaign, I never had much interest in it. I rather take a Battlecruiser MK3 and roam around the universe with a reduced risk of court martial.

Calling this game a "collector's edition" is like calling a used red solo cup a "goblet fit for only a king's mouth". Imagine a big disgusting bag of trash, and then dumping that into a septic tank and taking a long bath in there. That's basically what you're going to get with this abomination of a video game. The following two segments illustrates my first two playthroughs:
1. Spawned as the chestical soldier on Earth (elite combat marine with two gigantic chest pads no matter what gender) and some alpha guys that looked like me and were friendly started running up to me shooting. Infantry controls don't work with the "fully supported" xbox controller (but do with vehicles) so I switched to mouse and keyboard for this despite configuring it beforehand for the controller. Aiming with the mouse is a challenge considering the mouse is inverted by default for some reason. I killed one of them, sprinted towards the nearest building, clipped through it and was instantly killed.
2. Spawned as the chestical soldier again and, after slogging through the awful manual, figured out how to enter and drive a SUV with a machine gun ontop around the base. The controls are overly sensitive and incredibily awful. You have to directly target things if your vehicle has a free moving turret, instead of pivoting your mouse or something similar to manuver them around. I tried running people over but they just collect on your hood and get moved around. I shot at a giant yet noiseless patrolling tank a few times, with no reaction, then shot off into the desert by holding the "Down" direction on the left analog stick. The same stick the steering is controlled with, yeah, smart. The main developer, Derek Smart, didn't want anyone to see the truly awful level design outside of this base on Earth that also had truly awful level design, so the base defenses automatically started firing rockets at me as I drove far away from it. I drove over a lake, then into an ocean with my open-air car, and didn't drown even upon exiting. Since I had no idea where to go after spending about 10 minutes or more letting the car drive effortlessly over the oceanfloor, I quit the game and didn't bother looking at the rest of the game until the next day.
I have never dealt with a more needlessly complicated system of learning how to do anything. Even tabletop games, which can be fairly complicated, are more readily available to learn than this "turn to page XYZ to even sort of understand what I'm talking about" nonsense. This might fly in the days of Wing Commander and such, but the draw of certain "old school" style game elements just doesn't exist anymore unless you're playing an enthusiast level flight simulator or something. Seriously, page 4 of the tutorial throws every single blinking light at you at once, gives it a dumb 3 letter combination, and says to pause the game and just stare at the UI for awhile. How is that intuitive, or learning anything as you're doing it? By comparison, Elite Dangerous has a similarly complicated UI, with a lot going on in front of you, as well as the need to access the computers on the right and left sides of you at times, but the tutorials are broken down into small scenarios focusing on the basics before anything complicated. Slapping together a couple integrated Word docs that tells you how to play is just lazy, plain and simple. Telling me "go here, fly around the target craft at half speed because I said so, then shoot at it but DON'T KILL IT OR YOU LOSE" is not intuitive. Wouldn't "Collector's Edition" imply you made some improvements to these clearly outdated systems? Or is this part of the code that was only touched in one day, as detailed on Twitter? How does telling us the equivalent of "only the commander really works" in the game description on Steam, then giving us a bad experience in that one single class, tell us that the full upcoming game will not be completely bad as well?
I'm wearing headphones as I play this, and the crew randomly babbling things as soon as I jump into a ship makes me think this game is turning me into a schizophrenic. Is this the lost souls of those who played the game calling for me to join them in the underworld?
The controls are awful, and I'd like to re-emphasize that here. For example. instead of using the escape key to pause the game and display relevant background information like saving and such, there's 5 million different uses for Alt+*whatever key* instead. There's nothing in the key bindings of this game that screams "intuitive" or "well thought out". In fact, everything about this game's control scheme seems to indicate that it was designed to be played in the Eighth Circle of the underworld from Dante Alighieri's "Divine Comedy", alongside being whipped and having your body immersed in a lake of boiling pitch.
There may be some improvements I'm not aware of compared to the base game it originates from, but would you eat a turd if it has pink frosting and sprinkles on it? To me, and likely many others, this is just another failure of many attached to Derek Smart.

This is another one of those games that i would give a mixed review because of a good game/bad port. Let's start with the good game. Final Fantasy V may be one of the least favourites and more obscure titles, but i truly love this game. The story, contrary to many reviewers, is fun and engaging. Sure, it isn't deep or anything, but it's there and gets the job more than done. The same applies to the characters, both main and NPCs. But of course, what truly shines in this game is the job system, designed in a way that you can equip certain job exclusive abilities into other unrelated jobs, creating a huge amount of experimentation, and some combos are simply amazing. What i also enjoy here is the music, which is another masterpiece from Nobuo Uematsu. Final Fantasy V is a great and complete RPG which shoudn't be dismissed by fans of the genre.
But should it be the Steam version? I'll be honest right away: i didn't found this version to be terrible. I played in a windowed mode with a controller, and enjoyed playing this to 100% in this version, getting all items and achievements (which is a nice addition). But... to me the game didn't launch at first. There's an issue with the game only recognizing standard English characters for the Windows account name, and in order to play the game i had to create another account just to play this, which is absurd. That left a bad taste in my mouth, but besides that my experience was good the entire time. The auto-save makes the game very easy though (saving after each battle) and it doesn't delete itself when loaded as advertised. And speaking of saves, make sure to back-up your save manually, because the Steam Could only saves the main settings, which is also absurd. The price is also expensive considering it's age and that it's a mobile port (the main complain that everyone has). The port it's obvious, but it didn't distracted me. I even enjoyed the updated sprites (but not the character portraits). So, on sale, if you really want Final Fantasy V on your Steam library you can get it. It's a bad port, but the game is completely playable, or at least it was for me after the launch issue that i described earlier. If you really want it, go for it. Otherwise, you can always stick to another version.

I'm going to do something most reviews about this game don't do:
. First, I do have to address the Behemoth in the room: the issues people have with the port. I've watched a full playthrough of the SNES version (you can too on Youtube if you want), and in my opinion, this version looks better graphically as it is so much clearer. Just look at the monsters in combat on the SNES version, then look at them on this one. This one's monsters look gorgeous to me by comparison.
My only personal gripe about the graphics are the character portraits they used in this version. They're based on original concept artwork for the characters, drawn by Yoshitaka Amano. The problem is that this leads to a lack of cohesion when hair colors, accessories (such as glasses, etc.), hair styles, and more are completely wrong when compared to the in-game versions of the characters you see. Leaving the portraits out completely would have been better in my opinion. I ended up downloading a set of modified portraits from a Steam user's forum post in which he made the hair colors match and switched in a modified Terra FFVI portrait for Lenna (you'd be surprised how much it looks like in-game Lenna). Other folks had graphical glitches involving "tiling" while moving, but apparently there are files you can download if you search a bit in the forums and that will fix that problem if you have it.
Another gripe people have is that they dislike the eight directions of movement. The original had four. I've played those old SNES Final Fantasy games, and I was thoroughly thrilled when I found that I could move in eight directions in this game. It was wonderful. I could get around so much faster (straight line instead of zig-zagging up-left-up-left to go northwest, for example). Soem people dislike the look of the new character models. Look at the screenshots. Hate them? You'll likely hate this port. Genuinely don't mind them or like them? Cool. It's pretty obvious if you'll like or dislike them from the screenshots alone in this game. What you see is what you get, and I think they look nice. I wish they weren't so blurry and had more detail, but I'm fine with them as is.
Alright, I think that's enough about the port. I didn't want to say nothing about it, because it needs mentioning, but even if a game were the best port in the world, the quality of the game itself is often more important.
Your entry into this world will find you beset with very nice music. I've played all but FFXV and the NES Final Fantasy II  of the numbered series, and I much preferred V's soundtrack to XII (too much brass for my taste in XII), though many other titles in the series could contend for my favor. The sound effects are fairly old-school and I enjoyed them as well. I have no complaints about the sound and music of this game.
On the topic of grinding...it's not required in this game, but don't asssume that I'm saying I don't recommend it. If you don't care how much time you spend replaying bosses and enemy encounters trying to not get wiped with ease, and you are just naturally good at taking the time to try every little trick to progress in a game while at a low level, then you'll have a good time here. If you follow a walkthrough for every boss to look up the trick to beating them (not talking about elemental weaknesses), you could also manage without grinding. However, though I've completed all FF games pre-XV and post-III, I do not claim to be very good at FF games, nor am I really into long grinds. That said, I am perfectly fine with it if I don't have to spend too much time doing it and feel a steady feeling of being rewarded.
Unfortunately, your character level just isn't that important. I was level 40 and having difficulty with most bosses that came my way. Then I went into a cave and fought squirrels for...I'm guessing 8 hours or so. They give virtually no XP, but give ABP (ability points to level up jobs (jobs max at level 7 or earlier)), and I maxed out the jobs I needed (about 5-6 per character). Then I exited the cave at level 42, and was steamrolling over every boss for the rest of the game.
This took away from some of the fun of the gradual leveling growth inherent to FF games for me, because the game has a terrible ABP gain curve. You start getting 1 ABP in most battles. Although the gains go up to 3 and as high as 8 before the final act of the game, quite a few of these fights take longer than fighting very wimpy enemies that pay out small amounts of ABP. Then, at the final dungeon, you start getting 29 or so ABP per fight, and there are even rare monsters in the final areas of the final dungeon which give out more than 100 ABP per battle. When it costs 500+ ABP -per job- to hit the max level on most of the 25 jobs you can level in the game, it made grinding prior to the final "dungeon" very tedious for me. By the time the end credits rolled, I was bored and just glad to finally be done. Grinding is kinda worthless until suddenly you're too powerful for the boss of the game. =/
Lastly about the job system: use a job guide/walkthrough. Otherwise, you could spend far, far more time than I did training your jobs to get new abilities. I was bored, and I was only leveling jobs that I knew I needed! Each character had 15+ jobs they never touched once. Also, the game and its instructions do not tell you that your starting job, "Freelancer," gets most innate (passive) abilities from other jobs you've mastered, and that you get the highest attribute bonus among all jobs you master (so if you master Summoner and Black Mage, you only get the Magic bonus from Summoner because it's higher). This is a huge part of the game's mechanics to not mention in the game or its instructions, and I find it irresponsible that the people who made the game did not mention this. I cannot stress enough how important a job guide/walkthrough is if you are a person who cares about how they spend their time when playing a game.
Tip: Also, make Galuf a magic-user if you play, even though he has high strength stats. I can't say why because of story/spoiler reasons, but Bartz/Faris as physical attackers and Lenna/Galuf as magic-users is ideal if you're min-maxing your characters' offensive stats.
The positives I have about FFV's job system are that I like the numerous character models for each character while equipped with each job, and I like how you can equip an ability from one job on another job, making it easier to level less useful jobs, and helping to cover your party's weaknesses by having more options. Also, it's not FFIII's job system, so thank goodness for that. I started playing that before FFV, and FFV was a breath of fresh air by comparison.
Finally, I'd like to discuss...uh-oh running out of room. Finally, plot and characters. The characters aren't deep or interesting, but I really enjoyed the main team's "slice of life" interpersonal interactions when not being overly dramatic and things aren't blowing up or being sucked into vortexes. Towns feel a little samey at times and I did not care about the people in them. The villain is uninteresting and wants to kill/abduct everyone just because. Super cliche and lacking, failing to interest or excite me. FFIV is older and I preferred its story. That said, the self-sacrificing of characters en masse returns. This sort of thing should be shocking and emotional...not cause eye-rolling, as was the case here for me most of the time.
In closing, I thought the port was just fine. However, a weak storyline and some weak locations deflated my interest, and this game misses the mark a bit on grinding, as it is my opinion that very skilled players should be able to get by with very little grinding, while unskilled players should be able to grind a bit longer per area to become tough enough to proceed. My team was either puny or extremely over-powered, without enough middle ground for me to have fun.

The RollerCoaster Tycoon games have been a staple part of my gaming life since I was a knee high to a grass hopper....RollerCoaster tycoon world has ended this run with a game that doesn't deserve to be associated with its forebears.
Firstly, I know this is an Early Access game and shouldn't expect too much, but this was a true disappointment.  I have a fairly high end rig and this game ran pathetically; peeps don't walk and glide, fps is very low, coaster builder is laggy.  The graphics are just terrible, barely upgraded from RCT3.  The water is just dreadful....why does it look like copper sulphate solutions?! It's not that blue!
The coaster builder is a double-edged sword...the potential to build anything you want is brilliant...you can make the coaster into exactly what you want...it is just so damn fiddly!  One great positive is the testing stats overlay that you get...it highlights the areas of the coaster that has the highest nausea inducing spirals that can really help when trying to perfect a ride as well as pointing out where the excitement is highest; that aspect is brilliant.
All in all, I feel really disappointed with this game.  The number of bugs is staggering and issues is staggering.  I really wanted to love this game, but as it stands at the moment, I just can't.  In some respects, the developers have listened to the community from the pre-alpha but it still has light-years to go before I would recommend.
I just hope that the developers really try and fix this....otherwise its the end of a great series.  So far, the developers have certainly been fixing the major issues with posts and that.  I remain confident that with some time and feedback, they will turn this into the game that it should be.
EDIT 4/4/16:  Having played the game for a bit longer now, I can see the potential in this game about what could be.  Having changed the graphics settings to their highest (the autoconfig didn't do this) and their not actually that bad, so you can ignore that from my previous review!  I think I would upgrade my initial review slightly, but at its current state, I still can't recommend it.

Her Story, created and released by Sam Barlow of Silent Hill fame, is one of those games that often has critics questioning whether it should be called a “game” at all. It’s closer, perhaps, to a visual novel or a movie viewed out of sequence. Whatever you call it, it’s an enjoyable, compact experience that probably won’t have you lying awake thinking about it weeks later but tells an engaging story in an unexpected way.
Full Review Here:

This game is an example of nonlinear narrative done well. The premise of using a recovered police database with a semi-functional search facility is a sound premise for the narrative. The game is well written and the story is deliciously complex. In my first playthrough, I thought I had discovered everything within the first ten minutes. However, I was wrong. As I continued searching the footage, more and more questions became apparent and I was forced to re-evaluate my original assumptions. The game does have replay value for people who wish to explore those questions further. I strongly disagree with those who say it would be better to just watch the footage chronologically in YouTube. The non-linear gameplay style allows you to formulate conclusions from later sequences and then bring them into doubt with earlier ones. The player of the game is actively engaged trying to think of search terms to reveal gaps it the footage, which can be challenging. This is definitely a game. It is definitely narrative art. It is an excellent experience.

One of the best indie's I've played in a long long time.
I wasn't expecting much from this title.  I heard the narrative was good, and I liked the hook: Piece together a narrative from clips from police interrogations.
I absolutely adore logical puzzles, and I adore detective narratives.  Making a pot of tea and sitting down to the computer with the buzzing sound of the late night lights (in-game) really had me unexpectedly enthralled.  I only planned to play 10 or so minutes.  Before long, it was an hour and a half.  I was making notes, looking for clues, trying to understand Her Story.
Each little clip was another crumb, and the crumb trail was insatiable.  The story was interesting.  "Who was this?"  "What does that mean?" "There's a name!  I can really dig through a few videos now!"  Without spoiling anything this game really is about as far as you want to go with it.  Until you think you are happy with what you know about Her Story.

Her Story is a very interesting experience, personally I am a fan of visual novels and adventure games so this type of game is right up my alley. Going through the case files and investigatting everything so that I can get the full story and drawing my own conclusion at the end is pretty intersting. There isn't much much to say about the gameplay, you watch videos, decrypt stuff, research stuff, it's very basic but it works.
The performances during the live action video segments are well acted out and pretty convincing, Viva Seifert does an amazing job as the central character of the game.
The story of the game is pretty much a crime/mystery and I won't go into it in order to avoid spoilers but a few of the plot twists are pretty well implemented.
Her Story isn't a game for everyone and it is something you have to try for yourself to decide wether it is for you or not, but personally I can say that I would recommend this game even if it is for you to try it out for a few minutes.

In  the beginning you're given no context as to who the woman in the clip is or what she did, which a initially thought was a great idea until i reached about an hour & a half of playtime & all of a sudden the credits roll & i still didn't understand who this woman was, what her motivations for doing what she was alleged of doing were. I'm a huge fan of AVGN and have watch every single one of his videos several times. To see a game based on his outrages is such a brilliant idea. This game really takes everything that he hates about bad games, or they take some of his comments and make them an actual idea. (Especially the "Super Pitfall" reference was brilliant.)
If you've watched his videos you'll easily catch the references through out the game and the appearences of popular characters. Some of them are so awesome it brought a huge smile to my face (like the fireshark) and it's also nice being able to beat up the boss on the Atari stage. They are in no way overpowering a whole stage, just a small reference placed perfect in some parts of the game.
I liked that the stages had their own themes as well as that they tried to include his famous quotes in the game as a reference. I wouldn't have mind seeing more bats in the horror stage, as it always seems the old games have way too many bats than needed. I think my favorite stage was the Winter stage, just because of what happens after you defeat the first boss. Just brilliant and easily my favorite part of the game. Anytime you die, you get a randomly generated outrage from the nerd which is fun when there's a great mix up.
The graphics are well done and the music is very good. The controls for the most part feels very solid. I'm glad you can adjust the keyboard to your own liking.
So why don't I recommend this game?
Well, unfortunately whoever designed all these stages obviously ran out of ideas after taking the nerds outrages that don't fill a complete stage. So half the stages consist of instant death blocks. More than half of the deaths within the game will happen due to these blocks that are everywhere. Placed in hard-to-reach areas, walls of death blocks that changes between invisibility and jumping over them with a sketchy trampoline techinques. Did I mention they are literally everywhere in this game?
What would have been a brilliant platformer with great humor and references, ends up being a practice jump game to test your accuracy whether or not you're able to avoid these deathblocks or not. I guess the idea is making the game so utterly frustrating you will swear and scream like the Nerd, but even the games he played seem more fun than going through a stage of deathblocks. A lot of the games he did play featured some areas with frustrating jumps, but not to the extend that this game uses them.
If it wasn't for these tedious deathblocks, the game would honestly be very short. There isn't much variety to the stages other than being lucky enough to avoid deathblocks and occassionally shooting some enemies. It's like switching from one deathblock avoiding game to another. Just add some new sprites and backgrounds and voila, you are ready to make another test of frustrating accuracy. It feels quite sad that such a fantastic idea just ends up as a bland jumping game.
I can enjoy a game despite them being difficult. This isn't one of them though. Anytime I completed a stage I didn't get that rewarding feeling. In other difficult games, you complete the difficult part, then move onto another different, yet difficult task. It really was like playing the same stages over and over, with the deathblocks making up too much of my playtime than it was enjoyable. I enjoyed the parts of the game where these weren't present and quite frankly, I wouldn't have minded them being a bit here and there. It just feels that they are all over the game as a way to extend a very short game into something longer.

As a person who was watched the AVGN's how since the beginning, it amazes me to see how many (obscure) references have been put into this game. A 2D sidescroller that harkens back to the old SNES days, The Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is a smorgasboard of James Rolfe's ongoing Youtube sensation and celebrates every second of it.
Graphically the game has an inspired look. Meaning that pretty much everything in the game is an homage to something from the show, and the music is probably better than it deserves. While the presentation is top-notch, the gameplay is where the game falters. The game has the tendency to mock the faults of other games: not being able to see oncoming enemies beyond the screen, checkpoints that are placed at sadistic spots and instakills are only the tip of the iceberg. Alot of trial and error is in place here when it shouldn't. If you want to point out the mistakes other games make by being unfair to the player, don't make the same mistakes aswell.
Frustration aside, I still think this is a game you should at least give a try. The presentation is great, the soundtrack is unbelievable and it makes for some fun moments. You could do a lot worse.

This game has a lot of things to recommend it, most of which pale upon repeated playthroughs.
Upon first glance, it features a wide array of playable characters. However, the characters have a lot of overlap in abilities and the available equipment is constant across runs, leading to very few distinct-feeling characters. And one of the three characters in your party has to either be one of the 5 starting captains or a character that you have already used a lot. Still, there's enough variety to keep things interesting at the start.
The combat works in emotions and diplomacy in addition to violence, which is interesting and innovative at first. Ultimately, though, it's just a rock-paper-scissors elemental system by another name. It's also frustrating that each character has one style of combat that they suck at, meaning that you're essentially playing rock-scissors and just having to grind things out whenever your enemy picks rock. The splash-damage abilities are a little disappointing, too. Since regular attacks often one-shot weak enemies, a splash attack that hits multiple enemies for a third of their health is frequently useless. Once the novelty of winning a battle with kindness or insults wears off, what's left behind is underwhelming.
There are actually very few adventure paths in this game. You get one of three random ones at the start, then three new options open up (same each game), then three new ones (same each game), then two more (same each game), then one more (again, same each game), and that's it. The unique treasures, events, and dialogues are quite cool. That is, of course, until you discover that they aren't unique. You get the same ones each time, on each adventure, on each run-through.
I guess I'm being pretty negative about the game. And there's a good bit to be negative about. But that's only because I've played it too much. The game is great when you first start playing, and will remain great if you have the sense to stop. Buy this on sale, run through each of the adventures once, and never touch it again. You'll have good memories of a novelty game that didn't overstay its welcome.

This game is a must buy if you like strategy games or roguelikes.
I seduced a tribesman for a magic mask, I beat sheep to death for science, and I captured King Kong and sold him to the zoo because that's what Renowned Explorers do. It's all fair game on the way to fame and fortune.
This is the first time I've written a review on Steam.
That should give you some idea of how much of an impression Renowned Explorers has left me with in such a short amount of time. I HIGHLY RECOMMEND it to anybody who is a fan of King of Dragon Pass, Faster Than Light, or roguelike games. It's hard to describe because this game really is a breath of fresh air for any gamer that's played pretty much everything over the years.
It's not really like most other games.
The combat system is easily the most interesting mechanic I've seen in years. The last time I was this impressed by a new idea like this was probably when I first played Civilization because it was that different and new ideas in games don't seem to come around all that often anymore. It all feels like more of the same, except for this game.
You pick your leader, recruit your crew, and set out on an adventure. You can build a party up of different characters, and there's a lot to choose from. You unlock them as leaders to lead your party later.
The super deep "combat" system. I can't rave about this enough.
You can resolve encounters through skill checks before they happen sometimes, or by using aggression, devious, or friendly moves during them. Or, you can walk around the areas where you know they'll happen if you want. I mean, there's probably even more ways to handle a single encounter than that, but that's off the top of my head. That doesn't even get into the numerous strategies you can use while you're in combat. You don't have to stick with an aggressive approach for an entire encounter. You can switch halfway through to resolve it in a friendly or devious manner.
It's hard to explain. You just have to play it.
You MUST play it.
The game really gives you the feeling that you're exploring the world like Indiana Jones, Nathan Drake, or Lara Croft. You have your crew members, and everybody has their own strengths and weaknesses.
The art style is Adorable!
If you ever felt like all the wonder was gone in the world. Or like most games are too damn oppressively moody, then you'll really love the tone of the writing, the refreshing art style, and the humorous events that just seem to happen through the stupid decisions you make.
The cons:
I'm not sure I've found any yet. One bug that resolved when I exited the game. There was an enemy that kept running around my screen like he was on crack after he died. It was more funny than anything.
I solved it by saving and exiting the game.

A whimsical adventure exploring locations packed with character. Feels like a choose your own adventure game, remember those books when you where a kid?

Comparison to FTL are fair, but I feel like I have more control when playing this game based on information about each node, overviews of the adventures ahead etc.
At this stage I feel more locations and captains would be a good addition, which I assume is being added in the coming expansion. Also a global leaderboard would be great!
I find it hard to believe this game isn't more popular, because it is an absolute class act (with plenty of moustache references, excellent)! Highly recommended!!

(Note: I originally bought this game through Humble Bundle and played it directly through them, hence the lack of Steam play time here.)
As a big Metroidvania and brawler fan, I expected this game to be a homerun for me. And the first few hours I played were excellent. I loved the freedom of the combat and the ability to chain together lots of moves in new ways. I also appreciated the wealth of references.
But as the game progresses, you get flooded with new abilities (OP and unnecessary abilities IMO that ruin the rhythm of the game) and the once precise and tight controls become way over-saturated. The combat becomes muddled and convoluted.
On top of that, the game rapidly shifts its focus from combat to platforming, which is not its strong point. I had a blast in the beginning of the game chaining huge hit counts in very satisfying and visually appealing fights. Then some way into it, I have to make my way through almost Meatboy level platforming, only without the precision and quick respawn that dedicated platformers like Meatboy have. Where games like Meatboy and Dustforce are VERY hard, they don't feel unfair, and they focus on platforming mechanics so they can perfect them. Guacamelees platforming has terrible controls, and the platforming feels thrown-in. The game becomes crazy frustrating and promptly sucks all the fun out of it. If you're looking for platforming, leave Guacamelee on the shelf and go get Dustforce.
This game suffers from over-saturated mechanics and identity crisis. If you love brawlers and Metroidvania style games, you might get some enjoyment out of this, but my advice is don't get too invested.  If you want something that does brawler/Metroidvania really well, I suggest Dust (if you can get past bad story/voice acting), or even better, go buy Muramasa for about $12 on Wii or just emulate it. You'll have more visually unique game with better mechanics and longer campaign.

Okay, here's the deal. Every aspect of the game needs work. However, that being said, there are some very promissing aspects of this game. For example, the coaster building mechanics are top-notch. It combines the ease of piece-by-piece with the fine detained spline based editing to easily create specific track. However, you cannot "delete" a part of the track, only mess around with the nodes, which makes sense. Also, because it's so "realistic," you have to create realistic tracks, or it's not going to work. In the previous RTC games, you could slap together parts all willy-nilly and as long as it was a completed circut and didn't stall anywhere, it was "rideable." Not the case in this game, but I think it really makes you consider aspects you normally would not, so at the end of the day, you're more proud of what you've done. So good coaster building mechanics, but implementation still needs work.
Another example is the staff, I don't have much to say other than I'm not a fan of the "huts-that-take-up-space-and-provide-little-help-and-organization" way of doing it. I think parkitect has an amazing system where you just had break rooms placed about that increaded productivity.
The path placing and using is really the worst part. It's the only thing I absolutly hate about this game. It's extremely tempermental and I am always fighting it, sometimes to the point of tears. It's very annoying. (Pro tip: the large paths are the worst offenders, so just don't.) Also, because of the sudo-grid system, it's much more time consuming to place benches, trash cans, and lights. In RCT 1,2, and 3, I just went "lamp, bench, trash, repeat." With one per square, it was quick and painless and provided a system that met and exceded the requirements for the needs. Now, you have to pay super attention to place it exactly, and because paths don't like being even and symmetrical, it never looks good. And that's if it lets you place it! Yeah, it's really only a problem if you have OCD, but lets be real, that was one of the good things about RCT 2. I would like to see a mod or something that uses a more rigid grid. Also, while I'm on the topic of OCD, the grid that follows your mouse around (really nice, actually) has different weighted lines to mark large squares, which is normal. Well, the center line of the park DOES NOT MATCH UP WITH THE CENTER OF THE ENTRANCE!!! HOW?! WHY?! WHO?! And you can't extend the first bit of path and keep it striaght! IT BOTHERS ME SO MUCH!
Anyway, I can go on, but I think I'll leave it at this: It's very promising, and I'm really excited for a polished version. I'm going to recommend this game not because of it's current state, but because of it's potential. All of the bad reviews bring up fixable problems, and over time I'm sure they will get fixed and the final result will be a great game.

Not many people talk about Final Fantasy V, but it has one of the best stories of the series. It starts slow, but after awhile you will learn how it is magnificent.
Pros:
Very nice story
Cool classic job system
Well made character sprites
Awesome music
Cons:
Nothing at all

5/5
Story: I refuse to give any spoilers here, Just know that it's a very touching story of friendship; and, decisions will be made in game that will affect which ending the player will receive. It's a wonderful story and I will be doing another playthrough of this title.
Graphics: It seems this is where everyone gets hung up. I personally enjoy seeing the updated graphics. It fits much better for HD displays than the original pixelated super famicom graphics would.
Gameplay: The battlesystem uses the atb bar (this is the first Final Fantasy game to use this) The important thing for new players to understand here is the importance of switching classes constantly throughout the game to learn new abilities. This was interesting. I spent many hours just leveling up my classes to get new abilities to combine abilities with my team mates to DOMINATE in the ending game. Time well spent let's put it that way.This made grinding through the game less boring.
Music: Nobu Uematsu at his finest (nuff said)
Overall: If you are a fan of jrpg's check this game out. I love it and I Can't wait to spend another 72.8 hrs into this game.

Got this in a bundle some time ago, and just now finally got around to playing it.
Where to begin...
Let's get the negative out of the way.
-Outside of the ReadMe's, the game doesn't really tell you how to progress. Yes, you can search for inquiries, but, having no prior knowledge of the plot, you could spend a decent amount of time just typing in words to see if you get a hit.
-Only being able to watch 5 clips at a time, until rectified after you finish the game once, is a mild annoyance.
-The plot really asks you to have a suspension of disbelief.
Positives.
-This was a very interesting way, as convoluted at times as it was, to tell a story.
-The acting was convincing. Outside of aforementioned suspension of disbelief, I felt like this maybe could have happened.
-The retro feel of the desktop was nice, harking back to my childhood of the 90s.
-The ambient music and reflections you see in the desktop outside of clips added another layer to the story telling.
Final thoughts.
Is this game perfect? Not by any means, seldom are they.
Is this game fun? That answer is subjective, but, for what it was, yes, I enjoyed it.
Do I recommend it? If you are a fan of murder-mysteries, a stickler for retro technology, or just want a mildly fun way to kill a few hours, yeah. If you come into this game expecting cyber-noir detective work, or anything of the sort, you need look elsewhere.
I feel like myself a cyber-detector, yeah, 5 stars.

I probably should have liked this game, but instead I found myself flipping between bored and frustrated.
There's a complex story here, and the way it is constructed is very clever, guiding you to discover information that leads to more and more mini-revelations. But it's reliance of the player searching for the correct 'keywords' from the video's they've watched leads to a lot of dead ends where you've seemingly exhausted all you can think to search for until you've looking up guides and just typing in keywords off a list.
The videos themselves I just didn't find engaging. When the plot is being revealed it is fine, but often the details are tangential or just unrelated and mundane. Some might find that interesting from a character perspective, but spending half an hour listening to a fictional character talk about doing their laundry... that doesn't hold me interest. Neither do the hundreds of micro-snippets of footage that doesn't even tell a mundane story. Videos of nothing but the character going "Yes, that's right." "I don't think so.", perhaps on paper they can be integrated into a full-cut of the conversations that actually makes sense. But in the flow of the game, they're pointless red-herrings that waste your time.
This is a smartly designed, unique, game by a developer clearly interesting in making something very different. And the actress does a good job selling the main mechanic. But as much as I feel like a killjoy, I just didn't find it engaging to play at all.

There's no real gameplay, only story. So it's a good thing that the story is damn good. I won't spoil anything, but I will say that I'm impressed how a game which presesnts a story out of sequence can still tell it coherently and artfully, with motifs, themes, plots, subplots, and intrigues so masterfully managed. Highly recommended.

Second, combat still needs a lot of work. Currently, I took on an alligator on a 1v1 match. Me with a knife, him or her with it's alligator skin and sharp teeth. I only lost about 30% of my health even though I was attacking it with a knife over the course of the fight. Apparently the wildlife flinches if you hit them so they don't attack you back. Who was the genius who implemented that? Anyways, when you're in combat and in the middle of doing an action, you can't really move your camera. So when your character swings a knife down and your prey(or enemy moves), you have to watch as your character moves back into position and then you can slowly swing your character towards the enemy again. But the most ♥♥♥♥ed up thing would be that a different alligator took me from the 70% health I was at to maybe around 5% with just one bite. I was running from a lake when I saw two alligators next to each other. I figured I would try skirting around them so to save some energy but one turns to me, nips me on my heel, and I nearly die. Freakin' unbelievable. I mean, choose one or the other. If you want to make them dangerous, take away the flinching wildlife so that they're a force to be reckoned with. If  you want this game to be easy, nerf their bite or something. Seriously, that♥♥♥♥♥♥was outrageous.
One thing that's interesting about this game is that it uses this perception concept that's very similar to Tomb Raider(2013) where you press a hotkey and then everything turns black and white for Lara other than things that she can interact with. Same concept for this game, except that it draws on your stamina for some reason. It's okay I guess, although it shows me things that I can't even interact with some times. For instance, I'm in a village and I'm running low on hydration and hunger. So use the perception ability and I see a water pump and a metal bowl filled with water. I walk over to it but nothing works. There's no interact key and I'm left staring at this bowl of water as my hydration meter slowly drops down. Why are the devs making it more complicated than it is? Why doesn't it allow me to drink out of the metal bowl of which the water is coming from an underground source? Do I honestly have to craft some sort of cup or bottle to drink water out of a pump?
The gameplay itself is somewhat lacking. I admit, I was introduced to the survival genre through Minecraft so the first thing I usually do is I go up to a tree and see what I can do to it. In this case, my character just grabs a tree and shakes it. I allow it to shake it a few more times until the game doesn't let me anymore and I'm left wondering what the hell is it trying to tell me to do. Now I haven't played long enough to completely put all the mechanisms down to pat, I've lost interest pretty quickly. Also, having to hold down right click just to interact with items in the world? Are you kidding me? It might sound like a petty complaint but until you've played and realized the absolute horror it is to navigate throughout a room with a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of stuff on the ground, you won't understand the pain and agony I went through.
Lastly, I'm running a pretty powerful rig although it's not exactly the best(See my profile page for specs). Even so, I'm running this game on around 60FPS at max while sometimes it dips and stays around 40. Mind you, this is in 720p and the graphics look very subpar, especially during sunset. At sunset, it looks like all the props and assets were filtered with a weird bezel effect in photoshop.
Ultimately, the game could use some more work. I do understand that it's Early Access and I do understand that its a fairly new release. But if I'm gonna be completely honest, this market is completely saturated with dozens of survival games where you need something that puts you apart from another. Currently, this feels extremely bland. Of course, the graphics looks somewhat better than some of the other survival games out there, but the gameplay falls short by miles.
Thumbs down for the current Early Access game although I'm fairly optimistic that it'll be improved in the near future.

It's pretty simple. Here's a thing. Here's a box. Here's a bunch of snap otgether parts. Build a machine to do the thing.
Easily the best physics puzzle game I've played, as the great art style, and streamlined building tools make for an easy to pick up but increasingly difficult to master game.
Early access, and at the time of this review there are around 50 or so levels with a pretty competant selection of parts for building all manner of deadly war machines.
There's also easy to use god mode and sandbox modes (these prevent level progression) if you just like to build stuff, but the real strength of besieged is its simple task-based levels and freedom of design. Unlike most physics games, there's an actual game in here that's not just another sanbox experience, and that game is well designed, streamlined, and fun. There are no unlocks or currency. Just you, a limited building area, a task to complete, and a pile of parts. That simple system is leveraged masterfully to create a fun puzzle and building game that's both challenging and beautiful.
For eight bucks its already worth the asking price just for that game, and with more levels and multiplayer on the way I can't reccommend this enough. Go. Buy it. Build weapons of death. Lay waste to everything in your path.
