OVERALL THOUGHTS:
A good game that has two brilliant gameplay facets, that are let down by several smaller problems. However it shouldn't ruin the experience too much, as those "brilliant gameplay facets," are really freaking awesome. Would recommend, definitely.
STORY:
You play as a man named Becket who, despite actually having a name, is as quiet and as the Point Man from FEAR 1. The game begins right before it's predecessor ends, with Becket and a team of soldiers trying to find and secure Armacham employee Genevieve Aristide. After a simple first level that teaches you the basics of gameplay and gives you a few good scares, the operation goes south when the entire city is levelled from the nuke Point Man detonates in FEAR 1. You wake up in a hospital and discover you and your teammates have been experimented on, against your will, and now Alma is drawn to you, as well as a very stereotypical sergeant with all of armacham's military might intent on wiping out Genevieve Aristide, you, and anybody else who could spill the beans on the company's bad deeds. The over-arching story is a little nonsensical but is presented dramatically and it's very, very well done (except for a few not-so-good voice actors along the way) so it is forgivable. The story also expands on Alma Wade, the figurehead of the series, and turns her from spooky ghost girl into a character you actually can feel very sorry for, until her naked, wrinkled corpse begins hunting you and trying to... do things to you... The ending of the game is actually really good though, and even though I knew what was coming, I couldn't help but still be a little freaked out. It WILL make you want to either replay the game, or go and buy F3AR (Yes, they spell it like that).
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is pretty similar to the first game. It's a first person shooter with a heavy emphasis on strategic combat against squads of intelligent AI but also comes with levels that aren't just corridors (and encourage exploration), as well as some truly horrifying sequences. Unfortunately the game is a little uneven in some regards, as the action-shooty-shoot-bang side of the game feels rough compared to FEAR 1 with the AI seeming less intense and almost less intelligent , and a lot of the new features feel shallow and useless. However the enemies are still fun to fight, and are still much smarter than the average COD campaign AI. You won't use the optional "Flip cover" mechanic at all, however, as it's quicker and easier to duck behind something else than to press "e" and go into the slow animation of flipping a table. A few guns also feel stupid as well, such as the pulse gun. It's supposed to be like an energy bazooka thing that fires a big plasma ball that travels reaaaally slowly before melting anything it touches to bones, which sounds cool, but its clunky and awkward to use and doesn't even feel powerful, so instead of that I just used the awesome missile launcher as my heavy weapon, and it worked just fine. There is also an added feature of a giant mech walker ala Titanfall you climb into at certain points and wreck stuff with, and those two sections were amazingly fun and I loved them very much as it gives you the ability to grind through tough enemies like a hot knife through butter and blow holes through walls. It's empowering and a blast, and it's rare enough to keep from getting in the way of the horror.
Speaking of horror.... The horror lands on the side of horror that is a slow, creepy build up where your jumping at shadows and noises, to full on freaking the heck out when things escalate, and boy do they escalate. The first bits of horror you encounter in the hospital level left me horrified beyond words, then the ruined, nuclear waste of a city had even more potent scares and mutant enemies who could raise the dead to fight for them which was frightening, stressful, and a lot of fun to battle through. But, like the action part, the scary parts have their flaws too. The developers seem to have decided, "well there's a few parts in the game where you're just solving puzzles, or progressing through an area between firefights without shooting anyone... This'll be scary if just throw in a few spooky looking enemies, or those invisible ninjas everyone loved from the first game." Unfortunately, this was not a good decision. In the third or so level I got tired of blowing through the same enemies that once frightened me so badly, and while I loved the invisi-ninjas in FEAR 1 and was excited when they came back they too grew tiresome. Fortunately there must've been some devs who understood scariness, and after the third level those enemies were replaced by a much scarier opponent (and their scares lasted much longer) until much later in the game, when they were re-introduced and made very frightening again, and the invisi-ninjas don't show up enough to ruin the experience, but they will cause serious annoyance. Overall, the horror side is fantastic and can be downright terrifying as it makes you, the gun-toting soldier, feel weak and powerless as some young woman with godlike abilities is hunting you down.
SIDE NOTES:
- Alma is fully grown in this game, and she likes to wander around naked. There are also heavy forced-sexual themes, so this is especially not for younger players, or for those sensetive to those materials.
- While not a very graphically intense game, it did give my ancient Radeon HD 5750 some trouble before finally ending its life. The replacement card (an HD 6850) did just fine running the game, but it built up a bit more heat than I would've expected.
- While the game is fully enjoyable on mouse-keyboard, it is, unfortunately, a console port and plays better with a controller.
- The save system is annoying when first starting the game, as it only saves at checkpoints and the first checkpoint in the hospital level is really far in and I had no idea, so I wandered around the hospital for at least 20 minutes, did some stuff and got off only to get on later to realize I had to restart that level because I didn't hit that one checkpoint. All the other checkpoints in the game are well placed and non-bothersome, but that one is a pain.
- On the subway level I somehow fell out the map twice and had to restart from a check point. The rest of the game seemed rather stable on the bug-side.

For a long time, as a movie fan, I wasn't quite sure of the difference between a horror and thriller.  Later I was able to piece it together:  Both are about adrenaline flow, but only one actively tries to scare you.
I bring this up because it's exactly what acts as a parallel between the original FEAR entries (all three of them) and FEAR 2 Project Origin (and the Reborn DLC).  The original FEAR entries were intense games of cat-and-mouse, skulking about in the shadows hoping enemies with flashlights or automated turrets don't spot you, occasionally broken up by moments of first-person perspective horror more akin to Silent Hill than anything.  FEAR 2 drops this almost entirely - it has only a little bit of the surreal horror, and even that is played more as climactic narrative elements rather than memorable filler.  Each one of these scenes tells you something about the story, and as such they're less throw-away, but because of this, they don't scare you as much as they did before.  It's no longer a horror - it's now a thriller.
But having said that, FEAR 2 is a pretty outstanding thriller.  There are moments of genuine tension (like when some troops are resurrected around you in small groups), but by and large, it's an action game with a greater emphasis on intensity.  The atmosphere is solid, the gunplay is less "fun" than in most FPS titles, and the horror thematic elements allow the missions to take an almost random turn at any point, sometimes outright breaking reality, and this keeps you on your toes.  The campaign is also rather lengthy, with an absolutely AMAZING ending sequence, so all in all I most certainly recommend this game.
On a side note, the Reborn DLC is an excellent 90-minute or so secondary campaign that actually expands the story considerably in interesting ways.  Yes - it's DLC that ACTUALLY MATTERS to the future of the story.  For that alone, as well as the fact that it's just as fun as the rest of the game, I recommend getting the Reborn DLC if you can as well.

This game is sort of a bugged Flash thing, like you know, not the full games with thropies and such that you find on Kongregate, Newgrounds and other sites, but those games filled with pop-ups in Google-translated dedicated pages.
The negative thing is that they are all free..
This one has so many flaws.. let me start.
No tutorial at all, you don't even know what you have to do and what are your controls. You're put right into the game.
The game consists of a randomly-generated (every time you die) side-scrolling screen in which you are a red square and the platforms are black and gray squares - they will vanish after you jump on them.
On the left, you have a wall - I mean, a big black line - that comes after you.
You can also double jump, apart from the fact that the game's controls are so poor that you can't often forecast where you'll land or how many jumps you'll do.. it's really a mess, trust me.
The achievements aren't gaming-related. They unlock as you press each one of your keyboard keys. Yeah, you press them and get the achievements, that's all.
The other reason why they aren't gaming-related is that the game isn't really a game. It's an endless platformer with no objectives, no different levels and design, no tasks, no instructions at all are given.
You just randomly jump, fall, die and restart.
I made some screenshots just to let some other players see what the game is like, but really.. if you don't mind about the achievements, you'll find minimalistic platformers for free on every good Flash website.
This one has really no reason to exist in my opinion, if we consider it as a 1€ game. But even if it was free, believe me, there's really no fun here.

Review for this, I won't be afraid to use the word "Masterpiece", is long overdue. It is an amazingly competent and enjoyable game, on many levels. In this day and age this is very refreshing. And yes, I didn't repeat myself here. It is a game both extremely enjoyable overall, yet also beautifully designed both for the casual players and for the die hard fans of such games. Truly, this is one of the hidden gems and one of the top games that came in 2015.
But enough baseless praising. This game is essentially rogue-lite done right. There is no outgame progression, aside from opening new possible "captains" for your team of three. Which means you have as good of a chance of finishing it on your first try, as in any other attempt, if we disregard your accumulating personal experience with the game's mechanics. Captain roles can be opened in any order player desires and all characters can be used from the start as simple companions. While it may be argued that some of the locked captains are very strong, starting choices are good enough, desired captain can be unlocked in as much as one playthrough and mostly captains provide strong yet diverse bonuses to your party. Those bonuses, together with the choice of other two members and your playstyle form noticeable diversity in possible ways of playing.
There is some imbalance between usability of skills, but even that is kept in check with the ability of the player to choose his own adventures after the random starting one. You get a perfect basic description of each adventure, stating what playstyle and skills are perfered for its completion. And if something is going horribly wrong - you can always choose simpler expeditions after the second one, if you feel that your luck isn't as shining as you expected it to be. I can't emphasize enough how ingenious the gamedesign is in this diamond of a game, which tries to contain possible randomness and imbalance on every step, ultimately giving player every tool he needs to finish the game, bar exceptionally bad luck.
The gameplay revolves around series of expeditions both with Turn Based "overworld map" and Turn Based combat. Your endgame mission is to become, as the title suggests, the most Renowned Explorer in your club. And yet in another ingenious move, the "club" isn't some sort of faceless entity, leaderboard with only you as an existing figure. You do meet other explorers ocasionally, and may interact with them. You have different resources to both make use of and take note of. Three basic resources (Status, Research and Gold) both provide points for the end game and are spent between expeditions on enhancing your resource gathering, recieving different upgrades from a Scientific tree or buying equipment for your team. There are also Supplies and Resolve. First is usually spent while moving during expedition on the overworld map. Should you run out of supplies, you start incurring drastic debuffs, though you still can try to get few last items before facing the boss of this particular expedition. Resolve is lost if you fail certain events, take unnecessary risks or lose all HP on one of the teammates during combat. Should you squander all of your Resolve - you lose this game.
The game is using simple but well thought out system of "Friendly-Devious-Aggressive" playstyle, with most characters being addept at combination of the two out of three. WIth this comes the only real gripe I can possibly muster with this game - the Attack/Defence stats for Friendly/Devious are the same, yet for Aggressive are different. Basically that means, that in many cases you are attacked by Speeches and are attacking by Speeches, shadowing the necessity of Aggressive builds. Developers try, admirably I must say, to provide decent balance between those, but ultimately I must admit - it is nigh impossible to tackle this issue properly. Still, this system works extremely well most of the time, providing noticeable differences in playstiles even with the same party members used differently.
Overworld map of expedition is abundant with events and challenges, of which the turn based combat is anything but prevalent (except for expeditions specifically designed for aggressive parties). In many cases, combat can be circumvented. In other cases, you often can gain an advantage before important battles if you have certain non-combat skills at your disposal. But that is not to say that combat isn't important. Boss of each expedition will still be in your way, and each battle won provides a hefty combat bonus to one of the party members until the end of the expedition. Still, you can gain big advantages before quite a few boss battles using the non-combat skills, usually in different ways. And the game usually allows you to see the chances of success for each possible choice before making the ultimate decision. It might not be too far stretched to say that the Overworld experience on its own is worth the money this game asks.
But there is also a turn based combat. One would assume that it would be a mere add-on, poorly executed and without any time invested in it. Far from it, turn based combat makes full use of "Friendly-Devious-Aggressive" trio, making it a simple yet very important core mechanic. The battlefield is reigned by "mood". Mood being a combination of most used attitude of your party and that of the enemies. Depending on the combination, it provides different bonuses. For example, being Devious against Aggressive opponent provides you with +Dodge chance, while double Aggressive leads to a bonus Devious damage for whoever uses it. As you can tell from it, certain combinations are beneficial, and the mirrored ones are detrimental to your party. Not only that, but using Attitude attacks (majority of the attacks are those) can quickly shift the Mood towards different combination, especially when finishing off an opponent. That leads to an interesting tense combat, especially if you're getting the best reward from finishing the battle with the Attitude that would put the battle in a detrimental to you Mood. Many bosses shift their behaviour, if not all of their attacks, based on the Attitude you may use. And do not fear, most enemies contain a simple yet sufficient explanation of their strong points, weaknesses and possible big changes should you use particular Attitude attacks against them.
What else is there to praise? Art style is somewhat simplistic, yet vivid and pleasing. Animations are hilarious at times, which greatly helps with slight repetitiveness of the gameplay. Music and sound effects are much the same - simplistic at times, yet immerse you greately into the overall experience. The game oozes of love and passion that was put into it by the developers.
Not only that, but noticeable update to gameplay came out a while ago, completely free of charge. In this update they made some very drastic changes to certain aspects, like Research tree, Mood bonuses, various debuffs and characters. And you know what? The game became all the better. Developer that are both brave enough to change a lot, yet competent enough to make it ultimately worthwhile? On top of that, humble enough to provide it free of charge, when many others would make it a DLC (and do note, it would be worth money in my book)? I am baffled. People who made this game deserve all the praise and spotlight they can get, and even more on top of  that.
===================================================================

Not to be confused with a match-3 game, in Leona's Tricky Adventure, you click to change groups of gems, to make the gems in the left grid match those in the right.
It's a fairly simple formula, but compelling. It also features both charming graphics and catchy tunes that would feel right at home on a SNES.
Unfortunately, the difficulty rises far too slowly, and just as you get into the challenging puzzles, the game ends. On the other hand, it's still fun just to piece the puzzles together without brain strain.
It is a bit disappointing that puzzles featuring different gem groups are not used more often, but it's not a big deal.
There is also an issue where it's hard to tell when you've 100%'d the game, as there are a few more puzzles than you need to complete the game, and places that suggest you might be able to get to them if there were even more puzzles. Possibly more content was planned, but they didn't have time to finish it. There is still plenty of game regardless.
Oh, and there might not be an autosave. If there was, it wasn't working for me.
So, while a bit lacking in challenge and variety, Leona's Tricky Adventure provides a nice relaxing puzzle game with excellent presentation.

This cozy, relaxing puzzle game is the successor to Gem'X - one of the most loved Amiga games. It features the same classic Chris Huelsbeck soundtrack but extends the original game with charming new characters and map-based exploration.
The puzzles involve clicking on gems to change their colour to match what's on the right hand side of the screen. The gem you click moves two steps along the range of colours, and the gems surrounding it change one step. So you have to carefully plan your clicks. It's much more intuitive than I make it sound, and the game features a nice tutorial so the gameplay soon becomes clear.
An absorbing game that positively exudes good vibes.

I tried to stay positive, even though this game has had its fair share of negativity in the, ehh, recent past. I remained hopeful for the EA, and this review is keeping in mind that it's EA. Having played a few EA titles, and knowing how much a title can improve to final release, this review is negative, because I just don't see that it will improve enough to final release to warrant a positive review. Yes, it will improve, but I just dont see that without starting from scrath (again), this game can be salvaged. In any case, keep in mind that this review is of the first EA release.
But let me start with the positive. For me, at least, it runs smoothly and without problems. Performace wise, then, it's good. That is about all the positive I can say about it. Other than that, nothing positive to report, unfortunately.
The graphics are, without question, horrible. Nothing close to the "in game" screens we were shown before. The rides, the scenery, foliage, ground textures etc... I haven't seen any redeeming quality to any of it. There are several things I compare this to: RCT3, Planet Coaster (the competitor), Cities Skylines (built on the same engine), other similar sim-type games from the past 10 years. Without fail, I cannot think of any other high-profile game that is worse than the current state of RCTW.
Animations of rides are adequate I guess, but nothing to write home about. They could do with better physics simulations.
Animations of peeps - how they move that is - is atrocious. Even RCT3 did a better job at this. They perform several actions and show their emotions (e.g. having to go to the bathroom, hunger, anger, being sick etc.), but the animations are honestly just bad. Even their standard walking and running actions are awkward.
On that note, peeps look horrible. Colours, textures, shapes, everything. If you're into misformed yellow and brown blobs with creepy unexpressive and oversized eyes, this may be your thing. But no, they are not "cartoony", they just look like they stepped out of a game from the mid-90s.
What I may forgive the EA for is peeps, park workers (cleaners, medics etc.) walking through fences, buildings, off-grid paths, each other, to their destination. I may also forgive cleaners sweeping footpaths about 6 feet  away from where the dirt actually is. These can be fixed in future updates. But what will be a tall order to do is the seemingly faulty pathfinding of peeps to their destinations, which at this stage seems worse than in RCT3. The workers also seem to have a wonky work/pathfinding method to get to their next destination. For examply, just in RCT3, janitors are happy to walk straight past 10 puke piles to get to a dropped cup half-way across the park. These kinds of AI behaviours I am less optimistic can be fixed easily.
Paths are very hard to use. The three widths are ok, but their snap points are hard to use. This is a similar problem that Planet Coaster suffers from currently, that foodcourts with tighly packed shops are basically impossible to build. Maybe something that will be resolved.
This is personal preference, but should be inclued in the review: I am no fan of the pre-made and themed large food stalls and buildings. I much prefer a smaller footprint basic stall and build my own scenery/building around it. For me, at least, Planet Coaster has an advantage here. This is personal preference, if you like plop and forget, then RCTW is for you - just not for me at this time.
The coaster builder is actually not that hard to use. If I compare it to Planet Coaster's, I would say it's about the same level of difficulty to use. From me, no major complaints with the basic construction side of things. On the other hand, the graphics of coasters, their supports and the physics seem wonky to put it mildly. Much work needed here, but I think it could be done.
Overall mechanics and park management is basically a carbon copy of RCT3. Yes, the heat map and extra graphs may give you a bit more information about the park, and in the future there may be a few extra options in buildings, but overall it is exactly the same and nothing new to see. I also don't see any "placeholders" for future expansions in this realm to get me excited.
TLDR - in conclusion: very unpolished, which may be expected for EA. I personally don't see, however, how it'll be the game that was promised to the community - feels like at this point no matter how much the turd is polished, it remains a turd. Maybe there was too much hype from Atari (understandable marketing) making my expetations too high, but compared to my own expectations, this game falls short. If you have tons of $$ to buy both PC and RCTW, do so. It may be a fun game for a little while and worth the investment down the line. If you only have $$ for one, I'd recommend waiting and spending it on PC, because I don't think this one will be PC's match even at final release. I have both, and will keep both. But I am a sucker, and wouldn't recommend it to others.
I wanted to add a little edit to the end of this review to maybe clarify one point. This review may have been positive, but it is - and I fully acknowledge this - skewed by expectations. This is not my own preconceptions about what I expected the "next-gen" RollerCoaster game to be like, but rather by the expectations I had based on the promises made by Atari reps this past year or so. While Planet Coaster does look much better than RCTW right now, at least graphically, in terms of features it offers much, much less. But - and this is a big but - they folks at Frontier have been very honest with where the game is currently, what they are releasing in the Alpha and why, what they want to test and what kind of feedback they want. On the other hand, the folks at Atari have been spewing AAA, the best, so exciting, full of features, looks awesome, and other such language, which this game is not. At least not currently. So yes, a large part of the negative review is part of the humongous PR failure on Atari's part. If they had kept expectations realistic (not low, but realistic) and were honest what is actually being released - an unpolished pre-alpha stage of the game, I may have had a positive review. But not like this. If I take their word that this game has been in "final optimization and polishing" for the past four months, and is 90% complete, then no, I cannot give it a positive rating. Just wanted to clarify this point. :)

This game has so much potential, but the devs themselves say they're done with it unless they get a lot more money.  Um. Ok, well how about doing some minor tweeks, nope, we're done, we'll add more languages to try and sell in other countries, but otherwise we're done.  Um.. how about the random crashe... nope... ok, how about the icons which have no key to help you figure out wha... nope, we're done.
With that attitude it's no wonder sales aren't booming.  People don't necessarily buy a product, they buy their perception of the devs, in this case of video games.  People devoted to Apple products are devoted to them because they have a very simple credo, simple tech tnat works... and if it doesn't work we fix it.  They're not the most innovative, they're in no way the most affordable, yet people camp out for days to buy the next iteration of their products.
Alas, this game has SO much potential, but in the hands of these "done devs" it's going to be squandered.  I bought in for 5-bucks-ish.  I had hoped I'd be able to recommend it, but I can't, if only for the minor fixes that need to be applied and the disregard displayed by the devs in the community forum regarding their product.
I wish them luck in their future endevours but I offer one bit of advice, look at how the devs of The Long Dark did their product.... they did an early release, they raised a lot of money and people looked the other way when the little quirks of the game popped up, after all it's in early access, but the concept was so good it inspired many to buy into it, and the updates they would do along the way gave confidence that the audience was being heard and fixes were implimented.  More people bought in.
Devs, by saying you're essntially abandoning the game because you didn't raise enough money from it's sale tells all the consumers who've bought your game, you have no confidence in your product and the product itself didn't matter, it was all about the money.
Next go try two things... when you have a great concept like this do a GoFundMe to raise some of the money, and when the game is in this state release it as Early Access, players are much more forgiving if you admit you still have work to do, rather than release, not make enough money and essentially abandon the  game.  Because it's not really the game you're abandoning, it's the fan base, and we do remember.

-MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD-
++++ this is a rare game whose story makes excellent usage of its medium. the story cannot be delivered with the same amount of power without the mechanics that are provided by video games.
+++ at some point throughout the game, your investigation shifts from the predetermined goal of solving the murder case, to understanding the story due to personal curiosity. this is executed brilliantly, and lends particularity well to the open ending of the game.
- the search mechanic is unintuitive (no searches on metadata) because it doesn't function as proper search engines do. because of this, the difficulty seems a bit artifical at times.
-- there are effectively two parts to the story: but the first is boring and the second is contrived.
-- a corollary of above: its hard to care about most of the characters because of the lame story.
-- for a game that mostly consists of watching interviews, the acting is quite bad. it doesn't fell like the actor has put effort into immersing herself into the role of her character, so her performance and delivery doesn't feel genuine at all. sometimes its hard to tell if her poor acting is intentional (because her character is lying) or just because.
A very interesting game that is critically flawed because of the of the poor content that the game mechanics heavily depends on.

For a long time, as a movie fan, I wasn't quite sure of the difference between a horror and thriller.  Later I was able to piece it together:  Both are about adrenaline flow, but only one actively tries to scare you.
I bring this up because it's exactly what acts as a parallel between the original FEAR entries (all three of them) and FEAR 2 Project Origin (and the Reborn DLC).  The original FEAR entries were intense games of cat-and-mouse, skulking about in the shadows hoping enemies with flashlights or automated turrets don't spot you, occasionally broken up by moments of first-person perspective horror more akin to Silent Hill than anything.  FEAR 2 drops this almost entirely - it has only a little bit of the surreal horror, and even that is played more as climactic narrative elements rather than memorable filler.  Each one of these scenes tells you something about the story, and as such they're less throw-away, but because of this, they don't scare you as much as they did before.  It's no longer a horror - it's now a thriller.
But having said that, FEAR 2 is a pretty outstanding thriller.  There are moments of genuine tension (like when some troops are resurrected around you in small groups), but by and large, it's an action game with a greater emphasis on intensity.  The atmosphere is solid, the gunplay is less "fun" than in most FPS titles, and the horror thematic elements allow the missions to take an almost random turn at any point, sometimes outright breaking reality, and this keeps you on your toes.  The campaign is also rather lengthy, with an absolutely AMAZING ending sequence, so all in all I most certainly recommend this game.
On a side note, the Reborn DLC is an excellent 90-minute or so secondary campaign that actually expands the story considerably in interesting ways.  Yes - it's DLC that ACTUALLY MATTERS to the future of the story.  For that alone, as well as the fact that it's just as fun as the rest of the game, I recommend getting the Reborn DLC if you can as well.

Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is a love letter to the 8 bit NES era as well as the era that coined and defined the term NES hard! The game puts you in the role of the easily angered, foul mouthed, ill tempered Nerd as he travels through 8 levels of "Game Land" inspired by "Video Game Land" from the late 80s cartoon "Captain N: The Game Master" while the gameplay is inspired by classic retro games like Castlevania, Contra, Mega Man, Ninja Gaiden and others.
Each level has various nods to games from the past as well as games that The Nerd has reviewed on his web series. For example, the level "Beat it And Eat It" is inspired by the Atari Porn games for the Atari 2600, and the level "Boo! Haunted House" inspired by the "A Nightmare On Elm Street" and "Friday The 13th" NES games!
The most satisfying thing about this game is the challenge! Yes, areas of certain levels can be difficult and will even get you to curse like The Nerd himself, but that is what makes this game fun! The process of trial and error while playing through the game and being rewarded for beating the level instead of having you're hand held with a useless guide that shows you how to beat the level or give you recharging health or anything else that current games do nowadays. The game is still very fun as well as rewarding to play and gives you just that right amount of challenge that makes you want to keep on playing til the end!
If you are a fan of classic "NES hard" games like Castlevania, Contra, Mega Man, or Ninja Gaiden or are a fan of the AVGN character and his web series, then you should definitely get this game!

I recommend this game, but with stipulations.
(1) You have to appreciate 2D sidescrollers. Unlike Super Meat Boy, which at its most basic is attainable to almost anybody (thanks in no small part to it's quick respawn and limited screen length), AVGNA is rooted much more in old school games (as is to be expected). If you can't stand 2D sidescrollers from the NES or SNES era, you WON'T enjoy this game.
(2) You have to expect its difficulty. Beings as it was devised to emulate the atrocities (to an extent) that The Nerd reviews on his videos, this game emulates the difficulty perfectly. I didn't even attempt beating the game on normal or hard, where you have limited lives. It took me over 100 lives to beat the game on easy. Am I that bad? Probably; my hardcore gaming days are over. But the game is also just that difficult. You CAN'T get frustrated with the game, or else you will wind up making mistakes that will set you back (or just make you more angry).
Those stipulations aside, the game is enjoyable, and the final battle/stage will surely be a great "surprise" for any fan of AVGN. In fact, fans of AVGN will love the amount of references to the popular character and his videos. But I will say this - the game is short. The majority of its length of play comes from dying (and there are plenty of one-hit-kill objects in the game) and resuming at the previous checkpoint.
If you really like AVGN and can handle the above stipulations, the game is worth the price (though a sale price would help me encourage that). If you've never heard of AVGN and happened to stumble onto this game based on its old-school look, be advised of the above and note that there is LOTS of swearing in the game, and many humorous references will be missed.

Very good FTL like game. By that I mean it's a node based exploration game with limited time (supply in this case), each node being an event. Could be a series naratively driven stats rolls or an encounter. Encounters use a turn based tactical system with a strange and interesting emotion component. There is also a solid gameplay layer between expeditions where you can spend your various resources.
There is a good amount of replayability, especially if you want to unlock all the captains. With a total of 20 characters for a party of 3, I have yet to try them all. The game is also pretty hard so that's another replayability aspect. I've kinda beaten the game after about 10-12 hours of gameplay (I'm not sure how many playthrough, probably 5+) but by "kinda" I mean that I only survived all 5 expeditions, I didn't succeed the real goal of beating the top explorer. Doing that took another 2-3 tries.
This is definitely one of the underated gems of 2015, I would highly recommend it to anyone who liked the FTL system.

Renowned Explorers: International Society is an interesting blend of the rogue-like and strategy genres that sees you controling a team of three explorers going around the world collecting treasures in the hopes of becoming the World's Most Renowned Explorer.
Likes:
- a very unique combat system. You can choose to either aggressively dominate your enemies, insult them into despair, or become best friends with them. however, diffrent attiudes can easily wipeout your whole team. e.g, if you try to be friendly with an enemy who is aggressive towards you, you will suffer a armour debuff, making it more likely for them to hit you for high damage.
-The characters. With 20 playable characters who each have their own playstyle, strengths and weakness, every run is different
-Traits. each character has a trait/s that determine your chances in certain situations, for example, if there is a gaint boulder blocking your way, a character who has an athlete trait has a greater chance of succeding in that situation than someone who does not. in addition to that, characters can learn more traits through leveling,allowing you to customize your team to what you think will suit you best.
-The Challenge.  By moving throughout your expeditions, you use up your supplies. once they are all gone, your team will start getting debuffs like "-40% attack power". This will mean you have to think ahead of time if you should go straight to the final destination of the expdetition or explore some more to earn treasure at the cost of stats.
-Skill will win the battle. almost every attack in the game will hit at hundred percent, this includes enemy attacks aswell. even though it is a rogue-like game, a good strategy and equipment layout will always beat out sheer luck
Dislikes:
-Frame rate problems. Throughout playing RE:IS, frame rate seems to vary everywhere. you could be fighting at sixty frames one moment and have it drop to 30 the next. while this doesnt bother me to much, i can see how others who play   might find this irratating.
-The expeditions. Overall, there are 9 different expdeitions to go on, 12 if you count the first three starting expeditons that you dont get to chose from. while that seems like a quite a bit, some are very similar, for instance,  the Carribean expdetition mainly features pirates and monkeys and "The Emerged Island" offers voodoo pirates and voodoo monkeys, bascially reskinned pirates and monkeys.
Overall, I Highly recommend this game if your into rouge-like and strategy games. It has enough skill based combat, varity, and challenge to make it a game that deserves a spot in your steam library

Renowned Explorers: International Society is one of the biggest time vampires I've come across on steam. I have owned it for a little over 24 hours at the time of writing this review and I've got about 12 or so hours logged already, and I fully anticipate to log many more.
Lots of possible party combinations in tandem with the uniqueness of every character and the roguelike exploration elements make for something that I just can't get tired of playing. I like to experiment and try out various combinations and and see how they turn out with different playstyles.
The combat is refreshingly unique - it isn't too far removed from the type of turn based combat you'd normally see in these kinds of videogames, but it does a lot to distinguish itself from the normal with the use of moods and approach tactics and you can get rewarded for following certain tactics and moods for battles. You can write various research papers, which act as this game's tech tree, and further these rewards.
There's also over 100 different treasures to find in the game's state at the time I write this review, and it sounds like they will be adding more in due time.
I would like to see more expeditions, though, because the current con I have for this game is that, being a roguelike, I come across the same events too often. While there are plenty of events in each expedition, all of which are unique, this game would greatly benefit from having a wider variety of expeditions to choose from due to its nature. There are enough expeditions in the current game to keep me satisfied for a good while, though.
This game is tragically overlooked and I would rate it as a must buy. There's something here for everybody.

I've only taken a small bite out of this puzzling pie, and already I offer my praise to the chef. There's so much charm and quality in this modest little game that it's a crying shame it hasn't recieved more attention.
Judging from the screenshots, I thought this was going to be a match 3 Puzzle Quest style game. Turns out it's not like that at all. You have to make all the gems on the left panel match the ones on the right using a progressive upgrade system based on where you click (The gem you click upgrades two colors while the ones on the sides upgrade only one color). It has a kind of Minesweeper feel. It's not brutally difficult and it doesn't rush you in your decisions.
The music, sound effects, and graphics really sell the game for me. This feels like a puzzle game ported straight from the SNES. The aesthetics are relaxing and invoke pure delight whenever you finish a puzzle and see more of the map reveal itself. The music took me by surprise immediately upon entering the game. It's really nice.
On one hand, I'm ecstatic that I got this game dirt cheap in a bundle. On the other, I am saddened that it has recieved so little attention that it was relegated to bundle fodder in the first place. Good work should not go unrewarded, and I will be sure to spread the word about this charming little puzzle game as much as possible.
Because I don't yet know how much content is here, I can't confidently say that the game is worth the asking price of $9.99. But as I said earlier, it was dirt cheap in a bundle. I'd also recommend it whenever it goes on sale for sure. I will try to update my review as soon as I know more about the length.

You are Leona, you suddenly mysteriously find yourself in a mysterious land ... with mysterious hair. Before you stands a mysterious owl, he explains that stuff is %$&@ed up and that playing a mini-puzzle game on the arcade machine him behind will probably fix stuff. He would have solved the puzzle himself but he doesn't have hands, plus he's too stupid. He moves aside and lets you have a go at the puzzle game. You solve it in like 3 seconds, because you do have hands ... and you're smarter than an owl.
Thus begins your epic quest to solve all the problems of this land by solving these progressively harder and harder puzzles on all the arcade machines you come across. They are also surrounded by various dumb animals with no hands. As you solve the puzzles, rocks turn to trees, buildings are restored, sinkholes are filled, fox tents are replaced, crops are un-killed ... uhm ... oh yeah .... treasure chests are revealed and new paths appear. Don't ask how this works, but it does. It's based on a true story.
The puzzles are fun, and definitely become more and more challenging as you progress through the game. You will get stuck. You will be perplexed. You may even wish you didn't have hands so you could make someone else solve them for you.
This is a fun, addictive puzzle game. I'm not sure it's $10 worth of fun puzzle game so I'd suggest waiting for a good sale.

First of all, my review will be free of spoilers.
As I am a big Star Wars fan, I really love this game – not only because of being a SW fan. Can it also be loved by non-fans? It sure can! Two of my friends said they became Star Wars fans BECAUSE of KOTOR. Because it’s not just a good Star Wars game, it is one of the best RPGs ever (in my opinion KOTOR and The Witcher are the best RPGs). Instead of creating a wall of text, which I surely could, I try to keep it short and rate different aspects as positive (+), negative (-) or neutral/ambivalent (o) creating a wall of bullet points. Please keep in mind that not quantity counts, but your own weighting of the aspects. Especially neutral aspects can be considered positive by some and negative by others.
KOTOR clearly is such a beloved game for its story and atmosphere. Be ready to dive into the world of Star Wars settled about 4000 years before the movies.
+ Story: One of the best stories ever. Can’t say more because spoilers, but many seem to agree.
+ Probably the best plot twist ever: It features some more twists, but especially one is the best I have witnessed in all the movies, series, books and games I’ve watched, read and played in my life.
+ Many dialogue options. Even more dialogue options accessible when some abilities have been skilled (not only determined by the “Charisma” skill, but some other skills, too).
+ Big Star Wars universe: An influential source that greatly expands the Star Wars universe (at least the Legends universe). Was referenced by many following SW sources.
+ Nice plot: Overall, a nice plot.
+ Interesting side quests: Well-fitted into the world, but not always related to the main quest. Side quests are mostly on your way to the main quest. Good side quests for each companion, unraveling more of their background story and developing their own story.
+ Funny companion: One of the companions is a great comic relief and probably the most beloved companion by fans.
+ Different endings depending on playstyle (light side or dark side; canon ending is playing male and light side).
o Non-humans have their own languages, but after a while it’s repetitive to listen to the same audio files over and over again.
o Main character has no voice over (every other character does).
- Takes some time (hours) to truly feel great, storywise.
- Some story points seem repetitive in early-to-mid-game, at least the steps in between (thus, the plot leading to them) and the level design are distinct and creative.
+ Classical RPG based on the Dungeons & Dragons system adapted to fit into the SW universe.
+ Quite a bunch of different abilities and attacks.
+ Different playstyles: Ranged, melee, “mage” (well, The Force). Also characters can be skilled for being stealthy, tanky, DPS-y, good with computers, good with explosives, charismatic (dialogue options) and so on. (But stealthy seems to be quite useless in this game).
+ Customizable weapons: The stats of some weapons can be upgraded by having up to three slots for modifications. Colors of lightsabers can be changed.
+ Main protagonist/player character: Class, gender and appearance can be changed in the beginning, but not that much options (like up to ten different faces/heads per gender). Protagonist is always human.
+ Own “base of operations” where you can talk to all of your companions, upgrade/create some items and choose where to travel next.
+ 8 different companions: Main character can choose up to 2 companions when leaving the base of operations to go on with quests.
+ Quite long game: according to
29 to 44.5 hours of gameplay. The first two playthroughs took me 50-60 each, don’t know why. Maybe because I read and try out every dialogue option.
o Slow paced, more tactical gameplay: As its based und D&D system internally, it also feels like this while fighting. You don’t press button A for attack A and button B for attack B. Instead, you choose an enemy, choose one or more attacks and queue them up. Then you wait for the attacks to be finished. The game can also be paused anytime to think about your next step. Some will like this classical, slow paced gameplay, some will not and certainly miss some action.
o Difficulty: Most of the fights can be won by just letting your character(s) auto-attack your foes. So you sit back and watch. Some will like this, some will hate this. Of course, you can always interfere to end the battles faster and well.. have fun. Some boss fights may be very hard in comparison to most fights.
o Shops: You almost never need to buy stuff from vendors, because you will loot most of your good equipment. At least it saves you money. There are just a handful of powerful items that are worth buying from a vendor. In my opinion, just two are really worth (but not necessary) to be bought. You will notice them, they will be very expensive, but powerful modifications to your weapons.
- Takes some time to feel truly great. Because it takes some time, until (minor to medium spoiler)
.
+ Quite colorful, not that dull.
+ When blades meet, they actually clip and don’t fly through everything (like in SWTOR).
+ Different locations that also look and feel different.
+ Automatic skill option: You can let the AI decide what to skill for your characters. May not be the best skilling, but useful for those who are not interested in this. In addition, you also don’t have to skill like the AI proposes, but instead take its propositions as advice.
o Outdated graphics: Well, it’s an old game, but it’s one of the games you don’t get eye cancer from. There are newer games that are hard to look at. In fact, I consider it a quite “clear” style of graphics.
o Different fighting animations: There are some different fighting animations, but after a while you will know them all.
+ Voice overs: If I recall correctly, it features nice voice overs from well-known voice actors (for example Jennifer Hale).
+ Soundtrack: GREAT, absolutely fitting and SW-esque music! Jeremy Soule created an individual atmosphere for this SW era while keeping the spirit of John Williams original soundtrack. Truly a masterpiece!
+ Base of operations also catches the atmosphere of the original SW trilogy (you will see what I mean).
- Does not natively support widescreen and may have some problems with newer operating systems. To fix that, visit
, search for KOTOR and follow the instructions. Or google it.

TL; DR Version: Faithful remake of a stellar game with some baffling and sometimes outright bad design choices. Overall worth buying during a sale and you can't find another version, if only because the original game deserves more recognition.
---
This is a remake, and there are some big fundamental questions to consider when reviewing it in addition to the normal game review stuff:
Is the game a faithful recreation of the original experience?
Is that experience still worth having?
Do any new additions noticeably improve or hamper the experience?
The answer to the first question is a yes. All the content from the original game is here, transplanted over in such a way as to be unmistakable to this reviewer. It also includes the content from the GBA and iOS remakes, so in some ways this may be the definitive version, if what you're looking for is the most amount of content. The new translation is a bit of a wash, with some of the affectations given to the characters feeling a bit overdone, but I found nothing too cringeworthy as a non-Japanese speaker.
The answer to the second is unequivocally yes. FFV is probably the most under-appreciated game in the series. It has faults – most notably the very high random encounter rate in some areas and it's propensity to occasionally kill the player with unexpected overpowering monsters – but it's strengths are really, really strong. The continued refinement of the job system from FFI and FFIII gives it a lot of depth, often in ways the average game may realize. For reference, the series doesn't reach this level of depth in character customization again until Tactics. The soundtrack is very memorable and catchy (though that goes without saying for a Uematsu Final Fantasy). The monster design is quirky and imaginative, providing a nice variety as you push through the game. And probably more than any other game in the series, this one feels like an adventure in addition to being a quest. It feels just as much like you're trying to discover new things about the world as you are trying to save it, and that's something that not many games I feel can truly capture.
The answer to the third question is... tricky. The most obvious change is the artwork, specifically the new sprites for everything and the new dialogue portraits for the major characters. As many people have pointed out, these portraits are terrible. Most of them bear only a passing resemblance to the character they're portraying, and all of them feel over-designed, often with oddly placed baubles (Cid) or ostentatious clothing (King Tycoon) or completely mismatched hair styles (Galuf). The main character Bartz gets off particularly bad, looking so bizarrely feminine that I would never have guessed it was him had I not actually played the game. The new character models are also kind of a mixed bag. They look okay for Bartz, Lena, Galuf, and Krile (though I kind of prefer the bulkier SNES/GBA sprites), but Faris' are awful, betraying a key spoiler about the character before the player has had a chance to discover it for themselves.
Another major change that I noticed is the save system. The game makes a save after every battle and screen transition, and unlike other quicksaves this one can be loaded and reloaded as many times as you like. If you want to abuse this, it can trivialize some of the more difficult or time-consuming challenges, e.g. collecting everything from Karnak Castle.
The last major changes is the ability to move in eight directions by pixel, rather than in four directions by square. This is normally a pretty good thing, as it gives you more freedom to move around and dodge random NPCs who may have otherwise gotten in your way. Unfortunately, it can also lead to problems with your character getting hung up try to enter doorways, staircases, and narrow hallways, as well as causing problems trying to interact with certain objects.
The new changes ultimately aren't particularly beneficial, and I would say in some cases quite detrimental.
Finally, there's the normal review stuff not covered by discussing the games credibility as a remake - i.e. technical issues. This game has quite a few bugs which will likely never get fixed. The most annoying to me was the one with the battle cursor selecting a random command if they key was pressed too early, but a quick look around the Steam forums will show you that there are several more. Some people have said it lags, though I haven't found this to be true on my PC. Generally I found it pretty stable, but the annoying bugs were sometimes extremely frustrating.
So would I recommend this game? Begrudgingly, yes, though that has more to do with FFV deserving more recognition than it gets than anything to do with this remake. If one has the choice, though, I would highly recommend the GBA version instead.

Having completed the game and played for over 100 hours, I can safely confirm that game-play wise, this is certainly one of the best additions to the series. The combat itself is very reminiscent of Final Fantasy III given the job system although in this game it is significantly more fleshed out and less tedious to level up jobs and gain useful abilities at your leisure.
With this is mind I should mention that AP/Exp grinding in this game is now a menace of the past (be it for better or for worse) given the ability to speed up gameplay, automate it entirely or even do both at once. Some may consider this a problem as it makes the game extroadinarily easy by comparison, although the slew of bonus bosses, particularly within the Sealed Temple, help to mitigate this issue.
Outside of the gameplay I will concede that the game does feature a largely bland soundtrack compared to Final Fantasy IV as well as future games in the series. The only notable tracks on the OST being the well-known "Battle on the Big Bridge" and arguably "The Evil Lord Exdeath". Still, its par for the course given that of the first three games in the series and provides the game with a fairly comfortable, organic atmosphere - which brings me onto the next point.
This is one of the few games in the series where I would say the characterisation and dialogue works particularly well, as anyone well accustomed to the series is aware the dialogue of Final Fantasy games tends to be a bit on the cringe side (see
. On this iteration however, the game's tone assures one that it clearly doesn't take itself as seriously as its successors given the often absurd demeanor of some of the games more threatening characters (Exdeath and Gilgamesh) as well as being the first game in the series where the characters don't feel dumbed down or one-dimensional in any way.
Overall I'd say that this is certainly one of the most accessable games in the series, especially for those familiar with titles such as Bravely Defauly where job custimisation is mandatory. The combat is extremely fluid and is, at least in my opinion,  amongst the most enjoyable in the series. The only minor criticism being the rather ugly text boxes where character portraits are superimposed onto the text-space and the slight monotony attained from job grinding (in which case I'd recommend dual-tabbing with this game windowed, if you intend to play with an overpowered skillset).

I have only one word for this game: Planetbase. Both games are about same (managing space colonies), but Planetside works better than StellarHub. So, if you are looking for space colony management sim - go for Planetside.
And now for a little more expanded explanation - why I like Planetbase better:
1. Mechanics - while both games operate on more or less same mechanics, some of StellatHub mechanics make little sense - the whole grid-based construction makes me feel a bit weird along with weird cimilarity of modules, when it comes to their look, but the main weirdness is, of course, solar power points and gas clouds. For comparison - in Planetbase you have freeform placement of modules and furniture in them, the only limit is number of connections your module can have. Solar power plants can be built anywhere and work based on day-night cycle. And, of course, you don't have to pay for a right to build a new module - all you need to supply the needed materials.
2. Immerrsion. I hope that it would be improved in future, but right now Stellarhub does its best to break immersion in the game. Game does everything to show that it's just a flat map with sprites on top of it with little regard of what is there. Everyone walks over crates in the hub. Cargocrew digs into middle of the module and pulls crates from the floor. Sleeping outside of bedroom character rolls all over machinery in the room. Characters sitting in cantina sit above the table. As soon as you start to build something - everyone rushes there, because... because they love hanging in half-built zones instead of hanging in the lounge or bar or somewhere, where it would make sense. There are lots of sprites for sleeping, but there is only one for work for most crewmembers, so technican repairing something just kneels somewhere in the module (not even close to the problem point) and problem goes away. Things like oxygen leak don't seem to affect crew even slightest and they casually stroll into module with problem, etc, etc, etc.
There are some good points in the game - like ability to reassign your crew to do any task (In Planetbase - you can have a colony of food-producing botanists, who would happily die, because none of them would lift a finger to patch that broken oxygen generator) - but still it feels pretty unfinished at current state, bringing too little of its own mechanics and interesting points and a lot of weirdness like sun shining only over a special spot in space and so on.

StellarHub:
~~~~~~~~~
Every one of us looks up at the sky now and then. Sometimes to admire the stunning blue, and sometimes to be totally absorbed by the beauty of sparkling stars at night. Surely you must have wondered at some point, is there anything out there? Will the human race be able to live in space? Well, it’s time to find out – you’ve just been appointed captain of the StellaHub!
StellarHub is base building/strategy/management game where you have to build and manage an orbital station as well as survive the harsh environment in space.
Before you attempt to play this game, I strongly recommend that you complete the two tutorials available. They’ll help you to understand the basics of the game as well as part of the management system. It will take you around thirty minutes to cover both of them.
From here, you’ll be able to choose between several stars systems/scenarios or simply generate a random system to make the life on your new home even more exciting. You could start with a small, medium or large map.  Don’t be fooled by the words small (in relation to asteroids or pirates activities) or easy. StellarHub isn’t easy and you have to deal with constant events within the station, pirate attacks, asteroids impacts and even events that occur on earth which have repercussions for your station’s well-being. For example, there may be a food shortage, which will substantially increase the cost per unit of bringing some to your station.  If you have a farm, you could sell it back to earth for an awesome profit.
The gameplay is laid out as a grid, and it the middle of it you will have your main hub. Some of the tiles might have mining resources, sun and gas cloud-thingies from where you can produce oxygen. Other tiles could have asteroid fragments with an interrogation mark. With those, you’ll be able to send probes to discover if there are any additional resources, or just clear it so you can build a new station module on it. Tiles with locks on them mean that you are not able to build new structures there. However, if you build another main hub close to it, it will unlock those tiles and consequently you’ll be able to build new structures on them.
What I really enjoy in StellarHub is the management systems. First the staff; you can assign any of the staff to do a job on the station. The trick is to select the right person with the right professional traits suitable for the job. So, when you build a med bay, you would probably assign a person who has experience in first aid or surgery and not someone who enjoys cleaning or is an avid miner. That would probably give your patients new cavities they haven’t had before with a negative diagnosis called . . .  death! There is a good research tree where you can unlock new structures for your station. You’ll be able to hire people and purchase items from earth as soon as you build a supply spaceport, and sell items when you manage to build a trade spaceport.
Essentially, you need to have the right balance in resources, keep your staff happy and protect your station from pirates and asteroid crashes. Really simple, but can be hard to do!
Graphically StellarHub looks good and the controls work well.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Good building and management system
-	Randomly generated system (maps)
-	Good replay-ability
-	Achievements
Negatives:

The game revolves around searching a police database using a simple keyword filter to piece together 271(?) clips of a female being interviewed about her husbands murder. Though an interesting concept the execution is somewhat poor. A keyword may turn up 37 results but only the first 5 will be shown forcing the user to come up with better terms to refine their search. Though interesting this quickly becomes tedious as  most logical keywords will bring up the same few clips or the same 20+ most of which you cannot actually see due to the 5 clip limit. The interface also contains a "session" box you can add clips to and place in the correct order. To do this the user must examine the time stamps in each clip to deduce where they belong.  This feature is rather difficult to use as when a clip is added it is automatically placed at the end of the list and dragging and dropping it in the desired location it will swap it with the clip already located there rather than inserting it. When you already have 50+ clips having to drag a clip from the end slot by slot all the way to the beging is about the least enjoyable thing I can imagine doing. What the game fails to tell you is that this feature is entirely unnecesary. Ordering the clips is not required to win and once you have place everything in the correct sequence there is no option to view them as a whole. You must manually watch all 271 clips one by one...
After about 3hrs of play I had only unlocked about 60 clips, most of this time spent placing them in the correct order. Despite having discovered less that a quarter of the clips I had already learned enough to piece together 75% of the plot, twists and all. While still curious to fill in the blanks this coupled with the awkward controls/gameplay largely killed my motivation to keep going. At this point I only played the game as filler between more interesting tasks or as something to do while a movie buffered.
Even with the early reveal of major plot points the game could have still held my attention except for the fact it only has a single relatively bland character. The fact the interrogator is never seen is explained in game, if poorly, but no valid reason is given for why their voice is never heard. I can understand the choice from a development point of view as it "allows the player to feel as if they are the investigator" but I couldn't get past the flawed logic they used to explain it. Several other characters are discussed and would be viable suspects in a murder investagation matchig the situation described but they are never more than referenced as existing. Even a few brief or fragmented interview with some of these people would've really added depth and made the game/story more enjoyable.
Though not a terrible game I cannot justify the price for the overall amount of enjoyment I got out of it and would not recommend it to a friend unless the price dropped significantly.
SPOILER: If you want to play through in the most efficient, if not enjoyable, manner possible every video has the default user tag of "blank" and when searched will display in chronological order. So an initial search of "blank" will reveal the first five videos. If you then tag these in any way (ex: 1, 2, 3...) as you view them and add them to the session they will be removed from the next search for "blank". Repeat as needed. This will still take a very long time to complete.

Story
A woman is interviewed by the authorities about a murder that occurred in 1994. It’s up to you to piece together the massive amount of clips stored inside a Police Department’s database and uncover the truth behind her story.
Gameplay
Her Story places you in front of a Police Department’s computer with access to a large amount of clips and videos stored in the database. The desktop itself consists of a few shortcuts, including a Read Me file for instructions and a Log Off for when you want to take a break. Most importantly though it contains a windowed search engine that will scour the database for related clips based on the user’s search criteria. For example, if you search “Gun”, the database will reveal all the clips that contain the use of “Gun” and if it exceeds more than five results you may have to dig a little deeper (maybe “Gunfire” or “loaded gun.”) Now if in one of the videos you pick up on a word or scenario you think is worth noting, you may tag said video with your own thoughts or save it to a quick access pool for later review. Clips vary in length from fifteen seconds to a minute and a half, they also bear an icon in the thumbnail if you haven’t watched them yet.
From everything you know about the gameplay so far it probably sounds rather shallow, however it’s murky surface conceals the incredible depth Her Story has to offer. On my first playthrough I picked up on specific words and phrases throughout the initial few videos. Jotting them down, I pursued what I thought was important. Some lead me down dead ends and even related searches didn’t open hidden tunnels to continue through. There were also videos that walked me down longer paths that split to make more forks in the road. I found clips that ended too soon or were simply filler between others I had yet to discover, and some provided crucial insight to the case I was building.
After I completed Her Story I told my girlfriend about the game, she sounded eager to see what it was like. I reset the database to hide all of my searches and saved information and we started a new game. This is the part where Her Story floored me.
Alexandra watched the first four videos that I did, her next search was even the same as mine. However, the information she gathered from the nine or so videos she watched lead her down a completely different path. I was almost frustrated watching her search the database for keywords that (in my mind) were almost irrelevant compared to the clues in the videos she already watched. Alex constructed ideas that were so different than mine that it was almost more enjoyable to watch than play. I could go on about the differences between both of our experiences but that’s not the point.
Simply, Her Story offered an experience that was like no other. In other games you’ll hit a point where the objective can be reached using two, maybe three, tactics which are clear to almost any person that picks up the controller. Her Story hides the objective and offers the player an unlimited number of ways to find it. No two people will ever have the exact same experience and that is something truly incredible.
Replay Value
My first playthrough took about two hours and Alex’s took about three, both of us uncovered around 50% of the clips each time. Her Story is arguably short, however that is solely dependant on the player and their investigative prowess. New games have the ability of offering different avenues to search if you pick up on something you didn’t catch the first time, so it’s fair to say that Her Story is not just a “one and done.”
Wrapping Up
An experience like no other, describing her story as unique would be an understatement. Incredible performance from Viva Seifert, fair price tag, and a mystery that unfolds at the players will, Her Story is a must play.

I absolutely loved the first three RCT games and in 2014 when RCTW was first announced I was excited to see what the newest game could bring after ten years of new and improved gaming technology. Then the original developer was replaced, and the replacement developer was also replaced and the release date for RCTW kept getting pushed back from its initial “early 2015” date. Finally, at the end of Q1 in 2016, Nvissio and Atari released their Early Access Beta, a year after originally planned, and still not the final release. After playing RCTW for a couple of hours, I must say that I am somewhat disappointed in the progress that has been made after two years.
While the graphics are improved from it’s predecessor, RCT3, the game does look dated for 2016 and what game engines and computers are capable of (at a 1GB download I was kind of expecting that). Polygon reduction when zooming out is very noticeable, and trees go from leafy to a three shaded blob without any middleground. Additionally, the park visitors just look kind of… weird. They have a tendency to run almost wildly flailing their arms which just looks funny and the look only marginally better than their now twelve year senior counterparts. Rides on the other hand do look much better than back in 2004, but look more like they would be in a game released four or five years ago, not now.
The game is hampered by a number of bugs, with many people reporting that the game won’t load past 57% ( I have not had this issue myself). Additionally, there are issues with the game freezing and crashing at random times during gameplay, and on the “Frolicking Forest” map, the terrain editor only removes the polygons of the terrain and you still can’t place paths or rides unless they are above the previous terrain height.
Gameplay wise, it’s actually kind of fun but there are a lot of annoyances that really cut away at it after only a few minutes. The coaster builder is pretty fun, but it’s also pretty hard to just get a straight line out of it. It would also benefit from having a stand alone coaster builder built into the game instead of only having the option to load a map and build it during a game. Additionally, for a “beta” there is a wide variety of shops and stalls, but it is very limited ride wise, with only a handful of roller coaster styles and a few different “flat rides” with varying scenery to choose from which seems interesting considering it’s a game built around building rides at its core. Additionally, the roller coasters have to connect, no more building shuttle loops for an easy payday. The main annoyance that’s been plaguing me is that there is no area demolish. Every bush, shrub, and tree that is there when the map loads needs to be individually clicked on to destroy, with is rather tedious. I do like that there are now larger paths that can be built, but there are times when the game won’t let me make a straight path, especially when making a short path that connects to another path. Another annoyance is that you have to build shops and stalls offset from the main path, and have to build a path to connect it to the main path which adds in an extra step and is also tedious, especially when your path doesn’t want to just go straight.
Playing RCTW, you can see hints of the potential that this entry has, and with some polish and more development work, I do think that this can be a good game. However, with the way Atari has been treating this game over the past two years, I don’t really believe any major amount of progress will be made, and the game will forever be one of those “What could have been” examples.

If you're looking for Supreme Commander mark 2, you're looking in the wrong place.
Supreme Commander was a great if under-appreciated RTS. It was one of the first to introduce various sized units that could literally walk over their smaller brethren. It had an engaging storyline and was generally an interesting and worthwhile game.
This is not.
Supreme Commander 2 is a screensaver that happens to use the same graphics. Gone are the RTS elements that you have come to expect, and they've been replace with something more akin to a strategic mapping program. Your focus is less on building, battling and overcoming, and more on minutia.
Everything about this game reeks of desperation by the developers. The odor of their greedy profit-mongering can be felt in every underdeveloped, subpar, mediocre moment of this game. It is patently obvious that there was little to no real effort put into this game, with the sole focus being to churn out discs in a short time frame and sell them to fans.
To put this in Ian Malcolm terms they wanted to "patent it, package it, and slap it on a plastic lunch box. Now you want to sell it. You were so busy wondering if you could, you never stopped and asked yourselves if you should"

Original review: Good action-MOBA title with average optimization and a visual style akin to rainbow-puke. Whatever becomes of Battleborn, Gearbox needs to do something about the overabundance of color, as it is literally headache-inducing during matches where things get busy. Weapons are too big, models are too big and colors fly left and right, making the screen a mess where things are impossible to distinguish a lot of the time.
That aside, the core gameplay is good. The writing is clever, the characters have nice, interesting design. Here's the deal; it's worth trying out. People are pointing out that it's practically dead now-- that is absolutely NOT true. The problem is that match-making can take up time, depending on your area and the time of day. Nobody can pretend this is a very populated game, but if you're in the right place and know when to log in, you can find a game fairly quickly. Recently Gearbox added a new multiplayer mode, which is essentially grouping the different game types under one to cut down on queues and things are better. I reside in Europe and around afternoon-to-evening I can always find games to join.
Of note, especially for a game that's essentially a MOBA, is that it has one of the friendliest and politest communities around. Match-making will often throw you with or against lvl100 Commanders and most of them will be more than eager to lend you a hand, not blaming you for your sucking in the process.
Again, nobody can pretend that this is a densely populated game and I wouldn't discount the opinions of other players that have reviewed the game (especially if you're in Canada or Australia). I also didn't buy this full-price, which certainly contributes to my opinion of this. I would suggest waiting for a sale (or acquiring the game through a LEGAL/CERTIFIED third-party-seller) and give it a go. Honestly, it *is* a good game and it does deserve your attention. But be warned that you may need some time to get a handle on when to log in.
